headline: Ukraine war briefing: New political turmoil in Kyiv as prosecutor general resigns
trail_text: Anti-corruption agencies raid offices and arrest a deputy of Ruslan Kravchenko in case linked to alleged laundering of phone scam proceeds. What we know on day 1,658
body_text: Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, has resigned amid corruption accusations that saw anti-graft officers search his offices at the weekend as part of investigations into illegal call centres. Kravchenko has rejected any allegations against him, calling them “completely unsubstantiated” and denying wrongdoing. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (Sapo) announced on Saturday that they had uncovered a money-laundering scheme “led by an official in the prosecutor general’s office” and had conducted raids there. According to investigators, a corrupt network received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and “laundered fortunes amounting to millions”. Nabu published images of a safe filled with bundles of dollar bills, saying it uncovered five members behind the scheme, without naming them. A deputy of Kravchenko has been remanded in custody on suspicion of money laundering in connection with the case. Volodymyr Zelenskyy in 2025 faced protests that forced him to reverse efforts to make Nabu and Sapo subordinate to the national prosecutor’s office. According to the Swiss-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Crime (GI-TOC), illegal call centres employ about 60,000 people in Ukraine. On Monday, Kravchenko posted: “I have submitted my resignation as prosecutor general. I do not want the office of prosecutor general to be used as a tool in political confrontation. My position regarding the charges remains unchanged.” The new turmoil confronting Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, comes after a shootout between Ukraine’s SBU and GUR security and intelligence services. Kyiv is also bedding in new military leadership after Zelenskyy sacked the defence minister and was then forced by protests to sack Ukraine’s military commander-in-chief as well because of feuding between the pair. Russia resumed its attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine’s emergency service said late on Monday, as air raid alerts were issued in more than a dozen regions. It came after the expiration of a three-day halt in attacks while US envoys visited the Ukrainian capital and Moscow. Kyiv’s city military administration said at least two people were killed and seven wounded. The strikes damaged buildings across Kyiv, including a five-storey apartment block in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district. “Russians attacked Boryspil and Fastiv districts with drones,” the emergency service said. Social media channels monitoring air threats on Ukraine said Moscow’s forces had started to transport ballistic missiles and relocate heavy bombers from Russia’s east to airfields closer to Ukraine. Russia “does not rule out the resumption of the trilateral format”, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Monday, referring to possible talks involving the Russians, Ukrainians and the US. “But it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage,” Peskov added. US negotiators told European representatives during talks in Kyiv that Russia was showing a “new willingness” to negotiate over the Ukraine war, the French presidency said on Monday. “The Americans told us that there was a new willingness on the part of Russia to negotiate following the Duma [Russian lower house] elections, and we should prepare for a fresh start to the negotiations,” said an aide to Emmanuel Macron, the French president. Donald Trump’s administration, though, has repeatedly construed Putin’s willingness to meet US representatives and reel off his unaltered maximalist demands as a willingness to negotiate. Ukraine struck a Russian ⁠oil refinery ⁠in the Ryazan region, as ⁠well as oil-processing facilities in the ⁠Perm region ‌and Tatarstan, ‌Zelenskyy ‌said on Monday. Both attacks were confirmed by regional governors – in Perm the governor said one person was ⁠killed ⁠and four others were injured ⁠when one of the drones ‌damaged a residential building. A Russian ⁠attack damaged ⁠a British ⁠American Tobacco plant in the town ⁠of Pryluky in Ukraine’s northern ⁠Chernihiv region with no known injuries, BAT Ukraine’s ⁠press office said. Off-site power at the Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear ⁠plant in south-eastern Ukraine has been restored via ⁠the Ferosplavna power line, according to Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear corporation ⁠that is illegally in control of the power station. The plant had ‌been without ‌external power since 20 August and ‌reliant on emergency diesel generators for cooling of its nuclear fuel. The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed that repairs were completed during a ceasefire that it brokered. Latvia’s ⁠government plans to impose a 300% tariff on grain arriving ⁠from Russia and ⁠Belarus. Officials in ⁠Latvia and its neighbour Lithuania last week said they considered ending ⁠shipments of Russian grain through their ports after Moscow ‌stepped up the ‌transits in response to attacks by Ukraine ‌on its Baltic ports. The UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, said he was “horrified by reports that fully autonomous drones launched by the Russian Federation killed three Ukrainians last month”. Türk called for an urgent ban on such weapons. The New York Times has reported that a Russian drone guided entirely by an artificial intelligence system killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia on 6 July.

headline: Another Australian found safe after Nepal-Tibet floods – as it happened
trail_text: The day’s news as it happened
body_text: That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today. Before we say goodnight, let’s look at what made the top headlines: Former prime minister John Howard has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the debate over Australia’s immigration settings continues. Barnaby Joyce has defended One Nation’s super policy, saying it would have a “minute” impact on inflation. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has savaged the plan, saying it was a threat to the compulsory super rules. The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced two key pieces of legislation will be introduced to parliament this week to tackle corruption in the state. Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”. Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety. Jim Chalmers will release the latest intergenerational report on 21 September, which the treasurer described as “a snapshot of all of the changes we expect to see in our economy and in our society over the next 40 years”. Rising fuel prices, fears of further interest rate hikes and falling house prices have taken household confidence back towards the “deeply pessimistic” levels of last year, according to Westpac’s latest monthly survey. Guardian Australia and the ABC were once again refused entry to a One Nation press conference in Victoria. A dairy company founder and his daughter have been identified as the two people killed in a light plane crash, prompting heartfelt tributes and condolences. About 80 protesters gathered to demand an independent investigation into the death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom. Workers at the Arts Centre Melbourne have voted to go on strike for a full 24 hours this Friday, disrupting a one-night-only performance by US singer Macy Gray and the opening night of an international dance act. Another Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable, has today been confirmed safe and well and not requiring consular assistance. There are still 35 Australians missing. Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow morning! An Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable, has today been confirmed safe and well and not requiring consular assistance. There are still 35 Australians who remain unaccounted for in the region. Read more: Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom accuse One Nation of ‘practising censorship’ after shunning reporters from press conference Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom have criticised One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, for barring reporters from a press conference. Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the press conference at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff before they were asked which media outlet they were from and told to leave. AJF’s executive director, Peter Greste, said: Australia’s strong democracy means journalists have the ability to interrogate politicians on the behalf of the people who hire them – the voters. It isn’t always comfortable, but that freedom is one of the reasons our political system is one of the world’s most stable and effective. No individual politicians or political party should have the right to choose whether a media outlet can scrutinise them. This is democracy 101, when transparency and accountability are lost, citizens are deprived of their right and ability to know what is going on. Any politician deciding who gets to scrutinise them is practising censorship, and in a democracy, that’s something we should never accept. Following the latest updates in the Alan Jones trial? Nour Haydar and Amanda Meade will be answering reader questions in an upcoming podcast episode of Alan Jones on Trial. If there’s a piece of evidence, legal process, or courtroom exchange you would like them to explain, submit your question via email to australia.fullstory@theguardian.com. Workers at the Arts Centre Melbourne have voted to go on strike for a full 24 hours this Friday, disrupting a one-night-only performance of US singer Macy Gray and the opening night of international dance act, Burn the Floor: Luminous. Striking workers – including ushers, food and beverage attendants, stage managers, ticketing staff and more – will establish a picket line from 3.30pm and hold a rally from 6pm outside Hamer Hall, where Gray is scheduled to perform, on Friday. The state government-run Arts Centre is Australia’s largest performing arts venue, employing around 900 workers, some 600 of whom are casuals. Hundreds are expected to join the strike. The Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA), the Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) Victoria, and the Electrical Trades Union have been bargaining with the Arts Centre on a new enterprise agreement since March. Pay remains the sticking point. The expired enterprise agreement saw wages increase by 1% every six months, and many of the lowest (Band 1) wages in the expired agreement are now well below the national minimum wage. More than a third of employees are classified as Band 1. A spokesperson for the Arts Centre said all workers were paid at least the national minimum wage and that they had immediately adjusted the pay of workers whose wages had fallen below national baselines after the Fair Work Commission’s 2026 annual wage review. The Arts Centre has offered workers a pay rise of 3% annually, the equivalent of the Victorian government wages cap. But workers say they need a 7% annual pay rise to make up for wage stagnation since 2022. A union petition in support of the workers calling on the state government to increase funding to the arts and arts workers had nearly 3000 signatures at the time of writing. CPSU Vic Secretary, Jiselle Hanna, said: The decision to interrupt Macy Gray’s show has not been made lightly – but we are left with no choice until the government funds the Arts Centre properly. Vicki Ward (Minister for Creative Industries) has the opportunity to sweep in and stop this industrial action by committing to paying workers fairly. MEAA deputy chief executive, Adam Portelli, said: Workers are at a point where they simply can’t afford to accept another agreement that leaves them falling behind. This is about protecting the future of a major cultural institution as much as it is about workers’ pay. Outside the gates of Israel’s Canberra embassy, a lonely saxophone played as about 80 protesters gathered on Tuesday to demand an independent investigation into the death of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom. Frankcom was killed by the Israel Defense Forces in April 2024 alongside other humanitarians while driving to deliver basic aid to the Gaza Strip. The findings of an Israeli investigation last month suggested there was no suspicion of criminal misconduct surrounding her death despite a previous finding there had been failures in how the attack was carried out. No charges were laid. A group, dressed in red to symbolise blood, passed between them a white, tightly bound cloth, designed to look like the dead body of a baby, AAP reports. Mourning the life of his wife’s oldest friend, Karuna Ratna Bajracharya told the crowd: I’m losing my faith in humanity when there is no justice. I can see that when our leaders fail us, when justice fails, when international law fails. The protesters called for the Israeli ambassador, Hillel Newman, to be expelled from Australia. At the time Newman said he felt deep sorrow for Frankcom’s family but refused to apologise for the strikes on aid vehicles. Protesters say the response did not go far enough. Bajracharya, a lifelong Labor voter, said he was disheartened by the government’s sustained ties with Israel. He said: They have let me down dramatically. They have let down Zomi Frankcom. A letter to the minister in late August, understood to have been written by Australians previously onboard a Gaza-bound Global Sumud Flotilla, demanded an independent investigation into the IDF’s actions. The group had not yet heard back, Jewish pro-Palestinian activist Anny Mokotow told the crowd. Before reading out the letter, Mokotow said: We have to fight against this as much as possible. We do it for Zomi Frankcom and those who have died senselessly with her – for their bravery, generosity and selflessness. Federal eSafety commissioner failed to participate in Victorian inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes, report reveals Despite the centrality of apps and social media-type platforms to the incidents that triggered the Victorian government inquiry into anti‑LGBTQ+ hate crimes, the federal eSafety commissioner did not participate in it. Finding 37 of the report said: The Committee is disappointed that the federal eSafety Commissioner declined to participate in this Inquiry. The committee found that the community felt social media platforms should take greater responsibility for the “harmful targeting” of LGBTQ+ people on their platforms. It also recommended the state government advocate to the federal government for “a dedicated inquiry into best practice safety features of dating apps utilised by Australian users”, and to ensure that all apps operated under “an enforceable and strengthened Australian Online Dating Code”. Grindr and Match Group participated in the inquiry, but other apps did not. Victorian inquiry into LGBTQ+ hate crimes hands down findings Hate crimes against the LGBTQ+ community are under-reported, often not recognised as hate crimes by police, and frequently committed by “thrillseekers” enabled by “the relative permissibility of homophobic acts in society”, a Victorian government inquiry has found. A legislative council inquiry into anti‑LGBTQ+ hate crimes in Victoria handed down its final report to parliament this afternoon. It included 41 findings and 35 recommendations to the state government to strengthen prevention and policing of hate crime related to gender or sexuality, and to fund LGBTQ+ health and community organisations and legal centres to better support victims and the wider community. The inquiry found that there was significant mistrust of law enforcement among the LGBTQ+ community, which led to under-reporting of crimes against them. It also found police often did not recognise or record the prejudicial element of the hate crime when it was reported. The committee recommended practical tools be developed to stop hate crime falling through administrative cracks in law enforcement, and an independent evaluation of Victoria police’s LGBTQ+ awareness training. The inquiry was established after Guardian Australia reported in 2024 on a spate of more than a dozen, separate cases of gay men being allegedly attacked by people they met through dating apps. A dairy company founder and his daughter have been identified as the two people killed in a light plane crash, prompting heartfelt tributes and condolences, AAP reports. Ian Campbell, 56, and his daughter Hannah, 23, died on Monday morning when the aircraft crashed south of Brisbane, sparking a large grass fire. Tributes to the father and daughter highlighted the family’s support for their local community and Campbell’s contributions to the agricultural sector. The fourth-generation dairy farmer founded the Barambah Organics dairy farming company in Queensland and also ran Manana Pastoral in the Goondiwindi region, producing olive oil, lamb and beef. Goondiwindi mayor Lawrence Springborg said the family had the support, prayers and goodwill of the community, and the pair would be greatly missed. Campbell founded the Barambah Organics dairy farming company with his wife, Jane. Springborg told the ABC: We feel their grief deeply and what makes it also so hard is that the Campbell family were so generous in their support of the local community. The Campbell family had raised more than $70,000 for the Royal Flying Doctor Service and invested in agriculture, Springborg noted. National Farmers’ Federation president Hamish McIntyre said the loss of the father and daughter was an “absolutely heartbreaking tragedy”. Campbell was a highly respected figure in Australian agriculture and a longtime friend, he said. Hannah was a bright young woman with her whole life in front of her. McIntyre said his thoughts were with the family, their many friends and everyone touched by “this devastating loss’’. Guardian Australia and the ABC have again been refused entry to a One Nation press conference in Victoria. One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, is due to address the media over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use. Reporters from Guardian Australia and the ABC were escorted to the press conference at Crown Melbourne by hotel staff before they were asked which media outlet they were from and told to leave. Pickering has rejected his ex-partner’s claims as “false”. According to The Australian, he said in a statement: They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them. Reporters from The Australian, who broke the story, were not barred from attending the press conference. Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time The opposition started on housing, trying to pressure the government over its building targets, and the impact of its housing tax policies. They then pivoted to the tobacco excise and tried to wedge the government over some comments from NSW Labor premier Chris Minns questioning the current excise level. The health minister, Mark Butler, accused Angus Taylor of playing “follow the leader” with Pauline Hanson – the Coalition has pledged to cut the excise by 80% (a week after One Nation promised a 75% cut). Independent Dai Le asked the government to review her outer western Sydney electorate’s health priority status to bring in more doctors, but Butler said it was “complicated”. I’ll be honest, it felt like a pretty long and dry question time to me. And on that note, I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok for the rest of the afternoon. See you back here bright and early tomorrow! Rising fuel prices, fears of further interest rate hikes and falling house prices have taken household confidence back towards the “deeply pessimistic” levels of last year, according to Westpac’s latest monthly survey. Two-thirds of respondents now expect mortgage rates to rise, the survey showed, reflecting a near consensus among economists that the Reserve Bank will hike again this year and potentially as early as later this month. Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of forecasting, said fears of higher rates were weighing particularly heavily on the mood of mortgaged homeowners. As petrol prices push back towards $2.10 a litre, Hassan said “the mortgage belt is tightening up on spending plans”. Westpac’s gauge of house price expectations dipped but showed more respondents expected prices to be higher over the next 12 months than lower. A little over 32% expect property values to decline over the coming year, with 20% expecting no change and 42% anticipating an increase (6% weren’t sure). Westpac also today has joined the other major banks in predicting the RBA will hike again, picking the November meeting as the most likely time. Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, said, the main reasons for changing the call “are the growing evidence of a more resilient household sector, and a larger-than-expected impetus from a datacentre focused investment boom”. While the housing sector is playing out weaker than earlier forecast, the outlook for overall growth is now firmer and the tech sector is adding new cost pressures not evident previously. Jim Chalmers will release the latest intergenerational report on 21 September, which the treasurer described as “a snapshot of all of the changes we expect to see in our economy and in our society over the next 40 years”. The government is required to release an IGR at least every five years under the charter of budget honesty, but can be more frequent (the most recent was in 2023). In the words of Treasury officials, the reports “examine the long-term sustainability of current policies and how demographic, technological and other structural trends may affect the economy and the budget”. Artificial intelligence is likely to be a major feature of this year’s report, given its potential to transform the way we work and live over coming years and decades. That said, Treasury officials have already advised they expect AI will only help productivity growth return to historical levels, rather than unleash a new wave of prosperity. The IGR will also look at the effects of an ageing population on the economy and the country’s finances. The last IGR highlighted how compulsory super had lightened the burden of paying for aged pensions. The first IGR was delivered in 2002 under then treasurer Peter Costello, and this year’s report will be the seventh. After a final dixer to Mark Butler, the PM calls time on QT. Kate Chaney stands up looking annoyed – she was probably due to get the next question. Liberal MP Garth Hamilton asks Anthony Albanese if he will scrap a $5,000 cap on allied health services for veterans, instead of spending $150m on an “overseas climate talk fest” (the COP climate summit). It’s an issue the opposition pushed heavily last sitting fortnight – and called for the minister responsible to be sacked. Albanese says the government has increased the fees for allied health workers to stop disincentivising treatment for veterans. Now the review is after $5,000, that will be more than 12 visits. And then, if further care is required, if there’s a clinical need, then they’ll receive it. Importantly, changes will not impact veterans on the special rate disability pension, on the totally and permanently incapacitated pension, or determined to be catastrophic injured. These changes come into effect on July 27, and the government continues to consult. Butler refutes claim tobacco policies have ‘led to more Australians smoking illicit cigarettes’ Take three: Liberal MP Mary Aldred, who was on a Coalition-led parliamentary inquiry that recommended cutting the tobacco excise, has a go now to corner the government over the policy. She again quotes NSW premier Chris Minns warning on the impact of the excise policy, and asks if the health minister will “admit Labor’s failed tobacco policies have led to more Australians smoking illicit cigarettes?” The health minister, Mark Butler, says he begs to differ and that smoking rates have been going down despite the hiked up excise. I don’t agree with that. The Institute of Health and Welfare, which has been the statutory authority under governments of both political persuasions for many, many years, says otherwise as well. I think we should all be glad the authoritative body set up under statute, supported at least until today, by both major political parties, have said that smoking rates over the last three years have declined by about half a million on daily adult smoking rates. Labor fumes over Coalition question on tobacco excise Nationals frontbencher Anne Webster asks the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, why he is “refusing to protect his own constituents” by supporting an excise cut, after a tobacco store in his electorate was firebombed overnight. Mulino was asked about the firebombing in an interview this morning but wouldn’t provide any details on it. There’s a bunch of back and forth over whether the question is within standing orders or not. Milton Dick calls part of the question a slur, and the government argues that it doesn’t go to Mulino’s portfolio at all. Webster has another crack and asks why Mulino is “refusing to protect Australians …” which gets some more groans and Dick once again tells Webster to remove that part of the question completely. Finally we get to the answer. Mulino defends himself, saying he did answer the question about the firebombing responsibly, because, “what would’ve been irresponsible is for me to speculate on live TV about what actually happened this morning and what might have driven it.” Can I quote the illicit tobacco and e-cigarette commissioner: ‘Lowering tax on its own is not likely to resolve the criminal side of the market. It does not remove demand, eliminate supply, or the underlying profit opportunities, they, as the organised criminals, can undercut prices no matter where we see the excise.’ We have said repeatedly a responsible approach is to continue our policy on enforcement. Angus Taylor gets on to the wedge train and tries to pressure the government over comments from NSW Labor premier Chris Minns again, this time on the tobacco excise. This morning Minns (who has publicly questioned the efficacy of the excise remaining high) said: “It’s perversely driving a situation where you’re seeing more people, not less people, smoking because they’ve got access to readily available cheap [black market] cigarettes. The health minister, Mark Butler, says the government is “not interested in joining the Coalition, in following the leader, that he pathetically appears committed to be playing with the One Nation party”. We’re not interested in joining the Coalition in a price discounting war with organised crime. We won’t be joining in a policy plucked out of thin air, with one apparent objective, to go a little bit further than One Nation … And the member for New England [Barnaby Joyce] is pumping his fist. He knows what’s going on here. They know this follow the leader game that he’s playing. In the middle of his answer, Labor MP Matt Burnell gets kicked out for shouting too much. Independent MP calls for additional doctors in western Sydney Over to the crossbench, Dai Le asks if the government will review a mechanism that means her western Sydney community of Fowler doesn’t get “distribution priority area” status and can’t get additional doctors into the area. The health minister, Mark Butler, spruiks the government’s Medicare urgent care clinics and the increased number of students training to be doctors. Le makes a point of order, and says Butler is not addressing whether her area can be reviewed to access more support. Butler says the issue “is not particularly simple” and won’t commit to changes, just that he’s happy to engage with Le. Generally, distribution levers have distinguished pretty sharply between the big cities and rural and regional Australia so that doctors coming from overseas, which is the question the member asked, are required to practise for 10 years in rural and regional communities. Now, there’s parts of particularly outer suburban Australia, who are really struggling. Who have lower doctor rates per head of population than many parts of regional Australia. And we are grappling with that question. Every time we have an overseas doctor going to the cities, rural communities complain that’s taken from them. Happy to engage with the member more about that. It’s not particularly simple, though. Albanese says he has a few facts to provide the opposition on housing Liberal frontbencher Melissa McIntosh is next and asks the prime minister if he agrees with NSW premier Chris Minns that Labor’s housing taxes mean less construction and fewer homes in Australia. She adds, “since Labor’s budget, 421 New South Wales building companies have gone broke. Including Bathla Group, risking 14,000 affordable homes and apartments.” Anthony Albanese says he has a few facts to provide the opposition: Fact one, the latest ABS data shows that under this Labor government the total value of housing in Australia has gone from $10.1tn to 12.7tn, an increase of some 26% in just four years. Fact two, the median national house price in August was higher than it was a year ago. McIntosh raises a point of order and says the PM isn’t addressing her question which is whether he agrees with Minns or not. There’s some back and forth here, including an accusation that Albanese dismissed McIntosh with a flick of his hand. Albanese continues with some more facts, and says Labor is giving young people a crack at housing: Fact seven, annual construction cost inflation has fallen from a half-century high, under the Coalition, it was 17%. Today, it’s 3.8% under Labor. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson, is first up at the dispatch box today and asks if the government will confirm it’s on track to miss its housing build target by at least 300,000 homes (“woah” shout the opposition members). Wilson attributes it to toxic taxes delivering “a trifecta of housing failures. Fewer homes, higher rents, and confidence in the Australian housing market smashed.” The government had promised to build 1.2 million homes over five years to mid-2029. The housing minister, Clare O’Neil, says the housing crisis has been cooking for more than 40 years and then goes into a bit of a compare and contrast with the opposition’s policies. The combined effect of our supply measures as a government is going to build an additional 400,000 homes for Australians, a big part of that, Speaker, is our push on social and affordable homes. We have a fundamental belief on the Labor side of politics that the government has got to be involved in the task of housing Australians. Now, that 55,000 Speaker, we had a question here that relates to supply, do you remember how many homes they built, in nine years of government? 373 homes. Wilson then makes a point of order and says O’Neil isn’t answering the question. Speaker Milton Dick tells the minister not to “stray” into too much talk about the opposition. O’Neil won’t confirm the opposition’s number and spruiks the government’s housing targets and policies like previously increasing commonwealth rent assistance. In pictures: protesters rally for justice for Zomi Frankcom outside Israeli embassy Protesters are outside the Israeli embassy in Canberra today, demanding justice for Zomi Frankcom, the Australian aid worker killed in Gaza after the Israeli Defence Force struck an aid convoy. The rally was attended by politicians including Greens deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi, and independent senator, Lidia Thorpe. Albanese dodges question on UK banning commercial activity with Israeli settlements in the West Bank Anthony Albanese takes a final question on whether Australia will follow the UK’s lead and implement a ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The prime minister doesn’t weigh in on whether Australia would do the same, and says broadly: I’ve made clear on a number of occasions, we support a two-state solution in the Middle East. We think that is important for both Israelis and Palestinians to be able to live in peace and security. Choice between algorithm opt-in/opt-out is ‘empowering’, Wells says Anika Wells says the government’s position is a middle ground between an opt-in and opt-out model for algorithms. The communications minister says there will be a “pop-up” notification that will ask users if they want platforms to use an algorithm or not. The government’s statement explaining the draft legislation says: Users can choose to opt in to having their default feed include personalised content recommended by the algorithm. Alternatively, users can opt out of personally recommended content in their default feed and see the friends and creators they choose to follow. Wells tells the press conference that this makes it a “neutral choice” for users: You will have a choice about whether you want the algorithm or whether you want the following feed. That is a neutral choice that Australians will be able to make. It’s empowering. And the reality is lots of people are going to want to choose the algorithm. Lots of people follow it for entertainment, lots of people follow it because they like supporting small local business in their suburb. The prime minister adds later that if people want to continue doom scrolling, well that’s their prerogative. If people want to doom scroll, as you call it, that’s fine, that’s up to them. My colleague, Tom McIlroy asks Anika Wells how the government will stop “mission creep” around these rules and stop political content being drawn into the bill. The communications minister says there are six serious harms that are outlined under the bill for kids, while for adults there will be a ban on “just illegal content”. Digital platforms will be required to protect kids from serious harms including: There are six of those, which is content around the promotion of eating disorders. So like I said, a chatbot giving a teenage girl advice about how to exist on 600 calories a day. Misogynistic content that promotes hostile attitudes towards women, so that might be a particular platform, circulating content that women or girls are equivalent to beasts or animals. Pornography, content that glorifies crime or dangerous stunts, so, you know, there’s people at the moment that still can circulate that footage online. And then content that causes serious distress, and that includes abuse and cyberbullying, so that is like a chatbot, telling a teenager how to self-harm. So these are all things that the esafety commissioner currently grapples with and has for some time, but we are making those the six serious harms that will be regulated for Australian children. For Australian adults. It’s just illegal content. Albanese ‘emphatically’ rules out censoring political statements on social media Anthony Albanese is asked about concerns that the duty of care bill could amount to political censorship. Critics have claimed Labor is trying to use the legislation to shut down criticism of the government. The prime minister says he can “emphatically rule that out”. He says the bill is not about government control, but individual control. It’s not about censorship. It’s about giving people control themselves over what they see. We can emphatically rule that out. This is about basic safety standards online for online services and about the onus being on big tech to identify risks on their platform and to mitigate against those risks. Wells is also asked whether she will have the power to designate new forms of harm, she says: The rule making power exists elsewhere in the Online Safety Act. I used it, you’ll recall, to include YouTube in the social media minimum age laws when I became the communications minister, that would have been disallowable in the Senate. Nobody disallowed it in the Senate. Anthony Albanese says the digital duty of care bill will give people control over their social media, and require tech platforms to “protect children from harmful content, including content that promotes eating disorders, misogynistic content, pornography, and content that glorifies crime”. Albanese is joined by communications minister Anika Wells, as well as a group of advocates who have been pushing for digital safety. The prime minister says the bill is not about government control, and adds tech giants could face penalties of more than $100m for breaches. [This legislation] will require social media platforms to provide user empowerment tools that give people over the age of 16 genuine and enduring choice about what they see in their feeds. We’ll provide e-safety with the power to issue removal notices for nudify apps, all websites, and streamline the child cyberbullying and adult cyber abuse schemes, and will require digital platforms to document the measures taken to address harm to Australian users, and ensure measures remain effective over time. This is sensible, pragmatic, practical reform. It gives users choice, and it will hold the big tech companies responsible for inaction. This is not about giving government control. It’s about giving people control. Wells says: Tech companies have been running real time, unregulated product testing on Australians, and their platforms and tools have infiltrated our daily lives in ways that we could never have imagined. This is a global reckoning coming for big tech. Your questions answered in our brand new political newsletter – Politics, really: Have a question about the news you’d like answered by Guardian Australia’s politics team in Canberra? This week our team has been reporting on the government’s soon to be released digital duty of care bill. It’s a policy that will impact almost all Australians as we increasingly live our lives online. If you have thoughts or questions about how it will work, or why the government is continuing its regulatory agenda against big tech, please write in. We have also reported on everything from superannuation to US bases on Australian soil – if you have a question about any of those topics, we’d love to hear it too. Send us an email at politicsreally@theguardian.com, and don’t forget to sign up for the newsletter. Albanese and Wells to release Labor’s draft digital duty of care legislation We’re waiting for Anthony Albanese and the communications minister, Anika Wells, to stand up in the prime minister’s courtyard as they release the draft digital duty of care legislation. So far we know the Coalition aren’t fans, warning the legislation could “censor” people, while the Greens want some adjustments to make the rules stronger. We’ll bring that press conference to you shortly. Prime minister Anthony Albanese has savaged One Nation’s plans to allow people facing financial hardship to access some of their superannuation savings. Under the proposal from Pauline Hanson, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years. The full 12% compulsory super contribution would still be paid by employers, but 3% could be paid directly to the account holder by their super fund. Albanese told a meeting of Labor’s caucus that the plan was a threat to the compulsory super rules. He said. Once you lose the principle of universality, the policy starts to disappear. He referred to One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, who has struggled to explain the plan, including on ABC TV’s 7.30 program last night. Albanese said: If you watch [the Joyce interview], it’s clear that the policy has not been thought through. A group of neo-Nazis, including their high-profile leader, Tom Sewell, are at the high court in Canberra this morning. It’s the first day of hearings as the White Australia party, a political party that became the first to be outlawed under the federal government’s hate group laws, tries to overturn the listing in the country’s top court. The group’s lawyer this morning outlined their arguments; that the legislation breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, breaches the separation of powers. The group will also argue the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling overturning a ban on the Communist party of Australia. Sewell and many other faces of the White Australia party floated through the lobby during the morning recess without incident. We’ll bring you more as it comes. Greens in talks with Labor on carbon credits to fix koala park internal split The Greens are negotiating with Labor to avoid an internal split over a government plan to let New South Wales take millions of dollars’ worth of carbon credits for its planned koala national park. The federal party room met in Parliament House this morning. We understand they’re waiting until negotiations with the government are concluded to reach a final decision on whether to block the regulation, which is due for a vote next Monday. Bob Brown wants the rule blocked but one NSW Greens MP has said the federal MPs should wave it through, as we reported this morning: It’s not clear what the Greens are demanding in exchange for their support, though the general principle is that they want the regulation to ensure that coal and gas stay in the ground and more trees are protected. The party also decided to support the government’s amendments to its social media bill today. They are less certain about Labor’s reforms to algorithms, saying they want strong obligations on big tech and strong penalties if those are breached. That includes ensuring that users who do not opt into platforms’ algorithms get a similar level of service, rather than being punted to a substandard version of the apps. Smart Energy Council says Queensland government’s energy policy deliberately slowing renewables transition The Smart Energy Council says Queensland’s government is using energy policy uncertainty to deliberately slow the state’s transition to renewables. Since winning office in October 2024, the state’s Liberal National party government has extended the life of its coal-fired generators, which no longer have clear closure dates, killed renewable projects and the state’s renewables target, and tightened the state’s approval processes for green projects while loosening it for mining. The council’s chief executive, David McElrea, told the Smart Energy Queensland Conference and Exhibition this morning, in Brisbane, that it was part of a “a self-fulfilling strategy to make renewable energy uninvestable”. McElrea said: The overall strategy of the LNP government is clear: remove targets, erase closure dates, protect coal, make renewable investment harder and let the project pipeline thin – then point to the shortage you created as proof renewables cannot do the job. That is a self-fulfilling strategy to make renewable energy uninvestable. It is ideology, not economics or engineering. The premier, David Crisafulli, said the government’s energy policy was “working” and was delivering “affordable, reliable, and sustainable electricity”. He said: We have the youngest fleet of coal-fired power stations in the country and we’re investing in those to make sure that we have that base load power. We have an abundance of gas, and we see that as an important transition fuel. So we’re investing in that, and then we’ve got the most number of renewable energy projects in the country coming online. That’s a balance. Capital investment in the industry has seen a nation-leding decline in the government’s first year in office, dropping from 3202 and 14 projects in 2024 to just 510 and two projects reaching financial close in 2025. Labor has one standard in opposition, another in government, Greens say The Greens have also come out swinging over a report in the ABC today showing analysis from the Centre for Public Integrity that the Labor government granted hundreds of thousands of dollars to safe, marginal or target seats at the last election. Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May says the analysis shows the fund even handed the prime minister’s inner-Sydney electorate of Grayndler $6m for the Marrickville Golf Club. If this was a fair process, why weren’t other community organisations even given the chance to apply? Labor had one standard in opposition, when it rightly condemned the Morrison government’s sports rorts. Now it’s in government, it seems to think a different set of rules apply. You can’t condemn pork-barrelling in opposition and then hand out hundreds of millions of dollars behind closed doors when you’re in government. Spender says digital duty of care bill must still allow criticism of governments Independent MP Allegra Spender says she wants to ensure any digital duty of care bill doesn’t halt the right of people to criticise the government of the day. She also says the government should put truth in political advertising bills on the table. But Spender, speaking to News24, reserves final judgment, saying she still needs to look at the contents of the bill itself. I think to make sure that people still have confidence, that they can critique the government of the day, as they absolutely should be able to. There are certainly situations where people are deliberately lying in political advertising and there’s absolutely no recourse, particularly during an election … I hate the scare campaigns, it’s not up for me as a politician to decide, this is where the AEC [Australian electoral commission] or others could have a good role in terms of making sure that people don’t have lies in political advertising, because I think that is misleading and that is problematic. The government will soon release the draft bill, with the communications minister, Anika Wells, doing a press conference a little later. Liberal frontbencher and SAS veteran Andrew Hastie has taken aim at One Nation and defended his evidence to the Ben Roberts-Smith trial. In a newsletter to supporters, the WA MP threatened Pauline Hanson and her party director, James Ashby, with a “very costly exercise in time, money, and political capital” if they try to unseat him. It comes after a headline in the WA paper over the weekend, which splashed: “I’m Canning for you next”. Hastie said One Nation have attacked him over his evidence to the Roberts-Smith trial, and accused the party of not believing in the rule of law and not wanting to hold soldiers to a higher standard. I won’t take any more slander from One Nation. Not after they called me a traitor to my own country. I [gave evidence] with more than 20 other combat veterans and witnesses from the Special Air Service Regiment. Justice Besanko, in his ruling, found that I was a ‘straightforward witness’. For that, I’ve been called a rat, a traitor, a dog c—, and many other things. People I trusted have walked away from me or failed to defend me. Hastie says he seeks “no sympathy for the slings and arrows fired my way”. One Nation are working to unseat me because they don’t believe in the rule of law, nor do they believe in holding Australian soldiers to high standards of battlefield conduct. Now I’m calling time on cowards who have never served a day in the Australian Defence Force attacking my service record, my integrity, and my loyalty to Australia. Committee chair defends public servants over social media footage The chair of parliament’s power joint standing committee on intelligence and security, Labor senator Raff Ciccone, has come to the defence of bureaucrats worried about how footage of their appearances before inquiries is used online by politicians. The push comes after the defence department deputy secretary Celia Perkins told a hearing last week that public servants giving evidence did not consent to footage being shared on social media. Ciccone told the Senate last night the issue has been sitting uneasily with him for some time and, while he supported free use of footage, he said some politicians are misusing hearings. He criticised social media users unfairly attacking a senior female bureaucrat, including over her salary. We have seen senators accuse witnesses of not telling the truth, shifting the focus from what was said to what plays very well in a feed that rewards outrage over accuracy. There’s an old instinct in this country to cut down anyone seen as getting above themselves, and political content now packages that instinct as accountability. It used to carry a social cost. People who made a habit of it were seen as bullies. Now it carries a reward. An algorithm doesn’t care about whether we’re holding someone to account or tearing them down for clicks. It rewards both, provided they generate outrage. That goes to the heart of what this official was trying to say. Ciccone said it might be time for politicians to look at how evidence given to committees is used online and whether MPs need their own standards for describing evidence online. Read more: Grants went to Labor-held seats because we promised them, Mulino says The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, has said the overwhelming allocation of a grants program to Labor-held or marginal seats was “sound policy” that reflected the party’s promises. Mulino told reporters in Canberra the invite-only program had required projects to demonstrate community benefit. He said he didn’t have “specific details” when asked if any of Labor’s promised projects were rejected for lack of public interest basis. Asked about the grants flowing to seats where Labor won, Mulino said: The allocation across different electorates reflected the promises made. He also claimed successive governments had used such programs but could not cite specific examples, instead saying the government auditor general had previously said “these types of grants programs” are “sound policy”. He expressed no concern at the prospect of Labor doing this again at the next federal election, saying: I think that if we go to the next election with promises, people will expect us to deliver on those promises and I think that’s a reasonable expectation. Jacqui Lambie says she’s ready to fight big tech on algorithms Independent senator Jacqui Lambie wants to see a proper crackdown on the tech giants and social media algorithms and reckons the government won’t go far enough. Speaking to News24 earlier, Lambie says the government should go with an opt-in rather than opt-out approach, which would make no algorithms the default on social media platforms. Lambie says: We haven’t seen the bill, so I can imagine that there’ll be other things that need to be fixed in that as well and it won’t be tough enough. The problem is when governments are in they’ll go 70% of the way, and the other 30% is called courage, and that’s what they lack. Let’s have the fight [with big tech] because I’m ready because what it’s doing to our kids is disgusting. Government ‘seeking to censor’ social media with digital duty of care bill The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, has also been up having a word to the press gallery this morning, criticising the government’s duty of care bill. The government will release the draft legislation for consultation today. Wilson, like the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, claims the government is seeking to censor platforms. The problem we’ve got is the government is now actively seeking to censor, and has been active in attempting to censor any view they don’t like. What we need is laws that protect Australia’s national identity, our security, because that’s the umbrella in which all our rights and freedoms are anchored behind. Wilson says that harm minimisation on platforms is definitely important but that the government needs to be more transparent about it. The Albanese government has a long history of trying to censor, silence and bully voices they don’t like. We know that they tried to shut down access to public information through their freedom of information bill. Carroll has also announced the introduction of laws to give integrity agencies more powers, which will come into effect immediately once the bill is passed. The bill will give the anti-corruption watchdog Ibac the follow-the-money investigatory powers to trace public funds. This means they can investigate the conduct of private and third-party subcontractors. The definition of corruption will also changed to capture a broader range of conduct, including ones that don’t currently meet the threshold of a criminal offence. The special minister of state, Ingrid Stitt, says the new definition also includes a specific provision for elected officials, and that will include ministers, MPs and local councillors. She says: It means that they can be investigated for serious breaches to their respective codes of conduct. Stitt says, if re-elected, a second bill would be introduced to parliament next year, which would enact the remaining recommendations of an inquiry into the laws governing Ibac. The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, is holding a press conference to announce two key pieces of legislation will be introduced to parliament this week to tackle corruption. The first bill will establish a special prosecutor to work alongside the royal commission into the construction industry to lay charges against those found to have acted unlawfully on government Big Build sites. The bill also gives the royal commissioner the power to compel people to provide information or written statements, outside hearings. Carroll says the power will help the royal commissioner “get to the truth as quickly as possible”. He went on: No longer will anyone be able to use an excuse, ‘I do not have the information or I do not have any documents.’ If you do not have any documents, and the royal commissioner asks you to produce a written answer to a question, you will be compelled to do that under this royal commission … This is a law and a power that is only available at the commonwealth level, and I will now bring it into the state level as well. Jim Chalmers coming through the House of Reps doors to have a little word with reporters is becoming a more regular thing. It means the treasurer can get a couple of lines out to the media without having to do the full press conference. Chalmers and Labor are pretty keen to have a fight on superannuation with One Nation and the Coalition, and probably believe they’re on to a winner with the public. The treasurer tells reporters that the One Nation policy to allow people to use 3% of their super payments for mortgages and rents is “friendless” except for the shadow housing minister, Andrew Bragg. So this is a shambles from beginning to end. Instead of running from it, the Liberal party wants to photocopy it. And I think that says it all about the very dangerous and risky, anti-worker, anti-super ideology, shared by One Nation, the Liberals and the Nationals. He also points out that One Nation hasn’t modelled the impact of the policy. Barnaby Joyce ridiculed that idea this morning, asking why the party should have to model people “getting your own money”. ‘Australians are fed up’: Haines blasts community fund Independent MP Helen Haines has added her voice to the list of MPs angry over reports of Labor using a community infrastructure fund to allegedly pork-barrel money into target seats at the last election. The ABC has reported analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity that found the majority of money from an “invite-only” grants program was given to safe, target and marginal Labor seats. In a statement, Haines said: Australians are increasingly fed up with self-serving political establishment, and pork barrelling only further undermines trust in government and our democracy. Political parties should not be able to use taxpayers’ money to buy votes. Community need should come before political need. Haines was a leading figure behind the push to set up a national anti-corruption commission. One Nation super plan ‘not our policy’, Liberal senator says The shadow housing minister, Andrew Bragg, says One Nation’s plan to allow access to superannuation for mortgage and rental payments isn’t Liberal policy but doesn’t directly knock it on its head. He tells RN Breakfast the idea doesn’t address long-term structural issues around housing ownership in retirement. It’s a short-term factor that would help with cost of living relief, I imagine, but I don’t think it addresses that long-term structural challenge. So 30 years ago, you had about 20% of retirees renting. Now you’ve got about 30%, and in 20 years it’ll be about 40%. That is going to change the character of retirement. Bragg dismisses reports that the Coalition was cooking up a similar policy offering, and tries to put the pressure on to the government. He also won’t say whether the Coalition has modelled anything. I think it’s very telling that the treasurer, having destroyed the budget and destroyed the housing system, can’t even bring himself to have this debate. Instead, what he wants to do is to go and raise donations for the Labor party on the back of a public debate. Bragg is referring to a text blast that was sent by Jim Chalmers last month to supporters, claiming that the Coalition and One Nation were coming for superannuation and calling for donations. Joyce responds to Hanson loan reports: ‘I think we just get used to these stories’ Barnaby Joyce has tried to deflect reporting in Nine Newspapers this morning that Pauline Hanson has offered loans to her party since her campaign to re-enter parliament in 2016. One Nation has publicly reported it owes $400,000 in debts to Hanson. Hanson has refused to say whether she has charged interest on those loans. Joyce tells RN Breakfast we can probably expect more of these stories from those who are “scared” of his party. Joyce adds that he’s not an accountant for Hanson so he doesn’t have details of her financial affairs: I know that people have a pathological dislike of One Nation if they’re a socialist. I’m completely aware of that. And I imagine we’re going to get lots and lots of these stories, not only from the left, but from those who are scared of us, who are supposed to be on the conservative side of politics. So I think we just get used to these stories. They’re going to roll out. I mean, we’re under the microscope. I accept that. Barnaby Joyce is using every which way he can to say that One Nation shouldn’t have to model the impact of One Nation’s policy that would allow an individual to divert 3% of their superannuation to boost their pay. After a pretty heated exchange on 7.30 last night, Joyce is back on the ABC speaking to RN Breakfast, and there’s once again a lot of back and forth. He says having to model what happens to someone getting access to their own money is “conceptualised by socialism”. Is there an implication beyond it being their money? Do you model the money you get paid at the end of the week? Do you have to model that money before you get paid? Or do you believe you have an entitlement to your own money? … We shouldn’t have to model you getting your own money. When host Sally Sara then asks whether economists have backed the policy, Joyce ridicules the suggestion. Now we have to get economists to decide whether you get access to your own money … now we’ve got another group of people that apparently have to give approval for you to get your money. I mean, who else do you want to go to? Your local priest, Buddhist temple, before you get your money? It’s your money, for goodness sake. Mulino defends ‘invite-only’ grants program Daniel Mulino is facing the wrath of RN Breakfast host Sally Sara to explain exactly how the “invite-only” grant scheme is legit and above board and not pork barrelling. He says repeatedly that the scheme is “longstanding practice” that allows a government to deliver its election promises. (ie Labor promised money for parks, pools and sports ovals to seats that it either already held or really wanted to win and then this was the program to deliver that once they were re-elected.) Sara asks which other grants programs have been invitation only, but Mulino doesn’t know, replying, “I don’t have the background on how frequently it’s used.” He says: It is a specific kind of grants program which is designed to deliver election commitments and that’s something which is specifically set up after an election in order to allow governments to basically follow through on what they’ve promised to do. One Nation policy will leave people $25k worse off at retirement, Mulino says Superannuation is kicking off again today with One Nation pushing to allow people to divert 3% of their superannuation to their rent or mortgage. Cue the government cracking their knuckles ready to lash out against the suggestion that super should be messed with. The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, continued the fight on News Breakfast earlier: It took us decades to get to 12% superannuation guarantee and that’s a level that will provide people with a high level of dignity and security in retirement. To do what the One Nation party is suggesting will see somebody who is 30 years old, $25,000 worse off at retirement and a couple around $50,000 worse off. To unwind that is dangerous and undermines the whole superannuation system. What we’ve suggested over recent years is that the far better approach is to support people getting pay rises. We’ve supported increases in award wages and the minimum wage. The government will later today reveal draft legislation for new digital duty of care rules. But the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan says he doesn’t “think the government’s got clean hands” on the issue, and says the government shouldn’t be able to censor a person’s social media. The government argues that it is not censorship to ask digital platforms to remove harmful content, and allow users to choose if they want algorithms on their feed. Canavan told News24 this morning: I’m deeply sceptical of giving any government, whether I was in charge, or Anika Wells is in charge, I’m deeply sceptical of giving any government the power to decide what you read on your phone. ‘Invite-only’ grants program ‘standard practice’ says Labor minister The grants program is all above board and there’s nothing to see here, says the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, defending the government’s use of the Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program. Analysis by the Centre for Public Integrity showed $493m of the $560m fund went to safe, fairly safe or competitive seats for Labor. Mulino told ABC News Breakfast: It’s standard practice and longstanding practice for governments to set up these kinds of grants programs in order to deliver those election commitments. They’re different to the kinds of grants programs which are run in the ordinary course of government. And this program, as Catherine King has explained, is part of long standing practice and there are checks and balances in there. Ministers won’t approve programs in their own electorate and it’s an important way for governments to be able to deliver commitments. Independent MP Kate Chaney says reporting of an “invite-only” community infrastructure grants program by Labor shows “governments from both sides use taxpayer-funded grants to buy votes”. The ABC has reported the Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program committed tens of thousands of dollars to key seats, but 45 seats around the county (almost a third) were not invited to apply for this fund. Chaney says: This is pork barrelling, and we’ve seen it before. The Coalition had Sports Rorts, and now Labor is ‘park’ barrelling – money for parks and playgrounds, pools and sports ovals all promised during the election campaign. The Coalition’s colour-coded spreadsheet was Sports Rorts’ smoking gun, and this report shows that Labor’s pork barrelling is no different – same spreadsheet, different colour. Chaney says the Commonwealth Grants Rules and Principles has recommended the use of a competitive, merit-based selection process for grants – but so far those rules have been ignored. Good morning, Krishani Dhanji back in the hot seat here with you for another busy sitting day. The government’s focus is on social media – pushing ahead with a digital duty of care bill, and its legislation to increase fines and give the eSafety commissioner more power to tackle social media companies that breach the under-16s ban. There’s plenty going on here – let’s get stuck in! Howard claims US is Australia’s ‘ultimate security guarantor’ John Howard says the US remains Australia’s “ultimate security guarantor” despite its “unorthodox” president in Donald Trump. At ANU last night, the former prime minister said: Although there may be occasions for superficial provocation … [we shouldn’t] lose sight of the fact that our ultimate security guarantor is the United States. Howard said while on a flight from Hawaii back to Australia after the September 11 attacks in 2001, the then foreign affairs minister, Alexander Downer, urged him to invoke the Anzus treaty to show US solidarity. Howard said he spoke to then US ambassador to Australia, Tom Schieffer, about his decision during the flight, who he said was overcome with emotion. Howard believed it was this decision that would pave the way for the Aukus treaty becoming possible two decades later. The former prime minister John Howard has warned political parties against banning migration from certain countries as the debate over Australia’s immigration settings continues. The 87-year-old was in Canberra last night for an hour-long chat with Australian National University national security professor Rory Medcalf before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. The discussion began with last year’s alleged terrorist attack in Bondi, before turning to whether immigration settings can prevent terrorists from entering the country. Howard said the “law of averages” meant some people with nefarious intentions could enter the country but he did not believe the “evidence is overwhelming”. He continued: But I think the mood is overwhelming that we have to try very hard to stop terrorism creeping in under the cover of immigration, and you can’t do it by just stopping immigration, and it’s very hard to do it by stopping categories of immigration. When some people say you stop it by saying ‘we won’t take migrants from any country that has got a reputation for terrorism’, well, it might be a lot more limiting than those people imagine. Neither major political party has proposed a country-wide ban on specific countries for permanent migration. One Nation has said it would like to see country-wide migration bans on people coming from countries the foreign affairs department has listed as “do not travel”. Joyce has also defended his party’s policy allowing renters and mortgage holders to dip into their superannuation to boost their pay, saying it will have a “minute” impact on inflation. The superannuation industry has warned the policy – which Labor and the Coalition have said they do not support – would stoke inflation. The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive, Mary Delahunty, said the proposal would be “economically disastrous” and make people poorer in retirement. Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30, Joyce – the party’s Treasury spokesperson – said withdrawing your superannuation from your fund due to financial hardship was a “protracted” system. Asked if the party had modelled the inflationary impact of the policy, Joyce said it would have a minimal impact but did not point to any modelling: Now are you saying that it has no effect whatsoever? No, I wouldn’t say that but I’d say it is almost minute. Joyce says allegations against Victorian One Nation leader are ‘contested’ One Nation’s deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, has been asked about the party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, who continues to attract scrutiny over allegations made against him by an ex-partner about alleged drug use. Pickering said his ex-partner’s claims were false. “They are extremely hurtful and I just hope the public can see through them,” he said in a statement, according to The Australian. Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30 last night, Joyce said the historical allegations were “contested”. He said he did not hear about the allegations before story was published in The Australian on Monday: If he’s good enough to serve our nation in the defence force, as determined by our nation, then I presume he’s good enough to serve the people of Victoria. If we’re saying that any person will be held to account for any action they ever did, no matter how far in the past it was, I would suggest there are lot of people in this parliament who will no longer have a job Monday morning. Good morning Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live news coverage for Tuesday. Krishani Dhanji will be with you shortly. Let’s begin.
