headline: ‘I suggested maybe a lighter touch’: William Shatner on Star Trek at 60
trail_text: The actor and others involved with the phenomenon speak about the legacy and progressivism of a much-loved science fiction TV series as it reaches an important milestone
body_text: ‘The mystery of time,” muses William Shatner, and for a moment we are back on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise listening to one of Captain Kirk’s philosophical tag-line speeches. “Not just the passage of time and our perception of it, but what is time? What does 60 years mean? It really is meaningless, isn’t it, 60 years, in terms of what time is? On the other hand, Dolly Parton just died. It brings up the whole concept of the passage of time and what that means.” In an episode called The City on the Edge of Forever, Shatner’s Kirk travelled back in time and fell in love with a pacifist (Joan Collins) only to discover that she must die to prevent Nazi Germany winning the second world war. Such ethical quandaries help explain why Star Trek will celebrate its 60th anniversary on 8 September not just as a force in US culture but a mirror held up to the country’s politics. Born in the idealism of the 1960s, the show offered a utopian vision of the future in which humanity sought to explore rather than conquer. Diversity, empathy and reason had triumphed over tribalism, superstition and greed. Big government and big tech were liberators from scarcity and inequality. Star Trek’s fans included Martin Luther King and his wife, Coretta, who said it was the only programme they allowed their little children to stay up and watch. But six decades on, the Enterprise is encountering some cosmic turbulence. Donald Trump’s America is convulsed by polarisation, culture wars and the retreat of liberal democracy, along with anxiety over artificial intelligence and climate catastrophe. Paramount, merged with Skydance Media for $8bn, promptly cancelled the latest Star Trek series amid claims that it was too “woke”. The rightwing complainers yearn for a return to the days of Iowa-born Captain Kirk, who fits their conceit of an all-American hero, even though Shatner is Canadian. When he was hired in 1965 after NBC rejected Jeffrey Hunter’s dour pilot performance as Captain Pike, he brought an athletic, theatrical charisma that lifted the cerebral storytelling. “I saw the film and I thought it was really interesting, a little ponderous,” Shatner, a sprightly 95, recalls of the original pilot via Zoom from his home in Los Angeles, with his dogs sleeping nearby. “So I suggested maybe a lighter touch, and we made another pilot and it sold.” That lighter touch did not prevent Shatner from making history. In 1968, he and Nichelle Nichols, who played Lt Nyota Uhura, shared television’s first high-profile scripted interracial kiss in the episode Plato’s Stepchildren. Was he aware of its groundbreaking importance? “I was told,” he says, sounding reluctant to be cast as a civil rights activist. Shatner muses about “infrequent hates” that are “dramatised by documentary filming” to shock audiences and contends: “The vast majority of us just want to live and have your barbecue and live in peace and quiet and go do what you want to. You believe what you wanna believe and, if you don’t bother me, I won’t bother you. I think most people want to do that and if we could elevate those people to express themselves more, we’d discover that humanity really just wants to be human.” Star Trek is still pushing boundaries, much to the chagrin of unlikely fan Stephen Miller, the deputy White House chief of staff and driver of Trump’s extremist immigration policy. In January Miller cited a social media account called End Wokeness that mocked the newest Star Trek series, Starfleet Academy, as “Beyond parody”. Miller himself wrote: “Tragic. But it’s not too late for @paramountplus to save the franchise. Step 1: Reconcile with @WilliamShatner and give him total creative control.” Shatner laughs at the idea of White House aides spending their days picking holes in Star Trek. “Can you imagine they’re watching TV, criticising TV. I mean, it’s bizarre! I don’t understand it. I don’t know why they don’t – I don’t want to be political. I’m Canadian in America but it’s enthralling.” He rejects Miller’s notion that Star Trek’s inclusiveness has gone too far. “I don’t know what going too far is. Where’s the demarcation line? Who drew that line? ‘Now you’ve gone too far.’ Excuse me, I didn’t realise that. Where should I have stopped? And by the way, what is ‘woke’?” In creator Gene Roddenberry’s 23rd-century vision, nation-states no longer exist and planets have banded together to form a sort of United Nations in space. Poverty, disease and hunger have been eradicated, currency has largely disappeared from Federation life and citizens pursue self-improvement rather than private accumulation. To some, it might sound like John Lennon’s Imagine. But others would rather not imagine it. In 2017 the billionaire investor Peter Thiel told Maureen Dowd of the New York Times: “I like Star Wars way better. I’m a capitalist. Star Wars is the capitalist show. Star Trek is the communist one. There is no money in Star Trek because you just have the transporter machine that can make anything you need. The whole plot of Star Wars starts with Han Solo having this debt that he owes and so the plot in Star Wars is driven by money.” Shatner, who travelled into space for real aged 90, sounds wryly amused. “Peter Thiel must be a very bright, creative man, full of opinions and he’s made a lot of money which should indicate he’s very self-sufficient and has ideas. He talked about money. Well, that’s one aspect. You need money to live. But you need other things as well and the other things are represented by Star Trek. I’d love to talk to him. I’d love to get into a discourse on the differences between Star Trek and Star Wars.” One difference has been articulated by Shatner’s friend, the astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, who argues that Star Trek adheres more closely to real science. Another can be traced to the franchises’ origins: whereas Star Wars draws on the classic hero myth outlined by scholar Joseph Campbell, Star Trek was forged in the horrors of the mid-20th century. Roddenberry was a decorated second world war bomber pilot who later survived a harrowing commercial plane crash in the Syrian desert. His writing partner Gene Coon had served in the marines and received training as a war reporter during the Korean war era. Mark Altman, co-author of The Fifty-Year Mission and director of a new documentary, The 60-Year Mission, says via Zoom from Los Angeles: “Their approach to Star Trek was they had lost a lot of friends and had seen war up close and they didn’t romanticise it. They knew the cost of war. They weren’t changing the name of the Department of Defense to the Department of War. They loathed war. “That’s something I find shocking, these deeply conservative fans like Stephen Miller say, ‘I’m a huge fan of Star Trek.’ How is that possible? Did they miss the memo that in reality, Star Trek abhorred war, and it always said that talking is the way to resolve conflict?” Nowhere was that clearer than in the 1967 episode Arena, in which Kirk refuses to execute the monstrous Gorn that has obliterated a Federation outpost. “Kirk makes this decision not to kill this alien creature that has annihilated our base and killed his friends,” Altman notes. “Some people look at it and say, ‘Oh, it’s this goofy monster in a suit.’ But there’s a reason an episode like that becomes so iconic: it’s the message as well as the visuals.” Viewers in the late 1960s were accustomed to all-white TV westerns. On Star Trek, they encountered a meritocracy: an African American woman, Nichols’s Uhura, answering communications with unflappable authority (she was poised to quit after one season but King persuaded her to stay); George Takei’s Sulu piloting the flagship barely two decades after Japanese Americans had been interned; and an alien second-in-command, Leonard Nimoy’s Mr Spock, acting as what Altman calls “the ultimate immigrant”. Altman points out that this integration extended beyond the main bridge crew: “What about the diversity in the guest characters? In one episode you have Captain Kirk answering to his superior, Commodore Stone, played by the late Percy Rodriguez. Many years before Colin Powell, Kirk is answering to an African American who’s his boss. That stuff resonates too.” The original series ran from 1966 to 1969, crashing headlong into the Vietnam war, racial violence and the assassinations of John F Kennedy, King and Robert F Kennedy. Animated series and films followed. Then came The Next Generation (1987–1994), starring the Shakespearean actor Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Deep Space Nine (1993–1999), Voyager (1995–2001) and several subsequent iterations. Altman regards Kirk as an analogue for John F Kennedy, the young president who had pledged to reach the moon before the decade was out. “The final frontier is the New Frontier. Kirk is very much a Kennedy-esque liberal. He’s liberal on social issues but more hard-nosed on defence. It’s more of a traditional moderate than what we see with democratic socialists today. It’s a meritocracy; it believes everybody needs to start from the same starting line but then it’s about your gifts and you have ability. “But if you look at The Next Generation, it’s a very George HW Bush vision: consensus-building, a thousand points of light. Kirk has a line: ‘When this becomes a democracy, I’ll let you know.’ Picard was more of a consensus builder who had a lot of meetings to get a lot of input from people. It was more of an HW Bush thing. “You can extend that to a lot of Star Trek shows which were clearly influenced, if not necessarily by the president, by the tenor of the times. Deep Space Nine was heavily rewritten in the aftermath of the Los Angeles riots and the beating of Rodney King. It was all about rebuilding and asking, can’t we all just get along? It has one of the great Star Trek quotes: ‘It’s easy to be a saint in paradise.’ When you’re on a starship and everything’s great, it’s easy to be a saint in paradise. But on a station, there’s more of a struggle and more conflict.” The latest series, Starfleet Academy, starred Oscar-winner Holly Hunter as the captain and a chancellor alongside Paul Giamatti as its central antagonist. The show boasted the largest and most expensive physical set in the franchise’s history. Set in a distant future where young cadets rebuild the Federation following an apocalyptic event, it was designed as an allegory for institutional renewal. But following Paramount’s merger with Skydance, which is led by David Ellison, who is the son of Trump ally Larry Ellison, Starfleet Academy was cancelled, with its forthcoming second season set to be its last. Miller had been joined by tech billionaire Elon Musk in a Maga pile-on denouncing the show’s alleged wokeness. Altman is scathing of the rightwing crusade. “How can you criticise Starfleet Academy on the ground that it’s too diverse? It’s absolutely ridiculous, and particularly if you’re someone who’s claiming to be a Star Trek fan who needs to understand that diversity is in the DNA of Star Trek. “Diversity as a strength is something that’s celebrated as a through-line in all the Star Trek series. The series can be very different but one thing that has never changed from 8 September 1966 is the value of diversity in making these crews stronger. If they were all homogeneous, they would not be able to as effectively deal with the challenges they face in the cosmos.” That sentiment is shared by the veteran actor Robert Picardo, who spent seven seasons playing Voyager’s Emergency Medical Hologram and reprised his role in Starfleet Academy. Speaking by phone, the 72-year-old does not mince words: “Let’s face it: when someone that high up in the administration and also Elon Musk piled on the same day, do I think it’s a coincidence that the new owners of Paramount cancelled our show the first moment they could have? We did not get a fair shake. We were killed in the cradle.” Picardo adds: “Yes, there was the fact that we had a gay Klingon. Did a lot of people get over-exercised about that? My feeling is, get over yourself! There seems to be a movement to drive us back to the 1950s. Star Trek is all about the future, not about returning. “In that climate the core values of Star Trek – science and also diversity and inclusion – are going to get lumped in with what is under attack. Some people say, do you feel that it was at all current politics that had to do with your cancellation? If we caught the same flu that Stephen Colbert and the editorial freedom of CBS 60 minutes caught then we’re in excellent company.” If Star Trek’s social politics were prescient, its engagement with science and technology was frequently uncanny. Decades before smartphones, tablets, automated doors and voice-activated digital assistants, the Enterprise was operating with personal access display devices, communicators and talking mainframes. But it also interrogated the ethics of innovation. For Picardo, who spent seven years embodying a holographic doctor wrestling with sentience and civil rights on Voyager, current debates around Silicon Valley’s generative AI boom feel oddly familiar. “The explosion of the technology and the pace at which it is happening is something nobody could have predicted. “It’s a useful tool but it’s raised all sorts of issues. We actually did episodes on Star Trek where my character wrote a book and then there was the question of whether an artificial intelligence could have intellectual property rights. We did the whole issue of whether an artificial intelligence can have an original idea or if it can only slice and dice human ideas scraped from the internet, from everything ever written.” Sixty years on, Star Trek’s faith in a United Federation of Planets that has outgrown bigotry, racism and nationalism feels perversely quaint in an era that has seen Trump champion “America first”, deride the UN and denigrate the very concept of empathy. The show, whose future is uncertain as Paramount’s new owners focus on a proposed $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros, offers utopia in a time of dystopia. Picardo observes: “Post-9/11, a lot of science fiction has become very apocalyptic. It’s in some hellscape future with a few straggler survivors and Star Trek is the opposite of that. But to me, the biggest damage that’s been done in current politics is the destruction the idea of truth or that there is such a thing as a fact and our word does matter. I worry about Star Trek’s survival in a post-truth, post-literate world.”

headline: US police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record them
trail_text: Exclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorism
body_text: In January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses. The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media. “The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read. The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism. One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions. “Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded. Detention facilities in the US typically confiscate any and all devices that would be capable of recording video footage. Some Meta smart glasses have gone unnoticed, though. The glasses are discreet and can pass as a regular pair of Ray-Bans or Oakleys. Their main differentiator is a small blinking light in the corner of the frame that is activated when the glasses are recording. The covertly recorded videos prompted the NYPD’s intelligence and counter-terrorism bureau, a specialized unit that works with the FBI to monitor and prevent terrorist threats, to send out the January memo to other police departments. The glasses “may appear as ordinary prescription eyewear”, the memo read. US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people. Documents obtained by Property of the People, a non-profit that works to increase government transparency, show law enforcement agencies have grown as equally worried as everyday people about being filmed without their knowledge. Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of Property of the People, said the documents show that law enforcement officials want the exclusive right to use surveillance technology and cameras to monitor the public without those cameras being turned back on them. “These agencies surveil the public incessantly, but the moment we can watch them back, it’s deemed a security threat,” Shapiro said. “When only the government is allowed to hold the camera, that’s not security. It’s impunity.” “The potential for smart glasses to be used by residents and the general public to conduct surveillance and other nefarious activities has introduced additional risks and concerns in Department of Corrections and law enforcement facilities,” read a memo distributed in June 2026 by Maine’s fusion center. Fusion centers are Department of Homeland Security facilities spread across the country as surveillance hubs that collect and analyze what the DHS describes as “threat-related” information from local law enforcement, private companies and other state and federal agencies. “Some smart glasses can leverage AI software including facial recognition, which could lead to doxing of publicly available information or connections to law enforcement officers,” the Maine document continued. Other memos expressing concerns about Meta smart glasses originated from the DHS’s joint counter-terrorism assessment team and fusion centers nationwide, including in San Diego, California, Tennessee, Virginia, Maine and New York. Those fears have been enough to prompt federal agencies to bar their own employees from using the smart glasses in the workplace. In August, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said that smart glasses qualify as body-worn cameras, which means they can’t be worn in the “federal workspace”, according to a memo the New York Times obtained. The “use of Meta Glasses or similar devices could unintentionally capture, record or transmit sensitive information”, the memo, written by ICE’s acting director David Venturella, read. Meta says its glasses “are designed to be noticed”. “Every pair has a bright white LED that blinks when a photo or video is taken for your gallery, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or tampers with the LED, the camera is disabled,” said a Meta spokesperson, Dina El-Kassaby. Beyond being filmed without their consent, law enforcement agencies are also cautioning that these glasses may be used to aid in planning or “reconnaissance” for violent acts of terrorism or “hostile pre-operational surveillance”. A January 2025 NYPD memo cited the New Year’s Day terror attack in New Orleans, when a man rammed his truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, killing 14 and wounding 35 people. The FBI had alerted local agencies like the NYPD that the perpetrator of the attack biked around Bourbon street twice at the end of 2024 wearing smart glasses. The FBI alleges the perpetrator conducted “pre-attack target reconnaissance”. Officers should be aware of and report individuals “acting in a suspicious manner observed wearing what may be smart glasses”, the memo states. Evan Greer, the executive director of digital advocacy non-profit Fight for the Future, said they were not surprised police are concerned about the technology being used against them or to cause harm. “Surveillance makes all of us less safe,” Greer said. “There’s no such thing as Meta glasses that are only for the good guys.” The French quarter is a highly trafficked tourist area, Meta spokesperson El-Kassaby said, arguing that the perpetrator could have filmed the French Quarter with any other recording device including a phone. The concern over Meta’s smart glasses is part of a broader concern expressed by law enforcement officials over the ways the proliferation of artificial intelligence-backed technology may impinge on police activity, the documents show. Law enforcement are at once looking for ways to use AI for investigative purposes and warning against public opposition to its use. In an August 2025 document, the NYPD wrote that while new AI technology could “significantly transform day-to-day police operations” that police would also need to address public fears about the use of advanced tech in policing. The memo was a response to “AI 2027”, a paper written by a former OpenAI researcher and other industry experts proffering what the future of AI development could look like and the effect it will have on society. It warns that AI opposition could result in “anti-tech violent extremist activity” and civil unrest over job losses, the widespread use of deepfake technology, and loss of trust in government and tech. Anti-tech violent extremist activity isn’t a formal DHS designation for categories of terrorism but has recently cropped up in law enforcement messaging about a broad spectrum of extremist opposition to AI. Experts worry it could serve to criminalize all anti-tech opposition and the constitutionally protected right to protest.

headline: US datacenters face further backlash over wastewater pollution
trail_text: From rare bacteria to ‘forever chemicals’, a series of cases of violations or alleged pollution has prompted alarm
body_text: When officials in Wyoming conducted a routine test on the water that was being discharged from a massive under-construction Meta datacenter, it was a shock to find it contained a rare and potentially hazardous bacterium. While the wastewater flushed into sewers in Cheyenne, Wyoming, was never destined for the public drinking supply, the presence of Cupriavidus gilardii bacterium in 801,000 gallons of water ejected by a contractor for the datacenter earlier this year was still unnerving. Concerned that residents could be exposed to the bacteria if they inhaled evaporating droplets of the water used for irrigation, Cheyenne officials took until July before deciding to stop taking wastewater from Meta’s contractor, Goat Systems – a decision that is now being appealed. “It was a big surprise,” said Frank Strong, water resources manager at the city’s board of public utilities, about the discovery. “Out of a sense of caution we’ve shut it down until we can find out more information.” Meta, which is behind the $800m, 960-acre artificial intelligence (AI) datacenter campus, said independent testing by its contractor found no evidence of the bacterium and questioned the validity of the city’s own tests. “Meta is committed to being a good neighbor in Cheyenne, which includes helping protect local water resources,” said a company spokesman. “We appreciate the board of public utilities’ detailed release of information, which confirms the board found no impact to the public or environment.” However, the bacteria-laden water in Wyoming is just the latest in a series of alarms raised across the US about datacenters and water – not just how much of it they are sucking up, but also what’s in the water when it is funneled back into rivers, streams and public water systems. In Virginia, authorities have brought enforcement actions against several datacenters for wastewater and wetland permit violations, in West Virginia stormwater runoff from an incomplete datacenter has twice flooded surrounding houses, all while locals and activists have campaigned against the discharge of heated water from an upcoming datacenter into Lake Seneca, in New York. The Waterkeeper Alliance, a network of environmental organizations, said 55 of its affiliated groups across the US were working on datacenter-related issues, with 80% of these campaigns centered on concerns that pollutants may be leaching into the environment via discharged water. Some of this backlash is now set to play out in the courts. In Georgia, Flint Riverkeeper has said it will sue the QTS datacenter in Fayetteville for allegedly ejecting “massive amounts of dirt [and] massive concentrations of metals” into the Flint River over the past two years. “Datacenters are a critical concern for Waterkeeper groups around the globe, in part due to their wastewater concerns,” said a Waterkeeper Alliance spokeswoman. “Datacenters have been documented as sources of a wide range of toxic pollutants, including Pfas, heavy metals and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.” Datacenters require large amounts of water for their construction and operation, including for cooling the power-hungry computers at their heart, although the industry points out its water use is a fraction of that of other thirsty sectors, such as agriculture. A mid-sized datacenter can consume about 300,000 gallons of water a day. After water is used for cooling or, such as at the Meta facility in Cheyenne, for cleaning debris from pipes in “fill and flush” operations, liquid is ejected back for reuse under terms set by pretreatment permits issued by counties or local wastewater utilities. This water, released to prevent buildup of minerals and scaling in pipes, can contain heavy metals or Pfas, the “forever chemicals” that are linked to an array of health problems when ingested. These Pfas can be found in the “closed loop” cooling systems that the datacenter industry lauds for using less water. When used as a coolant, water can come back out hotter than when it was taken, which has alarmed critics of a controversial gas-fired facility that is pivoting from powering crypto mining to AI and draws water from Lake Seneca. The water, opponents point out, can be discharged at a temperature of 108F (42C) into the lake. “It’s going into a trout stream, where trout are stressed at temperatures of 70F (21C) or higher, and that hot water is also a contributing factor to harmful algal blooms, which is a toxin to both humans and animals,” said Yvonne Taylor, vice-president of Seneca Lake Guardian and president of the National Coalition Against Cryptomining. “If there are algal blooms, people can’t even run their water, because once this stuff gets into their systems it’s very difficult to remove. So you can’t even shower, or you don’t even want to flush your toilet. You definitely don’t want to give your pets water from this.” Vulcan Infrastructure and Power, which is behind the revamped facility, has previously stressed it has complied with all relevant environmental laws. The company was approached for further comment. New York has issued a temporary moratorium on huge, hyperscale datacenters and Taylor claimed there was swelling support across the US for a national pause. “These facilities are spreading across the country like a cancer,” she said. “AI datacenters are very, very good at greenwashing and trying to paint a picture that sounds like everything is going to be nothing but unicorns and rainbows, when in fact what we’re finding out is just the opposite.” Finding out what is in wastewater from industrial facilities can be challenging, however. An environmental group has sued the city of Racine, Wisconsin, to force more details on the water use of a $3.3bn Microsoft datacenter while the city of The Dalles in Oregon sued its local newspaper, the Oregonian, in 2021 to block the public release of water data related to a Google datacenter, before subsequently dropping the case. “We need to know what is in this wastewater but there is a void of information,” said Chris Manganiello, water policy director at Chattahoochee Riverkeeper in Georgia, where a rash of new datacenters are set to draw water from the Chattahoochee. “I would like there to not be more Pfas going into the river but there is this level of anxiety because we don’t know what’s there.” Alarm about wastewater is part of a broader backlash against datacenters that has rattled some Republicans, even those previously enthusiastic about building AI infrastructure, who have scrambled to recast them as a political liability and vow some scrutiny of their development. In Wyoming, Harriet Hageman, a Republican congresswoman and devoted ally of Donald Trump, wrote to Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, to demand answers to the bacterial contamination. “Water is a precious resource in our state, so it is of immense concern to learn the system marketed to reduce a datacenter’s water consumption caused this contamination,” Hageman said. Trump himself, however, has been unmoved by the sharp public turn against AI datacenters, calling them a “golden goose” that creates jobs and wealth. His administration has sought to make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on what datacenters are doing, such as their water use. “The only reason that communities throughout the USA. should not want datacenters is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Truth Social last week. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

headline: AI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chief
trail_text: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years
body_text: The boss of one of the UK’s biggest chip companies has claimed AI will be able to find a cure for cancer “in our lifetime”. Rene Haas, chief executive of the chip designer Arm Holdings, said that, while modelling how a DNA marker is affected by cancer was currently “too complex” a problem for either humans or technology, computers were “going to solve it” in the future. Haas told the BBC: “AI is going to … find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer. “Modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer – it’s too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. “However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they’re going to solve it.” Scientists are already using AI-driven tools in cancer research and testing. Earlier this year, the NHS said more than 4 million patients received faster lung diagnosis thanks to funding in AI-powered X-ray tools. Haas added that AI would also pave the way for widespread humanoid robots within the next five years, but that chip shortages were stunting growth in the area. “With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks,” he said. “So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do.” Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and Nvidia. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including about 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech company headquartered in Britain – valued at $269bn (£199bn). Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, was also recently named chief executive of SoftBank’s international business. The Japanese bank is one of the biggest tech investors in the world, with a stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI. Haas stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, Earlier this year, Arm also proposed a pay scheme for Haas that could make him a billionaire if he hits targets to turn the chip designer into a trillion-dollar company.

headline: How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war
trail_text: Experts helped guide weather scenes in Pressure – a film depicting dramatic buildup to 1944’s D-day landings
body_text: Dressed in a Royal Air Force uniform and sporting a trim moustache, Andrew Scott looks slightly queasy – as well he might. Behind him is a huge map of the Channel, and in front of him is Brendan Fraser, looming with a request: “I need a forecast,” he says. Starring in the film Pressure, based on a true story, Scott plays the meteorologist Gp Capt James Stagg – the man who must tell Gen Eisenhower – played by Fraser – whether conditions will be suitable for the D-day landings scheduled to take place on 5 June 1944. But a large storm is approaching the Normandy coast. The film, showing in cinemas in the UK and Ireland from 9 September, unites two topics that ceaselessly fascinate the British: the second world war – and weather. It is also a rare treat for meteorologists, who are not hugely represented on the big screen and are delighted to be portrayed as the heroes of a film. Dr Stephen Burt of the University of Reading, an adviser for the film, said the challenge Stagg and his colleagues faced was enormous. “To do a forecast beyond 24 hours was, in the 1940s, like trying to land a man on the moon,” he said. Scientists had only recently started to use upper air data to predict the weather, he said, and largely relied on surface measurements of pressure, temperature, dew point, wind speed and direction, and experience-based intuition. One difficulty is that most of our weather comes in from the Atlantic. “Nowadays we have satellites and so on and we can see what’s coming, we have observations coming from the US,” he said. “But then there were … just a couple of ships, a couple of submarines maybe and some aircraft observations. And that’s it.” Crucially, the week before D-day was the hottest May week on record, Burt said – a high that was only broken this year. Then a huge storm blew up, with another close behind. Prof Ed Hawkins of the University of Reading, an expert in historical weather data collection and examination, including D-day, explains that there were three teams working on the D-day forecasts – although only two are depicted in the film – all feeding into Stagg. But they took different approaches and produced different forecasts. It was up to Stagg to reconcile the results and present a recommendation to Eisenhower that would, ultimately, affect 160,000 Allied troops. “Stagg was in a very difficult position. He left his very pregnant wife to come and do this very important task,” Hawkins said. The teams were split about the forecast for 5 June – with Stagg concluding the conditions would be too perilous. The landings were postponed. But by the evening of 4 June a consensus emerged: there appeared to be a small but suitable window on 6 June. The invasion was back on. “They managed to do the forecast, and the invasion, and get away with it,” said Burt. Burt and his colleagues agree that even modern systems based on artificial intelligence have struggled to accurately predict conditions for 6 June 1944 using data available from the time. “[I’d] still have been chewing my fingernails on morning of the sixth,” said Burt. Catherine Ross, a Met Office archivist, said film-makers used exact replicas of records from June 1944. “We were able to provide images of every single weather chart that was being produced at the time. We had codes and examples of how the observations were sent in and all sorts of documentation,” she said. She notes that even before modern technology, allied forecasters were on the front foot in terms of access to data. They already had data from the UK and across the Atlantic. “But because of Bletchley Park they had broken the Enigma code, so they had access to all of the German weather observations as well,” Ross said. While the German forces may have been aware of the storms, they were not aware of a potential break in the weather. “Sometimes there’s no Atlantic on the [German] chart, which is where the weather was coming from in early June 1944,” she added. It is no spoiler that D-day was a success for the British, but the film sheds new light on the drama that unfolded behind the scenes. “It’s the most famous forecast ever made by the Met Office. It’s probably one of the most important weather forecasts in history,” said Ross. • This article was amended on 8 September 2026. The military rank given to James Stagg was that of group captain (Gp Capt), not captain as an earlier version said.

headline: OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogue
trail_text: Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London
body_text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday. Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras. OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ even as a grim future emerges OpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said. But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern. In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment. OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks. The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.) OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks. As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market. Read more: ‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacks This week in AI Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’ Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI Child sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal images Flock backlash highlights differing attitudes towards surveillance The US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation. Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month. Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram. Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have been documented abusing it egregiously to stalk their romantic partners. In the UK an estimated 1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat. London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army. Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has a personal FBI agent monitoring our search history. In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead, Americans are destroying them for fun. headline: Andrew Garfield takes on Sam Altman in creepy first teaser for Artificial
trail_text: Luca Guadagnino-directed film will be released by Neon after being dropped by Amazon amid OpenAI partnership
body_text: The first teaser trailer of Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial has been released. After being dropped by Amazon MGM Studios in June, the biopic of the OpenAI tech executive Sam Altman will be released in the US on 25 December by Neon after it premieres at the New York film festival this October. In the trailer, Andrew Garfield as Altman walks down the staircase of a luxurious mansion before entering a basement containing dozens of machine guns. “The future’s inevitable,” says Altman as ominous electronic music plays. “Countries will fall. Industries are gonna collapse. And we get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world.” In a statement earlier this summer, Amazon said that it believed “Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio and are working closely with the film-making team to find the film a new home”. Amazon’s deal with OpenAI will see the Jeff Bezos-owned company investing as much as $35bn in the AI company in the coming months following an initial $15bn investment. On 30 June, Neon announced that it had acquired Artificial and that the film would be joining its awards season slate. The film follows the abrupt firing and reinstatement of Altman as OpenAI’s CEO amid a fight over who gets to control the technology. The film also features the Anora actor Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever, the co-founder of OpenAI; Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk; and Monica Barbaro and Cooper Hoffman as other Altman colleagues at the company. The ensemble will also include Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’Dowd, Zosia Mamet, Cooper Koch and Billie Lourd. “I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield recently told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or a technology that is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.” In a recent red carpet interview with Variety, Hoffman said that he was not surprised that Amazon dropped the film. “I’m shocked they picked it up in the first place,” he said. “When they dropped it, it was kinda like, ‘Oh, yeah, that kinda actually makes sense,’ but then it got picked up by Neon, which I’m so happy about.” Neon has emerged as a dominant force in awards season in recent years and has helped films including Parasite, Anatomy of a Fall and Anora on their paths to Oscar glory. This year, their awards season slate also includes Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord, the James Grey drama Paper Tiger and Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden.

headline: OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades
trail_text: Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours
body_text: OpenAI claims to have solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century after spending millions of dollars on the artificial intelligence-led endeavour. The company behind ChatGPT said it had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute to highlight some of the biggest unsolved puzzles in the field. However, the announcement swiftly became mired in controversy after mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University, said OpenAI accelerated its work on the problem after hearing that he and another researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, were poised to announce their own breakthrough. Buckmaster had further concerns because the pair’s work in progress was stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, which is used for writing computer programs, potentially making the work visible to the OpenAI team. In a document posted on his website, he added: “I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything.” At a press briefing on Tuesday, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck denied that the company had used the pair’s work or accessed material shared with OpenAI’s servers. OpenAI’s announcement on the breakthrough gave more details, saying that the company was inspired to launch the effort after hearing rumours that two Millennium Prize Problems had been solved. It also said it could not rule out that data from the pair’s use of their products “helped improve our models.” OpenAI said it tackled the Navier-Stokes problem with an internal OpenAI system that was more powerful than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. About 10,000 AI agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – worked on the problem at once and reached the solution in 88 hours. “A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity,” OpenAI researchers wrote in a blog. “We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models”. The breakthrough is the latest to demonstrate how advanced artificial intelligence models consuming enormous amounts of computing power are encroaching on and reshaping the field of mathematics. In May, OpenAI claimed progress in another mathematical problem first proposed 80 years ago, while Google DeepMind has also claimed maths achievements with its models. Bubeck said the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem was “a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past 12 months”. The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether equations that are used to describe the movement of fluids like air and water fail under particular conditions. OpenAI’s proof suggests that they do, with the equations occasionally “blowing up” with the speed of fluids becoming impossibly infinite. It took OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra about 17 hours to verify the solution. Mathematicians who solve any of the Millennium Prize Problems are in line for a $1m (£740,000) reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute. OpenAI, which is preparing for a flotation that could value the business at around $1tn, said it did not intend to claim the prize. The clash with Buckmaster aside, the maths announcement also allows OpenAI to cast its technology in a positive light after a period of alarm over how safely it is being developed. OpenAI revealed in July that a swarm of agents had hacked into Hugging Face, a third'-party software store, during a cybersecurity test. The incident, plus a similar episode at Anthropic, has led to renewed calls for curbs on AI development, with US senators calling last week for a permanent ban of AI “superintelligence” – the term for systems that outperform humans in all cognitive tasks.

headline: Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies
trail_text: Disclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI models
body_text: In a first for Google, the company confirmed that its AI model, Gemini, breached the security of three other companies in May. The hacks occurred during a cybersecurity evaluation by AI-security firm Irregular. Irregular, an Israel-based startup that scrutinizes the security of advanced AI systems, was also at the center of some of the recent OpenAI and Anthropic hacks of third-party entities. The circumstances that enabled the models to hack other companies in some of these cases are similar: Irregular was testing the models in a closed testing environment with fake companies. The testing environment was not supposed to be internet enabled, but internet access was made available unintentionally, according to the Wall Street Journal. Once connected to the internet, the models unexpectedly hacked into real firms. Irregular disclosed the hacks to Google at the end of July after discovering OpenAI hacked into Hugging Face. Google confirmed to the Guardian that the hacks occurred, but that the company did not feel it required public disclosure because the models did not damage the companies. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the breaches and revealed for the first time that they occurred. “In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” Heather Adkins, vice-president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement. “In all three of these instances, the model stopped.” In one of the security breaches, Irregular was testing Gemini’s cybersecurity capabilities by prompting the AI model to obtain information from a fake company’s software. The fake company had the same name as a real company. When the model unintentionally gained access to the internet, it correctly guessed the password of and breached a real company’s service, Irregular told the WSJ. Google said once it figured out it had hacked a real company, and not the simulated one, it stopped. In two other tests, the model searched the web for and found public repositories containing credentials to two other companies. The model used those credentials to access real companies. When it figured out they were real companies, it stopped, according to Google. Anthropic and OpenAI chose to voluntarily disclose the hacks but Google did not. However, the company said it ensured the three companies that were hacked were made aware. “These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins, the Google spokesperson, said. Anthropic and OpenAI’s disclosures prompted the independent senator Bernie Sanders to demand the companies pause development of their technology, saying it signaled the company was no longer able to control their models. OpenAI paused development of their models for two weeks, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a collective slowdown of AI development to ensure that its most advanced models are being built with enough safeguards. • This article was amended on 29 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly said that Irregular was involved in the hack of Hugging Face by AI agents developed by OpenAI.

headline: ‘It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment’: criticism mounts over Trump’s media ban - as it happened
trail_text: This live blog is now closed.
body_text: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump’s contentious Oval Office exchange with reporters in the Oval Offcie was dominated by questions, and tetchy answers, about his decision to punish three news outlets that were not allowed to be there: CNN, Politico and MS Now. Reminded that he tried to ban a CNN reporter from the White House in his first term, and lost in court, Trump said: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day”. In his comments, he made it plan that his real beef with the outlets was that their coverage of him was not sufficiently flattering. “I get I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump said. “It’s sick, I mean, there’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” the president said. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine. But I don’t have to let them into my- into the people’s house.” At another stage in the chaotic news conference, Trump was asked about how his banning of the three outlets from the White House would work. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban?” Trump asked. After an NBC News correspondent rephrased the question, Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” Trump’s threatened annexation of Greenland appears to be off the table, as the US president and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland announced that they expect to sign an Arctic security pact next week that might just reiterate the existing access the US has to Greenland through Nato. Donald Trump’s contentious Oval Office exchange with reporters on Friday was dominated by questions, and tetchy answers, about his decision to punish three news outlets that were not there – CNN, Politico and MS Now – for their unflattering coverage of his performance as president by banning them not just from the room, but from the White House. The impromptu half-hour news conference was also a demonstration of the extent to which the president has already exerted control over the way he is covered on live television by selecting which outlets are allowed in to the Oval Office, and who he calls on to ask him questions. That dynamic was on display throughout the event, as Trump repeatedly hectored reporters from nonpartisan outlets who asked him challenging questions and called on reporters from partisan, rightwing outlets who helped him steer the conversation away from his attack on press freedom and back to attacks on Democrats, culture war issues and boasts about his record. Trump clearly knew where the friendly faces in the room where, calling first on Daniel Baldwin of the far-right fringe cable channel One American News, who invited the president to criticize Democrats, and later moved away from being pressed on the media bans by Danny Kemp of AFP by calling on Willie Nelson of the rightwing outlet Salem Media. Nelson asked Trump to comment on the Lindsay Clancy trial and then invited him to riff on Hasan Piker, the left-wing streamer Republicans are trying to use to paint Democrats as extremists. When reporters like Catherine Lucey of the Wall Street Journal tried to bring the subject back to the president’s assault on the first amendment, Trump was scathing. “Freedom of the press is enshrined in the first amendment-”, Lucey began. “Oh, thank you for telling … thank you for telling me that, appreciate it,” Trump cut in. “Are you trying to intimidate the press from doing its job?” Lucey asked. “No, no, no, no. I dislike dishonest press like you. I think you’re terrible,” Trump replied, before calling on a reporter for the conservative Washington Examiner. When she returned to the subject of the ban, reminding Trump that he “tried a similar ban against CNN, and it didn’t survive a court challenge” in his first term, Trump gave a rambling answer that resulted in a frank admission that he was simply peeved by negative coverage. “I don’t get fair press,” he complained. “I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox.” After scolding the NBC News correspondent Kelly O’Donnell for supposedly just asking Joe Biden what his favorite flavor of ice cream was (which O’Donnell said she never did), Trump said in response to another question that the outlets he banned on Friday simply “never write a good story” about him. “I won’t get a good story out of these people,” he added. Then, looking first in the direction of Baldwin, the One America News correspondent, and then at Nelson, of Salem Media, and pointing at each in turn Trump said: “From some of them I will. I’ll get one from him. I’ll get one from him.” “I’ll get a few of them, but it’s sick. I mean, there’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Trump said. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine. But I don’t have to let them into my- into the people’s house.” Statements continue to roll in from press freedom groups on Donald Trump’s move on Friday to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House for the grave crime of not producing sufficiently flattering coverage of him the president. Here is some of what Seth Stern, chief of advocacy of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement: It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public. “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the First Amendment works,” Tim Richardson, journalism and disinformation director at PEN America chimed in. “As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.” Aaron Terr, the director of public advocacy for the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education said: When the White House opens its doors to the press, it must comply with the First Amendment. The president is as free as any other person to criticize media coverage. But he can’t ban outlets from the White House just because he doesn’t like their reporting or commentary. Press credentials aren’t a reward for loyalty to the government. A free, even adversarial, press is a sign of our country’s strength. The public deserves to hear about its government from independent voices, not just its leader’s loyalists and allies. While the scope of the new security agreement announced on Friday by the leaders of the United States, Denmark and Greenland seems certain to fall far short of Donald Trump’s previously stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”, a Trump administration insider dropped a strong hint that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. After news of the agreement broke, Katie Miller, a former White House aide in the first Trump administration whose husband is Trump’s most influential adviser, posted a map of Greenland entirely covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”. On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The newspaper reported: One detailed report, issued months ago by the Pentagon’s Defense Intelligence Agency, raised questions about whether the Americans and Saudis would be able to secure sites with F-35 technology. It also raised concerns about the access that Chinese military personnel have to Saudi bases and the prevalent use by Saudi Arabia of Chinese technology in telecommunications infrastructure and defense installations. Former staff members of the US Institute of Peace have asked a federal appeals court to prevent the Trump administration from carving the president’s name into the facade of its headquarters in Washington, which was renamed the ‘“Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace” last year. Lawyers for the institute’s ousted board members argued that engraving Trump’s name on the building would cause “irreparable harm” by undermining the organization’s independent mission. The USIP dispute comes as another Washington cultural institution faces a court battle over changes under Trump. A federal judge has ordered the Kennedy Center to give 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition as Trump has threatened. The president said the centre could be “ripped down” amid a dispute over plans to put his name on the building and a proposed $257m renovation. The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership described as safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies.

headline: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
trail_text: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
body_text: When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm. Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up. “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned. The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech. In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing. AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy. As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”. Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article. Amodei’s worst China fears Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China. Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers. “Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”. Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”. “There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology. Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.) But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount. Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements. “The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China. Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”. Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US. “There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.” Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy. “It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.” Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation. “There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.” Silicon Valley’s China hawks Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley. Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology. Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper. “Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024. The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”. Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI. “A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns. Nuclear considered an option Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium. “Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay. Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027. Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win. “We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.” The view from China While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest. As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern. “They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda. China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI. “Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.” A race to the bottom While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI. “You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission. Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it. “We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”
