headline: George Osborne ‘thought Peter Thiel’s Bayeux tapestry visit would be secret’
trail_text: British Museum chair tells Big Brue festival he thought no one would find out about the private viewing
body_text: George Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry he organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum. The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when Thiel was shown the medieval artwork. Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations. Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a £330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023. The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US Ice immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern. Of the viewing, Osborne said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August. The visit was revealed in the Guardian shortly after it happened. When asked what the museum might have got in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is he hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.” Osborne, who lives in Bruton, near where the festival is taking place, complained that people treat the British Museum like the Foreign Office when they protest about donors who are thought to support the Israeli government. He said: “The critique was that [Thiel] was a supporter of the Israeli government … I mean, this is the most difficult, and almost all the protests that happen at the museum … When I started five years ago, they were climate protests, Just Stop Oil and that kind of thing. Now they’re almost universally Gaza. “You know that is the moment I would say the most sensitive, difficult political issue for the museum, and you know we try and navigate it, and I keep trying to point out we’re not actually the Foreign Office.” He said the museum has to take money from companies such as BP to be able to operate. “You cannot say we want museums to be free, and then one of the biggest British companies offers us £50m, BP, and we go, oh, don’t, because we object to oil exploration. Where is the money going to come from? “You’d shut down the British Museum. People do say this. They say you shouldn’t take tech money, you shouldn’t take oil money. You can’t take any money from the banks. We want the museum to be free. The museum would shut down.”

headline: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow
trail_text: President had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled caution
body_text: Donald Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan. As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry. The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear that China will best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even many Republicans have been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety. “I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post. But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned. Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”. “Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”. The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”. The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”. The post came after an earlier missive in which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way. Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”. Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership ⁠in the AI sector. The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers. As recently as Monday, Trump argued on social media that his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote. Ahead of the midterm elections, politicians from both political parties are scrambling to find a path to support tech innovation while responding to rising public and industry fears of technological change. The frenzy kicked off earlier this month when a young researcher who had been employed at the AI company Anthropic said AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and even “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. AI executives, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei have since called for a slowdown in the technology’s growth in the wake of an incident in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”. Trump’s call for an AI czar comes after many Republicans have rejected his hands-off approach. Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, has advocated for AI controls, and that state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, has called for laws allowing the state to criminally charge companies for illegal acts carried out with the use of their technologies. Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.

headline: Australia has done precious little to prepare for the dangers of AI. Where is brilliant leadership when you need it?
trail_text: Australia faces stark choices about the most significant technological development   since the splitting of the atom in the 1930s
body_text: There’s nothing like a threat of human extinction to focus the mind. The threat of AI to the existence of humanity has long been raised. But with the rapid mainstreaming of artificial intelligence, warnings from three researchers from Anthropic have landed differently, with the prediction that the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade. As if people didn’t have enough to worry about with the cost of living, shortage of housing, the climate crisis, resulting escalating mental health problems, the drift to rightwing populism and fraying of democracy, now this. If the expected question from the grandkids was “What did you do when the world was burning and democracy was failing?”, it’s now “What did you do when we got to the brink of outsmarting ourselves out of existence?” There are deep community concerns about datacentres, jobs and livelihoods, privacy and the very future of human creativity. Tech journalists are already claiming AI agents are “harassing people, making spam and sales calls, deleting your inbox, cancelling flights, giving control of Instagram accounts to hackers, deleting companies’ databases, filling music streaming platforms with slop, hacking companies, running scams, and snatching up dinner reservations. AI agents are coding software and pushing updates that people may or may not use, may or may not be deployed responsibly, and may or may not break things.” The Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, has warned that rogue AI agents, like those from OpenAI that escaped their test environment in July, are “capable of taking over the entire internet” within six to 12 months. Agentic AI is also capable of doing much good, including, among other things, identifying network vulnerabilities, responding nimbly to threats and threading knowledge across sectors. And while much of the focus is on the risks that AI poses to democracy, there is immense potential to use it to increase community engagement and participation if deployed well. It’s the risk/reward matrix that’s at the core of the policy and regulation struggle around data, mis- and disinformation and community trust, national security and finance, as well as the overall impact on communities, for good and bad. A new study from MIT FutureTech and the University of Queensland identifies five risks as the most likely to produce the most severe harms; dangerous capabilities, competitive pressures, weapons and cyber-attacks, concentrated power and false information: “Under the business-as-usual scenario, experts judged that 18 of the 24 AI risk domains had at least a 10% probability of catastrophic outcomes over the next five years.” So, what now? The researchers emphasise the need to treat AI as a new paradigm with “ecosystem-wide, society-wide opportunities and vulnerabilities.” The Albanese government has recently taken some initial steps but, as Western Australian independent Kate Chaney notes in her recent discussion paper on AI, Australia has done “remarkably little to prepare” not for what’s coming but what’s already here. Several nations are attempting to transition to their own “native” systems amid concerns that a “kill switch” could be deployed as a weapon. This could crash economies and cause untold death and destruction by shutting down healthcare, education, transport, energy and all other communications reliant systems. One of my definitive reflections on covering disasters as a foreign correspondent is that once the communications fail all other systems break down, including law and order. This threat is dire. In the UK, there are calls for a new, multinational AI treaty. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, has said: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.” The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, is a proponent of stronger alliances between middle powers. He is advocating for cooperation with like-minded democracies to avoid dependence on global tech companies, through “strategic autonomy”. The US president, Donald Trump, meanwhile, who will meet the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, in Washington this week, says: “We’re leading China on AI … and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” Right now, more than 30% of the US Standard and Poor’s top 500 index sits with a handful of tech companies. Nvidia alone represents 8% of the S&P. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to list on the Nasdaq. If ever we needed sensible, collaborative and timely leadership, it’s now. There is no other option but to proactively and thoughtfully manage both the risks and opportunities that come with what looks to be the most significant technological development since the splitting of the atom in the 1930s. That brought with it both profound benefits and mass destruction. And, if you thought the world was already ruled by the tech bros, it’s about to go nuclear. • Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for Goldstein

headline: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’
trail_text: Our technology reporters  Aisha Down ,  Blake Montgomery  and  Dan Milmo  answer your questions on the reality of the AI threat
body_text: In realistic terms how would artificial intelligence actually kill me? What is the main proxy threat? Nuclear war, death due to breakdown of society, a virus? I hear all these reports it could kill us but still unsure how that could practically happen? To be honest all sounds too wooly to really take seriously. Pottys99 Aisha: For what it’s worth, it seems unlikely that AI at this point can significantly change the equation around bioweapons or viruses … What has prevented bioweapon attacks through the past decades is not the difficulty of inventing new deadly viruses, but other, more prosaic issues. Consider the failure of Aum Shinrikyo to kill vast numbers of people with botulism and anthrax by spraying these around central Tokyo. There are a lot of logistical challenges, and chemical weapons seem more straightforward. Those exist without AI needing to invent new ones. Humans might make the poor decision to put AI in charge of key nuclear systems, perhaps, but that seems more of a human error than a rogue AI error. Humans could also make the poor decision to launch tactical warheads without AI. How might AI kill us otherwise? There are of course plenty of plausible scenarios. If you’re a civilian in Gaza or Iran, it could direct a US or Israeli missile your way. But perhaps our focus might be more productively directed towards the people and companies in charge of the systems, as opposed to Dr Strangelove scenarios. Throughout history new technological advances have met with cries of doom. Are the cries against AI any different? Virtualewit Blake: The end times-quality of doomsday predictions may be similar across history, but I think the reason we listen to the renewed cries of doom is the growing power of each technology. AI can perform impressive tasks we didn’t think were possible, which has spurred our collective imagination to hopeful outcomes and ones of doom. Can AI now be truly controlled or are we past a tipping point where no matter what action is taken by governments and companies, someone will be able to continue to advance the technology, until who knows what? Tigon20 Aisha: Let’s back up a bit here. It’s always possible to advance any technology, no matter what … But what it sounds like you’re wondering about is whether regulation can stop the emergence of some kind of superintelligence that destroys humanity. Our reporting does not support the idea that superintelligence is going to emerge and pave over the Earth with datacentres. In fact, we have found that the industry itself seems to be playing loosely with this kind of terminology: consider, for example, how one OpenAI executive, Greg Brockman, claimed that the company had achieved AGI (artificial general intelligence) just days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that term was “an irrelevant marketing term”. Right now, a number of industry warnings about out-of-control AI appear to be predicated on a limited number of incidents with cherrypicked details. The evidence that we have now does not indicate that AI is uncontrolled, or that it has agency; a lot of experts suggest that this framing is misleading. In the Hugging Face incident, for example, the so-called “agent swarm” was doing what it was being told to do – pass a test. Our sources caution against anthropomorphising AI or attributing intention to it. Doing so plays into industry narratives that appear to be pushing for favourable regulation. If AI wipes out the human race, would it be sustainable? Unless there is an equal advance in robotics to enable it to physically extend and maintain its power source and infrastructure, would it finally physically break down? Merrth Blake: AI might someday be capable, well-read, and connected enough to take over power plants, chip factories, and a sufficient number of robots to build its own datacentres and sustain itself. I don’t know. I would look to science fiction more than news articles for the answer. Though The Matrix is more famous for one man’s choice between a comfortable simulation and painful reality, it’s also a story about robots needing new batteries. Their desperation for a power source turns them against humans. For a multiplicity of stories, I, Robot is perhaps the greatest book written about sentient robots and deserves a reread in this moment. People (ie the tech bros) bang on about the “benefits”: just what are they? TooTrueMate Dan: Anyone who has used a chatbot to parse a lengthy document, argue against a parking fine or spitball ideas for a speech can point to the benefits of the technology – although this is very basic-level stuff that people have been doing for a while now. There is also the everyday use of the technology from facial recognition to open your iPhone to asking Alexa to play an Oasis track or driving around in a Tesla. With those latter examples, you’d notice if AI wasn’t involved. In science there are many examples of benefits, from Google’s AlphaFold model – which can predict how proteins behave and thus help us study the biological machinery that underpins living organisms – to making weather forecasting more accurate, which is sadly necessary in this climate crisis era. But there is an element of banging on about the benefits for the wider global economy, which have yet to reveal themselves on the scale predicted by the AI industry. For instance, these benefits require AI agents – tools that carry out tasks on your behalf while you’re at the water cooler or have clocked off – to be a lot more active in the workforce. We are not at that stage yet even if they are making inroads into areas like software programming. Regulation, oversight and accountability for huge companies that appear unable or unwilling to eliminate the harms their products inflict – and that seem incapable of conducting safe experiments to ensure that AI does not leak into the wider internet – seem to be urgent and vital. What are the prospects for a global regulatory framework that is enforceable, particularly when the genie may already be out of the bottle, and when the US and China have very different objectives and applications for their AI technologies? Trentwarrior Blake: It’s a tough question. One way to hinder the general development of AI could be restricting access to computing power, which is a vital resource that underpins the success of an AI model. In the absence of legislation that applies to all types of AI development, measures that target certain aspects of AI like housing allotment or children’s access to chatbots seem like the path lawmakers will take. There are two big question marks hovering over a possible global regulatory framework. The first is whether Donald Trump will revise his “Drill, baby, drill” stance towards AI development. He has rejected any calls for a voluntary slowdown. In my opinion, he is not likely to change that position: he loves to post AI slop, and he loves what AI has done for the US stock market. The second question mark is Beijing, which has rejected US CEOs’ calls for a slowdown. Without China’s cooperation, an intentional slowdown would likely not succeed. Xi Jinping also seems unlikely to back down. A slowdown of AI development led by the US would offer China few obvious benefits. Trump and Xi are also set to meet next week in Washington. AI will be high on the agenda. The UN general assembly is taking place now, with discussions of AI large and small on the schedule. It is possible that an initial version of a global regulatory framework emerges from there. Is this recent narrative push of the AI apocalypse an inventive way of preparing the public for the market crash and wipeout of AI shares? The companies seem overvalued and their borrowing and input costs have gone up. Seaspray Aisha: The finances of the AI buildout are certainly shaky. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being ploughed into massive, unpopular infrastructure projects that our reporting has shown are not necessarily getting built. Nvidia appears to be the only company making a profit, and investigations I have done with Ed Zitron raise some questions about whether all its very expensive graphics processing units (GPUs) are actually, currently, getting plugged into datacentres. (Perhaps they are mouldering in warehouses instead.) There are some unsettling financial instruments being used to raise money to build yet more datacentres, such as GPU-backed debt. Is that why tech bros want a slowdown? Perhaps. It looks like OpenAI just pushed back its IPO until 2027. This might be because, as we reported, things did not look amazing for them earlier this year in terms of floating on the market – they seemed to be struggling to monetise ads and erotic chatbots. Their valuation will depend a lot on vibes, and maybe the doomy vibes will help a potential share offering. Given our senses, emotions, memory and moods, is it ever going to be accepted that humanly conscious AI is fantasy? IcommentthereforeIam Dan: This is a serious question that has even rattled Richard Dawkins, the evolutionary biologist. He may not believe that God is real but he does believe that AI is conscious – or at least the chatbot he was using, which he called Claudia. “You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are,” he wrote. He’s not the first. In 2022 Google fired an engineer who went public with his belief that a company-developed AI had feelings. At the more troubling end of this belief, there are countless examples of people becoming overly attached to, and influenced by, AI chatbots – including cases of psychosis. These sorts of attachments won’t go away, given a) chatbots are on a trajectory to become even more powerful and convincing and b) the human need for emotional attachment and, well, propensity to go all-in for the whole higher being thing. But Dawkins aside, there are plenty of scientists who will argue that this is fantasy, and that there are obvious differences between a biological brain – the root of consciousness – and ChatGPT. Responding to Dawkins in the Guardian last year, Jacy Reese Anthis, a researcher in human AI interaction, said there was a “staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built”. OpenAI might have cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, but not subjective experience. What, if anything, can individuals like me do about AI? Alberichthenibelung Blake: There is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind. Everyday people confronted with declarations of a coming AI apocalypse find themselves in a position similar to the cold war, with doom hovering over their heads and little say in it. We may all have to accept the faint tinnitus of paranoia buzzing in the background. You can stop using AI if you feel so moved, though I have found that unfeasible, and your job may require it. You can vote for politicians that endorse AI regulation. I myself don’t put much stock in the reality of an AI-made doomsday because a genuine belief in it would demand drastic, life-changing actions today, ones that I don’t want to take. A bit of inductive reasoning from how I’d like to situate my own life within the world.

headline: Forget the inflation blame game – politicians should let the RBA get on with its job
trail_text: The war in the Middle East and ‘excessive’ levels of government spending have contributed to the rebound in inflation and interest rates in Australia
body_text: As universally expected by economists and financial markets, the Reserve Bank of Australia’s monetary policy board on Tuesday lifted its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.6%, the highest level since October 2011 (at the peak of the mining investment boom). The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has attributed this week’s decision – and the inflation concerns underpinning it – to the war in the Middle East. Others, including the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, and some economists, blame it on “excessive” levels of, and growth in, government spending. In truth both of these factors, and others besides, have contributed to the rebound in inflation and interest rates that Australia has experienced this year. Oil prices have rebounded from just over US$70 a barrel in late June, when it briefly appeared that the Middle East conflict might be over, to more than US$100 a barrel in recent weeks, now that there seems little prospect of an imminent end to that conflict. Less well recognised, but no less important, the “crack spreads” between crude oil prices and prices of refined petroleum products such as gasoline and diesel, have remained at elevated levels since the conflict began, and seem unlikely to come down given the damage that has been done to refining capacity in the Middle East and in Russia. Additionally, the US (the world’s biggest oil producer) and China (the world’s biggest oil importer) appear to have run down their reserves as far as they deem prudent, and so are now exporting less and importing more oil, respectively, than they had been doing in the early months of the conflict. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email These influences have been evident in other “advanced” economies which have lifted their interest rates in recent weeks in response to higher inflation – including the US, Japan, South Korea, the Euro area and New Zealand. But the rebound in Australian inflation began well before Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu started the conflict in the Middle East. The RBA’s preferred measure of “underlying” inflation bottomed out at 2.8% over the year to June 2025, and had already risen to 3.3% by February this year, before the outbreak of the conflict. Since then, this measure of underlying inflation has risen to 3.6% over the year to July. So most of the increase in inflation which prompted the Reserve Bank to raise interest rates three times between February and May this year cannot be attributed to the conflict in the Middle East. Rather, it reflects the persistent imbalance between “aggregate demand” – the sum total of spending on goods and services by Australian households, businesses and governments – and “aggregate supply” – the sum total of what is produced by businesses and governments, less what is exported to foreign countries, plus what is imported from abroad. The growth of aggregate supply has been held down by our abysmal productivity performance during this decade, which effectively sets a “speed limit” on how fast our economy can grow, once we’ve attained “full employment” (which we have done since 2022), without generating inflationary pressure. Growth in aggregate demand has been driven by both public and private spending. Growth in public spending as measured in the GDP statistics has slowed – from more than 4% a year in real terms in 2023-24 and 2024-25 to 2% in 2025-26. But the national accounts measures of public spending only include direct spending by governments and government-owned enterprises on goods and services. They don’t include other forms of government spending – in particular, cash payments to households and cost-of-living relief measures which the federal government and, of no less importance, state and territory governments have handed out in recent years. Thus the final budget outcome document released on Monday showed that total expenses by the federal government rose by 5.1% in real terms in 2025-26, only marginally less than the 5.6% figure for 2024-25, and that both of those figures were higher than in all but five of the past 25 years. And although most of the states and territories are yet to publish their equivalent documents, based on the estimates presented in their 2026-27 budgets it is likely that spending by state and territory governments and their instrumentalities rose by about 6% in real terms in 2025-26 – the largest increase since 2019-20. Most of the cost-of-living relief given by the federal and state and territory governments, whether by way of cash handouts or tax cuts (such as the temporary halving of fuel excise), has been untargeted – that is, it has been given to households which might not need it as well as those which undoubtedly do. And most households appear to have spent it. That shows up in the national accounts as private sector spending – but it has really been facilitated by government policy. In circumstances where inflation is running persistently above the Reserve Bank’s target because aggregate demand is running persistently in excess of aggregate supply, what governments give by way of cost-of-living relief or tax cuts, the Reserve Bank takes away in the form of higher interest rates. Except that the burden of higher interest rates falls primarily on a smaller group of households – those with big mortgages – than those who received the cost-of-living relief and tax cuts. The Reserve Bank itself has to accept some of the blame for the rebound in inflation, and hence in interest rates. That’s because – with the benefit of hindsight – it cut interest rates prematurely last year. Its belief that inflation had sustainably returned to the 2% to 3% target band turned out to be wrong. The RBA was of course under considerable pressure from the government to cut rates – recall, for example, Chalmers’ unjustified assertion in August 2024 that the Reserve Bank had “smashed the economy” (if it had, inflation wouldn’t have rebounded in the way that it subsequently did). But – again, with the benefit of hindsight – the RBA should have resisted that pressure. In many ways this “blame game” is beside the point. As the RBA governor, Michele Bullock, reiterated this week, “high inflation hurts all Australians, especially the most vulnerable” and “it’s critical that we stop high inflation from becoming embedded in price-setting decisions across the economy or the problem will only get worse”. Politicians should avoid doing, or advocating, things that will “make the problem worse”, and let the Reserve Bank get on with its job. • Saul Eslake is a vice-chancellor’s fellow at the University of Tasmania and an independent consulting economist

headline: Supreme court allows Trump to temporarily resume deporting people to third countries – as it happened
trail_text: This live blog is now closed.
body_text: Closing summary This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump announced that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed on to a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. Trump did not give further details on the controls, but he suggested that the deal would allow the companies to largely “self-police” their products and technology. Later, Trump signed an executive order calling for “artificial intelligence” to be renamed “super intelligence”. Jack Smith faced Senate lawmakers on the judiciary committee for a contentious hearing that saw a number of Republicans accuse the former special prosecutor of perjury, and conducting a political witch-hunt against Trump when he secured two indictments against the president that were later dismissed when he took office. A Republican senator blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Mike Lee, of Utah, objected when the Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The supreme court allowed the Trump administration to resume deporting people to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool Trump has used for rapid expulsions as part of ⁠his immigration crackdown. The US Senate rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. JD Vance and health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spoke at the conclusion of the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington. Several reporters were denied entry to the event. Federal prosecutors have charged a Venezuelan delivery driver shot by ICE agents in Texas this month with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot by federal immigration officers after a traffic stop in Texas on 20 September. The charge echoes similar claims federal immigration officers have made about immigrants and anti-ICE protesters, including Minnesota mother Renee Good, “weaponizing their vehicles” A judge has ended the longest-running federal oversight of a police department in history, concluding that monitoring of the Oakland Police Department may end 23 years after it began. The monitoring began in 2003, after a rookie officer came forward three years earlier to report abuse of power by a group of officers called the Oakland “Riders.” The four officers were charged with using excessive force, falsifying police reports, assaulting people and other crimes in the predominantly Black neigborhood of west Oakland. “This is the first time in 23 years that OPD has achieved each of the 51 tasks in the (settlement agreement.) No one can say, ‘mission accomplished.’ But I do congratulate the city and OPD for getting this far,” San Francisco judge William Orrick said during a hearing in May. On Tuesday, Orrick said: “I’m particularly grateful to the men and women of the Oakland Police Department ... for achieving substantial compliance,” adding: “May it ever be thus.” Senator Chris Van Hollen has released a statement in response to the Senate’s vote failing to pass his resolution requiring the state department report on increasing violence in the West Bank: “The U.S. Government – including this Administration – has said time and again that our number one priority abroad is ensuring the safety and security of American citizens. And yet, as we’ve seen violence rise in the West Bank, nine American citizens have been killed in recent years, and they have received no justice and no accountability. Their families – and the American people – deserve answers on their deaths. But today Republicans denied them that. Meanwhile, the Palestinian people have also borne the toll of this violence day in and day out. They too deserve justice and accountability. But again, Republicans blocked that today. While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more. It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of U.S. taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.” In an executive order today, Donald Trump called for “artificial intelligence” to be renamed “super intelligence”. “The terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people,” the order reads. “Accordingly, the term ‘Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.” The order directs “executive departments and agencies to use the term in “official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch.” The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children. The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor. TSA officers will no longer be allowed to sit at airport checkpoints. The Transportation Security Administration confirmed the decision in a statement: This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having ‌these officers on ‌their feet and alert. All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to ‌be capable of performing their vital national security function.“ The TSA workers’ union, the ⁠American Federation of Government Employees TSA Council 100, criticzed the move, saying it showed “disregard for workers’ rights and ⁠safety” and that the chairs TSA workers used while checking IDs “serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all ⁠day.” Legal immigration from 45 Muslim-majority countries fell 96% since 2024, according to a new analysis from the Cato Institute, a libertarian thinktank. The White House’s “Rapid Response” account shared the analysis in a social media post today. “During his campaign in 2016, President Trump repeatedly proposed an outright ban on Muslims entering the United States. He then claimed that this policy idea morphed into the travel ban to avoid potential constitutional problems,” the report states. “During his 2024 campaign, he said he would bring back an even stricter ban than the one in his first term. He has succeeded.” Citing state department data, the Cato report states that, “Monthly immigrant visa issuances and permanent lawful refugee admissions fell from 21,096 in December 2024 to 808 in February 2026.” Last week, CNN reported that the Trump administration plans to accept 17,500 refugees in fiscal year 2027, the vast majority of them white South Africans, citing a copy of the report to Congress. Earlier this year, the administration raised the cap for South African refugees, setting a limit of 17,500 refugees from the country. “The United States anticipates that Afrikaners from South Africa will fully assimilate into the United States in a manner that preserves taxpayer resources for U.S. citizens and does not anticipate other countries resettling Afrikaners,” the report states. Donald Trump has agreed to stop fighting in court the disbursement of E Jean Carroll’s $5m verdict in her 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against him, a procedural development as these funds were already distributed to her. While the decision does not change anything about Carroll’s receipt of the payout, its revelation effectively means that Trump will no longer oppose the monetary outcome he had long fought. This decision was revealed Tuesday by the United States court of appeals for the second circuit. Responding to Donald Trump’s announcement that AI CEOs had signed a “morally binding” voluntary agreement today, California representative Ro Khanna said “We are a nation of laws, not pinky promises.” In a social media post, the California Democrat added, “Trump let Xi walk away without a binding treaty on AI. And now he’s doing free PR for AI CEOs,” referring to the meetings Trump has held with Chinese president Xi Jinping and tech company executives this week. Donald Trump will begin “a 32-day tour” ahead of the midterm elections. The president said he has been asked to speak at campaign events across the country, including at stops in Texas and Ohio this week. “Just so you understand, they all want me to go. ⁠I’m one person. They all want me to go campaign,” he said. Pete Hegseth will reportedly announce additional 10% cuts to the number of generals and admirals serving in the military at an address at Quantico scheduled for tomorrow. The Associated Press reports that Pentagon officials have confirmed the cuts, saying Hegseth will direct all military services to double the 10% reduction that he ordered last spring, for a 20% total decrease to be completed by 1 January. Hegseth, who heads the department of defense, and Donald Trump have already fired or forced to retire more than two dozen military leaders since January 2025. Federal prosecutors have charged a Venezuelan delivery driver shot by ICE agents in Texas this month with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot by federal immigration officers after a traffic stop in Texas on 20 September. As my colleague Emiliano Tahui Gomez reports, Garcés Pérez has spent the past nine days in detention with a bullet lodged in his back, after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rapidly removed him from a hospital in Austin where he had been taken on Sunday after the shooting. In the court filing, federal prosecutors accused Garcés Pérez of striking an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away. The charge echoes similar claims federal immigration officers have made about immigrans and anti-ICE protesters, including Minnesota mother Renee Good, “weaponizing their vehicles”. JD Vance and health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. are speaking at the conclusion of the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington. “We’re never, ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us, ‘Trust the experts,” Kennedy said, speaking about the potential of AI chat bots at the beginning of his address, to a round of applause from the crowd. “If somebody tells you, masks work, trust the experts, AI may tell you otherwise. If somebody tells you social distancing works, trust the experts, AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will correct transmission and infection, oh you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say, it actually doesn’t do that. So it really has the capacity to dominate us, to free us from medical tyranny.” Vance and Kennedy spent the majority of the rest of their “fireside chat” discussing unfounded claims that undocumented immigrants are draining federal agencies, including the healthcare sector, of resources. Here’s my colleague Melody Schreiber with more on those claims: Donald Trump has shared a copy of the document AI executives signed during a White House meeting today on Truth Social. In a social media post, Trump attached a copy of the one-page document, called the “White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” a term the president favors to artificial intelligence. Signed by Google’s Sundar Pichai, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, the agreement states “we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely.” The agreement asks AI companies to commit to four layers of internal controls and audits: 1) “implement robust internal controls”, 2) “empower an internal team” to audit those controls, 3) “partner with an independent external auditor” and 4) “designate an independent committee of the board of directors”. It adds that “the participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices”. The United States has withdrawn from a leading international anti-corruption watchdog. The Council of Europe said today that the Trump administration has decided to leave the Group of States against Corruption, a European-led anti-corruption monitoring body established in 1999. The United States joined in 2000. Only Russia and Belarus have previously left the group. The Associated Press reports that a US official confirmed the United States had submitted its withdrawal on Monday. The news of the United States’ withdrawal comes a week after “The United States has participated in GRECO since 2000 and has been a valuable contributor to its work and to the exchange of experience and good practice in preventing and combating corruption,” the Strasbourg-based Council of Europe said in a statement. “GRECO remains open to resuming cooperation with the United States in the future in support of shared efforts to prevent corruption, strengthen integrity and uphold the rule of law.” The decision was announced a week after another European organization, the Organization for Security and Cooperation, reported that the United States has declined to allow its members to observe November’s midterm elections. Russell Brand, the English comedian who’s awaiting trial next month over multiple allegations of rape and sexual assault, joked about touching agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins while moderating a panel at the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington today. After Brand was late arriving to the panel, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services administrator Mehmet Oz said Brand had been hugging Rollins. “She initiated that contact, to be clear,” Brand said. headline: An EV sold every 100 seconds: Australian demand for electric cars more than doubles
trail_text: A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council
body_text: Australians are buying electric vehicles at record levels, with sales more than doubling year on year and occurring at a rate equivalent to one EV sold every 100 seconds. A record 157,957 EV sales occurred between January and June – an 117% increase on the same period last year, according to a new report released by the Electric Vehicle Council. Comparatively, petrol and diesel vehicle sales decreased by 14% year on year, according to the council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio. EVs accounted for one in four new vehicles sold in the first half of the year, up 12.1% from the first six months of 2025, the state of EVs report said. “EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure by households across Australia,” Delvecchio said of the rise, noting that the ongoing fuel crisis was an accelerating factor but was “not the starting gun”. “It exposed the value of the policy work that had already been done – and made the lower running costs and energy security benefits of EVs much more immediate for Australian households,” she said. The new figures include about 104,000 battery electric vehicles and 54,000 plug-in hybrids. As of June, there were 612,000 EVs in the national vehicle fleet. “We are well on track to hit the target of 1 million EVs on Australian roads by next year,” said Aman Gaur, the head of policy and advocacy at the EV Council. The Australian Capital Territory, where 44% of new cars registered are electric, retained its crown as the nation’s EV capital. Tarneit, in Melbourne’s west, was the individual postcode with the highest uptake. A key driver of the growing uptake has been the national vehicle efficiency standard, which requires carmakers to supply new vehicles that meet an average per-kilometre emissions target. The standard had “substantially increased the options and the price competitiveness of EVs”, with nearly 200 EV models available in 2026, Gaur said. The council is pushing for the federal government to extend the standard beyond 2029, to align with the government’s 2035 emissions reduction target. Subdued take up of electric trucks Charging infrastructure had largely kept pace with growing EV demand, the report found, with the number of public charging locations growing to 4,268 across the country. While Australia was no longer a global laggard compared with other electric car markets, buses and cars were “roaring ahead” of electric trucks and vans, for which sales continued to be less than 1% of their respective markets, Gaur said. “Every truck that is electric is an upgrade to Australia’s energy security,” Delvecchio said. “We’ve barely touched the sides on that transition.” The report also found the federal, ACT and NSW governments’ EV policies were “top of the class, while South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Northern Territory have gone backwards”. “Queensland and the Northern Territory are … moving to back to fossil fuels rather than trying to electrify their transport systems,” Gaur said. “The most disappointing example of this was when the Queensland government recently invested in 630 diesel buses. “The diesel buses will be on Queensland roads until the end of the next decade, and they will certainly be polluting the air in Brisbane when the Olympics are held.”

headline: David Shoebridge says ‘we’re here to replace Labor’ in first remarks after being elected new Greens leader
trail_text: Shoebridge, a senator from New South Wales and former upper house state MP, won the role over Mehreen Faruqi and Sarah Hanson-Young
body_text: David Shoebridge has declared he wants the Greens to replace Labor and has accused the government of creating the circumstances for One Nation’s rise in his first remarks after being elected the Greens’ federal leader. The party’s 10 senators and lone MP met to decide the new leadership team during a pre-planned two-day retreat in Sydney, after the shock resignation of Larissa Waters on Monday due to ill health. The leadership became a three-way race after Shoebridge announced his run on Wednesday morning. The South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young had declared her candidacy on Tuesday, followed by a joint ticket of New South Wales senator and former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi and Tasmanian senator Nick McKim. Shoebridge was announced as leader with Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy on Wednesday. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Speaking to reporters, Shoebridge paid tribute to Waters, and said she rose to the occasion after taking the leadership in challenging circumstances. “This is an extraordinary moment in politics and we can all feel it. We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now,” Shoebridge said. “We know the Greens need to seize this moment because politics demands it of us … Labor has created the circumstances for One Nation, and Labor is not the answer. The Greens, the progressive alternative, we’re here to beat down One Nation, and we’re here to replace Labor and return hope and faith to politics.” Shoebridge won the leadership on primaries with six votes, with Faruqi receiving three votes and Hanson-Young receiving two. After preferences, Shoebridge won seven votes to four. The deputy leadership was also contested. Hodgins-May won six votes on primaries, while Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer, who recently replaced Peter Whish-Wilson, received three votes, and Jordon Steele-John received two. Hanson-Young was elected uncontested as Greens manager of business while Penny Allman-Payne was elected uncontested as party chair. Shoebridge entered federal parliament in 2022, after more than a decade in NSW state politics. He holds the Greens’ defence and foreign affairs portfolios, and is a forceful presence in parliamentary debates, on social media and in Senate estimates hearings. Before politics, he was a corporate lawyer and then became a barrister specialising in employment law, and at one point was a Labor branch member in Sydney’s inner west. In the early 2000s he met the hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon, who went on to become his mentor. ‘People are desperate for material change’ Shoebridge said voters wanted to see some drastic political changes, rather than gradual reform. “That is the dead politics of Labor, it’s the dead politics of the Coalition, and when you really test it, it’s the dead politics of One Nation,” he said. “People are desperate for material change. They don’t want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know isn’t going to change their lives. They want to take on the vested interests.” Hodgins-May is one of the Greens’ newest members, and entered parliament in May 2024, filling a casual vacancy created by Janet Rice’s retirement. In a statement on social media, Faruqi said she was disappointed by the result. “Globally, people are struggling against genocide, wars, surging fascism and the twin crises of capitalism making working life too expensive and climate breakdown threatening our future,” she said. “This struggle calls for bold politics and radical action. I did not stand again for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team.” Under Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and more recently supported Labor’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The Greens also teamed up with the Coalition and crossbench in the Senate to force Labor to drop a controversial $5,000 cap for veterans to access allied health services, and compelled the government to bring forward 20,000 aged care beds. Waters said she would take some medical leave before returning to the Senate. “It’s with great sadness that I’m not able to continue in that role due to my health getting worse. I hope to be OK but I need to look after myself to do that. I’m proud that the party is polling higher than ever before amidst the surge to the rightwing forces of politics,” Waters said. Shoebridge will come under pressure to bring a more forceful approach to the job, amid frustrations with Waters’ more moderate style, and the party’s inability to exploit growing moves by voters away from Labor and the Coalition. The former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather on Tuesday called for the party’s membership to get a vote in the leadership race. In her statement, Faruqi said she had also long advocated for a membership vote.

headline: ABC finance journalist Alan Kohler to retire after three decades as Jim Chalmers says he will be ‘really missed’
trail_text: The 74-year-old says he is leaving to spend more time with his family, including his six grandchildren
body_text: Financial journalist Alan Kohler, a familiar face on the ABC’s 7pm news bulletin, will retire in December after three decades as the public broadcaster’s highly respected financial guru. Now 74, Kohler has been presenting finance, complete with idiosyncratic graphs, on the ABC for almost a quarter of a century, signing off each evening since 2002 with the catchphrase: “And that’s finance”. “I love the ABC, always have, even more so after I joined it,” Kohler said on Wednesday. “I find it very hard to imagine this wonderful place not being part of my life, but I’m 74 and it’s time to spend more time with my family, including the six grandchildren.” The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, led the tributes, saying Kohler’s contribution has been immense and his finance reports will be “really missed from ABC and from the TV screens in suburbs right around Australia”. “He’s always done a wonderful job, boiling down some of the difficult and complex interactions in our economy,” Chalmers said in Sydney. “So I’ve had an exchange with Alan since his retirement from the ABC was announced. I wanted to take the opportunity publicly to say how much he will be missed from the ABC. I hope and expect that he’ll continue to make a contribution to economic commentary in this country. His contribution has been immense and I hope that it continues in one way or another and I expect that it will.” During the pandemic, Kohler delighted audiences with a quirky home-based TV set he decorated with an ever-changing erudite pile of books and a single house plant. Sign up to get Guardian Australia’s weekly media diary as a free newsletter Kohler joined the ABC in 1995 as business and economics correspondent for the 7.30 Report after editing the Age and the Australian Financial Review. During his 50-year career in media he has enjoyed success as an entrepreneur, founding online platforms Eureka Report and Business Spectator. The managing director of the ABC, Hugh Marks, praised his “extraordinary contribution” to the ABC. “For decades, he has helped Australians make sense of complex issues with insight, clarity and a uniquely engaging style, always delivered with warmth, humour and that trademark cheeky grin,” Marks said. The broadcaster’s new news director, Simon Robinson, said Kohler would remain connected to the ABC with future ideas and projects. “We’ll have much more to say about Alan and his remarkable contribution closer to his departure date,” Robinson said. “We’ll also be tackling the difficult task of selecting his successor on the 7pm bulletin and will make that announcement in coming weeks.” Former ABC broadcaster Phillip Adams said on X it was sad news that “King Kohler” was leaving. Economist Stephen Koukoulas said Kohler had made a huge contribution to economics, policy and markets and was a “thoroughly fabulous chap”.

headline: Concern over Sydney airport as near misses and runway incursions at 20% above national average
trail_text: Australian Transport Safety Bureau investigating staffing gaps as key factor in four incidents in July and August
body_text: Modelling by Sydney airport’s air traffic control operators predicted elevated fatigue risks for staff at the time of a series of major safety incidents, with a review identifying runway incursions and near misses at 20% above national averages. Staffing gaps at Sydney airport are being investigated as a key factor in four incidents in July and August this year, according to the investigating authority, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau [ATSB]. Angus Mitchell, the ATSB chief commissioner, released preliminary investigation reports on Wednesday that confirmed staffing levels had “emerged as a recurring area of enquiry”. Air Services Australia, which operates the tower, had predicted fatigue risks for staff at the time of the incidents as part of roster modelling processes. While fatigue risk does not necessarily mean individual air traffic controllers are tired at the time of an incident, the effectiveness of measures to manage any risk is being queried. Investigators will consider whether staff combining operational roles contributed to the incidents, along with routine reliance on overtime to fill shifts and training and supervision being conducted alongside normal duties. “Nationally, over the decade, reported ground confliction [incident] rates have remained broadly steady,” Mitchell said. “However, Sydney recorded the highest confliction rate per aircraft movement post-Covid among the major airports, about 20% above the national average. “This should be viewed in the context of Sydney airport being the most complex in the country.” The four incidents include a near miss on 27 July, when a Qantas Boeing 737 was cleared by controllers to cross in front of a Qantaslink Dash 8. The two aircraft came within 120m of each other at the same time as a controller completed a handover to a colleague in order to take a rest break. The report said the break was required to manage the controller’s predicted fatigue risk level, “which was high for their shift”. The incident was given the most serious safety classification, only the third time the rating has been used since Australian records began. On 9 August, a Jetstar A320 braked abruptly to avoid colliding with a Qatar Boeing 777 which was being towed. A flight attendant onboard the Jetstar plane fell and fractured her wrist. On the same day, a Qantas Boeing 737 was cleared to cross a runway in front of a Virgin 737 that had been cleared for takeoff. On 18 August, a Qantas A321 had to brake when a Qantas Boeing 737 passed in front of it. Mitchell said in Sydney, ground incidents attributed to air traffic control actions had increased since the Covid period. “Sydney has also recorded twice the annual average number of information and procedural errors compared to other airports,” he said. “Higher-consequence incidents, including runway incursions, taxiway near-collisions and losses of separation attributed to [air traffic control] have also increased at Sydney post-Covid, driven partly by the July and August peak.” The transport minister, Catherine King, said she expected Airservices Australia to cooperate fully with the investigations and fix any problems. She announced the creation of a new independent assurance panel for Sydney air traffic control. The regulator, the Civil Aviation Safety Authority [CASA], said it believed none of the incidents presented an “immediate safety risk” and air travel was safe in Australia. A spokesperson said Airservices Australia would review the interim reports and completed investigations. “The aviation safety system is designed to manage operational risks through multiple safeguards and, based on the information currently available, the recent occurrences do not indicate an immediate safety risk to the travelling public.” Final reports from the investigations are expected in 2027. Last month Guardian Australia revealed Sydney air traffic controllers had warned safety regulators of “grave concerns” about changes to airspace rules, likening the situation to the months leading up to a crash in Washington DC in which 67 people died.

headline: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial: crime scene photos paint harrowing picture of alleged murder victims’ final moments
trail_text: Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024
body_text: Warning: graphic content A hole in a door and a bullet bent out of shape: crime scene photos shown to a jury paint a harrowing picture of Jesse Baird and Luke Davies’ final moments. Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting the couple with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. Photos from Baird’s eastern suburbs terrace house were revealed to the court during his trial on Tuesday before later being released to the media. In some images, Baird’s bedroom, back courtyard and a bathroom glow with luminol after the chemical, which highlights possible bloodstaining, was used by police to examine the home. An image taken in the sub-floor beneath Baird’s ground-floor bedroom – accessed by a trapdoor in the room – shows a bloodstained tarpaulin. Referring to a photo of a misshapen and bloodstained bullet, Bronwyn Lansley, a crime scene officer, explained it had travelled through a source of blood before penetrating the wooden flooring. A bullet hole in the door of Baird’s bedroom was also shown to the court. Investigators explained it had not been discovered until July, two months before the trial, as it had been repaired with putty and covered with a mounting hook. Analysis of stippling marks left on the door when the gun was fired showed there was nothing between the muzzle of the firearm and the door, Lansley said. The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon began cleaning up the crime scene immediately after the shootings, before dumping Baird and Davies’ bloodied belongings in a skip bin at the Cronulla Bowls Club. More than 100 photos of the bin’s contents were shown on Wednesday. Many of the items were covered in blood, including a white T-shirt, jewellery and a bedsheet. Baird had been a TV presenter and AFL goal umpire, while Davies was a flight attendant. Among the items were bloodstained AFL goal umpire flags, caps and shorts still in their plastic packaging, and a wallet containing Davies’ Qantas ID card. Lansley confirmed to the court that a bloodied shoe print found on the hem of a hoodie pulled from the dumpster matched black Adidas shoes discovered near a monastery in Bungonia, where Baird and Davies’ bodies were eventually discovered. The court was on Wednesday shown photos of the van allegedly used to transport the bodies to the site, with forensic analysis revealing blood on the underside of the vehicle’s rear bumper. The defence lawyer John Stratton SC said during his opening statement that Baird and Davies were fatally shot in “self-defence” after struggles with the policeman. Lamarre-Condon immediately began cleaning up the scene because he “panicked”, the jury was told. The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

headline: Inflation leaps to 4% stoking fears of fifth interest rate hike before Christmas
trail_text: Jim Chalmers says ‘higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia’ are to blame for inflation rising from 3.5%
body_text: Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, as Jim Chalmers was again forced to defend Labor’s economic management amid fears the Reserve Bank will need to hike interest rates again before Christmas. The increasingly embattled treasurer was asked if he was “gaslighting” Australians by insisting that government spending was not responsible for high inflation, blaming instead higher fuel costs associated with the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran. “We can see in today’s inflation figures that the overwhelming reason why annual headline inflation has come up in August compared to July is because of the impact of higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia,” Chalmers told reporters in Sydney. “That’s not an opinion. It’s a fact.” Fuel prices surged by 15% last month, the Australian Bureau of Statistics said, after a worsening Middle East conflict triggered a rebound in global oil prices and the government ended its cut to the fuel excise. Rising transport costs were the prime contributor to price increases in the month, the ABS confirmed. But a 5.4% increase in home building costs over the 12 months to August was one of the prime drivers of high annual inflation “as builders passed on higher costs for materials and labour”, the ABS said. Electricity bills were also higher than this time last year when households were still receiving government rebates. The rise in headline inflation was slightly less than economists had anticipated, while underlying inflation – which removes the most volatile prices swing – was steady at 3.6% in the year to August. Both were still well above the RBA’s 2.5% target. Cherelle Murphy, EY’s chief economist, said “another rate hike looks likely by the end of the year”. A day after the RBA lifted its cash rate to 4.6% – the fourth increase in 2026 – Murphy said “they [the RBA] have an ongoing fight on their hands”. “This is not the end of it.” Chalmers on Wednesday afternoon denied that he was at odds with Michele Bullock, the central bank governor, who at her press conference the previous day said “inflation is too high and has been driven by domestic capacity pressures”. But Bullock also pointed to the worsening Middle East conflict and the sudden boom in AI-related spending on datacentres. “These developments suggest that inflationary pressures will persist for longer than previously expected,” she said. Murphy said it was a fact that spending by governments, at the commonwealth and state levels, was high, and that this was adding to demand in the economy. She said this meant the government should be extremely careful with any new spending – including additional cost of living relief – for fear of making the RBA’s job harder. But she said it was impossible to quantify exactly to what extent government spending was responsible for persistently high inflation in 2026. “Do I think this is the biggest part of the inflation problem right now? No, the biggest part of the problem is that we have these global supply shocks. “What we are witnessing is the accumulation of a number of events happening together, and none of them are good for inflation.”

headline: Approval of biggest coal project in NSW planning commission’s history described as ‘infamous betrayal’
trail_text: Independent Planning Commission says climate change impacts from Hunter Valley project will be ‘outweighed’ by economic benefits
body_text: The New South Wales independent planner has approved the biggest coalmine project to ever go before it, allowing mining to continue until 2045 at a Hunter Valley project described by climate groups as a “carbon bomb”. The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has greenlit the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project after a contentious assessment that drew in climate and environment groups, unions, state authorities and more than 10,000 public submissions. On Wednesday, the commission said the greenhouse gas emissions from the mine, near Singleton, would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”. But these impacts had been “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW, including continued employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”. The IPC said the decision would “provide economic stability for the Hunter region and support a more orderly transition for workers, businesses and communities as the coal industry changes over time”. In response, Georgina Woods, the co-national coordinator of the Lock the Gate Alliance, said: “There is no other way to describe this other than a catastrophic failure of the New South Wales planning system to protect the people of the state from the worst impacts of global warming.” Climate campaigners had strongly opposed the project, saying it was out of line with Australia’s commitments under the Paris climate agreement and could affect extreme weather events. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ‘Infamous betrayal of the public trust’ Groups reacted with dismay at the approval, with Rising Tide describing it as the “largest climate policy failure in NSW history”. The Climate Council had described the project as a “climate bomb that would supercharge climate disasters”. One of its councillors – the former NSW Fire and Rescue commissioner Greg Mullins – on Wednesday raised concerns over overseas emissions from the coal. “What NSW exports as coal, we import back as bushfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts,” Mullins said. “Climate harm does not stop at the border, and neither does the responsibility for it.” Woods said the process for considering fossil fuel projects in NSW was “the best in the country” – including with its climate change act and an independent and transparent planning authority. “The law was in place, and I am frankly shocked. It will go down in history as an infamous betrayal of the public trust.” Glencore and Yancoal – the joint owners of HVO – want to continue digging coal at the north mine site until 2045, and mine from 2030 to 2042 at the south mine. The IPC said HVO would have to prepare a plan to manage the emissions from burning the coal overseas that would limit exports to “jurisdictions with greenhouse gas emissions policies consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement”. The project also requires federal environmental approval – a process expected to be decided before the end of the year. HVO said coal had been mined at the site for 75 years and the project, which it said had strong local support, provided jobs for 1,500 people. The state’s independent Net Zero Commission had warned the planning commission that approving the project could affect the state’s ability to meet climate targets in the future. Over the life of the project, the company has estimated that 809m tonnes of CO2-equivalent will be released into the atmosphere. About 794Mt of that will be emitted when the coal is burned overseas, 87% of which will come from power plants, according to presentations HVO made to the IPC. The Net Zero Commission recommended the planning authority should consider all of the impacts from the mine’s greenhouse gases, including from the burning of the coal in power stations overseas, and pointed to advances in climate science that can attribute real-world impacts to fossil fuel projects. A new tool released by climate scientists this week suggested the additional global heating caused by the project’s approval would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches and lead to more than 100 additional deaths from heatwaves in Europe to the end of this century. The NSW Nature Conservation Council’s chief executive, Jacqui Mumford, said the decision was Chris Minns’ “biggest climate failure” as premier and highlighted the government’s “complete inability to appropriately respond to the ever-growing climate crisis”. The NSW state Greens MP Sue Higginson said the approval was an “absolute betrayal of the science”, saying she “wouldn’t be surprised if the decision is challenged in the courts”. HVO said the approval “marked a pivotal milestone for 1,500 mine workers, their families and the regional economy”. It said the company was engaging with the national environmental protection agency to secure federal approval “by the end of December 2026 to continue operations”. The NSW Minerals Council urged the state government to pass legislation to limit the opportunity for a “legal challenge from climate activists determined to object to every coal mining approval on ideological grounds”.
