body_text: That’s a wrap on our live coverage, before we go let’s recap the day’s top headlines: NSW senator David Shoebridge has become the new Greens leader, replacing Larissa Waters. Steph Hodgins-May has been named deputy leader. Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, as underlying price pressures remained stubbornly high amid worries the Reserve Bank may have to hike again. Anthony Albanese and Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, announced early works are beginning on the second stage of the long-awaited train line to Melbourne airport – a 7.6km stretch of the train line from Albion to Keilor East. OpenAI’s Medicare breach has prompted a government-wide assessment of cyber systems to bolster Australia’s public sector against further AI threats. Two men and a teenage boy have been charged in relation to the alleged mistaken identity shooting of Sydney student Marco Tapia – including the person who allegedly held the gun – police say. A man has been charged with murder after the deaths of two men at Gurranang, about 25km north of Grafton in northern New South Wales, police said. ABC’s finance titan Alan Kohler will retire at the end of this year, capping a three decade-tenure at the national broadcaster. Laneway festival dropped its lineup for next year’s event, and there are some heavy hitters from both the international scene and Australian shores. Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow! ‘I am ready to play hardball’: Hodgins-May vows to take drastic change in new role Newly appointed Greens deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May said the role presented an opportunity to “reimagine what the future could look like if we put people ahead of those corporate profiteers”. Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, she said she was determined to represent Australians calling for greater action from the government. I am ready to play hardball … I’m listening to the Victorians, the Australians who are every day telling me they are distraught at the fact that this government is not doing more to help people. Incremental change doesn’t cut it when we are staring down the biggest El Niño on record, and the potential for immense droughts, floods, fires. Incrementalism won’t cut it on climate action. Incrementalism won’t cut it when we want to materially make lives better, so we are demanding more ambition and courage from the Labor party, but not expecting it. Hodgins-May said she would “take that responsibility incredibly seriously”. If that means playing hardball with the ALP and the Labor government, then absolutely. But if they turn around tomorrow and say, ‘Hang on, maybe we can do things differently,’ and serve us up some reforms that will genuinely change lives for the better, then I’m all ears and ready to go. We are ready to go as a team. Commbank becomes first of big four banks to increase home loan rates Commonwealth Bank has announced it will increase variable home loan interest rates by 0.25% per annum following Tuesday’s RBA rate hike. The changes will take effect from 9 October 2026. CBA Executive of Retail Banking Angus Sullivan said: Each customer’s circumstances are different, and our teams are ready to provide support, help them understand their options and consider what might work best for their situation. For some customers, the immediate priority might be understanding how their repayments and budget may change and where adjustments can be made. For others, it may be having a more detailed conversation with us about their finances. Peugeot announces major recall of over 500 cars due to ‘software issue’ The European car brand has recalled hundreds of vehicles in Australia over a “software issue” that could increase the “risk of serious injury or death”. A warning published on the Department for Transport’s website said the fault could cause the interior door handles to deactivate unexpectedly while the engine was running. The issue may prevent passengers from opening the doors from inside the vehicle, potentially leaving them unable to escape in an emergency. Peugeot estimated that 550 vehicles manufactured in 2024 and 2025 were affected. Owners of affected vehicles are being urged to contact their local dealership to have the software updated at no cost. NSW’s Greens condemn state government’s extension approval of Hunter Valley Operations coalmine expansions The party has criticised the state government’s planning commission for approving the proposal. The approval will allow Glencore and Yancoal’s Hunter Valley Operations to continue until 2045. The Greens said the mine will produce an estimated 809m tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent – about seven times NSW’s annual emissions. Greens climate and energy spokesperson, Cate Faehrmann, said the decision had “killed any chance of NSW meeting its own climate emissions reduction targets”. Each year, the Minns government falls further and further behind on reaching its net zero targets. The latest report from July shows that NSW is not set to reach its 2030 target until 2034 and its 2035 target until 2042. The Minns Labor government doesn’t care about climate action. It prefers propping up a dying industry, with even the International Energy Agency saying that global demand will decline from 2030. The signs of climate breakdown caused by the burning of fossil fuels are all around us and we’re facing a super El Niño here this summer. Meanwhile, the Minns government’s love affair with coal continues. South Australian police are investigating after reports of public fights at beaches. The possible move comes after “several disturbances along the metropolitan coastline late yesterday”, including reports of fighting at Glenelg and Henley Beach. Detective said it’s understood a small number of individuals were involved in public fights as several young people spectated. Police said they were alerted to the incidents through social media videos. They said no reports had yet been made to police and no injuries had been reported. Officers are working to identify and locate those involved. The force’s annual Operation Jericho monitors crime, public disorder and road safety along Adelaide’s coastline during summer. The new American ambassador to Australia, David Brat, has begun the new job, after presenting his diplomatic credentials to the governor general on Tuesday. Brat met Sam Mostyn at a ceremony at Government House in Canberra. The US embassy says Brat’s priorities in Australia include deepening the defence relationship, advancing the Aukus nuclear submarines pact, strengthening cooperation on critical minerals, and expanding trade and investment. In his first official act, Brat paid tribute to Australian servicemen and women by laying a wreath at the Australian War Memorial. “Australia has been our closest ally and friend for generations. It’s an honour to visit such an awe-inspiring tribute as Ambassador,” he said. US and Australian soldiers have fought side-by-side and stood shoulder-to-shoulder for decades in times of war and times of peace. I look forward to furthering our longstanding defence partnership during my posting to Australia. He said he looked forward to meeting Australians, including sport fans. “Both of our nations are crazy about sports, and I can’t wait to get out there, whether it’s tennis, NRL, AFL, rugby, or cricket,” he said. Mother of Marco Tapia wants people to remember her son ‘beyond the circumstances of his death’ Claudia Tapia, the mother of Marco Tapia, the Sydney student mistakenly killed in an alleged crime hit gone wrong, has released a statement after her son’s death. NSW police said earlier two men and a teenage boy had been charged in the shooting with a series of offences, including murder. A NSW official alleged the trio were “hired guns” by organised crime groups to commit the shooting, saying Tapia was a “completely innocent party”. Claudia Tapia said her family was “so grateful to NSW Police and everyone continuing to work on this investigation”. She went on: For our family, however, every development brings us back to the reality that Marco is no longer here. We want people to know who Marco was beyond the circumstances of his death. Marco was a warm, caring and loving 23 years old, a biomedical engineering student, a committed Christian, a youth leader, a volunteer, a martial artist, a boyfriend, a brother and our deeply loved son. … Marco had plans. He had purpose. He had a future, and he was already making a difference in the lives of others. His death is part of his story, but it must never become his identity. Marco was not simply a victim. He was our son, a brother, a boyfriend, a friend, a man of faith, a young leader and a biomedical engineer in the making, who was going to impact this sphere greatly. Officials said emergency services were called to the suburb of Engadine about 3.30pm amid reports a child had been struck by an ebike rider. A five-year-old boy was treated at the scene by paramedics for serious leg injuries before he was taken to Sydney children’s hospital. He is in stable condition. Officers were told the e-bike rider did not stop and left the scene before police arrived. They are searching for two people in relation to the incident. Anyone with information related to the crash has been urged to contact police. Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’ Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record, falling 1m sq km short of the long-term average, scientists have confirmed. Confirmation of the peak meant the four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and critical for marine life – had all occurred in the past four years. Satellites have been watching the continent’s sea ice since 1979, and this year data showed the sea ice peaked on 14 September at 17.59m sq km, about 1m sq km short of the average maximum, or an area roughly twice the size of Spain. Read more here: Minns defends NSW record on inflation: ‘We’ve been careful with public money’ The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has defended the Labor state government’s record on inflation ahead of the March 2027 state election, after former RBA governor, Philip Lowe, said public spending was adding to pressure. In comments in a podcast released by the Institute of Public Affairs today, the day after the RBA lifted the official cash rate to 4.6%, Lowe called for governments to cut spending and run larger budget surpluses to reduce pressure on inflation and interest rates. Figures this morning showed inflation jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%. At a press conference, this morning, Minns was asked about Lowe’s comments and whether the federal treasurer, Jim Chalmers, should cut spending. He said: Well, look, I’d just say that I think every government has a responsibility to do what it can to take demand out of the economy … The NSW treasurer [Daniel Mookhey] and myself have said many times that we have heard the advice from the RBA over the last two years that we need to be careful with public funds, and as a result, over the last four years, we’ve had the lowest increase in spending growth of any jurisdiction in the country … Now, I’m not going to make a long commentary about other governments. It’s up to them and their decisions, obviously. But we want to make it clear that we’ve been careful with public money, particularly the growth in public money, and that will continue if we’re re-elected next March. Jim Chalmers says he hasn’t met new Greens leaders before Jim Chalmers wished the Greens’ outgoing leader Larissa Waters well and said he hasn’t met the new leaders before. He said no party has the numbers in the Senate on their own, “so we engage in good faith with all parts of the Senate crossbench” and he expects that to continue. [It’s] very sad to hear that she’s been unwell, and she’s dealing with this condition. Larissa seems to me to be a really wonderful person, and I wish her well as she deals with the challenges in her health. When it comes to the new leadership of the Greens, I haven’t met the new leaders of the Greens before. Chalmers went on: I’m told that [Shoebridge] was particularly focused on the Labor party in his introductory remarks. I think it’s really important that we focus on the risks posed to workers and to our economy by One Nation, the Liberal party and the National party. … The government for its part is focused on delivering on its agenda, delivering real change, dealing with these pressures and challenges in our economy, and in the course of that work, we’ll play the cards that we’re dealt in the Senate and engage in good faith as we have been to this point. Shoebridge promises Greens will deliver ‘material change’ under his leadership David Shoebridge has promised the Greens will pursue “material change” under his leadership. He said people were “desperate for material change” and wanted more than gradual policy shifts from the major parties. He said: If you travel around the country, the call I’m not hearing is: ‘What do we want? Gradual change! When do we want it? In due course!’ That is the dead politics of Labor. It’s the dead politics of the Coalition. And when you really test it, it’s the dead politics of One Nation. They don’t want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know is not going to change their lives. Newly appointed deputy leader Steph Hodgins-May echoed the promise, pointing to the pressures facing Australian families. We have families who are desperate for secure housing. We have families who cannot afford to send their child to childcare. We have families who are deeply anxious about the climate crisis and are watching this Labor government wave through new coal and gas projects at this critical moment in time,” she said. I am here to say: ‘no, not on our watch’. I am here with David to bring a bold vision to Australia, to grow our movement. No ‘objective observer could contest’ oil prices behind inflation spike: Chalmers Jim Chalmers is pushing back against multiple questions about the cause of the inflation increase. He said: We can see in today’s inflation figures that the overwhelming reason why annual headline inflation has come up in August compared to July is because of the impact of higher global oil prices flowing through to oil prices in Australia. That’s not an opinion. It’s a fact. Chalmers went on to say there will be “all sorts of commentary made” but he didn’t think “any objective observer could contest that after today’s figures”. Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, is speaking after the inflation figures this morning showed inflation had jumped 4% in the year to August from 3.5%. Chalmers said Australia is not immune from the oil crisis in the Middle East, saying the conflict is “overwhelmingly” the reason for the figures. He said: These numbers confirm that the overwhelming reason why inflation went up in August in headline terms was higher global oil prices. In fact, all of the increase in annual headline inflation was from a combination of higher fuel costs and the unwinding of last year’s energy rebates. Chalmers went on to say amid “heightened global instability” he was encouraged to see “underlying inflation moderate in the month-to-month figures”. Inflation is still too high in our economy. That’s why it is so important that we are managing the budget in a responsible way. Former deputy Mehreen Faruqi ‘disappointed’ after Greens leadership vote Former Greens deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi has expressed her disappointment her party room did not appoint her leader in the ballot. In a statement on social media, Faruqi said: “Of course, I am disappointed the party room chose another direction, and know many others will feel the same way”. I did not stand again for Deputy Leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team. Faruqi said she had long advocated for Greens leaders to be elected by members “with enough time for thoughtful deliberation on who is best to grow our party”. I share members’ frustration that the opposite happened this week. Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party. I call on the new leadership team to set a timeline for one member, one vote. Senator David Shoebridge has thanked his party for its support following the unexpected leadership change in the Greens. Speaking in Sydney, Shoebridge said: If you’d asked me earlier this week would we expect to be here, I would have said no. Our party was rock-solid behind Larissa. But I can’t tell you how much of a joy it is going to be over the next 18 months – a lot of hard work – but what a joy it is going to be working with my colleague Steph. This is a moment where, between us, we are going to share the load. We’re going to cross the country. We’re going to deliver that sense of hope and opportunity that Australians are begging for and we are also going to meet the climate crisis. Shoebridge also paid tribute to outgoing leader Larissa Waters. She led with compassion, led with principle, showed what collective leadership can do. We were privileged to be led by Larissa. NSW senator David Shoebridge will become the new Greens leader, replacing Larissa Waters. Shoebridge, who ran on a joint ticket with Victorian Steph Hodgins-May, defeated Sarah-Hanson Young and outgoing deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi. A party announcement is due at noon. It comes during a two-day meeting of Greens MPs in Sydney. High and rising fuel prices drove the big rise in headline inflation, which was a little lower than anticipated. Underlying inflation, which trims out the more volatile prices, was unchanged at 3.6%, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Both measures remain far above the RBA’s official target of 2.5%. Oaka the rescue dog finds a new job as a koala protector, replacing Bear When Bear, the world-famous koala detection dog, entered retirement, his trainers feared the koolie’s little red fireground boots might never be filled. But now AAP reports Oaka – a two-year-old girl of the same breed with the same hyper-fixation on play – has entered the role, where she is tasked with smelling koalas not by their droppings, but by their fur, often metres above ground level. “It felt like we had struck gold twice,” said Josey Sharrad, the International Fund for Animal Welfare’s Oceania programs head. “The qualities that make dogs not a great family pet are often the qualities that make them become a detection dog.” The two-year-old was quickly adopted and now lives on the Sunshine Coast, training alongside a number of fellow detection dogs. Alongside drones and human spotters, she will be trained to spot koalas cut off from food and water following bushfires, floods and cyclones. While she will not be deployed until she is field-ready, the approach of what is expected to be another devastating bushfire season has added urgency. “Our koalas will need all the help they can get, whether it comes on two legs or four,” Sharrad said. Albanese defends government’s efforts on cost of living The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is answering questions in Melbourne, a day after the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates. Albanese said the Reserve Bank governor, Michele Bullock, made it clear yesterday that there are inflationary pressures in the economy that have been made worse by the war in the Middle East. That’s one of the reasons why we’ve looked for savings in the budget. How can you say you’ll repeal the measures that were put in place, such as the changes to capital gains tax and to negative gearing, which were put forward – and then say that you’re going to have a fiscally responsible policy? Alan Kohler will retire from the ABC at the end of this year, capping a three decade-tenure at the national broadcaster. Kohler joined the ABC in 1995 as a business correspondent and has been the lead finance presenter for the 7pm news since 2002. His trademark sign off – “And that’s finance” – has greeted viewers for years. He said in a statement: I love the ABC, always have, even more so after I joined it. I find it very hard to imagine this wonderful place not being part of my life, but I’m 74 and it’s time to spend more time with my family, including the six grandchildren. His last report will be 16 December. NSW police allege shooting of Sydney student ‘hired guns’ linked to organised crime NSW police are holding a press conference after two men and a teenage boy were charged in relation to the alleged mistaken identity shooting of Sydney student Marco Tapia. Three people, aged 22, 23 and 16, were arrested in Junee, near Wagga Wagga, yesterday. Once we have the opportunity to go through all of that and put it all together, we were able to identify that there was a strong case [allegedly] implicating these three males in this offence. Wife of Australian detained by Vietnam says she has concerns about his welfare Chloe Dang, the wife of a missing Vietnamese Australian democracy campaigner, said she hasn’t slept for days after her husband went missing during a trip to Cambodia. Tran Hiep, 50, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, earlier this month and reunite with his wife, but never returned. Dang said the government has since confirmed he has been detained by Vietnamese authorities on what have been described as “fabricated” charges. headline: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
trail_text: A year after his explosive tenure at Doge, the SpaceX CEO is back in the Trump administration’s good graces
body_text: Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House. A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations. The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year. Unlike Musk’s role at Doge – which drew heavy public criticism and costly boycotts of his products – the scope and goals of Project Meridian appear as if they will be much less time-consuming for the tech mogul. The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release. “We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.” Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare. Both have extensive defense department contracts through their companies, with Anduril’s business centered on the government purchasing products that it advertises as the latest advance in warfare. Gingrich was appointed as a member of the defense policy board in December 2020 during the first Trump administration but was dismissed less than three months later after Joe Biden became president. Going back to the 1990s, he has been warning about the threat of an electromagnetic pulse attack that could knock out US power grids.

headline: Senate Democrats block datacenter energy bill, saying ‘toothless’ legislation ‘misses the mark’
trail_text: Republicans supported legislation although Democrats said it wouldn’t effectively address energy consumption
body_text: Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation intended to offset the impact of datacenters on consumer electricity bills, calling it a “toothless” attempt to address a top voter concern ahead of November’s midterm elections. The Ratepayer Protection Act failed by a 57-to-43 vote, falling just shy of the 60 votes necessary to advance through the Republican-controlled chamber. Four Democrats – Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and both Georgia senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – joined Republicans in support of the measure. “Americans are calling for real solutions, real guardrails, real solutions on AI. Republicans’ toothless datacenter bill completely misses the mark,” the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said in a floor speech before the vote. Schumer assailed Trump for a meeting with top tech executives on Tuesday that the president said yielded a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. “Relying on ‘self-regulation’ is how we got into this mess,” Schumer added. Earlier this month, the House of Representatives had approved the bill by an almost unanimous vote. Datacenter construction and electricity consumption has grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has come increasing anxiety among voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills. The bipartisan legislation is an attempt by Congress to address those anxieties, and would have required electric utilities to consider adopting new standards so that datacenters pick up the costs of any necessary upgrades to transmission, generation and distribution, which can otherwise be transferred to households and businesses. It was proposed ahead of the 3 November midterm elections in which Democrats are campaigning on lowering the cost of living in their bid to regain control of the Senate and House. Its sponsor in the lower chamber was Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican who is a top target of Democrats, while the Ohio Republican Jon Husted championed the bill through the Senate. “It’s clear that big tech should be paying their own way, not passing the cost on to local communities and states – and this bill does that,” Husted said in a floor speech on Wednesday, urging Democrats to back the bill that the president had indicated he would sign. Though Ohio voted for Trump by an 11-point margin two years ago, recent polls have shown Husted trailing his opponent, the Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, who has accused the incumbent of bowing to the demands of the datacenter industry. While the proposal was seen as an attempt by Republicans Senate leaders to bolster Husted’s re-election chances, it also presented a quandary for the chamber’s Democrats, since voting it down could be seen as running counter to their pledges of lowering electricity bills. Nonetheless, the party’s leaders opted to oppose the measure, saying it would have been ineffective at actually addressing datacenters’ electricity consumption. The vote was one of the last the Senate is expected to take before the midterms. The chamber is scheduled to conclude its work on Friday, after which senators will return to their states to campaign.

headline: The people’s reboot? Inside the 2 October Guardian Weekly
trail_text: A pushback against big datacentres.  Plus:  Steve Reich at 90
body_text: As the alarm bells sound ever louder about the potentially existential threat of breakneck AI development, people far removed from Silicon Valley debates about the future of the artificial intelligence revolution are voicing other more immediately tangible worries about the building of the vast datacentres that power these entities. For this week’s cover story, economics and political writer Eduardo Porter, analyses why communities are pushing back against AI and the future that the big tech plutocrats want to create. These fears, based around environmental concerns over resource use and rapid societal change, are, he argues, far more complex than luddite attitudes or nimbyism. It’s a position exemplified by reporting from two rural communities in India and the UK where vast datacentres are already under construction or being planned. As Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan find out, the villagers of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, feel that government promises of a “golden age” that a hyperscale Google datacentre would bring them have been broken. Meanwhile, Sandra Laville meets protesters in Great Torrington, Devon, who sense that they are being kept in the dark about plans for an AI campus, one of Europe’s largest, in a Unesco-designated nature reserve. The US campaigner Elizabeth Humphreys, who joined a meeting in Great Torrington, told villagers: “This is a global issue; we are all connected.” And it felt like an issue where Guardian Weekly could bring together our journalism from correspondents across the world to highlight a subject that connects and affects us all. headline: ‘President of the Unites States’: White House’s AI accord includes spelling error
trail_text: Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI
body_text: The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday. At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”. It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents. Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control. Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth. Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social, and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed. The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error. The Guardian has asked the White House for comment The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”. Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats. External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI. The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September. Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI. While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.” The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.

headline: Economic growth in UK and US revised higher; diesel on brink of £2 a litre for first time – as it happened
trail_text: Second-quarter GDP growth on both sides of the Atlantic was stronger than first estimated
body_text: Time to wrap up.. The US and UK economies have strengthened their position as the fastest-growing G7 countries so far this year. Estimated UK growth in April-June was revised up to 0.5% this morning, following 0.6% growth in January-March. The Office for National Statistics reported that exports had been stronger than previously thought. The ONS also reported that UK household income grew at a stronger pace than previously estimated during the first six months of the year. The rise in income per head to 1.1% between January and June followed an increase in the level of economic growth that illustrated the resilience of the UK economy since the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East more than seven months ago. The US followed suit, with new data showing its economy grew at an annualised rate of 2.2% in April-June, or 0.55% in the quarter. Both economies also face the burden of higher motor fuel prices; in the UK, diesel is approaching £2 a litre for the first time. Elsewhere….Greggs has announced plans to close four of its factories, in a move that could result in 740 job losses over the next two and a half years. The bakery chain said it was consulting on the closures, which would initially cost £60m when including disruption costs and redundancy payments but then could create £20m of savings each year by 2028. Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach almost £2,000 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter. The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage. And finally, London’s stock market has posted its worst monthly performance since March. The FTSE 100 fell by 2% this month, including a small dip of 30 points or 0.3% tonight, to see the blue-chip index close at 10,606 points. Over in Germany, inflation has accelerated to its highest level since December 2023. On an EU-harmonised basis, inflation in Germany rose to 3.3% year-on-year in September, preliminary data from federal statistics office Destatis showed, up from 2.9% in August. Inflation was driven by energy prices, which Destatis estimates were 14.9% higher than a year earlier. In another blow, seasonally adjusted unemployment rose back above 3 million in September. The slowdown in US PCE inflation last month lowers the risk of a rise in interest rates in October, reports James Knightley, US chief international economist at ING. Knightley points out that a quarter-point (25 basis point) hike in rates at the Federal Reserve’s next meeting now looks less likely: “Today’s outcome supports the NY Fed’s John Williams’ comments yesterday that there is no immediate urgency for another rate hike and we now have only 9bp priced for the October FOMC meeting versus 18bp at the beginning of yesterday.” “Overall, the report shows a better balance to the US economy and suggests that the middle and lower income households, for whom income is so critical to spending power given the lack of financial assets, have been under less financial pressure than feared.” At the state level, real GDP across the US ranged from a 4.0% annualised increase in New York to a 2.3% decrease in West Virginia. Wall Street has opened slightly higher as traders welcome today’s lower-than-forecast PCE inflation reading. The Dow Jones industrial average has gained 37 points to 51,387 points in early trading, with the broader S&P 500 index up 0.3%. Investors may be hoping that it lowers the risk of a further rise in US interest rates soon. However, Adam Hetts, global head of multi-asset at Janus Henderson Investors, says: “Inflation pressures continue, albeit slightly below expected levels, with monthly headline PCE inflation at 0.3% and core PCE at 0.2%. Annual headline PCE, reading 3.4%, continues well above the Fed’s 2% target. The underlying economy proves resilient once again, with Q2 GDP growth revised up to 2.2% alongside a particularly strong Q3 GDP nowcast. While today’s inflation data is somewhat better than expected, strong labor and GDP data suggest the print is unlikely to derail consensus expectations for another rate hike before the end of the year.” American companies added more employees this month than forecast. Private-sector employment increased by 90,000 jobs in September, according to the ADP National Employment Report released today. That’s up from just 36,000 in August, and higher than the 70,000 economists had expected. Hiring was led by education and health care and leisure and hospitality. “It’s a strong report,” said Dr. Nela Richardson, chief economist at ADP, adding: “After a three-month slowdown, job creation rebounded and pay growth remained solid.” In a second piece of good US economic news, inflation was lower than forecast last month. The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price index rose by 0.3% in August, lower than the 0.4% increase expected by economists. Core PCE inflation, which strips out food and energy, only rose by 0.2% in the month. Newsflash: The US economy grew faster than previously thought in the second quarter of this year. New data just released shows US GDP grew at an annualised rate of 2.2% in April-June, up from a previous estimate of 1.5% growth. The upgrade is due to upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government spending. UPDATED: 2.2% is the equivalent of quarterly growth of 0.55%, so slightly faster than the UK which expanded by 0.5% in Q2 (we learned this morning). The industries which drove the US economy in the last quarter were real estate and rental and leasing, information, durable goods manufacturing, and finance and insurance, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). The diesel crisis could get even worse if Donald Trump decides to introduce an export ban on the fuel. The price of diesel has been pushed to record highs this year as supplies have swindled, due to the Iran war disrupting oil exports from the Middle East, and Ukranian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump has held crisis talks with advisers over whether to impose a diesel export ban, the Financial Times reports today, adding: Aides had presented the president with options including curbs on international diesel sales, people familiar with the discussions said, and administration officials have briefed foreign allies including the UK about possible disruption to their supplies. A White House official said Trump was “evaluating all the options on the table” to lower domestic fuel prices and that no decision had been taken on whether to suspend exports. While many central bankers are considering raising interest rates, ⁠Zambia’s central ⁠bank cut its benchmark lending rate by ⁠250 basis points to 10.75% today. The reduction ‌was much larger ‌than the 25-basis-point cut forecast by economists polled by Reuters. The move came after Zambia’s annual inflation rate softened to ‌6.1% in September, from 6.2% the previous month. It is near the bottom of the ⁠central bank’s 6%-8% target range and at its lowest level since ‌2018. Analysts have raised their 2026 oil price forecasts, Reuters reports. Benchmark Brent crude is now expected to average nearly $90 a barrel as disruption to Gulf exports offsets concerns over demand growth. A September survey of 30 economists and analysts forecast that Brent crude would average $89.05 a barrel in 2026 and U.S. crude $83.90 a barrel. Newsflash: the price of diesel in the UK has moved to the brink of £2 a litre for the first time. The average price of a litre of diesel has hit a new all-time high this morning, at 199.72p, its third daily record high in a row. That’s up from 199.53p a litre yesterday. Motoring body the RAC says: RAC analysis shows that while a third of forecourts (2,579) are now selling diesel for more than £2 a litre, the average price of the fuel has not yet reached the £2 point. Since the Iran war began, the average price of diesel has risen by over 40%, as the jump in crude oil prices drove up the cost of refined products too. The average price of a litre of petrol has risen too, to 174.54p a litre today. And over the last month, petrol has risen almost 13p (12.77p) a litre in September and diesel 16p (16.12p) – both are the third biggest monthly increases on record, going back o to the year 2,000. The RAC says: A full tank of petrol for a 55-litre family car now costs £96, £23 (£22.94) more than it did before the conflict between the US and Iran began. The diesel equivalent is £110 (£109.85), £31.54 more than 28 February. The AI sector could trigger financial stability if it does not deliver the significant productivity gains which have been promised, the Bank of England warns today. Its financial policy committee cite the surge of borrowing from AI companies, saying: Financing of AI-related investment continues to grow rapidly and is expected to remain on a strong upward trajectory. This is increasing the extent to which developments in AI could affect a wide range of investors and funding markets. An increasing volume of AI-related investment is being financed through debt issuance, with global issuance in 2026 expected to exceed that of countries such as the UK. The increasing indebtedness of AI firms combined with opacity and, at times, ‘circular arrangements’ that can be associated with this financing, can complicate the assessment of risks and could amplify losses if expectations disappoint. The BoE adds that government debt markets, as well as AI-linked assets, could be hit if investors reassess their expectations…. The Bank of England also highlights how the Middle East conflict has driven government borrowing costs to their highest levels in almost two decades, saying: The re-escalation of the conflict and the associated rises in oil, gas and refined product prices are leading to a more protracted negative supply shock to the global economy. This has contributed to sustained increases in sovereign bond yields across a number of advanced economies, to levels not seen since 2008 The risks of a financial crisis triggered by high energy prices and the AI boom have risen over the summer, the Bank of England is warning. The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee is concerned that the risk outlook has worsened since July; interconnected risks are more likely to crystallise at the same time, it says. The minutes of the FPC’s latest meeting, which took place on 25 September, highlight that the re-escalation of the Iran war has renewed uncertainty around growth and the path of interest rates in a number of advanced economies. Policymakers are worried that vulnerabilities in government debt markets, high stock market valuations and risky credit markets “crystallise at the same time”, which would create a crisis. The FPC also flags that “rapid advances in AI capabilities have increased cyber and operational resilience risks” – a nod to the recent reports of AI agents going rogue. However, they remain confident that UK households and businesses are resilient, and that the banking system is strong enough to support them in a stress. The committee says: The likelihood that interconnected vulnerabilities in the financial system crystallise has risen since the Financial Policy Committee’s (FPC) previous meeting. The re-escalation of the conflict in the Middle East has renewed uncertainty around growth and the path of interest rates in a number of advanced economies, re-intensifying the risk that vulnerabilities in sovereign debt markets, risky asset valuations, and risky credit markets crystallise at the same time. The rapid increase in artificial intelligence (AI)-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to developments in AI. At the same time, recent incidents in frontier AI have drawn further focus to the pace of AI development and associated vulnerabilities, including cyber and operational risks. The Committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks. The risk-on mood in the markets this morning is pushing up share prices and the pound. Sterling has gained almost half a cent against the US dollar to $1.327, while the FTSE 100 share index is 30 points higher at 10,666 points. British government bonds are rallying this morning, as the City welcomes the upgrade to UK growth announced at 7am. With prices rising, the yields on short and long-dated bonds are both falling. Two-year UK bond yields are down 5 basis points (0.05 of a percentage point) at 4.86%, while ten-year UK bond ields are 4bps lower at 5.356%. Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says the markets are in an “upbeat mood” as the UK economy surprises on the upside. A dip in the oil price is also helping. Brooks says: There was a double whammy of good news for the UK Gilt market this morning, with the upgrade to Q2 GDP, which was revised higher to 0.5% from the original estimate of 0.4%, This suggests that the UK economy was resilient to the effects the Iran war, the energy price surge and the rise in borrowing costs. Stronger services growth and rising household spending boosted the figure. This is fairly typical of the UK economy, which is service based, the real surprise was the strength of business investment and an improvement in the trade figures, which showed a boost in exports. GDP per head was strong too, at 1.1%, the highest level since the post-Covid boom, growth is now running at a 1.1% rate for the first 6 months of the year, which is the highest rate in the G7. The Gilt market likes what it hears, and is leading a major recovery in sovereign bonds this morning. The 2-year Gilt yield is down some 8bps this morning, and the 10-year yield is down 7bps. September has been a volatile month for global bonds, especially Gilts, and even with this recovery, 2-year Gilt yields are still higher by 30bps and 10-year UK yields are higher by 20bps. Over in France, inflation has jumped this month. Statistics body INSEE has estimated that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) should rise by 3.0% year-on-year in September, up from a 2.4% rise in August. INSEE predicts that energy prices accelerated again, driven by those of petroleum products and gas. Services inflation probably increased slightly thos month, while food prices are forecast to have accelerated, especially for fresh products. On an EU-harmonised basis, French inflation jumped to 3.4% this month, the fastest pace in more than two years. In another boost for the UK economy, Allianz Trade has upgraded its growth forecast for this year by 0.3 percentage points to 1.3%. In its latest Global Economic Outlook report, the international insurance company explains that the UK economy has performed better than expected in 2026. Allianz Trade says: UK business insolvencies have fallen 5%, bucking a 6% global rise and increases of 19% in the US, 7% in Germany and Japan, and 5% in France. Consumer spending and business investment have remained resilient, while manufacturing has rebounded and aerospace continues to power ahead. Households have sustained spending by reducing their savings rate, raising questions over how long that resilience can last. UK inflation is forecast to reach 3.4% in Q4 2026, as higher utility bills and input costs feed through to consumer prices. The Bank of England is expected to raise rates twice before year-end, taking Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4.25%. Rate cuts are not expected to begin until November 2027, with higher borrowing costs set to weigh on investment, housing and growth. Higher borrowing costs hurt demand for homes in September, the property portal Zoopla has reported this morning. Zoopla found that the number of sales being agreed this month fell by 9% compared with September 2025. The drop in sales came despite the number of homes on the market rising by 5% year on year, with the gap between supply and demand most acute in London and southern England. Annual house price growth has also slowed to 0.8%, the lowest level since July 2024, according to the latest Zoopla House Price Index. The average price of a UK home is now £273,000, it said. This morning’s upgrade to UK growth in April-June is a boost to Andy Burnham, analysts say, even though he didn’t take office until almost a month later. Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, says: “Still on a post-speech high, the upgraded figure is yet more good news for the UK’s still-new(ish) prime minister. The highest growth in the G7 for the first half is certainly a headline and one that will help keep nervous MPs in line for a while, plus it helps take off pressure for a new election - why risk it now when things appear to be improving nicely.” Ashley Webb, senior UK economist at Capital Economics, warns though that growth may slow towards the end of this year: The upward revision to real GDP growth in Q2, from 0.4% q/q to 0.5% q/q, suggests that the economy has been a bit more resilient to higher energy prices in the first half of the year than previously thought. This resilience may continue into Q3, but we still expect it to fade in Q4 as higher inflation takes a bigger bite out of households’ real incomes. The 0.5% q/q gain in Q2 real GDP followed unrevised growth of 0.6% q/q in Q1, with the breakdown still showing that the economy is no longer being heavily supported by government spending, which contracted by 0.5% q/q (revised down from -0.3%). Thomas Pugh, chief economist at audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK, agrees that growth will slow over the winter: “The upward revisions to Q2 GDP growth means the economy was even stronger in the first half of the year than we previously expected, despite the Iran war. What’s more, the composition of growth looks a little healthier. Surveys suggest that much of that positive momentum has been carried forward into Q3 meaning we have revised up our annual GDP forecast to 1.4%. “However, the next six months looks tougher with potential interest rate rises, a sharp increase in inflation and another tax raising budget all to come. That will drag heavily on growth over the winter. Shares in Greggs have jumped by 7.5% at the start of trading after it announced a pick-up in sales, and plans to cut 740 jobs. Investors are cheered that Greggs now expects “a modestly improved outcome for 2026”. Aarin Chiekrie, equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, says: “Greggs served up a tasty trading update, with total sales growth accelerating to 7.7% over the third quarter. This was driven by more settled weather in recent months, alongside ongoing menu development and product innovation. New store openings also played their part, with the group on track for 100-110 net openings this year, excluding 12 Express locations, making it easier for more customers to tuck into their freshly baked goods. Alongside cost inflation remaining at a manageable level of around 2%, the full-year outlook has modestly improved from prior guidance, which had pointed to operating profits of around £188mn. Encouragingly, the UK’s exports in April-June were much stronger than first estimated. Today’s national accounts show that export volumes increased by 2.8% in the quarter, revised up from the first estimate of a 0.5% rise. This morning’s growth upgrade underlines the UK’s status as the fastest-growing G7 economy in the first half of 2026. Growth of 0.6% in Q1, and 0.5% in Q2, put the UK ahead of other advanced economies this year – although on an annual basis Britain shares third place with Japan: UK bakery chain Greggs has announced plans to cut more than 700 jobs, despite a pick-up in sales. Greggs is proposing closing four of its production sites, which could lead to up to 740 roles becoming redundant. Greggs warns that with signs of greater inflationary pressures in 2027, it needs to cut costs to remain competitive. It says: We believe such changes, whilst difficult, are necessary to ensure Greggs continues to meet capacity requirements for growth in the years ahead in the most cost-efficient manner. Our immediate priority is to minimise the impact on our people where possible. We will enter into a consultation period shortly to work with trade unions and employee representatives of those affected to refine and develop these proposals. The proposals could cost £60m, but then save £20m a year. Greggs also reported 7.7% sales growth in the third quarter of the year, which it attributes to “continued menu innovation” and more settled weather. Those menu changes includes its new Steak & Stilton Bake, and relauched salads. Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to soar by £276 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter. The increase for the January to March quarter is well above the consultancy’s previous prediction of a 9% rise, with analysts blaming the uptick on the recent rise in gas market prices to three-year highs. It would take the cap to its highest level for four years. The AI boom may have driven UK business investment up in the April-June quarter. Gross fixed capital formation (which measures the acquisition of fixed assets by businesses, governments, and households) rose by 0.9% in Q2; the main drivers of the growth are “increases in other buildings and structures”, which would include data centres. Real household disposable income per head increased by 1.0% in April-June, following a decrease of 0.8% in January-March. That means people had more money left to spend, save, or invest after taxes and deductions, adjusted for inflation. headline: Seth Meyers on Trump canceling $1bn in federal funds: ‘Is he adding a waterslide to the reflecting pool?’
trail_text: Late-night hosts weighed in on Trump’s relationship with tech leaders and the White House’s new AI-powered site
body_text: On Tuesday night, late-night hosts discussed a Maha summit in Washington DC, the White House’s new AI-powered website and Donald Trump once again falling asleep on live TV. Seth Meyers On NBC, Seth Meyers focused on the president’s ill-phrased announcement of the US murder rate declining. “We have the best, uh, murder,” Trump said. “What are you talking about, ‘We have the best murder’?” Meyers responded. “It’s a murder rate, not a murder rating.” On Monday, Trump also took issue with the claim by the US ambassador to China, David Perdue, claim that he offered to sell weapons to China, saying: “I think he was probably talking about Taiwan.” “So wait, are you saying that we have an ambassador to China who doesn’t know the difference between China and Taiwan?” asked Meyers. “That’s like if Mr Met showed up to the stadium wearing a Yankees jersey.” Meanwhile, health officials in Florida have issued a local state of emergency after an outbreak of dengue fever. “Man, RFK Jr has only had the job two years and Florida is already turning into an episode of House,” the host laughed. The White House has also rebuked criticism of taxpayer-funded TV ads. They said “they are public service announcements that are ‘reminding Americans to love their country’”, explained Meyers, before quipping: “The clearest sign of a healthy relationship is if you have to remind someone to love you.” Trump reportedly told congressional leaders on Friday that he was revoking nearly $1bn in federal funding. “Oh God, what’s he doing to the reflecting pool now?” joked Meyers. “Is he adding a waterslide?” Meyers closed his monologue with news that the makers of a smart glasses brand have recalled frames after customers reported them overheating and causing burns. “Well, I hate to break it to you,” he said, “but no matter what smart glasses you’re wearing, you’re gonna get burned.” Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host discussed Trump hosting all the top tech executives at the White House for a lunch on Tuesday. The guest list included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and the House speaker, Mike Johnson, “who was there to ask if there was any way that AI could turn him into a real boy”. In a press conference, Trump announced that he was “changing the name” of AI from “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” “So far, everybody likes it,” he added. “Yes,” responded Kimmel drily. “I’m sure the guy whose company’s name is OpenAI is very excited about this development. “The idea that our guardrails against AI are being erected by an addled 80-year-old man … It’s like asking your grandpa to set up a wifi router in your house. You just wouldn’t do it.” The host moved on to talk about the new AI-powered government website America.gov. “A White House official called America.gov ‘a new front door for the federal government’,” said Kimmel. “You know, we need a new front door because Trump demolished the old front door to build his ballroom.” Kimmel added that Trump is still trying to blame all of America’s struggles on his predecessor, again branding former president Joe Biden “sleepy” in Oval Office remarks this week. Ironically, Trump fell asleep shortly after. “Only a few minutes after invoking the name ‘sleepy Joe Biden’, nappy Don Trump drifted off to dreamland on live TV,” Kimmel said. This week also saw the second annual Maha summit in DC in an event attended by JD Vance, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Mike Tyson. “You know we’re screwed when the sanest person in the group has half a face tattoo,” Kimmel said.

headline: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
trail_text: Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage
body_text: The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage. Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”. That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets. The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks. The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in. In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.” But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene. “In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said. However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.” A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth. But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”. “Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.” Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026. That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit. “The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said. “The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

headline: Hedge fund CEO gives $3bn to Carnegie Mellon University in historic donation
trail_text: Unprecedented university donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin will go toward building a new Miami campus
body_text: Carnegie Mellon University will receive an unprecedented $3bn donation from the billionaire investor Ken Griffin, making it the largest single donation in the history of US education. Griffin, 57, is the founder and CEO of Citadel, described as the most profitable hedge fund in history. The money is going toward a new Miami campus as well as big investments at the university’s longtime home in Pittsburgh. Part of the funding will be used to develop Carnegie Mellon’s presence in Miami, Florida, where Griffin lives and where Citadel is now headquartered. The rest will support priorities in Pittsburgh, including recruiting prominent academics and making attendance more affordable for students. The Miami campus will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and PhD students, nearly 300 faculty and more than 600 staff members, with construction slated to begin in 2027. $1bn will go toward Carnegie Mellon’s computer science school and other priorities, including financial aid, Griffin and the university president, Farnam Jahanian, said. The school will be renamed the Kenneth C Griffin School of Computer Science. “Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Jahanian said in a statement. “Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.” Founded by the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, Carnegie Mellon is particularly known for computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and the performing arts. Its School of Computer Science is ranked as the top undergraduate computer science program in the US. The planned Miami campus will take a different approach from the traditional academic-major model. According to the university, education there will instead be structured around “societal challenges”. The campus will concentrate on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation”. The expansion also reflects Griffin’s continuing investment in Miami and south Florida. Citadel moved its headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022, and Griffin has since increased his commitments to the region to about $2.4bn, according to Reuters. Those contributions include support for a Miami charter school network, the University of Miami, Miami Dade College, public schools and math tutoring. Griffin, whose net worth Forbes estimated at about $58bn, will also become a member of Carnegie Mellon’s board of trustees. The board already includes hedge fund billionaire David Tepper, a Carnegie Mellon graduate and donor. The announcement comes one week after Nike co-founder Phil Knight donated $1bn to establish an engineering college at the University of Oregon. Universities are increasingly seeking wealthy donors to expand science and tech programs as artificial intelligence drives economic changes. These large donations have generated concerns about how much influence the wealthy class has over higher education. Griffin has publicly criticized the use of political power for personal enrichment, emerging as one of the most vocal critics of Donald Trump and his administration on Wall Street. Earlier this year, he condemned how the president’s family appear to have made financial gain from their proximity to the White House.

headline: A ‘huge ego’ but effective: who is David Shoebridge, the polarising new Greens leader taking on One Nation?
trail_text: The 55-year-old senator is renowned for his sharp brain but he divides opinion and could face opposition from the party’s grassroots
body_text: The new Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has said he is “up for a red-hot fight” and hit out at One Nation’s “politics of hate”, signalling a more confrontational style of delivery under his leadership. The New South Wales senator, elected as leader on Wednesday afternoon after Larissa Waters’ shock resignation, said the minor party would show people it understood their anger and mistrust with mainstream politicians, and “show them who their real enemy is” – the elite 1%. “I think what people are looking for in this moment is a red-hot fight – a red-hot fight for them, a red-hot fight for their kids, a red-hot fight for a safe climate,” Shoebridge told Guardian Australia. “I think my political career shows that I’m up for a red-hot fight on these things.” Entering federal parliament in 2022 after more than a decade in NSW state politics, the 55-year-old becomes the sixth federal Greens leader since the party was created in 1992. Shoebridge leads the party after its devastating 2025 election outcome, which resulted in its former leader, Adam Bandt, and two up-and-coming lower house MPs losing their seats. While the Greens have maintained their primary support at about 10% to 12%, the rise of One Nation has meant they are no longer the main minor-party threat to future Labor and Coalition governments. The one-time barrister and corporate lawyer from Sydney’s wealthy eastern suburbs said his mission now was to show voters One Nation was not the answer they were looking for. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “When you get out and meet with Australians who are facing these kinds of challenges … working two jobs and still not being able to afford the rent, no one would criticise people for being angry with politics in those moments and searching for whatever answer they can find,” Shoebridge said. “Our job is to is to take them away from the politics of hate, the politics of racism that One Nation wants to provide in that moment, and show them who their real enemy is. “It’s not their neighbour who’s from the Philippines who’s working at the local emergency department. “It’s the 1%, the corporates that are literally stealing their future from them.” Shortly after Shoebridge emerged the victor of Wednesday’s party-room ballot, the former deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, posted a stinging criticism of the process. “I’ve long advocated publicly that Greens leaders should be elected by members with enough time for thoughtful deliberation on who is best to grow our party,” Faruqi said. “I share members’ frustration that the opposite happened this week. Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party. I call on the new leadership team to set a timeline for one member, one vote.” Shoebridge said he would give the membership a “real and direct say on the next choice of a federal leader” before the next federal election. “This is a process that will take months to work through with the party and work collaboratively with the party to deliver, and we are committed to having that in place before the next federal election,” he said. “After the election [it] will trigger an automatic vote for the next leader. That’s the timeframe we’re working to, and that’s the timeframe we’re committed [to].” The polarising NSW senator Shoebridge is one of the minor party’s newer additions but almost all of his upper house colleagues have an opinion about him. In his four years in Canberra, he has built up a reputation for being one of the most effective senators and political communicators. The Greens senator Barbara Pocock said Shoebridge and his deputy, Steph Hodgins-May, would “bring new energy and grow momentum on the issues that Larissa’s laid the groundwork for”. “Given the crisis in politics across our country right now, that is very welcome, and I think it will make a difference,” she said. The popular independent Australian Capital Territory senator, David Pocock, described Shoebridge as “smart” and a “hard worker”. “He recognises politics in our country is in a time of flux and I’m sure he will keep pushing hard and holding the major parties accountable as leader of the Greens,” Pocock said. Shoebridge’s role as the grand inquisitor of Senate estimates – of which many of his performances are clipped up and shared on social media to a much larger audience – has earned him praise and criticism. One of his Senate colleagues said no one gets under Labor’s skin more than Shoebridge. This month the government’s Senate leader, Penny Wong, took issue with his interjections. “Oh, the smartest man in the Senate is speaking again! So good to hear from you,” she said. Labor sources, who spoke under the condition of anonymity, described Shoebridge as annoying but “very effective” in the Senate, while others said he had “huge ego”. “In the face of an insurrection among the grassroots led by Mehreen Faruqi, Senator Shoebridge will have to convince the membership and his Canberra colleagues that the straight, white man from Woollahra is their best hope,” one Labor source said. A senior Labor figure said their honest assessment of Shoebridge was that he did not invest in relationships, liked things done his way and was not a natural negotiator. They pointed to a scenario when Labor offered the Greens the final seat on a joint artificial intelligence committee, as long as it didn’t go to Shoebridge. Waters refused, so Labor sent it to a vote in the Senate, where Shoebridge lost decisively to Pocock, 49 votes to 12. A former party colleague, Lidia Thorpe, said Shoebridge wasn’t a “team player”. While they had personal differences, Thorpe said she respected Shoebridge’s strong support for reducing Indigenous incarceration rates. “I just want outcomes for my people and if it means that he’s going to platform the same issues, then that’s what I’ll work with,” the independent Victorian senator said.

headline: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
trail_text: Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting
body_text: The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival. The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”. The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency. China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work. This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers. Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence. Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act, which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities. The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy. Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector. There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”. In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography, the embedding of hidden data in pictures online. Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said. Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics. “It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said. Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields. Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.” The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes. That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.
