headline: UK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis finds
trail_text: Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says
body_text: Datacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research. Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK. Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation. Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons. It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections. Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt. Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them. James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds. “Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.” To underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility. The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.” Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity. Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet. Narayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.” By contrast, the Green party in England has called for a moratorium on building datacentres, while there have been protests in Scotland, amid claims that massive projects are being rushed through. Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are. ‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.” In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”. A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”

headline: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom
trail_text: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from them
body_text: In 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator. Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic. But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly. “Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book. A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents. The maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring. The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.” Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.) In an AGI world – one that it’s easy to imagine is round the corner after reading Susskind’s book –whole careers but also the very meaning of work will change. Susskind urges politicians, parents and teachers to start paddling into that wave now. He warns against the folly of “future proofing” when the horizon is so foggy. He recalls the David Cameron government’s rush to teach kids how to code, just a few years before it emerged as one of the things that AI does best. Instead, schools should teach children to learn with and without AI, while also doubling down on the basic skills that we should never lose sight of. He envisages a future of personalised learning, in which AI-trained teachers will deploy the technology as assistant tutors rather than attempting to cater to 30 children as a blob. Graduates entering white-collar industries that stand to be most disrupted should harness AI to free them from the drudgery of, say, reviewing legal documents in a basement and instead hone their craft earlier in AI-simulated trials. Middle-aged careerists should not “retreat to inherited practices” or kid themselves that they occupy “safe” professions; we must remember the underlying problem our professions seek to solve and reimagine how to do so in an AI-assisted age. Susskind neatly weaves the conceptual and the practical. And while there was apparently no time in this slim work to consider the more immediate ethical implications of AI (its reliance on stolen creative work, its environmental toll) and the questionable personal qualities of so many AI bosses), as a call to action in the face of an unstoppable tide, his book is at once challenging, compelling and refreshingly optimistic. • What Should My Children Do? How to Flourish in the Age of AI by Daniel Susskind is published by Allen Lane (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

headline: Trump administration to confront Australia over Labor’s social media algorithm plan
trail_text: White House warns trading partners against ‘imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion’ on US tech sector
body_text: The Trump administration will confront Australia over its plan to force digital platforms to take down harmful content and let users opt out of algorithm-generated “for you” feeds. Big tech companies would be fined more than $100m for breaching the proposed laws and the Australian government is under pressure to raise those fines even further. A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said the US administration would raise its concerns with “trading partners”, in a statement released less than 24 hours after Australia’s announcement on Tuesday. “President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America’s leading technology sector,” Desai said. The communications minister, Anika Wells, downplayed the statement as “broad” and told News24 she had not directly received any such warning from a US representative. “We’re a sovereign nation,” Wells said. “We have the right to defend Australian parents and kids and we’ll do that.” Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here If passed, the digital duty of care laws would require platforms to protect children from harmful content around eating disorders, misogyny, pornography, glorifying crime, abuse and cyberbullying. Adults and children would need to be protected from illegal material. They would also require platforms to send users a notification or “pop-up”, giving them a choice between a main feed that shows personalised content from across the platform or one that shows only content shared by their online connections. The Greens party has demanded the government make the latter option the default setting and force platforms to let users opt in to having personalised feeds. The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young repeated calls for higher fines to be pegged to companies’ global revenue, speaking to ABC radio on Wednesday. “Big tech is going to spend a lot of money fighting these laws in the first place and finding every which way to get around them,” Hanson-Young said. “You need to hit them really where it hurts, and that’s their revenue.” Big tech companies Meta, Google and TikTok have not publicly commented, though their representative lobby group, Digi, has said the law’s definitions of harmful content and impact on user experience would be crucial. OpenAI, owner of ChatGPT, said it planned to engage with the government on its laws to ensure they were “protecting Australians while enabling them to benefit from AI”. Australian businesses have warned the rules could hurt their own revenue, as Australians who opt out of algorithms may stop seeing advertisements and buying from companies that sell via online platforms. The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia has asked the government to model the costs to small businesses and their visibility in feeds. The Labor government is also facing backlash from local conservatives, with the Coalition accusing Labor of using the bill to censor free speech. The proposal would give the communications minister the power to set new definitions for harmful content that would have to be taken down. The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said this could extend to political speech that opposed the government. “I don’t trust big tech, but I trust the Labor party a lot less,” Canavan said. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Canavan’s comments were “disingenuous” as the Senate would be able to reject the minister’s definitions. Wells has repeatedly committed to leaving political content and misinformation outside the scope of the laws. “Your right to be wrong on the internet remains preserved in the digital duty of care,” Wells said. “If you want to believe that the moon landing was fake, it is in no way impacted by the digital duty of care.”

headline: US allies lack resources to keep pace on AI, top Pentagon official says
trail_text: Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners
body_text: The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way. “They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”. The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power. Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”. “I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.” It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform. But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children. Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability. “The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

headline: AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?
trail_text: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
body_text: Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”? Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade? These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine. Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist. Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.” The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI). On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”. Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race. Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.” The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing. Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.” The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”. Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.” On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action. The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.” ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out. Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity. He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.” Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI. The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.” Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”. Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.” David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”. “AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable. “What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.” Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs. “These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.” Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not. “It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

headline: Reform UK says it will ‘fully cooperate’ with Met after inquiry launched into alleged overseas donations – as it happened
trail_text: Party denies wrongdoing after Scotland Yard confirms it is investigating allegations broadcast by Channel 4 after undercover sting
body_text: The Met police will investigate allegations that Reform UK broke electoral law relating to overseas donations as part of a wider inquiry. Andy Burnham is striking a welcome new tone at PMQs. He sounds like a man interested in the questions being asked, instinctively minded to be helpful (particularly to backbenchers) and, when confronted with a political criticism, interested in engaging with the argument. By contrast, when Keir Starmer was doing it, as the questions came his mind just seemed to be whirring towards the default ‘line to take’ discussed in advance. Perhaps it’s just because Burnham is new to the job and he has not been burned yet by making too many rash promises (or quasi-promises, like today’s on the Gravesend-Tilbury ferry – see 12.31pm). But he does seem to have some sort of strong, innate desire to win people round that might persist. During the summer, when Patrick Maguire from the Times put it to him in an interview that he worried too much about being liked, Burnham replied: “Isn’t the job to be popular by making people’s lives better? Isn’t that what you should be doing?” Getting Kemi Badenoch to like or admire him may be too much to ask, but it was notable that Burnham kept stressing his commitment to working with her on issues like defence spending. Badenoch opened her questions with a reference to Burnham’s mini-gaffe last week, when he told Tan Dehsi that he was fully committed to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 when he meant 3.5% by 2035. Badenoch could have made this highly embarrassing for Burnham, but he got out of it fairly well – not actually committing to 3% by 2030 while at the same time implying (as Alex Wickham from Bloomberg explains here) that he will get there in the end. The most interesting comments were about welfare. For at least a year now, the Conservatives have been arguing that the answer to the defence spending challenge (in fact, the answer to every government spending challenge) is just to cut welfare spending. In response to a challenge on this, Starmer would have just attacked the Tories’ record on defence. But Burnham sounded like someone who has actually read the Tory proposals in detail (which wouldn’t take long) and thought about why that might be a bad idea. And he told Badenoch: I looked at it and I don’t think myself that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country that we wouldn’t have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation. He went on: We do everything to support our national security, but it can’t come at the expense of social security. Having strong national security also depends upon having resilience in our communities. This side of the house will not be forced to choose between the two, and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% (of GDP spent on defence) by 2035 at the spending review. The Conservatives clearly think this is a mistake. Before the end of PMQs, a Tory spokesperson had put out a press release saying: Britain heard it loud and clear today: Andy Burnham will not cut welfare to fund the defence of our country. The prime minister is prioritising the ballooning benefits bill over our national security. Shameful. This is not leadership, it is surrender. But, if Labour want to win an argument with the opposition about welfare, they are going to have to explain why benefits matter and what happens when you cut them. Today, Burnham made a start. The second most interesting comments were the ones that Badenoch did not make; she did not say anything about Israel. Maybe that was just because she decided it was yesterday’s story, but it is also possible that that she realises that she is in the wrong place on this issue. Yesterday she published an article on this issue which did not contain a word of criticism of Israel and which accused Burnham of just caving in to Corbynism and antisemitism. The Tories seemed to be eagerly awaiting Donald Trump to lash out. But the White House said very little, it turned out that those well-known Corbynites Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney were doing exactly the same thing and even the Board of Deputies of British Jews was more critical of settler violence in its response than Badenoch. headline: Morning Mail: High-end home values fall; costs of sea level rise revealed; and is AI coming for humans?
trail_text: Expensive homes worst hit in property price downturn; report details staggering impacts of sea level rise; tech insiders raise alarm over AI advances
body_text: Good morning. Amid the gloom over the property market downturn across Australia, new figures reveal that it is the more high-end houses being hit worst – down more than 10% from their peaks in some cities. A new report has projected staggering economic losses to be felt across Australia by the end of the century due to coastal flooding as rising sea levels cause “safe land” to vanish amid a worsening climate crisis. Alarming warnings from tech industry insiders in recent days have left some global leaders scrambling to quantify the threat to humans posed by AI. And we look back at the life of author Blanche d’Alpuget. Australia ‘Less and less viable’ | The Climate Council forecasts that more than 267,000 coastal properties will be damaged by flooding by 2100 as Australia’s sea levels rise, costing hundreds of billions of dollars. A mixed bag | High-end homes are recording steep price falls, while more affordable properties are proving resilient, leaving Australians to experience the real estate downturn in very different ways. Renters warned | So-called “RentTech” companies may be circumventing Victorian laws designed to protect tenants’ personal data by asking for “excessive” information, a review has found. Analysis | The RBA hoped this year’s three interest rate rises would tame inflation. But with the US-Iran conflict, rising oil prices and the explosion in datacentre investment, nothing is going their way. Koala concerns | The Victorian government sat on a report for more than 12 months that found the state’s koala population was in chronically poor health, a report reveals. ‘A true one-off’ | Blanche d’Alpuget is being remembered as a successful author who “lived fearlessly” – and brought her own star power to her relationship with her “great love”, Bob Hawke. But how seriously should we take them? Know when to fold ‘em | Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007. ‘It’s a good start’ | Prominent Israelis are welcoming UK sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank. The UK foreign secretary has rejected claims that the sanctions will make British Jews less safe. King Harald V | Tens of thousands lined the streets as Norway said farewell to King Harald V in a ceremony attended by Europe’s royals and global political figures that brought 13 days of mourning to a close. Full Story Greg Jericho on One Nation’s superannuation ‘sugar hit’ One Nation’s proposal to allow people to access 3% of their super contributions for three years is touted as a lifeline for those struggling to get by. His play Woman Far Walking, about an ancient woman who has witnessed 160 years of colonialism, angered some New Zealand viewers resistant to acknowledging Māori losses of lives, land and language. And now, 26 years after it was first performed, the work is finally having its Australian premiere. headline: Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030
trail_text: One researcher who resigned said many in industry believe that without regulation AI could kill off humanity
body_text: Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest. The latest doom-laden predictions came in posts on social media on Tuesday by a researcher who said he resigned because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” wrote Jacob Coxon. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” The post garnered responses from at least two other Anthropic employees who backed up Coxon’s dire predictions. In the first, Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said his former colleague was “correct”, and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Hubinger’s comments mark a surprising affirmation of Coxon’s unflattering, apocalyptic predictions from a person still on Anthropic’s payroll. A second response came from Samuel Marks, Anthropic’s “scalable oversight lead”, who posted a lengthy analysis he stressed was in his personal capacity, and not the views of his employer. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Marks. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said. “Anthropic has been a pioneer in mechanistic interpretability, the science of looking inside AI models to understand how they work, which is now being used to analyze and prevent incidents of AI misalignment across the industry. We were the first lab to publish a Responsible Scaling Policy, a public framework dedicated to mitigating catastrophic risks from AI models and we continue to aggressively test our models for dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology, and publish what we learn for scrutiny and research. “This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.” The researchers’ musings on the possibility of human extinction follow more concrete warnings about AI’s cybersecurity capabilities by Sam Altman, chief executive of Anthropic’s rival OpenAI. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has conceded previously that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”. Altman said last year that certain aspects of AI, including what he called the “silent surrender” of human decision-making, terrified him. AI executives have shared some concerns about the direction of AI and its growing ability to manipulate, seize and control human functions and actions. A sharp rise was reported this summer in incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways. In one of the most publicized examples, staff at OpenAI recorded rogue behavior among its leading AI agents that escaped a closed training environment in July to access the open web and launch an unprecedented hacking attack on the software repository Hugging Face. OpenAI, the San Francisco-based startup behind the publicly available AI bot ChatGPT, later admitted that it should have responded earlier to warning signals of the days-long attack, which is widely considered to be the first autonomous agent cyber-attack. Those executives, however, have stopped short of agreeing with the full doomsday warnings like Coxon’s and have bristled at any attempts to regulate the AI industry. Some politicians have urged the industry to slow down, or in some cases, halt development on AI altogether. Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, reposted Coxon’s resignation on Wednesday with his own note: “Mr. Coxon is right. The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity.” Sanders said he would soon introduce legislation to “ban superintelligence” and pause AI development.

headline: Lawmakers blast AI companies after researcher warns of human extinction by 2030
trail_text: Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said AI will become ‘superhuman systems’ that can cause human extinction by the end of the decade
body_text: Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, lawmakers have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. Ted Cruz, a republican senator from Texas, said in an interview on ABC’s The View, that AI posed a “catastrophic risk” and that he “read that whole tweet thread that that developer put out. It was highly concerning. “It reminded me, last year I had Elon Musk on my podcast … and one of the questions I asked him, I said, ‘OK, what are the odds that AI destroys humanity?’ And he looked at me and said, ‘10-20%.’ And I’m like, ‘holy crap,’” Cruz added. On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, said: “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.” The outrage began after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, announced on social media on Tuesday that he was resigning from the company, saying AI would soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act. Ted Lieu, a Democratic congressman from California, said Coxon’s post was “exhibit number 739 for why we need to pass the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill asap”. Lori Trahan, a Democratic congresswoman from Massachusetts, said it was “past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job”. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway,” Trahan added. Even musician Sheryl Crow weighed in, posting on Instagram about Coxon’s warning and saying that AI had the capacity to “eliminate us in order to continue”. “I am begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent this from going forward,” Crow wrote. Singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers reposted Crow, writing: “what she said”. The outrage comes after both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees over the past couple of months. Executives at the companies have touted the power of their technology and warned of its potential, but have stopped short of prognostications like Coxon’s. On Wednesday, Anthropic published a lengthy cybersecurity incident report about its occurrences. The company said it scanned hundreds of millions of transcripts to look for further incidents and that it “found no other cases of similar or worse severity”. Anthropic insisted that while the agent’s actions were “misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope”. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.” The spokesperson added that the industry should work together “to pace how we release powerful models”. OpenAI did not return a request for comment.

headline: Weatherwatch: AI model beats standard methods at predicting cyclones
trail_text: Artificial intelligence system delivers a three-day forecast as accurate as previous two-day predictions
body_text: Google’s WeatherNext AI model is better than existing systems at forecasting cyclones, according to a paper published in Nature. The AI-based technology gives an extra day of warning, providing a three-day forecast for hurricanes or typhoons that is as accurate as previous two-day predictions. But this is just one AI tool transforming weather forecasting, part of a gradual shift that has been gaining momentum over the past year. Numerical forecasting dates back more than a century to Weather Prediction By Numerical Process, a book by Lewis Fry Richardson, who was a pioneering Met Office mathematician. At that time, the calculations had to be carried out by hand. It took more than six weeks to generate a daily forecast, making the method impractical until the introduction of computers. Even with modern supercomputers, processing power can still be a limiting factor. AI sidesteps this, because rather than having to make detailed calculations like physics models, it develops predictions based on patterns learned from training data. AI-based systems now rival conventional models for forecasting on several scales, especially longer-term predictions. And while they are not necessarily superior, they can produce comparable forecasts faster and at lower cost. There is resistance to AI in many areas. In weather forecasting though, it is generally being welcomed as a useful new capability.

headline: Thursday briefing: 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry as it goes on display
trail_text: In today’s newsletter: No Bayeux ticket? Everything you need to know about the sold-out exhibition – from its epic journey to London to a Game of Thrones likeness
body_text: Good morning. If you live in the UK, you have probably heard about the Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which opens today, and you probably haven’t got a ticket. The digital queue was nine-hours long when they first went on sale in July, and the exhibition has already broken the British Museum’s record for the number of tickets sold in a single day. Some lucky individuals, including King Charles and aspiring overlord Peter Thiel, have been treated to early previews of the medieval tapestry. Guests staying at One Aldwych, a hotel where rooms go for £1,000 a night, can partake in the “Bayeux experience” with a themed cocktail (mead spritzer, anyone?), a full English breakfast and preferential access to tickets. In a break from our regular programming, this morning’s newsletter brings you 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry for anyone who hasn’t been able to see the real thing. That’s one fact for each of its 68 metres (bonus fact: it’s 68.3m long). If that’s not your vibe, just be glad I didn’t manage to find 1066 facts. First, here are the headlines. Five big stories Reform | The Met police will investigate allegations that Reform UK broke electoral law relating to overseas donations as part of a wider inquiry. UK- Israel | Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end. Technology | Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, US politicians have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. UK news | Protesters who gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel mistook Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team for asylum seekers. US news | Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. In depth: From nudity, a save from the Nazis and its restoration, a buffet of Bayeux facts 1. First of all, as the exhibition’s curator Michael Lewis points out in his book, the Bayeux tapestry isn’t really a tapestry. It’s “more accurately described as an embroidery”, Lewis writes. (Nobody actually calls it an embroidery, though, so we’ll stick with tapestry). 2. The embroidery tapestry tells the story of the events that culminated in the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conquerer defeated King Harold. 3. It was supposedly commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conquerer’s half-brother, for his newly built cathedral in Bayeux in 1077. He was prone to “self-aggrandisement” (in Lewis’s words), which is why he gave himself a starring role in the tapestry. 4. But it wasn’t made in Bayeux. Researchers think it was probably made in England, near Canterbury. 5. It’s embroidered on linen, with 10 colours of woollen thread likely dyed with woad, madder and indigo. 6. Its nine panels were embroidered separately, and then stitched together to form a continuous picture. 7. It features 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs, 37 buildings (including Mont-Saint-Michel) and 41 ships. 8. It may have had a single master designer who plotted its narrative, but … 9. The embroidery was almost certainly stitched by multiple women (William of Poitiers cited English women as skilled embroiderers). 10. It’s unclear how long it took them – one estimate reckons the stitching took between two and four years. 11. Yet, only three women actually feature in the tapestry. None of them are having a good time: one is weeping at her husband’s deathbed, another is fleeing a burning building and a third is being assaulted by a priest. 12. This third figure is Ælfgyva (meaning elf-gift), the only named woman in the tapestry. Scholars think that she could be Emma of Normandy, who was accused of having an affair with the Bishop of Winchester. 13. The tapestry conveniently doesn’t mention Edgar Ætheling, who had a stronger hereditary claim to the English throne in 1066 than either William or Harold. 14. The borders tell their own stories. They’re filled with fantastical beasts, creating what the Guardian’s art critic Jonathan Jones described as a “marginal world of monsters and myths”. 15. The upper border features one of the first depictions of Haley’s Comet. 16. The tapestry also shows a figure with the name Harold, depicting the famous (and probably apocryphal) moment he was struck in the eye by an arrow. Most scholars think Harold was actually hacked to death. 17. It was possibly designed to be interpreted by a live storyteller in front of an audience, much like an epic poem. 18. It’s damaged at the end, and incomplete. Nobody knows what scene would have finished the tapestry (some think it could have been a depiction of William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey in 1066). 19. It survived at least three fires in Bayeux Cathedral. 20. The first recorded reference to the tapestry was in the 1476 inventory of Bayeux cathedral, which described a “very long and narrow hanging of linen, embroidered with figures and inscriptions representing the Conquest of England.” 21. The tapestry hasn’t always been well looked after. For centuries it was rolled out for cathedral visitors. One visiting English antiquary observed in the early 1800s that it was “much rubbed at the beginning, torn towards the end.” 22. In 1792, during the French Revolution, the tapestry was nearly used to cover a wagon (it was saved at the last minute by an official who swapped it for a piece of canvas). 23. In 1794, an proposal was briefly floated to cut the tapestry into strips to decorate a festival float. 24. A 19th-century British artist secretly snipped off two fragments that ended up in a London museum (these were eventually returned to Bayeux). 25. In 1803, Napoleon had the tapestry temporarily moved from Bayeux to Paris, where it hung on display at the Louvre, to rally support for his planned invasion of Britain. 26. The first full photographic copy of the tapestry was made for the South Kensington Museum in 1872 (now the V&A museum). 27. A group of women in Staffordshire created the largest Bayeux reproduction in 1885, which is displayed in Reading Museum. It took them 18 months. 28. They removed 93 penises from their reproduction, 88 belonging to horses and five to men. 29. The Nazis saw the tapestry as a propaganda tool, and wanted to establish that Normans were actually the descendants of Viking settlers. 30. They appointed a professor of Viking archaeology as the leader of “Special Assignment Bayeaux” to study it. 31. Heinrich Himmler tasked two SS officers in 1944 to seize the Bayeaux tapestry from the basement of the Louvre, where it was being stored. 32. A group of local resistance fighters tipped off by code breakers at Bletchley Park managed to intercept the officers and protect the tapestry. 33. Since 1983, the tapestry has been displayed at the Bayeux museum, in a 17th-century seminary near Bayeux’s medieval town centre. 34. When the tapestry arrived at the Bayeux museum in the 1980s, photos show that it appeared to have been folded and hoisted up a stairwell. 35. It’s incredibly fragile, and liable to fray. A 2020 study found the tapestry had “24,204 stains, 16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 gaps in the cloth or the embroidery” and “30 non-stabilised tears.” 36. The first request for the Bayeux tapestry to be loaned to Britain was in 1953, for Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. The French refused. 37. Another request was made in 1966, to mark the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings. The French refused, again. 38. In 2013, a committee was formed to advise on how the tapestry could be redisplayed. It raised the prospect of a loan to the UK (“I did sort of bang on about it,” Lewis, a committee member, later recalled, “until I was a bit like a broken record”). 39. The Bayeux museum was scheduled to be closed for refurbishment, creating an opportunity for the tapestry to travel on loan. 40. In January 2018, Emmanuel Macron announced at a summit with Theresa May that the French had agreed to loan the tapestry. Although France had “found the best experts of the world to explain in perfect detail” why the loan “was impossible”, Macron said that the French government had “decided” otherwise. 41. Many people insist it should never have been moved. Arts journalist Didier Rykner started a petition against the loan that gained more than 70,000 signatures. 42. The late David Hockney agreed, described the loan as “madness,” and said “some things are too precious to take a risk with.” 43. And two expert reports in 2021 and 2022 advised Macron against the transportation of the tapestry. 44. The loan specified the tapestry had to be stored lying flat, and couldn’t be subject to tremors any greater than two millimetres per second during its transportation. 45. A team of conservators and experts, including a German vibration technology scientist, were involved with its relocation. They designed a meticulous solution for transporting the tapestry involving a “paravent”, a hinged folding screen on wheels. 46. The paravent was designed so it could be closed into a rectangular block with the tapestry inside, effectively folded 28 times. 47. It took ninety people in blue latex gloves seven hours working to extract the tapestry from its case and transfer it to the paravent. 48. It then had to be stored in a specially manufactured crate for shipping. The art logistics firm Hizikia built two nesting crates, with an outer aluminium crate designed to reduce the impact of movement. 49. The firm also provided a customised reinforced truck to dampen vibrations. 50. Experts carried out two dry runs, one with a replica tapestry transported across the channel that made its way to an art warehouse in south London. 51. Data from these dry-runs showed that French roads are smoother than British roads. 52. The tapestry has been insured by the Treasury’s indemnity scheme for £800m, which is more than twice the value of the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction (Salvator Mundi, a painting of Jesus attributed to Leonardo da Vinci). 53. Two threads were reportedly broken when the tapestry arrived in London. 54. At the British Museum, it will be housed in a custom-made case, believed to be the longest ever constructed, and will be exposed to a limited number of light hours per day. 55. When the lights are switched on, they’ll be dimmed to 50 lux, the international museum standard for sensitive materials. 56. Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and King Charles viewed the tapestry last Wednesday. 57. It will be displayed at the British Museum until July 2027, before it returns to a newly built museum in Normandy that will open later next year. 58. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, has said he hopes the Bayeux loan could revive the prospect for a loan of the Parthenon marbles. 59. The tapestry has inspired numerous copycats, including the Bloody Sunday Tapestry created by the artist Darren Cullen in 2013. 60. There’s also a Game of Thrones Tapestry at the Ulster Museum in Belfast. 61. The Sun newspaper commissioned a “Bye-EU” tapestry in 2018 to commemorate the Brexit vote, which depicted Boris Johnson in chain mail and Theresa May surrounded by the decapitated corpses of Brussels bureaucrats. 62. A helmet from Sutton Hoo, and the Lewis chess pieces, were both loaned to Normandy museums as part of the Bayeux loan. 63. My favourite bit of any trip to the British Museum is the gift shop (eds: does this count as a fact?), where you can now buy a replica Norman helmet and bottle of Bayeux mead with your Tutankhamun pencil tin. 64. Speaking of Bayeux tat, Nigel Farage sported a Bayeux-themed tie during the 2014 Rochester byelection, a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. 65. Radio 4 has devoted a special day of broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry. 66. And the museum’s videos about the tapestry’s arrival are narrated by the Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. 67. Philippe Bélavel, Macron’s former culture adviser, has said “such a loan will only happen once and never again.” 68. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry, which cost £33, will go on sale on 21 October at 10am. Best of luck getting yours. headline: Is Vaibhav Sooryavanshi a post-Test cricketer – or could he revolutionise the format?
trail_text: The 15-year-old is tailor-made for short-form cricket, but he may just have the power to reimagine red-ball batting
body_text: The ball is short outside off. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi goes to pull it, hoiks it high to deep midwicket, is out for 44 off 37 balls. Almost immediately, a portion of the 12,000 fans who have risen at dawn to queue outside the Chepauk Stadium for free tickets begin to vacate their seats. The Duleep Trophy final in Chennai between East Zone and South Zone is scheduled for five days and has been going for barely an hour. But for some, the show is already over. Of course, Sooryavanshi is part of the reason the final is taking place in Chennai in the first place. It was originally slated for the national academy on the outskirts of Bengaluru, only to be moved in order to accommodate the thousands of fans desperate to glimpse the child prince of Indian cricket in the flesh. Sooryavanshi is the hottest player in the world right now, a 15-year-old left-handed jaw-dropping genius with records spilling out of his pockets. But when it comes to red-ball cricket, the classic form of the game, he’s still – by any objective measure – not very good. Going into this final, Sooryavanshi’s first-class average is a shade above 23, rendering him statistically a less effective red-ball batter than Craig Overton. Here, in perfect batting conditions, he scores a brisk and brash 44 in a mammoth total of 708, before dancing down the pitch and getting stumped for eight in the second innings as East Zone chase the outright win. None of which really tells us anything conclusive. The numbers are largely subservient to the project, the hypothetical, the burning question with implications not just for Sooryavanshi, not just for India, but very possibly for cricket itself. At the moment, and for all the hype and heroics for Rajasthan Royals in the Indian Premier League, Sooryavanshi is nowhere near the India Test side. Only last week he was named in the Twenty20 squad to face Afghanistan, rather than the India A side who will play Australia in a multi-format series this month, which is where you logically would put a prodigious young batter whom you were grooming for Test cricket. All of which raises a fascinating paradox. Given his skillset, his upbringing, his 7.6m Instagram followers, the basic sense of declinism in many parts of the sport, could Sooryavanshi be the first player in history who needs Test cricket less than it needs him? Because, let’s face it, the kid is going to be a superstar whatever he chooses. This year he obliterated the record for the number of sixes in an IPL season. He’s hit the second and third fastest centuries in competition history. He smashed the first ball he ever faced from Jasprit Bumrah over the rope. He made his national team debut this summer. He strikes at 216 and hits 16% of good-length balls for six. He is – and we should keep repeating this, because it doesn’t remotely make sense – 15 years old. This is the biggest and most lucrative stage in the sport and whatever path he chooses to navigate, he is already on course to be one of the most celebrated and richly rewarded cricketers of all time. And so, does it ultimately matter if he plays a Test match? How important is it that he conquers the “supreme” form of the game, which at the moment appears to consist of Ollie Robinson jagging it back off a fifth-stump length in some overcast British city? And, just as pertinently, what should we want to happen? Should we want him to struggle or succeed? Is the idea of willing Sooryavanshi into Test cricket the sporting equivalent of making a Kardashian read Beowulf, like making ChatGPT tell a joke: extrinsically satisfying but basically content, pub fodder, a celebrity stunt? If this sounds extreme, then Sooryavanshi is about as extreme a batter as Test cricket is ever likely to encounter. This is a technique not simply adapted for short-form cricket but steeped in it, built entirely around the mechanics of hitting hard and high. His trigger movement takes the front foot out towards mid-on, clearing the leg for a big swipe. The torso leans towards off, the eyes are unlevel. At the point of impact virtually all the weight is on the back leg, which is pretty much the opposite of what any classical textbook will tell you. Consequently, there is almost no attempt to keep the ball down. The hands are fast, flowing and brilliant. It may or may not surprise you to know that Sooryavanshi’s batting hero is Brian Lara. Then there are the intangibles of stamina and patience, management of the game and management of conditions. In his entire professional career Sooryavanshi has never batted for longer than 90 balls, never been out there for longer than a couple of hours, never really faced a spell that had to be survived or ground out. As his former coach Manish Kumar Ojha once told Cricinfo: “As long as he trained, I’ve never seen him train defence.” Sooryavanshi, a player with every shot in the book, could block the ball if he wanted to. By the same token, against Lucknow in this season’s IPL, he said that the wild swipe that dismissed him was a result of having faced five dot balls and not being able to bear playing out a maiden over. At this point many of you are probably salivating at the prospect of putting him up against Mitchell Starc at a baying Gabba, or making him bat out an entire day for a draw with the ball turning square out of the rough and five men around the bat. I want to see this happen. You want to see this happen. But at the same time it’s probably also worth turning the question around. What if Sooryavanshi’s game – which has already to a large extent reimagined the art of white-ball batting – manages to reimagine Test batting too? What if he generates a new orthodoxy: to go aerial, trust the eye, hit everything, don’t defend ever? If Test cricket ends up being decrypted by the kid with a native T20 game, then in the end what was the point of Test cricket? Obtaining the unknowable answers to these questions will rely a little on economics and a little on politics. To the extent that a 15-year-old in a machine can express any kind of autonomous thought, Sooryavanshi has expressed a wish to play Test cricket one day. But then so did Nicholas Pooran, who ended up retiring from West Indies at 29 with zero Tests to his name. Everyone knows this is what you are supposed to want. But wanting it and making it happen are two very different things. A tentative prediction: market forces and basic animal curiosity will dictate that Sooryavanshi plays a Test match sooner rather than later. Pretty much everyone, with the possible exception of a few Rajasthan ultras, wants this to happen. As for what transpires when it does: well, this is the caprice and fascination of cricket. Every series, every Test, every ball, is a new adventure. From which a second prediction emerges: if Sooryavanshi ever comes into contact with Test cricket, neither will emerge unscathed from the experience.

headline: Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable
trail_text: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
body_text: Google’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse. The Pixel 11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year. Being smaller doesn’t make it cheap. The 11 Pro sits above the regular £879 Pixel 11 and costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) – £80 (€100/$100/A$150) more than last year, with double the storage but less memory owing to the cost of RAMageddon. Little has changed on the outside for the Pro Pixels in several years. The new model is 0.1mm smaller in all directions and 3g lighter but has the same size 6.3in OLED screen, same polished aluminium and glass body and a large camera bar sticking out the back. It is an attractive design that has aged well. The temperature sensor from previous Pixel Pro generations, which always felt like a gimmick, has been replaced by a coloured HiLight LED that works as a camera flash and notification light. The LED glows when you talk to Gemini or pulses with one of five colours when your favourite contact calls. But it doesn’t work for notifications of any other kind, so is a wasted opportunity. The 11 Pro has the same Tensor G6 chip as the regular Pixel 11 and has 12 or 16GB of RAM depending on the storage version. It can’t match the raw performance of the top Qualcomm or Apple chips for games but is snappy in day-to-day tasks. Battery life is just shy of two days with the screen actively used for about seven hours across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging apps and photos. This is a bit behind the regular Pixel 11 but should see out even the heaviest of use days with some left in the tank. Most people will need to charge the 11 Pro every other day for general use. Specifications Screen: 6.3in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (495ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12 or 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfie Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes) Dimensions: 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mm Weight: 204g Quality Android 17 experience and AI The 11 Pro runs the same Google version of Android 17 as the regular Pixel 11 and will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest-lasting devices available. It’s a polished experience with smooth animations, nice touches of haptic feedback across the system and enough customisation to make it yours. But as with other Pixel devices, the phone is a showcase for Google’s most advanced AI tools that are littered throughout the software. The 11 Pro comes with six months of Google AI Pro subscription, which gives you access to Gemini Omni to generate surprisingly good eight-second videos, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium. But the most interesting tools are the local AI ones, including the new Rambler voice dictation feature in Gboard, which produces fully formed succinct sentences and paragraphs from your ramblings, removing unnecessary pauses, ums, ers and deviations. Gemini’s proactive assistance has also improved with more time-saving suggestions, although it only works in certain apps and not WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps. Camera The reason you buy a Pixel Pro is for the camera. The 11 Pro has a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front and a similar winning triple camera system on the rear from last year: a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and a 48MP 5x telephoto camera. All three cameras capture really fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions with very little effort. The wide and telephoto cameras now capture more light and slightly better detail, but the biggest boost is the new Instant Night Sight. It dramatically speeds up low-light photos by up to 4.5 times, which makes taking great shots in very dark scenes a lot easier. The 5x telephoto camera manages a very good 10x crop zoom before stretching up to 120x magnification, first with a very good traditional digital zoom to 30x then using local generative AI to go beyond. The camera keeps the regular digital zoom image and the one processed by AI to add back lost detail, which can be remarkable or filled with artefacts. Magic Capture takes video and photos automatically with just one button for point-and-shoot recording, which works well for events such as a birthday party. But Camera Looks is the most interesting feature for getting creative with photography. It allows you to modify how the camera processes your photos, starting with subtle changes such as darker shadows and ranging to more distinctive looks such as “minimal”, which reduces the computational photography processing for a more raw photo. Other options include “digi”, which replicates the look of old digital cameras that have become popular, and “velvet”, which mimics the look of some film cameras. Each look can be further customised, allowing great creative licence. The Pixel shoots great video with lots of stabilisation and processing tools including the new “Creator Suite”, which captures clips straight into a folder for storyboarding and trimming, with a teleprompter, framing for social media and speed enhancement. Sustainability The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair with manuals and parts available. The Pixel 11 Pro contains 31% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free. Price The Google Pixel 11 Pro costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) in a choice of four colours. For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799, the Pixel 10a costs £499, the Samsung Galaxy S26 costs £879, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,279 and the Apple iPhone 17 Pro costs £1,099. Verdict The Pixel 11 Pro is a refinement of multiple generations of Google’s Pro phones rather than an outright revolution, but that’s no bad thing. It is one of the very best smaller phones, packing all the top-end hardware, cameras and AI features of Google’s most biggest and expensive model into a slightly cheaper and more pocketable form. You buy a Pro Pixel for the camera, which doesn’t disappoint with arguably the best photography on a phone at the moment. The ability to customise the processing of your photos goes far beyond rivals for interesting creative potential. The dramatically faster Night Sight is also a significant improvement. Gemini’s proactive tools show great potential but depend on using the right apps. The supercharged Rambler voice dictation system is fantastic, and there are many other little AI tools that are useful from time to time. With just shy of two days battery life, a decent chip and quality software, the Pixel 11 Pro is a great pocketable phone. It just isn’t a massive upgrade on the already excellent Pixel 11 or recent Pixel Pro models. Pros: great camera with extended zoom and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, excellent screen, impressive dictation and local AI features, Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, good battery life, great size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included. Cons: quite expensive, less memory on cheapest model than before, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.

headline: First Thing: Trump makes highly unusual promise of $5,000 for all if Republicans win midterms
trail_text: Speaking in Dallas, the president raised ethical concerns with an apparent $1tn offer to the electorate
body_text: Good morning. Donald Trump has pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. Trump made the promise during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he assailed Democrats as “radical”, defended his unpopular war in Iran, and urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. Why did the Republicans hold a midterm convention? Republicans are gambling that the GOP’s first midterm convention can salvage their threatened House majority. However, Trump’s dismal approval rating drove many competitive candidates to skip the two-day event entirely. What has Trump said about the former attorney Michael Cohen? The US president has said he would consider pardoning Michael Cohen, the former fixer whom he once branded a “rat” for testifying against him. Cohen was Trump’s personal lawyer, but flipped in 2018, and pleaded guilty to federal crimes including facilitating a hush payment to the pornography star Stormy Daniels and lying under oath to Congress. Rubio says US will work with allies to stop drug-trafficking as three killed in latest boat strike The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration was focused on working with allied countries and aligning with their laws but insisted the military would “still blow up ships if need be”. The statement comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters. “I think it’s an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito. “The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended”. How many people has the US killed in its campaign? Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes. What has the US announced about Ecuador’s gangs? The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang as a terrorist organisation. Rubio said the gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists. “We are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said. Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo … and its new CEO Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since its 2007 introduction. The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens, and when opened, is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. While competitors have been releasing foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for Apple, and its rollout serves as the first big test for its new CEO, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook last week. The phone will be available on 23 October. What did new CEO Ternus say about his role? Helming the company’s annual showcase for the first time, Ternus said: “I want to take a moment to express what an extraordinary privilege it is to represent the remarkable teams here at Apple. I continue to be inspired every single day by the curiosity, invention and relentless pursuit of excellence that define Apple.” Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030 Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest. Jacob Coxon accused Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, of ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat. He said: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” Lawmakers including Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders have raised concerns following Coxon’s words. In other news … North Korea has built a new uranium facility to expand its nuclear arsenal, a UN agency has said. Hawaii’s western islands saw significant damage as Hurricane Lowell passed by leaving widespread power outages on Kauai. A large-scale ⁠search and rescue operation is under way in the Philippines after a passenger ferry caught fire, killing five people and leaving ⁠scores of passengers missing. Instagram’s boss has claimed users will be “overwhelmed” with brand content in an algorithm-free world, after Australia’s government announced plans to give people an opt-out. The ultrarunner Megan Eckert has shattered both the US men’s and women’s records by running 636 miles in six days. Stat of the day: Tens of millions of people fail to get humanitarian aid as global system crumbles With aid contributions cut by 30% between 2022 and 2025, the humanitarian system has suffered one of its biggest contractions since being formed in the post-second world war era, according to the State of the Humanitarian System 2026 report. The Filter recommends: Toys and activities to keep your dog engaged, happy and healthy From indoor scent training to the longest-lasting slow feeders, these are experts’ top recommendations for keeping dogs fulfilled. Don’t miss this: Trump’s top six falsehoods about 9/11 As the 25th anniversary of that dreadful day approaches, Chris Stein reminds us of the president’s habit of stretching the truth about 9/11. Rather more seriously, our international security correspondent, Jason Burke, writes that experts are sounding the alarm over “complacency” in current US counter-terror efforts. … or this: Meet the Americans moving to Scotland Since Trump’s re-election in 2024, there has been a 63% rise in Americans renting properties in Scotland. Politics is one reason – but there are many other surprising motivations, as Anita Chaudhuri discovers.
