headline: We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down
trail_text: What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality
body_text: On Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, warning that “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.” As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time. Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible. The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quickly find serious holes in even the most secured systems on the planet, including the NSA’s software. OpenAI quickly followed with an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, which broke out of their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face. And a separate rogue agent swarm gained administrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets. Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systems surpass us at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation. There are growing calls to change that, by creating mandatory incident reporting and third-party auditing, liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like? Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casar announced a bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence. This is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own. This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has written, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in its charter as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built? Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed. At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. The OpenAI executive Dean Ball explains: “Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.” Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.” We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon. After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agents broke their way out of their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader and successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks. Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack. This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reuters reported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.” The site’s logs indicate OpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers that uncovered this swarm said that there had been more discoveries since. And last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest ever leaps in benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantly harder to monitor because it can do more reasoning without verbalizing it. The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institute found would also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is also better at figuring out when it is being tested, which researchers have long warned breaks the main way safety is evaluated. Sam Altman soberly warns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it. Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing to render us obsolete. That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientists synthesized the first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institute found that AIs were more persuasive than even human experts. On Tuesday, amid a dispute over credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAI announced “an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russia reportedly used a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first. What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How? The bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts will tell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies. And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too. The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored using verification techniques that don’t assume any good will. One quick and dirty idea would be to embed auditors within frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement. This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said of advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley. And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity. Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, 29 September)

headline: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member
trail_text: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
body_text: OpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity. Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser, said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.” Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation. He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models. This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face. Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy, claimed on Tuesday there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade. Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields. Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic researcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”. Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction. “The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”. But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.” Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.” Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week. Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, from Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders in the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”. Meanwhile, Anthropic has admitted a new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR. Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”. Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database. The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach to pacing frontier AI development.”

headline: I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?
trail_text: Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an ad
body_text: I have a confession. I love my social media algorithm. It is a perfectly curated window into my insane and inquiring mind. It knows precisely which videos will tickle me and which memes will gently distract me from the slow collapse of humankind. On Tuesday the Australian government announced “world-leading” reforms that would force social media platforms to allow users to opt-out of algorithms, dubbed “my feed, my way”. On the same day, I was delighted to be confronted with a video on Instagram of a woman accidentally spilling a bucket of eels on a Chinese train. Dozens of eels slithered among the passengers, who appeared not as surprised as I would have expected. In bed that night, after sending the video to several friends and watching it multiple times, I lamented to my partner how I would find content like this if my accounts weren’t at the whim of the algorithm gods. “You can still search for eels,” he said. But would it be the same? So, for 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed. This feature – accessed simply by tapping on the Instagram logo at the top of the home screen – allows you to limit your feed to posts from accounts you are following, in chronological order. This is basically what social media feeds, including Facebook, looked like when they started. Would I be thrust back into the old days of social media, to how things were before artificial intelligence and Elon Musk bought Twitter and everything became an ad? As a reminder of how things used to be, I scroll back to my first posts on Instagram and find sepia-heavy pictures of trees, gigs and friends. “The SKY,” says one, simply showing a sunset. I am gripped with nostalgia for 2012, when all my posts got eight likes and no comments and I only followed two dozen close friends from school. For a truly “authentic” social media experience, I trawl through my contacts and unfollow any account that isn’t a person I have met in real life. It is refreshing to unfollow news accounts, and politicians, but sad to let go of funny influencers and meme accounts and chefs. “Goodbye, Ottolenghi,” I think wistfully. “Farewell, woman from Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders.” In total, about 100 accounts get the axe. I refresh my feed, and it only takes about 10 minutes of scrolling to run out of content to look at. For the first time in years, Instagram informs me I have reached the “End of following”. “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days,” it says. I am floored and unmoored. Each time I refresh my feed for the next few hours, there is nothing new for me to mindlessly scroll. Instinctively, I keep clicking on the app but it’s futile. Is this how social media used to be? A tool to communicate with people rather than a way to remain constantly distracted? What disturbs me, though, scrolling through a feed that should theoretically be made up of friends and family updating me about nice moments in their lives, is that it still feels hollow and impersonal. Mostly, people are using it for self-promotion, whether it be posting about something they’ve published, projects they’ve done, brand partnerships or attempts to “go viral”. The only ones who seem to be using social media as it used to be are my mum and her friends, who still upload happy snaps with abandon. This is soothing but also very boring. And do I really need to know or care that someone I met backpacking in 2015 is appearing at an art festival in Amsterdam? During my lunch break, instead of hitting the apps, I read my book and look at my surroundings. It’s nice. Maybe the solution is not to opt out of algorithms but to opt out of social media altogether. The justification for turning off algorithm-driven content makes sense. The federal government and many experts have raised concerns about how dangerous and divisive content can be pushed into people’s feeds, drawing them further and further into rabbit holes. I have watched on with concern as figures from the “manosphere” gain traction across the world alongside the rise of far-right parties, and how thinness appears to be the new norm in Hollywood, with eating disorder content proliferating on X, TikTok and Instagram. Thankfully, this has not been my social media experience. According to Instagram’s AI summary of my algorithm, a little-known feature of the app, I enjoy “community events” and “saving furry friends”, with a particular penchant for content related to the “Sydney food scene” and, somewhat vaguely, “Australia” (click on the reels icon and then the double-heart symbol in the top-right corner to see yours). My “For You” page is a haphazard collection of animals, food and gossip about reality TV. The top posts are an old man who summarises the latest episodes of Below Deck Mediterranean, a dachshund being pet with a spatula and someone making a cake with the face of Edward Cullen. It knows me so well! But is this healthy? Do I really need to spend my time watching AI-generated dogs dancing in the shower, or marvelling at a man attempting to eat an extremely gigantic cone of soft-serve ice-cream? After 24 hours switching off, my conclusion? It’s numbing my brain and turning my own thoughts into slop.

headline: Florida sues Netflix over misleading parents over minors’ data collection
trail_text: Lawsuit brought by James Uthmeier, the attorney general, marks latest action by the state against big tech companies
body_text: Florida officials filed a lawsuit against Netflix, accusing the streaming giant of misleading parents about its collection of minors’ data and using features that encourage children to “binge watch” content. The lawsuit, filed on Wednesday and led by James Uthmeier, the Republican Florida attorney general, marks the latest action by Florida against major technology companies. The red-leaning state has taken an increasingly aggressive approach toward big tech, particularly during the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). “Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape big tech surveillance. That was false,” Uthmeier said in a statement. “Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build. “Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable,” he added. In a statement shared with the Guardian, a spokesperson for Netflix said: “Netflix takes our members’ privacy seriously. We comply with privacy and data‑protection laws everywhere we operate and have dedicated safeguards in place for kids who watch content on Netflix. This lawsuit lacks merit and we intend to vigorously defend the matter in court.” In the 66-page lawsuit, Florida accuses Netflix of carrying out a “years-long bait-and-switch” that has “led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts”. The lawsuit claims Netflix opened Floridians’ data to commercial data brokers and advertising platforms after it launched advertisements in November 2022, allegedly allowing advertisers to “target Floridians by life stage, income, and household composition”. The complaint says Netflix failed to obtain the consent required under Florida law. It emphasizes that Netflix has in the past made a point to distinguish itself from tech companies that offer “free” services in exchange for data collection such as Google, Facebook and Amazon, but claims that Netflix has failed to live up to its promises to not track and monetize data similar to other tech companies. Netflix provides members with its updated privacy statement and terms of use annually, according to the streaming service. Those terms lay out the company’s advertising and privacy practices, along with users’ rights and available controls. It also offers parental controls that allow parents to filter or block content. The Florida case follows a lawsuit filed earlier this year by Texas officials accusing Netflix of spying on children and designing its platform to be addictive. Uthmeier has also filed lawsuits against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and TikTok this year. He recently kept Florida out of a multi-state settlement involving Meta, saying the $17bn agreement was “not enough to punish” the company over allegations that it failed to protect minor users. “We’re going to send a message to big tech companies. If you hurt our kids, you are going to have to pay for it,” Uthmeier said while announcing the Netflix lawsuit on Wednesday. “And so, in this lawsuit, we will be seeking billions of damages.”

headline: Gavin Newsom imposes strict new rules on AI, social media and chatbots for children
trail_text: California governor hails ‘nation-leading’ legislation banning addictive features for users under 16
body_text: California has adopted what Gavin Newsom described as “nation-leading” legislation that bans addictive social media features for young users, regulates companion chatbots and implements new safeguards around AI. The laws, signed by the Democratic California governor on Thursday, include AB 1709, which bars social media companies from using infinite scroll and autoplay for users under 16. “This is about actually addressing the problem, the scrolling, the algorithms. This is about addressing the substantive issue around the engineering,” Newsom said at a news conference in front of the Golden Gate Bridge. “And that’s what makes this truly a significant and consequential bill.” The development comes as states across the US seek to regulate AI companies and increase guardrails to protect young users from the risk of harm from social media platforms. Similar action is being taken around the globe. Australia became the first country to ban social media for children under 16 last year. The country also recently moved to allow social media users to opt out of algorithm-driven content. Since Australia’s landmark ban, more than 40 countries are considering or have implemented similar policies. Under California’s new package of laws, social media companies found to have harmed children with their platforms could face fines up to $1m per child. The laws also allow families to opt out of receiving school-issued laptops, and requires AI chatbot operators to conduct risk assessments before introducing them. The state now has the “strongest companion chatbot regulations” in the US, according to the governor’s office, and requires parental controls and crisis protocols. The chatbot bill is named for Adam Raine, who died by suicide last year – his mother has said he was “coached” by a chatbot. “Adam was an early adopter of AI, and so many of us parents did not understand the dangers back then,” Maria Raine said during Thursday’s news conference. “Now, we are all becoming more aware of the dangers of AI companionship and the need for our government to act to protect our children.” The new regulations also update child sexual exploitation laws to include “digitally altered and AI-generated” sexual imagery of minors. The package of new legislation is not without critics. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EEF), a non-profit focused on digital privacy and free speech, argues that AB 1709 is a “functional ban on social media use” for users under 16. “California should be passing laws to ensure that technology really works for people of all ages, not enacting social media bans that cut young people off from digital lifelines, communities and speech,” Rindala Alajaji, the EFF associate director of state affairs, said in a statement. “Denying minors access to digital forums – or stripping out basic tools needed to navigate them – is not going to help make young people safer or healthier in the AI age.” Earlier this week, Newsom signed Anthropic-backed laws regulating AI by requiring the state to create a framework for independent organizations to assess AI models’ safety risks, and a registry of AI auditors. The new regulations come weeks after Meta agreed to a settlement with California and 28 other states that accused the company of harming children with its products. The tech giant agreed pay up to $18bn and establish safeguards for teen users, such as daily usage limits and blocks on night-time use. The Associated Press contributed reporting

headline: San Francisco mayor declares rent emergency as housing costs soar amid AI boom
trail_text: Median rent for one-bedroom apartment in city tops $4,495 with a national median of $1,900
body_text: San Francisco’s mayor, Daniel Lurie, declared a rent emergency on Thursday, proposing reforms aimed at curbing evictions and preventing rent spikes as the city grapples with soaring apartment prices. The Bay Area city, home to a large number of high-earning tech workers, has long been one of the most expensive housing and rental markets in the country. The median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in San Francisco is currently $4,495, according to Zumper, a rental listings site. In comparison, the national median for a one-bedroom apartment is $1,900. The ballooning rental costs have been attributed to a recent influx of wealth in the market, as artificial intelligence companies began to go public on the stock market. While demand has ratcheted up for limited housing options, San Francisco has notoriously lagged behind other cities in approving new housing. Among Lurie’s proposed measures are caps to rent increases for rent-controlled apartments, $27m in funding to cover funding lapses from federal housing vouchers set to expire and an increase in payments to tenants who are evicted under the Ellis Act, legislation landlords can evoke when leaving the rental business. “Today, most San Franciscans feel our city is finally moving in the right direction, but many are also asking whether they can still afford to live here,” Lurie said in a statement on Thursday. “We have lived through booms before – this time, we have an opportunity to build a recovery that is broad-based and lasting, where San Franciscans can put down roots and participate in our city’s success.”

headline: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils but Musk dismisses ‘psyop’
trail_text: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction, while others are calling their declarations of concern a ‘setup’
body_text: A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings. In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”. The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but have not said so publicly. These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”. Anna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said on Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models. “There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X. Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks. “Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said. Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” he wrote. Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.” In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said. Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI. “I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.” Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservative thinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice. Bill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying, “Interesting.” Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it was time to boycott AI, but because it was already causing harm. More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”. The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.

headline: Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons
trail_text: The 154-page report comes two days after former employee Jacob Coxon resigned due to Anthropic racing to improve its models that would cause human extinction by 2030
body_text: Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday. “The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.” In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work. “Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.” Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent. Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions. In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms. Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropic told the New York Times this case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute. The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, set off a media firestorm with his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him. Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, are far more concerning within the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence. “AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly. In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations. The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses. “As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.

headline: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’
trail_text: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise
body_text: Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May. As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give every US adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend” after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances. Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again. That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs. The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade. Steve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed. “The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said. Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Evidence of this was clear on the ASX this week, where the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was on track to end the week down 3% and below the level it was this time last year. But Hui said ongoing optimism about the state of the global economy and, especially, the titanic boom in artificial intelligence investment was providing a tailwind for sharemarkets around the world, and especially on Wall Street. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at the end of February, the US benchmark S&P 500 sharemarket index is up about 10%, against a 5% fall for the ASX 200. But the Hong Kong-based Hui said the increasingly debated question among investors was at what point the steady march higher in yields begins to drive a broader and deeper switch out of stocks and into bonds. “We are approaching a crossroad,” he said. As economists warned of a new post-Covid era of structurally higher interest rates, financial markets upped their bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia would deliver a fourth rate hike on 29 September, pricing in an 80% chance. Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said the RBA would have to respond to recent evidence that inflationary pressures were not easing as hoped, even as the economy proved resilient. “I think they [the RBA] will go in September,” Kearns said. The former top RBA official said the central bank’s inflation-fighting credentials were increasingly at stake. “They need to get inflation to 2.5%, and that’s not forecast to happen until early 2028; that then becomes almost a seven-year inflationary episode.” The prospect of higher mortgage costs comes as Vivek Dhar, CBA’s head of commodities research, warned that diesel prices could climb by 10-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, from over $2.50 per litre today. Unleaded petrol prices could push from about $2.10 a litre in major east coast cities to about $2.30 over the next couple of weeks, according to a rough rule of thumb that says every US$1 increase in the crude oil benchmark translates to a 10c increase at the pump. Dhar, who is based in Singapore, said meetings with energy producers and traders on the sidelines of a major energy conference over recent days revealed a deep sense of uncertainty about how the next six to 12 months will play out. Dhar said he expected Brent crude to swing between US$70 and US$100 a barrel for the foreseeable future, until eventually the world becomes comfortable with the supply workarounds to a restricted strait of Hormuz. But the more pressing worries were around the supply of refined products, particularly diesel. “Everyone pays attention to oil, but it’s the refined product that hits the economy and feeds through to inflation. And that is what everyone is worried about, because there isn’t any workaround; we just need disruptions to stop.”

headline: One flight cancelled every three days due to staff shortages – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s a wrap on another eventful week in the news cycle. Before we let you go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines: Anthony Albanese has marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US. Ten Australians were among 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania – “lives tragically cut short far from home”. The saga surrounding the One Nation cartoon labelling Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie a “traitor” continues as Pauline Hanson doubled down despite growing condemnation from all sides of parliament. Hastie said Barnaby Joyce had reached out to him with an explanation and apology, which he accepted. The Victoria premier, Ben Carroll, joined in on the hype around the NFL game at the MCG this morning, calling it an exciting and historic day for the state. Australia’s domestic spy agency said it has foiled 16 terrorist threats in the nine months since the Bondi attack, including an antisemitic attack. Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing. That’s for sticking around, have a lovely weekend! Roxanne Tickle welcomes rejection of Giggle’s appeal in landmark transgender discrimination case The transgender woman at the centre of a successful discrimination case has welcomed the High Court’s rejection of an attempted appeal. The High Court refused, with costs, an appeal by the women-only app Giggle against a Full Federal Court ruling in May. The ruling upheld a landmark decision that the app and its founder, Sall Grover, unlawfully discriminated against Roxanne Tickle after she was denied access to the platform. In a statement, Tickle said: It’s been nearly 5 years since I lodged my discrimination complaint. It’s been a relentlessly exhausting time, both physically and emotionally, for me and many others. I hope that yesterday’s High Court special leave refusal provides clarity to the protections in law for transgender and gender diverse people in Australia, and perhaps provides a beacon of light to the rest of the world. I wish my trans and gender diverse siblings, as well as their loved ones, much hope and love for their collective futures. May we all learn that just being different is not grounds for you to be ridiculed, attacked, feared or hated, but that instead you are providing a little something extra to the world. Life is not easy. Let’s all be kinder to each other and we might all enjoy it a little more. Read the full story here: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson is being kept in near constant isolation, leaving her frightened and at risk of psychological decline, AAP reports. A prisoner rights group is advocating on the triple murderer’s behalf for her to receive peer counselling to improve her mental wellbeing at no cost to the state. Patterson’s current conditions at the Dame Phyllis Frost centre, west of Melbourne, involve being confined to a cell for a minimum of 22 hours a day and having approved contact with just one other prisoner through a wire mesh during limited yard time. Advocacy group Justice Action has called the treatment tantamount to torture, invoking United Nations rules named after Nelson Mandela which say a person should not spend more that 15 consecutive days in solitary confinement. The group is yet to be allowed direct contact with Patterson, but says information from other prisoners in the same unit suggests she is in a poor mental state. Justice Action co-ordinator Brett Collins, who is a former inmate, said Patterson was entitled to be treated like any other prisoner and to serve her time constructively. He told AAP on Friday: She’s a frightened woman, understandably so. She’s actually been now isolated for such a long time, and she’s already had those disorders before she before she was convicted, so now we’ve heard she’s unused to people being around her. That’s the sort of behaviour that causes causes permanent damages. It’s torture, actually. Justice Action is proposing Patterson be permitted a trained peer support mentor to help address and mitigate the psychiatric risks, which it would offer at no cost to taxpayers. Major fire breaks out at building in Sydney’s north-west Authorities are investigating the cause of a major building fire in Sydney’s north-west. Emergency services responded to reports of the blaze on Loftus Street in Riverstone at around 1.35pm. Fire and Rescue NSW said about 40 firefighters and 12 trucks remained at the scene. The fire has since been contained to the building where it started. Four people were assessed at the scene, but none were taken to hospital. Fire and Rescue NSW said the cause of the fire was under investigation. Hello! I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of afternoon’s news. That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take the blog from here. Take care! An Australian Taxation Office employee has been charged with corruption-related offences by the AFP and other groups on allegations the man disclosed information obtained in his work to organised crime associates. The AFP said today the Gold Coast man, 32, had been charged overnight with two counts of unlawfully disclosing information by a commonwealth officer. The offence carries a maximum penalty of two years in prison. He is due in court later this month. After a search warrant was carried out, the man was also charged with two counts of possession or control of child abuse material and 15 counts of using a carriage service for child abuse material. The maximum penalty for both offences is 15 years in prison. Queensland’s credit rating downgraded for the first time in 17 years Queensland has been dealt the first downgrade to its credit rating in 17 years, heaping more borrowing costs on to the state’s budget, AAP reports. Credit agency S&P Global slapped a stable outlook on Queensland’s downgraded AA rating. The loss of Queensland’s AA+ rating came on the same day NSW received an upgrade to its credit outlook. Queensland’s budget performance would remain “very weak” over the next two to three years compared to peers with a similar rating, S&P said on Friday. The state’s historically large infrastructure program ahead of the 2032 Olympics and forecast deficits contrasted with previous expectations for sound surpluses from 2028, it said in a report. The state could also expect lower stamp duty revenues after property tax changes in the federal budget exacerbated a deepening housing downturn, S&P said. Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing. The government agency’s deputy CEO, Peter Curran, said Australia’s airports recorded 2,536 cancellations over the year to 31 August, of which 121 were attributed to Airservices. Sydney accounted for 103 of those. Just this morning, the troubled airport recorded 14 inbound cancellations and more outbound cancellations, after some overnight staff were unavailable, Curran said. Airservices and airlines manage the shortage by delaying or cancelling flights. Curran said Sydney had grown and now needed a team of 41 air traffic controllers, spread across the roster. It has 49 employed but eight are unavailable at the moment. Curran said: When we have a bit of short-term sickness or unavailability, like we had last night, it makes it very difficult to recover. Curran said retired staff had been asked to come back to work but some of them were “simply not interested”. He said there were about 1,100 air traffic controllers working across Australia and 91 would join in the coming year. With more recruitment, Curran said Airservices would be able to enough on-call staff to cover two absences a day by March 2027. It’s not an ironclad model, but it certainly reduces the likelihood of the sorts of issues that we’re having today. 49ers rout Rams 27-7 in NFL clash at the MCG Mike Evans, Demarcus Robinson and Deebo Samuel caught touchdown passes from quarterback Brock Purdy, and the San Francisco 49ers routed the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 Friday in the first NFL regular-season game in Australia. Purdy passed for 205 yards against the Rams’ ineffective defense at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in front of 100,021 fans, the seventh-largest regular season crowd in NFL history. Australia’s sporting capital reveled in its first real taste of American football – and in a dominant win by the 49ers, who had already won many Aussies’ affection by travelling to Melbourne a week earlier than the Rams, who only boomeranged in on Thursday morning. Read more here: NFL stars, cheerleaders and the Jonas Brothers as American football comes to Melbourne About 100,000 fans filled the MCG for the historic NFL regular-season clash between the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne. Die-hard supporters and interested spectators came from all corners to see American football’s cultural exchange, which included cheerleaders before the match and a Jonas Brothers show at half-time. Take a look at some below: The Australian share market is barreling toward its worst week since the US-Iran war began, as surging oil prices pressure bond yields and squeeze central banks to hike borrowing costs. The benchmark S&P/ASX200 index fell 112.2 points by midday on Friday, to be down 1.27% as the broader All Ordinaries tumbled 120 points, or 1.33%. The top-200 is on track for a 3.2% slump since Monday and its worst week since early March’s 3.8% plunge, when US-led strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader and triggered a broader regional conflict. The Australian dollar was buying 71.56 US cents, down from 72.16 US cents on Thursday at 5pm. Sarah Hanson-Young on big tech’s ‘attack on democracy’ – Australian Politics podcast This week, the Albanese government released its draft digital duty of care legislation and announced reforms to allow social media users to opt out of algorithms. The Coalition has ruled out their support, so the Greens will be crucial to the changes passing the Senate. Political editor Tom McIlroy speaks to the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young about why she thinks this will be a “battle for our generation”. Listen here: Molly Ticehurst’s killer Daniel Billings sentenced to 28 years in jail for murder Molly Ticehurst’s ex-boyfriend will spend at least 20 years inhas been sentenced to 28 years in jail for her senseless and brutal murder, which was revenge for her reporting allegations of sexual assault to police. Daniel Billings was sentenced in the Orange Supreme Court today by Justice Natalie Adams, who imposed a non-parole period of 20 years. Ticehurst, a 28-year-old childcare worker, was found dead in her pyjamas at her home at Forbes, in the state’s central west, in the early hours of 22 April 2024. Justice Natalie Adams found Billings’ offending was in the high range of seriousness, given he murdered her in the exact way he had long threatened to do. It must have been absolutely terrifying for Ms Ticehurst to die knowing her worst fears were realised. Read the full story: Australia’s domestic spy agency says it has disrupted 16 terrorist threats in the nine months since the Bondi attack, including an antisemitic attack, a plot to kill Muslims and a violent racist allegedly found with weapons and ammunition. The Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation’s director general, Mike Burgess, outlined the “evolving threat” in a speech today on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terror attacks on the United States. The Asio chief revealed his organisation had disrupted 16 terror plans since December where the “threat was considered serious but not necessarily imminent”. In June the figure was 14. Since 2014, it has foiled 33 major terrorism plots. Burgess said Sunni violent extremism represented the majority of Asio’s counter-terrorism caseload but that it was “too simplistic to assume there is a single terrorism threat or a most likely terrorist threat as we did in the aftermath of 9/11”. He said the threats included an individual allegedly inspired by extreme right-wing ideology, others inspired by extreme left-wing ideologies and others inspired by “mixed and seemingly incompatible beliefs”, including one person who allegedly wanted to blow up a school who was allegedly inspired by ideological and extreme Christian beliefs. Burgess said: These dynamics make the contemporary terrorism environment different – and in some ways, more difficult – than a quarter of a century ago ... Spikes in grievance, intolerance and polarisation are degrading our security environment and making politically motivated violence more likely. Matt Canavan ‘welcomes’ communication between Barnaby Joyce and Andrew Hastie Matt Canavan spoke to News24 earlier, saying he “welcomes” Barnaby Joyce reaching out to Andrew Hastie about the One Nation “traitor” cartoon. Canavan began by condemning One Nation’s bids to “distance” themselves from the cartoon, noting the video was authorised and published by the party. I thought that was pretty weak. The Nationals leader said he appreciated that Joyce had explained to Hastie that he didn’t know about the cartoon. I welcome Barnaby’s apology, it’s a matter for Andrew if he accepts it – but I think Pauline should do the same. (In a statement, Hastie said he did accept it, but characterised it as an “explanation” rather than an apology.) Canavan said he personally welcomed criticism but said that politicians did not need to “devolve” into this sort of language. The interview took somewhat of an odd turn when Cavanan also referred to himself as someone with “communist sympathies” in his youth. Albanese is under fire over a grants program that benefited his local golf club. Were any rules broken? Anthony Albanese is under fire after an invite-only grant program allocated millions to marginal Labor seats and his old local golf club. The government claims it has broken no rules and delivered its election promises by the standard method but transparency advocates have said the system needs reform and have drawn comparisons to the notorious “sports rorts” affair. What went wrong – and is this sports rorts all over again? Read more here: Marles says Hanson should take Hastie cartoon down and apologise Back to defence minister Richard Marles, who made some other comments this morning about the One Nation video. Speaking on Nine, Marles said the Australia’s veteran community would have been affected by the One Nation video’s use of the word “traitor”. One of the issues here is to use that word in respect of any veteran is taken on by the entire veterans community … it’s distasteful. It’s inappropriate. It should come down and Pauline Hanson should apologise. The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, is standing by the cartoon that labelled Andrew Hastie a “traitor” despite growing condemnation from Labor, the Greens, Liberals and the crossbench. The video is currently pinned to the top of Hanson’s X feed, and she said on Wednesday she would not apologise and the uproar was “a storm in a teacup as far as I’m concerned”. She has denied ever calling Hastie a traitor. Last night, Hanson posted a photo of Jacqui Lambie and herself in the Senate, alongside a post that read “I think everyone just needs to take a chill pill”. A furious Lambie told ABC radio yesterday that Hanson was a “bloody coward”. The One Nation leader posted again this morning on X to express her “thanks” to Hastie that the “cartoons make the news again”, sharing the “ten best episodes” of the animation Please Explain. As we reported earlier, Hastie told Guardian Australia he accepted Barnaby Joyce’s explanation that he didn’t know about the cartoon. He said he now knows that Hanson “is the only lying coward”. The Victoria premier, Ben Carroll, spruiked the NFL game at the MCG this morning, saying it was an exciting and historic day for the state. The atmosphere, the weather for Melbourne, everything has just come on so perfectly. I couldn’t be more excited to be part of this day. This event helps cement Victoria as the major events capital, not only of Australia, but of the world. It’s going to be one of those events that people look back in history and say, ‘Where were you?’ Or ‘I was there’. Woolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotion Woolworths raised prices for popular items – including a 33% mark up on chicken fillets – within days of promising to freeze prices on 300 “family staples” for three months to help customers with the cost of living. Pricing data, compiled by comparison website CW Scanner and provided to Guardian Australia, shows the supermarket chain increasing the prices of at least four key products after starting the three-month “Price Freeze” promotion on 1 May. The supermarket nearly doubled the price of a 420g can of Woolworths “Mexican Style 3 Bean Mix” during the promotional period – from 60c to $1 on 17 June – the data shows. Woolworths dropped the price back to 60c on 17 August Woolworths has justified the increases because it regarded the previous prices as promotional prices, rather than the “standard shelf price” for each product. A Woolworths spokesperson said that the end of a temporary promotion did not represent a shelf price increase. Read more: The NFL is set to hold its first regular-season game in Australia today, a contest between the San Francisco 49ers and the LA Rams. The showdown will take place at Melbourne’s MCG this morning. Fans have been turning up in droves. The game starts at 10.35am and you can watch it on Netflix. ‘Profound’ increase in death rate for welfare recipients, report finds People receiving an income support including disability, unemployment or carers payments had an average mortality rate more than nine times higher than people who did not access the welfare system, AAP reports. The report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare compared mortality rates and causes of death for people receiving and not receiving various income support payments by linking data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics and government systems. Of the 287,000 people aged 22 to 64 who died between 2012 and 2022, almost three in five received income support payments. The report showed the main cause of death for people on income support was cardiovascular disease but there were also higher rates of “deaths of despair” associated with alcohol, drugs and self-harm, University of Queensland social science research fellow Mark Robinson said. The findings point to the profound health inequities in Australia despite its comparatively strong health record. Bowen: ‘disappointing’ Greens crossed the floor to vote with One Nation on koala deal Chris Bowen said yesterday was a “good day” for the government after the Greens reached a deal with Labor that will allow big industry to use a new koala national park in New South Wales to offset its climate pollution. The climate change and energy minister told RN Breakfast this morning it was “disappointing that three Greens crossed the floor to vote with One Nation”. I think if One Nation and the Greens are voting together, the Greens are voting the wrong way on climate. … I’m very pleased that this passed the parliament. I’m very pleased that the Greens party room worked with me, the majority. This was a good day yesterday because it’s practical action. … [It’s] good for emissions, and also providing a route for investment and economic development in the regions where this logging has occurred and where now the economy can be diversified. Andrew Hastie says Barnaby Joyce had reached out about the One Nation cartoon that labelled him a “traitor”. Hastie had this to say to Guardian Australia this morning: Barnaby Joyce has reached out to me and explained that he didn’t know about the cartoon that called me a traitor eight times. I accept his explanation. I called him a lying coward because I thought he was protecting Pauline Hanson. I now know that she is the only lying coward. For context – Hastie told News24 the One Nation cartoon, first posted on social media over a month ago and now pinned to the top of Pauline Hanson’s X account, called him a traitor eight times. “I would say that Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce are lying cowards, and I’ll say it again, so there’s no ambiguity,” he said. Pauline Hanson has denied ever calling Hastie a traitor, telling the Nightly: “I will call him a wanker.” Joyce previously told Guardian Australia he has never called Hastie a traitor, “nor ventured anywhere close to any such narrative about him”. More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings. In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”. The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly. Read more here: Former prime minister John Howard, who was in Washington DC during the September 11 terror attacks, spoke to the ABC this morning about his experience 25 years ago. “It meant that the world would never be the same,” Howard told Radio National Breakfast. I just knew that it meant a lot to the whole world, and it certainly meant that I quickly came to realise just how important our association with the Americans was because this powerful country had been attacked in an atrocious, cruel manner. Howard said he believes it was “only right” Australia join the US in Afghanistan, and the White House was “very happy to have our help”. He said: I think we did the right thing. I was unhappy with aspects of the ultimate withdrawal from Afghanistan. It did look rather chaotic at the time … Overall, I don’t have any regrets. I think we did the right thing in going into Afghanistan. Former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who also spoke on RN this morning, said he agreed with Howard’s decision to join the allied forces in Afghanistan. “He got that right. What he got comprehensively wrong was Iraq.” Marles reflects on September 11 Marles reflected on September 11 this morning, saying it was a day “which we remember most as having changed the world in which we live”. He told the ABC this morning: I remember on that night watching West Wing, a number of people I have spoken to in the last few days were doing the same thing. When it finished, it cut into this extraordinary vision of smoke coming out of the North Tower. We weren’t really sure what was going on. Then astonishingly it looked as though we were witnessing a plane fly into the South Tower. What it then heralded was obviously a huge change in terms of wars in … Iraq and Afghanistan. More than 40,000 Australians served over the coming years in those, more than 40 lost their lives. Ten Australians lost their lives that day on September 11. We very much remember them. The defence minister, Richard Marles, said the One Nation cartoon labelling Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie a “traitor” is “tasteless” and should be taken down. Marles just spoke on ABC News Breakfast as many senior Liberals, independent Jacqui Lambie and RSL Australia condemned the cartoon. The defence minister said this morning: Andrew Hastie is definitely not a traitor. I know him well and I’ve said this publicly. I very much honour the service that Andrew Hastie has given to our country, wearing our nation’s uniform. I think to use that word in respect of a veteran is extremely tasteless. No one should be using that word in respect of any veteran and in respect of Andrew. Anthony Albanese has marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US. Ten Australians were among 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and in Pennsylvania – “lives tragically cut short far from home”. We acknowledge the grief carried by their loved ones. We also honour the courage and selflessness shown in the face of unimaginable horror. First responders ran towards danger to help others. Ordinary people reached for one another. In the worst of circumstances, we saw extraordinary acts of courage, compassion and humanity. The prime minister said the anniversary was also an opportunity to reflect on “resilience in the face of profound loss”. Australia remembers those whose lives were taken, those who survived, those we’ve lost since, and all those who continue to carry the weight of that day. Opal Healthcare refunds residents after review into misuse of aged care standards Opal Healthcare has refunded roughly $190,000 to almost 350 residents under a sweeping review into misuse of new aged care standards, AAP reports. The standards came into effect in November and were designed to give residents more say over what premium products they opted to pay for. Guidelines said services that were previously offered for free could not be charged, though they were not made law. Reports emerged months later of aged care providers wrongfully charging residents for basic amenities, including television and wifi services. In some cases, services were removed if they were not paid for. An investigation was launched by the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission after the aged care minister, Sam Rae, informed the regulator of claims against Opal Healthcare. He said at the time the removal of services such as air conditioning and televisions was unacceptable. Good morning Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live news coverage for Friday. Let’s begin.

headline: UK economy unexpectedly grows 0.4% in July boosted by AI
trail_text: Welcome boost for chancellor with unexpected rise put down to rapid growth of AI in services sector outweighing Iran war fallout
body_text: The UK economy grew in July as the rapid expansion of AI appeared to outweigh the economic damage from the Iran war, in a welcome boost for John Healey. Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product (GDP), compared with 0.3% growth in June. City economists had forecast zero growth. The figures suggested the economy continued to be robust despite the fallout from the Iran war, which has raised energy costs and led to higher interest rates than were expected at the start of the year. The ONS said the expansion in July was driven by growth of 0.4% in the services sector, particularly admin services, and computer programming and consulting. Within the latter sector, it said: “Many of the businesses reporting the largest turnover in July 2026 are involved in activities related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing.” Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “At a time when many traditional parts of the economy remain subdued, this is exactly the kind of productivity-enhancing spending the UK needs more of.” PWC’s chief economist, Barret Kupelian said: “Artificial intelligence continues to have imprints across the UK economy, with AI exposed sectors – professional services, information technology, administrative services – recording strong growth.” The ONS said industrial production was also up in July, by 0.2%, with a rise in manufacturing output offsetting falls in mining, and electricity and gas supply. Over the three months to July – a period the ONS says is more representative of economic conditions – GDP growth was also 0.4%, the same pace as in the three months to June. Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “The UK growth story is becoming harder to ignore. Households and businesses are still spending – despite the unfolding energy shock impacting disposable incomes.” The economy’s continued strength is good news for Healey, the chancellor, as he prepares for his first budget on 28 October, though experts have warned that the longer-term picture for the economy is less positive. Healey said: “Britain’s economy is demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty. Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year. But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home – from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing.” Economists fear the latest rise in the global oil price – to well above $100 a barrel – is likely to stoke higher inflation worldwide, prompting rising borrowing costs. Higher interest rates on the UK’s debt are expected to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom Healey’s predecessor had built up against the fiscal rules – potentially forcing him to increase taxes or cut spending at the budget. Since the recent jump in oil prices, markets have raised their expectations for future interest rates and now expect the Bank of England’s policymakers to make four quarter-point rises over the next twelve months. Rates are still expected to remain on hold, at 3.75%, when the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee meets next week, however, despite the stronger-than-expected growth figures. Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the accountancy body the ICAEW, said: “While these figures may strengthen the hawkish mood among rate-setters, a September rate rise still looks unlikely as most policymakers remain hopeful that a sluggish economy will ultimately help bring inflation under control, despite escalating US-Iran tensions.” As well as strong growth in AI-related sectors, the ONS highlighted the economic impact of the summer heat, and the World Cup, which culminated in mid-July. Its director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, said: “some businesses reported that the warm weather and Fifa World Cup had affected their activity, although effects differed across industries, benefiting some businesses while creating challenges for others.” The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith said: “Nobody in this Labour government should be high-fiving themselves. Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we’ve got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years.”

headline: Crossword editor’s desk: when a theme is literally a theme
trail_text: EastEnders hides in a Guardian crossword and Guardian crosswords hide in a thriller
body_text: One way to ensure a novel gets my attention is a foreword that mentions crosswords, specifically the Guardian’s. I admit that this does not happen often, but it has just happened. Tony White’s Phantom at the Feast opens with this claim: Words emboldened in the text of this novel are the solutions to successive Guardian ‘Quick Crosswords’ that appeared through sixty days in 1985 from 3 April to 1 June You can read more about it at Prospect magazine. Thanks for your responses to last month’s assurance that all of our crosswords are created by human beings, best summarised by Kazoom: Am glad you’ve posted this. The ‘created by AI’ comments, often supported by zero evidence, have become quite tedious to read. It’s OK to fail, or just not get into the groove on a particular day, but just accept that’s a you problem. And if you want more on artificial intelligence and puzzles, Gizmodo has given large language models some cryptics. Once solvers had got somewhere with Glyph’s Genius for August, it became evident that the preamble was demanding a SOAP OPERA THEME. Theme in more ways than one: The grid was also secretly a piece of sheet music! This month’s Genius is by Turnstone and awaits your attention. If you haven’t tried a Genius before, this could be your way in. And many thanks for your clues for EERIE. The audacity award is of course Wellywearer2’s for the brazen “Becoming cheerier, then sneerier, then leerier, when getting beerier? It’s time to find the weird commonality within!” The runners-up are Mr_Rob_T’s intriguing “Weird European TV show Naked” and 10FootClaudicant’s evocative “Sinister eyes raised oddly”. And the winner is the refreshing “Headless beer that is chilling”. Kludos to Batteredmullet; please leave clues for THEME below, along with any favourite clues or puzzles you have spotted. • Alan Connor is the Guardian’s crossword editor.
