headline: Reform’s Robert Jenrick ‘very confident’ £72m donations are ‘perfectly legal’ – as it happened
trail_text: Party’s economic spokesperson says donations are a ‘breakthrough moment’ as Labour’s Angela Rayner warns of possible retrospective action
body_text: We’ll draw the politics blog to a close for now. Here’s a recap of the donations row around Reform UK. Reform spokesman Robert Jenrick insisted that the two £36m-a-piece donations from British crypto-billionaires are “perfectly legal’ and “entirely in line with the law as it is and with the law in the future”. It comes amid speculation on the exact timing and circumstances of when investors Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo gave the money to the anti-immigration party, as both had been living outside of the UK at least until this year. The Labour government currently has a bill in parliament, aimed at stopping foreign influence in UK politics, that would limit donations from British expats who’ve been back in the country for less than a year. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner warned that those law would apply retrospectively – potentially applying to the Reform donations – and so if the funds fell afoul of the new law, the party would have to return the money. Rayner said the huge donations had put the spotlight on mega-wealthy individuals and “who is funding politics” in the UK. Some political commentators say Reform will be laughing all the way to the bank with these earth-shatteringly large endowments. They’ll have the money now to majorly expand their electoral machine: place candidates in every seat, hire campaign staff to manage the races, print the leaflets, rent the billboards, blanket Instagram and TikTok feeds etc. But my colleague Peter Walker also points out some downsides for Reform in his analysis linked below. What are the downsides to receiving £72 million? “The first is that every time Farage presents Reform as the voice of ordinary Britons, his opponents can argue it is in reality the plaything of people who are wealthy and disconnected from everyday life to a degree almost unimaginable to most voters. Delo and Harborne are strikingly similar: cryptocurrency billionaires who are either based overseas – Harborne in Thailand, although he is electorally registered in the UK – or formerly so – Delo recently returned to the UK from Hong Kong. “The second, and arguably bigger, concern for Reform is the renewed focus this places on Farage’s own finances, and the perceived cloud of sleaze which has in recent months become more dense around him and the party.” Speaking of the PM, should note that Andy Burnham this afternoon has just completed a half marathon- the Great North Run from Newcastle to South Shields – to raise funds for homeless charity Changing Lives. He donated 15% of his first month salary to the group and has pledged further monthly contributions. Ending rough sleeping has been a priority for Burnham who made it his first pledge upon entering office in July. Last month he also unveiled a national plan to get people off the streets by Christmas. The U.S. president on his visit to Ireland has just been asked about the UK PM’s response to his remarks that he would “love” to see a united Ireland. “I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump had told reporters on Saturday in Dublin while sitting next to the Irish PM. “Now the UK will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing,” he’d said. Burnham said weeks ago that a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the UK is “off the table”- a position reaffirmed by Downing Street yesterday. But just now, Trump said “Everybody says that. And then things happen.” “By the way, I’ve spoken to him. Think he’s a very nice guy, tends to be on the liberal side unfortunately.” Then he went on to say that he believed Burnham was going to be “drilling in the North Sea, that’s my impression.” Rayner was also asked earlier on the BBC about the surge in anti-migrant protests, including those yesterday in Portsmouth, Tamworth and Glasgow where face coverings were banned. Police brought in the restriction after the September 5-6 weekend where hundreds of masked, black-clad men blocked entry to the Port of Dover and obstructed roads in Portsmouth in menacing scenes. “We’ve been really clear that there is a right to protest in this country, but it doesn’t give you a right to intimidate and act unlawfully… We’ve seen a surge of divisiveness and that has made communities feel more vulnerable and that is not acceptable,” Rayner said. She also described scenes earlier this week at a Portsmouth hotel as “completely unacceptable”. On Tuesday night, roughly 40 masked men had gathered outside the hotel, shouting slogans and banging on doors in the mistaken belief that a Pakistani youth cricket team staying there were newly arrived asylum seekers. “That’s completely unacceptable. That’s intimidatory behaviour,” said Rayner. “And I would say, hundreds of people walking down the streets, all dressed in black, with black balaclavas on, is intimidatory and crosses the line.” At yesterday’s protests in Portsmouth police tried to keep apart the two groups of protesters, with marchers chanting “stop the boats” facing off with demonstrators holding “stop the far right” and “stand up to racism” signs. As warnings surrounding the threats of AI continue to make headlines this weekend my colleague Dan Milmo has written a less pessimistic piece on the topic in his feature from the AI bootcamps aimed at addressing UK youth unemployment. The UK government is trying to address two of the greatest challenges facing the national economy: AI and youth unemployment and a pilot project in Preston comes with apprenticeship offer for Neets at end of three-week course. You can read more on it here: Elsewhere today the former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit and that rejoining the European Union’s customs union would be the fastest route to recovery. You can read more on that here While talking to the media this morning Angela Rayner also admitted that there was only a slim chance government will meet target of building 1.5m home. Labour’s manifesto pledge to build 1.5m houses by the next election was a “stretch target”, the communities secretary added, but said it was not being ditched and she was “definitely not giving up”. My colleague Jessica Elgot has her reported in detail here: Angela Rayner said she was pleased AI companies are “talking about the threats as well as the opportunities” after Elon Musk and Sam Altman backed a call for the industry to slow down development, PA reports. It comes after Anthropic boss Dario Amodei said he was concerned that since this summer, AI has been “advancing drastically faster”. Given the rate of development, Mr Amodei is worried that within six to 12 months, AI could be capable of leading a swarm that could take over the entire internet. The entrepreneur, whose company is behind the AI assistant Claude, shared a three-part plan for building the technology at a “balanced rate”. Rayner told Sky News: “I’m pleased that these companies are also talking about the threats as well as the opportunities that AI presents to us, and we have to work with our international partners, which is what we’re doing.” Describing the UK as “world leaders” in AI security, the communities and housing secretary added: “We have put robust systems in place here in the UK, like the AI Security Institute, to make sure we’re building resilience so that we get the benefit as well as really understand and protect against any risk.” Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat told Sky News: “The speed of change is also extraordinary, and this is where actually government can enable a conversation, but we simply do not have the speed to keep up with the advances that are happening. “And the reality is, we can’t pass laws against mathematics. “These are mathematical equations that are being developed in greater and greater speed, and we need to maintain that ability to protect ourselves.” Let’s put this £72m weekend windfall for Reform in context – not only the largest single donations to a UK political party ever, but also the equivalent essentially of an entire year of political donations in the lead-up to a general election. A total of £79m was donated to UK political parties in 2023, according to the Electoral Commission. A further £84m was given in 2024, the election year. This is just what’s been publicly logged. Reform is also facing allegations it has tried to hide foreign donations. It denies any wrongdoing. The data also shows how much has been donated to parties since the 2024 vote (not reflecting Reform’s latest endowments.) July 2024- June 2026 donations: - Tories: £37m - Reform: £35m - Labour: £21m - Lib Dems: 17m - Greens: £1.9m Will also point out here that across the Sunday politics shows this morning, neither Labour nor the Tories ruled out accepting such huge sums from crypto-billionaires in the future. Nigel Farage says that donations just go to putting Reform on a “more level playing field” with the more established parties. Angela Rayner was asked on the BBC, at least three times, whether Labour on principle would have accepted tens of millions of pounds from the industry if they had been offered it. She declined to give a direct answer, saying instead that the party has “very robust rules and a vetting process for where we accept donations from. And we have refused donations in the past.” Tom Tugendhat meanwhile highlighted “problematic” areas of the crypto industry, but also didn’t answer the BBC’s question directly. “Well, look, we’d accept money from reputable sources” he said, before turning to speculation on whether Reform had done their adequate checks. Reform has been describing these crypto billionaire donations – again the largest single gift to a British political party – as being from patriotic businessmen who “simply support our agenda”. Pressed by Laura Kuennsberg on the BBC: “And part of your agenda is being very pro cryptocurrency, which is their business?” Jenrick replies, “Um, not really”, saying first that he wants “proper” regulation of the digital currency which is a bit of a “Wild West”, and then advancing to the idea of gains for the UK in adopting crypto. Throughout this morning, he’s been referring to himself as Reform Shadow Chancellor. “Is there an economic opportunity for the UK from crypto? Yes, and I want, as Reform Shadow Chancellor of UK, to seize that so we can compete with Dubai and the United States.” “But that’s not what we’re doing here with these donations.” Reform has said if it wins government, it would raise a law to boost adoption of crypto, including through cutting tax on digital assets. They would also create a bitcoin reserve fund at the Bank of England. Just wanted to highlight this statement too from Jenrick, insisting to both the BBC and Sky this morning that wealthy donors wouldn’t get formal favours, if Reform were to come into power. He said “there are all these people in the House of Lords who are Tory donors. 24 out of the last 25 Tory Party treasurers sit in the House of Lords.” “Reform is different. We are not going to give peerages, or knighthoods, to people who go around giving us donations,” he says. A reminder that Jenrick was a Tory MP for 12 years (and the former shadow justice secretary) before defecting to Reform in January of this year. More from Jenrick on the BBC asserting that the donations from the crypto billionaires are legal. As I sketched out earlier, the Labour government has a package of laws going through parliament right now aimed at stopping foreign money from influencing UK elections. The foreign donor cap is currently set at £100,000. There are no restrictions on how much citizens living in the UK can give parties. But if a Brit returning to the UK wishes to give more, the new law states that they need to be living in the country for a full calendar year before they can do so. The issue with the laws perhaps applying retrospectively (i.e. from March) is that this could rule out these £36m a-piece donations from Harborne and Delo, as both of these crypto-billionaires have been living outside of the UK, and Reform may have to return the money. Jenrick says in the case of Harborne, he won’t go into his personal circumstances but, “even if that were the case, the donation that he’s made would still be a legal one in compliance with the law. So we see no reason why you’d have to return these.” Over on Sky, Conservative Tom Tugendhat was asked if the Tories were “rattled” by the money going into Reform. He says he “welcomes people supporting political activity” in a democracy- at this point, Sky’s Rachel Johnson cuts in – “even crypto billionaires who live in Thailand?” (referring to Harborne). Tugendhat then switches to his second point – the persistent murkiness over where Reform’s funds come from. He raises the issue of due diligence, noting it’s a legal requirement for each party to rigorously check the sources of their donations and highlights that Reform has faced allegations this past week after a Channel 4 undercover investigation appeared to show Farage’s senior aides attempting to circumvent the rules to accept an otherwise illegal injection of foreign funding. (Reform denies the allegations but Farage’s chief of staff and head of policy have stepped down and Labour has asked police to investigate possible offences. The Electoral Commission is also considering the allegations.) Tugendhat goes on to argue that regardless of these donations and huge sums, “British people can’t be bought” and it’s an “illusion” to buy influence in public office. He then also notes that these tens of millions have come from the crypto industry – noting that it’s the currency commonly used for laundering and to get around sanctions on foreign regimes like Russia and Iran. Earlier, Jenrick on Sky defended the donations saying he was “very confident” they’re “perfectly legal”. When pressed on whether Reform would return the donations if they were found to violate new law: “Who knows? I mean, if people try and do something retrospectively, then maybe.” To recap: In the past 48 hours, Reform UK has received a staggering sum of £72m from two crypto billionaires, the largest single donations in British political history. Christopher Harborne’s £36m donation, which he announced in the Telegraph newspaper yesterday, matches that given by another cryptocurrency investor Ben Delo on Friday. Would the new law capping foreign donations then make these latest Reform cheques illegal, if they apply restrospectively? Given both donors resided overseas, presumably at the time of donation. Rayner says she won’t be drawn on the individual donors in the Reform situation, and she doesn’t know their circumstances- i.e. where they were living at the time of donation- but she lays out what the law would entail, that it would apply from March. Harborne is still based in Thailand, while Delo is reported to have moved back to the UK since April. “With the retrospective action, anyone that’s received donations that doesn’t comply with … what is in legislation is currently going through parliament, would have 60 days to return that money,” says Rayner. ”That is not for those individuals, let me be really clear. I do not understand those individual circumstances, but that their retrospective action will apply from the 25th of March.” Meanwhile on the BBC, the government’s Angela Rayner says the huge sums show it’s all about “who is funding politics and if there are few individuals who fund power to power… in a democracy that is a concern.” Parliament is currently looking at new laws to cap foreign donations – Rayner again stresses Labour’s line that this restriction when it comes in should apply restrospectively. Sky’s just broadcast an interview with Jenrick who describes the bonanza donations as a “breakthrough moment” for Reform “from two patriotic businessmen”. (A reminder that Harborne has lived outside of the UK for years and is based in Thailand, and Delo until recently, was living in Hong Kong and was convicted of violating the US Bank Secrecy Act before being pardoned by Trump last year). Jenrick says the 2 x £36m donations “enables us to be battle ready for the election and to prepare for government.” He denies that the huge cheques mean that Reform is “in hoc” with the crypto billionaires, and says it wouldn’t buy them peerage or any other formal favours. Good morning and welcome to the Guardian’s politics live blog in what is a fairly tumultuous period in electoral financing. To recap: In the past 48 hours, Reform UK has received a staggering sum of £72m from two crypto billionaires, the largest single donations in British political history. Christopher Harborne’s £36m donation, which he announced in the Telegraph newspaper yesterday, matches that given by another cryptocurrency investor Ben Delo on Friday. The huge injection into Reform’s coffers obviously help fund the anti-immigration party’s operations leading into the next general election, to be held by 2029. But it has also further muddied the reputation around the party’s finances and who it says it serves. Reform has pledged more crypto-friendly policies i.e. greater adoption of the unregulated currency across the UK if the party were to come into power. Reform’s economics spokesman Robert Jenrick is on Sky and the BBC this morning to address questions over the massive donations and allegations it has sought to circumvent electoral law to receive foreign donations. There are also calls now across the political spectrum for a cap on donations from big-moneyed donors in the UK, a restriction that currently only applies to foreign donors.

headline: Obama reportedly urges Democrats to prioritize safety plan for AI
trail_text: Ex-president urged party at closed-door fundraiser to create sweeping framework, from safety ‘slow-down’ to job losses
body_text: Barack Obama urged Democrats to prioritize a “public conversation” about AI management and safety in a closed-door Manhattan fundraiser last week. The comments by the former US president reportedly urged the party to create a sweeping framework for everything from a safety “slow-down” to domestic job losses and children’s wellbeing. Obama’s comments follow a summer in which a band of rogue OpenAI chatbots hacked the company Hugging Face, towns across the country opposed datacenters and an AI researcher resigned in a viral social media post warning: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” AI leaders have recently expressed agreement that the race for technological superiority should slow, but have also sought to appease investors, whose stake in the technology is predicted to exceed $1tn in 2026 alone. “Once you are speaker,” Obama said to US House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York-Democrat, at the fundraiser Thursday. “I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” according to a transcript first reported by the New York Times. “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial. I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.” Obama later added: “I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety. Here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,’” he said according to the Times. Obama made the remarks as the US closes in on the midterm elections and Congress has taken little action on AI. While prominent Democratic lawmakers, and some Republicans, have called to regulate the technology, Trump has attempted to aid the AI industry by introducing legislation that would ban state regulations (the bill did not move forward). Democrats face an open presidential field in 2028. One major flashpoint for the midterm elections is datacenters that power AI companies. Both parties have since begun running ads that oppose them, as one of the few issues, “Maga Republicans and liberal Democrats” agree on, according to an NPR analysis. On Sunday, while on a trip to his Irish golf course, Trump told reporters that a lot of “very negative forces” are ⁠bringing up concerns ⁠about AI that “won’t happen”, and that his main concern was that the US remain the industry leader, according to Reuters. “We’re leading China in AI. ‌We’re the ‌most sophisticated country in the world, ‌and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” Trump told reporters when asked if ‌the AI industry should slow down or be more regulated. In the past, Trump has said on social media that anyone who opposes AI datacenters is likely “backwards and poor”. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he said on TruthSocial two weeks ago.

headline: ‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown
trail_text: From the Trump administration to AI experts, plans by the Anthropic boss to boost safety have spawned a largely negative response
body_text: The safety debate that ignited when whistleblowers last week warned that the most advanced AI poses an existential threat to humanity should come with a health warning: side effects include whiplash. It was only seven days ago that AI enthusiasts were cheerily toying with OpenAI’s newest model GPT-6 Astra which was marketed in part as a lifestyle tool to help people book tennis courts, run fashion companies and order takeaways. By Wednesday, cutting-edge AI started to look a lot less appealing when the resigning Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Yes, he was talking about artificial superintelligence – an as-yet-nonexistent version of the technology that outcompetes humans in most domains – but his comments, and the chorus of experts that echoed him, jangled plenty of nerves. Another lurch came when Anthropic revealed it had found users dodging controls to use its existing models “in ways that could support biological weapons development” – think novel mosquito-borne or bird flu viruses. It was all enough to make lawmakers in London and Washington demand brakes and bans on the most potentially dangerous types of AI development. And then this weekend, another sharp turn in the form of a three-point plan from the Anthropic boss, Dario Amodei, to “pace the frontier”. Never mind that his own employees had seeded the borderline panic only a few days earlier, Amodei was here to save us from fears of AI Armageddon, but not before his own spicy warning that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months. Sceptics doubted that claim, but it was enough for some to declare it a “code red” moment. In signs that a coordinated slowdown might not be just talk, some of Amodei’s precautionary ideas quickly attracted backing from his rivals – Sam Altman at OpenAI and Elon Musk at SpaceX. Perhaps there were reasons to be hopeful after a bumpy week: at least the AI companies were talking about a slowdown before anyone got badly hurt. In a nutshell, Amodei proposed three moves. First, each US AI company grants ongoing access to embedded third-party evaluators to check compliance with safety commitments, report incidents, ensure new AI models are not misaligned. Until now, such watchdogs have only been brought in at the companies’ behest or given limited access to systems to investigate when things go wrong. In the absence of any government-level independent regulator, this is a start. Second, he wants all companies in democratic countries building frontier AI models to establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress. Third, the world’s democratic AI powers would coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. This is likely to be the hardest step. Amodei suggested a baby step could be a narrow agreement prohibiting obviously dangerous uses of AI, such as for the production of biological weapons. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping in Washington DC on 24 September will test the prospects of any Sino-American coordination. An immediate political problem is that Donald Trump appears reluctant to confess to any AI fears. Amodei’s plan requires US government action and Trump said last week he had no concerns about AI leading to human extinction. He doubled down on Sunday, saying people were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. Losing to China appears to be a bigger worry in Trump’s AI calculus. “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” said Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, last week. “If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter.” People close to Trump also wonder why Amodei and the rest of the AI leaders do not get on with pacing AI development themselves. “The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” said David Sacks in response to Amodei’s blog. Sacks is co-chair of Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology. “Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system,” he told Amodei. Another criticism of Amodei’s call for “pacing” of AI progress to allow safety measures and guardrails to keep up has came from Prof Stuart Russell, one of the world’s leading AI experts. Amodei proposed a slowdown to free up time to make advances in systems to keep the AIs aligned to human interests. But Russell said this was “completely backwards”. “We don’t just set a slower rate of progress for capabilities and then hope that provides enough time to get the safety right,” he said. “We set the safety requirements and further progress occurs only when they are met. Imagine if a pharmaceutical company said: ‘We’re going to release a new cancer drug every year, and we hope that provides enough time for some clinical trials to be completed and for the results to be good.’” AI experts not working for the big labs were also suspicious about a plan for a global regulatory framework for AI drafted by the leader of the world’s most-valuable AI company. “Too little, too late,” said David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute. He added: “We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”

headline: Morning Mail: One Nation sleepovers at Rinehart’s revealed, Japan trips getting more expensive, and more AI alarm
trail_text: New podcast looks at who One Nation really stands for; scrutiny over Australia’s military exports; AI bosses back calls to slow development
body_text: Good morning. Today we launch The Populist: a podcast about how One Nation is gaining ground in Australia. The four-part series follows senior correspondent Sarah Martin as she uncovers the inner workings of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation – a party that has imported the modus operandi of the global populist right, including Trump-style attacks on the media. The Populist asks who One Nation really stands for and what influence its billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart has over the party. Elsewhere there’s speculation over the intended target of a Russian drone strike near the Ukraine-Poland border. And tech titans, including Elon Musk, say they’ll back calls to pump the brakes on AI development. Australia ‘Red lines’ legislation | David Pocock is among crossbench MPs who will pressure Labor to ban Australian goods from being used by the Israeli military. Sleepover at Rinehart’s | One Nation’s Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed overnight at Gina Rinehart’s Brisbane mansion after fundraising events, with Joyce conducting a live television interview about politics from the $20m home. He did not declare the hospitality to parliament because the billionaire is a “long-term friend”. End of the road? | The Japanese yen has now reached its highest level against the US and Australian dollars in six months. Is the era of budget-friendly trips coming to an end for Australian travellers? ‘They can get to incredible numbers’ | Rabbits are the biggest threat to Australia’s native species. And due to good rainfall and growing resistance to viruses, rabbit populations are booming. Sea lion death | South Australia has recorded the first death of an endangered Australian sea lion from H5 bird flu, amid fears for the protected species of which less than 12,000 remain nationwide. World Russia-Ukraine war | A train carrying former UK PM Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the intended target of a drone strike near the Poland-Ukraine border, officials say. AI alarm | Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic to “slow the pace” of AI development in a rare show of unity from rival developers. “Too little, too late”: critics remain suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdown. Middle East crisis | A pregnant woman was among more than 10 killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza; Iran-allied Houthis have said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in Saudi Arabia. headline: We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism?
trail_text: There are several answers, and none of them will be provided by tech. One thing we must do is identify the ingredients for human flourishing
body_text: Imagining the future as almost entirely bleak has somehow crept into the collective consciousness this year. Last week I was having coffee with an old friend. He was telling me about what his kids wanted to study when they went to university, when he suddenly broke off, stared into the middle distance and said, “I wish I’d never had children.” He’d been a father for 20 years and I’d never heard him say that. “Oh my god, why?” He loves his kids beyond measure, but right at that moment, he looked desolate. “AI,” he replied. “What about it?” It could have been anything AI-related at this point in time. Was it that AI was going to take all the jobs his kids would have done, rendering their lives impoverished and without purpose or meaning? Or was it environmental, with all the water and energy AI consumes that is going to create further stress on the climate and make the planet uninhabitable? Or was it the news that week that AI could “kill all humans” within the next 10 years? It was the latter. We talked listlessly about the “killing all humans” thing for a bit, then moved on. But the shadow had fallen and I started wondering: is the polycrisis that we are facing so overwhelming that we don’t even have the capacity to talk about it with urgency any more? Instead it’s just there, in the air, ambient, like pollution, each particle containing its own particular doomsday scenario – and the only way to be in this atmosphere is to be numb to it. Currently, for so many, all our past and future decisions are being refracted through this strange and dark moment. If you’re middle-aged, it looks like my friend, wishing (for a moment) you’d never brought kids into the world. Or it might be wondering if it’s worth continuing to work, if you’re not going to be able to enjoy a normal retirement. If you’re young, it looks like being unable to pick a university degree or vocation because you don’t know what professions or trades will be obsolete in a few years. Or wondering if it’s worth sacrificing and saving for an enormous house deposit, if you won’t have a proper job or future to service a 30-year mortgage. And if you’re older, it’s being grateful that you won’t be around to see it all unravel. There are several answers, or ways out of this nihilism we now face – and none of them will be provided by tech. The first is to wake up. Usually if someone was actually trying to kill you – if they broke into your house and tried to murder you – you would fight back. Yet we greet the news that AI could cause human extinction with a glazed indifference. It’s worth remembering that no one actually asked for AI, and yet here it suddenly is trying to kill us. And even if that’s averted, it’s embedding itself in our workplaces and in our emotional lives (ChatGPT may be the largest provider of mental health services in the US), robbing us of the capacity for critical thinking, and threatening economic and social stability. Why are we so numb in the face of what is – currently – a preventable threat? This numbness could be the result of almost 20 years of smartphones and social media where, addicted to entertainment, our attention spans have been shortened, and through our individualised algorithms, our capacity for organisation and collective action have been diminished. Or it could be the huge political power tech companies have that means all of us – including governments – feel powerless. It could be that the tide of this thing – this progress, the Last Invention – feels inevitable, and like the Luddites storming the factories, any resistance is ultimately useless. The next solution, after we wake up, is to return to first principles. What are the ingredients for human flourishing? Once we can articulate that, it’s like a rope that can guide us back to where we should be. Human flourishing is not having a machine to do your critical thinking for you – rather, it’s to engage in the pleasure and the pain of working things out for yourself. Flourishing is human-to-human relationships where we care for and nurture each other. It’s not talking to an LLM for 18 hours a day about our personal problems. Flourishing is having a direct relationship with the natural world – not the world through a screen, or the natural world itself destroyed and degraded to create more capacity for screen-based existence. These are all things worth fighting for. There is a place for technology in our world, it’s just that when we start hearing that it could destroy our world, we should wake up, shake off that numb feeling and start fighting back. Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the Sage

headline: Somerset ‘festival of ideas’ to measure whether its talks change people’s outlook
trail_text: Attenders will be asked to take part in tests to see if they have become more open to views they do not agree with
body_text: Festivalgoers sometimes report feeling they have a fresh perspective of the world when they make their weary way home after a stimulating cultural gathering. A new “festival of ideas” in Somerset is aiming to measure whether the beliefs and ideas of attenders and speakers really are changed by their event. People attending the Big Brue in the town of Bruton next weekend will be asked to take part in tests before and after to try to discover if what they have listened to has made them more open, optimistic, empathetic and tolerant of people with views they do not agree with. Beau Lotto, a neuroscientist and educator, said the idea was to turn the festival into an experiment “We have set up a number of panels with strongly opposing views. We want to examine if the festival can change perception of conflict. Can conflict be generative rather than degenerative?” Lotto said that finding out ways of understanding other people who see things in a different way was important given the febrile nature of much national and global debate. “Because of the polarisation in the world, there’s so much pessimism and negativity, partly because views are incredibly non-nuanced. Which means it feels very fragile. It’s very extreme.” Lotto did something similar at a Cirque du Soleil performance to test whether the wonder and awe people felt changed the way they interacted with other people. One of the experiments there was for an interviewer to drop their pens and see how people responded both before and after watching Cirque du Soleil performers. They found people were more likely to bend and pick up the pens afterwards. “People were much more pro-social than they were before. Much more willing to help than they were before.” Big Brue festivalgoers will be asked to fill in questionnaires and carry out simple tasks such as finding the midpoint of a line. Lotto said the line task could indicate which side of the brain the respondent was using – and might be different at the start and end of the festival, indicating a change. Panellists will also be invited to take part in the experiment. An ethos of the Big Brue, taking place in the grounds of the Hauser & Wirth Somerset gallery, is that conflicting views can be a good thing if they are aired under conditions that encourage curiosity, compassion, creativity and learning. So rather than bringing together speakers likely to have similar views, the festival has deliberately put together panels of people likely to have contrasting opinions. Lotto said he expected a session on artificial intelligence involving the former UK chancellor George Osborne, who now works for OpenAI, and Misha Glenny, who has written about the global race for dominance of the technology, to be lively. Two sessions with the Reform UK MP Danny Kruger may also be sparky. In one, he will discuss migration, in another, called Family Matters, he will be in conversation with his mother, the cookery writer and broadcaster Prue Leith. Parent and child disagree over subjects such as assisted dying and abortion. Even a literature session is being billed as a “poetry battle” in which the actor Dominic West and singer and activist Bob Geldof “go head-to-head to champion the poems they believe everyone else should love”. The journalist and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup, one of the festival founders and the host for the Kruger/Leith face-off, said: “The idea is not just to hold another talks festival. We’re creating a space where ideas are presented and tested, where disagreement is welcome so long as its agreeable, and audiences are participants as well as spectators.” Festival organisers also hope the rural setting – away from the “fray of the city” may be a good location for working out how to “disagree agreeably” – the theme for the talks programme. Another of the founders, the human rights lawyer Jason McCue said: “We firmly believe that progress comes from difference and disagreement, so we are here to stir things up and help make sense of the world.” • The Big Brue takes place on 19 and 20 September at Hauser & Wirth Somerset. For details: https://bigbrue.com/

headline: AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?
trail_text: After apocalyptic warnings about the the threats posed by AI, leaders like Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to ‘slow the pace’
body_text: Facing a public uproar over Anthropic researchers’ repeated warnings that artificial intelligence could kill all of humanity by 2030, the AI company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, issued a proposal at the weekend to slow down the technology’s advancement to ensure public safety. In a rare display of unity, the heads of the largest US artificial intelligence companies all agreed immediately. The OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and xAI owner Elon Musk posted support for Amodei’s proposal for slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”, with Altman stating he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman posted Saturday on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.” “Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward,” said Hassabis. Musk simply wrote: “Dario is right.” The AI CEOs’ warnings and promises open up a host of questions about how AI might be regulated, what risks it poses and whether the industry will actually slow down the fevered race to advance its technology. While lawmakers and the tech industry consider how to address growing fear and distrust of AI, many of the hurdles impeding comprehensive AI regulation remain the same as before last week’s apocalyptic declarations from a young Anthropic researcher. The US federal government is committed to a global AI arms race. Previous proposed AI legislation has wilted under intense, well-financed corporate lobbying. AI startups face the enormous pressures to release new, more powerful products ahead of upcoming trillion-dollar public offerings. Amodei’s pacing proposal has drawn heavy skepticism from critics and researchers who allege that AI firms are attempting to preempt more stringent government regulation and retain the status quo of power within the industry. Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Amodei’s proposal focuses on three main pillars. First, a commitment to outside evaluators given employee-level access to monitor risk. Second, agreements between democratic states on AI safety standards. Finally, global coordination with authoritarian governments such as China on security issues. Amodei and others in the industry have made similar calls for global coordination in the past, even before the industry’s recent warnings over models becoming too advanced and gaining autonomy. The AI industry, especially the factions within it that focus on whether the technology is aligned with humanity’s interests, has also long warned about its existential threats. Rahm Emanuel, former congressman and chief of staff to Barack Obama, tweeted: “I can tell you when the last time a CEO or an industry at large asked to be regulated: never. That’s what makes Dario’s letter so striking – it’s an admission that we’re driving down a dark, winding road on wet pavement with the headlights off. And where’s President Trump? Looks like he nodded off again.” AI firms have fluctuated on their emphasis on communicating the potential harm from their products, however, at times warning about apocalyptic effects of AI and at others promising it will bring about utopian prosperity. OpenAI, for instance, shut down a “superalignment” team in 2024 dedicated to studying long term AI risks and earlier this year disbanded another team intended to communicate how OpenAI would benefit humanity. While AI companies have made grandiose claims about the threats and benefits from their technology, they have also historically provided little transparency or oversight into how their models operate and spent millions in lobbying efforts to shape favorable legislation. The result of the AI industry’s narrative that it is too powerful, complex and lucrative of a technology to regulate, critics say, is that it has been allowed to essentially govern itself. “AI exceptionalism has led to a total failure to uphold our standards for what products are deemed safe for use,” Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, posted Sunday on X. Critics similarly see Amodei’s proposal as another instance in which the industry is seeking to set its own rules, in this case picking its own evaluators to monitor safety risks, instead of facing the scrutiny of more intensive government regulators. Alex Bores, a proponent of AI regulation whose failed bid for Congress spurred $24m in spending both for and against his campaign from AI-linked political action committees, warned that the AI lobby often seeks to undermine legislation while claiming to support regulation. “To everyone who genuinely wants real AI regulation, please don’t fall for their games,” Bores posted Sunday on X. Several critics of the AI pacing proposal from across the political spectrum expressed concern around Amodei’s proposal’s suggestion that the government could grant some form of antitrust waiver or exemption to allow industry coordination. Former officials, including Trump’s former “AI czar” David Sacks and Biden-era head of the Federal Trade Commission Alvaro Bedoya, suggested that the proposal amounted to an attempt at regulatory capture, which would benefit current industry leaders. “Antitrust law does not prevent AI companies from coordinating to make sure AI does not hurt people,” Bedoya posted on X, adding: “Antitrust law does absolutely prevent AI companies from organizing to prevent the entry of cheaper, upstart rivals because the bigger companies are burning cash and failing to achieve sufficient profitability.” The proposal’s calls for international coordination around AI and federal intervention also run up against president Donald Trump and his administration’s vows to turn the US into the dominant AI superpower regardless of safety concerns. The Trump administration has often framed AI development as a zero-sum contest against China for technological supremacy, an argument the AI industry itself has also promoted in the face of proposed government regulation. Vice-president JD Vance declared in a speech last year that the future of AI was “not going to be won by hand-wringing about safety”. On Sunday, Trump once again rejected calls for slowing down AI development while citing competition from China and telling reporters “whoever wins AI, wins”. “We could put guardrails. We can do this and that,” Trump told reporters while on a visit to Ireland. “But I think you have a lot of very negative ⁠forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen”. House speaker Mike Johnson likewise said Congress would not lead the charge on regulating AI safety, laying the responsibility at the feet of AI companies.

headline: Monday briefing: What do Reform’s record-setting £72m donations mean for the party – and our politics?
trail_text: In today’s newsletter: As Labour MPs scramble to realign later today around a bill that could stop donations like this in their tracks, a look at new game-changing donations to a party engulfed in financial scandals
body_text: Good morning. Nigel Farage has a confirmed talent for upending the laws of political gravity, and this weekend has been no exception, as he declared himself “humbled” by two donations of £36m each from cryptocurrency tycoons Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne. I’d shoehorn a joke about buses in here but, honestly, this feels too consequential for that. The largest single donations in British political history were made after a dismal party conference, the substance of which was all but obscured by the financial scandals engulfing Reform. As the financial dubiety continues, and the numbers of millions tick upwards to seem almost meaningless, it might be tempting to roll your eyes and focus elsewhere – but this is not the time to look away. These are gamechanging donations, transformative if used effectively at this stage in the election cycle, just as Labour has regained its confidence and the Tories are contemplating a comeback. As a bill that could stop donations like this in their tracks returns to the Lords later today, I spoke to Jessica Elgot, the Guardian’s deputy political editor, about what these millions mean and why they matter. First, a wrap-up of this weekend’s headlines. Weekend roundup Economy | Former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit – and that rejoining the European Union’s customs union would be the fastest route to recovery. Technology | Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace” of AI development. Amodei had cautioned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year. Sweden | With most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority. Ukraine | A train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways. Travel | The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report. In depth: More money, more problems? Let’s start with more detail on the donations, by businessmen who have amassed astronomical fortunes trading in cryptocurrency. Ben Delo, a previous Reform donor, has given £36m. Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned by Donald Trump last year. (A brief note here on how that story came to light: the Sunday Times approached Reform and Farage after a confidential source told them that Delo had donated to the party. Soon after, the Telegraph published an opinion piece by Delo himself, announcing the donation and trouncing the Sunday Times scoop. As Sunday Times political editor Ben Riley-Smith noted on X: “A fundamental part of political reporting – approaching for comment before publishing – just totally breaks down if this is what happens. Bad for both sides: Will increase the chance of inaccuracies.” Reform has used the same tactic with the Guardian, as we talked about in a previous newsletter.) Less than 24 hours later, another crypto donor was troubling the Telegraph’s op-ed page: this time Christopher Harborne – whose previous £5m gift to Farage is the one currently subject to a parliamentary standards investigation – announcing he had likewise donated £36m, saying: “My competitive spirit inspired me to match [Delo].” Taken together, these donations are unprecedented in British political history: £72m is bigger than the total sum spent by the seven largest parties in the last general election (about £67.9m) and almost double the total donations to all political parties so far this year (about £41.8m). *** Are these donations legal? “There’s nothing wrong with these donations that we know of,” says Jessica, her final four words doing a lot of heavy lifting in present circumstances. The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into that £5m Harborne gift, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024 and first revealed by the Guardian. Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing. It’s a legal requirement for every party to rigorously check the sources of donations, and, doing the media rounds yesterday, Reform’s economics spokesperson Robert Jenrick was sounding supremely confident that the donations were “entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, what it is going to be in the future”. Jenrick was referencing the representation of the people bill, going through parliament, which will bring in more stringent rules about foreign donations. Gifts to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March. Delo has recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong, while Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand. I don’t have space to get into it here, but if you’re curious about the path to becoming a crypto billionaire and the people who get trampled along the way, I’d recommend the actor and crypto investigator Ben McKenzie’s excellent film Everybody Is Lying to You for Money. (Yes, he’s Ryan in The OC). *** How could Reform spend the money? Reform has already vastly scaled up its party infrastructure since the general election, moving to new offices in London’s Millbank Tower, once synonymous with New Labour election operations. Press officers, graphic designers, videographers and regional organisers have augmented staffing capacity, but their wider policy offering is still weak. An injection of cash will probably mean more hires to address this, and perhaps even drafting legislation to boost Farage’s projection of a party that’s ready for government. Reform is expected to install campaign managers and branch coordinators in hundreds of seats across the country – as their list of 60-plus job vacancies indicates. And if this newsletter gig doesn’t work out for me, I might throw my bunnet in for the senior writer role advertised here – the application requires a 500-word letter, written in the style of Zia Yusuf, “setting out how the political class broke Britain and how Reform UK will fix it”. The donations also promise a massive boost to Reform’s visibility – they can pay for the big “air war” expenses incurred in coming byelections and council elections next year, more locally targeted online advertising and billboards, as well as getting creative with its TV studios. Reform now has the money to focus on labour-intensive data gathering in target constituencies as well, says Jessica, who predicts it will be “transformative” for the party. “You’ve got enough money now to spend on the granular and expensive work of going around every single constituency in the country making sure your data about voters, and non-voters, is bang on. And if you’re a party that wants to show that you’re on the march, they’ve got the momentum, you can dominate the airwaves, dominate people’s social media feeds.” *** Will this prompt a rethink on a cap for all donations? Labour MPs’ WhatsApp chats have been popping off over the weekend, Jessica reports, with anger that the government did not act last week to restrict domestic donations in the elections bill. Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, pulled her amendment proposing an annual cap of £100,000 after Andy Burnham dropped his support for it, following intensive lobbying from the party’s trade union backers, who argued it would undermine their ability to donate to the party. But the bill has its second reading in the Lords later today and, yesterday, communities secretary Angela Rayner suggested that the government was still considering amendments and that “it’s not as simple as we’re saying we won’t put a cap”. As Sunday turned into Monday, some unions appeared to be shifting their opposition while Labour MPs and donors were urging the government to look again at party funding rules. But Reform argues that – as a relatively new political force – it needs this cash injection to level the playing field with other parties and their far longer-standing donor arrangements. *** What about an early election? As Jessica reminds me, Reform will be able to splash its cash in the coming months because many restrictions on party spending don’t kick in until a general election is called. “Other parties are not spending that money now because they don’t have it. And their donors are not giving money at this stage in the cycle. So they won’t have any competition for those eyeballs whatsoever.” There’s growing chatter in Westminster that – if economic growth continues to inch upwards and Reform remains static in the polls – Burnham may go for an early summer general election next year. (With a note of caution from Jessica that there will probably be a backlash from hundreds of Labour MPs on course to lose their seats.) A major consideration for the prime minister is, of course, Reform – which remains, in recent polls, a couple of points behind Labour and a similar amount ahead of the Tories. According to Jenrick on Sunday, these donations enable his party to be “battle ready”, whatever Burnham decides. Meanwhile, Labour sent out an “urgent” fundraising appeal over the weekend, warning that Reform could “simply drown Labour’s message out in elections to come”. Clearly, £72m in cash is good for Reform. “But whether it re-energises the party, and voters think, ‘People are willing to give this money millions of pounds because they offer a radical reset and I want that, too’ or whether it adds to that perception of a party being bought by billionaires, it’s hard to say.” Crucially, it keeps everybody talking about Reform’s finances. After a summer marred by scandal, internal divisions and a damp squib byelection, and at a point when Farage’s own popularity ratings have plummeted and support for the party has stalled, that is last place Reform wants to be. The week to come Monday | First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff to discuss moves towards self-determination across the nations. Tuesday | The final report of the Thirwall Inquiry into events at the neonatal unit where Lucy Letby worked will be published. Letby was sentenced to 15 whole-life terms for murdering seven infants and attempting to murder seven others. Thursday | Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, will address the European parliament. What else we’ve been enjoying Much of the hand-wringing around the death of reading can seem uncircumstantial, but not this excellent column from John Harris on what it could mean for the future of our democracy in a time of “nonsense and poison”. headline: Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera
trail_text: Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed
body_text: Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices. The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. Unlike Samsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra or squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display. Opened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones. The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory support from last year, while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on the other Pro Pixels, replaces the camera’s flash. Specifications Outside screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi) Inside screen: 8in 120Hz OLED (372ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie cameras Connectivity: 5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes) Dimensions folded: 155.2 x 76 x 10.1mm Dimensions unfolded: 155.2 x 150.4 x 5mm Weight: 239g Faster chip but slightly shorter battery life The 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the other Pixel 11 models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance. The battery life is a little shorter than last year’s model and rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up. Android 17, Magic Cue and Gemini The Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months of Google AI Pro subscription. Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical display introduced last year. The bubbles system, which was primarily used for messaging apps, has been revamped to allow as many as five apps of any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen. The 11 Pro Fold will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available. Sustainability The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repair with manuals and parts is due to be available. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free. Camera The Pixel Fold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen. The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in the regular Pixel 11, which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of the Pixel 11 Pro. The Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media. The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellent Made You Look feature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos. Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones. Price The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799). For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,499.99. Verdict The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same. It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to the best from rival Samsung. As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel. But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get. Pros: just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates. Cons: very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.
