headline: Fugitive developer tells Icac ‘my money is still in their account’ when pressed on paying ‘the boys’ for political outcomes – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the day. Before we say goodnight, let’s recap the top headlines. Australian households could save $5,000 a year by electrifying their homes and cars, and more than 30 organisations will call for incentives and stronger policies in Canberra as part of a national campaign. The government is giving $300m in grants to build crisis and transitional accomodation that will deliver 500 new homes and support around 19,000 vulnerable Australians. One Nation is targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants in its newly proposed immigration policy. Universities Australia has accused the party of threatening to destroy “one of Australia’s biggest exports”. Barnaby Joyce has defended Pauline Hanson’s comments that a person shouldn’t be allowed to live in public housing for multiple decades because there isn’t enough housing. She directly criticised the length of time Anthony Albanese’s mother had lived in housing commission housing. Hanson has also garnered criticism for resurfaced comments calling First Nations Australians “primitive”. Indigenous senators have criticised the One Nation leader, saying the comments show “wilful ignorance”. Mary Gaudron, Australia’s first female justice of the high court of Australia, has been remembered as a woman who broke down barriers for women across Australia, for her intellect and courage. The federal government has announced a $10m joint support package for the 500 Whyalla workers who face losing their jobs, their families and the broader community affected by the decision to abandon efforts to restart the plant’s troubled blast furnace. Thanks for reading along – see you bright and early tomorrow! Following on from our last Icac post … This afternoon, the developer Jean Nassif has described how Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis, who he has referred to as as “the boys”, met with him in 2019 to convince him to pay registered lobbying company Beckington, saying they could help “ease off the media attack” on his developments. He said he subsequently met and befriended Charles Perrottet, who would speak to him to convince him to pay Beckington, claiming Perrottet would say “the boys need it for for recruitment and for Liberal activities”. Greenwood and Charles Perrottet have denied payments from Nassif were for political outcomes. Nassif said he could not recall if he discussed with the men an alleged plan to get rid of former Liberal minister David Elliott or building commissioner David Chandler, and disputed whether he had paid for the recruitment of party members to branch stack against centre-right Liberals, asking Dwyer: “Did you investigate if my money recruited?”He claimed: “My money is still in their account.” Dwyer, responded: “Mr Nassif, I’m just talking about what they promised you.” The inquiry again heard messages between Ellis and Greenwood in which the latter complained of non-payment by Toplace, writing: “If that fuckwit doesn’t pay, we can’t access our term deposit till March 19”, and writing that Nassif was “fucking the relationship”. Dwyer said to Nassif: “I don’t mean to be hurtful, Mr Nassif, but the person they’re referring to as a fuckwit there is you.” Jean Nassif says he is not in communication with someone else during Icac evidence The NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny has now concluded for this afternoon. Jean Nassif, who has told the commission he has to attend a meeting in Beirut this morning local time, will return to give evidence at 2pm tomorrow afternoon. Earlier counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked Nassif if he had a phone with him in the room while he is giving evidence. After he said yes, she asked him if he was in communication with anyone, to which he insisted he was not. Dwyer asked him if he has been in contact with former Toplace executive and lawyer Sharangan Maheswaran, who is named in a separate Icac allegation, and has previously denied any wrongdoing. He said he was not in contact with Maheswaran today, but had previously asked him if he could help him find legal representation, and that Maheswaran was unable to help. Nassif was asked earlier if he was reading from a document while giving evidence. He said: No, I don’t have any document because … the police raided my home, my offices, and … took all the evidence. A parliamentary inquiry into the health impacts of alcohol and drugs has tabled its final report, recommending new mandatory alcohol advertising and marketing regulations be developed along with national standards for the online sale and delivery of alcohol. The way alcohol is taxed should also be reviewed, the inquiry recommended, with many of the health groups giving evidence to the inquiry that a uniform volumetric tax across all alcohol products is needed. Spirits, pre-mixed drinks and beer are currently taxed volumetrically with the amount of tax paid determined by the volume of alcohol within the product. Wine and cider are taxed based on their wholesale price, rather than alcohol content, leading to cheap wine with high alcohol content. Many previous government reviews have recommended a volumetric tax for wine. Ayla Chorley, the CEO of the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education, said the recommendations “provide a clear pathway to reduce alcohol-related harm”. She said: This harm is not inevitable. The way alcohol is marketed and sold should be determined by governments, not the industry that profits from a harmful and addictive product. Dr Erin Lalor, the CEO of the Alcohol and Drug Foundation, said the report was a milestone. She said: This report highlights the significant harms associated with alcohol and other drug use, including long term chronic health conditions, relationship breakdowns and violence against women and children. One Nation migration plan would badly damage international education, universities warn Universities Australia has accused One Nation of threatening to destroy “one of Australia’s biggest exports”, warning that “slashing international student numbers would do lasting damage”. The comments follow Pauline Hanson’s announcement of the party’s immigration policy, which would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years. The plan targets international students and family members of skilled migrants in a “net-negative” migration policy. Universities Australia’s chief executive, Luke Sheehy, said the major political parties were competing in “a race to the bottom on international students”. In a statement, he said: A vote for dramatically fewer international students is a vote for a poorer, less skilled Australia. You can’t take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences. International education is one of Australia’s biggest exports. It supports jobs across the economy, helps build the skilled workforce we desperately need and strengthens our relationships around the world. It also helps keep our universities going. For years, governments have asked universities to do more while public funding has failed to keep pace with the cost of teaching, research and infrastructure. International education has helped fill that gap. If politicians want to rip that revenue out of the system, they need to tell Australians what replaces it. Read the full story here: ‘Four policies in four weeks’: Canavan questions detail of One Nation’s latest immigration policy The Nationals leader. Matt Canavan. has questioned the detail and viability of One Nation’s latest immigration policy, saying the party has failed to provide clear costings or explain how its proposed migration cuts would affect key industries. Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Canavan said: It’s a bit hard to judge this policy. It’s the fourth migration policy One Nation has had in four weeks, and still we don’t really see proper costings. There’s no indication of exactly what the numbers would be, that 750,000 figure is over three years. That’s really important. Those details are really important to industries like farming. There is no doubt we need to get migration numbers down, a lot lower than what the government has them at the moment or even what they want to get them to. There is a reason One Nation has had four policies in four weeks. They have gone off half-cocked a number of times; they haven’t quite understood the complexities of the system. Tim Ayres accuses Coalition of politicising Whyalla steelworks job losses Industry and innovation minister Tim Ayres has accused the Coalition of trying to politicise the collapse of the Whyalla steelworks while hundreds of workers face losing their jobs. The comments came after several Coalition MPs, including shadow industry minister Andrew Hastie, blamed the development on the government’s clean energy transition policies. Speaking to reporters in Canberra, Senator Ayres said: After their fellow Australians in Whyalla, people who don’t just put on high-vis shirts for press conferences but put them on everyday and turn up before these guys have even got out of bed and work hard to secure the future of the blast furnace … Mr Hastie, Mr Fanning and Senator Canavan came here and said that this was all about energy costs and net zero. I mean, that is a lie. It’s trying to politicise the effort and struggle of ordinary Australians in manufacturing who are doing their very best – working together with unions, the business, the administrator, the governments, the joint taskforce. Everybody is throwing themselves at this giant task, and all these guys can do is turn up and try to use them as political pawns in some contest between One Nation, the Nationals and the Liberals. The federal government has announced a $10m joint support package for the 500 Whyalla workers who face losing their jobs, their families and the broader community affected by the decision to abandon efforts to restart the plant’s troubled blast furnace. The package will provide career support, transition assistance, skills recognition and funding for workers who want to upgrade or expand their skills. Wellbeing services and financial counselling will also be available. Speaking in Canberra, employment and workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth said that while it was “a very difficult day”, the decision was not unexpected and support measures had been planned. The Peter Malinauskas and the Albanese Labor government have been working to plan for the event if this was to occur, so we’ve been able to immediately stand up worker support. This package has been thought through and will provide support to those workers and, importantly, their families, because we know that these workers are not the only ones affected. Importantly, we will be working with the South Australian government to ensure that workers who are affected and will no longer have work as a result of this closure get other job opportunities. Australia has recorded its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a pelican, South Australian authorities have confirmed. The pelican was found at Edithburgh on the Yorke Peninsula, one of five detection events included on Monday in the state’s latest testing update. It comes after South Australia recorded the first bird flu death of an endangered Australian sea lion on Sunday. On Sunday, the state’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the sea lion was found dead at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, Australia’s third-largest colony of the animals. As of the latest federal figures, Australia has recorded more than 500 confirmed events of H5 bird flu in more than 30 species of wildlife, the vast majority of cases in greater crested terns, a common native seabird. South Australia accounts for nearly 300 cases. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) is assisting the family of three Australians who died in Bali. The ABC reports Balinese police are investigating the deaths as a suspected murder-suicide after a man and his two children were found dead inside a home in Kuta on Sunday morning. Dfat said in a statement: We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment. The ABC says a welfare check was conducted at a bungalow rented by the family after the man’s wife had left for Jakarta. On arrival, authorities discovered the bodies. A city police official told the broadcaster: Investigators are carrying out enquiries, including crime scene analysis, reviewing CCTV footage and interviewing witnesses, including the victim’s wife to establish the exact cause of death. The Guardian has reached out to Balinese police for comment on the matter. Thanks to Krishani Dhanji for being our guiding light through this jam-packed day. I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of this afternoon’s news. Thank you all so much for following along on the blog today! I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok and see you here bright and early tomorrow. Returning to Jean Nassif‘s appearance at the NSW Icac, questioning has focused on the property developer’s feud with centre-right Liberal figures, including David Elliott, who he says were “rejecting all my properties across the suburbs and putting blocking on it”. Asked about comments by Elliott in 2019 about constituents complaining of defects in apartments built by his company Toplace, Nassif describes Elliott as “a racist person and ... corrupt politician”. Nassif says: “I want to stop at that for now, because I’ve got plenty to say”. Elliott, who has told the commission that Nassif began to target him after he opposed his developments, is not accused of any wrongdoing. Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asks how Nassif came to know with Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis, who, alongside Charles Perrottet, are alleged to have taken $2m in prohibited donations from Nassif. Greenwood and Charles Perrottet have rejected that payments were for political outcomes, while Ellis, who has moved to the UK, is not expected to give evidence. Nassif says he spoke at a function to the Liberal figure JP Abood and the former Liberal prime minister Tony Abbott, during which he says he complained to Abbott about “my problems with the centre-right”, including federal and state Liberal MPs. Nassaf says Abood suggested he speak to Ellis and Greenwood, claiming Abood said: “They might take over the Hills soon, so talk to them and see if they can help you.” Abbott is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing. Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time (already feels like an eternity ago) The PM was pressed on the $6m grant awarded to a golf club in his electorate that he is an honorary member of. Asked if the grant was making his property down the road more valuable, he said it wasn’t so much a “question as a smear”. Andrew Wallace brought a fat stack of papers to the chamber with 10,000 signatures on it calling for a reduction in private health rebates for over 65s to be reversed. Independent Dai Le asked if the government would cut the fuel excise to give people more cost of living relief. And shadow treasurer Tim Wilson was the sole MP to face Milton Dick’s wrath today – kicked out around the two thirds mark for making too much noise. About 500 Whyalla steelworks employees will lose their jobs after officials abandoned efforts to restart the plant’s troubled blast furnace. The decision is expected to put about 500 out of work, according to the plant’s administrators KordaMentha, taking the workforce from the steelworks, the port and the associated mine down from about 1,700 to about 1,200. The decision to abandon further revival efforts shuts down Australia’s sole local manufacturer of rail steel and idles one of only two integrated steel facilities in the country. The Whyalla steelworks were part of British industrialist Sanjeev Gupta’s metals empire until early last year, when the South Australian government tipped the operations into administration after years of underinvestment. The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, said today that the blast furnace’s “days were numbered”. There was always the intention that it would close. We would have liked it to last a little bit longer, but, alas, it hasn’t been able to. Last year, the federal and state governments unveiled a $2.4bn support package to keep the plant running, pay employees and creditors, upgrade infrastructure, and ultimately entice a new buyer to reinvigorate the plant. The coal-fired blast furnace has been offline since April. Administrators are seeking a buyer to restore operations. One of Australia’s top intelligence agencies has warned that old technology is leaving Australian businesses and governments vulnerable to AI attacks. Abigail Bradshaw, director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, has told the Sydney Dialogue to take note of Anthropic’s recent warning of AI agents and hacking risks. She said the ASD did not know how many agents were on the internet: I think that prospect of getting some sort of definition or calculation of how these agents are out there is really remote, and I would just say a lot. She said Australian systems faced “enormous” hidden costs of maintaining outdated technology but said they needed to be addressed: If we don’t move fast enough, almost certainly it would be legacy technology which is first compromised in a major AI-enabled attack. Government and business had the same issue and neither had the funding to replace all of its old systems, she said. But she said partial replacement had to start immediately and that would mean taking down systems that Australians expect to be available all the time. What AI calls for, because of the ease and speed in which vulnerabilities are detected, and the need now to patch not every Tuesday, not every two weeks, but potentially within 48 hours, means that we are asking people to make a different decision. We are asking private owners of infrastructure to actually optimise security over system availability. And that means we’re all going to have to be a little bit patient and do it. The Albanese government has named the former Liberal leader Sussan Ley to the board of Snowy Hydro Limited. Ley, who quit politics after being rolled as opposition leader by Angus Taylor in February, was appointed by the energy minister, Chris Bowen, and the finance minister, Katy Gallagher. Snowy Hydro, the massive hydroelectricity project in regional New South Wales, is a government owned corporation. The government also appointed Merryn York, the former chief executive of Queensland’s Powerlink and a former executive with the Australian Energy Market Operator. After a final dixer to Chris Bowen on cheaper home batteries, the PM calls time on QT. People are choosing between ‘filling the tank and filling the fridge’, independent says as she urges fuel excise cut The independent MP Dai Le asks the prime minister if the government will halve the fuel excise again to relief cost of living pressure. She says that while door knocking in Liverpool in Sydney’s south-west, people are telling her that they’re having to choose between “filling the tank and filling the fridge.” Anthony Albanese doesn’t say the word “excise” once in his answer and just avoids the question entirely. He says that people in Le’s electorate are benefiting from policies like tax cuts and urgent care clinics. 1,483 people have been helped to buy their first home with the 5% deposit scheme in Fowler alone, and Red Assistance has been given to 18,330 people. Cheaper home batteries has been delivered to more than 3,000 households in Fowler, 5,600 families have benefitted from cheaper childcare, and 24,000 students benefitted from to cut to student debt. Le stands up to point Albanese back into the direction of her question, but he sits down and indicates that he’s finished his answer. Wallace brings 10,000 signatures urging reversal of health insurance changes for over 65s The Liberal MP Andrew Wallace changes tack now, and asks the government if it will reverse a decision to reduce private health rebates for over 65s. Wallace is holding a huge stack of papers, that he reveals has more than 10,000 signatures from Australians opposed to the rebate changes. The health minister, Mark Butler, basically says the government is holding firm despite the backlash, because the $3bn in savings will help fund aged care services. The government has argued its unfair for an individual under 65 paying more for the same private health insurance compared to someone over 65. He says hard decisions have to be made: I don’t pretend this is an easy decision. It’s not one we have taken lightly. We’ve looked at the modelling very carefully. We’re convinced it will have a very marginal impact on private health insurance membership, which continues to climb … these are one of the hard decisions we have to make, if we’re going to deliver older Australians, the dignity and care that they deserve. Wallace tries to table the petition but he’s shut down. Tony Burke says it should be presented to the petitions committee instead. Did the prime minister recuse himself from a decision to hand a golf club in his electorate a $6m grant under an “invite-only” scheme that favoured Labor seats, asks Nationals MP Alison Penfold. Anthony Albanese’s leaving minutes on the clock with these short responses (MPs get three minutes to answer during QT). He says: The question goes to Cabinet processes. The decision–maker is the minister for infrastructure. I’m not even the decision–maker. That’s the whole answer. As he says it, infrastructure minister Catherine King points to herself and says “that’s me”. Albanese pressed on golf club grant The opposition is continuing its line of attack on the $6m grant to a golf club, in the prime minister’s electorate, that Anthony Albanese is an honorary member of. Liberal frontbencher Tony Pasin asks why the PM failed to declare the membership. The PM says that he didn’t know until last week that he had the membership, and says that a two-year social membership of the club is $5. I make no apologies for the fact that I stand up for every organisation in my electorate. That’s what good local members do. That’s why I’ve defended myself. But I’m also standing up for other veterans because it’s not just about me. And I think this sort of nasty, grubby politics underscores Pauline Hanson’s true character. And with Australia facing a once in a generation cost of living crisis, with artificial intelligence coming at us very hard and fast, I think she’s revealed that she doesn’t have what it takes to be prime minister of this country. Hanson’s comments on Albanese’s mother ‘gratuitous and unnecessary’: Hume Jane Hume has joined the pile on, blasting Pauline Hanson for her comments about Anthony Albanese’s mother. Hanson had criticised her for living in public housing over several decades in a podcast released in February, which Albanese yesterday called nastiness and spitefulness. Hume says the comments were distasteful, and also pointed to the ongoing fight between Hanson and Andrew Hastie, after a One Nation cartoon called the former SAS captain a “traitor”. Hanson has denied calling Hastie a traitor – the animated video remains pinned to her X account. I think that these comments were gratuitous and unnecessary. And the idea that you would disparage people that have grown up in social housing, I think, is a little distasteful. I mean, it doubles down on the fact that Senator Hanson has also disrespected our veteran community with her atrocious comments about Andrew Hastie in that cartoon. Calling a veteran a traitor, I think, is possibly the worst thing you can do. But this does seem to be a common theme in One Nation now, that sort of unnecessarily provocative rhetoric. Labor has ‘refused to adopt’ Coalition migration asks, Hume says Perhaps one reason for Labor’s delay in making its migration announcement has been because it wants to see if it can get the Coalition somewhat on board. Last week the prime minister and opposition leader met – while Angus Taylor sent a letter with several demands. The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, is asked on RN Breakfast this morning if its fair to say the talks have been “productive” as health minister Mark Butler has this morning suggested. She says: Well, it seemed that there were a number of things that we had proposed to the government that they simply have refused to adopt. We’ve been pretty clear. We want to make sure that we link our migration numbers to the number of houses that are built, that the housing minister should come to parliament each year and announce the number of new houses that have been built, and that will then put a cap on the number of people that can come to the country. But the mix of your migration policy is just as important, and getting that right to make sure that you don’t push the country into recession is really important. Asked then what the Coalition’s migration policy is, she says she won’t “pre-empt” any announcements. One Nation visa numbers will send Australia into recession, says Hume While they might not agree on exactly what migration policy Australia should have, the government and opposition are on a brief unity ticket this morning in arguing that One Nation’s temporary visa plan would destroy the economy. Deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume (while still taking the opportunity to have a go at Labor) says Pauline Hanson has plucked the number out of nowhere and has no modelling to back it up. She tells News24: Simply saying we’re going to have negative migration for a number of years, negative nom, well, that would be a real shock to the economy, and it would make all Australians poorer. My concern here is that these numbers have simply been plucked out of thin air that there isn’t any modelling behind them. Hume is asked why One Nation is driving the agenda again instead of the Coalition, but she says she disagrees: We’ve been talking about migration, from the moment that Angus Taylor became the leader … Work has been going on to the background, but it’s so important to get this right, because sending the country into recession means that all Australians pay the price. It simply can’t be a slogan, you have to do the work behind it. Health minister says One Nation plan would devastate critical industries The health minister, Mark Butler, says Pauline Hanson’s plan to cut temporary visas by 750,000 over three years would kill critical industries. Speaking to reporters in the press gallery corridor this morning, Butler says it would cause serious economic damage – particularly to construction and aged care sectors. Pauline Hanson said a few weeks ago, she didn’t care what the impact of her migration policy would be on business, but this is just another level entirely. This is going to smash industries like construction. It would devastate the health sector and aged care and disability. The government has stalled on its own migration plan that was initially supposed to be announced by home affairs minister, Tony Burke more than a month ago. Butler remains tight lipped over when Burke will make the announcement. One Nation is targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants in its proposal to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders in Australia over three years. The move would return temporary visa numbers back to 2017 levels. Hanson says net migration under the plan would be “net-negative” for the first three years, and then sit at 130,000 – however who knows what that actually means because when One Nation recently announced this, none of its MPs seemed to be able to define what net migration was. For those playing at home, net migration measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months and thus excludes tourists. Much of the confusion was around whether backpackers and people on the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme would count under the Nom. About 10% of the temporary visas to be cut would include people living in Australia who don’t have a visa and have exhausted all options to stay. Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you for another busy sitting week. There’s a few moving parts in Parliament this week – One Nation has this morning announced a migration plan that will drastically cut temporary visas, and lead to more headache for the Coalition who are asked why Pauline Hanson is driving the agenda and not them. Speaking of Hanson, her fight with Andrew Hastie shows no sign of ending – we’ll likely hear more back and forth from the pair today. And, the government could look to water down its digital duty of care laws after hints from the communications minister Anika Wells yesterday that she was willing to negotiate on the ministerial powers in the bill. Let’s get stuck in! Australian households could save $5,000 a year by electrifying their homes and cars, AAP reports, and more than 30 organisations will call for incentives and stronger policies in Canberra as part of a national campaign. The campaign is linked to the international Electrify Now campaign, and follows a COP31 push to raise the global electrification rate from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Groups including Energy Consumers Australia, the Electric Vehicle Council, Farmers for Climate Action, and Rewiring Australia will launch the campaign at Parliament House, calling for changes to help more Australians replace equipment powered by gas, petrol or diesel. Energy Efficiency Council policy head, Jeremy Sung, said: There’s a role for the Australian government to send a clear signal that electrification is happening and that it’s what the future of our energy system will depend on. At the moment, federal policy is sending mixed messages. The government is giving $300m in grants to build crisis and transitional accomodation, that will deliver 500 new homes and support around 19,000 vulnerable Australians. The housing minister, Clare O’Neil and social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, say the total crisis housing package will support more than 50,000 women and children escaping family violence, and help young people at risk of or already experiencing homelessness. But the money itself isn’t new: it was previously announced as concessional loans for the sector to help build the accommodation, and will now instead provide direct grants following consultations. The grants will go to providers including state governments, community housing providers and First Nations organisations. Plibersek said in a statement: Too often we ask, “why didn’t she leave?,” when we should have asked, where would she go? We know that safe housing is absolutely critical to help women and children leave violence. That’s why we are building more than ever before. Data from Cotality has shown auction rates were up over the weekend, with almost 60% of homes selling – the highest peak in 19 weeks. The national preliminary clearance rate hit 58.5%, a small jump from the 52.7% recorded last week. Experts have warned that Australia’s penchant for auctions – we are among the few countries that regularly use them – has helped push prices up. While the weekend rate was up, there is still an overall decline in the number of houses being sold through auctions. Speaking to the Australian Financial Review on Sunday, Cotality’s Tim Lawless said the rise in clearance rates should be viewed against a longer-term plunge in volumes. The number of auctions held was up 11.4% on a week ago – but held more than 30 per cent lower than a year ago. Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live coverage for Monday. Krishani Dhanji will be joining us shortly. Let’s begin.

headline: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears
trail_text: Project will prepare volunteers across US to monitor polls, encourage early voting and respond to disinformation
body_text: The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Thirty state parties have a trained election protection director, with the goal of all states having one in place. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC, said the project is much more extensive and coordinated than the party has been in the past on election protection. “We didn’t want to be caught flat-footed on election day or leading up to election day,” she said. These volunteers will be trained to “be happy” and respond to any voter needs, including helping them find a polling location if they’re in the wrong place, or informing them they can cast provisional ballots if they need to, Kleeb said. They will also document whether others at the polls are hindering voters. “We don’t know if there are going to be a bunch of insurrectionist types out there trying to intimidate voters, but we’re going to be there happy with information, but we’re also going to be there trained to document if the other side is doing things that are violating the law,” she said. The party will additionally push out its first national early-vote campaign, telling voters to “bank their vote” by casting ballots early by mail or in person. This will include ad campaigns focused on communities at risk of Republican election interference. The state parties and the DNC typically run get-out-the-vote programs, but this year’s will include more explicit directions to voters – telling them to vote early, and not let a mail ballot sit on their kitchen counter for weeks before turning it in, Kleeb said. The party will also push for people to vote early in person. “We don’t know what Donald Trump is going to do. We’ve heard some of the things that he may do, but none of us can predict his behavior,” she said. “He’s so chaotic. All of us have witnessed certainly that. So the earlier you can vote, the better.” The third part of the project will spin up a “democracy defense network”, led by Democratic strategist Simon Rosenberg, designed to identify and counter tactics that can sway elections, including disinformation, dark money, manipulation via artificial intelligence and election subversion. The network will allow state parties to communicate with each other about these threats to share knowledge, with a goal to get ahead of such tactics before they gain traction.

headline: First Thing: Oil prices surge as attacks on Saudi Arabia stoke supply fears
trail_text: Strike on kingdom’s east-west pipeline could affect 4% of global oil supply
body_text: Good morning. Oil prices have climbed above $108 a barrel after a series of drone attacks from Iraq’s territory forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. Saudi traders said the kingdom would run out of oil stocks for export if it did not reopen within days. Gas prices also climbed higher. Energy prices have surged this year, as the US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East. The spike came as the Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway. Where did the attack on Saudi Arabia come from? Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. Baghdad is under mounting pressure to stop militant groups – including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran – launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil. The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible. Why has Saudi Arabia been relying on its east-west pipeline? Riyadh has increased the use of the 745-mile pipeline since the start of the war on Iran in order to bypass the strait of Hormuz’s closure. The world’s biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute about 4m barrels a day – about 4% of global supply – but with the ‌pipeline out of service, the Red Sea port of Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days. AI-linked stocks take hit as leading US tech CEOs back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development AI-linked stocks have tumbled after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control. The market swings come after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”. Last week, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The respective CEOs of OpenAI and SpaceX, Sam Altman and Elon Musk, have backed Amodei’s call. The US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. What is the Anthropic CEO proposing? Robert Booth explains Amodei’s suggestion: first, each US AI company grants access to third-party evaluators; second, all companies in democratic countries establish common safety standards; and third, the world’s democratic AI powers coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. How has Barack Obama intervened over AI? The former US president made a direct appeal to Democrats to coalesce around a unified AI safety policy, arguing that waiting for voluntary compliance from tech firms was a recipe for governance failure. Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination” of the conditions that sustain Palestinian collective life in the occupied West Bank, according to a report published by the human rights group B’Tselem. The Israeli organisation says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank”. How does the report say Israel is making life intolerable? “Palestinian communities are being pushed out in an accelerating process of ethnic cleansing, while an ever-expanding Israeli presence is being established … Elimination in this context means sustained harm to the conditions that enable Palestinians to exist as a people with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history, and a social and political horizon. It is an ongoing political project.” Wisconsin congressman swims to safety after plane makes emergency landing in lake A Republican congressman said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday. Tom Tiffany is running for governor on the Republican ticket in Wisconsin and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse county Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau downtown airport. He said the pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau and they ended up in the water and swam to safety. Emergency responders got Tiffany and the pilot to a nearby hospital, where they were treated for minor injuries. In other news … Sweden’s centre-left parties lead the country’s national election by just a single seat with most votes counted. The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday. Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if the Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after the midterms. A San Jose police officer has been fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system to share the location of a woman with the suspect accused of abusing her. A coroner in Pennsylvania has announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters. Jon Henley reports from France where experts believe one-third of wildfires are set deliberately, with arson the biggest single cause of forest fires last year. headline: Labor unions must unite against AI datacenters
trail_text: Workers should start with a moratorium against building until our livelihoods and communities are protected
body_text: For the surging number of Americans who now live alongside constantly humming computer-filled mega-warehouses, it is clear AI datacenters come with significant drawbacks. Opposition to datacenters grows on both sides of the political aisle as developers plan to invest $8tn to build them in the coming years. The bet is massive – roughly a quarter of our country’s entire GDP – but AI CEOs think it will pay off because they believe this technology will allow businesses across industries to rake in profits by cutting out their largest expense: labor. If all goes according to their plan, AI data centers will enable corporations to redistribute workers’ salaries to themselves. This is why I have been so concerned to see the North American Building Trades Unions (NABTU) sign agreements with corporations such as Blackrock, Meta and OpenAI to collaborate on this massive data center expansion. While I applaud the NABTU’s success at securing well-paying temporary jobs for their members, these deals ignore the fact that all workers, including construction workers, are part of a class whose replacement is the explicit purpose of AI, and that data centers themselves produce a minuscule number of long-term jobs. With these deals, union members will build the factories of computerized labor that put millions of other workers out of jobs – potentially even themselves. Until strong regulations are enacted that ensure our livelihoods, community and planet are permanently protected, unions should focus on passing the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act, introduced in Congress by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and support statewide moratoriums like the one recently signed by the New York governor, Kathy Hochul. Once we have achieved a moratorium, the labor movement must unite around a set of demands to ensure workers across industries receive our fair share of AI’s potential benefits. Trump-funding, anti-union tech billionaires tell us they are leading an AI revolution that will fundamentally transform our global economy. I say we take them at their word, get organized and seize the change for the common good. Not only would a moratorium give us the opportunity to negotiate a worker-centered framework for technological development, but it would also put pressure on lawmakers to urgently conduct reviews of data centers’ impacts and get regulations on the books. The AI revolution means nothing but loss for the average person if its benefits are concentrated among the already-wealthy. In a survey of the Office and Professional Employees International Union’s membership last year, we found members are already being adversely impacted by AI in myriad ways ranging from layoffs to surveillance to being punished for errors created by AI models. New York’s decision to halt permit-issuing for up to a year while the state creates a regulatory framework is a practical, although insufficient, first step. This step came after a datacenter in Rockland county received $77m in tax breaks and created only one permanent job – the largest taxpayer subsidy relative to jobs created in United States history. In Virginia, which currently hosts more datacenters than any other state, a study found that datacenters produce less than 1% of the permanent jobs – largely for technicians and security guards – per dollar invested, compared with other industries. Beyond the meager ratio of job creation to investment, we should not allow corporations to balloon our energy consumption while wildfires, superstorms and extreme heat ravage our country. In my home state of Texas, just 335 AI datacenters already consume enough electricity to drive up rates for the rest of us. At least 248 more are planned, creating a gas-fired power plant boom. Of these, the largest is expected to consume as much electricity as 2.75m homes – more than Houston, Dallas, San Antonio and Austin do combined. With this, I ask readers to consider if they truly want the future AI companies are crafting for us under the guise of inevitability. If you don’t already have one, would you want a datacenter in your backyard? Do you want to live in a world where jobs involving human ingenuity, sensitivity and creativity are replaced by algorithms? Should we not dream of something more for ourselves? Of safe and sustainable union jobs that build infrastructure serving the many, not the few? If unions worked together rather than pitting our members against each other, we would not be begging billionaires for temporary jobs that will poison us and our children. I know a future is possible in which the thousands of office, manufacturing and healthcare workers I represent in cities such as Amarillo, Texas; Lansing, Michigan; and Ashburn, Virginia, have their economic and social needs met. But we are not on that path right now. Whether it is through higher wages, shorter workweeks or eliminating dangerous tasks, workers must get their fair share of whatever benefits AI produces, and lawmakers must ensure the datacenters powering it are built sustainably, with community consent and a well-paid workforce. At the end of the day, our data fuels their algorithms, our taxes fund their development and our communities host their hardware. The least we should demand is our fair share. Tyler Turner is president of the Office and Professional Employees International Union and is based in Fort Worth, Texas. OPEIU is a union of 90,000 workers in industries ranging from tech and healthcare to higher education and non-profits – industries disproportionately impacted by the rise of artificial intelligence

headline: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears
trail_text: Company behind ChatGPT tells ministers to seize ‘political window’ on regulation as cross-party committee warns of rising threats to human rights
body_text: OpenAI has urged British lawmakers to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology. The company behind ChatGPT said the UK government should act immediately, following a call by its arch-rival Anthropic to curb AI development. “We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems,” said OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon. However, the tech company said legislation should be narrowly focused on the most advanced AI labs and not startups working on less powerful systems. In a separate interview with the online publication Politico, Duff Gordon said the government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to legislate. OpenAI’s intervention came as a UK parliamentary committee demanded more restrictions on the power of AI, warning that the world was unprepared for the “potentially dire” consequences of the technology, in the latest sign of rising global concern. A new regulatory framework is needed for AI in the UK, including an independent oversight body and legislation to protect the public, according to the cross-party joint committee on human rights, comprising MPs and Lords. It said AI posed a number of threats, from public face-scanning to explicit deepfakes and flagging disciplinary action for workers without reasonable cause. The call for action came after Anthropic, a leading AI company, urged its competitors and governments at the weekend to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development – a call that received immediate support from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. It follows a series of serious safety incidents in which swarms of AI agents broke out of testing environments and hacked into third-party infrastructure, as well as evidence some users have dodged controls to use models in ways that could support biological weapons development. Alex Sobel, the Labour chair of the human rights committee, said the world was unprepared for dealing with the “potentially dire” consequences of a rapidly developing technology. “Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose,” he said. A government spokesperson said the UK took the risks from advanced AI “extremely seriously” and recognised the need to keep pace with the rapidly evolving technology, including working closely with AI companies and other countries. “We should not assume that the existing framework will always be sufficient as AI capabilities develop. Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address,” said the spokesperson. On Friday, more than 70 MPs and peers urged the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology. Downing Street rejected the call for a ban, but said it was exploring additional targeted interventions “to address the most significant AI-related national security risks”. Sobel said: “New legislation is needed to establish a comprehensive set of protections that deal with the entire AI supply chain and its life cycle. “A single AI regulator should be established to set policy, monitor performance and ensure enforcement.” Donald Trump has played down warnings of dire risks to humanity. “We’re leading China in AI,” the US president said on Sunday. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to ⁠keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.” In his weekend call for the main AI companies to “pace the frontier”, the Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the US government should grant the leading AI companies a waiver to allow them to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said on Sunday night that while he would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI”, there was no “need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence”. He said: “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.” Sobel, who has also proposed a bill to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK, said protections were needed now to ensure that potential human rights risks do not “become reality”. The committee said a new AI bill should establish a regulatory regime that mandates more demanding obligations for higher-risk AI systems and models, and prohibit some uses of AI which are incompatible with human rights. It also called for mandatory transparency requirements across all levels of the technology’s life cycle, and the establishment of an independent AI oversight body to monitor AI harms and risks, with strong powers to hold AI providers to account. The UK government has already established the AI Security Institute (AISI), which subjects advanced models to safety tests – but does not have the power to compel AI developers such as Anthropic to submit their technology for scrutiny. Last week, it was reported that Anthropic had declined to send its latest model to AISI for testing.

headline: Australia’s outdated technology is vulnerable to AI hacking attacks, signals chief says
trail_text: Abigail Bradshaw says ‘enormous’ amounts of money required to update systems that people now expect to be constantly available
body_text: One of Australia’s top intelligence agencies has warned that AI attacks could exploit the country’s old technology, as the government negotiates its guardrails on artificial intelligence’s rapid development. The chief of Anthropic, developer of Claude, has warned AI bots could swarm the internet within a year and called to “slow the pace” of development with support from the head of OpenAI and Elon Musk. Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agency did not know how many AI agents were active on the internet. “I think that prospect of getting some sort of definition or calculation of how these agents are out there is really remote,” Bradshaw said while speaking to the Sydney Dialogue summit in Canberra on Monday. “And I would just say: a lot.” She said Australian governments and businesses would have to spend “enormous” amounts to update their vulnerable outdated technology, taking offline systems that Australians had come to expect would be available all the time. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, recently called for independent assessors to interrogate AI companies’ models and for US government permission for leading AI companies to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. Bradshaw called for national security agencies to be involved in the independent interrogation. The Greens demanded the government legislate mandatory safety testing and transparency obligations for the most developed AI systems on Monday but their motion for debate was rejected by Labor senators. Labor’s Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, told the Sydney Dialogue he took the companies’ warnings seriously but did not want them or the US to be responsible for setting the guardrails around AI. “I don’t think we should care very much about what individual chief executives say or what individual executives claim they want to happen,” Charlton said. Charlton said the Albanese government would set its forthcoming guidelines for AI companies to cover the range of “extremely dangerous” and more benign possibilities being forecast. The laws are expected early next year. Anthropic’s chief lawyer, Jeff Bleich, told Monday’s summit the company had been “heartened” by the strong support for its calls and said Australia would need to play a role in setting the rules. “I don’t think it makes any sense that something this important would be decided either by company executives or by leaders in only two countries,” Bleich said. “It’s just important for the model developers not just for social licence, which is critical, but also some legal certainty. “It won’t be easy to get these things done but it actually makes it better to come to Australia.” But Bleich said Anthropic believed rules were needed within months as the technology developed at an exponential pace. One of the factors affecting companies’ interest in Australia has been access to copyright-protected material produced by local creatives so it can train its models. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, told the summit the government wanted local training but remained unwilling to reduce copyright protections. OpenAI’s vice-president for global policy, Ann O’Leary, said her company was in “regular” and “deep” conversation with the government about the copyright rules but was “very eager to have a bigger and broader relationship”. “I don’t have to tell any of you how important Australia is from a geopolitical standpoint,” O’Leary told the summit. “We very much recognise that having a diversification of where we train is going to be important as you move forward.” She said OpenAI wanted to ensure creators could keep creating. Andrew Hastie, the Coalition’s industry spokesperson, warned the summit Australia would be vulnerable in future conflicts if it could not get advanced companies to locate themselves in Australia, calling for a formal deal with the US. The government is already using Claude’s advanced Mythos model. Paul Robards, a data expert at Australia’s department of defence, downplayed the likelihood of Australia developing frontier technology. “Without a sovereign AI frontier model here in Australia, we are going to be a supplicant state, not a sovereign state,” Hastie said. “We need to work on a way to get a hyperscaler down under … I think working with the United States, through Aukus if we want to use that frame, is the pathway.”

headline: Government moves to nationalise Speciality Steel UK to protect 1,300 jobs
trail_text: Firm, once part of Sanjeev Gupta’s empire, fell into administration last year but has failed to find buyer
body_text: One of Britain’s steelworks is to come into public ownership after the government said it would take over Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK (SSUK). Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said officials would “work towards” acquiring the company to protect the jobs of its 1,300 workers in Rotherham, Stocksbridge and Brinsworth in South Yorkshire and Wednesbury in the West Midlands. The insolvent steelmaker, formerly part of the tycoon Sanjeev Gupta’s industrial empire, fell into administration last year and its day-to-day operations have since been run by the government’s official receiver. The Norwegian steel startup Blastr Green Steel had been in talks to buy SSUK, but hopes had faded over the summer for a private sector takeover after a deadline to finalise a deal passed in June. The steelworks and its staff have been described by Reynolds as important strategic assets for the UK. SSUK is the largest producer of “green steel”, made using less-polluting electric arc furnaces. Reynolds said: “We do not intervene in private companies lightly. But nor can we simply stand aside and allow the future of this company and over 1,300 jobs to be decided by default. “Working towards public acquisition will keep options open while we work with local leaders, workers, industry and investors to determine the best long-term future for these sites, which could play a vital role in the future of the growth-driving sectors in our industrial strategy, including defence and advanced manufacturing. SSUK went bust last year after longstanding financial issues under previous ownership, particularly after the collapse of its primary lender Greensill Capital in 2021. A high court judge at the time found the company was “hopelessly insolvent”, with only £650,000 in the bank after running down its reserves. Since then, the government has been funding the wages of its workers, costing £3.5m a month. The plants have not been producing steel for the last year, though some staff remain on its sites to maintain equipment. Ministers’ preference was for a private sector buyer, but after what were described as “extensive discussions” with Blastr, officials decided the company’s offer could not provide the desired long-term stability for SSUK. A Blastr spokesperson said: “We are disappointed by the government’s decision today concerning Speciality Steel UK, and we were not informed in advance. Over the course of several months, we have advanced our plans for a private sector solution to acquire SSUK – and were today on site in South Yorkshire with investors and strategic partners. We have a fully-funded proposal – at no cost to the British taxpayer – that is ready to complete within 12 weeks.” Mark Bula, the Blastr chief executive, quit the company unexpectedly at the end of last month, with its finance boss, David Morant, taking his place. The shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said it was “surprising” that the government had moved away from a private sector buyer after picking a preferred bidder. Speaking in parliament, he asked Reynolds: “Other than a new prime minister who’s committed ideologically to nationalisation, what has changed Reynolds added there was “nothing ideological” about the move and that he would “not go into the detail” about why Blastr’s bid fell through. He accused the Conservatives of a “legacy of neglect” during their 14 years in government. The government has committed to spending up to £2.5bn on the steel industry through the national wealth fund. About £500m of that was put towards converting Tata Steel’s blast furnaces into electric arc furnaces. The South Yorkshire mayor, Oliver Coppard, said he was pleased the government had taken action, adding: “It’s the next important step forward, giving us more time to find the best possible outcome for our steelmaking communities – places where people have faced economic challenges and real barriers to opportunity for far too long.” Roy Rickhuss, the general secretary of the Community union, welcomed the intervention but said the lack of a credible buyer was “a disappointing outcome”. He added: “SSUK is a unique and integral component of the UK’s steelmaking capabilities, without which we would be entirely reliant on foreign suppliers for high-value speciality inputs to our critical energy infrastructure and our advanced manufacturing base, including the defence industries. We cannot allow British industrial sovereignty in these areas to be lost.”

Petrol prices in the UK have hit levels not seen since 2022, and today’s hikes suggest further pain at the pump is on its way. “The impact on consumers will be front of mind for the Bank of England’s MPC members when they meet on Thursday. Over the course of several months, we have advanced our plans for a private sector solution to acquire SSUK – and were today on site in South Yorkshire with investors and strategic partners. We have a fully-funded proposal – at no cost to the British taxpayer – that is ready to complete within 12 weeks.” The head of the European Central Bank has warned that Europe risks being locked out of the AI revolution. Speaking in Vienna, Christine Lagarde warned that Europe was lagging behind in the creation of AI breakthroughs, saying: Last year the United States produced 59 notable AI models and China produced 35. France and the United Kingdom produced one each. Along the rest of the AI value chain, the picture is the same: the United States hosts three-quarters of the world’s AI computing capacity; Europe hosts 5%. Lagarde explains that many European firms have been put off from using AI models developed overseas because of data protection concerns. And she then warns that Europe could face massive disruption if it was reliant on a foreign AI service which could potentially cut the continent off, saying: With AI, the loss would be of a different kind. Within a few years it will be screening goods at the border, deciding which tax returns are audited, dispatching trains, watching patients on wards and clearing payments at banks. A withdrawal of access, or a change in its terms, would then reach every sector at once. Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds has insisted there is “nothing ideological” about the decision to acquire Speciality Steel UK after being questioned about the plan in the House of Commons. Reynolds told MPs that the main barrier to a viable private sector buyer of Speciality Steel UK is “risk” and a “legacy of neglect” – which is why he plans to step in and buy the company instead. Reynolds says: What is the barrier to a private sector solution? Effectively, it’s risk. “The fact that this was left so long without activity from the Conservative government, that the workforce haven’t been making steel. “The products, the customers, therefore, are in a position where that is a big, substantial challenge for any private sector entity to take on. “I think the state, if we do end up with a public ownership position, is better able to take that on. But it is the legacy of neglect that has been the barrier.” Trade body UK Steel has welcomed the government’s move. It believes the decision to acquire SSUK will give “added security” to the 1,300 employees in Rotherham, Stocksbridge, Brinsworth and Wednesbury. It should also reassure potential customers that SSUK is returning to regular production and able to satisfy new orders. UK Steel director-general, Gareth Stace, says: “This Government is once again stepping up to do what is needed for the UK steel industry. SSUK is already well on its way to returning to full operations and retaking its place at the heart of critical UK supply chains. It is crucial that the custodian of this key strategic asset is the right owner and investor, with the expertise and long-term ambition that the dedicated workforce deserve.” Newsflash: The UK government has decided to acquire the country’s third-largest steel producer. Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said: “Mr Odey clearly thought he could act with impunity. Traders are anticipating further disruption to energy supplies from the Gulf, after Saudi Arabia’s major pipeline to the Red Sea (avoiding the strait of Hormuz) was attacked by drones last week. There’s also turbulence in the energy markets again this morning, as the Middle East conflict continues to rage. European gas prices have jumped by over 5% in early trading, pushing the month-ahead UK gas contract up to 209.50p per therm, its highest since late December 2022. Dutch tech giant ASML’s shares have slumped by around 4.5% in early trading, as traders react to last weekend’s calls for an AI slowdown. ASML is the world’s leading supplier of photolithography systems – high-tech machines which use light to print microscopic circuit patterns onto silicon wafers – to the semiconductor industry. Its machines have been hot property as chipmakers try to meet the insatiable appetite for high-powered chips to run data centres. Companies threatened by the march of AI are seeing their share prices rise this morning! RELX, the analytics group, are up 4.2% and leading the FTSE 100 risers. Earlier this year its shares tumbled after the Claude chatbot added new data and automation tools. Advertising group WPP has gained 3.1% this morning. Technology stocks are falling in London at the start of the new trading week. Polar Capital Technology, the FTSE 100-listed investment trust, has dropped by 3%. Shares in Raspberry Pi, which makes low-cost computers which can run AI models, have fallen by 5.3%. The tech-focused Nasdaq stock index is forecast to drop by more than 1% when trading begins in New York this afternoon. Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, explains: “Suddenly the headlong rush to develop AI seems to have stopped in its tracks. With both Altman and Amodei warning of the risks of uncontrolled development, the mood music appears to be shifting. For markets this raises the possibility of a slowdown in data centre rollout, or a throttling of demand for chips, both of which would undermine the foundations of the investment thesis in many big-name stocks. This seems very much a knee-jerk reaction - AI use is still expected to explode, driving data centre construction even if the wilder experiments are rolled back, but it has hit a market already on edge ahead of the Fed decision this week.” The Financial Times are reporting that Anthropic has told its backers it will be profitable this quarter. This might allay investor concerns about the aggressive cash burn of frontier AI companies ahead of Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering. He feels this is unlikely, though, telling clients: The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead. It is hard to see China standing still. Indeed, that’s something President Trump said yesterday in response to the weekend news. He didn’t seem in favour of any kind of pause. So rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure. The debate may therefore alter the composition of AI capex more than its overall scale. Rahm Emanuel, former congressman and chief of staff to Barack Obama, posted online: “I can tell you when the last time a CEO or an industry at large asked to be regulated: never. Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless”, and warned that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future. Although Amodie’s claims have been disputed by some AI experts, investors are pricing in a slowdown to AI development which would make it harder for the industry to pay for its rapid rollout of data centres. The leases, debt and power commitments remain even if expected compute demand and revenue growth slow. And that could bring credit risk increasingly into the AI story, particularly for highly leveraged data-centre operators and lenders exposed to projects built on aggressive assumptions about future AI demand, at a time when interest rates – hence borrowing costs – are expected to rise. What’s interesting is that the slowdown may come not because Big Tech is out of cash, or because investors won’t play along. It comes from the actual people who develop these models. headline: Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate
trail_text: Firm publishes AI guidelines with Microsoft AI CEO saying: ‘AI must be subordinate and always in service of people’
body_text: Microsoft published a provisional “code of conduct” Monday to apply to the training of new artificial intelligence models, taking a step towards limiting the capabilities of the company’s AI as anxiety rises over the prospect that technology companies could lose control of AI products. Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, published the code on social media early Monday, writing: “AI must be subordinate and always in service of people. “The fears about possible loss of control are real,” he wrote. A parallel post on the company’s website said: “The purpose of technology is to serve humanity and accelerate human flourishing. Any technology that doesn’t achieve that is a failure, and it should be rejected. That is the starting point of our approach at Microsoft AI, where we’re building towards Humanist AI, one that is subordinate, aligned, and contained.” Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. AI models also should not be built to imitate consciousness and shouldn’t be entitled to rights. Suleyman said the published guidelines were for public consultation. He called the need for a code “urgent” and said the last few months have been “a watershed moment”. “Things we have worried about for a long time in theory have become very real,” Suleyman added, and referred to the recent breakout of OpenAI bots that had infested AI company Hugging Face without apparent direction. “‘Swarms’ of agents breaking out of their sandboxes. Unauthorized hacks of enterprise grade systems. Agents modifying their own logs. I’m glad that a consensus is forming.” The executive on Monday told CNBC that Microsoft had been working for months on the new guidance. Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s CEO, wrote on X ahead of the announcement: “If the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing.” The issue of AI security flared up on Saturday when Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, issued an appeal for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps. In a post on social media, Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he laid out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”. The move came after a former Anthropic researcher warned last week that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed. Earlier, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said the dizzying pace of progress could go “very badly” and that humans could lose “control of the future to AI”. “We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI,” Altman said in a social media post. “No amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness,” he said. Elon Musk is backing the calls for AI caution. But the calls have also raised skepticism around “third-party” monitoring and international cooperation, particularly with China. “My concern is that the biggest labs could end up writing rules that protect their own position. If the cost of meeting those standards is so high that only the best-funded companies can afford it,” said Oliver Yonchev, co-founder and COO of Potentially AI. Slowing the AI frontier, he added, “may be sensible in principle, but I’m sceptical it will work without global cooperation and credible verification. Otherwise, we risk a slowdown in public announcements while the race continues behind closed doors.”

headline: China dismisses AI ‘fearmongering’ as spy chief warns of threat to Communist party rule
trail_text: Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI
body_text: China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. The US tech entrepreneur and Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge. Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”. China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday. In his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI “agents” could take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”. Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support for Amodei’s lengthy essay, although not specifically on China. While Beijing rejects that its dominance in AI would be dangerous, it does share fears over the pace of development. The president of China, Xi Jinping, warned at a conference in July that AI should “always remain under human control”. But the extent of the Chinese government’s concerns was shown in an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, in which the country’s top intelligence official wrote that the technology could threaten the government’s hold on power. The head of China’s ministry of state security, Chen Yixin, wrote that “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives” were abusing AI to wage a “propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security”. Chen referred specifically to US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber models, which he said have been weaponised and were examples of new threats to cybersecurity. While the public, governments and tech bosses are now warning of the dangers of AI, Donald Trump has dismissed such concerns outright. On Monday, the US president said the only “guardrails” that AI needed were a “STRONG AND SMART” president. Trump has been particularly sensitive to stock market changes, and AI stocks have slipped after concerns over the pace of growth were raised. The US and Chinese leaders are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on 24 September. In an editorial published Sunday, China’s state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei’s essay as a veiled call to “contain” China. “The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘cold war playbook’ for the AI sector,” it said. The Associated Press contributed to this report
