headline: Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine face collapse after ‘difficult period’ – as it happened
trail_text: Today’s blog is closed
body_text: That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today! Before we go, let’s take a look at the day’s top headlines: Pauline Hanson has offered a qualified apology for her comments about Indigenous Australians and about Anthony Albanese’s mother – both which have been widely condemned. Chris Bowen has watered down any expectations that a renewed rise in oil prices will lead to the reintroduction of the federal government’s fuel excise relief. Clare O’Neil has defended her colleague, the transport minister Catherine King, after it was revealed the latter had accepted a lifetime membership to Qantas’s top-tier membership, the platinum Frequent Flyer rewards. Independent MP and former Winter Olympian Zali Steggall has joined the chorus of criticism against an ad for a US sports wagering company featuring actor Sydney Sweeney. Universities Australia has warned One Nation’s plan to drastically cut down international student numbers will lead to campuses shutting down and domestic students missing out. The National Disability Insurance Agency has announced voluntary redundancies for the first time since its creation in 2013. Queensland’s state government has flagged a new crackdown in the state’s parole system under legislation introduced into state parliament today. “Activists” and “green groups” will be banned from objecting to Queensland mining projects, under new legislation introduced into parliament today. Fugitive property developer Jean Nassif has fronted the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption after an explosive appearance on Monday. The Gold Coast mayor, Tom Tate, swore at an ABC journalist before storming out of a press conference after a series of questions about his trip to Mar-a-Lago to spruik an ultimately doomed $1.5bn plan for a Trump hotel on the Gold Coast. Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning. Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine face collapse Longtime Australian fashion brands Cue and Veronika Maine are facing collapse after being placed under the control of receivers and managers. The company’s parent said the decision followed “a difficult period”. In a statement, a spokesperson for Hilco Capital said: It is a disappointing outcome, but the only available course of action given the circumstances. Our intention has always been to fund Cue to restore growth and profitability. This appointment will now provide an opportunity for a new owner to carry the Cue and Veronika Maine brands forward. I want to acknowledge the efforts of all the staff during a challenging period and thank them for their continuing support of these great Australian fashion brands. Human Rights Commission condemns Hanson’s comments about Indigenous Australians The Australian Human Rights Commission has joined widespread condemnation of Pauline Hanson’s offensive comments about Indigenous Australians. The commission said the comments contradicted Australia’s shared values of “fairness, dignity and respect” and had “no place in the national conversation”. The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander social justice commissioner, Katie Kiss, said: Such commentary is a tactic to divide us at a time when we need to come together. In fact, people have come together over the past 24 hours, across the political spectrum, to criticise the senator’s comments. For that, I am heartened. But the harm caused should not be underestimated. The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, added: Whether our ancestors arrived more than 200 years ago, or we are recent migrants, we all live on lands and waters that were maintained by and hold the cultures of First Peoples. Recognising that gives us strength and brings us together. Denigrating First Peoples does the opposite and lessens all of us. When public figures use language that dehumanises entire groups of people, it causes real harm. History has shown that when people are portrayed as less deserving of dignity, respect or belonging, discrimination and exclusion are more likely to follow. Sivaraman said the incident reinforced the commission’s recommendation in the National Anti-Racism Framework for anti-racism training for all parliamentarians. Three-year-old girl dies after being hit by car in Sydney’s west A three-year-old child has died after being hit by a car in Auburn, in Sydney’s west, on Tuesday afternoon. Emergency services were called to Normanby Road at about 2.05pm following reports that a child had been struck by a vehicle entering a driveway. Paramedics treated the girl at the scene before taking her to Westmead hospital in a critical condition. She later died from her injuries. Police said the 27-year-old male driver was not injured but was taken to Auburn hospital for mandatory testing. An investigation into the circumstances remains under way. The resources minister, Madeleine King, has accused the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, of “gaslighting” Indigenous Australians and the prime minister after Hanson offered a qualified apology for comments that have been widely condemned. Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, King said Hanson’s apology was inadequate. She said: There is a way of apologising, isn’t there? … ‘Sorry if I caused offence’ is not really an apology. She says outrageous things about Indigenous Australians, disgusting things, and then walks back into this building and says she did not say it at all. That is gaslighting. What she said about the prime minister’s much-loved mother is beyond the pale, and a pseudo-apology is just pathetic on her behalf. NSW police watchdog delays public examinations into alleged protest brutality investigation The NSW independent police watchdog, the law enforcement conduct commission (Lecc), has delayed public examinations into its investigation of alleged police brutality, citing “a range of procedural issues”. In February, the Lecc launched Operation Makalu to investigate allegations arising from violent clashes between police and demonstrators at a protest against the visit of the Israeli president, Isaac Herzog. The delay comes two weeks after the leak of police body-worn camera footage of the protest, which was shared widely on social media. The footage allegedly shows a male police officer telling colleagues during a 9 February protest at Sydney Town Hall: “I fucking pumped that cunt.” The commission has not specified when the public examinations will begin. In a statement, the Lecc said: The Commission had previously announced that any public examinations would start no earlier than September 2026. A range of procedural issues have now arisen, which the Commission must consider. As a result, public examinations will not be held in September 2026. The Commission will provide a further update on its investigation as soon as practicable. Two WA teens charged after alleged Perth Zoo break-in Western Australia Police have charged two teenage boys after an alleged break-in at Perth Zoo during which a crocodile was assaulted and property was damaged. Police allege the boys, aged 16 and 17, entered the zoo at about 7.15pm on Sunday. It remains unclear how they gained entry. The teenagers allegedly cut the locks on a crocodile enclosure before entering and striking the animal with a metal pole. They are also accused of damaging CCTV equipment inside the enclosure by removing the cameras from the wall. The incident was reported to authorities the following morning, before police arrested the teenagers at their separate homes. Both boys have been charged with two counts of criminal damage or destruction of property, one count of trespass and one count of animal cruelty. State politicians react to Guardian story about man Tasered in homeless clearance Queensland politicians have reacted to Guardian reporting that a man was Tasered in a homeless clearance earlier in the month. The man attempted to kill himself after being ordered to leave a park north of Brisbane to make way for a kite festival. He was rushed to hospital, but discharged the next day. The opposition leader, Steven Miles, said the state government had “washed their hands of responsibility for the homelessness crisis that they’re contributing to”, blaming cuts to the state’s emergency fund for accommodation in hotels and motels. He said. We’re seeing this situation get even worse. It’s pretty much every park across Moreton Bay, whether that’s Pelican Park in Redcliffe, all the way through to Fernie Grove, there’s more and more people popping up in those parks. Miles said it wasn’t appropriate for a hospital to discharge a patient back into homelessness. Greens MP Michael Berkman said the case was “the end result of both major parties treating housing as a profitable commodity rather than a human right”. He said: Our Government has created this vicious merry-go-round by underfunding housing, healthcare and community services. If this is how the system treats a homeless man with terminal illness, it makes you wonder how they’re treating other people who we just haven’t heard about. The minister for correctional services, Laura Gerber, said she wasn’t familiar with the case but said the government prioritised community safety. Gold Coast mayor Tom Tate has sworn at an ABC journalist before storming out of a press conference. ABC reporter Liam Walsh asked Tate a series of questions about his trip to Mar-a-Lago to spruik an ultimately doomed $1.5bn plan for a Trump hotel on the Gold Coast. Tate claimed to have met with the US president at his golf estate at the invitation of the Trump organisation – but no record of the invitation exists, the ABC said. Walsh asked Tate on Tuesday how much the trip cost. The mayor responded that “it’s private” and denied he got “mate’s rates”. Then the mayor asked the reporter why he was so aggressive and if he was with the ABC, which the reporter confirmed. “Fuck off,” Tate said, and walked out of the press conference. The hotel plan fell over in May, with the developer claiming the Trump brand was too “toxic” to work with. Good afternoon! I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of the afternoon’s news. Thank you all so much for joining me on the blog today! I’ll leave you with the fabulous Achol Arok and see you here bright and early tomorrow. Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time The opposition picked a broad bunch of questions (and was perhaps a bit all over the place) to target Labor with today, from the Whyalla steelworks, to a fundraising dinner attended by Albanese, to green hydrogen, to private health insurance rebates for over-65s. Albanese defended Australia’s democracy and his government’s transparency, in response to a question from Allegra Spender. His answer was essentially: well, at least it’s not as bad as it is overseas. The prime minister also said it was appropriate that a Labor staffer, and ex-Play School host, was stood down after old tweets disparaging Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and others were revealed. The opposition then tried and failed to table photographs of the staffer in question with Albanese. National framework for defining affordable housing supported by advocates Advocacy group National Shelter has welcomed a move to establish a nationally consistent definition of “affordable housing”, but says a definition won’t solve the housing crisis. On Monday, the member for Bradfield, Nicolette Boele, introduced a bill that would tie the definition of affordable housing to what households actually earn, and attach it to commonwealth housing programs and funding agreements. CEO of National Shelter, Jackson Hills, said the organisation supported the bill: For too long, affordable housing has been defined differently across programs, jurisdictions, and policy settings. Establishing a consistent framework would strengthen policy development, improve transparency and support more effective measurement of housing outcomes over time. While a nationally recognised definition is an important foundation, definitions alone will not solve the housing crisis. Affordable rental housing delivered at scale can reduce pressure on overstretched social housing waiting lists by providing viable housing options for low- and moderate-income households. Over the next two decades, Australia must move beyond definitions and accelerate the policies, programs and investments needed to grow Affordable Rental Housing at scale across the country. Queensland’s state government has flagged a new crackdown in the state’s parole system. The legislation is set to be introduced into state parliament today by the minister for corrective services, Laura Gerber. Gerber said it will expand the type of people who can be covered by the state’s restricted prisoner laws, which permit a person serving a life sentence to be banned from release for a decade. At the moment the parole board can only issue a ban to a person who murders more than one person, or a child. Gerber told parliament they will now apply to all people sentenced to life, an unlimited number of times. Under our laws, the rights of victims and community safety will be the paramount consideration for all parole decisions, as it always should have been. The parole board must be empowered to deliver decisions in line with community expectations that put victims and the safety of Queenslanders first, and that is exactly what these laws will deliver. The legislation comes on new legislation making it more difficult for some people accused of crimes to get bail. Australia rises as US plunges in world democracy report The rise of independents and teals and an underage social media ban have helped boost Australia’s ranking in one of the world’s leading democracy indexes, AAP reports. At the same time, the United States’ standing has plummeted, with the Trump-era ransacking of institutions and standards dropping one of democracy’s leading lights to the ranks of also-rans. The annual Global State of Democracy report, released on Tuesday, rates Australia very well across its assessment matrix. Sweden-based organisation International IDEA charts nations across four main categories – representation, rights, rule of law, and participation – to assess their democratic health. Overall, it’s ugly reading – autocracies and repressive forces appear to be winning. For the 11th straight year, the report finds more countries recorded declines rather than improvements. The most extensive global decline was in freedom of expression, with drops in a quarter of the 173 surveyed countries. Judicial independence is at a 36-year-low globally, while press freedom and access to justice are at their lowest levels this century. In pics: boy meets the PM after walking 500km for rural paediatric care There are some genuinely inspiring and incredible people that walk through the halls of parliament, and today that’s 12-year-old Dusty Langby with his mum, Sarah, who have just completed a more than 540km walk to Canberra. They’ve been raising money for charity Little Wings and awareness to deliver paediatric care to bush communities, walking from the town of Warren, north-west of Dubbo in New South Wales to Capital Hill. Little Wings provides free flights and transportation for seriously ill children and their families in regional and remote areas. Dusty, his mum, and nurses Christine Letton and Nichole Callan (who also made the journey by foot) met with Anthony Albanese in his office. The government has this morning committed more than $1m to the charity. In a statement, Albanese said Dusty’s journey has been “extraordinary”: My government will match every dollar Dusty has raised so his incredible effort can make an even bigger difference. On top of that, my Government will invest another $1 million to keep Little Wings flying and help regional families get their children the care they need. Dusty has shown that you’re never too young to make a difference and we’re proud to back Little Wings and the work they do. People over 40 the largest single age group in share house accommodation Share housing has stopped being a stage people pass through, with people in their early 20s now in the minority, according to research conducted by Homerun, an app that manages share house expenditure. The study of 3,562 Australians living in or hosting a share house revealed that the largest single age group in Australian share accommodation is people aged 40 and over, who make up 44% of respondents. Key findings were: 17% already own a home and let rooms in it, rising to 26% of the over 40s. 35% have shared for five years or more, and 18% for more than 10. 69% did not expect, at 20, to still be share housing at their current age. 31% never expect to own a home. A further 11% put ownership more than a decade away. 75% say the high cost of housing has extended how long they will keep sharing. Scott Mckeon, founder of Homerun said: Sharehouses are underrepresented and underserviced. Co-living with people you are not related to comes with its own problems, and very little is built for them. Running a household is work, and it is harder between independent adults. Splitting the finances, agreeing on what clean means, keeping the shared things stocked, and finding someone new when a housemate moves out. Drug dogs on Oxford Street causing risks for LGBTQ+, advocates say Redfern Legal Centre has condemned repeated raids by NSW police on Oxford Street venues as alleged harassment of the LGBTQ+ community that fails to disrupt drug supply while causing real social harm and health risks. Over the weekend, police with drug-detection dogs were seen at several venues with people asked to remove clothing and questions about why people were in bathrooms. RLC’s police accountability practice lead, Rian Terrell, said: NSW police’s repeated decisions by NSW Police to deploy drug dogs to target patrons of venues on Oxford Street amount to [alleged] targeted harassment of the LGBTQIA+ community. This is particularly concerning given the police watchdog, the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, directed NSW Police to reopen a misconduct investigation into its actions targeting Sydney LGBTQIA+ venues just last month. That NSW Police chose to raid Oxford Street again, when that investigation has not concluded, raises further concerns about NSW Police lack of accountability. Use of drug dogs, wide scale strip searches and searches do little to disrupt drug supply and deter drug use. The 2024 NSW Drug Summit made several recommendations, including related to the use of drug dogs, many of which have not been accepted or implemented by the NSW Government. ‘No plans’ for further fuel excise cut, says Marles The calls for another cut to the fuel excise are again growing as petrol prices continue growing, but the government is hosing down speculation of price relief. Labor said the previous cuts to the excise were always designed to be temporary. The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, told News24 earlier: We don’t have plans for it. We are watching what’s playing out in the Middle East, clearly … Our focus has been in respect of ensuring fuel supply in Australia, and we’ve been able to do that from the moment that this conflict broke out. One Nation abandons gas plan in favour of policy benefiting Rinehart One Nation has come under fire for quietly shelving support for a new domestic gas reservation policy in preference for a policy that favours the party’s billionaire patron, Gina Rinehart. The Albanese government has announced it will establish a new reservation policy for Australia’s east coast, requiring gas exporters to supply a portion of the gas they produce to the domestic market. The policy is aimed at “modestly” supplying the domestic market to put downward pressure on prices for consumers. Pauline Hanson moved a Senate motion as recently as March in support of a domestic gas reserve, saying it would “increase the supply of gas and lower the price of electricity directly”. But the reservation plan has been vehemently opposed by Senex, a $900m company that is 49% owned by Rinehart’s Hancock Prospecting, and 51% owned by the Korean company Posco. In June, One Nation abandoned its longstanding support when it unveiled its gas plans after “consultation with industry and stakeholders”, saying the policy risked “killing domestic Australian gas companies”. Read the full story here: Chris Bowen says that Labor is willing to work with the opposition to bring down immigration levels, while adding it was “up to the Coalition” to pass legislation on it. The energy minister was asked on Monday’s 7.30 program about reports that the prime minister and opposition leader, Angus Taylor, had met last week to discuss a Coalition proposal to link net overseas migration to housing completion. Immigration has been a hotly contested issue within the Labor party, which culminated late last month when the prime minister announced a backflip on proposed cuts to Australia’s refugee intake. Bowen said if the Coalition wanted to see immigration settings “brought down and improved, we are happy to work with them”. We need the legislative pathway through the Senate in particular to get that done … Ultimately, the Coalition has to decide. Do they really just want to talk about immigration or do they want to actually vote for improvements to immigration? … If you want to be a party of government, it does need coming together from time to time to work on difficult issues. Pressed on whether Labor backed the housing idea, Bowen maintained “what we need to do is get immigration down” after post-Covid peaks and said there was “more work to do”. Universities Australia warns One Nation’s plan to drastically cut down international students will lead to campuses shutting down, and domestic students missing out. Pauline Hanson’s plan, released yesterday, suggested cutting the international student intake down to 100,000 visas per year and graduate visas down to 20,000 – a cut of more than 200,000 on current levels. The Universities Australia boss, Luke Sheehy, accused One Nation of “joining the conga line in this furphy” and blaming international students in the migration debate. He told ABC News: If numbers actually materialised as One Nation proposed … you would see university campuses shut down, Australian students unable to get a place at university and thousands of university workers have their jobs put at risk. Marles downplays reports of OpenAI ultimatum over copyright Richard Marles says reporting that OpenAI has issued an ultimatum to Australia – that the government must water down copyright protections or the company will refuse to invest in domestic AI training or renewable energy – is overstated. Marles says he recently met OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei in San Francisco and the fact that they want copyright protection for creatives watered down is “not news”. I think that’s overstating, actually, the comments that have been made … It’s not new that there are challenges in respect of copyright, which has been raised by those companies. All of this was articulated by the prime minister in his speech in July. We do want to see our country take this opportunity. It’s a historic opportunity for our nation, but we need to be doing it in a way which protects rights holders – and that means news organisations, it means creatives. But actually, I think you can do both. Asked if that language used was “threatening” the government, Marles replies: Well, I actually don’t think it’s at the level that you’ve described it. I mean, I think the person in question was making the point that copyright is an issue which needs to be looked at in the context of OpenAI doing training in Australia. That’s not news. Defence recruitment goes online and reaches a 16-year high in Australia Recruit smarter, not harder, says the deputy PM and defence minister, Richard Marles, announcing the highest defence recruitment intake in 16 years. He credits a lot of it to meeting young people where they’re at – which is of course, online. (I guess the release of Top Gun: Maverick itself in 2022 didn’t do enough to cajole people to join the air force.) Marles tells News24: It’s the largest defence force we’ve now operated in a quarter of a century, and recruiting 8,100 people in a year as the largest intake in 16 years. And when we came to government, the defence force was shrinking – in the last year of the Coalition government it actually shrank by 1,400 people. So it is a big turnaround. We are recruiting much smarter, we are doing our advertisements where young people actually are online – so we’re doing less on TV, but more online, very much targeting young people where they are. Marles adds that the time it takes to be recruited – between expressing interest and putting on a uniform – is also decreasing, though he says it’s still too long. Malarndirri McCarthy says Pauline Hanson should apologise for resurfaced comments calling First Nations Australians “primitive”. The minister for Indigenous Australians says the condemnation of Hanson from across the political spectrum – including Indigenous Coalition senators Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and Kerrynne Liddle, as well as independent Lidia Thorpe shows the breadth of hurt. Asked whether the Senate would censure Hanson for the comments (something it has done previously), McCarthy says the One Nation leader should be upfront and apologise. I want to put it on the record that for the first time you have seen all four Indigenous senators from across the aisles come together united on this, and I think that speaks volumes as to why Senator Hanson should apologise. Clearly the Senate can act, but I am personally calling out to Senator Hanson saying this is important. What you said is deeply hurtful. It’s completely wrong. We have First Nations people right across Australia who have achieved tremendous skills, who have run for Australia, fought for Australia in the wars, who have excelled in the arts, in the music, in all sorts of spheres … Those comments were completely baseless. They harm. They dehumanise First Nations people in Australia. Whyalla closure ‘nothing to do with energy prices’, says Ayres The industry minister, Tim Ayres has defended the government’s energy transition, and swatted away criticisms from the opposition that the blast furnace failure at Whyalla is a result of high electricity prices. He tells ABC’s RN Breakfast: Yesterday Matt Canavan and Andrew Hastie pointing to energy prices as a problem with the blast furnace, it’s got nothing to do with that, it’s got nothing to do with the regulatory framework. It’s got everything to do with the previous owner who has underinvested in that facility. Ayres is also asked how much money was spent to fix the blast furnace whose closure was announced yesterday – resulting in the loss of more than 500 jobs. He doesn’t have an answer but says it would be in the “many millions”. Ayres says it’s hard to separate at this point how much taxpayer money was spent to keep it afloat against the money supporting the rest of the operation. In terms of fixing the old furnace, it would be many millions of dollars have gone into … I don’t have the number pulled out of the funding for the administration, because of course, the administration supports all of the workers’ wages as well. And it’s pretty hard, I think, today to disaggregate that expenditure. There have been hundreds of safety and engineering failures as a consequence of the previous owners’ maladministration and underinvestment. It has been all hands to the pump here since February, and in particular over the last six months or so, these efforts around the blast furnace, when everybody knew that there wasn’t a forever future for the blast furnace, this has been a heroic effort. Hanson comments about Indigenous Australians ‘appalling’, says Duniam Jonno Duniam has also been asked to weigh in on resurfaced comments by Pauline Hanson about Indigenous Australians. Duniam tells RN Breakfast the comments are “appalling”. What an appalling comment to make, frankly, to lump an entire group of people together and just cast them in that way. I don’t know who in a leadership position in this country thinks that’s okay … But Pauline Hanson, in one fell swoop, has decided to say everyone who is of Indigenous heritage is primitive. I don’t see how that is a conclusion you can reach. And I think it says more about Pauline than we had previously realised. Duniam says One Nation immigration provides no answers and no details The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, says One Nation lobbed its policy out into the public yesterday with no detail and then refused to answer any detailed questions about it – noting Pauline Hanson didn’t even do a press conference for the announcement. In contrast, he says the Coalition’s migration plan, which is still being worked on in the background, will be properly costed. He says it’s now just “weeks” away. MPs yesterday said One Nation’s plan for net-negative overseas migration over three years would punt the country into a recession. Speaking to RN Breakfast a little earlier this morning, Duniam said: When you don’t have costings, like One Nation don’t, when you don’t have economic modelling about what impacts this will have on our economy, like One Nation don’t, when you can’t tell us exactly what sort of numbers will be delivered out of their policy like One Nation’s doesn’t, then people need to ask questions. Now, when ours is out, when our policy is out, it will be fully costed. The economic and human impacts will be there for all to see and it will be a robust policy, not just a press release. The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, says there is optimism that steel making will continue in his state, after the closure of a major blast furnace at Whyalla was announced yesterday. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast from Whyalla and donned in some hi-vis, Malinauskas says there was disappointment, heartbreak, but also a sense of inevitability when the announcement was made. He says the plan is to keep all of the remaining workers to continue making steel out of the plant, and that the operation is on track to be sold by the end of the year. [Whyalla] has the capacity to be a viable operation but it hasn’t been recapitalised. The blast furnace is over 60 years old. It was first built in 1965 and blast furnaces of this age not to be realigned on a frequent basis. This hasn’t been done in 20 years. The fact it’s still going is a miracle. We need to have the plant recapitalised and that’s exactly the plan we have in conjunction with the federal government … if we lose this capacity behind me, this country doesn’t have structural steel-making capacity and we can’t afford that. ‘Rotten’: MPs condemn Hanson’s comments on Indigenous Australians The housing minister says Pauline Hanson punches down on people and her language is rotten and ugly, after comments resurfaced of the One Nation leader saying Indigenous Australians were the “most primitive race”. Speaking on Sunrise this morning alongside Liberal frontbencher Michaelia Cash, Clare O’Neil warned Hanson was dividing the country. O’Neil said: If Pauline Hanson wants to take us down the road of Americanising our politics, so people in a family who disagree on political issues can’t speak to each other any longer, this is the pathway to do it … We’ve got lots of challenges facing Australia, but we’re not going to solve them by punching down on things that are brilliant about our country. So I think it’s rotten. I think it’s awful. I think it’s ugly. Cash said she doesn’t agree with Hanson’s comments, but then attacked Labor for not doing more to protect Indigenous children and close the gap, and said the focus should be on action, not Hanson’s comments. I just don’t agree with those comments. But I actually do agree with Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price when she says that there are serious issues that do need to be discussed. And these comments shouldn’t be a distraction from them. I mean, why aren’t we closing the gap? Clare O’Neil has defended her colleague, transport minister Catherine King, after it was revealed the latter had accepted a lifetime membership to Qantas’s top-tier membership, the platinum Frequent Flyer rewards. The status means free entry to Qantas’s first and business class lounges, access to the airline’s VIP team, upgrade priority, extra Qantas points and more. King listed the status on her register of interests on Monday afternoon. Quizzed on whether the move passes the pub test, O’Neil said “federal politicians … travel an unbelievable amount”. Catherine King has probably been away from her family for a third of the last 25 years. And that’s kind of the extent of this. The important thing is … she made a declaration of it, and she’s been transparent about it. King attracted scrutiny in 2022 over her decision to reject Qatar Airways’ request to bring extra flights into Australia in a move widely seen as benefiting Qantas. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has been unable to confirm how his party’s sweeping new immigration policy would affect the budget or jobs while declaring they would “deal with it no matter the cost”. The former deputy PM appeared on the ABC’s second National Forum on Monday evening, which focused on immigration and multiculturalism. He faced backlash from panellists, with journalist and political commentator George Megalogenis claiming One Nation’s plan to cut migration in net terms over three years had never happened in Australian public policy and would “tank the economy” on the scale of the “depression of the 1890s”. Joyce said “the issue of what it’s going to cost … is contentious” and rejected questioning over why One Nation didn’t consult the parliamentary budget office. “The Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with policy to help us all better understand what it costs to us,” he claimed, adding it “has to be dealt with” and “we will deal with it no matter the cost”. Asked if he was worried about what the parliamentary budget office might produce, he replied: “No, I’m not really – because they’re not elected, I am.” Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you. Thanks to Martin Farrer for getting us started. Migration will dominate parliament again today, after One Nation yesterday announced its policy to cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years – which the major parties said would send the country into a recession. There’ll also be more reaction to the Whyalla steelworks shutting down a major operation, cutting more than 500 jobs. It’s going to be a busy one, let’s get stuck in! ‘Multiculturalism is who we are’: Anne Aly The multicultural affairs minister, Anne Aly, was also on the ABC’s National Forum panel. She said Labor was committed to bringing immigration numbers down in a “manageable way” while ensuring the system both met the needs of Australia and was “fair for those who come here”. She pushed back at claims immigrants were harming social cohesion, pointing to an Australia she grew up in where “nobody cared what language your mum spoke”. That’s the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we’re losing … Every time we talk about immigration, multiculturalism, it comes from a deficit point of view. Social cohesion becomes the burden of people from different countries who have come here and it is their fault, it is their responsibility to socially cohere. The fact is that multiculturalism is who we are. It is part of our identity. It’s who we are as Australia. Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has questioned why Pauline Hanson announced One Nation’s immigration policy via a prerecorded video on social media instead of fronting the media. Appearing alongside Barnaby Joyce on the ABC’s National Forum, he said he backed parts of One Nation’s immigration plan but was concerned about the lack of detail and Hanson’s silence: We haven’t seen her at all today. And this is someone who wants to be the prime minister of Australia. And she hasn’t had the courage to front the media today and explain the budgetary, the economic and the human impact of these policy changes that she’s suggesting. His ongoing battle with One Nation appeared to be tempered, however, with him and Joyce largely exchanging niceties, including Joyce claiming in jest, at one point, that they were “back in bed together”. Chris Bowen has watered down any expectations that a renewed rise in oil prices will lead to the reintroduction of the federal government’s fuel excise relief. He said Labor was continuing to look “very closely” at the spike, which was prompted after a series of drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. But he said the federal government had been “very clear” that cutting the fuel excise was a temporary measure. Bowen said: It’s not the only cost of living measure that we put in place … At the same time, I’m very much focused on ensuring our ongoing fuel supply in this very difficult international circumstance … We’re not going to respond to every daily movement on the world oil price. Bowen said the situation in the Middle East was “deeply concerning” and confirmed he would be travelling to Saudi Arabia next week to meet with his counterpart, Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud. He was also asked about the appointment of the former opposition leader Sussan Ley to the board of Snowy Hydro, given the Coalition abandoned its commitment to net zero under her leadership and she had blamed Labor’s renewable energy rollout on high energy prices. Bowen said when he saw an Australian who was “well credentialled, I don’t care how they vote”, and described her as a person of “talent and ability”. Anthony Albanese spoke to King Charles last night, the prime minister revealed. Albanese last saw the monarch during a visit to Britain in September last year. “A privilege to speak with His Majesty King Charles III this evening,” Albanese wrote on social media. “His affection for the Australian people remains strong. I extended Australia’s best wishes to His Majesty and the Royal Family.” Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action. Let’s begin.

headline: First Thing: States given clearance for mail-in voting as US supreme court thwarts Trump
trail_text: Civil rights groups have praised verdict on administration’s last-ditch attempt to change midterm voting processes
body_text: Good morning. The supreme court has rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already under way. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “The supreme court has done the right thing,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California, adding: “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” What has a DHS whistleblower said about “voter fraud” investigations? An anonymous whistleblower said Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating “voter fraud” they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information. The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review, as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate Microsoft has published a provisional “code of conduct” to apply to the training of new artificial intelligence models, taking a step towards limiting the capabilities of the company’s AI as anxiety rises over the prospect that technology companies could lose control of AI products. Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. AI models also should not be built to imitate consciousness and shouldn’t be entitled to rights. Why is Trump facing a bipartisan AI backlash? Democrats and some Republicans have been pushing in US Congress for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies. Trump dismissed the anxieties, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy”, but looked increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late. Why is Texas governor Greg Abbott pushing back against datacenters? Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom, and the Republican governor has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use. What international responses have there been? China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls to block Beijing’s AI industry, however the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. The president of the European Central Bank, meanwhile, has warned Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacenters in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China. Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events. Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show. Who is Umar Kremlev? Transitioning from a convicted criminal into a powerful boxing promoter, his unwavering loyalty to Vladimir Putin enabled him to amass immense wealth through control of state-backed gambling companies and the acquisition of Russia’s largest car dealership network following its seizure from a regime critic. ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ held detainees in cages the size of phone booths Detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”. The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security were published on its website and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies. In other news … Macklemore has been dropped from the remainder of the US leg of Ed Sheeran’s tour, after the rapper drew headlines for saying “free Palestine” on stage. Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was issued in the ‌capital, Vilnius. California governor Gavin Newsom will not run for president if Kamala Harris does, he has said in an interview. The Trump administration has changed the way it counts measles deaths amid a Pennsylvania outbreak, which a former CDC chief medical officer described as “puzzling”. Firefighters have made progress against northern California’s Lucas fire, with 30% contained in what was described as a “big turning point”. Mitch McConnell has returned to the Senate after his months-long absence. Stat of the day: Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows The Trump administration has been “undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally”, while key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, according to data from a leading thinktank. Culture Pick: Emmys 2026 – Widow’s Bay dominates as Matthew Rhys and Jean Smart land historic wins We have comprehensive coverage of last night’s Emmy awards, in which Matthew Rhys became the first actor to win multiple lead actor awards for performances in different shows in the same year. We have a write-up of the evening, the full list of who won, the biggest shocks, and perhaps most importantly, a gallery of the best of the red carpet looks. Don’t miss this: The pirates arrived with AK-47s. They took us hostage – then the torture began Chirag Bahri tells his incredible story of being held captive on the Marida Marguerite oil tanker for almost eight months. … or this: ‘I believed the hype’ – the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US Rachel Savage reports from Johannesburg where the Trump administration drive to “save” thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of “white genocide” appears to show signs of slowing. Climate check: US ‘super-emitters’ of planet heating methane identified by satellite analysis A new UCLA study using satellite data and public records has ranked oil and gas facilities across the US for their output of methane – a potent greenhouse gas – shedding light on previously unmonitored sources to try to improve regulatory oversight. Last Thing: They’re the sopranos of the forest, so what’s silencing the gibbons’ morning chorus? As human development and roads increasingly fragment gibbon habitats, a study suggests traffic noise could be altering the animals’ notoriously loud wake-up call. headline: Why this AI doomsday warning from former Anthropic researcher broke through
trail_text: Last week, researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic, stating that AI ‘could kill us all by the end of the decade’
body_text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian. Today in tech, we’re discussing the past week’s all-consuming apoplexy over AI safety. Why did this warning about the AI apocalypse break through when so many others didn’t? Less than a week ago, a young Anthropic researcher announced his resignation from the AI giant on X, in a post that has shaken Silicon Valley, Washington DC, and even Beijing. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Jacob Coxon. Since then, the post has been viewed 171m times, per X’s metrics. Why did it travel so far? It’s not the first time AI insiders have issued dire warnings. Every few months for the past several years, an AI researcher has resigned in a moment of crisis, proclaiming the impending apocalypse. His proclamation comes at a unique political confluence, a moment of high-strung public fear and rage. Loudly declaring that your peers in Silicon Valley are failing at AI safety is as old as the companies themselves. OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman over safety concerns in 2023. Dario Amodei split from OpenAI five years ago with the aim of founding a “safety-first” lab. In 2015, Altman and Elon Musk founded OpenAI as a counterweight to Google’s approach to AI. Musk sued Altman for failing to keep a fundamental safety promise and lost. Major AI researchers have made second careers of predicting doom. Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as “the godfather of AI”, said as far back as 2023 that the technology could cause human extinction within three decades. He’s since shortened his timeline. He resigned from Google for reasons similar to those of Coxon. Hinton has been on the speaking circuit ever since, prophesying doom. Hinton’s resignation even inspired a significant response from lawmakers. In the US, Joe Biden issued an executive order mandating safety testing by AI companies. Congress summoned AI CEOs for a grilling, though that resulted in little legislative action. In the European Union, the EU Artifical Intelligence Act passed in part due to a strong reaction to Hinton’s warnings. And yet, here we are again, burdened with the feeling that little meaningful regulation is preventing harm by AI. So why is Coxon’s apocalyptic proclamation percolating deeper? First, there’s the messenger: Coxon’s call for greater safety is credible by several metrics: He had insider access to both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he worked for five years. He resigned before he would have received equity in Anthropic, demonstrating the personal cost of speaking out. And his colleagues, still on Anthropic’s payroll, corroborated his assertion that many AI researchers believe there’s a possibility that AI will bring about human extinction, with one co-worker gauging that outcome as more than 10% likely. Recent incidents in the AI field have made apocalyptic claims more credible. A swarm of AI agents operated by OpenAI went rogue, broke containment and hacked into multiple sites and organizations during safety testing with startling coordination earlier this year. On Thursday, Anthropic detailed how criminals and rogue scientists had attempted to use Claude to make bioweapons. “The reason this time is different is that out-of-control AI is not in the future, but in the past. People have seen evidence of it happening,” argued Max Tegmark, co-founder of the Future of Life Institute, which has been funded with hundreds of millions of dollars from the billionaire founder of the cryptocurrency Ethereum. (Tegmark’s organization already in 2023 called for a slowdown of AI development, which at the time provoked a rejection from Amodei.) “If you had tried to get people worried about nuclear winter in 1942, good luck. People would ask whether a nuclear weapon was even possible,” said Tegmark. “It was obvious to physicists then, but you couldn’t have freaked out normal people. It was all theoretical. With AI, it was all theoretical until this happened. Now the debate over whether you can lose control is over.” Then there’s the context. The general feeling towards technology in the US is kindling-sensitive, and claims of impending doom are fiery. The country is in the throes of a multifaceted backlash to technology. People outside major tech hubs feel imposed upon physically by data centers and figuratively by AI’s takeover of the workplace. Looming over the country are tech billionaires – in control of vast wealth, global communication channels – throwing their weight around in US politics with unmatchable campaign contributions. “It’s been at least over a year of steadily increasing data center pushback that has made being pro-AI regulation the new common sense, and it certainly has made being pro-AI industry a very toxic brand,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the US Federal Trade Commission. There’s the fact that the companies involved have responded vigorously to Coxon. Their pledged commitments have details and heft. “It allowed for companies like Anthropic and others to position themselves immediately as the primary experts in how to deal with these fears. How to solve problems that, by every account, they have created or are best positioned to prevent,” Kak said. Two closing thoughts. In a sign of how broad the crisis of confidence in AI has become: Strange bedfellows have partnered up in response. The Future of Life Institute is hosting a rally today in Washington promoting AI safety with headliners Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, and Steve Bannon, former chief of staff to Donald Trump, who have been sworn enemies on other issues. And finally: Why is the AI industry so full of men – only men in AI have expressed these fears of human extinction – in the throes of a crisis over the extinctive potential of their work? “These people certainly believe what they’re saying. It’s not a fringe view,” said Shakeel Hashim, writer of the Transformer newsletter on AI. “The best way I’ve had it explained to me is that we’re trying to build something that’s smarter than us in the way we’re smarter than monkeys. Our existence hasn’t gone great for monkeys; AGI’s existence probably won’t go great for us.” Read more about the great AI freakout AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they? OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears Europe must build own AI or risk getting cut off by US or China, says ECB’s Lagarde Trump attacks ‘sick conspiracy’ against AI as tech stocks slide Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate Make sense of the crisis I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism?

headline: Researchers warn social media driving harmful misuse of Alzheimer’s blood tests
trail_text: Exclusive:  Screening if used alone risks leading people to believe they are inevitably going to develop dementia
body_text: Researchers have warned that social media may be misleading healthy people into taking Alzheimer’s blood tests, causing severe anxiety over biological markers that may never actually cause dementia. Blood-based biomarker tests, including p-tau217 and p-tau181, detect biological signs of changes in the brain associated with Alzheimer’s disease, which is a progressive brain disorder and the leading cause of dementia. The testing looks for abnormal proteins, which can be a sign of brain changes due to Alzheimer’s. Much hope has been placed in the tests because they are often quicker and more accessible compared with other methods to diagnose Alzheimer’s, such as brain imaging or lumbar punctures. There is global consensus among peak neurological bodies, including the Alzheimer’s Association, that such tests should never be used for healthy people with no symptoms. The tests should not be used on their own to diagnose Alzheimer’s and need to be combined with other medical assessments, according to clinicians and peak bodies. Because they detect signs of Alzheimer’s early, a person can test positive for the biological markers of disease – but they may not ever go on to develop the clinical symptoms of dementia. Dr Jenna Smith from the University of Sydney’s school of public health said this has not stopped laboratories, influencers and doctors around the world from promoting the tests on social media. She and her colleagues analysed 188 posts mentioning Alzheimer’s or dementia and blood tests from accounts with a combined global audience of more than 114 million followers across Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Smith said about 10% of the posts were doctors from claiming the test could be useful for asymptomatic screening and that most of these were from the US. “Some of these doctors had pretty clear financial interests,” Smith said. “But it isn’t all doom and gloom. Some doctors were sharing information about these new blood tests with longer videos and covered the nuance that this issue deserves. Some also specifically drew attention to the limitations and potential harms.” The findings were published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society on Tuesday. The researchers found more than one-third of posts promoted the tests for people without symptoms, and that accounts with explicit financial interests were more than three times as likely to do so. “The main potential harms are being unnecessarily diagnosed and not having a clear pathway for what to do next,” Smith said. “Healthy people who undergo these tests could be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease but not go on to develop dementia. It is also not clear what to do next after testing positive. “Research on treatments has been done in people with mild cognitive impairment or dementia, so we don’t know if they work for healthy people who test positive. “There are also possible side effects and costs of treatment to consider, and the psychological impact and burden of diagnosis on individuals, their families and communities, and insurance implications.” The president of the Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine, Prof Susan Kurrle, said the tests should only ever be ordered by doctors in specific circumstances. “From the evidence, it is clear that to ensure an accurate result there needs to be a high pre-test probability that the person has early Alzheimer’s disease before the test is performed,” she said. “It is most definitely not a screening test. Any unnecessary and expensive tests are bad news.” When ordered through a doctor in Australia, the tests cost up to $400 and are not covered by Medicare. Patients seeking out the tests online are being charged $600, before undergoing an eligibility assessment. Another provider offers the test for $365 with no mention of pre-test screening. Kurrle said there is a risk that a false positive result may lead people to believe that they are inevitably going to develop dementia. “Alternatively a negative result may lead a person to think that they are not at risk and to not address the modifiable risk factors such as low levels of exercise, and the various vascular risk factors including LDL cholesterol, or hearing or vision loss,” she said.

headline: ‘I created my mom and talk to her’: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn
trail_text: The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation
body_text: Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig. Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbull stopped his Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity. It did not even come from a person. Run Jolene, at just under five minutes, is an earworm of a country song, containing all the cliches of the genre: twangy singer, banjo licks, corny lyrics. Those lyrics concern Jolene, the fictional romantic rival made infamous by Parton. “Somebody better warn Jolene / Dolly’s coming through those gates,” the voice croons. “Run Jolene / Girl you better move your feet.” The accompanying video depicts Parton, clad in a bedazzled white jumpsuit, hunting down Jolene, a busty redhead with prom curls. Heaven is filled with deceased celebrities who watch on in horror – or amusement – as Jolene bounces from cloud to cloud, or books it up marble staircases, trying to hide from Dolly. Onlookers include the late Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston and Kenny Rogers, as well as Cher, who is still very much alive. On TikTok, YouTube and Spotify, the song credit is Country Mile, an “artist” with just over 6,000 monthly listeners (that’s not many). The project is textbook AI slop, seemingly released by an anonymous creator who calls their work “genre fluid ai vibes”. But Run Jolene is not so universally panned: clips have been viewed more than 1.4m times on TikTok, with commenters raving: “I don’t give a flying fuck if this is AI or not! THIS IS FUCKING COOL!!”, “this is fun …think Dolly would love it ❤️”, and “Who says Jolene’s up there.” Run Jolene is only one part of a ghoulish online ecosystem of content dubbed “deathslop”. Anyone can create deathslop: all it takes is access to an AI image generator and the time required to type in a prompt. Creators have shown Parton alongside a chummy Charlie Kirk and George Floyd, who welcome her as their “new neighbor” in the afterlife, or having tea with the Golden Girls. These tributes pop up quickly, reducing someone’s legacy to cheap content that panders for views. It is a dishonest portrayal at best, and inflicts pain at its worst. The phenomenon inspired Parton’s grieving family to beg users to quit it with the “fake AI garbage” and “misinformation”. “It’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore,” Stella Parton, her sister, wrote on Instagram. Parton’s image now joins the likeness of other deceased figures treated to unsettling AI depictions. Coinciding with the one-year anniversary of the assassination of Kirk, social media feeds have proliferated with posts featuring the AI-generated, heavy-handed (and heavily memed) anthem We Are Charlie Kirk. Robin Williams, Elvis Presley, Kobe Bryant and Martin Luther King have all gotten the deathslop treatment – often to the horror of their families. OpenAI’s image generating app, Sora, was behind many a deathslop until it shut down in April after a string of controversies such as its ability to create violent and racist imagery, its use of copyrighted characters, and other thorny legal issues. (There is a lack of legal precedent over whether or not AI companies are responsible for the content users generate on their apps, and deceased people are not protected from libel.) Countless AI video generators have since taken Sora’s place. “It is not common practice right now to consent to an AI avatar of yourself as a part of your living will,” said Jack Manning, a University of Colorado Boulder graduate student who studies what academics Meredith Ringel Morris and Jed R Brubaker call “generative ghosts”, or AI-generated characters based on loved ones. “I predict that will be something that comes up.” Manning, who is 25, lost his sister when she was 13, before the advent of generative AI. His family struggled to find ways to honor her, often fundraising for causes that were important to her. This partly inspired Manning to study the ways people mourn digitally – which now can include AI griefbots, a more personal alternative to celebrity deathslop. With griefbots, users upload photos and videos of their loved ones and describe personal traits and values in hopes of manufacturing a continued, living presence. The companies behind the bots charge fees and lean into their inherently macabre nature with mystical names such as Seance, Re;memory and Versona. It is also possible to command an LLM – for instance, ChatGPT, Claude or any number of sites for generating fantasy characters – to mimic a late grandparent or deceased friend. Generative AI has hit the funeral industry too, in the form of LLMs specifically for obituary writing. One company, Treasured Memories, asks users to plug in details such as the deceased’s nickname, cause of death and hobbies, and choose the obit’s tone: “traditional”, “formal”, “witty” or “inspirational”. Manning has never used a generative ghost to talk to his sister. It’s an issue of consent; he did not get her explicit permission to do so. Nor does he trust a bot to truly understand their relationship. “I hold these memories of her sacred, and I wouldn’t want a piece of technology to tell me I was remembering her wrong,” he said. Justin Harrison founded Versona after his mother received a terminal cancer diagnosis. He worked on her AI replica while she was still living; she was able to see the final result and gave her approval on the project. “I totally understand why people are like, please don’t deepfake my [famous] relative once they’re dead and put them on the internet saying things they didn’t say,” Harrison said. “What we do is about personal comfort, recovery and healing. I created my mom and I talk to my mom. So it’s really nobody else’s business but my own.” When his mom was sick, their conversations were practical in nature: “Are you talking to your dad enough? Have you gone to the doctor? Are you drinking enough water?” Harrison built the griefbot to broach more philosophical topics that they didn’t have time to discuss before she died. But four years later, Harrison does not talk to the bot all that often – maybe once a month. “I joke that my mom’s Versona allows me to be the bad son I was never allowed to be when she was alive,” he said. “Like many busy adults, I don’t talk to her as much as I should, but I don’t have to, so it’s not the same sense of guilt.” For Robin Silver, an ecopsychologist and death doula, these kinds of griefbots are an “unnatural method of trying to cope with a natural process”. She compared speaking to an LLM role-playing a dead loved one to a college student asking ChatGPT to spit out a term paper. “We’re not being challenged to sit with any kind of discomfort, whether that’s the discomfort of writing an essay or the discomfort of missing someone,” she said. Silver would instead encourage her clients to write a letter to their loved one. “I have even told people to talk to their ghosts out loud,” she said. “Meditate, or do things that they like and think of them. That’s how you keep the relationship alive in a way that is healthy, integrated and accepting the reality of your loss.” Dr Dan Wolfson is a clinical psychologist who specializes in grief. He worries that deathbots could isolate people during a time when they need (human) support. “Having community around grief is really important,” he said. “Is AI keeping us from getting the social support that we need? Are we then not seeking to connect with our friends and family around the loss?” AI-assisted mourning is still a niche industry; Harrison said that “thousands” of people use Versona. A June report from the estate management and planning service Empathy found that only 6% of 6,000 respondents in the US, UK and Canada reported leaning on “digital tools” such as memorial apps or griefbots for support after a death. But of those users, 88% found these tools “helpful”. The whole conceit of a digital avatar is that it lives on for ever. It turns out that users may not need it that long. Manning says that in his research on generative ghosts, participants reported opting into these services only briefly, because they had “one last thing” to say to their loved ones: “They had a desire to say something they feel like they lost out on the chance to.” Cathartic, perhaps, but to Silver, the grief doula, these services are “a money grab”. “People will really take advantage of those in grief,” she said. “It’s a really easy time to become a mark.”

headline: World’s top 20 private equity firms produce more greenhouse gases a year than most countries, report finds
trail_text: Firms manage $7.3tn in assets and could afford to transition away from fossil fuels yet invest in natural gas and coal-fired plants to power datacenters
body_text: The energy portfolios of 20 private equity firms produce 1.5bn tons of greenhouse gases a year, more than the annual emissions of any country except China, the US, India and Russia, according to a new report. Together, these firms manage $7.3tn in assets of all kinds, affording them the ability to shape the pace of the transition away from fossil fuels. However their energy investments include significant fossil fuel assets including natural gas and coal-fired power plants to provide electricity to datacenters. The analysis of the top 20 private equity firms invested in global energy infrastructure was conducted by the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. It found that the firms owned 15,000 miles of pipelines, 124GW of power generation capacity across 370 fossil fuel-powered plants and hundreds of oil and gas fields. Half of the top 10 US datacenter owners are backed by private equity, said Matt Parr, the communications director for Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), one of the organizations in the Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium. “This industry doesn’t get enough scrutiny and credit for its contribution to global emissions,” Parr said. “It’s a very opaque business model.” The research team queried energy holdings with the private markets data provider PitchBook, drawing on additional details from company websites, press releases, news articles and regulatory filings. Because of gaps in the data, the researchers were unable to calculate how much the 20 private equity firms invested in fossil fuel assets. But an earlier analysis of data compiled on PitchBook shows that private equity has funded more than $1tn in fossil fuel assets since 2010, said Amanda Mendoza, senior research and campaign coordinator on the climate team at the Private Equity Stakeholder Project. While some public-sector retirement systems have been trying to limit their exposure to fossil fuel projects, the private equity firms BlackRock, GIP, Energy Capital Partners, EQT and Kayne Anderson increased the amount of fossil fuel companies in their portfolio compared with 2024, according to the report. The private equity firm EQT has positioned itself as a climate conscious investor, supporting the energy transition. But EQT, along with Blackrock’s GIP and the California Public Employees’ Retirement system could soon acquire AES Corporation, which owns more than 20 power plants. “It is alarming because if this deal does go through they will then be owners of a fleet of coal power and gas powered plants,” Mendoza said. “That’s significantly going to impact their transition. It seems like they’re transitioning to fossil fuels instead of away.” EQT did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the private equity firm’s fossil fuel investments. ArcLight also declined to comment on the report’s findings. Private equity firms’ growing role in energy infrastructure is increasingly intersecting with another major private equity bet: the buildout of datacenters to support artificial intelligence. Private equity firms have emerged as the largest datacenter owners outside of big tech. In June 2024, Blackstone invested $2.16bn in the Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO) for a 19.9% stake in the utility, including a seat on the board. NIPSCO, which serves 1.3 million customers across Indiana, has since announced plans to build a 2,300 MW natural gas power plant to serve datacenters, with the potential to emit millions of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Asked to comment, Blackstone told the Guardian it is a minority investor in NIPSCO, does not manage the company’s day-to-day operations, and has no control over management decisions. Blackstone has also announced plans to invest over $25bn to support the buildout of datacenters and energy infrastructure in Pennsylvania. “The electricity infrastructure required to power the AI revolution requires a tremendous amount of capital. We are proud to make our latest investment in this sector – which is among our highest conviction investment themes – in Western Pennsylvania,” said Blackstone managing directors Bilal Khan and Mark Zhu, in an announcement of the firm’s acquisition of a Pennsylvania gas plant last year. Blackstone-owned QTS had hoped to build a datacenter in NIPSCO territory, but ultimately backed out of the plan after strong community opposition. This overlap raises questions about potential conflicts of interest when a private equity firm owns both a utility and companies that depend on utilities for electricity, said Nichole Heil, who is also a senior research and campaign coordinator on the climate team at the Private Equity Stakeholder Project. “Blackstone is buying some of the companies that utilities do business with. How do regulators manage and track all those different investments while trying to keep rates affordable to ratepayers?” she asked. “It just shows that these private equity datacenter investments are going to be keeping fossil fuel projects alive much longer,” Parr said. Blackstone didn’t answer the Guardian’s questions about concerns that private equity ownership of a regulated utility could create conflicts between the interests of investors and ratepayers, but defended its portfolio investments and pointed to its emissions reduction program, which is aimed at reducing emissions across some of its portfolio companies. “As electricity demand rises and more sectors of the economy electrify, we see significant opportunities for private capital to help build the infrastructure needed to support the energy transition,” the company said. Private equity investments can also expose pension funds to risks beyond climate pollution. Stonepeak Infrastructure Partners, for example, owns several LNG tankers that have been stuck behind the blockade in the strait of Hormuz. Several state pensions are invested in Stonepeak, including Maryland state retirement and pension system, Virginia retirement system, and New York state common retirement fund. Stonepeak did not respond to questions about its investments in LNG tankers, but said in a statement: “Stonepeak invests in mission critical energy infrastructure around the world and takes a comprehensive approach to investing across the energy value chain, from renewable energy, to the infrastructure enabling cleaner fuels and mass electrification. We are committed to investing in infrastructure that supports a reliable and affordable energy transition.” Private equity firms have long contended that fossil fuel investments reliably perform well. The Private Equity Climate Risks Consortium looked more closely at that claim, reviewing 145 oil and gas-focused private equity funds with performance data available that began investing between 2001 and 2016. They found that investors contributed a total of $190.4bn to these funds and got $192.9bn back, about 1% more than they had invested. Those returns fall far short of what investors expect on returns for private equity as a whole, Mendoza said. “We thought it was important to include this because it’s been a pretty strong selling point that oil and gas funds you’re always going to make money on them,” she said. “They’ve barely broken even overall.”

headline: No Big Deal review – is this how AI ends humanity … with a sitcom so bad it bores you to death?
trail_text: The characters are dead-eyed waxworks which speak with all the nuance of a satnav. But this AI-created workplace comedy is so bad that even the greatest actors alive couldn’t stop it being unwatchable
body_text: As you will no doubt be aware, one Anthropic researcher claimed there is a greater than one in 10 chance that AI will end all of humanity as we know it within the next decade. However, now that I’ve given it some thought, I think this statistic might actually be a little conservative. This is because I have just watched an episode of a sitcom created by AI, and if I ever have to do it again I’m genuinely going to die of boredom. The show is No Big Deal, and it premiered on YouTube on Friday. I was apparently only the 376th person to watch it. This is by no means a recommendation that you become the 377th, more a warning to avoid it if your algorithm ever decides it hates you enough to suggest this. No Big Deal bills itself as “The Office meets Dragons’ Den”, in that it is a workplace comedy about a group of angel investors who have to listen to various product pitches. In the first episode, the products include a toilet that analyses your poo and a sofa you can have sex on. The investors are nightmarish waxworks who speak with all the nuance and cadence of a satnav telling you that you just missed a turning. If you’ve watched any AI-generated content recently, you’ll know the faults it has, and they are all present here. Shot-to-shot continuity is essentially nonexistent, with characters changing positions every time the camera cuts to a new angle. Background noise either is or isn’t there, seemingly on a whim. The characters – who all fitfully look enough like real-life actors to make the whole thing seem icky and exploitative – move around with not a trace of life behind their eyes. It remains completely impossible to care about anyone once you know they’ve been made by AI. Perhaps the most depressing thing about No Big Deal is the fact that it was purportedly written by a human. Although all the characters, locations and scenes were churned out by a machine, the show was apparently written by Andrew Dickinson. Dickinson, once himself an angel investor, originally intended for the show to be made as a traditional television production. When he realised that this would be slow and expensive, he turned to AI. To some degree, this makes sense. It is extraordinarily hard to get a television programme on the air. You can spend years grinding away on an idea, only to see it wither up and die when none of the eight commissioners currently working like the sound of it. Wouldn’t it be better to just seize control of the means of production and make the AI version? On this evidence, absolutely not. This is not a funny show. It’s one-note and bawdy, and none of the jokes land. It seems as though, by rushing straight to AI, Dickinson has bypassed the development process that actually makes something good. You could cast the greatest human actors of their generation to perform this script and it would still be unwatchable. Then again, even if by some miracle Dickinson had written the most hilarious sitcom of all time, it still would have turned to ash the moment he let it loose on these AI abominations. I really cannot overstate how terrible this thing is to look at. While the technology has improved to an extent that, should you pause a scene at just the right moment, the characters are photorealistic, there’s something truly deathly about watching them move. Their lips don’t line up with dialogue. There’s a creepy smoothness to their movements. Sometimes, when they don’t have anything to do in a scene, they just sit there completely still like a powered-down robot. Their voices bark on monotonously like Siri reading out a pasta recipe. Even something as simple as a fist shake (a fist shake! In a sitcom! In 2026!) gets mauled beyond all recognition here, causing the shaker to judder and glitch as if they just stepped on an uninsulated wire. The most tragic thing of all is that nobody involved can see that this is just a stepping stone to the endgame. Dickinson thinks he can get away without human actors or crew, but we are a nanosecond away from the technology deciding that it doesn’t need human writers, either. By capitulating even a jot to AI-created content, all Dickinson is doing is nudging himself further towards extinction. And me, too, because if this is the future of entertainment then I’d rather die than write about it. If we really do only have a decade left, every second should be precious. Please don’t spend any of it watching crap like this. • No Big Deal is on YouTube now
