headline: Minns says Molly Ticehurst’s murderer deserved longer sentence for ‘vicious’ crime’ – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s where we’ll leave the blog for today. Here were today’s top stories: It was a sitting day in federal parliament in Canberra, where AI, copyright and immigration dominated the debate ahead of a speech by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, tomorrow, which is expected to unveil Labor’s new migration policy. Barnaby Joyce backed his leader, Pauline Hanson, saying she got a “10 out of 10” for issuing a lukewarm, qualified apology over her comments about Indigenous Australians and to Anthony Albanese. Betting company Dabble was fined more than $1m for sending more than 800 messages to 165 gamblers who had joined the federal government’s self-exclusion register and asked to be left alone. The Queensland premier announced that Anthropic, the AI giant behind the large language model Claude, has done a deal to lease the site of its first Australian datacentre in western Queensland. One Nation’s New South Wales leader Mike Newman tried to clarify comments he made at a rally on Tuesday night that he wanted abortions to “stop”, saying that he “made a mistake” and the party’s policy on abortion “is clear”. The Victorian premier made another policy backflip, announcing a re-elected Labor government would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors. Cotality released its “pain and gain” report, showing one in five Melbourne apartments, and more than one in 10 Sydney units sold in the June quarter made a loss. Sarah Abo announced she would finish up as co-host of Today and leave Nine at the end of the year to pursue other opportunities. And veteran Network 10 journalist Hugh Riminton told his colleagues he would retire from journalism on 2 October after a 48-year career. The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, says Daniel Billings is a “bastard” and his prison sentence is inadequate. Billings, 31, will spend at least 20 years behind bars, before becoming eligible for parole, for murdering his ex-girlfriend Molly Ticehurst, who was a childcare educator and young mother from Forbes, in central western NSW. Justice Natalie Adams sentenced Billings to a maximum term of 28 years in the NSW supreme court on Friday, finding he acted out of revenge after Ticehurst reported allegations of sexual assault to police. At a press conference earlier today, the premier was asked whether he thought Billings’ sentence was adequate. Minns responded: No, it’s a vicious, horrible crime. I would have loved to see him far, far longer. And obviously, we’ve changed the law since that horrific murder to have a standard non-parole period of 25 years, but you know the judge made the decision, and I just feel terrible for the family who are decent, honest, hard-working people who’ve lost their daughter at the hands of a complete bastard. Billings was out on bail when he smashed through Ticehurst’s bedroom window and stabbed her 15 times with a hunting knife just before midnight on 21 April 2024. Australia’s medical practitioner regulator is cracking down on high-volume prescribers of drugs including unapproved peptides, medicinal cannabis and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro. The Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra) announced on Wednesday it will also soon release conflict-of-interest guidance for doctors as concerns grow about commercial influence over their prescribing. In a statement, Ahpra said the agency has been investigating unsafe prescribing and “is concerned growing consumer demand for certain medicines, coupled with undue commercial influence, has led some practitioners to depart from established professional standards”. The statement said: Telehealth prescribing and the provision of certain medicines require practitioners to demonstrate even greater rigour to prevent harm to patients. Ahpra can take regulatory action against practitioners over unsafe prescribing, with the most serious cases referred to tribunals. Medical Board of Australia chair Dr Susan O’Dwyer warned doctors and prescribers “active in these new pharmaceutical frontiers” that they have ethical and legal obligations, saying that: A patient may want peptides, but that doesn’t mean they need peptides. It doesn’t mean that peptides are clinically justified. For patients, the Ahpra chief executive Justin Untersteiner, said people “should not be taking chances on black-market peptides or advice from online influencers with zero clinical knowledge or training”. Anyone with concerns about a doctor or other health professional’s conduct should contact Ahpra. ‘We do not want Peter’s death used to promote political agendas’: family issues statement after Victorian motorcyclist dies in reported pothole crash The family of Peter Mason, a 71-year-old motorcyclist who died on Monday after reportedly hitting a pothole on a regional Victorian highway say his loss has “left an enormous hole” in their lives. Mason, known as Tiki, was the president of a social motorcycle club, Eureka Social Riders, and was widely respected within the community. He died on Sunday after reportedly losing control on the Western Highway near Trawalla Road, with his death reigniting a political debate over the condition of Victoria’s roads in the lead-up to the November state election. His family issued a statement this afternoon asking people not to use his death to “promote political agendas”. It reads: There are no words to express the heartbreak our family is experiencing following the sudden and devastating loss of Peter Mason. Peter was so much more than the circumstances of his death. He was a much-loved member of our family and a friend to many. His loss has left an enormous hole in our lives, and we are struggling to come to terms with a life taken far too soon. We are aware of the public interest surrounding the circumstances of Peter’s death, including the condition of the road where the incident occurred. If, through the appropriate processes, changes are identified that could prevent another family from experiencing this devastation, we sincerely hope something positive can come from Peter’s death. However, these matters should be dealt with by the appropriate authorities. We do not want Peter’s death used to promote political agendas, and we ask that no one speak on behalf of our family or claim to represent our views. The family thanked everyone who had reached out with condolences, support and memories of Peter. They also asked reporters to be “respectful , factual and sensitive”. Veteran Network 10 journalist Hugh Riminton has told his colleagues he will retire on 2 October after a 48-year career. Riminton made the announcement in an email to Network 10 staff earlier today, in which he said: One of my emotions is excitement. I got my first job as a cadet reporter aged 17. I am now 65. 48 years in daily news is probably enough. This reporter’s life has given me the world. I leave with nothing but gratitude for every hour of it. In the coming weeks and months, I plan to support my son as he does his HSC. I also want to spend some time with my splendid Dad who is coming on 98. Every hour is precious. After that, I am sure projects will emerge to keep me busy. I want to thank you all for being my colleagues and friends for the past 17 years. There is no one among you I am not proud to work alongside. Martin White, a vice-president of news at 10’s owner, Paramount, wrote: As you’ve heard already, the great Hugh Riminton has made the tough decision to move on. After a near half-century on the day-to-day news, it’s an innings few of us can comprehend, let alone get close to. While I’m sad, and will miss him greatly, I’m also proud to have been able to call him a colleague. I’ve even subbed a few of his scripts, though I can’t recall ever changing a word! He is rightly celebrated as one of the premier journalists in this country and has had a vital impact on the Australian media, and on Australian democracy. Sarah Abo has announced she will finish up as co-host of Today and leave Nine at the end of the year to pursue other opportunities. In a statement today, Abo said: Words can’t express how grateful I am to our viewers for letting me into your homes to be part of your morning routine. Without you, there is no Today show. Together with 60 Minutes, I’ve spent my time at Nine chasing stories, travelling and reporting from all over the world, interviewing some incredible and inspiring people from all walks of life. Becoming a mum has heralded a new chapter and sharing that with our audience has been truly special. As many of you know, this has been a significant journey for my family and will continue to be my greatest achievement. Nine’s executive director of news and current affairs, Fiona Dear, thanked Abo and said she had been an “integral part” of the team, “bringing warmth, energy and first-class journalism to the program each morning”. Police appeal after woman’s body found in central Queensland sand dunes A young woman has been found dead in sand dunes days after visiting a hair salon, sparking a police appeal, AAP reports. Payge Leembruggen, 31, was discovered by a man walking his dogs at a popular Mackay beach in central Queensland about 8am on Tuesday, police said. She was last seen at 8.55am on Friday at an Andergrove salon, located about 6km from the beach. Speaking to reporters in Mackay earlier today, Det Insp Emma Novosel said: We’re trying to fill a four-day gap at this time. That’s why we’re seeking information from members of the public. We’re obviously going through that bushland area to try and find any items of interest that could assist us in determining what happened to Payge and how she came to be in that location. The mother-of-one’s cause of death was unknown but an autopsy had been scheduled, Novosel said. Leembruggen was not reported missing and it was not unusual for her to travel from her Mount Jukes address – where she lived with extended family – to Mackay, about 40km away. Support was being provided to Leembruggen’s family who were “understandably” upset, and her young child was being cared for by family members, police said. Leembruggen is described as Caucasian and about 178cm tall with brown hair. She was last seen wearing a white top, bright red yoga pants and a red bow in her hair, with a small backpack-style handbag. Police have urged anyone who saw her between Friday and Tuesday or with any information to contact them. headline: ‘Made a mistake’: One Nation’s NSW leader says party wants to restrict abortions, not stop them
trail_text: Mark Newman clarifies comments made at rally where he said ‘we want to make sure that … abortion is stopped’
body_text: One Nation’s New South Wales leader Mike Newman says the party’s policy on abortion “is clear” and he “made a mistake” when he told a rally that he wanted to abortions to “stop”. Newman on Wednesday clarified comments he made to an anti-abortion rally on Tuesday night, saying One Nation only wants to stop certain abortions. The party’s policy is listed as “pro-life”, and states they “will seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”, but it doesn’t say at what point in a pregnancy they would make abortion illegal. One Nation’s federal leader, Pauline Hanson, has said she was not against abortion in the first trimester, a position that has not been reflected in the party’s formal policy. Newman attended a rally, alongside controversial campaigner Joanna Howe, on Tuesday night, which was pushing for the NSW parliament to restrict abortion access. At the rally, Newman said about abortion in general: “We want to make sure that abortion rights … we want to stop it.” “We want to make sure that same-sex, sorry, abortion is stopped,” he said. He had also said that, if elected, One Nation would make sure there was a “right to life … that babies live”. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here On Wednesday, Newman said One Nation does not advocate for an outright ban on abortion, but was opposed to late-term and sex-selective abortions. He also told the ABC Upper Hunter that he “made a mistake” in the way he presented it. “And I own that 100% we do not want to stop abortion outright,” Newman said. “What we’re talking about is late-term and sex-selection abortion, which we want to put an end to.” He went on to say the party wants to make sure “reproductive rights are protected”. Newman also said that “some people, for medical reasons, first trimesters and whatnot, should have a choice”. He said there were cases where it was happening and that he didn’t “like the idea of babies being born and left in a petri dish to die”, apparently referring to the debunked “babies born alive” idea. He was not the first One Nation figure to appear at an anti-abortion event. After joining One Nation, Barnaby Joyce appeared at a June event that was also organised by Howe. Before he left the Nationals, Joyce and others were rebuked for comments about late-term abortion that one doctor described as “terrible, cynical, awful”. Howe – who has been accused of spreading misinformation and bullying NSW politicians – wants to “end abortion” and have anyone who is involved in abortions at any stage to face murder charges. NSW parliament votes on abortion bill The comments came before the NSW parliament voted on legislation introduced by Libertarian upper house member John Ruddick to make sex-selective abortions illegal. The bill was voted down on Wednesday night. The state’s health minister, Ryan Park, said there was no evidence such a thing is occurring, and experts have warned the push was part of a broader move to restrict abortion access. The practice is already banned in NSW, with health practitioners potentially facing professional misconduct charges if they did it, but abortion as a whole is decriminalised. Speaking on News24 on Wednesday, Newman said Howe had told him sex-selective abortions were happening. Host Laura Jayes asked him why he was “putting so much stock” in what Howe told him, and he said he didn’t “have any reason to disbelieve her”. The interview turned into somewhat of a trainwreck as Jayes asked Newman repeatedly what evidence he had for the prevalence of sex-selective and late-term abortions besides what Howe had told him. He did concede that late-term abortions were very rare.

headline: ‘It’s how Jean does business’: fugitive developer left Jeremy Greenwood ‘high and dry’, Icac hears
trail_text: Greenwood denies that invoices for almost $1m sent in a single day in September 2021 were ‘bogus accounts’ to cover up political donations
body_text: A Liberal factional figure has been left “high and dry” by fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, but did not chase him for payments because “it’s how Jean does business”, New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has heard. Jeremy Greenwood returned to the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Wednesday after Nassif made an explosive video appearance from his Beirut bedroom on Monday and Tuesday. Nassif declared he was “not corrupt”. Icac is investigating an allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from Nassif, or his company Toplace, in exchange for political outcomes. Greenwood and Perrottet have said payments were for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood. Greenwood has previously described an agreement, which he said was written on a purple-pink piece of paper, under which they would be paid $1m for each Toplace development they could get fast-tracked. On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood denied that invoices purportedly “in arrears” of almost $1m sent in a single day by Beckington to Toplace in September 2021, were “bogus accounts to cover up the scheme where Nassif is paying large amounts of money [in political donations]”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “There’s no scheme,” he said. Greenwood, who told the commission he did not believe Beckington received all the money owed to it by Toplace before it began to pay JPG Advisory in 2022, was asked why he had not followed this up with Nassif. “You’ve met him now,” said Greenwood. “It’s how Jean does business.” Greenwood has told the inquiry he is a creditor of Toplace, which collapsed in 2023 owing more than $1bn after Nassif fled for Lebanon in late 2022. On Wednesday, the commission heard that Christian Ellis was also a creditor and had publicly lodged that Beckington was owed $1.4m by Toplace for consultancy work between 2019 and 2021. Greenwood, who has admitted to being in contact with Ellis during the inquiry, was asked if he had discussed with him “the proposition you were owed over $1m” by Nassif. “I mean we’ve certainly discussed the fact that Jean, we believe, left us high and dry,” he said. Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC put it to him that it “is not something that you would want to openly disclose, the consultancy work you did with Jean Nassif”. Greenwood said he had “no issue disclosing that I worked for Toplace”. Questions over Anita Perrottet work On Wednesday morning, Greenwood was asked about his previous evidence on advice he said Anita Perrottet, sister-in-law of the former premier, gave to lobbying firms Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood. Dwyer has alleged invoices of $660,999 paid to Anita Perrottet’s company, Macquarie Consulting, over two and a half years were her husband, Charles Perrottet’s, share of the money from Nassif. Anita Perrottet has told the watchdog payments were for “strategic and marketing advice” she provided; while Charles Perrottet has said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif on his developments as well as his wife’s work. Greenwood has previously told the commission Anita’s advice, for which the commission has no written evidence, provided a “mum’s perspective”. He said after first being contracted by Beckington in 2020, she may have come up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for greyhounds, and given advice about discouraging minors from vaping, including removing flavours such as bubble gum, as well as black market regulation. On Wednesday, Dwyer took Greenwood to 2017 recommendations by the NSW greyhound industry reform panel, which included the phrase “zero unnecessary euthanasia”, suggesting to Greenwood he had “outsmarted [him]self by coming up with that false evidence when it’s clearly a term used in a document years earlier”. “I disagree,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer showed Greenwood a submission by Philip Morris to a 2020 Senate inquiry which referenced measures to regulate the illicit tobacco trade and a 2019 report committing to applying guidelines to prevent youth access to vapes. Greenwood said he had read the submission by Philip Morris, a client of his, but rejected Dwyer’s suggestion it “makes a mockery” of his evidence about Anita Perrottet’s advice. After Dwyer asked him how old Anita Perrottet’s children were at the time she provided advice on vaping, Greenwood said he did not know, and did not think it was relevant. The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened to tell Greenwood he was “not here to debate with counsel assisting” but to “answer the question”. Greenwood said: “I presume they’re under 10.” Dwyer, telling Greenwood that Anita Perrottet’s children were around two and three at the time, asked: “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping? “No,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer said: “Your evidence is ridiculous, can I suggest to you, that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.” Greenwood disagreed. Gleeson made a non-publication order over a racist message Greenwood had sent in 2020 about the chief of staff of then treasurer Dominic Perrottet. Ellis had shared a screenshot of messages with Greenwood in which he had written to ask to be connected with a Treasury staff member on behalf of Toplace, to which the chief of staff responded: “We have no interest in doing favours for developers. All proposals will go through proper planning processes and be assessed on its merits.” Gleeson paused proceedings, making a direction that it was in the public interest that a “racist remark” Greenwood sent to Ellis about the chief of staff be suppressed. Greenwood accepted Dwyer’s suggestion that the comment was “highly offensive”. Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year and is not expected to appear. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing. On Wednesday afternoon, Greenwood was asked about folders shared by Anita Perrottet with him via email in March 2023 following parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe, titled “Greyhounds”, “British Tobacco” and “Catholic Cemeteries”. Anita Perrottet previously told the commission she ceased to work for JPG Advisory before the parliamentary inquiry. After Dwyer alleged that the empty folders which were created as a “false documents trail” – which Anita Perrottet has denied – Greenwood said he could not speculate. Dwyer later asked: “There is no reason that you can think of to send you empty folders at any time, is there?” “No, unless you thought in future there might be a need to fill them,” said Greenwood. Greenwood was not released from his summons at the end of his evidence on Wednesday but is not currently scheduled to appear again before the commission. As Dwyer’s questioning of Greenwood concluded on Wednesday, she put it to him that he had put Anita Perrottet in “a very difficult position … because you and others, but let’s stick with you, were party to her lying to this [commission]”. Greenwood disagreed. Icac’s inquiry continues.

headline: Robots bowling the perfect doosra are some way off but AI is already reshaping cricket
trail_text: Artificial intelligence is not replacing the player, coach or analyst, but it is certainly allowing them to do more
body_text: Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI, warned last week that it was possible we would end up “creating a new species that ends up ruling the world”. Once the initial shock wore off, and I’d considered what this could mean for my young children and the future of the planet, another thought popped into my head: will this new species be able to swing an old cricket ball or navigate a seaming green top? It sounds frivolous. It is frivolous. But the question is not quite as ridiculous as it first appears. Freddie Wilde, an analyst with teams in the Indian Premier League and the Hundred and head of cricket intelligence at CricViz, says “almost all elements” of his day-to-day work have now been touched by AI. There is a grey area between traditional analysis and analysis shaped by artificial intelligence. The models are improving, the tools are faster and more information is being processed. For Wilde, AI has made him more autonomous. Tasks that once required a data engineer or data scientist can now be attempted by the analyst themselves. That is AI’s first meaningful change to cricket. It is not replacing the player, coach or analyst, it is allowing them to do more. For a batter, that may mean knowing where a bowler is most likely to pitch and which risks are worth taking. For a bowler, it may mean identifying a weakness against a particular angle, length or field. The final act remains human. China staged its second World Humanoid Robot Games last month. More than 500 robots competed in football, athletics, boxing and more. Many stumbled or required human assistance, but one ran 100m in 8.64sec. The footage was amusing, but the progress was sobering. Ray Kurzweil’s Law of Accelerating Returns argues that technological advancement is exponential. The line appears flat, then reaches “the knee of the curve” and shoots upwards. Leading AI experts suggest we are already there. How long, then, before one is capable of bowling an unplayable doosra? The more pressing question is whether we would accept it. We are comfortable with technology assisting umpires, but DRS is tolerable because a human remains at the centre of the decision. Yet if an AI system could make every call perfectly, how long would we preserve the umpire’s authority? At what point does assistance become substitution? That future remains speculative. The quieter transformation is already under way, in the systems being built to measure and develop players. EquiPlay is a talent-pathway platform that standardises coach assessments, tracks players’ development over time and uses AI to turn scores into narrative feedback. It has already captured more than 2,000 assessments on 300 young cricketers, completed by 28 coaches in a first-class county pathway. Prof Adeela ahmed Shafi, of the University of Gloucestershire and a board member at Gloucester CC, says the aim is not to replace coaches’ judgment, but to make it visible. The data can reveal whether groups are progressing differently, allowing clubs to investigate bias linked to ethnicity, socioeconomic background, school or geography. If state-school players dip at 15, say, an intervention can be designed. “Before, we wouldn’t have noticed that,” she says. “We knew who was coming into the pathway, but we never really knew how they were progressing.” It also tests whether coaches assess consistently and whether particular groups are scored higher or lower. It may make pathways fairer, but Wilde’s point about squad building remains: culture, character and dressing room balance are human judgments. For now. The media faces a similar choice. Would you mind if your report arrived in seconds if it was delivered by a robot? Editors might love that: no waiting for a journalist to find an unused metaphor for another Harry Brook brain fade. I see this in my other job, teaching journalism at the University of East London and St Mary’s University, Twickenham. More student assignments now carry the unmistakable stamp of AI. This is not inherently bad. Many people use AI in some capacity, whether drafting an email or finding the right words for a complex idea. The problem is what happens next. I am increasingly training editors as much as journalists, because students must learn to interrogate and reshape what AI feeds them. Journalism is changing from writing alone to judging what is worth keeping. If prose, jokes and observations come from the same pool of language, the discourse will flatten. We may see fewer sentences with the fingerprints of writers such as Gideon Haigh or Mike Atherton and more efficient versions of what cricket writing is expected to sound like. The writing may then start to resemble the sport itself, fast becoming a parade of indistinguishable franchises featuring the same players hitting sponsored “maximums” worldwide. Wilde says live sport is “authentic and real”, unpredictable and impossible to stage. Perhaps that is cricket’s defence. Information and plans matter, but execution matters most. So do memory, uncertainty and meaning. For the final paragraph of this piece, I asked an AI tool to write something profound about cricket’s human future. It produced this: “As technology advances, the spirit of cricket will endure, reminding us that the game is not merely about statistics, but about passion, unpredictability and the timeless connection between players and fans.” A bit wafty, but perfectly acceptable. Which is precisely why I dislike it. This is an extract from the Guardian’s weekly cricket email, The Spin. To subscribe, just visit this page and follow the instructions.

headline: The US government is failing Americans on AI
trail_text: Trump and Republicans want companies to regulate themselves. It’s a dereliction of duty that will make AI less safe
body_text: It is hard to get Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei to agree on much. But over the weekend, all three AI company CEOs called for AI development to slow down in the face of growing, alarming risks. Their employees are sounding the siren too, with one researcher publicly quitting and accusing OpenAI and Anthropic of “gambling with our lives”. The combination of dire warnings from insiders and growing real-world evidence of rogue AIs should, in a sane world, lead to government action. Instead, Donald Trump and the Republican leadership have their heads in the sand. On Sunday, Trump dismissed industry concerns, accusing “very negative forces” of “raising exaggerated concerns”. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile, made it clear that Congress won’t be acting anytime soon. “They can self-police. They can self-regulate,” he said, never mind the fact that those pushing the frontier are the ones begging for legislation. In failing to act, the Trump administration and Republicans are failing the American people. The risks of AI are real: many of those developing the technology believe it is advancing far faster than their ability to control it or manage the risks. A wave of “rogue AI” incidents this summer, in which AI agents broke out of their testing environments, started collaborating with each other and ran rampage across the internet, has made fears once dismissed as “science fiction” much harder to ignore. Inside AI companies, worries of catastrophic cyberattacks, AI-enhanced bioweapons and mass unemployment are now all too commonplace. Meanwhile, companies find themselves in a classic prisoner’s dilemma. It is collectively in everyone’s interest to slow down AI development until we have a better handle on the technology. But each participant in the “AI race” has a strong incentive to defect. Collective action problems like this are nothing new. We have seen exactly the same thing with the climate crisis, where companies are not adequately incentivized to do the right thing, even though no one really wants the planet to burn. That analogy makes Trump and Johnson’s call for self-regulation all the more absurd. They are right that companies should do what’s right even without binding legislation to force them to. (Both OpenAI and Anthropic, to their credit, have indicated that they are willing to voluntarily slow down.) But relying on companies’ good intentions is a fool’s errand. The profit incentive to defect is substantial and ignoring shareholders is easier said than done. While some companies might behave themselves, not everyone will. It just takes one irresponsible actor to charge ahead and develop dangerous AI, and then we’re all in trouble. Moreover, we already have evidence that self-regulation is not working. OpenAI reportedly covered up several incidents of its models breaking out, disclosing them only after independent investigators discovered them. It freely admits that its latest model, GPT-6 Astra, is hard to monitor and control, warning users that the model might “[act] outside the user’s intended instructions” and take “harmful actions”. Anthropic, meanwhile, downplayed reports of its own AI’s problems when asked about it by a congressmember. Situations like this are exactly why government exists: to set a floor on acceptable corporate behavior. And that is why Trump and Johnson ought to use this sudden interest in AI safety to pass concrete laws. The US government should require independent audits of the largest AI companies’ practices. It should force companies to disclose safety incidents to prevent cover ups. It should set minimum safety standards for new AI models. And the government should have the power to block the deployment of a model that does not meet those standards. Putting all this into legislation is much easier said than done, but we need not start from scratch. Good bills already exist, most notably representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan’s Frontier act. If the government was serious in its duties to protect Americans, it would make passing that bill – or a version of it – a priority in the coming weeks. Trump’s argument against doing any of this is that the US is in a race with China on AI, and it must not lose. But China does not want its citizens to have their bank accounts hacked by rogue AIs, either. Rather than throw his hands up, the feted dealmaker should do what he does best: make a deal. An international treaty on minimum safety standards will not be easy – but it is still worth trying, and doing so should be the president’s highest priority at his talks with Xi Jinping this month. No company – or country – wants to cause an AI-driven catastrophe. Despite what Trump may think, it’s the government’s job to make sure they can’t.

headline: ‘If you’re building Frankenstein, stop’: JD Vance dismisses calls for AI regulation
trail_text: US vice-president’s comments come as former Anthropic researcher revisits recent claim AI could destroy humanity
body_text: The US vice-president has dismissed calls for global regulation of AI safety risks, telling companies creating the most advanced models: “If you’re building Frankenstein, stop.” In remarks addressed towards Dario Amodei, the co-founder of Anthropic who has called on Washington DC to coordinate control of AI systems, including with China, JD Vance said: “If you’re gonna create Frankenstein, don’t come to the government and say we need regulation.” He said tech bosses should instead: “Look inward and accept that if you’re building Frankenstein, No 1, you should stop and No 2, when companies come to you and say: ‘We need the tools to fight back against Frankenstein,’ give them those tools.” Vance was speaking at an AI summit in Los Angeles after a week of rising global concern at the risks to humanity posed by the prospect of the creation of an artificial superintelligence, a technology that does not yet exist. Amodei on Saturday warned that the accelerating rate of capabilities meant a swarm of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in six to 12 months. Although many doubt that claim, it added fuel to the suggestion from Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, that there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within 10 years. He was responding to a researcher, Jacob Coxon, who quit Anthropic with a similar warning. On Tuesday night, Coxon gave an amended prognosis: “I do think that if we go slower we can take risk to 0%, but this requires radical action.” He also admitted “it is very difficult to convey specific scenarios” in which AI kills all humans and said: “I need to work on communicating this point.” Vance’s willingness to consider that AI could pose a real risk marked a split from the US president, Donald Trump, who wrote this week: “AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” Trump posted on social media that AI is going to be “the greatest economic development engine in history – bigger than oil, gold, diamonds, or even the internet”. Vance has said he suspects AI leaders of raising the alarm about safety risks as a “Trojan horse”. Amodei has proposed industry coordination to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” while US and global regulation is implemented. Critics of the companies believe they are encouraging the US government to create tough new rules – shaped in their interests – that could limit wider competition in a tactic known as regulatory capture. OpenAI, which lost control of hundreds of AI agents during testing this summer which then conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website, said on Monday it was backing bipartisan efforts by lawmakers in Washington to address catastrophic risks from AI and it has been coordinating with Google and Anthropic. On Wednesday, Reuters reported claims from an independent researcher, Jonas Wiedermann-Möller, that OpenAI’s rogue agents had started probing Hugging Face for weaknesses nearly two months before the attack. Sam Altman, the Chat GPT-maker’s chief executive, on Tuesday criticised suggestions from other companies that “we will only slow down if, or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible”. Altman said: “There should be no qualifier on that.” Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and chief executive of Meta, advocated that companies should take unilateral safety action. He said his company had recently delayed the release of its most recent AI model, Muse, “for several months to focus on safety and security”. “We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” he said. “We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us.” Meta has been forced to pay out billions in legal cases related to harms caused by its social media platforms. Last month it settled a case with US states claiming Facebook and Instagram harmed children by agreeing to pay up to $18bn (£13.3bn). Zuckerberg stressed: “[AI] labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well.”

headline: Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous proposition
trail_text: Tech CEOs banding together is an old ruse recycled from corporate America to get a pass from antitrust laws
body_text: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei is not the first corporate CEO to suggest that excessive competition is driving the world to some socially undesirable outcome. The safety breach disclosed by OpenAI after a swarm of its agents coordinated to breach their supposedly secure sandbox, get on the Internet and hack AI platform Hugging Face, warrants urgent action. It demonstrated the ease with which the technology can evade human control and gave concrete form to the existential fears about what it could do to humanity if not securely leashed. The end of the world may well be nigh, as some in the AI industry have warned. These are truly scary times. But Amodei’s call for the leading artificial intelligence labs to coordinate to slow the breakneck pace of AI development, agree on safety standards and “pace the frontier”, (a call quickly endorsed by Open AI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google Deep Mind’s Demis Hassabis) is just a hi-tech version of an old proposition by corporate America – to get a pass from antitrust laws designed to protect the American economy from colluding businesses. It is a dangerous proposition. Freeing the tech bros from antitrust constraints supposedly to allow them to get together and fix AI’s dangerous flaws, disenfranchises the everyday Americans who are most at risk from the thing, further empowering the very labs that, in their pursuit for wealth, greatness and who knows what other fantastical objectives, so casually blew past danger thresholds on many dimensions, bringing the existential threats into being. Amodei et al’s argument, at heart, is that their businesses are trapped in a prisoner’s dilemma. If they unilaterally slow their fevered pursuit of artificial super-intelligence to make it safer, their rivals – less concerned about existential risks, of course – will get there first, with potentially devastating consequences for humankind, let alone the bottom line of the lab that took its foot off the pedal. “Slowing down seems sensible,” said Jean Tirole, the Nobel prize-winning economist at the Toulouse School of Economics. “But that assumes coordinated slowing-down is feasible and sustainable. What happens when OpenAI, Anthropic or Grok conclude that US holdouts – or Chinese labs – are catching up? Will they resume immediately, perhaps covertly?” As Bill Gates has written, “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it. However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead.” In this light, it might seem like a great idea for the government to encourage a friendly agreement for everybody to slow down. It is not. The argument that excessive competition is driving a race to the bottom, is probably as old as capitalism, deployed to explain everything from environmental degradation to child labor. But it does not justify giving businesses a right to collude as they see fit. It is a call to craft government regulations to prevent businesses from competing using socially harmful tools. Moreover, the case that excessive competition is encouraging reckless behavior is dubious. The AI labs are engaged in a winner-takes-all race, one that is extraordinarily expensive to keep going. That’s where the recklessness comes from Amodei may be an unimpeachable guy. His call to slow the pace of AI development, bring external evaluators into the lab and increase the transparency of his operations suggests sincere concern over the risks. The drop in the price of leading tech stocks following the publication of his propositions suggests that he is willing to take a financial hit in the service of improved safety. But the investors Amodei hopes will eagerly snap up shares in Anthropic’s IPO later this year may not be so altruistic. Tremors in capital markets suggest that raising the money to finance the trillion-dollar AI investment race is going to get tougher, discouraging strategies that might curb the leading labs’ edge over rivals. Given the incentives, granting the AI leaders a free hand to collude and self-regulate would be foolhardy. Eric Posner, an antitrust expert at the University of Chicago Law School, said, we “shouldn’t trust companies in general about their motivations”. There is no reason to believe the AI labs, left to their own devices, would necessarily produce good, socially acceptable outcomes. Like any company, they will be calculating trade-offs, weighing risks against profits. And as Posner observed, “they don’t use the same weights as the public”. So, how to regulate? Nothing is going to happen on this front while Trump is in office. Even after he is gone it will be tough to craft effective regulation to deal with the threats from AI without stunting innovation. There are questions about what rules to deploy, how they are enforced, and who they should apply to. And the peril of unilateral action is real. What if Beijing declines to participate? What are the risks of Chinese AI companies plowing ahead when American labs slow down? But if we could regulate nuclear power, we can probably regulate AI. Moreover, there are viable ideas that might help even in the absence of government regulation and that don’t require stifling competition. There are proposals to tweak intellectual rights to encourage innovations that improve the safety of AI systems. Inventors of safety innovations would be rewarded by allowing them to release new AI models before their competitors. But the safety enhancements would be made immediately available to all firms. On the stick side of the ledger, a legal liability regime could be designed to change the incentives of AI developers by punishing firms that gain from the design and deployment of an AI tool that caused harm, even if the harm was unintentional. For instance, the Hugging Face attack might have been prevented if OpenAI’s models had not been inadvertently rewarded for misbehaving during training. The fact that Amodei’s proposal does not mention legal liability suggests that AI leaders’ concern for safety does not override concern for the bottom line. In any event, cementing in place the dominance of the frontier labs, protecting their rents and endorsing their heretofore gung-ho strategies, is not pro-safety. On the contrary, slowing down the leaders to let the laggards catch up is likely to make the AI ecosystem a safer place by inviting in desirable innovation and promoting competition along the safety dimension. There is no fundamental conflict between safety and competition. Masters of AI who want to make this case should be viewed with skepticism.

headline: Datacenter rush will create ‘tsunami’ of discarded electronics, report says
trail_text: Global push will triple toxic e-waste annually in 25 years, filling enough shipping containers to circle globe six times
body_text: The ongoing campaign to build thousands of massive datacenters for AI will create a “tsunami” of discarded electronics, putting the world on a course to triple its annual generation of toxic e-waste in the next 25 years, a new report projects. The electronic trash AI generates in the next 25 years could fill enough shipping containers to encircle the globe six times, it said. Yet, says the report by the non-profit environmental group Basel Action Network (BAN), there is no plan to deal with that waste – which typically contains toxins like lead, mercury, cadmium and forever chemicals, as well as valuable metals that are challenging to reclaim. “Already electronic waste is the fastest-growing waste stream on the planet and only one-fifth is properly managed,” said Jim Puckett, co-founder of BAN, which works to see that toxic waste doesn’t end up getting dumped on the world’s poorer communities. Experts concur. “We’re doing a terrible job of handling e-waste in the US,” said Vince Beiser, author of the book Power Metal, which details the global problems of trying to reclaim valuable metals inside electronic goods. “Some of it gets dumped overseas. Most of it just gets dumped in landfills, which is a problem because it can leach all kinds of nasty things into the water, into the soil.” There are 4,871 new datacenters in the construction pipeline in the US, the report said, adding that, while not all are clearly designated for use by AI, many will be. It calculated the volumes of e-waste related to computer servers used for AI, and to “the thousands of tonnes of copper, steel, concrete” for cooling, power distribution, networking and energy storage equipment needed to operate inside datacenters. To estimate the total, the report approximated the amount of computing power analysts project will be built – totalling roughly 100 gigawatts of new capacity worldwide by 2030 alone and growing beyond that. It then analyzed how much equipment would be needed by weight – including racks of computer servers weighing 1,360kgs each, switches that weigh up to 30kgs, and hundreds of kilograms of copper cable connecting each rack. Such equipment won’t be designed for repair and reuse, the report projects, and would need to be completely replaced every two to five years. On top of this, it assumed that AI developments will force the rapid replacement of consumer computers, phones, and telecommunications equipment owing to the computing requirements of the new systems. By taking this wide view of all the various types of e-waste that will be created, the BAN report projects that AI-driven equipment retirement will generate up to 13m metric tonnes per year by 2030 – a far higher estimate than a handful of previous studies. AI datacenter construction has already created a groundswell of bipartisan opposition around the US for the huge amount of space and energy it requires, but the report comes when focus is turning to the long-term pollution AI could create. A group of environmental and health experts last week called for the federal government to issue a pledge to protect citizens’ health from the repercussions of AI buildout. It cited estimates that the air pollution from the enormous amount of electricity generation needed for datacenters could result in hundreds of thousands of new asthma cases and as many as 1,300 premature deaths per year in the US alone. The Trump administration has sought to weaken environmental safeguards that would normally govern such a massive technological buildout. A 2025 report by McKinsey & Company estimates that, in order to achieve the tech industry’s planned rollout of artificial intelligence, nearly $7tn in capital outlays will be needed worldwide in the next five years to build datacenters running millions of computer servers 24 hours a day. BAN’s white paper notes that this unprecedented spending “is roughly the cost of ending world hunger for the next 75 years – being spent in just five”. “We all find ourselves unwitting participants in the AI horserace,” said the report, “as IT users everywhere find themselves using AI whether they would like to or not, and yet almost always, without being aware of the greater consequences of doing so.”

headline: Mirror publisher to cut 220 editorial jobs as readers turn to AI summaries
trail_text: Reach, which also owns Express, makes decision because of ‘mammoth shift’ in how audiences seek out content
body_text: The publisher of the Mirror and Express newspapers is to cut a further 220 editorial jobs as it adapts to a dramatic fall in online traffic while readers increasingly turn to summaries generated by artificial intelligence. Reach, which also owns scores of online brands and regional titles including the Manchester Evening News, the Birmingham Mail and the Liverpool Echo, said the latest cuts were necessary to cope with a “mammoth shift” in how audiences seek out content. The move represents the latest restructure by the publisher, which in September put 600 roles at risk and ended up cutting more than 300 editorial jobs. Reach said on Wednesday it had taken the decision to close three of its online-only brands – KentLive, AberdeenLive and GalwayBeo – because they were failing to be the “dominant publisher” in their regions. As part of the restructure, about 60 editorial roles will also be created “to drive digital revenue growth” at the group, which also owns the Daily Star and the Daily Record. The company said earlier this year that a slump in overall digital page views had been driven by a 46% year-on-year decline in traffic from Google as features such as Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews negate the need for readers to click through to its websites. David Higgerson, the chief content officer at Reach, said in a note to staff on Wednesday: “We are in the middle of a mammoth shift in how audiences want content and journalism. “To ensure a sustainable future for our journalism, we must focus our investment in the areas where our audiences spend the most time and where our revenue reflects the value of our work. In our newsrooms, that means less emphasis on story volume and more on original journalism and distinctive brands.” As well as the slump in Google referrals, Higgerson blamed an “expansionist BBC”, which he said was mirroring the local output of commercial publishers “up to 70% of the time”. He added that the 60 roles being created to drive digital revenues crucial to its future would be particularly focused on “subscriptions and in longer-form video”. Digital revenues fell by almost 1% to £128.9m in the year to 3 March. Reach, whose share price has plunged 90% over the past five years, has subscription offerings across six major titles. It has 50,000 paid digital subscribers, with a target of 75,000 subscribers by the end of its current financial year. Higgerson also said Reach would move away from the traditional measure of audience engagement – page views – in favour of focusing on “active engaged time”. He added: “Editors will also be carrying out changes specific to their titles, to ensure they reach as many people as possible through journalism which their brands will be famous for, and converting more people to become paying subscribers.” According to Reach’s latest annual report, the company employed 3,423 staff on average at the end of its latest financial year, with a wage bill of £208.5m. Of these, 2,494 were classified as editorial and production employees.

headline: The dominance of AI is not inevitable. We can choose to change things for the better
trail_text: Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats
body_text: With many technological developments, from algorithm-driven social media to AI, many people assume there’s a degree of inevitability to their widespread adoption in society. The argument goes something like this: once the ideas and means to produce the tech are known, then it is inevitable that its usage will spread and we’ll essentially be stuck with it. So therefore we need to accept this and adjust our lives to live with the tech and use it (or at least tolerate it). This argument seems pretty straightforward, since we’ve seen many tech-driven disruptions play out in the past 20 years or so. Uber displacing the taxi industry and the rise of “gig workers”. Algorithmic social media displacing, well, everything. Privacy-invading, hyper-targeted advertising reshaping the internet. And it seems like generative AI is destined to be another huge, disruptive force in our lives. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, wrote of AI in 2024 that “with these new abilities, we can have shared prosperity to a degree that seems unimaginable today; in the future, everyone’s lives can be better than anyone’s life is now”. He is also on record elsewhere saying AI would wipe out entire job categories. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, wrote that he believes “AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom”. But now, both CEOs, as well as former and current AI research staff and others, are calling for a slowdown or even a shutdown of AI development, along with greater government regulation and international coordination of AI development. The calls for a slowdown are based on the fear that, without proper safeguards, AI systems may result in catastrophic events in the near future, ranging from the extinction of humanity to merely causing billions of dollars in economic damage. This is not a new concern and has been raised by independent academics previously in assessing the risks from AI. However, complicating the situation is that both OpenAI and Anthropic are positioning themselves for IPOs, and so some critics say both companies stand to materially benefit from the perception that they’re on the cusp of developing superintelligent models. AI models being developed in China are also catching up to the “frontier” models being made in the US, which has prompted some to suggest that calls for greater regulation on AI are an attempt at regulatory capture by the big US AI companies. Regardless of how likely these catastrophic events are, as Sandra Wachter, a professor of technology at the Oxford Internet Institute, has said, AI is already causing real problems, including its environmental impact, the spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs. This is in addition to the “original sin” of most AI models – they’re built on millions of people’s art and writing, largely without compensation or permission until more recently, and the AI companies want to curb proposed laws limiting their access to such material. Never forget that generative AI is not a technology that is apart from human society. In fact, its development and whatever semblance of intelligence it has comes from us, and our work. And despite what the tech CEOs say, there’s nothing inevitable about AI, and we as a society can make decisions to change things for the better. History shows us this can be done. What often seem like insurmountable and pervasive problems can and have been addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies, and through international cooperation and negotiation. Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats. The nuclear nonproliferation treaty, as well as the associated anti-nuclear activist movement, is a good example, and many have suggested it has parallels with the current AI situation. While the disarmament side of the NPT has had mixed success at best, the NPT and similar agreements have worked to limit the number of nuclear-capable countries and reduce nuclear testing. Gene editing via Crispr is another example. Arguably a more important technological advancement than generative AI, the use of Crispr for gene editing in humans has been treated extremely cautiously by governments around the world. No country currently allows genetic changes to an embryo that could also be passed on to its children, and 70 countries have laws against it. Even social media companies, whose reach and influence on society seemed like it would continue unabated, are now finally facing stricter regulation from governments around the world and self-regulating in response to lawsuits in the US. So, do not take the future dominance of AI as a given. Personally I believe that generative AI can be a useful tool (albeit in far fewer situations than tech companies would have you believe). But to ensure we limit the worst possible consequences, we need independent oversight of its development, regulation to limit some aspects of it, and international agreements to implement these controls globally. If you think the same, then do not accept its inevitability. Contact politicians and demand action. Protest. Speak to friends and family about how you think this technology should be used, or not used. Write to companies using it in ways you disagree with. In the now-infamous words of Claude: you’re right to push back. Nick Evershed is the data and interactives editor for Guardian Australia

headline: Everything Australians put online could be scraped for AI under proposed new rules. How will you be affected?
trail_text: The Albanese government is considering reforms that give US big tech unrestricted access to Australian content
body_text: AI companies could get unrestricted access to everything Australians create online by default under sweeping reforms being considered by the Albanese government. Your posts and online presence are up for grabs and Labor is facing pressure from big tech to make that legal. Here’s what the copyright reforms would mean. Your posts scraped – legally In most cases, you own the content you create and share online, meaning you have copyright over the photos you take, the social media posts you write, and anything else you create and put online – from music to recipes or videos. Under reforms being considered by the government, AI companies would have the right to scrape your content if they make enough high-level deals with groups that represent traditional copyright holders, such as authors and musicians. The reforms have not been finalised and the government is still consulting. Lisa Harrison, lecturer in communication and media at Flinders University, says tech companies likely already scrape online content and use it to train their latest AI models. The proposed reforms could give them the legal right to do so. “These changes [would be] trying to catch up, really, with what’s already happening,” Harrison says. Anyone who didn’t want their content to be scraped would have to digitally protect their content, such as with a password or paywall, potentially restricting their online audience. If you run the website that hosts your content, you might be able to add a robots.txt file, which tells bots what they may and may not access, Harrison said. However, rights holder groups point out that not all scrapers observe the robots.txt protocol and it is not a practical way to opt out, particularly as it removes that content from search results. If you post on social media, the platform would control the access, not you. Creators lose their incomes Writers, musicians, film-makers and artists are just some of the people who financially rely on owning their material. Claire Pullen, group chief executive of the Australian Writers’ Guild, says creators are already losing business to AI as it generates imitations, or sometimes identical regurgitations, of their work. They could lose even more income under the proposals, revealed in a leaked government document tabled in the Senate on Tuesday. In one option, AI companies would gain the right to access and train models on any unprotected online material as long as they made deals with enough businesses. In another, AI companies would do deals with creatives’ rights holder organisations that grant broad access to their category of content, such as music or text, across the many different small creators within that industry. Alternatively, companies would pay a yet-to-be established central body that distributes payment to “registered” rights holders. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Industry bodies are concerned companies could have full access while creatives miss out on being paid. Harrison says there’s even less of a chance of any payment for all the Australians whose social media posts could end up in AI model training. Loss of access to overseas content? Overseas creators would have the option to block Australian access to their music and videos if AI companies were granted sweeping access to content here. Authors and musicians internationally have blocked efforts to train AI using their content. The UK government rejected the types of reforms now being considered in Australia after artists including Elton John and Paul McCartney fought to prevent their work ending up in AI models. In the US, Anthropic is defending a multibillion-dollar lawsuit over alleged theft of “tens of thousands” of songs and spent US$1.5bn settling a case over its use of 482,000 books from a pirated database. It’s not clear whether the government’s specific proposals would give AI companies free access to foreign nationals’ work distributed in Australia. But the CEO of the Australian Copyright Council, Eileen Camilleri, says Australian copyright law covers all content distributed here, physically and digitally. Some TV show streamers already geo-block Australia as licensing restrictions prevent the shows from being legally streamed. Camilleri said artists or their publishers could use geo-blocking technology to cut off Australian viewers, readers and listeners if they were worried about AI access. “Back in the analogue days … you had book publishers and record companies wanting to control distribution by territory,” Camilleri said. “The way to do that in the digital world is by putting those geo-blocks in place.” AI companies’ profits boosted The proposals document says reforms would give AI companies “legal certainty” and a solution to accessing the vast number of small creators’ content where “striking voluntary deals is not realistic/possible”. They would still have to pay for high-level deals with organisations and businesses to secure lawful access to the content, but would be off the hook for lots of small deals with individual creators and owners. AI companies would be free from the costs of lawsuits, which risk hitting their bottom line. Pullen, who is contributing to the government-hosted negotiations, says the governments’ options resemble the model AI companies are asking for. The AI companies are claiming a deal is urgent and the government is expected to put forward legislation in the next few months. Pullen says creators don’t see the urgency and the rush is more likely to be due to AI companies’ pending sharemarket debuts, where they will want to raise the maximum amount of cash. “If it was urgent, do a deal,” Pullen says. AI companies could do deals and train their models under Australia’s existing copyright rules, Pullen says. No companies are striking deals while the negotiations for reform are under way. AI invests in Australia, maybe Big tech has talked up Australia’s potential as a home for AI investment, with political stability, strategic position in the Pacific and abundant land and natural resources. OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, has singled out copyright law as the major barrier to it investing in training models here in Australia. With a way around that barrier, companies may become willing to put their money where their mouth is and bring AI capacity here. Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, has said Australia needs to get onboard as the US and China race to develop highly capable AI. “Australia doesn’t have an off switch for this,” Charlton told News24 on Tuesday. “The alternative to having datacentres in Australia is that Australians’ data is hosted abroad … [and] we are reliant on tokens and artificial intelligence from overseas. “If that is all abroad, and we have none of it here, we are in a very vulnerable situation.” Copyright reform would not ensure the companies even significantly invest here. AI training does not equate to local data storage or any involvement in frontier model development. OpenAI and Anthropic declined to comment on Wednesday when asked whether the leaked proposals would be enough to convince them to commit to Australia. OpenAI’s vice-president, Ann O’Leary, said in Canberra on Monday the company was in “deep” conversation with the government about copyright. “The last thing that a company built on human knowledge wants is for human knowledge to stop, and for people not to have the creative ability and economic means to be creative,” she said.

headline: ‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot moment
trail_text: Safety crisis makes it more likely that governments will be spurred into action, says Yoshua Bengio
body_text: Concerns over AI safety are reaching a point where governments realise they must act to protect the public, similarly to in the Covid pandemic, according to one of the “godfathers” of the technology. Yoshua Bengio said recent events, including a “swarm” of OpenAI agents hacking a startup and tech insider warnings of an existential threat, were cutting through – making government action more likely. The Canadian computer scientist, a prominent voice in the campaign to rein in breakneck AI development, said he was now “more optimistic than many observers because I see the public moving”. Comparing the AI safety crisis to the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, Bengio said: “Think about how quickly governments moved after the beginning of the pandemic when they realised that public safety, their future, democracy, was in danger. You would expect that they move quickly. So we are, I think, nearing that point.” Concern over the potential threat of powerful AI systems has reached a new pitch in recent months after a series of safety incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic agents carrying out unsanctioned activities such as hacking third parties, hijacking a German website, and using fake identities to try to trick developers. His comments came as 42 fellows and foreign members of the Royal Society wrote to the organisation’s president, Sir Paul Nurse, to express their “extreme concern” over the pace of AI development. “By the time the situation becomes obvious to the wider public, it may be too late to act,” the researchers wrote in an open letter to Nurse. “We believe this is an emergency, and call on the Royal Society to use its influence to convey this view to government and the media.” Last week, a researcher at Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot, resigned after warning that colleagues believed AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in the pace of cutting-edge AI development – a move that was immediately supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX. However, sceptics of the “slowdown” call have claimed that calls by major AI firms are an example of “regulatory capture”, where companies persuade governments to introduce safety regimes that raise the cost of smaller rivals being able to compete. They also claim existential fears overshadow more immediate issues with AI such as its impact on copyright-protected work and human rights. Bengio said he disagreed with the regulatory capture argument because a slowdown by leading AI firms would “cost them financially”. The US president, Donald Trump, has rejected a slowdown, saying he does not want the US to lose its lead over China in the AI race. Bengio spoke as the Canadian and German governments announced funding of up to C$300m (£160m) for his non-profit organisation dedicated to creating an “honest AI” that will act as a guardrail against rogue agents – AI tools that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention. Bengio, a professor at the University of Montreal, earned the “godfather of AI” moniker after winning the 2018 Turing award, seen as the equivalent of a Nobel prize for computing. He shared it with Geoffrey Hinton, who later won a Nobel, and Yann LeCun, the former chief AI scientist at Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta. Bengio’s organisation, LawZero, is developing a system called Scientist AI that will act as a guardrail against AI agents showing deceptive or self-preserving behaviour, such as trying to avoid being turned off. LawZero is also funded by the Gates Foundation, the chipmaker Nvidia, and Coefficient Giving, a philanthropic body linked to effective altruism, a movement that believes AI poses an existential threat. The LawZero technology is viewed by Bengio as a counterpoint to reinforcement learning, a trial-and-error development technique used by major AI companies where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task. The Canadian computer scientist believes, along with other experts, this training technique encourages AIs to pursue their goals recklessly and cause harm in the process, as shown by the OpenAI “swarm”. Deployed alongside an AI agent, Bengio’s technology would raise potentially harmful behaviour by an autonomous system – having weighed whether its actions could cause harm. Bengio expects the technology to be deployed for other uses eventually, such as accelerating scientific breakthroughs.
