headline: Trump blasts interest rate uptick and claims ‘hostile’ Federal Reserve board made decision ‘only for political reasons’ – as it happened
trail_text: This live blog is now closed.
body_text: This brings our live coverage of the second Trump administration to a close, but just for the day. We will be back on Thursday with more. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump responded to the Federal Reserve’s unanimous decision on Wednesday to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, by demanding a massive cut in rates. The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. Congresswoman Joyce Beatty, a Democrat and Kennedy Center trustee, has filed a motion for an emergency hearing on the performing arts venue’s apparent closure. Asked why it is so important to him to have his name inscribed on the Kennedy Center, a memorial to another president, Trump said he deserves “recognition” for saving the venue. If not, Trump said, “It’ll end up being ripped down. Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader who returned to work this week after a months‑long absence, had to be prompted by colleagues as to how to vote near the start of a televised meeting of the Senate agriculture committee on Wednesday. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, cancelled votes currently scheduled for Thursday, meaning that lower chamber lawmakers will now head back to their districts for the midterm recess a day early. The change to schedule means that the House will avoid voting on Republican congressman Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Speaking in North Carolina, Trump explicitly compared his effort to blame Democrat Roy Cooper, the former governor and Senate candidate, for the brutal killing of a young Ukrainian refugee, Iryna Zarutska, last year, by using false information, on the infamous 1988 Willie Horton ad. Speaking in North Carolina on Wednesday, Donald Trump repeated his false claim that it is the war in Ukraine he’s failed to stop, not the one in Iran he started, that has caused a spike in diesel prices in the United States. After repeating his false claim to have ended eight wars, Trump said, “we’re working very hard to get Russia-Ukraine” settled. “The one that’s the toughest is Russia-Ukraine. They hate each other. The two leaders hate each other so much,” he continued, falsely suggesting, as he has before, that Volodymyr Zelenskyy is to blame for hating Vladimir Putin, the dictator who ordered the bloody invasion of his country. “You know, hatred is very interesting. War is very interesting, but it’s too bad,” Trump went on. “And that’s what’s driving actually, that’s the war that’s driving up the diesel prices.” Meanwhile, in Washington, Republican senators who are more clear on who is to blame for the war in Ukraine celebrated the passage of a bill that will give the president the power to impose sanctions on Russia, and tariffs on other countries that buy its oil, even though doing so would likely drive fuel prices even higher. “I applaud the House’s passage of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act—it’s long past time we cut off the funding for Russia’s war machine at its source,” senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, posted. “This legislation will tighten the screws on Putin and impose real costs on those financing his war.” “We are now one step closer to arming President Trump with the tools he needs to deplete Russia of the little economic power it has left and bring much-needed peace to the region,” senator Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican, wrote. Congressman Joe Wilson, a South Carolina Republican, has written a letter to the National Hockey League’s commissioner to protest the appearance of Washington Capitals star Alex Ovechkin in a campaign ad for Vladimir Putin’s party, United Russia. In the letter, posted on social media by the congressman on Wednesday, Wilson expressed “serious concern” over Ovechkin lending his celebrity to support “the dictatorial political party of Russian war criminal Vladimir Putin, who actively works to oppress the people of Russia by outlawing freedom of speech and fair elections.” Wilson notes that, as the Guardian reported on Monday, images from the ad campaign published by a leading Russian newspaper showed that Ovechkin appeared alongside a series of key figures in Putin’s government: Mr. Ovechkin shamefully appeared in a campaign video alongside senior figures of the Putin regime, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of the Kremlin propaganda outlet RT. The advertisement comes ahead of Russia’s September parliamentary “elections” and represents an alarming instance of one of the National Hockey League’s most prominent players lending his image and international celebrity to a political organization that has enabled Putin’s brutal rule and his ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine. Even more disturbing, this United Russia campaign includes Maria Lvova-Belova, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for her role in the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory. “An NHL superstar appearing in campaign propaganda for Putin’s political party cannot simply be dismissed as an activity wholly disconnected from the League,” Wilson added. “I therefore respectfully request that the NHL review this matter and clarify what policies, if any, govern the participation of active players in political advertisements or propaganda on behalf of dictatorial political parties and foreign political regimes,” the congressman wrote. “I further request that the League and the Capitals organization clarify any endorsement of Putin’s party is not a official position of the NHL or the Washington Capitals.” The letter was also sent to Ted Leonsis, the owner of the Washington Capitals. Beneath his signature, in blue marker, Wilson added an impassioned, if imprecise, handwritten note: “Putin is a convicted war criminal!” Putin, the Russian president, has been indicted by the International Criminal Court, along with Maria Lvova-Belova, for the forceable transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia, but neither has yet been tried or convicted. Wilson, a strong supporter of Ukraine, is perhaps best known for disrupting then president Barack Obama’s address to Congress in 2009, by shouting “You lie!” in what was then considered “an extraordinary breach of congressional decorum”. After running through many of his familiar talking points, including a gratuitous attack on his predecessor Joe Biden, Donald Trump wrapped up his speech in North Carolina and departed to the even more familiar strains of YMCA. In his address to supporters in Gastonia, North Carolina, now in progress, Donald Trump tried to blame the state’s former governor, Roy Cooper, who is now the Democratic nominee for the Senate, for the brutal killing of Iryna Zarutska, a Ukrainian woman who was killed on a train in Charlotte, North Carolina last year. Trump began by describing Cooper as a “murderer protector” before repeatedly making the false claim that DeCarlos Brown Jr, the man arrested and charged with killing Zarutska, had been released from prison by Cooper. “He was released by Cooper,” Trump said, incorrectly, after describing in gruesome detail the video of the killing. While Republicans have tried to blame the fact that Brown was not in jail in 2025 on a 2021 COVID-era prison settlement as he result of a lawsuit over prison conditions during Cooper’s term as governor, in fact Brown had been released from prison on 20 September 2020 after completing a sentence for a previous crime. Despite that fact, Michael Whatley, the Republican Senate candidate Trump is in North Carolina to campaign for, claimed in a social media post in September, which featured video of the killing of Zarutska: “Cooper bears direct responsibility for this heinous act and must answer to the public about why he prioritizes criminals over public safety.” Earlier on Wednesday, Whatly repeated the false claim in another post, writing: “Iryna Zarutska would still be alive today if Roy Cooper’s soft on crime policies didn’t put her killer Decarlos Brown Jr back on the streets of Charlotte.” “This is a lie,” a Cooper campaign spokesperson told Fox News in February. “Decarlos Brown was not released from prison as a result of a court-ordered settlement but in fact served his full sentence and was not released early.” During his speech, Trump paused to show the crowd 80 mug shots on a giant video screen. The fact that nearly all the faces of the suspects were Black revealed the lack of subtly in the president’s appeal to his mainly white audience. During his State of the Union address in February, Trump introduced Iryna Zarutska’s mother in the gallery and made a different false claim about her alleged killer, wringly claiming that the man who stabbed Zarutska was an undocumented immigrant, calling him, “a hardened criminal set free to kill in America came in through open borders”. Trump’s attempt to frame Cooper, by falsely claiming that he had let the Black man who killed Zarutska free, echoed the 1988 attack ad run against the Democratic presidential candidate Michael Dukakis, which blamed the former Massachusetts governor for crimes committed by Willie Horton, a Black prisoner released on a furlough program, who raped a white Maryland woman and bound and stabbed her boyfriend. “By the time we’re finished,” Lee Atwater, the campaign strategist for Dukakis’s Republican opponent, George HW Bush, said at the time, “they’re going to wonder whether Willie Horton is Dukakis’s running mate.” The Willie Horton ad was produced and distributed by a former employee of Bush’s media adviser, Roger Ailes, who went on to create Fox News. As he so often does, Trump spoke the subtext out loud, telling the audience that his attack on Cooper was inspired by the Willie Horton ad. “Years ago in Massachusetts, there was a governor named Dukakis, Michael Dukakis, you remember, who had a very substantial lead for president,” Trump said. “He was going to win easily, but he allowed a man named Willie Horton out of jail. Willie Horton was a bad guy, really bad guy. Same thing as this. Same as- same exact thing.” Trump went on to exaggerate the scope of Horton’s brutal crimes, falsely claiming that “he raped and murdered, raped and murdered again and again. And he ended up killing three women.” “Overnight, Dukakis took a rousing lead of 15 points and lost the election in a landslide. Because of that one advertisement,” Trump said. “They put it on just like we’re putting this on, because we have to make sure that Michael Whatley gets into office”. Asked by a reporter in North Carolina why it is so important to him to have his name inscribed on the Kennedy Center, a memorial to another president, Donald Trump said he deserves “recognition” for saving the center no one else seemed to think was in dire condition until he took office. “It’s a mess,” Trump said. “The Kennedy Center for many years has lost tens of millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions of dollars ... For me to go and fix it – I’m quite capable of fixing it – and then have to subsidize it for years to come, because you will lose with the Kennedy Center – they were losing hundreds of millions of dollars and sometimes hundreds of billions – this is before I got involved. So, for the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. “It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape. You see steel falling down. You see plaster falling off ceilings. You see a lot of dangers. It’s been very badly maintained for 25 years,” he continued. “I’d like to be able to save it, but it’s going to take a lot of subsidy into the future. And for us as an administration to want to do that, I think the Trump administration should be recognized.” Speaking to reporters at the airport in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Wednesday, Donald Trump scoffed at the idea of Canada being driven to join the European Union as a result of the trade war he launched against the North American country. “I think it’s laughable,” Trump said in remarks clipped and posted on social media by the White House. “The whole thing with Canada, Canada’s been a terrible trade partner. No, I don’t see that. If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things. So, if they do that, if Europe does that, with a bad intention – if it’s a good intention, that’s fine – if it’s bad intention we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.” Speaking to reporters on his way to give a rally speech in North Carolina, Donald Trump denied that his hand-picked Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, had defied him by voting to raise interest rates, claiming that he had advised Warsh to vote as he did. Asked if he still has confidence in Warsh, despite the rate hike Trump deplored, the president said: “I do. I mean, I’m relying on Kevin, but he’s got a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people. And the interest rates are too high. They’re not appropriate,” Trump replied. “I told Kevin, I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board because it’s just not going to matter.’ The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing. They’re a bunch of politicians. They are people put on by politicians.” “We should be paying the lowest interest rate anywhere in the world because we have the strongest credit,” he added. “If we wanted to get rid of deficits, which we could do with the swipe of the pen with every country, we’d make a trillion and a half dollars a year. We’d pay off our debt. We’d do all sorts of things. But we haven’t chosen to do that. But at some point, we will. Interest rates are too high.” Later, asked again about Warsh, Trump said: “It doesn’t matter because he doesn’t have the votes... No matter how good a job, he’s got a hostile board... They’re raising that only for political reasons, and that’s a raise against Trump.” As fans of Donald Trump wait for the start of his remarks in North Carolina, a live feed showed they were just treated to Sinéad O’Connor’s rendition of Prince’s Nothing Compares 2 U. It was not clear what the Republicans in attendance made of the tune, given that the late Irish singer was for a time a hate figure for American conservatives, after she tore up a photograph of Pope John Paul II during an appearance on Saturday Night Live in 1992, and said: “Fight the real enemy.” The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago. The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support submitting the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results. However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead. The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports. It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions. Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill. The US Department of Defense’s chief technology officer, Emil Michael, dismissed safety concerns raised by the leaders of artificial intelligence companies in an interview with CNBC on Wednesday. Michael, a former Uber executive, previously led the Pentagon’s efforts to press Anthropic to allow the defense department to use its Claude AI model for fully autonomous lethal weapons or domestic mass surveillance. Michael repeatedly said he opposes increased government regulatory oversight of AI companies and claimed that the alarms raised by leading AI firms were part of a “coordinated campaign to scare people to make irrational decisions that benefit” those firms. He also suggested, as he had in a Fox News interview on Monday, that “the fear-mongering” is driven by an ideology called effective altruism. “The amount of dollars being spent in DC now, directly and indirectly by this effective altruist movement,” Michael said, “I don’t think the country has ever seen. “I think in the next few years, you’re going to see more dollars poured into this sort of industry from a lobbying standpoint, and to specific congresspeople and senators, than we’ve ever seen before,” he added. “And the promoters of some of these extinction death-cult-like philosophies are part of that effort.” When Michael was asked if he favored the Trump administration seeking to nationalize or take partial government stakes in AI firms, he replied: “I hope not.” He pointed out that the AI giants could become some of the biggest companies “in the history of the world. In America, that’s a good thing. We want others to come up alongside them. We don’t want government to get in the middle. trail_text: Mohammad Abedin denies statement was written by a former Labor councillor under investigation for allegedly blackmailing a colleague, inquiry hears
body_text: A Sydney estate agent says he used ChatGPT to help write a statement provided to the New South Wales corruption watchdog, but denied it was written by a former Labor councillor under investigation for allegedly blackmailing a colleague, an inquiry has heard. Mohammad Abedin told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday he could not explain why a document titled “Mohammad Abedin statement.docx” was sent by Sharangan Maheswaran to the lawyer who witnessed Abedin’s statement, but denied it showed Maheswaran had written it. Abedin accepted he had no evidence for an allegation of “a dodgy deal out the back” mentioned in the statement about the former Strathfield mayor, Matthew Blackmore. Blackmore is not accused by Icac of any wrongdoing. Icac is investigating whether Maheswaran and fellow Strathfield councillor Karen Pensabene engaged in conduct towards Blackmore in a way “that involves the dishonest or partial exercise of their official functions and/or a breach of public trust, including conduct which could involve blackmail” and possible breaches of the Surveillance Devices Act. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Maheswaran, who is expected to appear before the commission on Friday, has denied any wrongdoing. The former councillor was also a lawyer to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company, Toplace. Nassif, who is under investigation for allegedly making $2m in prohibited political donations to Liberal party figures, insisted he was “not corrupt” in an explosive appearance at the inquiry earlier this week. On Thursday, the commission heard that Abedin, who came to Australia in 2004, had employed Blackmore at his real estate agency, but fell out with him after he left the business in 2023, taking clients. He said he subsequently came to be personally close to Maheswaran, who Blackmore had previously introduced to him, accepting counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin’s suggestion that they discussed their “mutual dislike” of Blackmore. “Yes, of course. I hated him [Blackmore]. He took the business away,” he said. On Monday, Blackmore alleged he had been threatened, followed and his children secretly recorded after he refused to honour an agreement with Maheswaran and Pensabene to step down as mayor. Abedin was asked about the statement he provided to Icac containing the allegations against Blackmore. He said he voluntarily provided it, and did not do so at Maheswaran’s request. The allegations included a “a dodgy deal out the back” from Blackmore’s work on council. After Abedin said the allegation was “just my perception”, and accepted that he could not recall any evidence to support it, presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, asked: “So what is your evidence?” “Your honour, I have no evidence,” said Abedin. After he initially he said could not recall if Maheswaran had helped draft the statement, Abedin said: “I don’t remember how I did it, ChatGPT or myself.” Curtin asked: “So you told ChatGPT what it was that you had to say about Mr Blackmore, and ChatGPT prepared a statement?” Abedin denied this, but said: “I put things with my word[s] and … the context of the letters. They make it in order, as you can see, bullet point and numbering, and devices help to make it more correctly wording [sic].” Curtin took Abedin to a message sent by Maheswaran to the lawyer who witnessed the statement in August 2023, before Abedin signed it, sharing an attachment titled “Mohammad Abedin statement.docx”. “That’s your statement that you say Mr Maheswaran never saw before you signed it,” said Curtin. Abedin denied this. On Thursday afternoon, he was shown the signed and unsigned statements, which Curtin said were “one and the same”. Under repeated questioning, Abedin accepted that the documents were the same, but insisted that he, and not Maheswaran, had written the statement. Curtin, saying Abedin was “quite clearly lying to this commission”, said: “I want to give you one more chance. The case is this, is it not? Mr Maheswaran prepared that statement, not you.” Abedin rejected this, saying the statement was “prepared by me”. Later on Thursday, Abedin said he may have shared “my draft final copy” with Maheswaran. Icac’s inquiry continues.

headline: Queensland to create outback boot camps for youth offenders – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: It was bad day to be a microphone in Canberra – what a hectic sitting day! Before we go, let’s recap the top headlines: The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, has revealed long-awaited migration changes at the National Press Club, after plans for a speech more than a month ago were derailed. The government will cut off pathways for international students to remain in Australia, and crack down on individuals living in Australia without a visa, under its new migration plan. Deputy opposition leader Jane Hume said the government has been “all over the shop on immigration”, and cannot support its proposal without seeing further details. Net overseas migration eased to 292,000 in the year to March, from 299,000 in December, according to new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Australia has broken into the top 10 of the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report, ranking eighth out of 148 countries – its highest ranking ever. Tanya Plibersek and Katy Gallagher have announced plans to close gaps that have allowed family and domestic violence perpetrators to continue causing harm through the child support system. Plibersek said the new child support legislation will enforce travel bans of child support dodgers – meaning they won’t be able to fly overseas. Labor has backflipped on a decision to cap allied health support for veterans after wide backlash. The veterans affairs’ minister, Matt Keogh, said the cap will be removed after consulting with veterans. Pauline Hanson has rebuked a reporter for asking about her decision to team up with Fatima Payman, who previously called her racist, to demand more staff. Queensland’s government has passed legislation allowing it to establish outback boot camps for young people convicted or accused of crimes. And finally, here’s a tl;dr on what happened during question time. Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning. NSW government introduces legislation cracking down on contract crime The NSW government on Thursday introduced to parliament legislation cracking down on contract crime. The move came after Marco Tapia, 23, was shot inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine early on 1 September. Two teenage boys have been charged with murder after the shooting death of a university student in Sydney this month, which police say was a case of mistaken identity. Premier Chris Minns said his thoughts remained with Mr Tapia’s family. He said. I can only imagine to have a son who’s done absolutely nothing wrong, living his life and being [killed] in his bed The age of the people who have been accused of these offences is worrying for everybody.” Opposition leader Kellie Sloane labelled the arrests deeply shocking and concerning. She said: It is no wonder that people in Sydney’s southwest and west are frightened and I don’t blame them. Read the full story: The independent research institute the Centre for Public Integrity has warned that federal government agencies are deploying opaque automated decision-making tools as part of an opaque system, creating major accountability gaps potentially depriving people of fundamental review rights. In a submission to the government inquiry on Artificial Intelligence, the Centre wrote that it is concerned the increasing use of algorithms is creating “significant accountability gaps” requiring new legal frameworks. The submission said: At the most basic level, individuals may not know whether automated decision-making has been used at all in a decision affecting them. Even where its use is known, there may be insufficient information about the particular system involved and the material upon which it operated, including relevant algorithms, code, datasets and, in the case of generative AI, prompts and other instructions. This opacity stops meaningful scrutiny of whether government systems produce discriminatory, biased or otherwise unfair outcomes, the submission says, and this may “substantially impair an individual’s capacity to understand and challenge a decision”. It comes as Guardian Australia has reported the government’s implementation of an algorithm to assess the entitlement of older Australians to government-funded aged care support at home could not be overridden when it made wrong decisions. It has left older Australians without the care and support they need, leading to worsening health and earlier entry into aged care. Centre director Dr Catherine Williams said: We have been here before. Robodebt showed what happens when automated systems are allowed to make decisions affecting people’s lives without adequate transparency, accountability or review rights. To prevent piecemeal reform like we have seen with the Aged Care Bill, a single, principled framework must be implemented. The submission calls for an audit and registry of all automated tools across commonwealth agencies. Shadow health and aged care minister Anne Ruston said Freedom of Information (FoI) documents reported by Guardian Australia show the government “shut out its own staff and frontline assessors from a decision that directly affects older Australians”. You cannot tell Australians a qualified human is in control, while designing a system where an assessor cannot override an algorithm-generated result. The federal government stripped frontline health workers of the power to override an algorithm used by aged care assessors to determine how much government-funded home support older Australians are entitled to, forcing them to accept the algorithm’s outcome even when it under-assesses peoples needs. FoI documents show the department’s own staff warned removing the ability of assessors to override wrong outcomes was contrary to assurances they had provided to assessors and in public statements, and would likely break the trust of the sector. Ruston said: Technology can support an assessment but must never replace professional judgement or stop an assessor responding to an older Australian’s individual circumstances. Read more: Government to face Senate scrutiny over compulsory BasicsCard scheme after broken election promise Last week, the government broke an election promise to “scrap the discriminatory Cashless Debit Card and make the BasicsCard voluntary” by repealing a clause that would have ended the compulsory nature of the scheme in July this year. Tomorrow, the Senate Community Affairs References Committee will be hearing from groups about the government’s changes to the policy, which blocks purchases like alcohol and tobacco until 2033, Data from the Department of Social Services shows there are 33,061 people on income management programs, known as the BasicsCard and SmartCard. More than 82% of participants identify as First Nations, with the vast majority on the scheme living in the Northern Territory. Ahead of the inquiry tomorrow, Accountable Income Management Network Simon Schrapel said: The Government’s proposed changes aim to shut down future Parliamentary review of a regime that has proven to be ineffective, discriminatory, costly and harmful for many participants. And yet here we are with a government having no road map to end compulsory income management. Instead they have pushed through legislative changes to remove self-repeal dates and the periodic review of income management by the Parliament, backtracking on their promise to end these policies. Income management disproportionately targets Aboriginal people and communities. It undermines basic human rights, creates stigma, is fundamentally racist and has consistently shown to deliver minimal if any benefits for participants forced onto the scheme. The Accountable Income Management Network continues to call on the government to end compulsory income management. If the Government was serious about implementing its policy commitment to ending mandated income management then this latest proposal to remove legislative self-repeal dates is a funny way to go about it. It will only serve to make the Government less accountable for a policy that has failed at every hurdle. Deputy opposition leader Jane Hume said the government has been “all over the shop on immigration”, and cannot support it’s proposal without seeing further details. Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hume said the Coalition had not seen any legislation: The Coalition cannot respond on whether we would support legislation unless we have seen it. This government has a track record of putting together legislation that contains things that are inevitably going to wedge the Coalition, that we simply cannot support for one reason or another, and then accusing us of being uncooperative. If the minister has legislation that he would like to bring to the parliament he would like us to consider, absolutely, go ahead, please do it. We want to see it. Labor always tries to find a wedge and the political angle. This is too important for a political angle. WA police officer stood down after allegedly assaulting his five-week-old baby A Western Australian police officer has been stood down and charged after allegedly assaulting his five-week-old baby. The baby was taken to Perth Children’s hospital as a precaution. The 30-year-old man has been charged with aggravated common assault and is expected to appear before a magistrates court on Thursday. The Asylum Seeker Resource Centre has accused the government of turning its back on migrants, international students and asylum seekers in an attempt to “appease the far right” as it announces its migration policy. In a statement, ASRC chief executive Kon Karapanagiotidis said the government must remember that “behind all of this are human beings”. They are our neighbours, our colleagues, our friends and our families. They are part of us. And all of this for what? To make Australia smaller, meaner and more divided in the hope that cruelty towards migrants and refugees will win back votes from the far right? There is no bottom to this race. There is no amount of cruelty that will ever appease the far right. Pauline Hanson has already made that clear, and the Coalition is already demanding more. How much of its soul is the Labor Party prepared to sacrifice chasing people who will never be satisfied? Karapanagiotidis said the organisation “will not stand by while migrants and refugees are used as political punching bags”. Queensland’s government has passed legislation allowing it to establish outback boot camps for young people convicted or accused of crimes. The Youth Justice (Circuit Breaker) Amendment Bill 2026 passed into law this afternoon. The Liberal-National party government made an election promise to establish two camps run by non-government organisations in rural or remote locations in the state for up to 60 children. Under the act, children can be sent to the remote prisons for up to six months either as a condition of bail or as a sentence for a conviction. Experts compared the facilities to the boot camps created under the government of Campbell Newman. A KPMG report later found they weren’t an effective way to reduce recidivism and children should not be detained in remote locations. The Youth Advocacy Centre warned there was a risk children could be mistreated in the camps, as the new centres will have less oversight than Queensland jails. Minister for youth justice Laura Gerber said the law would give courts “a powerful new tool to deal with repeat youth offenders by removing them from the community they have caused harm to and ordering them to Circuit Breaker Sentencing, an intensive rehabilitation program”. Labor and the Greens voted against the bill. Good afternoon! Thanks to Krishani Dhanji for guiding us through what has been a jam-packed day. I’ll be here to see out the rest of the afternoon. Thank you all so much for joining me in our journey on the blog today – it’s been busy to say the least! I’ll leave you with the wonderful Achol Arok for the rest of the afternoon. Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time The Coalition started on migration today, asking why the government hadn’t reduced its migration targets in today’s announcement. Tony Burke said cutting migration further would “trash” the economy. Jim Chalmers then accused the Liberals of having their policy developed by One Nation “in the cockpit of a plane donated by a billionaire” The Coalition finally got the prime minister to say that he hadn’t provided Rhys Muldoon a reference for his role as an Australia Day ambassador (on the second attempt today). Anthony Albanese was asked about whether he would increase funding for the AI safety institute – while talking up the institute, he wouldn’t commit more money. Milton Dick had a bit of a moment confusing two different MPs, which the Coalition took full comedic and political advantage of when he apologised for the mistake. A failed New South Wales bill has been labelled “a familiar strategy from the anti-abortion playbook”. The Libertarian upper house member John Ruddick had introduced a bill that claimed to ban sex-selective abortions. Experts say such a practice is not occurring, has already been banned within the health regulations, and that the attempt to “ban” it is part of a broader strategy to recriminalise abortion. The bill was defeated 21-16 on Wednesday night. Family Planning Australia’s chief executive officer, Sue Shilbury, said the decision underlined that abortion is healthcare. She said: It is reassuring that measures which could recriminalise abortion care and undermine safe, equitable and timely access were rejected. Criminalising any aspect of abortion care is an attack on women’s health and the doctors and nurses caring for them. This bill was a familiar strategy from the anti-abortion playbook attempting to chip away at women’s reproductive rights bit by bit. One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, spoke at a rally for the bill organised by controversial anti-abortion campaigner Joanna Howe, where he claimed the party wanted to “stop” abortion – a claim he later said was a mistake. Abbott says Australians don’t want frontier wars or ‘drug wars’ in War Memorial Tony Abbott has said the Australian War Memorial should not be dedicated to the frontier wars between Indigenous people and settlers, just as it should leave out the “drug wars” in suburban Sydney. The former prime minister said the massacres should not be considered a war between nations, nor even a civil war, addressing the “Imperialism and Resistance” conference at the memorial today. He said: What about the fights between First Nations which were frequent and often deadly? How could events such as the Eureka Stockade or even the apprehension of the Kelly Gang be excluded? ... It would be a big stretch to ask the Australian people to describe as war all acts of politically motivated violence, as it were, or of violence between significant groups of people. I mean the tabloids might say there’s a drug war in western Sydney, but I don’t know whether we would want to put that into the Australian War Memorial for instance, however serious. The Australian War Memorial has no separate gallery on colonisation but is considering more work to reflect the conflicts after the first fleet’s 1788 arrival. Abbott said there were “lots of terrible things that undoubtedly happened” and singled out a court case over the 1838 Myall Creek massacre as a “regrettably rare show of British justice”. He accused colonial Queensland’s native mounted police of “indiscriminate killing” which went “unrecorded as a matter of policy”. But he downplayed an academic’s massacre map and their estimate of 11,000 deaths from conflict as a “guesstimate”. Researchers this week estimated there were roughly 2.2 million Indigenous people before 1788, with fewer than a tenth thereafter. Abbott declined to comment on the study but said it was “way, way, way larger” than previously recognised estimates. He said: Obviously, population decline from let’s say 300,000 to 100,000 is a catastrophic decline. Question time ends And after that final dixer, the PM brings question time to an end for the fortnight. Milton Dick has helmed a bit of chaos in the House. Meaning to call on the member for Hume, David Moncrieff, for a dixer, he instead accidentally calls on the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell – an honest mistake. Everyone laughs it off and he apologises, which leaves the Coalition roaring with laughter. “That’s how you do it!” shouts Nationals deputy leader, Darren Chester (a nod to Anthony Albanese not apologising over melon-gate). Dan Tehan gets up to acknowledge the apology, but Dick laughs it off and tell him to sit down and be serious: Yes, we don’t need acknowledgement, we need you to resume your seat. Albanese questioned on funding for AI Safety Institute Independent Kate Chaney asks if the government will increase funding for the AI Safety Institute, after AI leaders just this week said the technology was developing faster than it can be controlled. Anthony Albanese spends most of the answer talking about how good the institute is but doesn’t say whether he’ll give it any more money. Chaney tries to make that point – that she asked about funding specifically – but Milton Dick says the prime minister is being relevant. It’s just been established, it’s just been established, less than one year ago … we want to make sure this follows best practice. Perhaps that means it’s too soon to give it a funding boost? After ducking questions in question time yesterday and today, Anthony Albanese finally gives a us a clear “no” when asked again whether he provided Rhys Muldoon a reference for his Australia Day ambassador role. It’s fourth time lucky for the Coalition. Albanese dodges questions on his ‘foul-mouthed friend’ Anthony Albanese has continued to dodge questions on whether he provided a reference for Rhys Muldoon, the ex-Play School host who was sacked from a casual Labor staffing role with Tasmanian senator Richard Dowling after old slur-ridden tweets were resurfaced. Liberal frontbencher Angie Bell says the prime minister twice avoided the question yesterday and asks a third time if a reference was ever provided to what she calls his “foul-mouthed friend”. The prime minister repeats lines that Muldoon’s social media posts were “completely inappropriate”. I’m advised that Mr Muldoon has been Australia Day ambassador since 2014. It’s clearly not appropriate for that to occur. And as I have said I wasn’t aware of his comments until they were raised in the media. Neither was Senator Dowling. Senator Dowling took immediate action and that is appropriate. There’s no mention of references. No dollar figure on government spend on green hydrogen How much has been spent on green hydrogen asks One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce. Spoiler alert, halfway through Chris Bowen’s answer Joyce stands up to make a point of order because we’ve got no dollar figure. Bowen says there are a few different programs that could fund green hydrogen, some only disburse money when green hydrogen is actually produced. Bowen says more broadly that green hydrogen is still an important part of the energy transition and takes a swipe at the opposition: I want to give credit where it’s due. I stand on the shoulder of giants because my predecessor as Minister for Energy, the member for Hume, said, on eight occasions that hydrogen would be responsible for $50 billion of additional GDP by 2050. “Hydrogen. Not green hydrogen!” shouts Angus Taylor from across the despatch box. After the point of order, Bowen still can’t get us a dollar figure, but says he’ll come back to Joyce with an answer. Coalition calls for Keogh to apologise following allied health cap backdown The veterans’ affairs minister, Matt Keogh, has been asked to apologise to veterans and resign after he this morning announced a backflip on the government’s controversial $5,000 allied health caps. Keogh says the government listened and engaged with veterans – which causes the opposition to arc up. Veterans have accused Keogh of not meeting with them or hearing them. He doesn’t apologise – and unsurprisingly doesn’t say he will resign. We committed to listen, and we did. And we heard. We have responded as part of that, we are not proceeding with the threshold. But we are also ensuring that we are increasing that access to allied healthcare by maintaining that increase in fees so that allied health professionals will continue to service our veteran community, which is so vitally important. Keogh says the government has passed legislation through the Senate today that goes to 40 of the recommendations from the royal commission into defence and veterans’ suicides. The opposition tries to make a point of order, but Keogh sits down, indicating he’s finished his answer. Albanese challenged to face workers in Whyalla Changing tack, Liberal MP Tom Venning asks Anthony Albanese whether he will visit Whyalla and face the hundreds of workers who have lost their jobs “under Labor’s future made offshore”, before he heads to New York. Albanese is leaving tomorrow morning – so won’t go. But he tries to do a bit of a compare and contrast on how many times he’s gone compared with the opposition. I’ll compare how many times I’ve been to Whyalla compared with the frontbench there. We’ll add it up. I don’t know if the member for Canning [Andrew Hastie] has been to Whyalla or the leader of the opposition, he’s probably been there to check that it was still there. Remember when they were in government they said it would disappear off the map? ‘They’ve got a lot of nerve’: Chalmers hits back as Coalition attacks Labor on productivity Tim Wilson has gone for a bit of a character hit on Jim Chalmers, asking how many more chances the treasurer will get – between “Labor legend Bill Kelty’s” criticisms of him, Labor backbenchers briefing out their budget concerns to the media, and reports that he’s switching from a 20-year to 30-year averages for productivity to “pump up his numbers”. Chalmers seizes on the third point and says the opposition “has a lot of nerve” asking about productivity, accusing them of presiding over the weakest decade in over 60 years in terms of productivity. They’ve got a lot of nerve asking about productivity. They did nothing, nothing about productivity in their wasted decade of missed opportunities in office. One of the first things I did as Treasurer was to get rid of the Coalition’s dodgy productivity assumption and make it more realistic on the advice of the Treasury department. He says the government’s long term productivity assumption sits at 1.2 – somewhere in between the UK which uses 1.5, the US that uses 1.4 and New Zealand that uses 0.9. Over to the crossbench, Greens MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown asks whether the government will legislate to force datacentres to build at least enough renewables to power themselves, and in the mean time, place a moratorium on new datacentre approvals. Anthony Albanese says these discussions are being had and that datacentres will be forced to build renewables, but they won’t be forced to only use renewables for power. He also doesn’t want a moratorium on approvals. If there is surplus energy in gas, for example, in some areas then we would allow that to be used on the proviso that it does not put pressure on the system and therefore put pressure on prices that ordinary Australians are paying. Why is that important? That’s important because you need social licence for these institutions. We’re working constructively to make sure that that social licence is available, is absolutely critical. We have said very clearly that we must shape AI or it will shape us. Parents, teachers, coaches have a role in preventing radicalisation: Burke Jumping back to the end of his address to the National Press Club, Tony Burke was asked about reports in The Australian documenting four major terror plots that had been disrupted since the deadly Bondi beach shootings in December. The alleged schemes were all thwarted in the first six months of the year, with five males, including three teenagers, charged. Burke said that work is under way right now to consider changes to the terror threat level system, including possibly changing categories such as “probable” to give the public a better understanding of the likely threat. Burke mentioned advertising related to the national security hotline and said a real risk was young men and boys engaging with people or AI chatbots online and becoming radicalised. We’ve talked today about what comes over the border and who comes over the border. Can I also say we need to be really careful about what comes over the browser. We have real national security risks there, particularly for young people. So, one of the challenges in any advertising campaign there is, what do we do for parents to notice what signals there might be? Burke said parents, teachers, school coaches and other trusted adults were best placed to notice small changes in behaviour and language which might indicate possible risk of radicalisation. In those cases, he said it could be advisable for adults to call the government’s national security hotline. All calls are investigated and care applied to help children and families. The advertising campaign on that, I think, is the biggest risk that we need to get moving on. Because that’s the bit that people are most likely to be unaware of. Nationals MP Kevin Hogan is up next and asks the treasurer how the government can be trusted when it’s blown a $7bn hole in the budget after the prime minister said the refugee intake would remain at 20,000. For the backstory on that one, read here. Jim Chalmers decides to take a quick jab at his counterpart, shadow treasurer Tim Wilson, joking that the opposition probably gave the question to the Nats, not expecting him to still be here in QT (because he pretty often gets kicked out). He says more seriously that the government is working to make the migration system “robust” and one that works in the national interest. Then decides to get a bit personal again. The difference between this side of the house and that side of the house is our migration policy is determined by cabinet ministers in the cabinet room. The Liberal party’s migration policy is determined by One Nation in the cockpit of a plane donated by a billionaire. Barnaby Joyce fist bumps the air at the shout out. Angus Taylor begins and asks why the government did not announce new cuts to migration levels today. Tony Burke, who has raced back to parliament from the National Press Club, says doing so would trash the economy. Let me say this to the leader of the opposition, as I said to the National Press Club today. If you make cuts too deep, too hard in the immigration system, you trash the Australian economy. “You’ve already done that mate,” shouts someone from the opposition benches. Burke asks Taylor if he’s been listening to his own backbench who have been calling for more backpackers to support regional areas. Does he understand that the people who have jobs at our universities, funded by international education, are Australian citizens with real jobs? Does he understand that the people who work there have real jobs? Does he understand that the small businesses that exist off the back of international education also are people with real jobs? What we don’t need is random dog whistling and someone wanting to claim that … they want all the numbers to be lower except every visa that might affect their electorate. “That’s a slur!” shouts Taylor. Burke: tougher compliance measures will force ‘behaviour change’ My colleague, Tom McIlroy, asks Burke how many more people will leave under his new enforcement measures. There are tens of thousands of individuals who have had their visas rejected and then exhausted legal options to remain in the country. Burke says new compliance officers and beds in new detention centres will help get those numbers down. It’s not 250 permanent places. So, you’d certainly turn over more than four in a year, and sometimes you’d only have people in there for a couple of weeks, sometimes even less than that. The behavioural change is actually the biggest outcome. So, we’re dealing with something that Australia hasn’t done for 11 years. He adds that there’s a deterrent effect, where previously six to seven people would depart voluntarily for every person brought into detention. The real change is effectively for people to be self-managing and working on the basis that ‘this is a country where, if I’ve no longer got a visa, I should leave’. Tony Burke says that the prime minister did not intervene last month when he was first due to unveil the migration plan at the Press Club. He says the first reports of his speech being cancelled came a day after he’d discussed the decision with Anthony Albanese: It was a bit hard for me to go back and say ‘I’m upset that you’re not agreeing to something that he had agreed to yesterday’, but journalists were saying he hadn’t. Things are also all good with Jim Chalmers, Burke stresses, after reports the two weren’t seeing eye to eye on the policy. This morning other cabinet ministers sought to play down any tensions in the cabinet over the plan. Asked, “are you still mates?”, Burke says: Yeah, absolutely. Add that to the list of things I’ve read that have surprised me about myself! I’ve had all sorts of arguments that I wasn’t aware of, as I’ve watch the news over the last six weeks. Migration plan ‘improving supply and reducing demand’ in housing, says Burke Burke is asked whether the policies will help put downward pressure on housing and rental costs. At the beginning of his address, the home affairs minister tried to rubbish claims that migration is the leading cause of housing unaffordability. He said a huge change from the last century is that less people are living in a home together, and more people are living by themselves, meaning you need way more housing stock to accommodate those choices. He tells the press club these measures will help bring in more trade and construction workers to build more housing while decreasing the total number of migrants competing for housing. It’s never going to be the only issue. But obviously anything you do that improves supply, you know, we’re both here, we’re both improving supply and reducing demand. We’re doing the two things that should help with exactly what you’ve described. Tony Burke says it would be an “own goal” for the country to drop migration numbers further than what the government is planning over the next few years. The budget anticipates net overseas migration will drop to 225,000 in 2027-28. He says any more than that risks critical industries. He tells the press club that other parties (One Nation) are proposing to stop temporary skilled workers being able to bring their families which would stop many of them coming and “will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy.” How many doctors at the moment, the proportion of doctors who come to Australia, come with family attached to their application? 50%. How many construction workers come with family attached to their application? 50%. How many nurses and aged care workers come with family attached to their application? Two–thirds … Imagine half of the construction workers who we have to build the houses that we need, not coming. Imagine two–thirds of the people who we rely on in aged care or nursing not coming. That’s the impact of those policies. That’s what those lower numbers do. And if that’s the debate I’m walking into, I am all in. ‘Some of what’s been written is very wrong’: Burke on humanitarian visa reports We’re onto questions now and Tony Burke is asked about media reports that the government was considering stripping working rights for asylum seekers or that an individual would only have three months to apply for asylum. Burke says, don’t believe everything you read. This is the problem we want to solve, but we will insist on solving it in a way that doesn’t undermine the decency of us as a country and doesn’t undermine the fact that we do believe – and the government does believe – for example, the classic one was those [Iranian] footballers, where they came to Australia, they were completely honest about the visa they applied for, they intended to go back, circumstances changed when they were here, and we were a good and decent country. We should continue this. I don’t think there’s much public appetite for people who know they don’t have a valid claim, being able to game the system. There are ways of working through that. I’m not going to go any deeper than that. There are some pretty significant changes to the backpackers’ visas that Burke is announcing today. Right now you have to do 88 days of regional work to qualify for a second year of the working holidaymaker visa. Under the new changes, that only gets you into a ballot to then get a chance of remaining here for the second year. Then there will be a further ballot for the third year, for those who have spent six months of their second year working in a regional area. This is where the government will be cutting down a lot of visa places. Burke says: What you will be qualifying for is a ballot. Not everybody will get through because we need to have some control and certainty of what those numbers are. The ballot for year two will be limited to 45,000. For reference, last year there were 57,000 people who qualified. Year three, with the exception of the UK, is something that is not part of any free trade agreement, that third year, it was something that was introduced not that long ago. We will be seriously limiting year three down to a ballot system of 5,000. Now, last year, there were 31,000 in this group. I like Tony, but honestly, he was the greatest no-show since Amelia Earhart when he didn’t turn up to the Press Club … What I’ve heard thus far is that it’s an exact replication, but not to the extent of what One Nation is doing. He says Jim Chalmers will have to come with him for the return – claiming what will be announced today won’t match the economic modelling in the current budget. Modelling is perhaps a bit of a sore point for Joyce at the moment, after he was asked a serious of questions about whether One Nation had modelled its migration plan and couldn’t come up with a coherent answer (the answer was no). I will be watching this with absolute fascination and some trepidation, and I’ll be waiting for Jim Chalmers to explain his new budget. Plibersek troubled by alleged behaviour from Brethren church during election Tanya Plibersek alleges she saw first-hand members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian church physically intimidating her colleagues during the election campaign. Two of the most senior members of the church have been compelled to appear before the electoral matters committee. Hundreds of the church’s members volunteered for Liberal members and candidates around the country in 2025. The church also denied reports it had secretly paid far-right individuals to disrupt the Labor campaign, during the church’s last appearance at the committee. Plibersek tells RN Breakfast: I was on polling booths with my colleagues like Sally Sitou. I was out there in Reid with her in those last weeks of the campaign, standing there for hours at a time. She would be surrounded by men a foot taller than her, stopping her physically talking to or giving information to voters. I would think secretly paying known rightwing figures to disrupt events and pretend that they are just disgruntled citizens having their say is certainly immoral, if it’s not illegal. And physically intimidating Sally Sitou, who’s a head shorter than me, with big blokes standing around her, physically stopping her talking to voters, I think that’s pretty troubling and it’s certainly not what we want in our democracy. Tanya Plibersek says the new child support legislation (which my colleague Tom McIlroy brought you a moment ago) will enforce travel bans of child support dodgers – meaning they won’t be able to fly overseas. Plibersek says there is more than $2bn of unpaid child support in Australia. She says the system can be used as an “insidious form of domestic violence where you can continue to harass or intimidate your ex”. She says the new rules will help recover “some” of the outstanding debts. If people move from the private collection system to the agency collection system, so the child support agency collection system, it’ll give the child support agency the ability to go after that outstanding debt. We got 200 cases where the debt is more than $150,000, we got one case where the debt is more than $2m. The next piece of legislation we introduce will actually have transport or travel bans on people who have, outstanding child support debts of more than $10,000, will be automatically stopped from leaving the country and that is a strong incentive for people to pay. We also investing more in resources from the tax office to go after people who haven’t been lodging tax returns. We know that one of the ways that minimise their child support or avoid paying is by saying I’ve had no income or have had much less income than they’ve actually had. ‘You don’t know that at all’: Plibersek rejects cabinet division over migration Tanya Plibersek doesn’t want to say much about migration this morning, other than the broad-brush statement that migration is essential to Australia and the government has already brought net migration down significantly from Covid peaks. The social services minister also doesn’t want to talk about whether there was any internal cabinet division over Tony Burke’s proposed migration changes. There’s been plenty of reporting out there in recent weeks over division in the cabinet being part of the reason why it’s taken so long for the policy to be announced – it was initially due to be revealed at the National Press Club more than a month ago. Plibersek tells ABC News Breakfast: don’t believe everything you hear. You don’t know that at all. That has been reported and you can’t always believe what you read in the newspapers. I don’t talk about what happened in cabinet but I can say to you that it is a very constructive discussion that focused on the real issues here. Which is making sure that our immigration system is fit for purpose, that it meets the needs of our country, and that – and by the way, that we continue to celebrate the contributions that migrants to this country make today and have made for many, many years. Asked again whether she’s saying there were no disagreements, Plibersek replies, “I’m not speaking about what happens in Cabinet, I never do.” Good morning Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting day of the fortnight. Thanks to Martin Farrer for getting us started. And the sitting fortnight is going out with a bang today with the Labor’s long awaited plan finally being unveiled at the press club today. We have a fair sense of where some of that will land – including a restriction on international students bringing their family with them, and cracking down on “visa-hopping” – and we’ll bring that speech to you live from 12:30pm. No doubt the Coalition will want the government to go harder and cut more, the Greens will want more compassion and fewer cuts, and everyone’s going to be comparing the plan with One Nation’s. It’s going to be a big one – let’s get stuck in. Tanya Plibersek and Katy Gallagher have announced plans to close gaps that have allowed family and domestic violence perpetrators to continue causing harm through the child support system. The new laws will scrap legal requirements that mean any information provided by one parent be shared with the other parent, stopping situations where sharing that information could put children or a parent at risk. Families will also be supported to recover more unpaid child support debts when they move into official arrangements, and new rules will be created to remove the harm that can arise from family tax benefit debts caused by child support payers against their former partners. In a joint statement, the social services minister and the finance minister said: There is almost $2 billion of unpaid child support in this country. There are almost 100,000 parents and carers in the child support system who have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family and domestic violence. Australian children deserve better. This is the first stage of the most significant reforms to child support in decades, helping create a system that is safer, simpler and more effective for Australian families. Australia has broken into the top 10 of the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report, ranking eighth out of 148 countries – its highest ranking ever. The 2026 report marks a significant climb for Australia, moving up 35 places from 43rd since the Albanese government took office. The government credits this historic high to improved political representation (including a majority-female cabinet), expanded paid parental leave, wage increases in female-dominated sectors and new investments in women’s health. Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the ranking “slipped to an all-time low of 50th under the previous Coalition government” and acknowledged that the work must continue: The job is not done and we will continue to focus our efforts on lifting wages, ending gender-based violence, increasing female representation in workplaces, investing in women’s health and more. The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, said the record ranking was “not by accident”, also recognising areas for improvement: We know there is more work to do across our priorities of ending violence against women, valuing care, improving women’s economic empowerment, improving women’s health outcomes and strengthening women’s leadership and representation – this is just one measure that shows Australia is moving in the right direction. International student visa changes expected International students will see some of the biggest changes in the reform of immigration settings. Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. The vast majority of students will now be expected to be required to come alone. Burke gave a preview in parliament yesterday. We do need to get net overseas migration down. We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy. Burke’s speech kicks off at 12.30pm today. Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia under big changes to the country’s immigration system. The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, will reveal the changes today at the National Press Club, after plans for a speech more than a month ago were derailed. Burke’s plan is designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy. His speech is titled: “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”. The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, introduced during the Howard government, allowing more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country. Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament. Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action. headline: Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada
trail_text: US president responds as Mark Carney seeks to move closer to Europe and diversify defence ties
body_text: Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first ever associate member – an idea he derided as “laughable”. The US president said that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.” Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, a day after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited his country to become the EU’s first “associate member”. Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. She said: “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength. In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.” In response to Trump’s comments, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions. “It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans. Once again, we have a relationship ⁠with Canada, and we are fully entitled to seek to deepen it,” Haddad ‌told Public Sénat TV channel. A European Commission spokesperson said: “As our president made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of the relationship with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.” Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade. After meeting EU leaders in Strasbourg on Wednesday, he described the EU and Canada as “natural partners, united by shared values” and said that both sides were focused on “a deeper partnership that reinforces our mutual sovereignty to create more opportunities and prosperity for our peoples”. An associate membership agreement would have to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states, who generally support closer ties with Canada, but were taken by surprise by the term. Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU. In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the US, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition. The force is a rapid response ‌military partnership comprising 10 North Atlantic Nato member states including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. On Wednesday, Carney and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, held a bilateral meeting at the ground of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves. The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and ⁠challenges presented by ⁠artificial intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However, it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. Von der Leyen said on Wednesday that it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. “We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said. She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

headline: Big AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play along
trail_text: Universities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
body_text: AI companies like OpenAI are insinuating themselves into the pathway from education to work. Soon they may claim it entirely, a disastrous result for students. We know that students are using AI at school and at university. In conversations with those I teach, I’m struck by the trust many place in it. They turn to ChatGPT and similar tools for personal problems as well as study help. Some even doubt their abilities without AI. Institutions are working hard to adapt. But we need to urgently look up from the use of AI to pay attention to big AI companies’ attempts to take over the educational pipeline, else we lose sight of the people that matter, our students. The industry has spent the past few years making our young people afraid of unemployment. Now it’s claiming to have a solution: more AI. On a website introducing its new certification programs, OpenAI gives a peek into the bigger picture. The company says it wants to “connect learning, certification and real economic opportunity in one clear journey, laying the foundation for our upcoming OpenAI Jobs Platform”. That means offering education, credentials and access to work – owning the entire pipeline, infusing AI at every step. The company is positioning itself to directly compete with universities. I don’t mean that we’ll soon see shiny new ChatGPT campuses. These companies don’t need to build a university out of bricks and mortar to take over key parts of higher education. They already own the tools where learning and work are increasingly happening – next, they can compete with universities by brokering access to employment. As big AI companies search for a business model beyond subscriptions, universities need to be alert to this threat and urgently protect their position. Otherwise, the possibility of an independent path for students may be lost. Big AI is slowly commandeering the pathway Even though many young people are ambivalent towards AI, it’s easy to see why they’d trust a service that’s explained accounting calmly and patiently for the 20th time and counselled them through a breakup. Now OpenAI is extending its close relationship with students even further, hiring students as campus ambassadors. The recruitment ad for joining what the company calls the Student Collective promises prospective campus leads “robust training in our tools, funding, swag and access to a community of remarkable peers”. Such a program gives OpenAI even greater access to students. This is a familiar brand strategy. Getting inside a community is a way to win trust and influence. It also gives you data that can inform your next move. At the same time, AI companies are getting boots on the ground within employers. The OpenAI Deployment Company launched this year, with “more than $4bn of initial investment”. It’s sending over 150 “forward deployed engineers”, a military metaphor used to describe engineers embedded in companies, to the “frontlines” of its network of organisations to re-engineer work around OpenAI’s tools. But a company that is at the centre of shaping work across industries also sees and influences what employers are looking for. That puts OpenAI in a powerful position to broker the relationship between students and employers. It can help shape the skills employers want, while becoming increasingly involved in how students learn those skills and prepare for work. So, OpenAI will have insight and influence over students and their learning on one hand, and employers’ workflows and needs on the other. With that, all that is needed for OpenAI to unbundle universities is credentialing. And it’s doing that, too. In collaboration with companies including Accenture and John Deere, OpenAI is now offering certificates meant to lead to employment opportunities. Currently, the focus is on AI tooling and literacy. That’s not new – tech providers have always taught people how to use their tools. The difference this time is how the credentials fit into a larger ambition to capture every step of the journey from learning to work. Look at the language it uses to sell the delivery of the program: “A full learning experience is available directly inside ChatGPT, where learners can practice real tasks, receive feedback in context, and reflect on their work in a single environment. ChatGPT acts as the tutor, the practice space, and the feedback loop.” A single learning environment, and one clear journey. OpenAI could soon be selling young people a one-stop-shop for learning, credentials and a job, all heavily dependent on its tools. We shouldn’t hand the pathway to work to big AI I understand that the picture I’ve painted here may be appealing to some. Students are nervous about their futures, and employers are urgently seeking workers with the ‘right’ skills. But there is a human, societal, and potentially economic cost to making this particular journey so centralized. Consider what a 23-year-old recently told the Wall Street Journal when discussing the appeal of “white-collar apprenticeships”: “Companies want to help mold you into the employees they’re looking for.” That may be so, but if commercial actors own the pathway from education to work, how will the next generation learn who they are and could be outside of the immediate demands of these structures? And what happens when what employers are looking for changes as technologies evolve and bubbles burst? Society – and students – need education to be more than a quick-turn-around response to the whims of today’s increasingly fragile market. Universities can and should offer an alternative path to a totalizing “single environment”. So let’s not compete on big AI’s terms. Rather than turning to AI to speed up grading or rushing to use bots as a stand-in for teachers, we need to focus on what OpenAI cannot so easily provide: independence, access to expertise in context, productive struggle and social connection. Memories are made when others – both peers and educators – see your efforts, and recognise who you are and who you are becoming. Not long ago, Sam Altman and peers had declared the job apocalypse. We should be wary when the same companies that warned young people that their future is uncertain offer them “one clear journey” towards a different version. Education should leave space and time for finding your own way, beyond a mold offered up for profit. Ella Hafermalz is an associate professor of work and technology at the Kin Center for Digital Innovation at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
