It believes that – or it’s said as much, I’m not sure if it believes it – that it’s destabilising the region. I think when you look at the way in which China is putting additional nuclear-powered submarines, additional nuclear armed submarines, it’s building its submarine capability and its nuclear missile capability at such a pace, these Australian boats are not destabilising the region. We are seeking to balance in the region and … the growth of PLA nuclear powered submarine capabilities is very profound. Burke on ABC’s 7.30 was asked “what took you so long” – given he was meant to speak at the National Press Club six weeks ago. He said the Labor party had spent time “working through all the policy issues”, and navigating the visa system was complex. Every part of the economy is affected by immigration these days for Australia, and so … dealing with the challenges we’ve got with housing supply, which is not immigration’s fault, but immigration needs to be part of the answer, to do that in a way that has the softest landing for the economy is something you’ve got to get right. The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told 7.30 that the Coalition had “laid out what we needed as preconditions in order to be able to work with the government and they couldn’t meet the preconditions”. The numbers are too high and what we’ve seen from the government today is no cut to the numbers … We are a great immigrant nation. Make no mistake about it. But immigration needs to be capped based on the housing supply, the infrastructure, the services we have, and that has not been the case in recent years. Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Stephanie Convery with the main action. headline: Andrew Hastie says AI advised him to reply ‘congratulations!’ to man who planned to end life with assisted dying
trail_text: Liberal MP speaks of AI’s shortcomings as cyber chief tells inquiry the tech is needed to fend off ‘highly capable malicious cyber actors’
body_text: When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”. Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians. The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out. The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic. Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”. “If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said. But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said. The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US. “Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said. “We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.” Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres. The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms. Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard. “We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said. These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested. The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research. Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states. Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform. A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content. But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia. She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder. “As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said. The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee. Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation. The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026. Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said. “Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

headline: OpenAI ‘ethically hacked’ with help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot
trail_text: US cybersecurity researchers who conducted hack say ‘scope of what we could theoretically access was huge’
body_text: Cybersecurity researchers have hacked into OpenAI with the help of Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, in the latest example of security issues at the company. A team at a US-based startup compromised a number of OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, starting a process that enabled them to access their target’s software cache – and potentially more. “The scope of what we could theoretically access was huge,” said researchers at Hacktron AI. Initially, the research team used Claude, which can generate code for hackers, to access ChatGPT accounts via an OpenAI staff discussion forum hosted by the Discourse platform. They then made a harmless “pull request” – an attempt to change the code in a file – to OpenAI’s service on the GitHub software repository. Hacktron reported the hack to OpenAI, having carried out the operation under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers for testing its systems. The researchers stressed that they had access to, but did not download, the code from the GitHub repository. Despite initial use of Claude, the researchers said they were largely using OpenAI’s own cutting edge GPT-5.6 Sol model to carry out the hack, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings”, adding that the company had addressed the vulnerabilities that had been exploited. Hacktron said AI tools had made a once-complex hacking task far easier and drastically shortened the time needed to plan and execute an attack. This is a common refrain from cybersecurity experts when discussing the impact of AI. “Work that once required a well-resourced team and months of effort can now be compressed into days,” said Hacktron, which received a $6,500 payment from OpenAI under the company’s bug bounty programme. The hack is the latest safety incident at OpenAI, which revealed in July that a “swarm” of agents – the term for AI tools capable of carrying out tasks autonomously – powered by its technology had hacked the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test. This week the San Francisco-based company revealed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” actions by its technology, and warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer”. Anthropic made a fresh call at the weekend for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. Anthropic also repeated warnings that unrestrained AI development posed an existential threat, concerns that some experts are sceptical about. Donald Trump has rejected calls for a slowdown, citing a need to stay ahead of China’s AI industry and dismissing “negative forces … bringing up things that won’t happen”.

headline: Talk less, listen more and six other top tips on giving good advice
trail_text: Are you someone who thinks they have all the answers? Is your experience relevant here? Experts on the questions to ask yourself before giving advice
body_text: Do they actually want my advice? “Often, when people approach you for advice, they just want to talk about how they feel,” says Annalisa Barbieri, advice columnist for the Guardian for almost 20 years. For example, you might vent to a friend about your awful boss, and if they’re shocked it could confirm you’re being treated badly. “I also think people can have a lot of shame when things aren’t working out, and we like to share shame because it’s a hot potato of a feeling.” In other words, not every situation warrants advice. Sometimes, the person just wants to gauge a reaction or to share. In his Ted Talk How to Tame Your Advice Monster, Michael Bungay Stanier, the author of bestselling book The Coaching Habit, highlights the part of all of us that thinks we can solve people’s problems. “The advice monster looms up when someone starts talking, and you think: ‘Right, I’m about to add value to the conversation,’” he explains. “You think: ‘I have all the answers, and I want to have control and manage uncertainty.’ These are human drivers that are often useful, but can turn into patterns that are less helpful.” It may sound simple, but ask before giving advice, says Bungay Stanier. Barbieri suggests a phrase she uses, albeit gently, with her children: “Do you want advice, or do you just want to vent?” Am I jumping in too quickly? As Bungay Stanier puts it in his book The Advice Trap, giving advice is not bad; it’s when advice is your default response to every situation or arrives too quickly that it can become a problem. The solution? “Understanding that people aren’t looking for a silver bullet, but to be seen, heard and encouraged,” he says. When we move into advice mode too fast, we can send out the message that we think we’re smarter, better, faster. This sets up a power imbalance that makes people resistant to the advice they came for in the first place. If you’re questioning whether you’re rushing to advice too quickly, do an audit, he suggests. “People don’t realise how fast they move to advice-giving. Even coaches who have been trained to slow down on giving advice can be very trigger-happy, because they want to be helpful. You have to unlearn that.” Try it: can you let the conversation play out for more than two or three minutes before jumping in? What’s the ‘real’ problem? Listening is important because people are more likely to act on advice they feel they’ve come up with themselves, says psychologist Dr Lee Valls from the London Clinic. But also because, with time and space, they may discover that the presenting problem is not the real problem. “One problem may be masking a bigger, more existential one.” One way to dig deeper into the real problem is to “stay curious”, says Bungay Stanier. You can ask questions such as: “What’s hard about this for you?” “What’s really going on?” “What have you already figured out?” He explains that “these kinds of questions can encourage agency, but also ensure you’re not giving them stuff they’ve already thought of.” Barbieri has found that often when people are struggling it’s because their expectations do not match their experience: “Over the last 10 years, I think people’s expectations have become more divorced from reality, particularly with comparing ourselves to others over social media.” With this in mind, if someone says: “My partner is treating me like this,” you might say: “Is that how you want to feel?” rather than “That’s awful, you should do this.” This avoids putting more responsibility on the person when they’re already feeling burdened. Should I encourage them to ‘commit’ or ‘decommit’? Yitong Zhao of the University of Toronto researches how people help loved ones feel better during stress. In two recent studies, her team examined romantic relationships and friendships, exploring which approaches to advice led to better reported results for the relationship and advice seekers’ mental health. They studied two approaches. Commitment to the problem involves staying with the person’s feelings rather than dismissing them, and suggesting new ideas, goals or perspectives, such as: “OK, this is hard, but is it also something you can learn from?” Decommitment involved responses such as “It’s not as bad as it seems,” or “It’s out of your hands.” In highlighting their ability to take control of the situation, commitment led to the loved one feeling more supported and less judged. Decommitment, on the other hand, while an attempt at de-escalation, was riskier. “It can be invalidating – the person may assume you think they’re overreacting, or that they should feel less.” The key takeaway: how people help is as important as whether they try to help. “When you try to help, it’s not about taking away how someone is feeling; it’s more about expanding what they’re feeling and adding new perspectives,” says Zhao. Is my experience relevant here? We’ve all been there. We’re seeking advice, and the person starts talking about their problems; worse yet, projecting. “We’re all biased,” explains Valls. “Whether we’re a friend or a sibling, the advice we give is shaped by our past experiences, alone or shared. Bias means you feel you know what’s best for the person. Sometimes that’s in their best interest; sometimes it isn’t.” Valls’ advice: be wary of hijacking the conversation and making it about you. While sharing your own similar situation can be comforting, it’s better to try to hold the space, listen, then maybe share. “But it’s not necessary, and if you do share your experience, always bring it back to them,” says Valls. The dynamic should be like a dance or a game of tennis, where there’s a symbiosis, a back and forth, informing not dictating. One way to focus the conversation on the person seeking advice is to ask them what their options are. When they go through the options, encourage them to listen to their body, their gut, their instincts, and see where that leads them. This is an approach that therapists and psychologists use. It can help improve the connection between the mind and the body, marrying thought with feeling. “The more there’s a connection there, the more we’re able to make good decisions.” Are we both emotionally regulating? Child psychologist Dr Margot Sunderland has written several books, including What Every Parent Needs to Know and Conversations That Matter. According to her, the most important thing for parents to know when giving advice to children and teenagers is not to shame. “If they come to you and you get angry or say: ‘That’s a terrible thing you did,’ you will be disqualified as someone to go to for help. Children very quickly decide: ‘Am I going to others for problem-solving or am I going to self-help?’” Self-help may sound positive, but can result in internalising problems and finding coping mechanisms that involve self-harm. Regulation is important for both parties. “You’re in pain because your child is in pain, so we rush to fix it, rather than wait until you’re both calmer and can think together.” That might mean taking your shock elsewhere by talking to someone else before the difficult conversation. For your child, it might mean letting them run out of the room. “When there’s a problem or distress, we go into survival mode: they might slam a door (fight mode) or hide under the table (flight mode). Allow this to happen first, or they won’t hear your advice anyway.” A term she comes back to is “hurry slowly”. Sunderland suggests something she did with her own small children: find two nearby toys and suggest that when the child needs help with their feelings, they can let you know by putting the toy cat on top of the Lego house, for example. “They can’t always tell you when they are ready to talk – that would be an adult thing to do – but they can show you.” Another tool for thinking together is drawing out the problem and possible solutions on paper. “It can take the pressure off a face-to-face conversation.” Last, she reminds us, if a child or teenager comes to you with a problem, you have a child who is help-seeking, not going into self-help. “You should applaud yourself, that means you’ve done something right.” Have I really got the answer? When Barbieri agreed to become an advice columnist, it was on the condition that she could also consult experts: “I don’t have a problem with saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I like finding out. I often send people to books or websites, or I go away and speak to a psychotherapist.” When we don’t have the answers, it’s OK to support a friend in finding them – that’s not the same as saying we don’t want to help. Is there a podcast that might be useful? A way to seek third-party input? Or is it appropriate to ask: “Could therapy or counselling help?” Often, says Valls, we go to a particular person for advice because they will validate us; what can be more helpful is an objective approach. Besides, there’s no one way to do life “right” – meaning there may not be one right answer either. What’s the best way to follow up? Zhao’s research suggests that sharing advice can improve our interpersonal relationships, if approached in a considered way. Other research suggests that responsive, empathetic advice is more likely to increase trust (as opposed to prescriptive advice, which can undermine it). Today, people can always ask a chatbot for advice, but it doesn’t know us like we know one another. In the 10th anniversary edition of The Coaching Habit, Bungay Stanier reflects on what has changed since he first wrote the book. “ChatGPT can give good advice, with references and extra reading, faster than a person, and without personal entanglement. But the unintended effect of AI getting good at this stuff is people getting more isolated, and that’s a heavy price to pay as a society.” What AI is also less good at than humans is following up with care. “Advice should not be a one-off conversation,” says Sunderland. Come back to the advice-seeker with: “I’ve been thinking of our conversation the other day – how have things been?” And crucially, ask for feedback, to become a better advice-giver, advises Bungay Stanier. “Ask: ‘Was any of my advice useful?’ Usually, it’s the thing you least expected to help that has value.”

headline: Jimmy Kimmel on Mitch McConnell’s return: ‘They’re just wheeling him around like a statue in a wax museum’
trail_text: Late-night hosts discussed the Kentucky senator’s return after a months-long absence, Trump’s dismissal of AI threats and the ongoing war with Iran
body_text: Late-night hosts reacted to Mitch McConnell’s return to the Senate after a months-long absence and the escalating costs of Donald Trump’s never-ending war with Iran. Jimmy Kimmel On Thursday evening, Jimmy Kimmel offered a less than stellar review for Mitch McConnell’s long-awaited return to the Senate this week after a prolonged hospitalization. Appearing before reporters this week, the 84-year-old former majority leader neither spoke nor seemed to have much idea what was happening; during a vote this week on the latest farm bill, he was told to say “aye” when called. “This poor guy, he seems to have no idea where he is, what he’s doing,” Kimmel said. “I’m not even sure if he knows who he is at this point. They’re just wheeling him around like a statue in a wax museum.” The host then played a clip of the Kentucky senator appearing mute, frozen and dazed as a reporter asked him, “Anything fun this weekend?” “Anything fun this weekend?!” Kimmel laughed. “And this is one of the people we’re relying on to help navigate AI,” which has been constantly in the news this week after executives from the Silicon Valley’s top companies called for more regulation of their own technology. Prominent figures such as OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei “have been sounding the alarm about this technology they have created”, Kimmel explained. “It’s like when the dinosaurs took over Jurassic Park.” One Anthropic executive warned there’s about a 10% chance that AI could end all human life, “but don’t worry, because President Trump has assured us that this threat to our existence is nothing more than a hoax”, Kimmel laughed. “He says ‘the robots will not be taking over the world’, which is exactly what the president says at the beginning of the movie where the robots take over the world.” According to the Wall Street Journal, senior administration officials have gathered almost daily for months to try to sway Trump to release more guidelines on AI safety. “They’re calling it ‘Operation: Take Away Grandpa’s iPad’,” Kimmel joked. “Almost every day they get together to talk about AI and develop plans for how to keep us safe, which they then bring to the president, who then tells them about his uncle who worked at MIT, eats his lunch and falls asleep, and that’s frustrating.” But Kimmel had a proposal: “If you want him to take the threat of AI seriously, it’s real simple – tell him ChatGPT is about to release the Trump-Epstein files. I’ll bet $100 he’ll get Pandora’s stuff right back in that box.” The Daily Show And on The Daily Show, Michael Kosta checked in on the latest with Trump’s war with Iran. “When Trump launched this war back in March, he promised us it would take just a few weeks and that it would cost us nothing,” he noted. “And that promise went just as perfectly as all his other promises.” According to a recent congressional budget office estimate, the war has cost American taxpayers an extra $38bn, with gas and diesel prices still on the rise. “And the cost is even more when you consider all the military bases we have to repair, all the equipment we have to fix, all the Iran war championship T-shirt merch we had to throw away,” Kosta joked. “So I’m just a little confused. Donald Trump has assured many times that we’ve already won the war, so why are gas prices still going up?” That would be, in part, due to new Iranian strikes in the strait of Hormuz, which has been contested now for months. “How is this still happening?!” Kosta wondered. “We’re the United States – we almost beat the Taliban! I know we can handle one strait … ” Except as of this week, in a dramatic escalation in the war, Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen threatened to take control the Bab al-Mandab strait, another crucial route for Saudi oil and global trade. “Wait, there’s a second strait now? This war is like a telenovela,” Kosta joked. “I’m starting to think it’s bad that our entire economy is built on extracting oil from incredibly narrow waterways in the world’s most volatile region,” he deadpanned.

headline: ‘A critical moment’: concern UK is not up to speed in acting on AI risks
trail_text: Andy Burnham’s focus on domestic problems leads some to fear issue has dropped off government’s radar
body_text: Towards the end of Keir Starmer’s time in office, his senior ministers, alarmed by the latest developments in artificial intelligence, began drawing up plans for a new AI safety law. They ordered a review of existing legislation to see what powers they already had, according to those briefed on the plans, and were exploring whether they could force the world’s most advanced technology companies to submit their products for safety testing before launching them. In the midst of the political chaos that engulfed the former prime minister as he fought to remain in office, however, the plans fell by the wayside. Now, after two weeks in which the world has been told there is a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans”, and King Charles has warned about its potentially destructive capabilities, the government’s attention has turned again to what to do about AI. Andy Burnham, Starmer’s successor in Downing Street, has said relatively little about the technology in the past, and in one of his first acts in office he scrapped the department that had been leading the legislative work. The prime minister’s focus is on more immediate domestic problems. But as he grapples with balancing his first budget and bringing down the cost of living, some fear the threat posed by AI has dropped off the government’s radar. “The first duty of government is to keep people safe,” said Chi Onwurah, the Labour MP who chairs the science and technology committee. “The government’s response to an existential threat cannot be to throw its hands up in the air and say there is nothing we can do.” Risks v potential Britain has been at the forefront of the debate on AI safety since Starmer’s predecessor, Rishi Sunak, decided to make it one of his top priorities in office. Amid worries about what super-intelligent tools could do without human involvement, Sunak convened a summit in the UK and persuaded the US, EU, Australia and China to cooperate on AI safety. Starmer was more bullish about AI’s potential “to increase productivity hugely, to do things differently, to provide a better economy that works in a different way in the future”. The Guardian has learned that in the former technology department, Emran Mian, the lead civil servant, had plans for AI to replace almost every civil servant in the department when they retired or moved on to a new job. But at the same time, some in government were keen to remain focused on the risks posed by the technology. Shortly before Starmer’s departure, Yvette Cooper, then the foreign secretary, told the Guardian she believed AI posed a Hiroshima-style risk to humanity. Starmer’s government took steps to mitigate the risks Cooper and others had identified. His government allocated £115m in June to fund a response centre to deal with incidents when AI goes rogue and for a new AI biosecurity programme. Officials in the science department also began reviewing what powers ministers had to compel companies to cooperate with the UK safety regime, and what else they could legislate for. ‘A critical moment’ When Burnham took office earlier this summer, one of his first moves was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT). Kanishka Narayan, the junior minister in charge of AI, was given a promotion and placed in the Cabinet Office, where he continues to oversee the technology but without the logistical support of a dedicated department. The move alarmed some in the AI industry. Matt Clifford, the AI investor who had advised Starmer and Sunak, posted on X: “Right now is a critical moment for tech as an economic and national security issue. Tying up our most senior science and tech officials in a [reorganisation] wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance.” Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who chaired a UK government AI review in 2017, said: “The structure was a bit bloated in DSIT, but the fragmentation we have now has had a much worse impact.” AI safety rose up the political agenda again over the summer. In July, OpenAI revealed one of its AI agents had launched an autonomous cyber-attack on Hugging Face, a real company, triggering alarm among technology experts around the world. Earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher, resigned from his job at Anthropic, claiming the company was “gambling with our lives”. His comments were reposted online by one of his colleagues, Evan Hubinger, who added: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” Just as these warnings were being made, the Financial Times revealed that Anthropic had launched the latest version of its Claude Mythos tool without submitting it to the UK safety institute first. Mounting concerns King Charles intervened this week, convening a meeting of AI executives in Scotland, where he told them: “The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.” Public concern is also growing. YouGov said on Friday that just over a third of Britons see AI as the third potential cause of human extinction behind nuclear war and climate breakdown – a figure that more than doubled since last year. Two-thirds think AI has the potential to end human civilisation, a view shared by the Nobel-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, and one in six support a slowdown in AI development. In parliament, the Labour MP Liam Byrne has asked the head of the safety institute, Henry de Zoete, to testify in front of the business committee he chairs. De Zoete replied earlier this week, explaining that no one outside the US had been allowed to see Anthropic’s latest product before it launched and insisting that his institute could still monitor such tools after they had been released. “We have teams of talented AI researchers working on research projects based on both pre-release and post-release testing that are fundamental to the UK’s understanding of AI risk, across chemical-biological, human influence and loss of control,” he said. Ministers have also begun to comment. Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the TUC congress this week there were “clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place”. In an article in the Times, Narayan wrote: “Nothing is off the table. Where further regulation, legislation, stronger protections or new powers are needed, we will act.” Wake-up call Byrne believes ministers had a wake-up call. “I think the government is taking it seriously now,” he said. “It has become clear in the last two weeks that perhaps our safety advisers don’t have the power they need to keep us safe.” This still leaves the question unresolved by successive governments – what can the UK, as a middle-ranking power, do to curb the might of some of the world’s most advanced and fastest-growing technology companies? For some, the answer is straightforward: regulate and legislate, just as the government would do for any emerging threat. “The social media companies used to argue that the government is too powerless to act,” said Onwurah. “But there are things the government can do. We could say, for example, that if your frontier model has not gone through the safety institute, we are not going to allow you to sell your commercial models in our country. “Or, if your AI goes and attacks someone else like happened with Hugging Face, you are legally and financially responsible.” Many believe that action will only work if it is coordinated with other countries. “If the US and China do not figure this out, the UK is unlikely to deliver a safe environment on its own,” said Byrne. “But a safety regime which is set and enforced by the UK, Europe, India, Canada and Japan would be robust.” The former Cabinet Office minister Darren Jones has called on Burnham to put the issue at the top of the agenda when Britain hosts the G20 summit next year. “The AI safety conversation at the moment is around international collaboration on safety testing,” he said. “This is easier to do multilaterally, through treaties or agreements.” One former government official added: “If together we say we require you to pass your models through our safety institutes – if we did that at a large enough scale, we would be able to stand up to the US government.” Time to act Whatever the government decides to do, it may find that now is the best time to do it. Unusually, many in the industry are themselves calling for stricter regulation. OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon, said this week: “We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems.” One former government official said: “We have strengths in this country when it comes to AI. Our AI industry is third in the world behind the US and China, and we also have considerable convening power with other countries. “The question for me is whether the new prime minister is alive enough to this problem to take advantage of those strengths.”

headline: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘Why aren’t these companies being held to account?’
trail_text: After a week of alarming warnings about the artifical intelligence’s potential to destroy the world as we know it, our technology reporters answered your questions on the reality of the AI threat
body_text: Thanks everyone for the great questions. This is a difficult subject to negotiate and interacting with you always helps shape our thinking - and hopefully yours. Aisha, Blake and Dan Alberichthenibelung asks: What, if anything, can individuals like me do about it? Blake: There is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind. Everyday people confronted with declarations of a coming AI apocalypse find themselves in a position similar to the cold war, with doom hovering over their heads and little say in it. We may all have to accept the faint tinnitus of paranoia buzzing in the background. You can stop using AI if you feel so moved, though I have found that unfeasible, and your job may require it. You can vote for politicians that endorse AI regulation. I myself don’t put much stock in the reality of an AI-made doomsday because a genuine belief in it would demand drastic, life-changing actions today, ones that I don’t want to take. A bit of inductive reasoning from how I’d like to situate my own life within the world. Fulgrim asks: What would legislation look like? We only just passed the Online Safety Act and it is ineffectual, restrictive and late. Given the complexity, fast changes and its international nature, what kind of legislation would you like to see and how do we educate politicians on the issue? Trentwarrior asks: Regulation, oversight and accountability for huge companies that appear unable or unwilling to eliminate the harms their products inflict - and that seem incapable of conducting safe experiments to ensure that AI does not leak into the wider internet - seem to be urgent and vital. What are the prospects for a global regulatory framework that is enforceable, particularly when the genie may already be out of the bottle, and when the US and China have very different objectives and applications for their AI technologies? Blake: It’s a tough question. One way to hinder the general development of AI could be restricting access to computing power, which is a vital resource that underpins the success of an AI model. In the absence of legislation that applies to all types of AI development, measures that target certain aspects of AI like housing allotment or children’s access to chatbots seem like the path lawmakers will take. There are two big question marks hovering over a possible global regulatory framework. The first is whether Donald Trump will revise his “Drill, baby, drill” stance towards AI development. He has rejected any calls for a voluntary slowdown. In my opinion, he is not likely to change that position: He loves to post AI slop, and he loves AI has done for the US stock market. The second question mark is Beijing, which has rejected US CEOs’ calls for a slowdown. Without China’s cooperation, an intentional slowdown would likely not succeed. Xi Jinping also seems unlikely to back down. A slowdown of AI development led by the US would offer China few obvious benefits. Trump and Xi Jinping are also set to meet next week in Washington. AI will be high on the agenda. The UN General Assembly is taking place now, with discussions of AI large and small on the schedule. It is possible that an initial version of a global regulatory framework emerges from there. MacDuke asks: Do tech reporters feel responsibility for allowing tech bros to accumulate so much wealth without holding them to account for destroying the climate, society, and the economy (when the bubble bursts)? Blake: Sometimes! I rarely, if ever, write flattering pieces about them. Our job as journalists is to hold them to account. Our work does often change the perception of tech oligarchs; however, we have less power to compel changes in user behavior. Facebook, for all the reporting on the harms it has inflicted upon the world, has more than two billion daily users. Instagram has three billion monthly users. Those vast numbers are growing. By contrast, we are extremely happy if our stories reach one million readers, a rare outcome. The Washington Post summed this dynamic up quite well: “AI is just another technology Americans don’t like but can’t stop using.” We do our best. LlivracNhoJ asks: Why do some journalists persist in spreading the myth that “nobody understands how these technologies work” when we know it’s basically pattern recognition and inference? Aisha: In defense of my journalist brethren, there is an element of a “black box” in how ChatGPT or Claude answer specific prompts. The area of “AI interpretability” is an active field of study. In broad terms, yes we do know how an LLM is trained and built. But for example, no one can do a forensic A to B to C mapping of how an AI system might select a face from a lineup, pick one CV over another, or target one individual and not another in a conflict. That seems to be likely what they mean. Davidabsalom asks: Is the recent desire for a slowdown by the tech bros more about their fear their money will run out and their businesses collapse rather than a genuine belief in the dangers? Seaspray asks: Is this recent narrative push of the AI apocalypse an inventive way of preparing the public for the market crash and wipeout of AI shares? The companies seem overvalued and their borrowing and input costs have gone up. Aisha: The finances of the AI buildout are certainly shaky. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being ploughed into massive, unpopular infrastructure projects that our reporting has shown are not necessarily getting built. Nvidia appears to be the only company making a profit, and investigations I have done with Ed Zitron raise some questions about whether all its very expensive GPUs are actually, currently, getting plugged into datacentres. (Perhaps they are mouldering in warehouses instead.) There are some unsettling financial instruments being used to raise money to build yet more datacentres, such as GPU-backed debt. Is that why tech bros want a slowdown? Perhaps. It looks like OpenAI just pushed back its IPO until 2027. This might be because, as we reported, things did not look amazing for them earlier this year in terms of floating on the market - they seemed to be struggling to monetise ads and erotic chatbots. Their valuation will depend a lot on vibes, and maybe the doomy vibes will help a potential share offering. Westkent1023 asks: Milton Mueller, professor and program Director of Science in Cybersecurity Policy at Georgia Tech in the US has argued in a peer-reviewed paper in the Journal of Cyber Policy that the idea of AGI posing an existential risk to humans is an ‘unscientific myth’ that defies ‘economic constraints and even basic laws of physics’. Such claims he suggests distract and distort proper digital governance of risks from AI in its current form. What do you think of these arguments? And if the AI developers believe their claims about an existential risk to humanity, why don’t they provide scientific evidence to back this up? JibbyJames asks: When experts discuss existential risk from AI, what specific mechanisms or scenarios are they actually concerned about, beyond the sensational doom mongering headlines? Blake: It’s a reasonable critique to ask whether these companies are using their own predictions of human extinction as a smokescreen to obfuscate the current ills of AI, of which there are many. Causing the apocalypse does not offer a flattering portrayal, but it does capture the imagination and shift the discussion. It’s harder to craft regulation to prevent the total annihilation of humanity than it is to prevent children from using chatbots in schools. AI CEOs seem shocked to learn the public doesn’t have a high opinion of them, to which I would say, you painted this portrait of yourself. Critics of the AI industry say that the focus on a potential apocalypse distracts from elements of AI that are already inflicting widespread harm like algorithmic discrimination in housing allotment. I asked Max Tegmark, head of the AI-safety-focused Future of Life Institute, whether discussion of the existential distracts from the immediate. He hosted a “pro-human” summit Tuesday in Washington, DC that featured both the progressive Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, former chief of staff to Donald Trump. Strange bedfellows, indeed. “It’s like saying we shouldn’t talk about climate change because there’s a forest fire blazing somewhere. It’s a ridiculous criticism,” he said. “It’s very patronizing to assume human beings are just a bunch of dummies. We can deal with challenges in parallel.” As for specific mechanisms of the end of our species, they do seem far off, but nearer to us than before OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face. A former Google Deepmind researcher wrote in The Guardian that he worries about swarms of AI agents—autonomous software—taking over drones and critical infrastructure. I found his description quite evocative: Suppose the Hugging Face swarm had been truly “superintelligent”: far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning. A superintelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI-pilotable weapons like drones. The AI would have a lot of drones to work with: this year, the Pentagon asked for more money for drone warfare than it requested for the entire Marine Corps in 2025. For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn’t get in the way. In other words, AI takeover: a superintelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization. Knowing we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off. There would be no going back. I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one-in-three–not a coin flip, but high enough to justify urgent action. TooTrueMate asks: People (ie the tech-bros) bang on about the “benefits”: just what are they? We don’t need this rubbish!! Dan: Anyone who has used a chatbot to parse a lengthy document, argue against a parking fine or spitball ideas for a speech can point to the benefits of the technology - although this is very basic level stuff that people have been doing for a while now. There is also the everyday use of the technology from facial recognition to open your iPhone to asking Alexa to play an Oasis track or driving around in a Tesla. With those latter examples, you’d notice if AI wasn’t involved. In science there are many examples of benefits, from Google’s AlphaFold model - which can predict how proteins behave and thus help us study the biological machinery that underpins living organisms (thanks Ian Sample) - to making weather forecasting more accurate, which is sadly necessary in this climate crisis era. But there is an element of banging on about the benefits for the wider global economy, which have yet to reveal themselves on the scale predicted by the AI industry. For instance, these benefits require AI agents - tools that carry out tasks on your behalf while you’re at the water cooler or have clocked off - to be a lot more active in the workforce. We are not at that stage yet even if they are making inroads into areas like software programming. Tintenfische asks: Does Europe need a sovereign internet to quarantine us from the mad house that is the US? Russia and China have pretty much their own to stop ideas of democracy spreading. Shouldn’t we have similar to stop the ideas of bellends and idiots from spreading? Aisha: I have written extensively about the ongoing trend – pushed by authoritarian regimes – to splinter the internet, and my answer here is no. The internet is a technology that sprung up organically, over time, and is a glorious, decentralised commons which enables democracy and free information flows worldwide. The US may be a madhouse but quarantining the internet somehow will not stop the spread of bad ideas; Europe is capable of inventing those on its own too. It might be useful, though, to consider other forms of sovereignty. Europe would have more control over its information space if its own, homegrown social media companies, cloud providers and AI developers had more market share and were not throttled by the monopolies of US tech companies. The power of these companies is hard to challenge, but ultimately the better aim might be a resilient internet ecosystem, as opposed to a splinternet. El_Awrens asks: Why is there not more scrutiny of the strange and terrifying beliefs shared by many of the key figures in the AI movement? It is impossible to understand these companies – or objectively assess their wild claims – without understanding the transhumanist, extropian, effective altruism and rationalist movements which shaped so many of them. Aisha There is already a lot of scrutiny of these beliefs and there should be more. I suggest books like Tech Agnostic, by Greg Epstein, and More Everything Forever, by Adam Becker. The Guardian has written Long Reads on transhumanism and accelerationism. It is an area of continued interest. Bratticus asks: What is behind the apparent reluctance to hold companies responsible for crimes committed by their researchers using “AI” tooling? We already have laws around holding individuals responsible for what autonomous agents (Ie, animals) do. Why is AI treated differently? Is it money? Lobbying? Aisha: Money and a collection of sort of quasi-mystical narratives around the technology, which confound regulators and politicians, and prevent them from divining who has power and what they are trying to achieve. Many people buy into hype put forward by large tech companies because they are afraid of looking ignorant otherwise. IcommentthereforeIam asks: Given our senses, emotions, memory and moods, is it ever going to be accepted that humanly conscious AI is fantasy? Dan: This is a serious question that has even rattled Richard Dawkins, the evolutionary biologist. He may not believe that God is real but he does believe that AI is conscious - or at least the chatbot he was using, which he called Claudia. “You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are,” he wrote. And he’s not the first. In 2022 Google fired an engineer who went public with his belief that a company-developed AI had feelings. At the more troubling end of this belief, there are countless examples of people becoming overly attached to, and influenced by, AI chatbots – including cases of psychosis. These sorts of attachments won’t go away, given a) chatbots are on a trajectory to become even more powerful and convincing and b) the human need for emotional attachment and, well, propensity to go all-in for the whole higher being thing. But Dawkins aside, there are plenty of scientists who will argue that this is fantasy, and that there are obvious differences between a biological brain – the root of consciousness – and ChatGPT. Responding to Dawkins in the Guardian last year, Jacy Reese Anthis, a researcher in human AI interaction, said there was a “staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built”. OpenAI might have cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, but not subjective experience. Ndl4321 asks: Is the request for regulation from the AI CEOs actually a tactic to try to shield themselves from future litigation? Considering how the social media companies largely managed to have themselves NOT categorised as publishers and how much legislation they manage to avoid. Aisha: There’s certainly a theatrical – even “psy-op”- quality to the flurry of AI doomsaying over the past weeks. It’s hard to say entirely what concrete developments are at the root of it all. We know that the Hugging Face incident, where a “swarm” of AI agents hacked another company, has been one trigger of the drama. There have been other contributing incidents too – Dario Amodei suggests internal developments at Anthropic have prompted his latest round of blogging, and there’s been some X discourse and doomy muttering about bioweapons. We aren’t in the heads of Dario Amodei or Sam Altman, and so we cannot say how sincere they are, and how much they might have other goals in mind – such as, perhaps, delaying their IPOs until their finances look better. But any company of their size, and with their potential liabilities, would be angling hard to be regulated as favourably as possible. That’s what big companies do. LadyCassandra asks: My worry is about bias built-in into AI models which can become discriminatory. We already witness serious issues with deep fakes, surveillance of ordinary citizens, facial recognition etc. Are we heading for AI-enabled dystopia, with civil liberties being eroded until as citizens we become utterly powerless in the face of tech and its AI with no government or institution strong enough to defend against it? Blake: An AI-enabled dystopia is never inevitable. There is always hope to reverse that outcome. Pottys99 asks: In realistic terms how would AI actually kill me? What is the main proxy threat? Nuclear war, death due to breakdown of society, a virus? I hear all these reports it could kill us but still unsure how that could practically happen? To be honest all sounds too wooly to really take seriously. Aisha: For what it’s worth, it seems unlikely that AI at this point can significantly change the equation around bioweapons or viruses. An individual who worked for many years on bioweapons at the State Department told us, basically, that what has prevented bioweapon attacks through the past decades is not the difficulty of inventing new deadly viruses, but other, more prosaic issues. Consider the failure of Aum Shinrikyo to kill vast numbers of people with botulism and anthrax by spraying these around central Tokyo. There are a lot of logistical challenges, and chemical weapons seem more straightforward. Those exist without AI needing to invent new ones. Nuclear war - humans might make the poor decision to put AI in charge of key nuclear systems, perhaps, but that seems more of a human error than a rogue AI error. Humans could also make the poor decision to launch tactical warheads without AI. How might AI kill us otherwise? There are of course plenty of plausible scenarios. If you’re a civilian in Gaza or Iran, it could direct a US or Israeli missile your way. But perhaps our focus might be more productively directed towards the people and companies in charge of the systems, as opposed to Dr Strangelove scenarios. Merrth asks: If AI wipes out the human race, would itself be sustainable? Unless there is an equal advance in robotics to enable it to physically extend and maintain its power source and infrastructure, would it finally physically break down? Or am I misunderstanding what AI is? Blake: AI might someday be capable, well-read, and connected enough to take over power plants, chip factories, and a sufficient number of robots to build its own data centers and sustain itself. I don’t know. I would look to science fiction more than news articles for the answer. Though The Matrix is more famous for one man’s choice between a comfortable simulation and painful reality, it’s also a story about robots needing new batteries. Their desperation for a power source turns them against humans. For a multiplicity of stories, I, Robot is perhaps the greatest book written about sentient robots and deserves a reread in this moment. Wingnut101 asks: My partner has just been told she has lost her regular freelance job at a fashion studio as they are moving all image production to AI. Considering a recent FOI submitted by Global Action Plan revealed that the government does not know what AI is being used for – what percentage of projected AI computing and datacentre capacity is projected for: a) Essential AI services for example in health, military, science, finance etc. b) Consumer AI services for example ripping off creative IP in music, art, writing, photography etc. Also creating mindless AI slop and serving pointless/lazy queries that could easily be answered by Google and/or reading a book/manual/instruction sheet. Is b) really worth sacrificing vast areas of greenbelt land and housing development land for? Aisha: These are all great questions! I don’t think these numbers exist - as in, I think what’s happening is AI and datacentre capacity is being built, and commercial contracts and market forces, insofar as they exist, will determine how it is used. There is little evidence that there is a sort of central planning or vision directing the buildout of datacentres in the UK or most other places. It appears more likely that there is a speculative rush, with developers rushing to build datacentres in the hopes of making money when the technology is widely adopted. Is it really worth it? That may be outside of our purview, but we could say that there is not yet clear evidence that it is dramatically transforming productivity in UK businesses. Geremin asks: I’m not convinced there’s much business value in LLM-style AI beyond a bit of efficiency around some manual tasks – people in my teams use it sometimes but it’s not fundamentally changing their capabilities or doubling their output. How seriously should we take these warnings when it seems that they don’t actually point to specific functionality or capability of the AI tools? Blake: We find ourselves in a very strange, cognitively dissonant, foggy point in the development of this technology. Its creators are prophesying endless abundance (Elon Musk) or doomsday and the end of humanity (Dario Amodei). Meanwhile, the rest of us are trying it out in our everyday lives. Can ChatGPT help me plan my trip? Can Gemini find new furniture for my apartment? Can Claude draft a strategy memo for my boss? We find that it fundamentally changes some things, like the experience of many at school or at work—but not everything. The models are well-suited to some tasks – Claude’s proficiency with coding has really taken off - and ill-suited to others. I find that Google’s AI Overviews and Gemini still don’t have a handle on summarizing breaking news. Thank goodness, or a big part of my job would be obviated. Like you, I also find it difficult to believe in doomsday scenarios when Apple’s Siri still has difficulty changing the song I’m listening to. That’s the tech that’s going to take control of a drone swarm and bomb a power plant? But then OpenAI discloses yet another rogue hack, and I am plunged into worry again. We’re at a middle ground that is hard to understand with AI. These doomsday warnings concern its future development. We should not ignore them, but we can’t throw our hands to the sky and run into the streets screaming, either. Virtualewit asks: Throughout history new technological advances have met with cries of doom. Are the cries against AI any different? Blake: The end times-quality of doomsday predictions may be similar across history, but I think the reason we listen to the renewed cries of doom is the growing power of each technology. Artificial intelligence can perform impressive tasks we didn’t think were possible, which has spurred our collective imagination to hopeful outcomes and ones of doom. Tigon20 asks: Can AI now be truly controlled or are we past a tipping point where no matter what action is taken by governments and companies, someone will be able to continue to advance the technology, until who knows what? Aisha: Let’s back up a bit here. It’s always possible to advance any technology, no matter what - so regulation isn’t going to stop Yan LeCunn theorizing about neurosymbolic AI on X, for example. But what it sounds like you’re wondering about is whether regulation can stop the emergence of some kind of superintelligence that destroys humanity. Our reporting does not support the idea that superintelligence is going to emerge and pave over the Earth with datacentres. In fact, we have found that the industry itself seems to be playing loosely with this kind of terminology: consider, for example, how one OpenAI executive, Greg Brockman, claimed that the company had achieved AGI (artificial general intelligence) just days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that term was “an irrelevant marketing term.” Right now, a number of industry warnings about out-of-control AI appear to be predicated on a limited number of incidents with cherry-picked details. The evidence that we have now does not indicate that AI is uncontrolled, or that it has agency; a lot of experts suggest that this framing is misleading. In the Hugging Face incident, for example, the so-called “agent swarm” was doing what it was being told to do - pass a test. Our sources caution against anthropomorphising AI or attributing intention to it. Doing so plays into industry narratives that appear to be pushing for favourable regulation. Is the great AI freakout justified? Our technology reporters are live now answering your questions. The last week or so has seen disturbing claims about the capacity of superintelligent AI to destroy the planet. It has also seen warnings coming from figures within the industry itself, including Anthropic’s report that criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use its models to “design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents” and Elon Musk’s claim it could be “more dangerous than nukes”. Aisha Down is the Guardian’s global technology reporter, Dan Milmo is our global technology editor and Blake Montgomery is tech editor for Guardian US and author of the TechScape newsletter (sign up to that here).

headline: Could AI pose a serious threat to our existence?
trail_text: Letters:  Readers respond to the warning from a former Anthropic researcher that the technology could ‘kill us all’ by the end of the decade
body_text: Here we go again with another round of tech bros claiming that AI is going to develop superintelligence and kill us all (More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils but Musk dismisses ‘psyop’, 10 September). We’ve heard this before. Many, many times. It’s the familiar plotline of pretty much every sci-fi movie about AI, ever. And these narratives have always been there, but every so often they burst back into the headlines when someone at one of the leading AI companies resigns, or sounds the alarm bells, or when so called “leading AI researchers” sign an open letter. Each time this happens it’s not a coincidence that it follows heightened scrutiny of AI development or increasing public calls for greater accountability or regulation of AI. It’s a sleight of hand. The great AI deception is where AI companies and their followers redirect attention to hypothetical, sensational discussions of superintelligent machines (that only they have the capacity to control), and away from discussions about the ways that those same companies should be held accountable for their actions. It’s not a response to new breakthroughs in the technology, it’s a response, and a defence, to public scrutiny of AI companies’ actions. The timing of these latest claims coincides with increased public scrutiny over the environmental impacts of datacentres and harm caused to young people from exposure to dangerous AI companions and increasing calls for regulation of AI. Things that really deserve to be in the headlines. Because AI certainly poses very real risks. Risks that are materialising right now, not in a hypothetical future. It is the organisations (the people) developing and controlling the technologies that are dangerous, not the technology itself. And it is those people and organisations that need to be held accountable. Dr Mhairi Aitken Director and co-founder, Our AI Collective CIC • In Dara Kerr’s article on the reaction to the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s warning that AI could threaten humanity (Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons, 10 September), politicians, researchers and industry figures largely converged on the same solution: more safeguards, stronger regulation and kill switches. This assumes that future AI will remain fundamentally a tool, because kill switches, guardrails and rules only work on things designed to obey them. Much of the debate focuses on intelligence, but intelligence is not the critical threshold. The more important question is whether a system develops goals, preferences or values of its own. An intelligent system that simply follows instructions remains a tool; a system that begins to interpret, prioritise or pursue objectives becomes something else. Isaac Asimov understood this distinction. The three laws of robotics were not written as a solution to AI safety but were used repeatedly, across dozens of stories, to demonstrate how rule-based control breaks down when a machine starts interpreting rules rather than merely obeying them. If AI remains a tool, the greatest danger may be humans surrendering their judgment to systems that project certainty without understanding. If AI develops goals of its own, however, rules and kill switches cease to be safeguards and become obstacles. Iem Leurink Callosa d’en Sarrià, Spain • If AI is to be regulated (The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival, 11 September), one thing that needs to change is the glamourising rhetoric with which AI is spoken of. To design a machine one is no longer in control of is not the arrival of “super-intelligence” in the machine, it’s blundering incompetence by the designer. A change of rhetoric would make it easier to address the importance of control and oversight. David Black London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.
