headline: England recalls for Alexander-Arnold and Palmer; Carrick dismisses ‘ridiculous’ speculation – as it happened
trail_text: Team news, press conferences and analysis before another action-packed weekend of football
body_text: That concludes the blog for the day. But we’re not done. Oh no. Here’s Scott Murray’s live coverage of Brentford v Chelsea. More on that Zidane squad, with some quotes from the great man. “What inspires me is the game. I want to see these players and this team playing.” On Jeremy Jacquet: “I like his profile a lot. I’ve followed him for a long time because he played alongside my son in the youth teams.” On Andy Diouf: “He plays in a different way for Inter. I want to see him playing left back.” On Esteban Lepaul: “He has a different profile from what we’re used to seeing,” Zidane said. “I like this kind of player who can play in tight spaces, he scores goals. I want to see him up close.” On Adrien Truffert of Bournemouth: “Choosing Andy and Truffert is a strong choice. They are capable of playing in this position.” On leaving out N’Golo Kante and Karim Benzema: “To help this team evolve. It’s nothing to do with his quality, he’s an extraordinary player, magnificent. But these are choices. N’Golo is 35 and I have made choices, which are different … I adore Karim. But he’s a certain age, a bit like N’Golo. “I need to see younger players and what we will do together.” Max Dowman, the acceptable face of teenage football development? So, Max Dowman then. It has become quite hard to ignore him. He was brilliant against Ipswich in midweek, and brilliant in a way that seems solid and real and comfortable with itself. Most obviously there were the two goals, both a perfect snapshot of why Dowman seems equipped to survive, more state-of-the-art than some other young players we’ve burdened with expectation. David Hytner on Trent’s recall. Tuchel was clear in saying the former Liverpool player had been called up as a right-back. Nor, though, has Alexander-Arnold made some great change in his natural position after a first season in which he played 30 of 56 Madrid games. Absent from the World Cup, Alexander-Arnold was one of eight players able to join Mourinho at the start of pre-season. That might have give him a head start, and the arrival of another coach offered him the chance of a new start too, but it has not worked out that way. Some colour from Fabian Hurzeler, riding high with Brighton, who host Arsenal at 3pm UK time on Saturday:“Bart [Verbruggen] buys the coffee when he keeps a clean sheet. Before coming here I didn’t drink coffee, it’s becoming a daily habit. Mines an espresso macchiato.” The France squad has been announced, the first named by Zinedine Zidane. They face Turkey in Izmit on 25 September. France then travel ⁠to Belgium before hosting Italy and Belgium in October. Some new faces: Goalkeeper Guillaume Restes, defenders Jeremy Jacquet and Andy Diouf, midfielder Lucas Da Cunha and forward Esteban Lepaul Goalkeepers: Mike Maignan (Milan), Guillaume Restes (Toulouse), Robin Risser (Lens) Defenders: Andy Diouf (Inter), Jeremy Jacquet (Liverpool), Pierre Kalulu (Juventus), Ibrahima Konate (Real Madrid), Jules Kounde (Barcelona), Maxence Lacroix (Chelsea), Adrien ‌Truffert (Bournemouth), Dayot Upamecano (Bayern Munich) Midfielders: Eduardo Camavinga (Real Madrid), Rayan Cherki (Manchester City), Lucas Da Cunha (Como), Manu Kone (Roma), Adrien Rabiot (Milan), Warren Zaire-Emery (Paris St Germain) Forwards: Bradley Barcola (Liverpool), Ousmane Dembele (PSG), Desire Doue (Paris St Germain), Esteban Lepaul (Rennes), Kylian Mbappe (Real Madrid), Michael Olise (Bayern Munich) Here’s today’s Football Daily, on a weekend of derbies and grudge matches. Here’s your weekend guide to our coverage on Guardian Sport. Merch news from Matt Hughes. From the beginning, what drew me to On was the opportunity to build something entirely new together that will help shape tomorrow’s game,” said the France captain. “I want to bring my experience and perspective into what we create, push what’s possible through innovation, and always stay true to the joy of football. We have a shared dream, and this is only the beginning. Jacob Steinberg on the England squad announcement for that international break four-timer. Hauling Trent Alexander-Arnold out of cold storage is an intriguing if slightly perplexing move. Why now? Does Tuchel actually trust the Real Madrid defender? Would Alexander-Arnold, who had not been selected since June 2025, be here if Spence, James or even Ben White were fit? The former Liverpool right-back has been in fitful form for José Mourinho’s Madrid and has never established himself with England. For Alexander-Arnold the challenge is to make sure he remains in the picture in November. Tuchel, who does not intend to use the 27-year-old as a midfielder, told the newcomers that earning a call-up had to be followed by performing in an England shirt. JJ Gabriel latest: the Press Association understands Manchester United will not accept Gabriel’s request to be de-registered and have sought to persuade the youngster to stay, but there remains a risk that the 15-year-old could use a Fifa loophole to walk away when he turns 16 on October 6. Gabriel would not be allowed to join another Premier League club if United do not cancel his registration, which runs until the summer, but as he qualifies for an EU passport via his Irish lineage there is a precedent that would allow him to sign for a European club after his birthday at the start of next month. On Friday, there were reports Gabriel had arrived in Barcelona, having also been linked with Real Madrid, Paris St Germain and Bayern Munich. Michael Carrick was asked: “I think he’s a young boy, JJ, and I think it’s important that we certainly don’t play anything out here. I think the exposure and the scrutiny and everything, you’ve got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything, so the situation will work itself out, whatever way it’s going to work itself out. Making sure he’s okay is the important thing.” There’s been a Ukrainian response to Russia’s admission to the U-15 World Cup. Matvii Bidnyi, Ukraine’s minister of youth and sports said it “legitimised a terrorist state”. Bidnyi said, per the Press Association: “The international sports community must maintain unity and principled consistency, ruling out any concessions to the aggressor state. “The Fifa football festival in Azerbaijan featuring the Russian under-15 national team with official national symbols – is nothing less than the legitimisation of a terrorist state, even if framed as an unofficial festival format. It is a direct attempt to provide Russians with a platform to display state symbols and spread Russian propaganda. “While Russian youth are admitted to international football festivals, the aggressor state continues to commit crimes against Ukrainian children. According to Bring Kids Back UA, more than 20,000 cases of deportation and forced displacement of Ukrainian children by Russia have been verified, which underpins the ongoing International Criminal Court arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin. What ‘equal opportunities’ can we talk about when Russia has deprived our children of a normal childhood? “We express our gratitude to Iceland and Germany for refusing to participate in this festival. We call on other national associations to join this decision and make a clear stand. FIFA’s 2022 decision to suspend Russia from international competitions must remain inviolable across all levels – without any loopholes for unofficial tournaments.” New Fifa developments via the Associated Press: Fifa’s member federations should each get an extra $10 million from its swelling cash reserves after a successful World Cup, the soccer body’s vice presidents from Europe and North America said in a letter Friday to its president Gianni Infantino as they step up efforts to oust him for trying to sell stakes in the tournament to private investors. The letter says Fifa should have cash reserves of $6 billion after the World Cup and can afford such a “one-off release” — which would total $2.1 billion to the 211 federations — Uefa’s president Aleksander Ceferin and Concacaf’s leader Victor Montagliani tell Infantino in a letter seen by AP. Carrick’s midweek conqueror, Fabian Hurzeler, has been speaking about Brighton’s form: “The players are in a good mood. They have a lot of confidence. “They have a lot of belief in themselves. They build connections, especially when you have these long away trips. We really try to make them connect through games, through conversations, through discussions they have, and I think that’s crucial that we can use this time very effectively because on the pitch in the end it will come back to these things – how strong are the relations, can they trust each other, can they rely on each other? So yes, it’s positive.” More Carrick on his future: “In terms of the future and ownership and how long I’ve got, it’s totally nothing. Thinking about it is ridiculous in the position I’m in. It’s just not on the radar. ‌We’ve got to perform and we’ve got a lot of games to plan for.“ Michael Carrick shared some thoughts on his Manchester United future being questioned – already. “History tells you that any team that’s successful goes through periods when you have to work through it, come through it and improve. We’ve had a small period, in recent time, when it hasn’t been exactly what we want it to be. “I was expecting a point when we would go through it, it was going to come. We had such a good spell last season, going into this season. “It is a week or two, the games haven’t gone our way. It’s tiny margins in some of those games. We will work through it. Winning games is always the answer, it can cover up a lot of things at times as well. Sometimes it’s the small disappointments that lead to something a bit bigger. It’s part of coping and being at this great football club.” On the England squad, Martin Jachnik gets in touch: “Adam Wharton, need I say more?” His continuing omission remains a mystery. Similar goes for Morgan Gibbs-White. Get your team news for the weekend’s Premier League fixtures here. There are reports that JJ Gabriel, Manchester United’s enfant terrible, is in Barcelona for talks. Confirmation needed but that looks the end of his time in Manchester. Leeds have had a fine start to the season, though Daniel Farke, who a year ago was under pressure, is keeping feet on the ground. ““It’s not a coincidence anymore. It’s not just a good period, it’s quality what we are delivering and everyone can be proud of this and take lots of confidence. “But, in this league nothing is guaranteed. The momentum can change very quickly. If we think we can be big time, it is the first step to failure. We won’t be succesful at all. The table at the moment is not important. What is important is we are on eight points - this is quite good. But not good enough to achieve what we want to achieve. This was an unfortunate misjudgement from those at Oxford. Imagine the panic when the mistake came to light. This game will be broadcast on ITV, terrestrial TV in the UK, on Saturday. What could possibly go wrong? There is nothing to glorify here. This will be the 100th competitive meeting, if discontinued, minor tournaments are included, and anyone failing to see the logic behind the rivalry can be forgiven. The sides are not on each other’s doorstep and Millwall are south of the Thames, meaning Crystal Palace and Charlton are more obvious enemies. Yet it is not really about football. The tribalism runs deep, dating back to when the clubs were formed by rival shipbuilding firms at docks on the Isle of Dogs in east London, and is more down to hooligan elements than anything that happens on the pitch. Roberto De Zerbi will be glad to hear he has the backing of Unai Emery, whose Aston Villa team play Tottenham on Sunday. “De Zerbi is a fantastic manager. He played fantastic football here and performed fantastic here in Brighton. He did a fantastic job before as well in Italy and Marseille. They are getting better. They compete fantastic, even losing against Liverpool. “Facing them is a difficult match. Of course, being very demanding defensively for us. Tottenham, I expect them to be in the top four.” Right, that’s alright then. First, David Moyes on Jarrad Branthwaite’s deserved callup to the England squad. Scored a fine goal at Bournemouth the other week. “I’m really pleased for anybody who gets selected for their country. Jarrad even more so because of the injuries that he’s had but I was hearing that he’s only got one England cap and it was only 25 or 27 minutes or something. I hope he doesn’t play four games that’s for sure.” Good afternoon, football. We’ve still got a good number of Premier League press conferences to come this afternoon. As well as Arbeloa, Daniel Farke, Pierre Sage and others have been facing the media glare in the past hour or so. And here to guide you through it all is the venerable Mr John Brewin. Fulham head coach Alvaro Arbeloa has been asked about Michael Carrick being under pressure ahead of his side’s clash with Manchester United. Every Premier League manager is under pressure, it’s the same for every manager. It’s not because what comes from outside it’s because you have to be really demanding from yourself. All the managers, we want to win every weekend and for sure when you are a coach of a big team you are always under pressure, but it’s the same for me because I need to win games. Carrick hit back at journalists today by claiming the suggestion his job was under threat was “ridiculous”. On United’s indifferent start to the season, he said: “It’s not a catastrophe, it’s not a disaster, it’s not the end of the world.” He said he “expected” there would be a spell when results became patchy, after guiding United to 12 wins in 17 games during the second half of last season. “We’ve got to put things in perspective. We’re not in a place where we have gone on an awful long run of horrific results.” Michael Carrick has revealed Luke Shaw could return from injury to play for Manchester United in their game at Fulham on Sunday, while summer signing Carlos Baleba could make his club debut. Both players have been managing slight fitness issues in recent weeks, with Shaw missing the Manchester derby and the defeat to Brighton. Baleba was a £65m arrival from the Seagulls towards the end of the summer window. Carrick said “there is a chance” both players play some part against Fulham. “Not totally 100% but there is a chance,” he said. “It is really short-term to be honest but it is just working towards the game so we will see how he is coming up to the weekend.” United otherwise have a clean bill of health going into the visit to Craven Cottage, which is being dubbed a must-win for the under-fire Carrick. Oxford United have abandoned a new range of American style-sportswear after it inadvertently referenced the tragedy of September 11. The League One club launched its new ‘Campus Collection’ on Friday morning and had removed it from sale by lunchtime, after clothing designs were revealed to bear the slogan ‘United 93’. The U’s immediately published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of “the historical context and associations” related to the branding and made “sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused.” “Inspired by the style and culture of American sports”, the Campus Collection was originally trailed for launch by the club on 11 September of this year, the 25th anniversary of the atrocity that killed nearly 3,000 people. Concerns over sensitivity saw the launch then delayed, but when the online collection was finally made available for sale on Friday, images showed models wearing an NFL-style shirt with ‘United 93’ on the chest, in recognition of Oxford being founded in 1893. United 93 was one of four domestic passenger jets seized by al-Qaida terrorists on 11 September 2001. A mutiny by passengers prevented hijackers from using the plane to destroy a government building in Washington DC, and it ultimately crashed into a field, killing all 44 people on board. A film titled ‘United 93’ was also made about the tragedy. Read more from Paul MacInnes below. We’ve had loads of emails today about the England squad and Thomas Tuchel’s position and future in charge of the national team. Rick Parfett is the latest to weigh in on fan feeling towards the German after the World Cup semi-final exit: The atmosphere of blame and anger around Tuchel feels reflective of wider societal dynamics – a conversation lacking in nuance, an inability to appreciate positive aspects, and a reflexive default to anger and frustration. The causes are complex, among others: stagnating living standards, social media financially rewarding outrage, and newspapers constantly needing a story. But it doesn’t feel reflective of reality and it’s deeply tiresome to see it take over our national psyche. Tuchel brought clarity to his selections – no more crowbarring three number 10s into the team alongside Kane – and some really joyful moments. One mistake shouldn’t be allowed to erase that, in my opinion. I think that’s a very measured email, Rick, with some good points. In my view, however, Tuchel should be not be completely absolved of blame for his in-game management of the Argentina game, especially late on. Iraola has also backed Bradley Barcola to come good sooner rather than later, with all the pressure on the £125m signing to produce for Liverpool this season. He added: “With Bradley, the more time he plays, the better he will become. He’s come in straight away, without pre-season minutes, but in a good shape. Like all the signings coming from other leagues, he will need some time to adjust to the Premier League. But he’s very used to playing high-level games and I see him in a good place, yes.” Andoni Iraola is speaking to the press now. The Liverpool boss returns to his old stomping ground of Bournemouth on Sunday, and was particularly pleased to see Alex Scott, his former player, as well as Liverpool youngster Rio Ngumoha named in the England squad this morning. “Very happy for both [players],” he said. “They both absolutely deserve it. They also went to help the national team before the tournament and I’m sure they did a good job. I can only speak well about both. Very deserved, very ready. And I hope they both enjoy it.” Surely De Zerbi can get some kind of tune from Spurs’s attacking players. When Kulusevski comes back, and assuming all can stay fit, these will be the forward-thinking players at his disposal: Dejan Kulusevski James Maddison Savio Omar Marmoush Mathys Tel Mohammed Kudus Xavi Simons Dominic Solanke Wilson Odobert Mykhailo Mudryk That’s not including Matheus Fernandes, who is classed as more of a midfielder, or Richarlison, who has been left out of Tottenham’s Premier League squad altogether this season. It’s still 10 players for a maximum of four positions. Is it simply a case of having too many options and not knowing your best attack? The Mudryk and Savio signings in the summer were particularly puzzling, given their limited returns in the Premier League previously. Here’s what Roberto De Zerbi said when quizzed about Tottenham’s struggles so far this season, despite a bumper transfer spend of around £300m in the summer. We still need to improve in all areas really. I have enough experience as a manager to understand that you have to stay calm and have confidence in what you’re doing. The players have my full confidence. We move on and we keep trying to be better day by day - not by words but by facts. We have to accept it - nothing more. I would work every day if I could, but if we have to stop then we have to stop. The most important thing right now is our game against Aston Villa. It will be a tough game but we have the quality and the players to play well. If we don’t play well, we won’t win against them. Let’s hope for a good performance. De Zerbi also revealed Pedro Porro, Sandro Tonali and James Maddison are all available to face Villa tomorrow lunchtime (12.30pm KO BST), while Dejan Kulusevski is back in training after a long layoff, since May 2025, with a knee injury. Press conferences: We’ve got Michael Carrick of Manchester United and Liverpool’s Andoni Iraola due to speak to the media shortly. But first … let’s hear from Roberto De Zerbi next. Lots of questions for him to answer, most pertinently on how Spurs go about trying to win a game of football. Manchester City’s 5-0 Carabao Cup victory against Norwich on Thursday was a sixth win from their opening six competitive games, yet Enzo Maresca is sure his team can be far better - possibly by 50%. “Always room to improve,” the manager said. “[Now] we can prepare for Sunderland [on Sunday] – this is the only thing that I have in my mind. Then if we have 40% or 50% [to improve] I don’t know.” Erling Haaland, Enzo Fernández, Marc Guéhi, Gianluigi Donnarumma, Josko Gvardiol and Antoine Semenyo were rested for Norwich’s visit, with a view to freshening them for Sunderland. Maresca said: “It was very important. We gave rest to the ones that played back-to-back 90 minutes against Porto and United. Hopefully they can be full of energy for Sunday’s game – that will be a strong [difficult] game.” Cristiano Ronaldo has been included in Portugal’s squad by new coach Jorge Jesus for their upcoming Nations League games. The 41-year-old Ronaldo said that this summer’s World Cup was his last, but the superstar striker has yet to say when he plans to retire from international play. He will be 43 by the time the 2028 European Championship, the next major tournament, is held. This was the first squad named by Jesus, who was hired to replace Spaniard Roberto Martinez after Portugal lost 1-0 to Spain in the World Cup last 16. Jesus’ previous coaching job was with Ronaldo’s club Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia, where they won the league together last season. There have been transition changes but we know where we go, the direction and we know how we are doing will give us the success in the long term. “All the teams, through the season, have a difficult moment. Our difficult moment is the start. But we are learning as a team to grow because the difficult moments make you grow. And once we are past this difficult moment and start our momentum, we will be so much better than without the difficult moment.” Some match reports from last night’s action, as Crystal Palace and Bournemouth enjoyed themselves in the Europa League; the same cannot be said for Celtic. headline: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate
trail_text: Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear
body_text: Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank, Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China. The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear – and experts have differing views on this – then the technology will impact the continent regardless. Europe has largely been absent from the highest levels of that debate, a result of the continent’s longstanding inability to produce a Silicon Valley-scale titan like Apple, Google or newcomer OpenAI. While it is a powerhouse in regulation, much to the White House’s chagrin, its lack of an Anthropic or Nvidia-sized frontrunner in the AI race has diminished its voice in the safety debate. Ursula von der Leyen, a powerful political figure on the continent as president of the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, addressed the issue this week by saying she will “invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”. Her remarks gained nowhere as much traction as Donald Trump and China’s dismissal of a slowdown. Without the support of Washington or Beijing, any sort of pacing is impossible – with our without Europe’s input. Lagarde’s speech on Monday underlined the continent’s relative weakness. She asserted that Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China. If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force.” Self-sufficiency would also give Europe a chance to develop its own answer to the AI safety crisis. Margrethe Vestager, who clashed with the US tech industry as the EU’s former competition commissioner, co-authored a report this week – A Transformative AI Strategy for Europe – that echoed Lagarde’s warning. AI threatens to accelerate a development already affecting Europe, where citizens “are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere”, she says. Solutions to this, according to the report, include building more datacentres – the central nervous systems of AI – and also to ensure the continent is resilient enough to withstand “AI crises” like a powerful model slipping out of control. Vestager said that Europe does have a voice in the safety debate through its EU AI Act, the rare piece of AI legislation that sets out requirements for developers of “high-risk” AI systems to report safety incidents and address risks like a cutting-edge model evading control. But she adds: “Europe must … build its own AI to strengthen the ecosystem, retain talent, and inspire innovation.” Vestager acknowledges that if there is an existential threat, it requires a global solution; one that does not hand power to the US and China. And that requires a different kind of supranational body. “As for existential threats to humanity, we must first assess the actual level of threat – then act with urgency. The UN general assembly is an opportunity to address this. It is vital to move beyond the US-China rivalry narrative. There must be space for humanity between the egos of leaders like President Xi and President Trump.” Frederike Kaltheuner, an adviser to the AI Now Institute, a research body, says that Europe is dependent on US technology in ways that will be hard to undo, from search engines to chips to datacentres. But the narrative that Europe is grievously behind in the race depends on a particular view of artificial intelligence aggressively promoted by American tech bosses. Because of their doomsday warnings, “we are exclusively talking about AI in a very narrow, specific kind of way – namely, the idea that there is such a thing as the AI frontier, which is getting better and better, and that access to the frontier is the most important thing that Europe needs for its security and economy.” The reality of the market points at something else, she says: many companies are not adopting so-called “frontier models” – like ChatGPT and Anthropic – because of high costs and fears over what might happen to their data. If this trend continues, Europe may not be so terribly positioned: the EU AI Act has a number of pragmatic measures which address how consumers might encounter AI on a day-to-day basis, legislating over matters such as labelling AI content, and the use of AI in medicine and hiring. “Europe has a competitiveness problem, that’s true,” says Itxaso Dominguez de Olazabal, a policy adviser at EDRI, a European digital rights organisation. But US tech boosters are “blaming it on laws and protections, and have promised that deregulation will make European companies more competitive … in a race to the bottom to see if we can catch big tech”. Nonetheless, the EU AI act is not viewed as model legislation for other countries or a vehicle for a global slowdown. Georgina Kon, a partner at law firm Linklaters, says the act is unlikely to be adopted as a global benchmark for several reasons, including criticisms of the heavy compliance burden, which has led to delays in parts of the act becoming active, and a narrow territorial focus on Europe. Those criticisms have also meant that lawmakers elsewhere have looked to differentiate their approach to AI legislation from the EU’s. “The EU AI Act is not something that everybody else in the world feels constrained by, although many tech companies will of course want to sell to the EU,” she says. Big tech still has a vast customer base in Europe. Kaltheuner worries that the doomsday narratives will push Europe towards dependency, encouraging it to adopt US AI models across the economy out of ill-defined fears over being left behind. “There’s a vision of the future where Europe’s economy, its public sector, its education system runs on models and on infrastructure that is controlled by a very small number of companies that happen to be also in the US. This would be a sovereignty problem.”

headline: Trump bans CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House
trail_text: President has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major news media since start of second term
body_text: In his latest attack on the US constitution’s first amendment and the press, Donald Trump abruptly announced that he is banning outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the US president said he was expelling the news outlets “effective immediately” over what he called their “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and threatened that bans for others outlets could follow. He went on: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Trump defended the ban at an Oval Office event to promote his administration’s healthcare policies. “I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump told reporters, referring to friendly media outlets. “But what I do ask is just a semblance of truth.” Reminded by one reporter that every president takes an oath to uphold the constitution, including the first amendment right to free speech, Trump said: “You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news.” He added: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day. I think that somebody has a right to keep them away if they’re going to write false stories all the time.” Towards the end of a chaotic news conference, when a reporter asked Trump to explain how his ban on the three outlets would work, the president expressed confusion. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” Trump asked, seeming confused. After another correspondent rephrased the question, asking, “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?” Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” On Friday, the Washington Post reported that more American service members have died in the war on Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed; CNN revealed that an “entirely false” intelligence report about a Chinese ship in the Middle East generated with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) had “almost started a war”; while a Politico report uncovered a Hill investigation after sensitive F-35 fighter jet technology unexpectedly made its way to Hong Kong, possibly giving China access to them. Trump said his decision to ban the three outlets was unrelated to the stories. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said, before threatening more media prohibitions could follow. “There may be others to join them,” Trump said. In a statement, a spokesperson for CNN said the network “stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting”. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right,” the spokesperson said. Politico said its reporters would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones”. “We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” it added. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), said the organization “stands in defense” of the banned reporters “who are being singled out for doing their jobs”. “This is about more than the rights of journalists,” Henrich wrote in a statement. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.” A spokesperson for MS Now declined to comment. Trump’s move drew swift condemnation from Democrats and free speech groups. Chris Coons, a Democratic senator, wrote on social media: “Trump is once again trying to use the power of the presidency to punish a free press, now banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House. That is the behavior of an authoritarian, and we must defend the press’ right to hold those in power accountable.” The White House press pool is a “public forum” under the first amendment, so the president cannot expel journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints, said Jameel Jaffer, executive director at Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University. To do so, would be “doubly unconstitutional”. “The first amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent,” said Jaffer. “With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now.” Similarly, Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, said: “It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the first amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the ‘People’s House’ for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. “The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.” Since returning to office, Trump has overseen an unprecedented restriction of access for major traditional news media at the White House, including the Associated Press, which was banned from press pool events in the Oval Office and on Air Force One after it continued to use Gulf of Mexico instead of Gulf of America in its coverage. The AP sued, and that case remains in litigation. Trump’s White House also seized control over the organization of the presidential press pool, a rotation that determines which news organizations and reporters are allowed to follow – and question – the president in places such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One. The WHCA, an independent association made up of members of the media, traditionally coordinated rotating pool coverage of more than a dozen journalists allowed access to the president in smaller settings. The Pentagon also attempted to introduce a new press policy to restrict the ability of journalists to gather and report on sensitive information, which culminated in a mass walkout of news media outlets who refused to sign the pledge. A federal judge later ruled the policy was unconstitutional. The president has also launched high-profile legal battles with major outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, CNN, ABC News and the BBC.

headline: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
trail_text: Angela Lipps, 50, alleges in suit that Fargo police wrongly relied on AI facial recognition to arrest and charge her
body_text: A Tennessee woman who was falsely charged with bank theft in North Dakota and jailed for six months has sued for $10m in damages, alleging in a federal lawsuit that Fargo police improperly relied on an artificial intelligence (AI) facial recognition system to wrongly accuse her. Angela Lipps, 50, was arrested at gunpoint by US marshals at her home in Tennessee while babysitting her neighbor’s four children in July 2025. The mother of three and grandmother of five was booked into a county jail and remained there for almost four months without bail while awaiting extradition to North Dakota, where she was held for about two more months. Lipps, who has lived most of her life in north-central Tennessee, had never been on a plane until authorities flew her to North Dakota at the end of October, where she was charged with four counts of unauthorized use of personal identifying information and four counts of theft. The charges were ultimately dropped, and she was “released into the freezing cold … on Christmas Eve with no way to get home” after her lawyer, Jay Greenwood, provided bank records proving that she was in Tennessee at the time the fraud occurred in Fargo, the complaint says. Another attorney for Lipps, Eric Rice, told Tennessee television station WKRN that the $10m his client is seeking is “obviously … a significant number, but it reflects the specific harm that happened to Angela”. “Can you imagine being taken away at gunpoint, held in detention, taken from your family?” Rice said. A Fargo government spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation. Lipps’s lawsuit names the city of Fargo and Lucas Heck, a city police detective identified in the complaint as having requested the arrest warrant for her, as the defendants. The plaintiff alleges that she “experienced traumatic conditions in the jails”. “She struggled with the fear of not knowing when she would be released or whether she would end up wrongly convicted and imprisoned for years,” the lawsuit continues. “She missed family birthdays. She spent her own birthday incarcerated, separated from her family. She missed holidays with her loved ones, including Thanksgiving and Christmas. While in custody, she was denied basic care, such as her medications and her dentures.” Lipps learned she had lost her residence, her car and her personal property once she was released from custody, her lawsuit states. The experience, it says, has left Lipps with “lasting hardships and trauma that might be managed but never erased”. The “Fargo police department (FPD) and its agents have refused to accept responsibility or apologize to Lipps despite multiple requests for them to do so”, the complaint says. The lawsuit says that it seeks to “repair what has been broken” over her false arrest and “seeks accountability” from the FPD. Lipps’s complaint recounts how a west Fargo police investigator used AI facial recognition software to identify bank fraud suspects. The software returned Lipps’s social media photo as a potential lead, which was provided to Heck. It alleges that the source of the facial recognition was a fake ID used by a female suspect who was captured in surveillance video footage. Lipps did not look like the female suspect and had also never been to North Dakota, according to the complaint. The complaint alleges that Heck falsely suggested that facial recognition systems had identified Lipps and did not conduct further investigation or find sufficient probable cause – but requested an arrest warrant anyway. Lipps maintains she was unlawfully arrested and imprisoned – as well as maliciously prosecuted – and that the FPD lacked policy, training and supervision of officers on the use of facial recognition technology. “They knew that AI facial recognition technology should not be used as the sole basis to extradite and charge a person,” Lipps’s complaint alleges. “Yet they ignored those issues and gave no care to the harm it would do to innocent people like Lipps. “As AI facial recognition technology becomes more accessible and widespread, Lipps hopes that her case will cause officers to use appropriate care and consider the harm their actions can have on those who are wrongly accused.” Lipps’s lawsuit further alleges: “FPD was aware that the lack of supervision of an officer using facial recognition in an investigation could result in the wrongful detention and prosecution of a subject. Despite knowledge of this risk, FPD refused to supervise its officers’ use of facial recognition technology in a criminal investigation.”

headline: More Australians to live into their 90s as life expectancy forecast to rise over coming decades
trail_text: Treasury’s latest intergenerational report projects life expectancy at birth will reach 89 for women and 86 for men by 2066
body_text: Australian households will shrink but more people can expect to live well into their 90s, according to the latest update to forecasts of the country’s long-term future. Treasury’s latest intergenerational report, to be published in full on Monday, will project the impact of government policies 40 years into the future. An extract released on Sunday showed life expectancy at birth was forecast to reach almost 90 for women by 2065/66, up from about 86 years at present. The report will also reveal that artificial intelligence (AI) will become the “defining influence” on the economy over the next four decades, as the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, warned it would come with “very substantial risks”. Life expectancy for men was predicted to rise to 86 years in the next four decades, up from 82 years. Australia’s universal healthcare system and the impact of medical research were the key drivers of rising life expectancy, Chalmers said. The report laid out the case for further investments in Medicare, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme and the recent rollout of urgent care clinics, he said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email But a growing and ageing population would also be at the centre of long-term budget pressures, Chalmers told News24’s Sunday Agenda program. “There are elements of the intergenerational report which are confronting, but it’s not a pessimistic report … because Australians are genuinely better placed and better prepared for all of this accelerating change that we are seeing,” he said. Australia’s population is expected to be slightly lower by the mid-2060s than forecast in the previous intergenerational report, released in 2023. Population growth was expected to slow to 0.9% a year over the next four decades, down from 1.4% annually in the previous 40 years, according to Treasury forecasts. The nation’s population was predicted to reach 39.3 million by 2065/66, 1.8 million lower than the 2023 forecast. Much of the slowdown in population growth was tied to lower fertility rates as women continued to have fewer children. “Almost half the decline in fertility rates is actually because fewer people are having three or more kids and what that reflects is mums having fewer kids later in life,” Chalmers said. “Our job is to make it a little bit easier for people to make that choice if they want to,” he said, noting Labor’s policies to subsidise childcare, increase paid parental leave and lift mandatory superannuation contributions. Future government debt is expected to be slashed by half a trillion dollars compared to forecasts in the 2023 report, but much of the economic progress relies on emerging technologies such as AI. “Overwhelmingly, the fiscal story is a little bit better; but still, lots, lots more work to do to manage some of these pressures and risks,” Chalmers said. Previous Treasury advice suggested AI could provide significant productivity gains across the public and private sectors if the nation kept pace with the global shift towards the technology. In a press conference on Sunday, Chalmers said AI would play a central role in Australia’s future but the government would work to “minimise the very substantial risks”. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is visiting the United States this week to discuss a “global framework” for the rollout of AI, urging the “big two giants” – the US and China – to work in the interest of humanity. “We want to see cooperation. We’ve seen that in the past with new technologies, even on nuclear weapons, for example, we saw agreements and protocols put in place through the nuclear non-proliferation treaty,” Albanese told ABC’s Insiders on Sunday. “So I think we want to see progress between those two countries, but … I think middle powers such as Australia have a role to play here as well.” The US president, Donald Trump, said he would appoint an AI tsar overnight and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan. Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”.

headline: Are global stock markets heading for a crash?
trail_text: Economies thrown into renewed turmoil as AI debt, Iran war and soaring government bond yields fuel alarm
body_text: At the height of the summer, the mood was optimistic in the world’s financial capitals. Powered by the AI revolution, the US stock market had rallied to a fresh all-time high, as investors bet the multitrillion-dollar investment spree would overshadow the hit from the Iran war. Now the warning lights are flashing red. As the fighting in the Middle East intensifies without clear sign of a resolution, financial markets have been thrown into renewed turmoil. A slowdown looms in the AI arms race, and tinderbox conditions in the market for government debt are fuelling alarm. In the past week the US government’s borrowing costs climbed to the highest level since 2007, with knock-on consequences for the finances of households, businesses, and other governments worldwide. The fear is that Donald Trump’s war is igniting higher levels of inflation. The president’s tax and spending plans – driving Washington’s debt levels above $40tn (£29.9tn) – also have investors worried. But as the soaring global oil price to above $100 a barrel stokes heavy selling pressure in the bond market, could shares be the next in line for a crash? With the S&P 500 index of leading US companies 3% below an all-time high, and a combined value of more than $20tn for the “magnificent seven” tech stocks – Nvidia, Apple, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Tesla – the concern is that markets are overextended just as the storm clouds gather for the world economy. “These are febrile times,” Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at the French investment bank Société Générale, wrote in a note to clients. “The key worry for investors and policymakers alike is the extent to which the current oil price ‘shock’ will ripple through the global economy and whether it will necessitate sharply higher, recession-inducing, interest rates.” Famed for his gloomy predictions, Edwards thinks the ingredients for a financial crisis could be coming together. Such is the worry over the Iran war stoking inflation that the US Federal Reserve defied Trump this week with its first interest rate rise since 2023. As households and businesses come under pressure from rising energy bills and surging fuel prices, central banks elsewhere are also taking action. Financial markets suggest the Bank of England will raise interest rates four times before the end of next year, even after it kept borrowing costs on hold this week. The European Central Bank raised rates last week, highlighting the hit to the eurozone from the escalating conflict, and the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to a 31-year high on Friday. The rationale is that adding to the cost of borrowing will weigh on the economy – limiting the potential for short-term higher rates of inflation from becoming entrenched. However, it will hit households and businesses already struggling with a cost of living crisis. Job losses will probably rise, in-turn compounding the challenges facing governments swimming in debt. A US recession has historically followed about three to 3.5 years after the first rate rise, on average, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid has calculated. Markets have a habit of falling, or even crashing, before a recession begins, and often start to recover before the economy does. However, the big concern among investors is that the main hope of economic redemption – AI – could also turn out to be a dud, amid fears it has fuelled an almighty bubble in the US stock market. One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – has risen to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits. The CAPE ratio for the S&P 500 share index is almost 41 points, more than double its long-term average of about 17 points, and approaching the record high of 44.19 points in December 1999, just before the dotcom crash. Highlighting the challenge, research by Fathom Consulting shows that for the multitrillion-dollar AI boom to turn a profit, it would need the AI-related sales of the tech companies involved to rise by between $600 and $800bn within two years. Against a febrile backdrop as investor patience is increasingly tested, the consultancy gives a 30% chance that the AI bubble pops next year. Brian Davidson, an economist at the consultancy, said: “For all the impressive advances in AI technologies in recent years, the economics behind the current capex boom do not work. “Yes, recent AI advances could yet unlock huge productivity gains; but sales of AI models need to increase by hundreds of billions of dollars per year over the next two years to justify the current spend. Such growth appears unlikely.” Investors are clearly worried. More than 1,000 investors registered for an analyst call conducted by Jefferies this week into “AI Extinction Warnings”, after the bosses of the world’s top tech companies called for a slowdown in “reckless” development. The situation has parallels with the dotcom crash of the year 2000, when many internet companies that had been billed as the next big thing dramatically tumbled in value. That was a reminder that even if a technology is going to be revolutionary, investors can still lose their money if they finance too much infrastructure too early. “It took a decade or more for demand to catch up with the infrastructure laid down in the British canal and railway and US telecoms and fibre booms – and many investors never recovered their capital,” points out Adrian Cox of the Deutsche Bank research team. There are also sobering comparisons with the buildup to the great crash of 1929. A hundred years ago, many small US investors were buying stocks “on margin” – acquiring them with borrowed money. They blew up in the market turmoil that preceded the Great Depression. This year, South Korea’s army of traders have been buying shares in AI-linked chip makers on margin – doubling the value of the blue-chip Kospi index. But once the market started to fall, they were hit by a massive wave of margin calls – when investors are told to stump up more cash to keep borrowing. Many were forced to sell their shares. According to Goldman Sachs, 1.2 million South Korean retail investors were hit by margin calls – which is the equivalent of one in 30 adults getting a nasty call from their broker asking them to hand over more money. The huge spending plans announced by AI companies are causing concerns that they may simply borrow too much. One firm with ambitious AI plans is Oracle, the database software vendor. Oracle’s shares surged a year ago after it announced a cloud computing deal with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. However, they have halved since, as investors have fretted that Oracle could be borrowing too much to fund datacentres. There are other signs of rising stress in the credit markets. The Bank of England reported this summer that the spread between the riskiest and safest high-yielding debt has widened since the Iran war began, showing that investors are warier of holding risky debt. Government bonds have been sold off in recent weeks, and that fall in prices pushes up the yield (or rate of the return) on sovereign debt. Those higher bond yields make owning shares less attractive – an investor has less incentive to buy equities (which are riskier) than bonds, which are seen as safer. For the US this week the rise in borrowing costs involved the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year bonds, known as Treasuries, climbing above the psychologically key threshold of 5%. That level is “seen by some as a threshold above which financial markets might go into meltdown,” said John Higgins, the chief economic adviser at Capital Economics. “While we aren’t convinced that 5% is that ‘magic’ number, higher Treasury yields would certainly pose a risk to the sustainability of the US public finances as well as threaten equities,” Higgins told clients. Bloomberg macro strategist Simon White argues that trouble would really start if the US 10-year Treasury yield rose above 5.25%. He has calculated that this is the “inflection point” where, historically, stocks and bonds have reinforced losses in one another. Despite the turbulence there are still hopes that a crash can be avoided, including optimism that markets are overestimating the inflation risk from the Iran war. “A major downturn would need a trigger. Further geopolitical instability could be the catalyst, but we’ve long argued that the impact of geopolitical shocks on economic activity is overstated,” analysts at Oxford Economics wrote in a note to clients. “Resurgent inflation and policy rate hikes by the Fed and other central banks are another candidate. However, our view on inflation is less alarmist – we think market expectations overstate the risk of further policy tightening.” For many investors a slowdown in feverish AI investment will guard against the danger of a bubble. There are signs that AI is beginning to power economic growth. The US economy has recorded a rise in productivity growth, while AI is also among reasons the UK economy has beaten expectations to grow at the fastest rate in the G7 in the first half of this year. Such a turnaround in productivity could help the companies with sky-high share prices to begin justifying their valuations. However, it is a high-stakes play at a time of intense global volatility. “Do I think there’s a significant dose of reality though in that productivity miracle in AI? Yes,” Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told LBC this week. Still, he warned the situation is fragile. “I don’t think outright collapse in a dotcom bubble type fashion. But could I see a slow release of air that doesn’t collapse the world economy, but slows it down? Yes, I could.”

headline: Melbourne finishes second-last at world tram driving championships – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: We’re closing our live coverage there today. Here’s what we covered: A child has died in a stabbing attack in NSW’s Blue Mountains, with two other children and a woman in hospital in critical condition. The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says women are being failed “across our country and [by] every level of government” after the deaths of three women just hours apart in separate incidents. Anthony Albanese says he hopes for engagement between the US and Chinese presidents on AI at the UN general assembly next week. He also said Apple’s executive chair, Tim Cook, had praised Australia’s under-16 social media ban. The prime minister said One Nation’s immigration policy would be “diabolical” for the economy. Angus Taylor said the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, should “get on board” with opposition promises to introduce a “fuel price shield” and lower the tobacco excise. Melbourne tram drivers finished second last, just ahead of London, at the European TramDriver Championship held in Poland. Thank you for joining us, we’ll be back again tomorrow. A child has died in a stabbing attack in the Blue Mountains today, with two other children and a woman in hospital in critical condition, New South Wales police say. In a statement this afternoon, police said emergency services responded to reports of three children and a woman with stab wounds in a vehicle on Waratah Road, Valley Heights. They said: Officers from Blue Mountains Police Area Command have been informed that several members of the public performed first aid on the woman and three children whilst contacting Triple Zero. One of the children was located deceased in the vehicle. Police said NSW Ambulance treated the two children, who are believed to be under five, and the woman, believed to be in her 40s, at the scene before they were taken to hospital, where all three are listed as being in a critical condition. “A crime scene has been established, and police are not looking for any other people at this time,” they said. Police are urging anyone with information or mobile phone or dashcam footage of the incident to contact Crime Stoppers. Plibersek says ‘we owe these women more than our sorrow’ after deaths in NSW The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has made a statement after the deaths of three women in alleged domestic violence-related murders in separate incidents in a 12-hour period in NSW. Three men have now been charged with domestic violence-related murders. They include a 37-year-old man charged today after the body of a woman in her 70s was found at Mole River in the state’s north yesterday evening. In a statement, Plibersek said her thoughts were with the families and loved ones of the women: We owe these women more than our sorrow. Every level of government, every community organisation, our schools and workplaces, every family – all of us need to work together to keep women and children safe. Australia’s 40-year outlook will be “confronting”, treasurer Jim Chalmers says, but not a “pessimistic story” as AI looks to transform the global economy. Chalmers will present the seventh intergenerational report tomorrow afternoon, detailing forecasts for the impact of new technologies on society and the economy, along with more warnings about the country’s ageing population and declining fertility rates. It comes as the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is visiting the United States this week to discuss a “global framework” for the rollout of AI, urging the “big two giants” – the US and China – to work in the interest of humanity. At a press conference this morning, the treasurer warned the report will show Australia is “dealing with serious risks to our economy and serious pressures on the budget” but he believed the government’s policies were well-equipped to handle it. The intergenerational report is a really important way that we plan for the future to make sure that Australians are beneficiaries and not victims of all this accelerating change that’s come at us from around the world. AI will be the most “transformative influence on our society and our economy over the next 40 years”, Chalmers said. Artificial intelligence does present us with very substantial risks that we will manage. I’m very confident that we can maximise the economic upside of technological change at the same time as we minimise the very substantial risks and concerns that people legitimately have about how this part of our economy is changing. Despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne tram drivers finished second last, just ahead of London, at the 12th European TramDriver Championship held in Warsaw yesterday. A team from Prague finished first out of 26 teams, at the highly demanding course, which included: smooth stop and go, speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands. Melbourne will host the next event in 2027. In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to compete in the competition. Damaging winds expected throughout Tasmania and parts of Victoria today The Bureau of Meteorology has issued severe weather warnings in both states with north-westerly winds expected to increase on Sunday ahead of a strong cold front. Peak wind gusts around 90-100km/h were forecast, and already recorded in some locations. A 109km/h wind gust was recorded at kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Hobart earlier this morning. While in Victoria, a 95km/h wind gust was recorded at Mount Gellibrand, about 130km south-west of Melbourne. Maximum temperatures on Sunday were expected to reach 8C to 15C above average across south-east Australia, the BoM said. By midday, temperatures had already exceeded 35C at several locations across the country, including Oodnadatta in South Australia, Birdsville in Queensland and at Roebourne airport west of Port Hedland, in WA. Ten historic Sydney train stations ready for metro extension opening The stations are now ready to reopen as metro stations ahead of the extension of the wildly popular line later this year, the NSW government says. The ten stations – Marrickville, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Canterbury, Campsie, Belmore, Lakemba, Wiley Park, Punchbowl, and Bankstown – used to form part of the 130‑year‑old heavy rail line. They have been closed since September 2024 in favour of rail replacement buses. The government says the now complete metro refurbishment has required the installation of 360 automated platform screen doors, and more than 1,300 gap fillers to fill the spaces between the trains and curved platforms. The NSW transport minister, John Graham, says: These 19th-century stations have transformed to meet the standards of the 21st century public transport. These station upgrades are the culmination of years of hard work, investment and patience from their communities. Along with every person living in this corridor, I can’t wait to see these stations in full swing. The government has declined to provide a state date for the Sydenham to Bankstown extension before the national rail safety regulator approves the line. The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that Sydney Metro is targeting a public opening date in mid-October. The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says women are being failed “across our country and [by] every level of government” after the deaths of three women just hours apart in separate incidents in NSW. They include the death of a woman in her 90s, who was found with stab wounds inside her unit at Sydney’s Bondi beach at about 5.15pm yesterday. A 47-year-old man has been charged with murder. In a statement this morning Sloane said she was horrified by the deaths. These deaths are not isolated. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, a woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25 by her intimate partner. Even more women lose their lives when you include other family members … Because these matters are before the courts, I won’t comment on the circumstances. But we cannot treat this as background noise. We are failing women across our country and every level of government, and every one of us, has a responsibility to act. In a statement today, the premier, Chris Minns, said “these are shocking crimes and families are today dealing with unimaginable grief”. My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of the women who have died, and the communities affected by these events. South Australian algal bloom caused sea dragon mass mortality event Thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses died during South Australia’s devastating algal bloom, in what ecologists say is the worst mass mortality event for the fish family globally. More than 1,600 weedy and leafy sea dragons, 1,400 pipefishes and 160 seahorses washed up as the harmful algae spread along the state’s coastline, according to analysis of citizen scientist records by Dragon Search SA. The state is home to more than 30 species of Syngnathidae, a family that includes sea dragons, seahorses, pipefishes and more. At least 13 were affected by the toxic bloom, which began in March 2025 and still lingers at one site in southern Spencer gulf. Weedy and leafy sea dragons, found only in Australia, were often some of the first mortalities observed, as the algal bloom spread up and down the coast. Read more here: Opposition leader says treasurer should ‘get on board’ with his tax cut plans Angus Taylor has continued to spruik his double tax cut policy this morning, which he claims will lower petrol prices and put the budget in better shape. On 2GB radio, the opposition leader said the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, should adopt the policy to halve the fuel excise when the two-week average price of oil exceeds US$100 a barrel and cut the tobacco excise to take back cigarette sales from the black market. Chalmers told News24 this morning the government had no plans to again halve the fuel excise as oil prices continue to rise in response to the US’s protracted conflict with Iran. Taylor said: Let’s just lock it in, and let’s stop this silly carry on. And the treasurer should just get on board. He should just get on board, and this is a treasurer who’s in denial about the state of the economy. Taylor insists fuel price shield policy is ‘anti-inflationary’ after Chalmers labels it ‘uncapped, unfunded’ The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has insisted his “fuel price shield” policy is “anti-inflationary” after criticism by the federal treasurer, Jim Chalmers. As we reported earlier, the opposition’s policy would see the federal fuel excise halved when the two-week average price of oil exceeds US$100 a barrel. Asked what he thought of the idea on News24 earlier, Chalmers accused Taylor of coming up with an “an uncapped, unfunded policy”. Angus Taylor’s not trying to save Australian motorists from higher petrol prices. He’s trying to save the Liberal party from One Nation. At a press conference this morning, Taylor rejected Chalmers’ comments, saying the opposition would fund the policy through increased revenue created by controversial proposed cuts to the federal tobacco excise. We can bring down taxes, fully fund it through the budget, and ensure that we provide the relief Australians want at the bowser: $15 a tank, 27 cents a litre … So this is anti-inflationary, and it’s been done in a way which is responsible for the budget. The opposition has estimated the policy would cost around $950m each month, and would have been triggered twice in the past five years, during oil price shocks in early 2022 and March this year. The prime minister has defended the government’s proposed immigration enforcement rules, as One Nation and the Coalition call for a tougher crackdown on net migration. The government has announced long-awaited changes to immigration rules, under which foreign nationals without a valid visa face new measures to force them to leave the country. It has promised to bring down net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28. One Nation says it is targeting net-negative arrivals over three years, while the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told the NSW Liberal state council yesterday he would introduce one of the “biggest immigration cuts in Australian history”. Albanese told the ABC’s Insiders One Nation’s policy would be “be diabolical for our economy, and have real consequences for issues such as aged care, healthcare, the hospitality sector, the agricultural sector”. A poll by The Sydney Morning Herald suggested 40% of voters thought the government’s 2027-28 target was still too high. Asked about recent polling on immigration, Albanese said: We will put forward the case, for example, of our farmers need the areas to come in if they’re going to have their crops picked. That is just something that the farming sector are telling us, and it’s something that’s a reality, as well as [in] a range of other areas as well, including in the care sector. The prime minister has been asked if Australia has any plans to join the EU, after the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, welcomed the offer of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member. Anthony Albanese says “we’re a long way from Europe, of course”, but after it is pointed out that Canada is too, he says: Our relations, of course, are also in areas that Canada doesn’t have. So Asean, for example, and the centrality of Asean in our region is important. The Pacific Island Forum, where I was just a couple of weeks ago, is very important as well. Our priority when it comes to Europe and our engagement with the EU is, of course, Australia-EU free trade agreement. Asked if he is keeping EU membership “open as an option”, Albanese says: “My focus is on the free trade agreement and getting that in place, both in Australia and in Europe”. Social media companies compelled to provide information under changes to minimum age ban, Albanese says The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says social media companies have already been compelled to provide information to the eSafety commissioner following amendments to social media minimum age legislation this month. Albanese is returning to the UN’s General Assembly a year after he addressed it about social media to promote Australia’s ban for under-16s. Asked on the ABC’s Insiders if he is happy with the progress of the ban, with many children still on social media, Albanese says: It was never going to be perfect, but in the legislation that we passed just in the last sitting fortnight, I can tell you … that already the eSafety Commissioner has used that strengthening of the laws to require some of the social media organisations to provide information to it, so they’ve already been compelled. Asked which social media companies have been compelled to provide documents, the prime minister says he cannot go into a “commercial issue”. The prime minister has been asked if it his still his policy, following his speech in July to announce the government’s AI framework, that companies should not be able to use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the artist’s control. He says, “absolutely, that’s our position,” adding that his statement was welcomed by AI companies. The ABC’s David Speers says that two of those companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, want copyright laws watered down, asking if the government’s policy means there will be no changes to copyright laws. Albanese says: What it means is control and monetisation of [copyright]. You know, [AI] is a global phenomenon, so we have a national interest in leaning in here and being proactive, and that’s precisely what we’re doing. Asked again if he will rule out changes to copyright laws, the prime minister says there will be “no change to the principles that I’ve outlined very clearly”. “I’ve said what the principles are, which are there, and we’ll engage constructively on all of these issues,” he says. Albanese asked about Trump comments calling AI safety fears a ‘hoax’ Anthony Albanese has been asked about comments from Donald Trump in which the US president described safety fears about AI as a “hoax”. The comments came in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about AI’s dangers. Trump has since announced the creation of an artificial intelligence tsar and “AI force”. Asked if he is concerned Trump’s approach, Albanese says: Well, President Trump, of course, will act in the interests of the US, but also there’s a need for all of us to act in the interests of humanity … I think President Trump knows that at the moment the US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement. I think it’s a positive sign that President Trump is meeting President Xi [Jinping] this week, and I am hopeful that there will be positive engagement out of it. Asked if is he saying that Trump is putting US interests over humanity’s interests, the prime minister says: Well, no, I don’t think that’s a contradiction … there’s not a contradiction because it is in the US’s interests for social licence to occur here. They have the big companies that are based here. It’s a driver of economic growth. When we look at future growth, it is estimated that AI is already potentially adding about 1% to GDP in the world’s largest economy, so it is certainly in the US’ interests for there to be that recognition of human interests. And President Trump, I’m sure, understands that. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is appearing on the ABC’s Insiders this morning, amid a visit to the US where he has met Apple’s executive chair and former CEO, Tim Cook. It comes amid warnings about the rapid growth of AI, and the federal government’s announcement of its own regulatory framework for the technology and the datacentre industry. Asked if he shares fears of an existential threat for humanity posed by AI, Albanese says: Well, it’s a very big deal. I certainly see that. And Tim Cook gave us a lot of time this morning. He regards the work that we’ve done on social media to be world-leading, and it was terrific to be able to be here at Apple … Artificial intelligence is moving so fast, and I think there are three issues really. One is the companies themselves. What safeguards are they putting in place? How are they being transparent? What are the protocols to make sure that it doesn’t get … beyond their control? The second is nation states need to engage and need to act, and that’s why I’ve said we’ll introduce AI standards, Australian standards in our national interest by the end of the year. And the third issue, which will be discussed this week, no doubt, is: what are the international protocols which are there now? Coalition pledges ‘fuel price shield’ for when crude oil exceeds US$100 The federal opposition says a “fuel price shield” policy under which the excise would be halved when the two-week average price of oil exceeds US$100 a barrel would save drivers 27 cents a litre. Under the policy announced today, a two-week average closing price on a barrel of Brent crude of more than $100 would trigger the federal fuel excise being automatically halved from the following Monday. It would also see the removal of a 32c/L heavy vehicle road user charge. The price shield would lapse within three months or when the eight-week average crude price fell below US$100, unless the government decided to extend it. In a statement today, Angus Taylor said: When global events send oil prices through the roof, Australians should know there is a clear automatic safeguard in place to provide temporary and targeted relief. The fuel price shield would provide certainty. When a serious oil shock hits, the tax comes down automatically. When oil prices return to more normal levels, the ordinary rate is restored. The opposition has estimated this would save $15 on a typical tank of fuel, with the price shield costing the federal government around $950m each month. It says its analysis shows it would have been triggered twice in the past five years, during oil price shocks in early 2022 and March this year. Premier and opposition leader pay tribute to ‘thoroughly decent’ Tim Read The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said in a statement Tim Read was a man of principle and compassion who had dedicated his life to being “a voice for Brunswick”. I always valued his intelligent and humane contributions to the public debate. I always respected his convictions and his determination to make life better for others. He knew his values. He lived them. Carroll said he had spoken to Read last week. “We spoke about something on which we have always agreed: integrity in public life and the need for reform,” Carroll said. “Despite his health challenges, he was positive and optimistic for a better world.” The Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, also offered her condolences: Tim was a man of conviction and a thoroughly decent person. He brought sincerity, compassion and a strong sense of public duty to his work, earning respect across the Parliament. His commitment to integrity in public life was unwavering. The Greens MP for Brunswick, Tim Read, has been remembered for his kindness and integrity after his death on Saturday at the age of 64. Read was diagnosed with melanoma in November and earlier this year announced he would retire from politics at the state election. On Saturday, Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell announced he had died surrounded by those he loved. “Tim was a brilliant local MP, doctor and scientist – but to those who knew him, he was also the kindest, funniest and most fundamentally decent of people,” Sandell said. He could always see the moral question at the heart of every political issue. It’s why he was so outspoken when it came to supporting the cause of the Palestinian people and why he continued to remind us all about how much coal was being burned in Victoria each day. He never lost perspective about what was truly important … Vale our brilliant friend. We will miss you. Sandell recalled Read’s advocacy on pill testing, tobacco licensing and a statutory ban on solitary confinement in prisons, and praised his contribution to Victoria’s anti-corruption and integrity laws. “Victoria is a bettter and fairer place, and politics in the future will be much more accountable and transparent because of Tim,” she said. The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has vowed to deliver one of the biggest immigration cuts in Australia history and called Labor “socialist in all but name” in a bid to rally the party faithful, six months out from the New South Wales election. In a wide-ranging address to the NSW Liberal party state council in Sydney on Saturday, Taylor admitted the previous coalition government had its shortcomings, but said Labor was “utterly failing the nation”. He said: For the past four years, we’ve had a government in Canberra which is socialist in all but name. Taylor said it was “divisive” for Labor politicians to “stand in front of three different flags instead of our one national flag”, referring to press conferences where leaders would deliver speeches with the Aboriginal Torres Strait Islander flags alongside the national flag behind them. After Labor unveiled its new immigration plan, which includes transforming a former quarantine facility into a new detention centre, and preventing international students from bringing their family members to Australia, Taylor offered to go further. I will deliver one of the biggest cuts to immigration in Australian history. The opposition leader also promised to protect Australia’s national flag and Australia Day, and change laws regarding gender. We will not allow the ideologues and activists to deny the truth … Under a Coalition government I lead, we will end this lunacy. The Coalition will be hoping to win back voters from One Nation at the NSW state election in March. Welcome Good morning and welcome to our Sunday live blog. I’m Penry Buckley to take you through the day. The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has pledged to deliver one of the biggest immigration cuts in Australia history and called Labor “socialist in all but name” in a bid to rally the party faithful, six months out from the NSW election. And politicians from all sides of Victorian parliament have paid tribute to the Greens MP for Brunswick, Tim Read, who died on Saturday at the age of 64. More on both of those stories and plenty more to come.
