headline: Hastie ‘open minded’ on return of baby bonus to counter ageing population concerns – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s where we’ll leave things. Here were the key things we covered today: The government’s seventh intergenerational report was released, which found there will be more Australians dying than being born in 40 years’ time. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the report highlighted the challenges facing Australians in a “more fragmented and uncertain world”. The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said Australia’s telecommunications system is “failing”, after handing down the report from an inquiry into problems in the sector, which made 11 recommendations including that the government consider nationalising triple zero. The ACT government announced a reward of $500,000 for information that helps conclude a series of unsolved murder or missing person cases, including a possible Ivan Milat victim, Keren Rowland. Police alleged that a mother was behind a stabbing attack on three young children in the New South Wales Blue Mountains on Sunday that left one dead and two others fighting for their lives in hospital. A cool change swept across much of the east cost after an unseasonably warm weekend. Thanks for joining us – we’ll be back tomorrow to bring you the latest. Andrew Hastie has weighed in on the latest intergenerational report, saying he’s “open minded” on government financial incentives to encourage people to have children. The report, released earlier today, found there will be more Australians dying than being born in 40 years’ time, and examines the fundamental challenges of managing an ageing population at a time of rapid change and lower economic growth. It also outlines how Australia is at the cusp of a new and uncertain age of artificial intelligence that will shape the economy and society over the coming four decades. Hastie was interviewed on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program a short time ago, where he said: “The real problem is of course that family formation is being delayed because people can’t get into home soon enough, and families are having less children. “It is a real concern that our fertility replacement rate is projected to drop further, to a historic low at the moment of about 1.39 I think it was, and we want Australians to have a better chance of getting into a home, forming a family and having children of their own.” Asked if he would support a Peter Costello-style baby bonus to incentivise Australians to have children, Hastie said he was “pretty open minded”. The Liberal MP noted there were mixed views on whether the baby bonus among economists but he said he would “support anything that allows young Australians to form families soon enough”. Hastie said: I have three kids myself, they are a great blessing, I love children. I’d love other Australians to have kids as well, and part of the challenge is getting them into homes sooner and making the economy work for them. The New South Wales Greens MP Abigail Boyd has urged the state government to invest more in frontline domestic and family violence services after a horror weekend of alleged domestic violence. Boyd has called for an immediate increase in funding of a minimum $200 million investment to address what she described as “chronic funding shortfalls … causing calls to go unanswered”. In a statement, Boyd, the Greens’ spokesperson for gendered violence and abuse, said: Services are operating at up to nine times their funded capacity and waitlists are at an average of two months with some stretching for months on end. Whenever we see cases like the ones we saw over the weekend, politicians wring their hands and express their sadness as though they have no power to prevent these tragedies from happening. These issues are not new, nor are the solutions to solve them. Reports, studies, testimony and evidence have all demonstrated for years where the shortfall is and how to address it. In a $135 billion annual state budget, even if funding was increased, it would still add up to less than half a percent of total annual expenditure. I think most people in NSW would think that’s a small price to pay to prevent these horrific crimes. Her call comes after police earlier today said they would allege a mother was responsible for Sunday’s stabbing attack on three young children that left one dead and two others fighting for their lives in hospital. Bystanders were first on the scene after finding the three children and the woman with stab wounds inside a vehicle at Valley Heights in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, yesterday afternoon. On Saturday, three women were allegedly murdered inside their homes within a 12-hour period, in three separate incidents across the state. The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has said Australia’s telecommunications system is “failing”, after an inquiry into problems in the sector recommended the government consider nationalising triple zero. The Senate committee, which delivered its report earlier today, began the inquiry into the Optus triple zero service outage of 18 September 2025, which has been linked to multiple deaths. The inquiry, which was expanded to cover problems with other telcos including Telstra, which experienced its own outage in July this year, resulted in 11 recommendations to overhaul the system. Speaking after the report was delivered, Hanson-Young said: Australia’s telecommunications system is failing and it’s failing because for too long these big corporations have been able to regulate themselves and yet they are essential services. People should be able to know that they need to call triple zero, their mobile phone will work regardless of where in Australia they are. One of the key recommendations is urging the government to look at nationalising triple zero. At the moment it’s a service that is managed by Telstra with support from the other telcos. These companies are not putting the safety of Australians first. They’re putting their profits first and they can no longer be trusted with Australia’s vital triple zero service. Hello, I hope you’ve been having a nice day. I’ll take you through the rest of the news this afternoon. That’s all from me. Catie McLeod will take things from here. Take care. Asic begins proceedings against former CEO of company behind Supercheap Auto, Rebel and Macpac The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) has begun civil penalty proceedings against the former CEO and managing director of the Super Retail Group, alleging he breached his duties and provided misleading information to the board and the market. Asic alleges Anthony Heraghty failed to disclose conflicts of interest that arose from an alleged undisclosed relationship with a senior executive at the company. Those failures, Asic says, included continuing to supervise the person and making decisions affecting their employment, including remuneration, rewards and a redundancy package. Super Retail Group is an ASX-listed public company and the parent company of a group that has retail interest including Supercheap Auto, BCF, Rebel and Macpac. Heraghty was the CEO from March 2019 to September 2025. Sarah Court, the chair of Asic, said in a statement: The allegations in this matter raise important issues about governance, transparency and trust in the information provided to boards and the market. This case is not about private relationships, but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders. Asic is seeking declarations of contravention, pecuniary penalties and disqualification orders. Heraghty has not yet filed a defence, according to The Sydney Morning Herald. The ACT government will offer a reward of $500,000 for information that helps conclude a series of unsolved murder or missing person cases, including the death of Keren Rowland, a 20-year-old nurse killed in 1971 whose family believe she was the first victim of serial killer Ivan Milat. The government said the rewards will apply to five new cases in addition to three others that have had rewards attached to them since 2012. Officials said while some of the cases relate to long-term missing persons, they hope the rewards will encourage a witness or someone with information to come forward. The other cases include those of Elizabeth Herfort, who was last seen in 1980; Megan Louise Mulquiney, last seen in 1984; Troy Hugh Forsyth, who was fatally struck by a van in 1987; and David Abuoi, who was last seen in Canberra in 2012. The ACT minister for police, Marisa Paterson, said in a statement: The families of these five people have never given up hope of getting answers regarding what happened to their loved ones. Half a million dollars is a strong incentive for someone to tell police what they know. If you know anything about Keren, Troy, David, Elizabeth or Megan’s matters, we are urging you to come forward. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said artificial intelligence will play “a pivotal role” in driving Australia’s long-term productivity growth. The AI revolution is the most consequential new emphasis since the 2023 report and the biggest economic transformation of our lifetime. The productivity, investment and labour market impacts of AI will be dramatic. The IGR shows from 2030 onwards each extra 0.1% of productivity growth from AI could improve the bottom line by 0.7 percentage points and reduce gross debt by 0.3 percentage points within a decade. Chalmers said Australia needs to be focused and deliberate in adopting AI to realise its benefits. We are well positioned with Australians adopting AI at a higher rate than almost every G20 country, but the productivity boost from AI depends on translating that into better ways of working. More from the treasurer’s response to intergenerational report Jim Chalmers outlined the five major challenges identified in the intergenerational report: The impact of the “AI revolution” on the economy A “fragmenting world” shaped by growing geopolitical tensions The transition to clean energy A growing and ageing population, accelerated by falling fertility rates Changes to the industrial sector, driven by AI and the energy transition Chalmers said the challenges needed to be addressed through a holistic approach: There’s no separating these five accelerating shifts from each other or from their consequences for our budget or our economy. A smaller workforce means a proportionately smaller income tax base at a time when pressures on social services and tools of statecraft, including defence, will be growing, not easing, along with the fiscal risks of climate change and more frequent disasters. Chalmers said it was “remarkable” that the budget was strengthening despite those pressures, with government spending over the next 40 years expected to increase by significantly less than previously forecast. Tasmanian jumping castle tragedy wind gust ‘unprecedented’, inquest hears A jumping castle that became airborne due to a freak “dust devil”, killing six primary schoolchildren, was tethered at only four of eight anchorage points, an inquest has been told. The children died during end-of-year celebrations at Hillcrest primary school in Devonport on 16 December 2021. A long-awaited inquest began in Tasmania on Monday after years of delays due to criminal proceedings against the castle’s operator, Rosemary Gamble. Gamble operated Taz-Zorb, which set up inflatable equipment at the school. She was found not guilty of criminal workplace health and safety breaches in 2025. The events of the day and the tethering of the castle and other devices would be placed under “extensive examination”, counsel assisting the coroner Maree Norton said on Monday. Gamble was supervising on the day and had a policy of not operating the castle if winds were tipped to exceed 25km/h. The Bureau of Meteorology forecast for 16 December was light winds, reaching 15 to 20km/h by the evening, Norton said. Several witnesses, including teachers and nearby residents, said the morning was largely windless before a “mini-tornado” hit around 10am. In 2025, the magistrates court found Gamble could have taken further steps in relation to the castle’s anchorage, but even if she had, it would have made no difference to the outcome. The coroner can make different findings but cannot make rulings of criminal guilt. – AAP The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has delivered the Treasury’s latest intergenerational report, examining the potential impact of government policies over the next 40 years. Speaking in Canberra, Chalmers said the report highlighted the challenges facing Australians in a “more fragmented and uncertain world”. The world is becoming more dangerous, more unpredictable, more unequal, and more divided. And these aren’t just individual threads, they’re part of a bigger fraying of that intergenerational promise of better times. Accelerating change is putting more pressure on people. It’s eroding trust in the institutions of democracy. It exacerbates the strain felt by younger Australians and younger generations in particular. Chalmers said the report identified that Australia faces serious challenges but said the country is well prepared to manage them. This intergenerational report shows that we face very serious risks and pressures, but that we are better placed and better prepared for them … this report also shows that we have a better plan to maximise our opportunities and minimise our risks, to grow our economy and lift living standards, embrace new technologies and share the benefits. Queensland’s premier says bipartisan plans to reduce the number of foreign visa holders allowed into the country is “nuts” and could risk spiralling food prices and damage to regional communities. Labor, the Liberals and One Nation have all recently released plans to cap or slash migration. Last week the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, released a plan to slash net overseas migration from 292,000 this year to just 225,000 in 2027-28. “I think that’s nuts,” David Crisafulli said on Monday, referring to the idea of reducing visa numbers year on year. He said: Without it [migration], you go into a country town during a fruit picking season, for example, and without those short-term visas, you won’t get a beer at a pub, and a farmer won’t be able to pick his or her produce, and those towns grind to a halt. But if you don’t love those little towns as much as I do, see it through a self-interest point of view. The things you put in your trolley are going to be a hell of a lot more expensive if there’s not a sensible discussion around making sure that people can go into regional areas and do the kind of work that they have done for a long period of time. Crisafulli said the country needed a discussion as much about welcoming new Australians who wanted to build the country of the future as about how best to accommodate them. Four Australian sea lions test positive for H5 bird flu in South Australia Four more endangered Australian sea lions have tested positive for the deadly H5N1 bird flu at an important breeding site in South Australia. The animals, including one pup, were among several found dead on the Pages islands near Kangaroo Island, state authorities said on Monday. SA recorded the first H5 death of a sea lion eight days ago, with fears about how deadly virus will impact populations of the endangered pinniped. Experts estimate that about 12,000 Australian sea lions remain, most of which are found in SA. The Pages islands are one of three sites in the state with large breeding colonies, according to Parks SA. Authorities identified three positive sea lions on North Page Island and one on South Page Island via aerial wildlife surveillance operations. Several dead pups were also found, but tested negative for H5 bird flu. Invasive Species Council chief executive Jack Gough said: We haven’t seen the mass deaths in pinnipeds that the experience in South America and Antarctica suggests may be coming but multiple deaths in a single location could indicate that devastation is just around the corner. We’re now about to see millions of migratory birds arriving in Australia as part of spring migration as well as breeding events around the country which could be a new phase in terms of the level of devastation. The WA government has called off the search for a shark that killed a Perth man on Friday, after a minister had ordered a catch-and-kill directive. WA police said a 63-year-old man was bitten by a shark while swimming at Sorrento beach. The swimmer’s body has not been found. In a statement, the Department of Primary Industries said it had concluded water and land based patrols around Sorrento beach. There was no evidence of white shark activity in the area yesterday and a significantly diminished chance of catching the individual shark involved in the fatal incident on Friday. Beaches in the City of Joondalup from Marmion to Iluka were set to reopen at 10am local time. On Saturday the WA fisheries minister, Jackie Jarvis, revealed she had greenlit the order. She said in a social media post: Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if captured. More Australians forecast to live into their 90s Australian households are expected to shrink but more people can expect to live well into their 90s, according to the latest update to forecasts of the country’s long-term future. Treasury’s latest intergenerational report, to be published in full on Monday, will project the impact of government policies 40 years into the future. An extract released on Sunday showed life expectancy at birth was forecast to reach almost 90 for women by 2065-66, up from about 86 years at present. The report will also reveal that artificial intelligence (AI) will become the “defining influence” on the economy over the next four decades, as the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, warned it would come with “very substantial risks”. The industry is already reeling from the this month’s arrival of the varroa mite parasite. Tom Bidner, an apiarist from the Atherton Tablelands, west of Cairns, said 44 colonies had been stolen from three different beekeepers. Read more: Foreign minister Penny Wong has spoken with her Palestinian counterpart, Varsen Aghabekian. The pair agreed that senior officials from both governments should meet in coming months to strengthen bilateral relations and discuss key priorities. The pair spoke on Friday night, with Aghabekian briefing Wong on progress on the Palestinian Authority’s reform commitments. “Australia is committed to a two-state solution,” Wong wrote on social media on Monday. I spoke with Palestinian Foreign Minister, Dr Varsen Aghabekian, about the PA’s reform agenda and our joint efforts to strengthen Palestine’s institutional foundations. We also discussed the devastating situation in Gaza. “I reiterated that Hamas must play no role in the State of Palestine. The pair agreed that Israel must halt its illegal settlement activity and hold perpetrators of settler violence to account. Wong also told Aghabekian that Australia continues to press all parties to implement the Gaza peace plan in full and facilitate unimpeded humanitarian access to Gaza. ‘Things are getting worse,’ Kellie Sloane says after alleged DV incidents Kellie Sloane, the NSW opposition leader, also spoke about a series of alleged domestic violence incidents in the state in recent days. Sloane told ABC News Breakfast this morning: Something is broken and we’re failing women in our state and our country. It’s a national crisis … Every time this happens, we treat it as a wake-up call. People say we need action. We need to talk to men about respect. We need to talk to women about being respectful. We need more funding. We’re in a hopeless situation where things are getting worse. So, you know, this is not just the responsibility of government, although government has a responsibility to properly fund and manage this, but it needs to be a whole of community response. Our sporting clubs, dads in the homes respecting their wives, talking to their kids about what respect means, and then neighbours checking in on people as well. The Coalition’s education plan to reduce First Nations content from the curriculum would give Australian children a “broader perspective of history” according to Dan Tehan. Speaking to Radio National, the Liberal MP said: We won’t be becoming apologists for who we are. We’ll becoming proud of who we are, what we’ve created as a nation and what we can contribute to the rest of the world. It’s all about getting the balance right and that’s what we’ll be seeking to do in how we have the curriculum taught in schools. Those western civilisation values, in particular, are what is at the heart of who we are as a nation. We want to make sure that that is equally part of the curriculum as it’s taught to young Australians. The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, revealed on Saturday that a Coalition government would remove cross-curriculum content about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and culture, Australia’s engagement with Asia, and sustainability. He said they should instead be delivered as discrete, planned topics within history, geography or science classes – rather than taught thematically across the curriculum. Read more: The NSW premier, Chris Minns, spoke earlier this morning after a spate of alleged domestic violence crimes this weekend. He said: We have numerous examples and allegations of individuals who [are] alleged to have committed horrifying acts against what are often defenceless family members. This is confronting and incredibly violent, but we can’t become numb to the pain or the violence that we see. We still need to take action and commit ourselves across government agencies, law reform, our prisons, New South Wales police, and education and other aspects of government agencies, as well as across civic society, to confront domestic violence when we see it. NSW police detail ‘horrific’ scenes after Blue Mountains stabbings Peter McKenna, deputy commissioner for NSW police, just spoke after an alleged stabbing attack by a mother against her three young children, which left one child dead and two others in critical condition. McKenna said the mother, aged in her 40s, is also in critical condition after the incident, which took place in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, on Sunday afternoon. He said police responded to “horrific” scenes and officer were confronted with a “barbaric” attack. “I can’t remember a weekend like this in my career,” the deputy commissioner told reporters. McKenna said the woman, if she recovers from what’s believed to be self-inflicted injuries, would probably be charged with murder and attempted murder. He said the family was not known to police. The woman’s husband is supporting his two children in hospital and has assisted police with their investigation. Read more here: Plibersek says polls ‘not great’ but Labor focused on cost of living Tanya Plibersek says the Labor party isn’t focused on polling, despite the results. She told Sunrise this morning: The polls are obviously not great, but we are not focused on the polling. What we’re focused on is making a real difference in people’s lives. We know that they’re doing it tough. We hear that. … In every part of our government, we are wholly focused on taking pressure off Australians. We know they’re feeling it because they tell us. Plibersek said the government needs to remain focused on cost of living and taking pressure off Australians while making sure wages grow. We want Australians to earn more and keep more of what they earn through lower taxes. … It’s those sorts of practical things that make a difference to people’s lives. That’s what we need to focus on as a government and that’s what we’ll keep doing. Albanese and Labor hit record low popularity in latest Newspoll Anthony Albanese is the most unpopular he has ever been since becoming prime minister in 2022, a new poll shows. AAP reports The Australian’s closely watched Newspoll tally has slugged the prime minister with a minus 27% net satisfaction rating, with only about a quarter of Australians now saying they would cast their vote for Labor – the lowest in nearly 15 years. The week before receiving a record-breaking belting in the 2025 election, former Liberal leader Peter Dutton scored minus 24% on the same metric. The major parties combined performed abysmally in the latest poll, with 54% of those surveyed now supporting someone other than Labor or the Coalition. One Nation is continuing to dine out on the mass exodus with a leading 30% of the primary vote share, but Australians still prefer Albanese to Pauline Hanson as prime minister. The rise of Way Dynamic, Australian folk-pop musician It’s been a huge couple of years for Way Dynamic, the Melbourne multi-instrumentalist whose real name is Dylan Young. His 2025 album Massive Shoe is about to be re-released internationally after Young signed with the indie giant Jagjaguwar. The likes of Elton John, Djo, Zane Lowe and Elijah Wood have sung his praises. Have a read about the musicians’s rise above, and take a listen to his music below on this fine Monday morning: Australians won’t be hit with card surcharges from 1 October Debit and credit card surcharges will be eliminated from 1 October, as part of Reserve Bank reforms that will do away with extra checkout fees on Visa, Mastercard, and Eftpos payments. The RBA estimates the changes will save consumers about $1.6bn a year in surcharges, but the big banks and credit companies are likely to recoup the costs of processing transactions in other ways, including through fewer perks for cardholders. What will happen now? Angus Taylor says the Coalition would cut the tobacco excise to fund halving the fuel excise, despite health experts sounding the alarm about the move. Speaking on Nine’s Today, the opposition leader said his party’s policy to slash the fuel excise in half when global prices hit US$100 over two weeks “won’t put pressure on inflation, despite what the treasurer is trying to say, he has it wrong”. When asked about previous criticisms from health experts about slashing the tobacco excise and what it would mean for anti-smoking efforts, Taylor said: I think the health experts need to explain why they’re OK with … organised crime in this country, criminal gangs in this country, controlling the tobacco trade. 80% of the trade is illegal. You can already buy a packet of cigarettes for 15 bucks a pack or less. So I mean, seriously, we can’t take those comments seriously. NSW domestic violence rental reforms in effect from today Rental reforms which make it easier for victim-survivors of domestic violence to leave a rental property in NSW are in effect from today, the state government says. Under the changes, victim-survivors no longer need to notify people they share a lease with they are leaving a rental property, cannot be held responsible for damage caused by domestic and family violence, and must be asked for permission to publish images of the property that show their belongings. The government says victim-survivors have now have broader rights to change locks without landlord consent. The NSW fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, said the reforms “deliver on the Minns Labor government’s promise to make renting fairer by replacing unsafe, outdated laws with practical, compassionate protections which put victim-survivors first”. During debate on the laws, which passed last year, the cross bench and domestic violence advocates raised concerns that last-minute changes to laws on pets in rentals, making it easier for landlords to prevent pets, would make it harder for DV victim-survivors who want to find a safe place to go with their animals. Domestic Violence NSW Deputy CEO, Pia Birac, has said today’s changes “remove some of the practical barriers that can make it harder for women to leave violence and rebuild their lives”. Now we need to build awareness and understanding of these new protections so women can confidently exercise their rights and the professionals around them can support them every step of the way. Dan Tehan says fuel excise cut when oil price high a ‘sensible’ plan Dan Tehan, the shadow minister for energy, said Gallagher’s criticism of the Coalition’s fuel plan wasn’t fair. Tehan said the call for a 50% cut to the fuel excise whenever barrels of oil top US$100 was a “good, sensible, practical measure” that would help Australians deal with a cost of living crisis. He told RN: [What] I would say to Anthony Albanese and the Labor party is get out amongst the people and see what’s happening in your electorates because people are hurting because of cost of living … We have the discipline to be able to do the policy work to make sure we can offset policies like this so it won’t be inflationary and it will provide much needed relief to people, and they need it now. Tehan maintained the plan would be funded by the promised cuts to the tobacco excise, which would allow the plan to “not be inflationary at all”. Katy Gallagher, the federal finance minister, said the government doesn’t think a Coalition plan to halve the fuel excise whenever oil prices skyrocket is a “good idea”, saying it is an “unfunded, uncounted promise” from Angus Taylor. The government halved the fuel excise for three months earlier this year amid the war in Iran and then discounted it at a small rate until August. Taylor has proposed to institute that plan whenever Brent crude oil averages US$100 a barrel over a two-week period. Gallagher told RN Breakfast the government was not considering the same: Obviously we’ve helped when the war started with some changes to the fuel excise but we’ve shifted, and [are] including in the budget, to providing more permanent cost of living arrangements, including through the tax system, to make sure that that ongoing cost-of-living help is there permanently, not just in these one-off arrangements, which, when we’ve got higher inflation, could be difficult in the economy. She said the government hasn’t been considering further cuts to the fuel excise. Our decisions have been built and baked into the budget to make sure that that cost-of-living help is permanent. You know, the sooner this war in the Middle East stops, the better. New diplomatic postings for Cairo, Port Moresby and Dili Foreign minister Penny Wong announced the appointments of three people to lead Australia’s diplomatic posts in Cairo, Port Moresby and Dili, as well as the consulate in New York as we reported earlier. Wong said Joel McGregor would serve as Australia’s next ambassador to Egypt; Jamie Isbister would be the next high commissioner in Papua New Guinea and Lucienne Manton would be the new ambassador to Timor-Leste. Australia takes the world as it is and seeks to shape it for the better – these diplomatic appointments will deepen Australia’s connections abroad and increase our ability to influence where it matters. NSW to lead Australia with solar panel recycling mandate New South Wales plans to introduce Australia’s first mandatory solar panel recycling scheme to ensure the materials are recovered rather than sent to landfill. The state launched consultation on the design of the stewardship scheme on Monday amid prolonged delays at the national level. Around 14,000 tonnes of solar panel waste was generated in NSW each year, which was expected to grow to 89,000 tonnes by 2045. The proposed scheme would require solar panel manufacturers to take responsibility for the end-of-life management of their products, helping fund collection, recycling and resource recovery. NSW environment minister, Penny Sharpe, said: NSW has embraced rooftop solar, and now we’re making sure those panels don’t become tomorrow’s landfill problem. Solar panels contain valuable materials that can be recovered and put back to work. “NSW is getting on with the job,” Gayle Sloan, the chief executive of the Waste Management and Resource Recovery Association of Australia. The state was implementing mandatory battery stewardship and intended to finalise solar panel regulation by the end of 2026. She said: The solar model can then be adopted by other jurisdictions or transition to a future Commonwealth scheme. That is tangible reform: establish the rules, set a deadline and create a pathway for national action. Australia is a leading destination globally for datacentre investment and has seen a near doubling of capital expenditure in this area since the 2023 IGR. It comes as Albanese will be face-to-face with Donald Trump at a gala reception hosted by the US president during the high-level week. We have a view about artificial intelligence that there needs to be appropriate safeguards put in place, and I will advocate that privately, the same as I will publicly. Depending on how long the empanelment process takes the court may hear the crown’s opening statement in the afternoon. Justice Natalie Adams will preside over the trial, which is slated to go for two to three months and include a brief of evidence with more than 200 witnesses. The case has received significant media attention and Lamarre-Condon’s trial is also expected to attract substantial public interest. Anthony Albanese has named former News Corp executive Siobhan McKenna as Australia’s next consul-general in New York. headline: Tree vaccines and gene-edited butterflies among biotechnology projects funded by UK ‘invention agency’
trail_text: Exclusive: The tax-funded brainchild of Dominic Cummings hopes to find ways to speed up wild species’ evolution
body_text: Vaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail butterflies are among 14 tax-funded projects from the UK’s “invention agency” aiming to accelerate nature’s ability to adapt to the climate crisis. The £54m accelerated adaptation programme from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria) – a public body that funds high-risk, high-reward tech projects – aims to investigate applications of biotechnology that can speed up wild species’ evolution and help them to adapt to new threats such as global warming and disease. The 14 teams announced on Monday will receive a share of an initial £30m in grants over the next two years. They will develop tools to protect native British wildlife species, including the English oak tree and critical pollinators such as the buff-tailed bumblebee, said Yannick Wurm, the director of the accelerated adaptation programme at Aria. The world’s natural environments are changing so rapidly owing to the climate crisis and human pressures that many species can no longer adapt quickly enough, said Wurm, a professor of evolutionary genomics at Queen Mary University, London. “This cohort is a first exploration of how we can harness some of the powers of biotechnology to responsibly help wild animals and plants to overcome challenges they face,” he added. The projects aim to work alongside conventional nature conservation measures, such as protected reserves, to give environmentalists a new set of “precision tools” that Wurm compares to mRNA vaccines for humans. Aria is the brainchild of Dominic Cummings, the former chief adviser to Boris Johnson, who said it would fund “crazy” ideas that could “restore Britain’s place as a scientific superpower”. The publicly funded body has attracted criticism for its research into controversial geoengineering techniques and grants that have given millions in UK taxpayer money to US tech companies and venture capital firms. Matt Clifford, Aria’s chair, was forced to stand down this month over what one senior MP called a “clear conflict of interest” after taking a job with Anthropic, the developer of the AI chatbot Claude. One team announced on Monday, led by researchers at the University of Exeter, will use Crispr-Cas9 gene-editing on the swallowtail, a butterfly on Britain’s red list of endangered species, to increase its resistance to insecticides used widely on farms. Another project developed by Rothamsted Research, the 180-year-old agricultural research facility in Hertfordshire, will edit the genes of long-lived tree species such as oaks to reproduce in months rather than decades, meaning they can rapidly develop adaptive responses to drought and invasive pathogens. Environmentalists across the planet have debated using increasingly powerful biotechnology and gene-editing techniques to aid conservation. At the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s (IUCN) world conservation congress last October, more than 90 NGOs raised concerns that these technologies will irreversibly alter natural systems with unpredictable effects. The ban was narrowly rejected after 250 scientists signed an open letter to highlight the potential benefits of synthetic biology, which could allow small islands to eliminate invasive mice that threaten more than 100 birds and reptiles. Instead, the IUCN adopted its first global policy on synthetic biology, including a set of stringent criteria for proposed solutions. This IUCN policy has been one foundation of Aria’s ethical policy, said Marie-Claire Cordonier Segger, the chair of the programme’s ethical and social responsibility advisory committee. Although the projects are intended for the wild, none of the experimental solutions will be released during the programme, which will last until 2030, said Cordonier Segger, a professor of international law at the University of Cambridge. “The decision was made early to have the strongest possible code,” she said, adding that all grantees will work in secure labs. Chris Thomas, founding director of the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York, said the projects that Aria is funding offer potentially valuable tools at a time when many species and ecosystems face drought, pathogens and other threats. Skin-eating chytrid fungal infections, which have caused population declines in more than 500 amphibian species, seems a “particularly worthy target” for these new approaches, said Thomas, who is not involved in the Aria programme. Biologists have so far had few options to prevent the spread in the wild, leading the Boston-based research lab Cultivarium to propose their project in partnership with Imperial College and Queen Mary University, London. It would genetically engineer a bacteria that lives on amphibians’ skin to produce proteins that “bind and stop” the infection, said Henry Lee, Cultivarium’s co-founder. “We’re not genetically engineering the amphibian; rather what we’re trying to do is we’re trying to give them a shield,” he said. Another project aims to prevent ash dieback – a fungal disease that is expected to kill half of Britain’s ash trees – by injecting the tree with RNA molecules that interfere with the fungus’s ability to infect. “So it is like giving the tree a vaccination,” said project lead Sarah Christofides, a mycologist at Cardiff University. But Thomas cautions that the impact of these solutions will probably be “modest” and difficult to assess. While 90 amphibian species have gone extinct owing to chytrid infection, others show signs of adaptive resistance, he said. Making certain species within a pond more resistant will inevitably affect the species not targeted, he added. To think that these interventions have an important role to play in preventing biodiversity loss “is probably pretty naive”, he said. To be deployed in the field, solutions will not only have to prove they are effective in the lab but win approval from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has tightly controlled the releases of genetically modified organisms. A further £24m will be allotted to projects that have shown success over the initial two years. Wurm said he hoped that a handful of successes would be “world-changing”. Ultimately, our “most urgent challenge” is to halt and reverse human-controlled drivers of environmental change, he said, but these projects aim to offer solutions in the places where we cannot.

headline: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
trail_text: Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday narratives’
body_text: The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”. Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”. “2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.” Coxon’s remarks, which were backed by two other researchers at the maker of the AI system Claude, prompted an international debate about the dangers and lack of oversight of AI as companies race to develop ever more powerful models. US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents. Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, Sam Altman, the boss of the ChatGPT maker OpenAI, and Elon Musk have called for development of the technology to be slowed down. However, Donald Trump has dismissed anxiety over the AI development as a “hoax” and a “conspiracy”, adding that a slowdown could give China the edge. On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, said the US and China had agreed to set up an AI dialogue mechanism to alert each other to help contain the technology’s potential dangers. Huang said predictions of an extinction-level event caused by AI were “not grounded in science”. Huang also claimed AI companies’ recent calls for national and international safety regulation aim to duck existing laws that would hold them to account. Citing recent cases where AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI triggered cybersecurity incidents during testing, he said there were plenty of laws to tackle the problems. “You have cybersecurity unauthorised entry laws, you have damage liabilities … if your product does harm, if your product doesn’t perform as you promised, and if you entered into contracts with companies for service level agreements, there are plenty of laws associated with that. My point is, apply those first. And don’t let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.” He continued: “Now, go and read between the lines. They’re actually not asking for more laws. They’re asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that’s a problem.” On Monday the the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) thinktank published a paper arguing that countries risk “profound and compounding disadvantage” if they fail to embrace AI and fall behind other nations. However, it also warned that the institutions meant to support the choices leaders would have to make were not equipped to do so. “The previous [industrial] revolution transformed our world over generations, AI will do so within a decade,” said Tony Blair in a foreword to the paper. “New capabilities are emerging at an extraordinary pace, with profound implications for economies, education, science, labour markets, public services and national security. But the risks are equally profound and growing, and so too is public concern. “Today’s political leaders… must make hard choices that will signficantly alter their countries’ trajectories. However, the institutions of the modern state meant to support political leaders in making these choices are simply not equipped for what is coming.”

headline: Fears over interest rate rise and jobs send UK consumer confidence to three-year low
trail_text: Blow to John Healey before budget as UK households face ‘notable strain’ on their finances
body_text: Fears of a steep rise in mortgage payments and increasing job insecurity have sent UK consumer confidence tumbling to a three-month low, according to a leading survey. In a blow to John Healey before next month’s budget, the S&P Global consumer sentiment index dropped to 42.7 in September from 42.9 in August, indicating “a notable strain on financial confidence across UK households”. The chancellor could announce tax rises in his first budget to offset the rising cost of government borrowing, which has soared in response to the conflict in the Middle East. S&P Global said consumers were concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England. More than 50% of 1,500 respondents said they expected a rise in the cost of borrowing over the next year. Fixed-rate mortgage costs have already jumped to multi-year highs in the UK, while the threat of artificial intelligence and caution among employers about hiring new staff sent consumer confidence in the jobs market plunging to its lowest level in three-and-a-half years. The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate rose to 5.88% on Monday, its highest since 16 April and up from 5.84% last Friday, while the average five-year is at its highest since October 2023, at 5.92%, up from 5.88%, data from Moneyfacts showed. The rise in mortgage costs is expected to add about £150 to monthly mortgage payments, based on a typical loan of £250,000 over 25 years, since the start of March 2026. Official figures have shown that the average direct debit to cover monthly mortgage costs has risen over the past four years from about £600 to £900. Maryam Baluch, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a downbeat mood was spreading across UK households “as improved sentiment surrounding the new government is eroded by renewed worries over energy prices, the cost of living and job prospects”. She said: “Against a backdrop of rising volatility in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East, households increasingly reported difficulties accessing credit, suggesting that expectations of tighter monetary conditions are beginning to feed through to borrowing conditions. Together, these factors point to cautiousness about both financial prospects and pose some downside risks to the broader economic outlook.” Analysts believe the jobs market has proved resilient since the US attack on Iran and a steep rise in the cost of fuel and energy, but a steady decline in the number of payrolled employees over the past six months and a drop in vacancies to a five-year low have shown employers are worried about their profitability over the next year. The British Chamber of Commerce has called for the government to give businesses extra support after a series of tax rises over the past two years, including an increase in employers national insurance payments. A survey by the business organisation of 5,000 companies in the second quarter of 2026 found that only 17% were planning to increase investment in the coming months, a post-pandemic low. Last week, Andy Burnham said he will need to take “difficult decisions” on the economy to ensure that it “remains on track”. In response to the growing clamour for tax cuts to support businesses and households hit by the cost of living crisis, the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, said at his party conference that the UK should cut fuel duty to offset some of the rise in petrol and diesel prices at the pumps. The German government on Monday announced plans for a cut in tax on fuel of about 15p to take effect on 1 October. Healey could limit his tax rises to wealthier groups, including a rise in capital gains tax. However, analysts say he is unlikely to raise sufficient funds from discreet tax rises to pay for higher defence spending and the rise in debt costs while preserving a reserve buffer, often referred to as headroom, of at least £20bn.

headline: Air traffic control failure ‘fixed’ after flight disruption in Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England – as it happened
trail_text: UK transport secretary Heidi Alexander warns ‘there may be some delays as things reset’
body_text: Crude oil prices have fallen a lot today, with Brent crude sinking 3% to $100.79 a barrel, down $3.14 a barrel. Wall Street has opened higher, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 1%, as expected, amid new optimism around artificial intelligence and trade, after US and Chinese officials held “constructive” talks in New York, according to both sides. They came ahead of a summit n Thursday between US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington. European stock markets have bounced between 0.6% (UK) and 1.4% (Italy), while government bond yields have retreated from Friday’s highs, as lower oil prices raised hopes of less inflationary pressures. Our main story: Flights have been disrupted in parts of the UK after National Air Traffic Services was hit by its second technical issue in a fortnight. A number of departing and arriving flights were severely delayed and dozens cancelled on Monday with disruption affecting Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England. The fault was reported to have occurred at Nats’s second control centre, at Prestwick in Scotland and fixed by about 10.30am. Airlines including British Airways and easyJet reported immediate cancellations. A total of 35 flights have so far been cancelled across UK airports, according to the analysts Cirium. The failure came less than two weeks after a major incident at Nats control centre in England disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers, and only three days after the release of an initial report into that incident by Nats promising to “continually improve the critical service we provide”. A Nats spokesperson said: The issue in our Prestwick centre is now fixed. We are working with airports and airlines to safely lift air traffic regulations as quickly as we can to minimise any further disruption. Passengers should still check the status of their flight with their airline. We apologise for the disruption. Jason Geall, executive Vice President, global SME at American Express Global Business Travel, said: The UK air traffic control disruption is the latest reminder that disruption is the new normal in travel. Our data shows disruption alerts have surged 300% over the past three years, while the number of impacted travelers has risen 600%. While leisure travelers get in a queue, business travellers have help at their fingertips - a combination of smart technology and real people ready to step in. That’s the difference a modern managed travel programme makes when plans fall apart. Thank you for reading. We’ll be back tomorrow. Take care! – JK Labour has been warned its “skills revolution” to tackle youth unemployment risks failure, after its flagship apprenticeship scheme enrolled only 160 young people in its first eight months, our economics correspondent Richard Partington reports. The shortfall, highlighted in a report by the Fabian Society, leaves the government well off track of achieving its ambition of 30,000 “foundation apprenticeship” starts by the end of this parliament. As part of plans to tackle the nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet), Labour announced in May last year what it called “radical skills reforms”, including the proposals for foundation apprenticeships. These posts are paid jobs for young adults with attached training for a minimum of eight months. However, official figures show there have been only 160 such starts between August 2025 and April this year. About 308,000 people have enrolled into an apprenticeship of any kind in England in the academic year so far, according to the official figures, an increase of 9% from the same period a year earlier. More than half of all apprenticeships are taken up by over-25s, while under-19s accounted for a fifth of all starts. We’d like to hear from employers who have taken on apprentices. What has your experience been like? Have apprentices benefited your organisation? What have been the biggest challenges? What changes or government support would encourage you to offer more apprenticeship opportunities? If you’ve decided not to recruit apprentices or would like to take on more than you currently do, we’d also like to hear why. What barriers have you faced? Are funding, costs, administration, training requirements or finding suitable candidates making it difficult? Novo Nordisk shares fell sharply as the Wegovy maker’s boss set out turnaround plans and faced tough questions from analysts over its pricing power and dealmaking strategy ahead of looming patent expiries. The Danish company’s share price is still down 5.2% in Copenhagen this afternoon. The success of its Wegovy and Ozempict shots made it Europe’s most valuable company in 2024, but since then the shares have plummeted, as Novo lost market share to US rival Eli Lilly, the maker of diabetes medicine Mounjaro and obesity drug Zepbound. Novo intends to launch more than five blockbuster drugs by 2030 and deliver more than 150 billion Danish crowns (£17.2bn) in annual sales in 2035, chief executive Mike Doustdar said at the drugmaker’s investor day in London. The company is scrambling to reassure markets that it can navigate patent expiries for semaglutide — the active ingredient in its anti-obesity drug Wegovy and diabetes medicine Ozempic — in the early 2030s. This means that generic drugmakers can make cheaper versions of the blockbuster drugs. Novo launched a pill verson of Wegovy in the US at the start of the year, which has been very popular, and went on sale in the UK at online and highstreet pharmacies on 6 July. Evan Seigerman, analyst at BMO Capital Markets, said Novo’s plans “may be underwhelming for investors” as the 3.6% revenue growth was already priced in by the market, leaving the “burden of proof” on management to demonstrate execution. When Doustdar took the helm about a year ago, he announced 9,000 job cuts and other cost cutting measures, including 5,000 job losses in its home country of Denmark, out of a workforce of 78400. The staff departures have reached 13,000 in total over the past year, the drugmaker said today. He said the company had the financial firepower to do larger acquisitions rather than just small bolt-ton deals, but would focus on the “quality of the deal” rather than the size. Doustdar said Novo would become “a larger and more diversified company by 2035”. It intends to launch CagriSema, a next-generation obesity drug, next year. The ABTA, the trade association for UK travel agents, tour operators and the wider travel industry, has expressed its frustration about the latest travel disruption caused by an air traffic control failure. It asked the government to consider whether National Air Traffic Services, which is partly state-owned, “should be made to compensate the wider industry for such events”. Luke Petherbridge, ABTA’s director of public affairs, said: This is the second Nats incident to cause disruption in the last fortnight, and fourth in recent years. It’s simply not good enough. The industry and travelling public will want answers – not only on what has gone wrong, but critically how the system is going to be made more resilient to avoid future outages. These incidents cause inconvenience to travellers and significant financial costs for airlines and the wider travel industry, including additional work and costs for ABTA’s tour operator and travel agent members. As these Nats issues are entirely outside of travel companies’ control, the government should seriously consider whether Nats should be made to compensate the wider industry for such events. Fears of a steep rise in mortgage payments and increasing job insecurity have sent UK consumer confidence tumbling to a three-month low, according to a leading survey. In a blow to John Healey before next month’s budget, the S&P Global consumer sentiment index dropped to 42.7 in September from 42.9 in August, indicating “a notable strain on financial confidence across UK households”. The chancellor could announce tax rises in his first budget to offset the rising cost of government borrowing, which has soared in response to the conflict in the Middle East. S&P Global said consumers were concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England. More than 50% of 1,500 respondents said they expected a rise in the cost of borrowing over the next year. Fixed-rate mortgage costs have already jumped to multi-year highs in the UK, while the threat of artificial intelligence and caution among employers about hiring new staff sent consumer confidence in the jobs market plunging to its lowest level in three-and-a-half years. The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate rose to 5.88% on Monday, its highest since 16 April and up from 5.84% last Friday, while the average five-year is at its highest since October 2023, at 5.92%, up from 5.88%, data from Moneyfacts showed. The rise in mortgage costs is expected to add about £150 to monthly mortgage payments, based on a typical loan of £250,000 over 25 years, since the start of March 2026. Official figures have shown that the average direct debit to cover monthly mortgage costs has risen over the past four years from about £600 to £900. Maryam Baluch, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a downbeat mood was spreading across UK households as improved sentiment surrounding the new government is eroded by renewed worries over energy prices, the cost of living and job prospects. Against a backdrop of rising volatility in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East, households increasingly reported difficulties accessing credit, suggesting that expectations of tighter monetary conditions are beginning to feed through to borrowing conditions. Together, these factors point to cautiousness about both financial prospects and pose some downside risks to the broader economic outlook. Disruption caused by an issue with air traffic control systems is “very regrettable”, Scottish first minister John Swinney has said. Speaking to the Press Association during an unrelated visit to Edinburgh airport, the first minister said: It’s very regrettable that there’s been an issue with the air traffic control system today and that members of the public have experienced disruption as a result. I’m glad the issues are now resolved and that flights are able to take their normal course, but it demonstrates of all organisations, particularly the air traffic control system, having resilience, being able to withstand issues in the systems, so that people can rely on the services that are being provided. So, we’ll engage with the national air traffic control service to ensure that these issues are addressed and that the resilience is necessary for these systems is available at all times. Here are a couple of pics from affected airports. On the air traffic control issue in parts of the UK, the prime minister’s spokesperson acknowledged that it is “deeply frustrating” for passengers, reports our political correspondent Aletha Adu. There’s a review that is ongoing, and the transport secretary has been clear that we need to urgently understand why the issue wasn’t discovered and fixed before it caused chaos. Engineers have fixed the problem, and systems are resuming. But we recognise this is deeply frustrating for passengers, particularly after a recent incident, and it’s crucial that our national infrastructure is fit for purpose now and in the future. And we’ll make sure the aviation sector is as resilient as possible, so passengers can get to where they need to be. Here’s a round-up of our main stories today: Airbus is expected to hire as many as 900 more workers in north Wales to build its long-range A321 jet, as the aircraft maker invests £150m to ramp up jet production. The company has a backlog of more than 5,000 of the planes, and will make an initial 480 new hires at its wing production centre in Broughton to help meet soaring demand. Airbus is understood to be planning a similar number of hires next year at the group of factories, which have about 6,000 people working there. The move will include restarting production at its West Factory, which used to make the wings for its double-decker A380 jet, but was converted into a warehouse after the company made 1,700 people redundant across its UK sites during the pandemic. The West Factory will be retooled to build the new aircraft which can fly 240 passengers from the UK to the east coast of the US. Jerome Blandin, head of Airbus Wing, said: Investing in our capacity strengthens our industrial footprint, creates high value jobs that support the wider UK aerospace sector and ensures we remain competitive in the years to come. The investment comes after Airbus said it would also expand a wing factory in Belfast over the next few years to help it build more of its smaller A220 planes. Locking the UK out of a new EU scheme to protect industries from Chinese competition would be an “own goal” and risk up to 250,000 jobs in the bloc, the British car industry has warned. Most of those jobs, 69,000, would be jeopardised in Germany, France and Spain but also in central and Eastern Europe, according to a new study by Oxford Economics commissioned by the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). SMMT’s arguments comes days after the chancellor, John Healy, urged EU finance ministers to include the UK in its definition of Made in Europe legislation. They fear if UK industry is locked out then EU manufacturers may no longer buy British parts for assembly lines. The government is also warning that it won’t commit to a second EU-UK summit unless Made in Europe is discussed amid fears over opposition in France to including Britain and other countries such as Japan who are warning that their EU bases should be included. Mike Hawes, head of SMMT, said: The EU is rightly focused on strengthening its industrial base, but the UK remains fundamental to Europe’s automotive ecosystem and is therefore essential to that ambition. Excluding the UK from ‘Made in Europe’ would be an own goal, weakening competitiveness, reducing scale and limiting consumer choice. Ryanair has stepped up calls on the Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe to resign immediately, or for transport secretary Heidi Alexander to sack him. This latest Nats failure which is affecting its Prestwick control centre is disrupting flights operating to and from Dublin, Edinburgh, Newcastle, Manchester and a range of airports across Scotland, Northern England, and Ireland. So far, more than 25,000 Ryanair passengers are expected to be affected, with more than 140 Ryanair flights delayed and delays exceeding three hours. This latest system failure comes just days after Nats published its preliminary report into the 8 September failure. Ryanair said: Today’s disruption raises serious questions about Nats’ operational resilience and why, after repeated system failures, there is still no effective back-up system capable of preventing widespread passenger disruption. The report confirmed that the permanent software fix identified following the 8 September failure had not yet been implemented and remained under testing. Ryanair’s chief operations officer, Neal McMahon, said: Just three days after NATS assured airlines and passengers that it had introduced a robust ‘mitigation plans’, its flight data processing system has failed again. More than 25,000 Ryanair passengers have already suffered disruption, with over 140 Ryanair flights delayed, yet NATS still cannot tell passengers when this disruption will end. Martin Rolfe’s report claimed that another failure was ‘unlikely’ and that NATS could recover more quickly if one occurred. Those claims have been exposed as completely worthless. Just three days later, passengers are once again suffering lengthy delays because Nats has failed to deliver either a reliable system or an effective back-up. After the August 2023 collapse, Martin Rolfe assured parliament that it was a ‘once-in-a-lifetime event’. Then Nats collapsed again on 8 September, disrupting more than 2,000 flights. Now, just 13 days later, the same flight data processing system has failed once more. How many times must UK passengers suffer disruption before Martin Rolfe is replaced by somebody competent? Another review, another report and another round of empty promises will not fix NATS. Martin Rolfe has presided over repeated system failures, repeated passenger disruption and repeated failures to deliver an effective back-up system. Enough is enough. Martin Rolfe should resign today. If he will not, then Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander should fire him and appoint somebody capable of delivering the resilient ATC service that UK passengers and airlines deserve. headline: Health, wealth and housing: here’s what forecasters think Australia will look like in 2066
trail_text: The country will be home to 40 million people, but fewer people will be having even fewer babies
body_text: Australia in the 2060s will have an older population that is working harder while facing the rapid expansion of AI, the climate crisis and mounting geopolitical tensions. The intergenerational report – a predicted snapshot of life in 2066 – shows the population will grow to 40 million but fewer people will be having even fewer babies. Here’s what life is forecast to look like in 40 years’ time: How wealthy will we be? The intergenerational report says household wealth will continue to rise into the 2060s, but younger people will experience “smaller gains” compared with previous generations. Wages and living standards are expected to grow “sustainably”, driven by productivity growth. But several economists have said the government’s long-term productivity forecast of 1.2% growth is a stretch, and lower productivity will affect overall wealth. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Households will have more super and rely less on the aged pension in retirement. The report’s medium-term expectation, ie within the next 10 or so years, shows the median superannuation balance will increase for 65 to 69-year-olds from $204,000 in 2024 to $450,000, not adjusted for inflation. The government projects superannuation drawdowns to rise to almost 6% of GDP by 2066, while spending on the aged pension will fall from 2.3% to 1.8% of GDP. But an ageing population and a reliance on income tax will put more pressure on working-age Australians. The current inability of younger generations to crack into the housing market will have longer term impacts, which the government says it hopes to turn around through its tax changes. Will there still be a housing crisis? Home ownership is a key theme of the report and, while it does not predict the 2060s home ownership rate, it provides sober insight into today’s housing crisis. Had home ownership rates remained at 1981 levels, an additional 250,000 people aged 25 to 34 would now own their own home, with or without a mortgage, according to the report. Declining housing affordability has deepened intergenerational inequality, it notes, with tax concessions – such as negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount – contributing to the problem. Treasury estimates 80% to 90% of investor housing lending had gone towards buying existing housing stock rather than new dwellings since 2019. There will be more people dying than being born For the first time, deaths are projected to outnumber births by the 2060s, with the number of people aged over 85 tripling, and life expectancy increasing due to better healthcare and lifestyles. Life expectancies will increase to 89.5 years for women and 86.1 for men. The birthrate is expected to decline considerably from 1.44 babies per female to 1.34 by 2066. The report estimates the population to be 39.3 million, 1.8 million people fewer than projected in the 2023 report. The report expects more women and older people to be working but the ageing population will reduce the overall share of people in the workforce and the number of taxpayers, putting pressure on future budgets. Despite this, Australia is well placed, the report says: “The working-age population is projected to continue growing, supported by ongoing migration, while many Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries are projected to experience declines”. The changes will also require a drastic increase in health spending, with health expenditure expected to rise from 4% of GDP in 2026 to 6.2% in 2066. One-third of the projected increase is linked to ageing. AI will create productivity gains The economic and social implications of artificial intelligence are “profound” and will have a greater impact than any other technological boom, the report says. However, its ultimate impact depend on how it develops and how broadly it is adopted. There are also concerns AI will fuel misinformation and cybersecurity risks. “The challenge for Australia is to harness and share these benefits widely whilst mitigating its potential to generate societal harms such as misinformation, scams and malicious cyber operations,” the report says. There’s no evidence yet of AI taking future jobs, but that it will increase productivity by making some tasks automated. Australia will be in a good position to “capture value” from AI, due to Australia’s location, land, and energy and water resources. Effects of climate crisis ‘uncertain’ Australia is well placed to meet the global energy transition, with vast renewables resources, but the broader effects of climate change 40 years from now are “highly uncertain”. Australia’s uptake of rooftop solar and batteries is the highest rate in the world and expected to increase, with the cost of solar photovoltaic (PV) modules and battery energy storage systems falling by 80% since 2015. But the report says global heating will have the greatest impact on major cities with lower elevation, while hotter temperatures could reduce productivity of workers, affect agricultural crop yields and damage tourism. It warns the increasing severity and changing frequency of climate-related events “will require stronger risk management approaches” from the government. By 2066, Treasury modelling shows heat stress could reduce crop yields by 3.6% under a 3C+ scenario, or 1.2% under the Paris-aligned scenario.

headline: Labor claims Victoria’s new datacentre rules are strongest in Australia but critics point to ‘huge loophole’
trail_text: New rules include a ban near schools and require datacentres to source their own renewable energy, but won’t apply to projects already in pipeline
body_text: Datacentres in Victoria will be banned in residential areas, required to use renewable energy and contribute to the community but regulations won’t apply to existing centres or dozens currently planned. On Tuesday the premier, Ben Carroll, and the artificial intelligence minister, Anthony Carbines, released the government’s sustainable datacentre action plan. “These are the strongest, clearest rules for datacentres in the nation,” said Carroll, though he admitted the rules wouldn’t affect the more than 50 existing datacentres nor those currently seeking planning approval. The new rules include a ban on datacentres near schools and childcare centres and in rural areas that cannot support them, along with a 150-metre buffer zone between new developments and homes. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Datacentres will be required to source their own renewable energy and will have to pay for connection costs and network upgrades. They will also need to use recycled or non-drinking water for cooling or offset their usage. The action plan revealed 19 datacentre applications in the pipeline were seeking a combined 19,714 megalitres of water per year – or 4% of Melbourne’s current supply. Currently, the 50 existing datacentres use less than 1% of drinking water in both Melbourne and Geelong. The government said new datacentres will also have to give back to the community via a “local investment guarantee”, which could include jobs, Tafes and parks. They will also be required to employ Victorians during construction and train people for long-term jobs when up and running. The plan also includes mandating “fair community consultation”, as well as existing noise limits, and fire and safety rules. The federal government had previously flagged plans to require all new datacentres to be powered by renewable energy rather than coal and gas, but was forced to back down on the mandate after opposition from Queensland and the Northern Territory. Carroll said he had consulted the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the lead-up to the state’s announcement while Carbines said their plan would be “likely adopted” by federal laws, expected in 2027. It’s a shift for the state government after the former premier, Jacinta Allan, vowed to make Victoria the datacentre capital of the country last year. Belinda Dennett, the chief executive of peak body Data Centres Australia, said the new rules were “disappointing” and could cause investment to “relocate” to other states. “Datacentre investment has been incredibly important to the Victorian economy. Other states have seen the opportunity, and they are lining up for it,” she said. Datacentre company CDC welcomed the new regulations, with its chief executive, Greg Boorer, saying it provided industry with “greater clarity”. But the Victorian Greens spokesperson, Sarah Mansfield, said the lack of retrospectivity created a “huge loophole”. “If Labor genuinely believes these protections are necessary, they should apply to every datacentre in the pipeline,” she said. “Otherwise communities will rightly ask what the point of these new rules are other than to save Labor seats 10 minutes before an election.” There has been growing community opposition in the lead-up to the November election, particularly in Labor-held seats. They include Footscray, held by Labor’s Katie Hall on a 4.2% margin against the Greens, who ran a “stop AI datacentres” day of action in the electorate on Saturday. NextDC has lodged an application with the state government for fast-tracked approval to expand its Footscray datacentre, known as M3, to cover 10 hectares, drawing 225MW of power and running 24/7. Some residential homes are within 15 metres of the datacentre’s boundary, which is zoned in an industrial area. Hall is a long-term opponent of the datacentre’s expansion. But the new rules will not apply to the project. The shadow attorney general, James Newbury, said Carroll’s plan was “irrelevant” because datacentres are “currently being built in the wrong spots”. He said the Coalition would release its own policy prior to the November election. NextDC has also bought 169 hectares of land just outside Geelong, which had been earmarked for future residential development. The Labor MP for Lara, Ella George, expressed concern about the acquisition to the Age in July. There are also Syncline Energy’s plans to develop a 350-hectare, 2.4GW datacentre in Plumpton, in Melbourne’s outer north-west, which is opposed by federal Labor MPs Alice Jordan-Baird and Sam Rae. The proposed centre is larger than any currently operating in Australia and would consume more electricity than is generated by Victoria’s largest power station, Loy Yang A.
