headline: Halt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to say
trail_text: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem
body_text: Ed Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem. When he addresses the faithful on the final day of the gathering in Brighton, the party leader will call for a global pause on super-intelligent AI, comparing it to a nuclear arms race that could result in technology that could “destroy us all”. Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchers that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say. Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development. “As liberals – we know that something as existential as nuclear weapons or climate change cannot be left in the hands of a powerful few. And so it must be with AI. We can’t leave it to Mark Zuckerberg, to Sam Altman, or to Elon Musk to save us,” Davey will say. On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. But Davey will say the plan “doesn’t come close to meeting the scale of this threat” and “only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros”. It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced that the party proposed a big tech levy and promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images. Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use of Meta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said. On Sunday Davey set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies. Davey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens. “It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.” Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market. The Lib Dem leader did praise Burnham for wanting to reform adult social care, but told Sky News the “jury is out” on whether Burnham will deliver as prime minister. But Davey was positive about some of what Burnham has done. “I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”

headline: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
trail_text: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
body_text: The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil. Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world. The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government. On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait. The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating. “We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said. The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result. “Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump. As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly. The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance. Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan. The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending. Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur. Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer. They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks. Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting. Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday. Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality. Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.” Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home. Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy. On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said. Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture … “To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.” Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming. The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration. Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.

headline: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges
trail_text: Boosting productivity could result in four extra years of good health for people on average, report says
body_text: The NHS in England could prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and boosting productivity, a report says. Research by the Health Foundation found the health service has been held back for decades by excessive regulation, short-term planning and insufficient capability to deliver major change. But rewiring the NHS, the world’s largest single healthcare system, by harnessing new technology, empowering staff and increasing capital investment could save both lives and money, it found. There is “substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS”, which could result in up to four extra years of good health for people on average, the report said. In terms of where deaths could be prevented, focusing on diagnosing cancer earlier and finding people with high blood pressure or conditions such as diabetes quicker would be key, it added. The report called for a series of changes, such as releasing the NHS from unnecessary regulation, reporting and compliance tasks, as well as launching a “test-and-learn” approach to scaling up things that could improve productivity, such as use of artificial intelligence. “Our analysis suggests that if the NHS in England achieved outcomes closer to the best-performing comparable health systems, without spending more each year, it could potentially result in 18,500–20,600 fewer deaths each year from treatable causes and 2.5 to 4.5 additional years that people spend in good health on average,” the report said. Increasing NHS productivity is “sometimes … seen as exhorting hard-working staff to work even harder, in a system already under considerable strain” but this view must be challenged, it added. “At its heart, productivity means achieving better health outcomes from the resources available.” The biggest issues affecting productivity included the “constant churn”, too many targets, and not enough focus on health outcomes. Researchers also heard from staff how poor IT wasted clinical time, how limited estate and equipment constrained healthcare and how gaps in administrative support shifted additional work to clinicians. While AI offered opportunities, the “NHS has repeatedly struggled to take advantage of the potential”, the report said. Anita Charlesworth, report author and senior economic adviser at the Health Foundation, said: “This is mission critical for the NHS, which cannot simply keep doing more of the same. “The problem is not a lack of committed and talented people or an absence of ideas; it is that the NHS is not set up to deliver sustained productivity growth. “Our research points to a fundamental redesign of the operating conditions – not another disruptive reorganisation, but a reset to make improving productivity a defining focus for the NHS over the next decade and beyond.” Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents and supports the health and care system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said he agreed more could be done to deliver further productivity gains but there were “big barriers” that would need to be addressed. “Lack of capital investment has been a long-running drag on NHS productivity. More must be done to turn the tide on years of neglect … We also agree that a more streamlined, supportive regulatory system which encourages local autonomy and innovation will be vital for future progress.”

headline: Trump says he’ll probably lose lawsuit brought by news outlets he banned from White House, blaming judge appointed by ‘TRUMP’ – as it happened
trail_text: This live blog is now closed.
body_text: That concludes our coverage of the second Trump administration for today. Here are the latest developments: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Newsrooms including the New York Times and the Washington Post also decided to hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight as part of the collective effort. More here. The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here. Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social. Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here. At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration. The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here. Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here. A long-running legal fight over Missouri’s congressional map took another turn Monday when a federal appeals panel ruled in favor of new districts backed by Donald Trump, even though the US supreme court has blocked those districts from being used in the November election, the AP reports. A three-judge panel of the eighth US circuit court of appeals said Missouri should use the new Republican-drawn US House districts in the November election, just as the state did in its August primary. To revert to its prior districts for the general election would violate the US constitution, the appeals judges said. However, the ruling has no immediate impact. That’s because the federal appellate panel delayed the effect of its order for a week to allow time for an appeal. The US supreme court already has twice sided against the Trump-backed map and had blocked enforcement of a lower court order favoring the map pending a potential appeal and eventual decision by the high court. Missouri is currently set to run its November election with the same congressional districts it used in 2024 and 2022, following prior decisions by both the Missouri supreme court and the US supreme court. Read the full story here: In a press conference held on Monday, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani was in disagreement with Donald Trump’s decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, and instead welcomed all members of the press at Gracie Mansion in New York. “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in – is everyone, no matter the opinion or the critique, that we engage,” Mamdani said. US Senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff are asking California attorney general Rob Bonta to look into the claims of a whistleblower alleging the Department of Homeland Security is ordering officers to impersonate voters to access online voter data. According to the senators, officers in a unit of the US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), an agency within the department, are being tasked with investigating 40 subjects per day. The whistleblower claims that officers were instructed to pull citizens’ personal data from federal databases and enter it into the state website to gain access. “The Trump Administration appears to be undertaking this rushed effort to find – or manufacture – evidence for its baseless election conspiracy theories of widespread voter fraud ahead of the 2026 midterm elections,” reads a letter by the senators. “Inaccurate claims of ‘unlawful voters’ and erroneous federal law enforcement records can result in serious consequences for Californians, including many naturalized citizens.” “The Trump Administration may also use these claims to further threaten state and local election officials in California and undermine or challenge the election results themselves,” the senators added in the letter. US Representative Ro Khanna said on Monday that the shooting of a Venezuelan man in Texas by a federal immigration officer “demands a full investigation”. “No one should be shot in the back and denied urgent medical care,” Khanna wrote in a post on social media. “The shooting of Venezuelan DoorDash driver Wilber Garcés Pérez by ICE in Austin demands a full investigation.” Khanna added: “Abolish ICE. Prosecute rogue agents.” Earlier today, Garcés Pérez pleaded for better medical care. “I haven’t received any medical attention. I’m in a lot of pain,” he said. My colleague Emiliano Tahui Gomez is reporting the latest details on the shooting: The US is planning to reopen a former cold war-era ⁠military base in southern Greenland and set up a military presence at an east coast base, Reuters reports. Sources told the wire that an agreement is expected to be signed by the US, Denmark and Greenland on Tuesday at the United Nations general assembly in New ‌York City. One of these military bases, Mestersvig, ⁠is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol. The other post is Narsarsuaq, where the population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Bluie West One military base in the 1950s. The agreement follows the announcement of an Arctic security pact between the US and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, following pressure from Trump to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force. In his remarks today, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani said he shared “very strong opinions” on “how we can keep immigrant New Yorkers safe” during his meeting with Donald Trump, especially regarding temporary protected status (TPS) for immigrants in the United States. Mamdani said he told the US president “how important immigrant New Yorkers, especially Haitian New Yorkers, are not only to the fabric of our city, but also to our city’s economy, to so many of the industries that build our city, and the stability that is in the president’s hands”. In June, the US supreme court ruled in favor of the Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians. Zohran Mamdani was asked whether he challenged Donald Trump on the banning of CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds. “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in,” Mamdani said at Gracie Mansion in New York City. “It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump said. In response to a question about whether the ban was put in place as a distraction from the war in Iran and high gas prices, Trump said: “I’m not.” “I’m only doing it because I think the press also has an obligation,” Trump said. “I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair. And if they’re fake news, I really think I have an obligation not to allow them into another very special house. This is a special house, Gracie Mansion. Well, the White House is the most special of all houses.” New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani and President Donald Trump spoke ahead of the UN General Assembly this week following a closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion on Monday. “One of the focuses of the conversation the president and I have been having is about the possibility of building more housing here in New York City,” Mamdani said. “We’ve spoken about Sunnyside Yard,” he added, referring to the 180-acre railyard in Queens, “and it’s a real pleasure that just today we’ve agreed to set up a new level of that conversation between our housing and operations team at City Hall and the White House team.” “I can tell you that Sunnyside’s a big job,” Trump said. “I’ve been watching that for 35 years. Everybody’s wanted to do something with Sunnyside Yards.” “You’re going to need a lot of federal approvals and probably some federal money to do it. But it’s always been a great location,” Trump added. Republican senator Chuck Grassley called for an embargo on diesel exports. And Republican congresswoman and Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson called for measures to tamp prices and bring an “immediate” end to the war in Iran. Trump is beginning a busy week of diplomacy. An ICE agent shot a DoorDash driver in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. headline: British Columbia sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over Tumbler Ridge mass school shooting
trail_text: Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use
body_text: British Columbia has sued OpenAI, saying a mass shooting at a school in the Canadian province could have been prevented if the company had warned local ⁠law enforcement that the shooter ⁠had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday, names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence. Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van ⁠Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. “The people of Tumbler Ridge have endured an unimaginable loss, and they deserve answers and accountability,” said Niki Sharma, British Columbia’s attorney general, in a statement this week on the suit. AI companies are facing increasing scrutiny over how their products may lead to a range of harms from cyberattacks and disinformation to facilitating violence and worsening mental health. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits from family members of victims in the British Columbia mass shooting, as well as the family of a victim in a Florida State University shooting from earlier this year. Altman published a letter in April to the community in Tumbler Ridge saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted ‌law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never ‌followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says. The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being ‌demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit. One survivor, Maya Gebala, recovered from being shot three times, including in the skull. She suffered catastrophic brain injuries and permanent disabilities from the attack, according to court documents. Gebala’s family has documented her life since the shooting in online posts, including sharing images of her celebrating her 13th birthday this week. A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.” British Columbia alleges that OpenAI has failed to take proper accountability and action for the killing, however, with Sharma stating that the company must strengthen its safeguards and increase transparency on its products. “To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community,” the attorney general said. The province’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent ‌the shooting. Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by suicide. The incident, one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history, devastated the small northern mining town and shocked the country. It also prompted Canadian officials to call in OpenAI executives for questioning, as well as resulted in a call between Canada’s AI minister, Evan Solomon, and Altman. Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting. The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack. After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the ⁠account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law enforcement. The lawsuit comes after a series of cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, including lawsuits related to a mass ‌shooting at Florida State University last year. In June, Florida became the first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.

headline: Trump’s bizarre social media blitz leaves world guessing ahead of UN address
trail_text: President has been posting on Washington arch, AI and his ‘25 top achievements’ – the chances of an uplifting speech appear slim
body_text: The annual gathering of the United Nations general assembly has historically been a platform for US presidents to display their most serious face and a positive vision to the world. From Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower to John F Kennedy and Barack Obama, over eight decades US leaders have used the setting to expound on grand themes before a global audience at pivotal moments in international affairs. As world leaders and officials gather in New York for the yearly event, and Donald Trump prepares to address them on Tuesday, how he will contribute to this historic catalog of remarks is a matter of speculation. The US president has spent recent days blitzing social media on a variety of topics, from his planned triumphal arch in Washington to a bid to rebrand artificial intelligence, as he contends with an unpopular war and low approval ratings that threaten to drag down his party in November’s US midterm elections. His previous addresses to the assembly suggest that the chances of a non-divisive and uplifting message are low. Last year, Trump shocked the august gathering in his first appearance since returning to the White House the previous January by declaring to those present that their countries were “going to hell” while launching a full-frontal assault on the UN and the concept of open borders. In 2018, during his first presidency, Trump drew laughter from fellow leaders when he opened his address by claiming: “In less than two years, my administration has accomplished almost more than any other administration in the history of our country.” The previous year, he had attacked longstanding allies, singling out Germany for its energy policy, and declaring that the US “can no longer be taken advantage of, or enter into a one-sided deal where the United States gets nothing in return”. This time around, Trump’s recent social media activities hinted at an even more volatile than usual state of mind from a leader who can be erratic at the best of times. Arguably the most eye-catching was his declaration in an early Sunday morning post that he intended to turn his highly controversial planned arch in Washington DC into a military storage facility, claiming – without providing evidence – that the move was requested by the US military. There was a surfeit of others. A post headlined “His Hemisphere” and depicting Trump gazing at a map of the globe ominously hinted at an imperious tone he could strike, less than nine months after US forces seized the former Venezuelan leader, Nicolás Maduro, in his compound in Caracas and spirited him and his wife to New York. The Trump administration has since trumpeted a deal giving it control over a significant segment of Venezuelan oil reserves. In another post, Trump postures as the defender of AI – denouncing recent fears that its rapid development could presage the destruction of the human race. Instead, he painted it as the latest target of “many hoaxes, all generated by the radical left dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our country” and announced his plans for an “AI force”– headed by an “AI Czar” – in the image of the space force, established during his first presidency. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our country’s GDP,” he wrote. “We are leading China, and the rest of the world, and I intend to keep it that way.” There is every chance Trump returns to previous themes at the UN on Tuesday. In an echo of his 2018 speech, on Friday he posted a list of his “Top 25 Trump Achievements” since returning to office. Trump’s appearance before the general assembly will be his first since his fateful decision to launch, in tandem with Israel, a war against Iran in February. The conflict – despite his predictions that it would last a few days, and result in the collapse of Tehran’s Islamic regime – shows no signs of ending. The regime still stands. Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that was a conduit to one-fifth of the world’s oil exports before hostilities began, has sent global energy prices soaring and stoked inflation in the US, challenging the prospects of Trump’s Republican party in November’s midterms. Polls show a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has further deflated his approval ratings. Further piquancy to Trump’s political dilemma is likely to be added by the presence of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, at the UN. While Trump has signaled a willingness to meet his Iranian counterpart, Pezeshkian – a relative pragmatist, under pressure from regime hardliners to stand firm and avoid compromise with an enemy still branded by Tehran as “the great Satan” – is thought unlikely to agree to such an encounter. The sting of being snubbed by an Iranian leadership he likes to depict as “dying to make a deal” could add further fuel to a fiery speech before the general assembly and witnessed by a global audience. Traditionally, US presidential speeches to the UN go through a long drafting process and are subject to reviews by the state department, the Pentagon and the intelligence community, as well as fevered last-minute rehearsals. That all may still hold true for this address. Yet equally likely is a no-holds-barred, scattergun diatribe, rehashing the themes of Trump’s recent social media output.

headline: Jetstar staff to waive extra baggage and seat fees as industrial action escalates – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for today. Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines: The City of Sydney has banned smart glasses in all its pools, libraries, gyms, childcare centres and town halls. Anthony Albanese has joined the leaders of more than 20 countries in signing a statement calling to bring the rapid growth of artificial intelligence under control. The Greens have called for a national authority to oversee the triple-zero network, which is responsible for emergency call operations. A pilot of “ground rules” hearings will reduce distress and trauma for complainants in sexual assault trials alongside other reforms being introduced to NSW parliament today, the state government says. A medicinal herb found in cold and flu supplements will be phased off Australian shelves over links to severe allergic reactions. Police in Sydney are appealing for information after a man allegedly performed a Nazi salute in the inner city suburb of Newtown on Saturday. NSW police are investigating possible organised crime links after 11-year-old boy was shot in a Sydney apartment. The Reserve Bank governor has said migration is holding up Australia’s economic growth, not adding to inflation, as the government defends its plan to tighten the immigration intake. Victoria has confirmed two new cases of deadly H5 bird flu in fur seals on the state’s coastline. A mother has been charged after allegedly fatally stabbing one child and seriously injuring two others in the Blue Mountains. Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow morning! A New South Wales mother has been charged after allegedly fatally stabbing one child and seriously injuring two others in the Blue Mountains. Emergency services responded to reports of a stabbing at a property on Waratah Road, Valley Heights, at about 12.45pm on Sunday. A five-year-old child died at the scene, despite witnesses providing first aid while waiting for emergency services. Two other children, aged one and three, were taken to hospital and are in a critical but stable condition. The woman, who is in her 40s, was also found at the property with critical injuries. She has been charged with murder and two counts of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to murder. She was refused bail and will remain in custody until her next court appearance next month. Jetstar staff to waive extra baggage and seat fees as industrial action escalates Jetstar staff will escalate industrial action this week, with union members expected to waive extra charges for passengers during a busy travel period. The Australian Services Union (ASU) confirmed that protected industrial action will commence at 12.01 am on Wednesday and run until midnight on Thursday. The timing coincides with the Victorian and Queensland school holidays and precedes the AFL Grand Final. While workers will assist passengers as normal, they won’t collect extra fees on the airline’s behalf, waiving or recording excess baggage, seat selection and late fees as $0. ASU national assistant secretary, Scott Cowen, said the dispute is about fair pay, highlighting Jetstar’s recent annual results showing domestic earnings up 15% and international revenue up 14%. Our members are still turning up to look after passengers, but they won’t be collecting extra fees on Jetstar’s behalf until Jetstar shows that it is serious about its workforce. The ball is now in Jetstar’s court. Members voted in favour of protected action following a ballot in late August, seeking wages aligned with other Qantas Group employees, higher penalties, improved leave, weather protections and job security. A Jetstar spokesperson said operations will not be impacted by the action and that it is “committed to working constructively towards an outcome”. We’ve put a comprehensive and fair offer on the table that includes pay increases, improved penalty payments and allowances, as well as more flexibility in rostering. This is a great package for our people which also allows us to keep investing in our fleet and grow our network while keeping fares low, despite escalating fuel costs impacting the industry. Victoria has confirmed two new cases of deadly H5 bird flu in fur seals on the state’s coastline. A long-nosed fur seal was found dead at Gabo Island in East Gippsland, while an Australian fur seal was reported at Rye back beach on the Mornington Peninsula. Both animals were identified about a week ago through community reports, with tests now confirming the presence of the virus. The state’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said: Timely reports from the public are helping our teams respond quickly, investigate cases and build a clearer understanding of where the virus is present. The cases followed news on Monday of four Australian sea lions, including one pup, testing positive for bird flu, at the Pages islands near Kangaroo Island in South Australia. Victoria’s environment department reminded members of the public to stay at least 30 metres away from marine mammals that appear unwell, and to keep children and pets well clear. People can report sick or dead wildlife to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. Peter Greste says Trump media protest should serve as warning for press freedom in Australia Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom executive director, Peter Greste, has warned that attacks on press freedom in the United States should serve as a warning to Australia. His comments came after major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration barred journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Speaking to the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Greste said: We need to be very careful about not normalising these kinds of behaviours. This is the latest in a fairly long history, a long period of attacks on press freedom and freedom of speech and all sorts of ways by the Trump administration so I think what it shows us is unless we stand up and take note and speak out, whenever these things happen, we do run the risk of these kinds of assaults being normalised and treated as part of a new normal. It is very dangerous for democracy and we have to stop it. Greste said the developments should serve as a warning to Australia, pointing to domestic examples such as One Nation recently barring Guardian Australia and ABC journalists from its press conferences. The example of the United States shows that we can see press freedom being chipped away at the edges. The fact that we are at this particular point I think tells us here in Australia that we cannot take press freedom for granted, and the US has always been held up as that bastion of freedom of speech and freedom of the press because it has the first amendment protected it in its constitution. We don’t have anything like that here in Australia so I’m concerned that if we do not heed the warning from the United States, if we do not recognise the press freedom in Australia is in fact extraordinarily vulnerable, we risk finding ourselves in a very difficult place. Rohan Dennis’s lawyer warn of ‘personal affront’ risk for presiding judge A judge who warned former Olympic cyclist Rohan Dennis he could expect to be jailed if he drove while banned might feel personally affronted that Dennis had breached the ban, his lawyer has told a court. Dennis, 36, received a suspended 17-month jail term and a five-year driving ban in 2025. It followed a guilty plea over the events leading up to the death of his Olympian wife Melissa Hoskins. Despite the suspended sentence over his head, Dennis was allegedly caught driving with two children as passengers on 11 June. AAP reports that in the South Australian district court on Tuesday, Dennis’s lawyer, David Edwardson told Judge Ian Press that it would be inappropriate for him to deal with the matter from every perspective. The perception that Your Honour ... might be personally affronted at the fact that – having given an opportunity to a man by way of a suspended sentence and having given the caution or warning of the potential consequences – that that of itself carries with it almost the inevitable outcome. The prosecutor opposed the claim, stating there was nothing inappropriate about a defendant receiving a standard warning about the consequences of not abiding by a good behaviour bond. Suspension extended for Royal Australasian College of Physicians director A director of the Royal Australasian College of Physicians has had her suspension extended by the charities regulator until early December. In May, the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC) suspended Dr Sharmila Chandran, the president-elect of one of Australia’s oldest medical colleges, until 20 September for allegedly contravening a direction from the NSW work health and safety watchdog. It followed months of conflict within the RACP’s board, which culminated in an extraordinary general meeting in April to which police were called. Prior to her suspension as a responsible person of the RACP, which is a registered charity, Chandran had been due to become president and board chair at an annual general meeting on 29 May. On Friday, the ACNC decided to extend Chandran’s suspension until 4 December, noting that “although the RACP has made progress in addressing the governance and workplace safety issues identified by SafeWork NSW, it has sought an extension of time to comply” with an improvement notice. Chandran said: I have been suspended as a director by the ACNC for simply writing emails to the senior leadership team, emails which in my opinion were always respectful and professional … In my view the regulatory process to date reflects, among other things, retaliatory targeting and victim-blaming of a whistleblower, racial discrimination, bullying and harassment, and institutional bias. Asked for comment, an ACNC spokesperson said: By law the ACNC cannot speak publicly about the circumstances of any charity, apart from referring to information published on the Charity Register, or unless an exception applies in limited circumstances. Michele Bullock has said the AI investment boom could be a bubble, with no sign that it is improving efficiency and every sign it’s adding to inflation. AI stock prices are soaring again after Facebook owner Meta debuted a new AI agent and saw its shares rise 11% on Monday. The Reserve Bank governor said it’s not yet clear whether share markets’ strength will be sustainable. Speaking in Sydney, she said: All central banks are a little bit worried about that. It might not be a bubble but it might be and if it unwinds in a disorderly manner then that could have implications for the financial system and also for real economies … Some people think it’s a bubble, some people don’t. I don’t have a particular view one way or the other, but it’s a risk that I think we’re watching. She said the RBA and top central banks all agreed AI was “the great white hope” to make economies more productive but there was little sign it was yet to happen, with rapid adoption and investment in datacentres just adding to inflation instead. She said: We’ve got this awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand and the AI boom is adding to that demand, ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forwards. The Reserve Bank governor has said migration is holding up Australia’s economic growth, not adding to inflation, as the government defends its plan to tighten the immigration intake. Michele Bullock said Australia’s weak economy and lack of efficiency gains mean immigration and bigger populations are responsible for higher activity, at a CEDA lunch in Sydney. She said: It’s fair to say that, the extent [activity] has been growing over the last few quarters, it’s been growing due to population growth. Bullock rejected the idea that immigration just meant more people entering the country and pushing up prices. She said: The point is it also adds to supply because a lot of those people come in and they work. And therefore, when we think about it, we typically think that it probably is much of a muchness. She said the housing market was the exception, as new immigrants did not immediately generate new housing supply. Where it bites is the housing market, because the housing market can’t respond …. That’s where you tend to see pressures arise. That’s all from me. Achol Arok will take things from here. Take care! House price slide is in ‘lower range of downturns’, RBA governor says The Reserve Bank governor said house prices are falling lower than other recent downturns in the market but from a “pretty unaffordable” level. Michele Bullock has said the drop in prices “doesn’t look entirely out of line” with past experience, at a CEDA lunch in Sydney. She said: It’s a slight dip down after a very long run up. And I think there was a feeling, certainly for this most recent correction, that housing was in effect becoming pretty unaffordable. … You can see that the downturn is sort of in the lower range of downturns in the past, but it’s certainly not out of the ballpark, of the sorts of downturns we’ve seen in the past. Bullock said the downturn was due to interest rate rises, with only 5% of mortgages on fixed rates. The government’s tax reforms had “very directly” impacted the market as well, she said. Housing approvals for investors have just dropped. They’ve dropped for everyone but they’ve really dropped a long way for investors, so it has changed the dynamic for investors, whether it’s worth investing in housing or not. She said economic activity would be hit as slower home sales meant fewer people buying new furniture and fittings, while lower house prices would leave some people feeling poorer and less likely to spend. Political fight over gun buyback after boy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney apartment The shooting of an 11-year-old boy in Sydney’s north-west was a “tragic reminder” of the danger of guns, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, has said while the opposition defends “backflipping” on a gun buyback. The Liberal opposition voted with Labor in support of a buyback last year, but on Saturday pledged it would scrap Labor’s firearm ownership caps for primary producers. The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, instead proposed a commission of inquiry into gun laws and a freeze of any buyback. Caps for farmers and professional shooters would also be scrapped. The police minister, Yasmin Catley, called the Coalition’s plan a “stunning backflip” and said it would leave more guns in circulation. Read more here: NSW police are holding a press conference after an 11-year-old boy was shot in the face in Sydney yesterday. Supt Naomi Moore said officers found the boy with the injury on arrival. He was treated at the scene and taken to hospital, where he remains in critical condition. Moore said there were a number of people in the unit at the time, and officers have spoken to some of them and are looking to speak to others. Some of those present at the time of the shooting “are not currently cooperating with investigators”, she said. Three men, all 18, were arrested last night. Two have been released pending further investigations, and one was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence and had bail refused. Moore said several of those in the unit were known to police, adding: I want to reassure the community this shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts. However, a number of individuals that were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police, and their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators. Angus Taylor said shadow housing minister Andrew Bragg’s idea to use superannuation as collateral for housing purchases is “not our policy”. Taylor was asked about Bragg’s idea earlier today. The opposition leader had this to say: Superannuation is Australians’ money. It’s Australians’ money. They should have choice in it, that’s why we strongly support self-managed super funds. But the proposal you’re talking about there is not our policy. As we reported earlier, Bragg said the “general idea” behind the proposal “is we want to have a country where more people are retired homeowners, and one of the most worrying trends we have is the growth in retired renters”. Bragg added: That doesn’t seem to be the best outcome for all people, which is why we’re having this debate, because we want to be a nation of homeowners. Australian shares edge higher after shaky start Australian shares have already handed back most of an early lead after optimism about the AI boom didn’t translate into significant upside for the local exchange, AAP reports. The S&P/ASX200 rose 0.24% as the broader All Ordinaries gained 0.3%. The top-200 spiked almost 49 points at the open after a tech-led rally on Wall Street overnight, but an unconvincing bounce from under-pressure mining stocks and a lack of follow-through for bank stocks left it on track for yet another flat session. Local energy stocks weighed heavily on Tuesday, as hopes of US-Iran talks sent Brent crude down to $US101.10 a barrel, while diesel prices in the US and Europe have hit record highs. The Australian dollar is buying 71.05 US cents, down from 71.28 US cents on Monday at 5pm. Man linked to suspicious death charged with bribing public officials in Bangladesh A man has been charged with bribing public officials in Bangladesh to stop police linking him to a suspicious death, in a first in Australia’s courts, AAP reports. An Australian-Bangladeshi woman’s death was deemed suspicious by local authorities when her body was found in Bangladesh in September 2024. The Australian federal police began investigating the death due to the woman’s dual citizenship status, seizing international transaction records from banks in Sydney and Brisbane. Police allege a 51-year-old man known to the woman conspired with people in Bangladesh in the two years after her death, transferring about $90,000 to bribe public officials to remove his name from police records. Raids were carried out on Monday at homes in Goodna and Redbank Plains, in Ipswich, south-west of Brisbane, where authorities seized an electronic device and arrested the 51-year-old. He was charged with bribing a foreign public official, an offence which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in jail. Any attempt to corrupt investigative processes, whether in Australia or overseas, was a serious criminal matter, AFP Cmdr Stephen Jay said. “We will continue to work closely with our domestic and international partners regarding this investigation,” he said. The Redbank Plains man is scheduled to appear before Brisbane magistrates court later on Tuesday. It is the first time the AFP has put an allegation of foreign bribery of a public official for personal advantage before the court. Bangladeshi police are conducting their own investigation into the woman’s death. Solar and wind generation meet record 80% of power demand on Australia’s national grid Sunshine and wind met 80.4% of demand on Australia’s main power grid on Saturday, setting a new high bar for renewable electricity. Solar panels on rooftops provided more than half of the power used in the national electricity market, the grid that supplies the eastern states, South Australia and the Australian Capital Territory, for 30 minutes around lunchtime. This was complemented by solar and windfarms, and a small amount of hydro (1%). Fossil fuels, coal and gas, contributed 20%. The energy minister, Chris Bowen, said the milestone meant there was “more clean, cheap, sovereign energy powering our homes and businesses than ever before”. Read more here: Coogee shark attack survivor Stewart says skin graft has failed Leah Stewart, who was bitten by a shark at a Sydney beach, says a skin graft has failed as she continues her recovery. The 34-year-old mother and school teacher was attacked while swimming at Coogee beach in Sydney’s eastern suburbs on 13 June. As part of her treatment, doctors took skin from her right thigh and grafted it on to her injured left thigh. In a social media post, Stewart said she was “devastated” after doctors confirmed the operation has failed. Unfortunately, this is not the post I was wanting to do, but I had my graft checked yesterday and it was confirmed that it failed. Feeling pretty devastated, had quite a few tears. And now, I’m not really sure where to go from here. Stewart said despite the failure, the operation had offered her some reprieve from using a vacuum-assisted closure machine. It’s been three and a half months and my leg is still open. I guess the only good thing is we’re trying something different, having a little break from the vac machine, which means I can move a little bit more freely. Police in Sydney are appealing for information after a man allegedly performed a Nazi salute in the inner city suburb of Newtown on Saturday. NSW police released images of a group of men, who were seen walking along Australia Street at about 5.40pm. The men were allegedly yelling offensive comments before one of them stopped and performed a Nazi salute. The group then continued on their way before they were approached by a woman. They allegedly made offensive comments towards her. Detectives are continuing an investigation into the incident and have asked for anyone with information to come forward. In a post to social media, authorities released photos of people who police believe can assist in their investigation. The BBC has deleted a post and issued a correction after footage of the wrong Fitzroy River was used in relation to the Olympics 2032 venue in Queensland. In a story about the central Queensland venue titled “River with 500 crocodiles chosen as Olympic rowing venue”, a giant reptile is shown lurking in the Fitzroy River. However the footage showed Western Australia’s Fitzroy River – about 3,500km away. The BBC had since issued a correction, stating: “an earlier version of this video included footage of the Fitzroy River in the Kimberley region of Western Australia instead of the Fitzroy River in Queensland. The BBC’s post appeared to no longer be available on Tuesday. The Queensland government had been under pressure to reconsider the rowing venue since pitching it in March 2025, but it was endorsed last week by the IOC, World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide. Emergency bushfire warning for residents near Kingaroy in Queensland Queensland officials have issued an emergency warning for people in the rural locality of Teelah to seek shelter now amid a very dangerous bushfire. The warning applies to an area around Stretton Drive and Scott Close. Teelah is about 115km north-west of Brisbane, near Kingaroy. Boy accused of plan to threaten people and cause harm in Queensland city A boy has been accused of planning to threaten people in a Queensland regional city, AAP reports. The teenager has been charged with acts in preparation to cause death or grievous bodily harm along with possession of a knife in a public place and possession of violent extremist material. He was also charged with possession of a knife in public and violent extremist material in Maryborough, north of Brisbane. He is set to face court after detectives searched a Maryborough address on 27 August. Multiple electronic devices and other items were seized during the search, police said. Police said investigations were continuing but there was no ongoing threat to the public. The boy will appear before the children’s court later today. A medicinal herb found in cold and flu supplements will be phased off Australian shelves over links to severe allergic reactions, AAP reports. Andrographis paniculata (andrographis), also known as green chiretta, has been barred from new medicines entering the Australian market, the Therapeutic Goods Administration announced on Monday. Existing medicines containing andrographis will not be removed from the market immediately, but the TGA has encouraged suppliers to recall products containing the herb. Native to India and Sri Lanka, andrographis is commonly used in Ayurvedic and Chinese traditional medicine to support immunity and combat cold and flu symptoms. Around 80 products containing andrographis are listed on the Australian market, some of which are available from supermarkets, health food stores and pharmacies. The ingredient has attracted growing industry concern in recent years after reports of anaphylactic reactions and one fatality in June 2024. Victoria police warn of heightened family violence risk on AFL grand final day Victoria police have issued a warning ahead of the AFL grand final this weekend, saying officials know there is a heightened risk of family violence during major sporting events. “This is because we see families come together and offenders may use periods of extended contact to increase their abusive behaviours,” a Victoria police spokesperson said this morning. There were 315 family violence incidents on AFL grand final day in 2025 and 301 in 2024. The spokesperson added: While we have not seen a significant increase in family violence incidents on Grand Final Day or the extended weekend in recent years, we urge the community to look out for each other and report any incidents to police. There is never an excuse for family violence and Victoria Police will ensure each crime is investigated and all offenders are held to account. Andrew Bragg, the shadow minister for housing, will float a new proposal for homebuyers to use their superannuation as collateral for mortgages. Bragg will detail the idea during a speech today. He told ABC NewsRadio this morning: The general idea here is we want to have a country where more people are retired homeowners, and one of the most worrying trends we have is the growth in retired renters. Now, there’s nothing wrong with renting of course, but for a lot of people, they would rather live in their own house in retirement. And so we want to make sure that we’re properly calibrating all the options people might like to have in their working life to use their own savings to promote home ownership. When asked if it would be risky for people to take out loans larger than they could service, Bragg said the risk right now is the current trajectory for older renters. Today’s address is about setting out the rationale for having a more sophisticated debate. … We are becoming a country which is going to have a lot more retired renters, but also people potentially with quite high superannuation balances. That doesn’t seem to be the best outcome for all people, which is why we’re having this debate, because we want to be a nation of homeowners. Police interviews able to be used as evidence-in-chief in NSW sexual assault trials under new rules More on today’s changes to the Criminal Procedure Act in NSW … Under the changes, recorded police interviews will also be able to used as evidence-in-chief in sexual assault trials, requiring complainants to only provide their evidence once, including in the case of a retrial. The NSW Women’s Safety Commissioner, Hannah Tonkin, says: Allowing complainants’ pre-recorded evidence in chief to be used during sexual assault trials will enable them to give their account much earlier, in a safe setting, and to start rebuilding their lives sooner. The government is also amending the law around the handling sexual assault complainants’ counselling communications so that courts can only consider them when it is necessary, rather than automatically or out of an abundance of caution. University of Sydney-led research, due to report back in mid-2027, is considering alternative models for reform. Recent reporting has revealed how complainants’ counselling records, including audio recordings, have been used by alleged perpetrators’ legal teams. Minns says shooting of 11-year-old ‘very tragic reminder’ of danger of guns The NSW premier, Chris Minns, says the shooting of an 11-year-old boy in north-west Sydney is a “very tragic reminder of how dangerous guns are”. An 18-year-old man was charged yesterday with concealing a serious indictable offence after the incident, while two other 18-year-old men were released pending further inquiries. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast this morning, the premier said: It’s obviously an incredibly distressing situation. It’s the subject of a major police investigation. I understand the adults in the house are not cooperating with police. We just urge anyone that has any information about this horrible event – we’ve got [an 11-year-old] in a serious condition in a NSW hospital – to come forward. It’s also a very tragic reminder of how dangerous guns are, and often the people who are the victims of guns, are innocent people, many times they are children. They’re very dangerous, and we need less of them in our community. Minns was asked about comments made by police deputy commissioner Peter McKenna after a spate of violence over the weekend, including the alleged murders of three women. McKenna said the government needed to be “throwing every resource” at domestic violence prevention. Minns said: Well, Peter’s an incredibly straight talker on these issues, and he’s 100% right. I mean, the number of violent crimes against often innocent people, innocent family members is hugely distressing. It’s an urgent emergency for our state and we need to throw everything we possibly can at it. A pilot of “ground rules” hearings will reduce distress and trauma for complainants in sexual assault trials alongside other reforms being introduced to NSW parliament today, the state government says. Ground rules hearings, which are already used in child sexual assault proceedings in NSW, will be piloted in sexual assault trials at Parramatta, Wollongong and Dubbo district courts from March next year until 2030. They will provide directions about how complainants will be questioned, including the duration and manner, topics put to them and aides to support their evidence. The government says hearings will require pre-trial discussion about jury directions regarding consent and differences in accounts “without compromising the accused’s right to test the prosecution case”. The NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, says: Sexual assault complainants and witnesses are especially vulnerable in our justice system. We want to help them give their best evidence by ensuring they do not need to tell their story multiple times and deterring inappropriate and irrelevant questioning in court. Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young spoke this morning about the idea for a national authority to oversee the triple zero network, which is responsible for emergency call operations. A Senate committee said yesterday in a report that triple zero should be taken out of private hands. The plan would move control of Australia’s emergency call system away from commercial entities like Telstra to a dedicated public authority. Hanson-Young told RN Breakfast this morning: At the moment, Telstra is contracted to do this work. The taxpayers pay it. That’s your money, my money, every Australian taxpayer’s money to fund the operation of triple zero … We think it’s time to really consider bringing that back under independent control so that the customer, the public, the safety is put first – it’s not seen as some kind of chore or add-on for a privately run company … There needs to be an overhaul of the telecommunications laws. Standards and reliability guarantees must be in the law. Compensation must be available for people. And triple zero must be run for the safety of people, not the profits of corporations. Jim Chalmers was also asked earlier if the government would support a national royal commission into violence against women and children. He said the government had chosen to increase resourcing for child and family violence and domestic violence, adding to the ABC: We’re trying to deal with the sources of all of this violence, whether it be more security in the housing system, whether it be the monetised misogyny that we see online – there are a whole range of factors feeding in here. We do acknowledge that all of this violence is obviously entirely unacceptable. It’s horrific in every way. That’s why we’ve increased the resources and that’s why we all need to do better to do everything we can to make a difference here. The Minderoo foundation put out a new report yesterday that found tech-based abuse disproportionately affects women, particularly on dating platforms. It found that 99% of women surveyed said they had experienced at least one instance of tech-based abuse on dating platforms in the past three months. Chalmers says Australia has ‘a lot going for us’, despite ‘pretty serious’ economic pressures The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, is making the media rounds this morning after the release yesterday of the intergenerational report. He said the government remains optimistic, despite some “pretty serious budget pressures and economic risks”. He told RN Breakfast: We’ve got a lot going for us as well. And one of the things we’ve got going for us, even in the context of these very substantial budget pressures that come from things like ageing and other pressures in our economy, is we’ve actually got a budget which is substantially stronger than other countries. Chalmers stressed that the difficulty of entering home ownership remained the “defining intergenerational challenge” facing too many Australians. We could have left everything exactly as it was. We could have acknowledged the intergenerational unfairness that exists in the housing market and done nothing about it. We chose to make some difficult changes. Tanya Plibersek says we need to use ‘all of our big systems’ to better tackle domestic violence Tanya Plibersek, the minister for social services, said she was struck that a spate of alleged domestic violence incidents this weekend weren’t previously identified by police. Plibersek spoke to RN Breakfast this morning, saying that fact showed how the country needed to use “all of our big systems”, including health, mental health, the school system, Tafe and the university sector to help identify and tackle risk. She said: All of these big points of contact as potential systems where we can identify that there is a risk that there’s family, domestic or sexual violence happening and be able to intervene earlier. She went on to say increased funding was part of the solution and “bigger changes” were needed: It’s not just about funding. There’s also, I think, a much broader role for our community … Support for victims and survivors, making sure that we’re intervening earlier, enhancing supports for children and young people, focusing particularly on sexual violence, which is the area where we’ve seen really extraordinary growth in incidents, focusing on reducing online harms and holding perpetrators to account. All of these things will be part of our second action plan as well. Anthony Albanese has joined the leaders of more than 20 countries in signing a statement calling to bring the rapid growth of artificial intelligence under control. “AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law,” the statement said. Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks. The Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, Spain’s PM, Pedro Sánchez, and European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, also signed the statement. “Artificial intelligence has the potential to improve lives, to strengthen our economy and productivity, and to massively advance science and medical breakthroughs,” Albanese said. But humans need to be in control of it. If it’s going to be successful, then we need to make sure that humans are at the centre of everything that occurs. Albanese told reporters Australia had played a “central role” in the statement. I was in direct discussions with [Finnish] president [Alexander] Stubb, and we continue to engage with our neighbours. The statement also sounded the alarm on AI systems being able to circumvent safeguards and gain unauthorised access to several systems. The signatories called for AI companies to develop transparent safety protocols and for governments to develop common standards for the technology. It also urged the UN to explore options to create an international institution that could set out AI standards. Good morning, Nick Visser here to take over for Martin. It’s a gloomy morning here in Sydney. Let’s get to it. Anthony Albanese has met with Ursula von der Leyen on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly, to talk free trade, China, critical mineral and AI. The prime minister and president of the European Commission were joined by the president of the European Council, António Costa. The trio discussed geopolitical issues, including ongoing support for Ukraine, the situation in the Middle East and Iran, as well as relations with China and the Pacific. They also agreed to continue deepening cooperation on economic security – including on critical and emerging technologies like artificial intelligence. Cooperation between the EU and Australia when it comes to critical raw minerals was also on the agenda, ahead of the Team Europe business mission to Australia next month. “They agreed to remain in close contact with a view to explore the potential for further strengthening and deepening of EU-Australia relations,” a statement read. It comes after the EU invited Canada to become an associate member – though the council has no such category – with some speculating Australia could follow suit. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says the Albanese government is committed to doing “everything we can” to address to domestic violence after a horrific weekend of violence in New South Wales. Chalmers made the comments to ABC’s 7.30 program last night after a mother allegedly fatally stabbed a child and wounded two others in the Blue Mountains and, separately, three other women were allegedly murdered inside their homes across the state. Chalmers noted expert views that a lack of accessible housing played a role in domestic violence, along with the “magnitude” of misognystic content online. He also said frontline staffing was crucial. I work closely with the prime minister and [women’s minister] Katy Gallagher and the relevant ministers to make sure that police and others get the resourcing they need, working with state governments. Jim Chalmers says migration is necessary to support Australia’s ageing population, and can help the nation as birthrates tumble. The three-yearly intergenerational report found that the declining birthrate meant more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time – the first time the report had made such a prediction. Chalmers told 7.30 Australia’s birthrates were falling faster than anticipated just a few years ago, because people are taking the decision to have smaller families later in life. He said, in this context, “any objective observer would conclude that we need responsible levels of migration” to support the ageing population: Migration is a force for good in our economy and in our society. We will continue to make the case for getting that net overseas migration down in the most responsible way, that balances all of the key considerations in our economy and in local communities. His comments come after the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, last week unveiled long-awaited changes to immigration rules, promising to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28. The City of Sydney has banned smartglasses in all its pools, libraries, gyms, childcare centres and town halls. The council agreed to update signage and guidance to prevent people wearing the glasses in community facilities, due to growing privacy and harassment concerns. In a statement, Greens councillor Matthew Thompson said his motion included exemptions for those who use the glasses as accessibility devices, including those with vision and hearing loss. He urged the federal government to do more to regulate the glasses and prevent their misuse, saying that: Overseas we’re seeing women being targeted and harassed in public and recorded without their consent. We don’t want what’s happening in the US to happen here. That’s why we’re banning smart glasses and other wearable recording devices from all of our pools, gyms, childcare [centres], libraries and other council spaces. Cheap wearable devices like smart glasses are already flooding the market. But instead of stopping this problem, the federal Labor government has dumped it on to councils to sort out. We need an import ban on these cheap, intrusive devices until we have stronger privacy protections and clear standards implemented nationally. Last week, Sydney’s Canterbury-Bankstown council introduced its own restrictions on the technology. Its mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools. In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools. Melbourne’s Yarra council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms. Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Nick Visser with the main action. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says the Albanese government is committed to doing “everything we can” to address to domestic violence after a weekend of violence in New South Wales. More coming up.
