headline: Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him
trail_text: US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state
body_text: Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state. Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader. But this seemed more shocking. The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting. Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience. Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise. The US president twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-western former Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979. Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests last January, weeks before the war. “The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons. No definitive death toll has been established. But previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations – even including those previously stated by Trump himself – have been much lower. The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran. Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes. “It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.” US actions in Venezuela, where special forces last January seized the strongman president, Nicolás Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries – as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard”, if it felt its interests threatened. “Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump declared. He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with the interim Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60% of the world’s oil. “It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump said. There was outright antipathy for the international criminal court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people”. “We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said. Given his pugnacious stance towards US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his general assembly speech a year ago, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration. This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, as a “great leader” – a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger”. He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country”, just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex. With that issue seemingly settled – at least for now – the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence, or AI. Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labelled a “hoax”. Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” (“it makes it sound fake – and it’s not fake”) and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents. “Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”

headline: Previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart shortlisted for Booker prize
trail_text: The two authors are in the running for the £50,000 award alongside a Pulitzer winner, a science fiction legend, a comic writer and a debut novelist
body_text: This year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison. Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November. James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time for The Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list. Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in a Guardian review. Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! This year, she is shortlisted for The Things We Never Say, which departs from the well-known cast of characters in her previous novels to introduce the history teacher Artie Dam, whose comfortable life on the Massachusetts coast is threatened by a secret, and by the realities of a changing US. Harrison, who judged the prize in 2022, is shortlisted for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in an unnamed Kent coastal town. The book, “as its title suggests, is about everything”, wrote Michel Faber in the Guardian. “It burrows deep into our psyches – into the psyche of our civilisation – and exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now.” The shortlisted books “took risks”, and they “could not be replicated by artificial intelligence – these are very human books”, said the writer Raymond Antrobus, who is on this year’s judging panel alongside the chair Mary Beard, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, the writer Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. Kennard made the list for Black Bag, his comic campus novel about an actor in his late 30s who takes a job involving attending lectures in a black leather bag as part of a psychological experiment. Completing the shortlist is Perry, the sole debut novelist, with May We Feed the King. The book – which won this year’s Waterstones debut prize – is about a modern-day curator tasked with dressing rooms in historic houses, who becomes increasingly obsessed with the life of a medieval king. Four of the shortlisted titles are by men, and three of them – Black Bag, The Disappearers, and John of John – explore masculinity and male sexuality. That the shortlisted authors are predominantly male is “quite surprising, because generally speaking the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”, said Cocker. The masculinity theme may come down to men “having to rethink their role”, he added. Beard said she doesn’t think it’s a “very masculine” shortlist, while Lockwood half-joked that “all these books are gay”. Among the surprises on the shortlist was the absence of American author Emma Cline, whose novel Switzy, which follows a man suffering from dementia travelling to a euthanasia clinic, received positive reviews across the board, amid predictions that it could win the overall award. British author Gwendoline Riley also failed to make the cut with her longlisted novel The Palm House. The judges said the shortlisting meeting lasted approximately three hours. The five other books that didn’t make the shortlist were The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis, Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman, The Renovation by Kenan Orhan, All Them Dogs by Djamel White, and The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams. This year’s prize was open to books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026. Last year’s prize was awarded to David Szalay for his novel Flesh. Recent winners include Samantha Harvey for Orbital, Paul Lynch for Prophet Song, and Shehan Karunatilaka for The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida. • Explore the shortlist for this year’s Booker prize and, for a limited time, get all six books for only £79 at guardianbookshop.com. headline: Middle East crisis: Trump says Iran will make a deal after US midterms – as it happened

body_text: Donald Trump has called on nations to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices, as he gave a bellicose defence of his administration’s foreign policy and decision to strike Iran. “I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” the US president said in a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror … and oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict.” It comes as numerous US allies have complained about soaring energy prices and growing international instability during his US administration. He also denied that the US was running short of critical munitions (“we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using”). But instead of letting the future continue to veer toward fragmentation, transactionalism and mistrust, he called for “a world built on interdependence – and sustained by a dense web of economic, political, social and technological connections.” You can watch the address here: Russian president Vladimir Putin held ⁠a phone call with Saudi crown prince ⁠Mohammed bin Salman ⁠today, Reuters reported. They discussed the security ⁠situation in the Gulf and the need to keep ⁠vital waterways open, according to the Kremlin. It said ‌the two ‌leaders held a detailed exchange ‌of views on the situation in the Middle East and emphasised that a political and diplomatic settlement remains the ‌only viable path forward. They also “underscored the need for a swift cessation of hostilities” in Yemen amid the deteriorating military and political situation there. “The ⁠importance of ensuring the safe and unimpeded passage of vessels through the region’s international waterways, including ‌the Bab el-Mandeb and Strait of Hormuz, was emphasised,” the Kremlin said. Iran’s national airline said it had not received any ban on serving neighbouring countries, a day before US sanctions are due to be tightened against the Iranian aviation sector. “Iran Air has not received any notification or official instruction from the civil aviation authorities of Turkey, the Republic of Azerbaijan, or Iraq regarding a halt or suspension of the airline’s flights to Istanbul, Baku and Najaf,” the company said in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA. Earlier this month the US blacklisted the Iranian aviation sector and threatened sanctions against any organisation working with Iran’s airlines, AFP reported. Gaza’s health ministry said in its latest update that at least 1,399 people have been killed by Israeli attacks since a supposed ‘ceasefire’ was signed between Israel and Hamas last October. Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by the US to end the war on Gaza, which includes the Israeli withdrawal from the strip and the disarmament ⁠of Hamas. Israel says Hamas has been violating the deal. Gaza’s health ministry said on Tuesday that 73,919 people, mostly women and children, have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since October 2023, when Isreal launched its assault on the territory following the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people, mostly Israeli civilians, were killed. A number of legal and rights experts have concluded that Israel has committed genocide – considered the most serious international crime – against the Palestinian population of Gaza. Israel denies the charge, despite the widespread evidence that supports the conclusion. The US secretary of State, Marco Rubio, has confirmed that the ⁠US is ⁠open to speaking with Iranians at the UN ⁠General Assembly, but said no meeting is currently scheduled (see this post for more details). “We’re ⁠open to that. I don’t ‌think anything ‌is scheduled at this point, ‌but we’re certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of ‌leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about,” Rubio told NBC News. “And that is the fact that Iran can never ‌have a nuclear weapon. They just simply can’t,” he added. The renewed US-Iran efforts to resolve the dispute about control of the strait of Hormuz comes amid reports of Saudi Arabia attacking areas under Houthi control in Yemen. Among the latest reports is of an attack by Saudi Arabia on a prison in northwestern Yemen that killed nine detainees, according to a Houthi official, who spoke to the Saba news agency, which is affiliated with the Iran-backed militia. “Nine prisoners captured during recent events were killed last night when the Saudi enemy targeted a prison” in Al-Hazm, in Al-Jawf governorate, Houthi official Abdelkader al-Murtada said. The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen’s capital since 2014, seized the country’s Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government. Saudi Arabia, an important US ally, has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters’ positions in the highlands, according to the Houthis. Here is some more analysis from our diplomatic editor, Patrick Wintour: A fortnight ago Iran said it had reached agreement with Oman for a new agreed temporary route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz that would then be lodged with the International Maritime Organisation. The bulk of the route goes through Iranian waterways in the north of the strait. But the meeting planned for the Gulf States to endorse the route was cancelled by Saudi Arabia after what it regarded as Iranian-induced attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthi forces in Yemen. Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted the route had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways passed: Iran and Oman. Iran had also said the waterway would not be opened even after the route was agreed until seven other conditions were met largely related to lifting the sanctions, asset freezes and broader US aggression towards Iran. Only after that could the issue of Iran’s nuclear program be considered. The US has been countering this week by trying to impose an aerial blockade on Iran, threatening third countries not to allow Iranian civilian planes to fly in and out of Iran from their airports. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said all Iranian planes will stop flying worldwide from Wednesday. Tehran appears to have relaxed its preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz, saying it is prepared to do so within seven days so long as the US takes reciprocal steps to ease the pressure on Iran. Previously Iran had set seven onerous pre-conditions for lifting the blockade including “an end to war on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to cease all aggressive actions against Iran including sanctions. The new position emerged ahead of backstage negotiations at the UN General Assembly in New York this week and was briefed by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo. The official claimed the position had been approved by the Supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, and the Supreme National Security Council. The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) in a statement not directly referring to the report said there was no contradiction in staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammed Ghalibaf in remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament this week. Iran, the Japanese news agency reported from Tehran, was seeking signs from Washington that it is prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward an end to the US military blockade of Iranian ports and a halt to military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. If such steps are taken, Iran is prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official. These preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other authoritative figures in the previous 48 hours. It is sometimes the case that initially appealing offers from Iran emerge to be more complex once the small print is examined. But Tehran is under growing pressure due to US engineered restrictions on the exports of its oil playing having havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation. The official insisted there was no chance that Iran’s president, Massoud Pezeshkian, will meet the US president while in New York. Pezeshkian has not been directly involved in the negotiations with the US and does not have the independent authority to make concessions to the US. As broadly a reformist, he is also not fully trusted by the IRGC and hardline politicians in Tehran. Some hardliners oppose negotiations with the West as a matter of principle. Others argue that Iran holds the upper hand as energy markets come under further pressure worldwide. We are seeing reports that the Houthis have said that strikes carried out by Saudi Arabia in the northwest of the country killed at least two civilians. “A mother and child were killed, while her husband and two of her other children were wounded in strikes carried out by the Saudi enemy in the Al-Batin area of Al-Hazm, in Al-Jawf province,” the Iranian-backed militia’s news agency said, citing the Houthi health ministry. Iran is ready to ⁠reopen ⁠the strait of Hormuz within seven days ⁠if the US ⁠eases military pressure and lifts ‌its ‌blockade on Iranian ‌ports, a senior Iranian official has told the Reuters news agency. There is no more immediate detail on how exactly this reopening would work in practice and the US hasn’t commented on the report, which we have not been able to independently verify. The official ‌also told Reuters that the Iranian delegation to the UN General Assembly has full authority to revive diplomacy with US officials. Visible traffic through the strait of Hormuz has dwindled to a trickle, but some tankers are continuing exporting oil by travelling with their transponders off to avoid detection. A total of 17 commodity vessels transited the strait over the weekend, down from 37 ‌a week earlier, shipping data showed on Monday. Before the war, an estimated 120 vessels crossed the strait each day. Despite the reduction in journeys through the strategic waterway, oil prices fell for a fourth consecutive session yesterday amid fresh prospects for renewed diplomacy. As we mentioned earlier in the blog, Tehran and Washington exchanged ‌threats ⁠on Sunday, although the US president, Donald Trump, said he probably would be open to meeting his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, who is travelling to New York for the UN meeting. Among Iran’s previous conditions to reopen the strait included an and to the war on “all fronts” – referring to Israel’s assault on Lebanon – and the release of frozen funds. The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil. Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world. The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government. You can read the full story here: Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi has already arrived in New York. He said Iran’s main objective is to “defend the legitimacy, rights and interests” of the Iranian people at the UN general assembly, which he describes as “a major international platform”. He said the gathering comes at a time when Iran is still defending itself against a “cowardly” war waged on it by the US and Israel that has resulted in many deaths. Araghchi referred to the 156 civilians, including 120 children, who were killed by a US strike on the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab on the opening day of the war as among the victims of the war. In his comments to journalists, which were published on Araghchi’s official Telegram channel, the Iranian foreign minister picks up on the title of this year’s theme of the UN general assembly: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”. He said the title “shows that all countries acknowledge that there is no longer any trust and confidence in this organization has been lost, and this is unfortunately due to its ineffectiveness in establishing international peace and security.” He went on to say that a number of countries act as if they are above international law, condemning the west as hypocritical for pretending to care about human rights while remaining “silent” when Israel, for example, is allowed to “do whatever it wants”. Araghchi said Israel has been committing crimes across Lebanon, Gaza, Palestine and Iran without any “serious condemnation”. “Therefore, it is natural that no trust remains in an organization that is influenced by these countries, so the discussion of restoring trust is an important discussion and provides an opportunity to talk to the world about how trust in the UN has been lost and how it can be restored,” Araghchi said. The statement comes ahead of the first debate of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where representatives from 193 countries are gathering for an intense period of high-stakes diplomacy. The debate opens on Tuesday, runs through to Saturday, and concludes on Monday, because no sessions are held on Sunday. Today’s morning session (from 1300 GMT time) is due to be kicked off by an address from the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, and will be followed by a speech from the US president, Donald Trump. Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak at the UN meeting tomorrow. On his way to New York this morning, he vowed to “firmly defend” his country’s positions. “We emerged with our heads held high, and this is a source of dignity and pride for all of us. Therefore, we will firmly defend our positions in international forums,” he said. “We will make the best possible use of this opportunity to convey Iran’s plight to the international community. We will firmly tell our adversaries that, despite all the unfairness and injustices, the Iranian people have stood their ground,” he said. Pezeshkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to set foot on American soil since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on 28 February 2026. In a joint statement, the Group of Seven (G7) foreign ministers called on Iran to end military support to Houthi forces in Yemen. The ministers representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US said “we call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions”. “All threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” it added. They also called on Iran “to end its arming of and support for the Houthis,” alleging Tehran is in violation of past UN security council resolutions. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a UN embargo, and has said it only supports the group politically. However, smuggled Iranian weapons have been seized from shipments bound for Yemen, and a report by UN experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies. According to a report in the New York Times, the US president, Donald Trump, has wavered for weeks over whether to act on appeals from Saudi Arabia for military help in fighting the Houthis. On Wednesday, the president had reportedly met with advisers and said he did not favour strikes. But the following day, his close ally, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, called Trump again to ask for his help to halt the Houthi’s rapid advance, the outlet reported, citing administration officials. After this phone call, Trump reserved his position and told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis, according to the report. But by Sunday, Trump had changed his mind again and said there would be no US airstrikes against the Iranian-backed rebel group, at least for now. The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group, as it agreed to stop targeting shipping in the Red Sea. The US has directly kept out of the conflict ever since. Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and government forces supported by Saudi Arabia has killed 154 people in the past two days, military sources told the AFP news agency, and has sparked a refugee crisis. “The death toll from Saudi airstrikes, clashes and artillery fire in the governorates of Taiz, Al-Jawf, Marib and Saada stands at 118,” Houthi military sources said, while government sources reported 36 killed in their “ranks”, according to AFP. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that started in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally recognised government from Sanaa, the country’s capital, driving it south towards Aden. A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states subsequently intervened on behalf of the ousted government, with a mostly aerial campaign that was condemned for its deadly impact on the civilians of Yemen. Neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen’s mountainous terrain, and the Houthis remained in control over the northwest, where most of the population lives. The two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, which, despite some skirmishes, largely held until July, when a Saudi airstrike hit the runway of the airport in Sanaa, preventing the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a high-ranking Houthi delegation. The already shaky UN-brokered ceasefire has since completely collapsed, with the two sides exchanging missiles, drones and air strikes. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would “change the geography of the war” if the US escalates the conflict, after Donald Trump issued fresh threats against the Islamic Republic. In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump said “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future”, adding that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”. A spokesperson for the IRGC, Hossein Mohebbi, responded with a warning that if the US were to launch fresh attacks against Iran, Tehran would use “new weapons with capabilities into the battle”. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Mohebbi was quoted as having said. “Our targets will no longer necessarily be the same as before,” he said, according to the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, adding that Iran has targets that have not yet been struck. The comments come as the US and Iran remain locked in an impasse over the strait of Hormuz and after attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The Houthis, who operate independently of Iran’s instructions, have seized territory along the country’s Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital shipping route that links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Saudi Arabia has used it as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have also attacked oil facilities and other types of infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, in response for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The attacks have further disrupted energy markets, pushing up global fuel prices, including in the US, where consumers have been hit hard. Iran hugely benefits from the Houthis fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on the US to relent over Iran, which has insisted it will not allow the reopening of the strait of Hormuz until all its conditions have been met. With diplomatic negotiations stalled, traffic in the strait continues to be severely disrupted, with Iran firing on commercial ships and demanding it first approve passage along its authorised route. In response, the US, which started the war on Iran alongside Israel in February, is maintaining a counter-blockade of Iranian ports while intensifying economic pressure. The US has also fired on commercial shipping in the region and has killed Iranian civilians in its strikes.

headline: Trump praises Burnham despite tensions over AI, Chagos Islands and Iran
trail_text: US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York
body_text: Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos Islands and the war in Iran. At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister. Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran. UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead. On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure. Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US. Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”. Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops. In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year. But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology. “The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said. “Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution.” Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks. In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia. “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said. But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”. However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK. UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial. But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way. “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.” Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”. In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”. Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade. “Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said. Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

headline: Trump defends actions in Iran and Venezuela in UN General Assembly address amid rising tensions with allies – as it happened
trail_text: This live blog is now closed.
body_text: Closing summary This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Speaking at the UN general assembly, Donald Trump re-issued his threat to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into Hell” if the regime didn’t capitulate and make a deal.” He also said he was “working closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine” to end the disastrous war, defended his administration’s actions in Latin America – including the midnight raid to arrest former Venezuelan president Nicólas Maduro, defended his drone strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, accused Mexico of being effectively controlled by the cartels, and said it was “unacceptable” for the US to share a border with a nation under such conditions, pointed to regime change in Cuba and said he would reject any calls for a “globalist scheme” to control artificial intelligence. Shortly after his UN address, Trump signed a Greenland deal, which Greenland’s prime minister Jens-Frederick Nielsen said “underlines the importance of the Nato alliance.” In tricky, carefully worded paragraphs, she said the agreement “recognises the US defining historical and ongoing contributions to the security and defence of Greenland,” but it also “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.” Trump and New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani appeared friendly after a ‘wide-ranging’ meeting at Gracie Mansion. Trump said he hoped Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader. Trump told a CNN reporter at the UN general assembly on Tuesday that he was “surprised” the outlet was covering him, saying it ‘shouldn’t be here’ after he banned the network alongside Politico and MS Now from the White House on Friday. Answering a reporter’s question following her first appearance of the midterm campaign season, Kamala Harris said, “The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing.” At a joint press conference on Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced that the federal government was removing 760,000 enrollees from Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces. Trump said he is working on a ‘massive’ Belarus, pivoting away from main supplier Canada amid an escalating trade dispute, and moving instead toward an ally of Russia. Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian. Senator John Curtis, a Republican from Utah, published a letter calling for a key Senate committee to investigate Trump’s son over his personal and business dealings with foreign governments, as well as his shady ventures in cryptocurrency and predictions markets. Curtis’ letter follows a bombshell report from ProPublica that found a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, had helped bankroll Trump Jr.’s lavish Bahamas wedding. The Republican National Committee has sued top election officials in New Jersey, alleging they failed to produce public voter roll records, including the addresses of noncitizen voters. The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts. Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is currently imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza. Kamala Harris called Donald Trump’s decision to ban three news organisations from the White House “absolutely abhorrent.” Answering a reporter’s question following her first appearance of the midterm campaign season, Harris said, “The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing.” Harris had been speaking at a roundtable on Black maternal health in Michigan alongside Senate-hopeful Abdul El-Sayed. “He’s trying to stifle the ability of journalists to let the people of America know what’s really going on with their government,” Harris said. 60 Minutes’ blockbuster interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, failed to provide a major ratings boost for the Sunday show, according to audience figures released Tuesday. Sunday night’s episode of the newsmagazine show drew an average of 6.77m total viewers, the third-smallest audience in the past 25 years for the second episode of a season, adding to a disappointing debut for Bari Weiss, who, as CBS editor-in-chief, rewired the show, firing several high-profile correspondents in the run-up to the new season. The 59th season debuted on 13 September with an audience down sharply from the 58th season debut, drawing 7.94 million viewers compared with 10 million for last season’s first episode. Angela Paxton – the Texas state senator who is currently divorcing US Senate-hopeful Ken Paxton – encouraged Republican women to vote the party “even if we’re mad at them,” the Texas Tribune reports. Paxton said she was divorcing her husband on “biblical grounds,” citing allegations of adultery, in 2025, shortly after her husband announced he would challenge longtime Texas senator John Cornyn. She has not commented on her husband’s race since announcing the divorce, including excluding his name from a list of endorsements in statewide primary races. According to the Tribune, Angela Paxton addressed a meeting of the Texas Federation of Republican Women on Friday. In a speech titled “The Elephant in the Room” she encouraged the attendees to vote for the party even if they disliked an individual candidate. “We have more control over that seat and the future when we control the seat — when it’s still in the family, even if we’re mad at them,” she said. “But if we lose it to the other team, the nuances that we want to fix with maybe a certain candidate are nothing compared to what it’s going to take to get it back, right?” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer says the shooting of a Venezuelan man by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday “is a direct result of Trump ordering ICE agents to continue deadly traffic stops.” “ICE must provide a full accounting of what happened, why deadly force was used, and why despite billions in funding agents are still roaming around without cameras and accountability,” Schumer said in a social media post. After the shooting, Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine. Since then, the remains of Iran’s hardline leadership have dug in, blockading the vital Strait of Hormuz, a key artery of oil shipping, and launching waves of drones and missiles at US bases and ships in the region. The US has retaliated by striking Iranian targets and oil tankers, and by imposing withering economic sanctions aimed at forcing the regime back to the bargaining table. A series of top Republicans heading to Iowa and New Hampshire – key states in the presidential primary – have raised the possibility of a contentious 2028 field for the GOP nomination, The Washington Post reported on Tuesday. Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian. Escobar, a Democrat who represents El Paso and surrounding areas on the US-Mexico border in west Texas, conducted an oversight visit last month at the Camp East Montana ICE tent facility housed in the Fort Bliss military base, after two separate “disturbances” had been reported there in recent weeks. But when she arrived to scrutinize conditions at the camp, the largest ICE detention center in the country, she said she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. Despite a federal judge ruling in favor of the lawmakers last December, there have been subsequent reports of ICE officials placing limits on or turning away members of congress when attempting to conduct oversight visits. “Oversight, during the second Trump administration, has certainly been significantly more challenging than during the first Trump administration,” Escobar added. The announcement on Monday shows Washington’s willingness to pursue dialogue with Minsk despite its repression of dissidents and support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The visit to Gracie Mansion, ahead of the president’s speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday, was a measure of Trump’s apparent respect for the 34-year-old mayor of his native New York. It was the first presidential visit to the historic riverside residence in 45 years, following Ronald Reagan, who met there with Ed Koch in 1981. headline: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China
trail_text: Fears persist about Trump ‘sucking up’ to Xi on Taiwan, but few concrete outcomes anticipated from US meeting
body_text: When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors. The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics. Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.” One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of ⁠OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a ⁠state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening. ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’ In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement. Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said. Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, which called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”. China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots. China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots. Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.” Trade tensions persist Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November. Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power. Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.” China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running. ‘This is not a G2’ One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship. But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again. Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers. “They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary. China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation. Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making. Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran. When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022. Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.” High vibes, low ambition The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit. Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.” Democrats in Washington have urged Trump to raise concerns over China’s treatment of political prisoners, but are already sounding the alarm that he could make too many concessions to Xi. Senator Tammy Duckworth told an audience at the Center for American Progress thinktank on Tuesday: “He’s not very good at making deals with the PRC [People’s Republic of China] that they actually follow through on. If you look at the result of the last summit they had, they promised the purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft and $17bn in agricultural products. Neither one of those has come to pass.” “At the same time, he violated our longstanding position on Taiwan by engaging in discussions on arms sales to Taiwan with President Xi,” Duckworth added. “I worry that it’s going to be a repeat of that and President Trump basically spends too much time sucking up to President Xi. He’s very distracted. When he focuses on the Indo-Pacific, it’s about him cozying up to an authoritarian regime at the expense of our friends and allies in the region.” Additional research by Yu-chen Li

headline: Shoebridge says US submission on online safety laws an ‘extraordinary intervention’ – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today! Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has denied Australia’s proposed digital duty of care laws are about government control after the Trump administration accused the legislation of being “viewpoint-based censorship”. Despite the row, Albanese posed for a selfie with Trump at the UN assembly in New York. Anthony Albanese has met Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, at the United Nations – the first time the pair have been together since Albanese’s comments about melons in a controversial podcast. Parenthood chief executive, Georgie Dent, addressed the National Press Club in Canberra today on new research that shows the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The royal commission into allegations of corruption on Victorian government construction sites has begun, with commissioner Chris Kourakis kicking off proceedings by asking his associate, Peter Tantalos, to read out the letters patent, which formally established the inquiry in August. Randwick council announced it intends to ban smartglasses across Sydney’s eastern suburbs beaches. Sydney’s inner west council has also moved to ban smartglasses and other wearable recording devices in its facilities, including pools, change rooms, childcare centres and public toilets. Sydney airport saw some flights delayed or cancelled this morning amid a blanket of fog that settled over the harbour city. Continuing on aviation, Qantas announced its 18-hour direct Sydney-New York flights will start in mid-2028, predicting it will cut travel time between the two cities by three hours. A $1m reward has been offered for information about four-year-old Gus Lamont, who went missing almost a year ago. Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning. The Greens senator David Shoebridge has accused the United States of interfering in Australia’s domestic politics after the Trump administration criticised the government’s proposed opt-in algorithm reforms. In a submission overnight, the Trump administration warned the measures risked becoming a mechanism for “viewpoint-based censorship” and called for American platforms to be exempted. Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Shoebridge said: It’s an extraordinary intervention in our domestic politics, that’s what we have seen. The US embassy issuing, basically, a slap down to the Australian government on a piece of domestic legislation that the Australian parliament should be deciding on, not Washington. It is almost unprecedented in my experience to see a foreign government in this country through their embassy … so overtly try and dissuade the Australian parliament from taking actions to protect the Australian public. Shoebridge said the US “needs to be brought to heel by the rest of the world” as global discussions continue over artificial intelligence safeguards and the power of major technology companies. NAB says it is working to fix online bank outages affecting customers Continuing our coverage of the NAB outage, the bank said it is aware of the reported issues and has launched an investigation. NAB said the issues have affected “a number of our digital channels” including internet banking, its mobile app and broker digital services. In a statement to social media, the bank said the issues “are not limited to” its online services: The issue is also affecting our phone services, and customers may be unable to contact us by phone at this time. Our teams are investigating and working to fix this as quickly as possible. NAB ATMs remain available. We’re sorry for the inconvenience and thank you for your patience while we work to restore services. We’ll share updates as they become available. A NAB spokesperson said: Most services have now been restored. Some business customers are continuing to experience login issues via NAB Connect, and we’re working as quickly as possible to resolve the remaining impacts. National Australia Bank (NAB) customers are reporting an outage affecting access to the bank’s online services. According to DownDetector, reports began at about 1pm, peaking at more than 2,000 reports at about 3.30pm. Users have taken to social media to say they are unable to access their accounts. NAB has been contacted for comment. ‘Chaos, confusion’: cop recalls jumping castle tragedy A veteran police officer has described the chaos and mistakes that followed a deadly school jumping castle tragedy, saying unclear chains of command created confusion, AAP reports. An inquest which began on Monday is examining the circumstances of the tragedy, safety processes and whether there were any departmental deficiencies. Tasmania Police constable Dean Wotherspoon was one of the first officers to attend the Hillcrest primary school accident on 16 December 2021. Students Addison Stewart, Chace Harrison, Jye Sheehan, Jalailah Jayne-Maree Jones, Peter Dodt and Zane Mellor died after a freak “dust devil” wind gust lifted the jumping castle into the air above the Devonport school grounds. The leading forensic officer told an inquest on Wednesday: I think the phrase perhaps is organised chaos. There were a lot of people doing their utmost to save children. Police officers, school staff, paramedics all doing what they could. It was nothing like I had seen. Rosemary Gamble, the operator of Taz-Zorb, which set up the inflatable equipment, was in 2025 cleared of criminal workplace safety breaches. Good afternoon! I hope today has been nice to you. I’ll be here to take you through the rest of the day’s news. That’s all from me today folks. The blog is now in the capable hands of Achol Arok. See you next time! Sydney’s inner west council has moved to ban smartglasses and other wearable recording devices in its facilities, including pools, change rooms, childcare centres and public toilets. Inner west councillor Kerrie Fergusson said that the technology is likely “just the beginning of many new challenges for local councils”. For people with vision or hearing impairments, they offer a new level of independence. But they can also discreetly record high-definition video and live-stream, creating genuine privacy concerns … This isn’t tearing down new technology like a bunch of 19th-century luddites, but ensuring AI technology properly serves our community without compromising its privacy or civil liberties. Council staff have been asked to report back on how the ban will be implemented, including conditions of entry and signage requirements. Exemptions will be provided to people who rely on the technology as accessibility devices. As reported earlier this morning, smartglasses could soon be banned across Sydney’s eastern suburbs beaches Coogee, Clovelly and Maroubra under a motion put forward to Randwick council. It has already banned the technology at the Des Renford leisure centre, citing “growing community concerns” about their potential misuse. It also follows City of Sydney councillors voting to ban smartglasses at council gyms, childcare centres and pools on Monday. Police appeal for information after Wagyu cow ‘unlawfully’ shot and butchered in Queensland Detectives from Queensland’s Rural and Stock Crime Squad are appealing for public information, after a Wagyu cow was “unlawfully shot and butchered for meat” on a property in Queensland. Police believe trespassers entered the property in Farnborough on 13 or 14 June. Investigators urge anyone who noticed suspicious activity or captured dashcam footage along Fishing Creek Road, off Farnborough Road, between 13 and 16 June to contact police or Crime Stoppers. Parenting advocate Georgie Dent tells National Press Club that Australians should get 52 weeks paid parental leave More on the national press club address today by Georgie Dent, Parenthood chief executive … Dent cited Treasury data showing that having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years of parenthood. Dent said families need two incomes to stay afloat in the current economy and even with both parents working, they have less breathing room in their household budget. For many families it feels like a cruel game of whack-a-mole … For parents of young children seeking to raise and provide for their family one obstacle towers over the others: early childhood education and care. Too many face an impossible bind. They cannot access it, they cannot afford it, or they cannot trust what is available. This isn’t perceived: the options families have are largely determined by what the market has delivered. Dent will call for a policy pathway from government for the provision of 52 weeks of paid parental leave, up from 26 weeks currently paid for by taxpayers, and meaningful parental leave for fathers and partners. The speech comes after Monday’s intergenerational report showed that, for the first time, more Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years’ time. Read more here: Press Club says it will never ban journalists from ‘doing their job’ The host of today’s national press club momentarily interrupted question time to say it will never ban journalists from “doing their job”. Just another message, we’re going to depart for our theme for a second. [There is] a lot of news at the moment, and in recent months, about journalists not being able to, you know, attend press conferences, et cetera. Just a note on behalf of the national press club that no journalists will ever be banned from doing their job here. The message was greeted by applause, before returning to the topic of childcare costs. This press club comment comes after US president Donald Trump banned journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. In Australia, the ABC and the Guardian have called on One Nation to reverse its ban on select media outlets from press conferences amid warnings the party is practising censorship and actively avoiding public scrutiny. Journalist Peter Greste has written for Guardian Australia about how these circumstances show “why Australia urgently needs a media freedom bill”: Anthony Albanese has met Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, at the United Nations – the first time the pair have been together since Albanese’s comments about melons in a controversial podcast. The PM has repeatedly rejected suggestions he made offensive comments about a gift of two melons from Takaichi on the Bush Deep podcast in early July. Japan’s ambassador to Australia downplayed any possible offence and said Tokyo had been reassured by the Australian government that Albanese’s comments had been misunderstood. Albanese wrote on social media, in a post that included a photo with world leaders including Takaichi: Working with our international partners. Standing up for Australian interests. Finding global solutions to global challenges. Australia’s voice matters at the United Nations. And it’s here that we’re delivering for Australians back home. While in New York, Albanese has met Britain’s Andy Burnham, the French president Emmanuel Macron, Pedro Sanchez of Spain and the US president Donald Trump. Plan to shift $4bn of NDIS spending snagging on lone holdout state Health minister Mark Butler says he is frustrated that Queensland is the only state or territory not to sign up to the government’s Thriving Kids program, a week before the first phase is due to begin. The health minister told ABC Radio on Wednesday: I’m a little frustrated they haven’t signed because all other states and territories, Liberal and Labor alike, CLP government in the NT has signed on. The Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, was shirking a responsibility he had previously promised to accept, according to Butler. He said: I can’t imagine a Queensland government that, for the next 15 months, would sit on its hands and pretend it does not have a very serious obligation to follow the rest of the country. Frankly [it should] implement commitments that the premier made at the national cabinet meeting earlier this year. Gus’s parents, Josh Lamont and Jess Murray, have spoken in a video shown by police. Williams said Gus was “learning so much and had such a bright future ahead of him”: He should have celebrated his fifth birthday and his little brother’s first birthday with us. Lamont thanked family, friends, the community and those who were part of the search for Gus, and said: We believe someone knows something. Someone knows what happened to Gus.
