headline: John Green got an astronomical following from his books. What came next? ‘I’m still competing for clicks’
trail_text: Returning with his first-ever adult novel, the bestselling author reflects on fame, YouTube and his brother’s AI controversy
body_text: By his mid-30s, John Green had done pretty well for himself. His debut novel, Looking for Alaska, had won a prestigious award for young adult literature. He and his brother, Hank, had launched a popular YouTube channel, where they regularly posted videos about their lives. With their combined incomes, Green and his wife were able to cobble together a living, buying a house and starting a family in Indianapolis. And then, in 2012, he published The Fault in Our Stars. “The week that book came out, it sold more copies than all of my previous books had sold in hardcover combined,” Green recalled in a recent interview with the Guardian podcast Stateside with Kai and Carter. “Up until that moment, I’d been very cavalier about sharing my life online and offline, and it was only in the wake of that that I started to realize the cost of that. People started coming to our house, sometimes quite late at night. We had young kids – babies – back then. People don’t always have the best boundaries.” The Fault in Our Stars follows the story of Hazel, a 16-year-old living with cancer, who falls in love with a fellow cancer patient. Powered in part by Green’s online fandom, the book sold more than 20m copies – enough for every person in the state of New York to have a copy, and then some. In 2014, Hollywood adapted it into a movie starring Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort. After the film became a blockbuster, raking in more than $300m at the global box office, Hollywood started adapting Green’s other books, too. Today, Green is as famous as an author can probably get. He has published another young adult novel and two nonfiction books – all of which also became bestsellers. His YouTube channel with Hank, Vlogbrothers, now has north of 4 million subscribers. The brothers have posted about practically every topic imaginable, from giraffe mating to presidential tax platforms to what it feels like to spend 15 hours in a Target. But he remains decidedly ambivalent about his popularity. It doesn’t feel nourishing, he said. It feels like empty calories. “It was uncomfortable to talk about, because how do you not be grateful for this overwhelmingly wonderful thing in your life?” Green said. “I have a friend who’s a very successful author, and I remember she said to me once: ‘Of all the good things that ever happened to me, fame was the worst.’ I think that’s a pretty good way to think about it.” Green decided to work through his mixed feelings in his new book, Hollywood, Ending. Released this week, the book follows two young actors who make a movie about Andy Warhol, fall in love, and try to stay sane as they sell pieces of themselves to the internet and the Hollywood publicity machine. It’s Green’s first novel in nearly a decade, and his first-ever for adults. But it still feels like a classic John Green book – thanks, predominantly, to its ardent belief that art, and other people, can help us survive anything. In an era in which more and more people must market themselves on social media, courting the dizzying highs and crushing lows of fame, Green still hopes we’ll find something better. I spoke with Green about the moral complexity of the attention economy, what he wishes he had done differently as a pioneering YouTuber and his brother Hank’s recent AI controversy. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. Watch the Stateside podcast episode in full here. CS: This book is so much about fame and the various machines that create and perpetuate celebrity culture: journalists, social media, movie studios. Why was this something you wanted to write about? JG: It used to be that this was a question mostly for celebrities, mostly for actors and to a lesser extent novelists. Now, it is a question for everyone because we all participate in this attention economy. We all transform our private lives into publicly consumable goods, whether that’s posting about our dog’s death on Facebook or our marriage on Reddit or whatever. These questions about how best to handle the publicization of one’s private life are no longer rarefied. I guess the overriding question was: is it worth it to make art in an age where art will inevitably be so commodified and will cost us so much in the making? I feel like the moment your fame really kicked into a different gear was with the publication of The Fault in Our Stars in 2012. When did you realize: “Wow, I have really hit something new here?” I remember I was on the road for about a month touring. I got home, and I called my agent and I said: “When does this end?” And she said: “You don’t really choose.” How did you feel in that moment? Both excited and trapped, which I think is the nature of celebrity a little bit – that it’s exciting and also claustrophobic. You have a choice about how public to make your life. You don’t really have a choice about the public’s response to that. On the other hand, it was wonderful to have the book reaching so many millions of people. Living with all that at the same time was both exciting and challenging, like it is for the young people in Hollywood, Ending. It’s much harder for them because I was 35 years old and married and had kids and the foundational relationships in my life were pretty set. When this happens when you’re 22, as it happens to a lot of people, whether they’re influencers or actors, you often don’t have those relationships. It can be really disorienting. It sounds to me like you’re saying: “This thing that was happening around my house, around my family, that was more real.” Why did the excitement around the book feel unreal? I don’t think it ever feels real, to be honest with you. I think it always feels like that’s happening to someone else. One of the things that [Andy] Warhol saw coming is that people don’t really see famous people as people. They see them as both more than people and less than people. They objectify them in every imaginable way. They feel free to comment on their bodies, they feel free to comment on their work as if they weren’t people, and so on. The other thing is that I wanted really badly to be successful. I think I wanted much more than would be healthy to be successful. I had no concept of what it would actually feel like. It was really rewarding to have so many people respond to the books and the story so generously. But the fame part of fame was quite empty. Why did you want fame in the first place? I don’t think I was liked very much in middle school. I really struggled with making friends. I thought that if I was famous, then everyone would be my friend and like me. That turns out to be a little bit of an oversimplification. A lot of people don’t like you, right? The nature of being famous is that everybody has an opinion about you, but not everybody has a positive opinion about you. That’s one thing that I hadn’t really thought very hard about. The other thing is that compliments simply don’t penetrate. I believe people in the abstract when they say that my work has been helpful to them or that it has been meaningful for them, and I’m extremely grateful for that. I don’t want to disbelieve them because that would dishonor the gift that they’ve given me by investing in my work and by bringing their deepest selves to it. But the criticism just penetrates in a different way. I believe it, because deep down there’s something about me that believes I don’t deserve any of this and I’m an impostor and I’m not a very good writer. You and your brother Hank have been creating videos for YouTube since 2007. How do you feel about your legacy as a pioneer of the social internet? Hank and I try really hard to do interesting, useful, fun, meaningful stuff in online spaces that build community and also make the world suck less. I hope that we’ve been able to do some of that. But there’s no question that just participating in an algorithmically generated internet is morally complex. You’re competing with Mr Beast for clicks. Even if I’m making an educational video that’s intended for high school students to be able to understand US history or physics or organic chemistry or whatever, I’m still competing for clicks with people who will do or say literally anything for clicks. Do you think, feeling the way you feel now about the social internet, you would have started making YouTube videos if you had to do it all over again? I’d do it again because it’s been an amazing experience and it’s been such a gift in my life. I might do it without my face in the videos, to be honest with you. That’s the big difference. A lot of my educational video friends don’t have their faces in their videos, and I find that admirable. But so much of the community you build is, frankly, parasocial. Yeah, it is. It is face-based. It’s hard to imagine not doing it that way. Actually, the time when Hank and I both realized that we weren’t actually in control of what we share was when Hank got cancer a couple years ago. We realized one of two things was gonna happen. One: Hank was going to, for the first time in 20 years, take eight months away from making Vlogbrothers videos without an explanation. Or, two: he was going to be forced to talk about having cancer in public. Hank ended up dealing with it beautifully by not just talking about having cancer, but by sort of science-communicating his way through cancer treatment, which is a very Hank Green thing to do. What do you make of the fact that in the age of the social internet, so many people, particularly young people, really just wanna be famous? The fame itself is a goal. Not only is the fame itself a goal, fame has become so decoupled from wealth that no longer is fame a guarantee of financial security. I have a friend, for example, who was a famous TikToker and also worked at the Gap. People would come to the Gap where they worked and be like: “Why are you working?” They would be like: “For money. Because this is where I work.” I suspect that young people want to be famous for the same reason I wanted public attention, which is that I thought it would fill a hole inside of me. What fills the hole is real connection, which is the relationships that are gonna sustain you through everything you have to survive. It’s interesting that you’re saying this. In an interview you did last year with the New York Times, you talked about feeling like people believe the internet fills a hole – but then, you didn’t really want to tell young people not to try to use the internet to heal themselves. I’m wondering if you have different advice for young people now. It’s so hard. I’m going through this now with one of my godchildren, where when you don’t have the relationships that you want to have in your community because you’re different – as I was – or because your interests are too niche or whatever it is, you find connection online. I was part of the first generation of people who found that, in 1993 on CompuServe. It was revelatory, to be able to not be stuck inside of a body that was frail and embarrassing and full of failure, and instead to be this creature online where I could really connect with people. Some of the people I connected with, I’m still connected to. I’m so grateful for that. Yet at the same time, it can’t replace what we experience with real life connection. I do feel a little differently than I did a year or two ago. I do think we have to build meaningful relationships with each other in meat space, as they say online. I think it’s very helpful to be reminded that my body is made out of meat, that even the thinking parts are made out of meat. It’s very easy online to lose track of the fact that you’re a mammal. You’re much, much, much closer to being a squirrel than you are to being an artificial intelligence. I feel like in the book and in this conversation, you are suggesting that fame is corrosive to us and that the online attention economy is not good for us. But having a social media platform, having a personal brand, being on camera – that is all stuff that more and more people just have to engage with, not in order to necessarily be famous, but to have a professional life. How are we supposed to move forward? What the book concludes, I hope, is that we have to seize the reins of power and understand that we have more power than we think we have as internet citizens, as creators online. I remember suddenly becoming conscious on the set of The Fault in Our Stars that everyone cared what I thought. The reason they cared what I thought was not because I’m an incredibly compelling person, but because I had millions of followers on Twitter and at any moment I could blow up the movie. Understanding that with the sacrifices involved in participating in the social internet – there is also an exchange of power. Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk don’t have all the power, as evidenced by the declining role of X in society. They have a lot of power. They have too much power. Way, way, way too much power. But, combined, we have more. Hollywood, Ending is to some extent about how much you have to feed the content beasts in order to succeed. So I did want to ask about a recent dust-up that Hank was involved in, where he was accused of using AI to write part of a script for a video. He addressed the controversy. He said that AI did not write the script but admitted to relying on AI more and more to research his work. That’s honestly understandable to me, because he really produces a lot. Hank suggested that you and he had spoken and that you had some criticism of his AI use. Are you comfortable telling me about those criticisms? Yeah, it’s more than being critical of his AI use in particular. I have my own opinions. I don’t use LLMs and don’t see a need to use them in my work. It was more about the fact of what you just said, which is Hank makes a lot of stuff. I think especially in the last couple of years, Hank has been obsessively trying to get everything in his head out into the world and I think that is not healthy. We’ve had that conversation and that’s part of being a brother. Hank’s had those conversations with me many times before. Trying to get everything out of your head seems like a pretty reasonable response to a bad health scare. Yeah, I think it is a reasonable response to mortality. I think the more reasonable response – not that I’m here to lecture my brother – is to invest in your core relationships. You have expressed mixed feelings about people seeing too much of you in the art you make. I have spent this interview very much reading you into Hollywood, Ending. How do you feel about that? You haven’t read into it in a way that makes me uncomfortable, so I feel fine about it. There are other things you could have read into it that would have bothered me. It’s uncomfortable to be read into the book because I don’t want to be a character in the book. I have written two nonfiction books now and six novels, and writing fiction is so much more vulnerable and intimate than writing nonfiction. Why is it more vulnerable? It just is. Because I have to go to deeper places within me. I have to go to places that nobody else knows about, not even the people closest to me. That’s really hard work, but it’s good work because I’m asking the reader to do the same. I’m asking them to bring their deepest selves to the story, to bring their own particular traumas and fears and loves and losses to the story in a way that no one else can. That’s asking a lot. So I have to do the work on the other side to make that worth it. Hopefully. Hollywood, Ending by John Green is out now via Dutton Books

headline: UK economic outlook brighter as new government measures will boost growth, says OECD – as it happened
trail_text: Oil prices reverse earlier declines to rise above $100 a barrel again
body_text: Wall Street shares have fallen moderately and government bond yields rose, as crude oil prices reversed earlier falls and rose above $100 a barrel again. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, has been on a rollercoaster today and is now up 2.5% at $101.61, a gain of $2.3 a barrel, after five days of declines. Chip-related companies saw their shares slide, with AMD down 2.1%, Nvidia losing 1.1% and Intel 3.2% lower. Meta Platforms shares rose 1.3%, adding to its 10% plus jump this week as its new personal AI agent Muse has been a hit. Over here, the FTSE 100 index in London is holding on to modest gains, trading 0.25% higher at 10,736. Other major European indices are trading lower. Our main stories today: Thank you for reading. We’ll be back tomorrow. Take care ! – JK Business growth in the US has picked up to its fastest pace in more than five years and hiring also rose sharply in September, while price pressures also intensified. The composite PMI output index from S&P Global, a closely-watched monthly survey, rose to 58.4 from 56 in August. The services business activity rose to 58.7 from 56.5 while the manufacturing output index leapt to 56.7 from 53.1. Any reading above 50 indicates expansion. Employment rose sharply, with jobs added at a pace not seen for over four years, as firms sought to meet rising demand. Backlogs of work continued to rise at an increased rate and supply chain delays intensified, pointing to a lack of operating capacity which fed through to higher prices. Input costs surged on the back of the recent spike in energy prices, adding to a worsening inflation picture. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said: US business continues to boom, with output growing at the fastest rate for over five years in September. Historical comparisons suggest that the latest survey data point to annualized growth of around 5% with a 4% gain now signalled for the third quarter as a whole. To put the growth surge in context, barring the spike in demand following the opening up of the economy after the COVID-19 lockdowns, the latest improvement in business activity is the greatest recorded since early 2015. Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services. However, this growth is being accompanied by some of the most severe supply chain bottlenecks seen in the near-two-decade survey history if the pandemic is excluded, with companies also reporting increasing problems finding suitable staff. Backlogs of work are consequently rising sharply. While this accumulation of uncompleted orders bodes well for the further expansion of output and capacity in the coming months, it also indicates that companies are developing more pricing power, and hence is a worry for the inflation outlook. Firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices seen during the month, which will add further to the upward pressure on selling prices and inflation in the coming months. Air fares in Europe will rise “dramatically” next summer, by as much as 10%-20%, Ryanair has forecast, with airlines unable to absorb continued high oil prices. Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary said a lack of refinery capacity meant jet fuel was likely to stay 40% higher than crude oil, and predicted several airlines could go bust this winter. He said Ryanair itself would trim its capacity in the coming months, sending fares upwards, to avoid the high cost of unhedged fuel, around 20% of its fuel needs. He added: If I was planning a holiday I’d be booking [flights] today. There is only one way air fares in Europe are going next summer and that is dramatically upwards. Speaking at a press conference in London, O’Leary repeated his calls for the sacking of Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, after the latest outages of air traffic control services in September. He said Ryanair was calling for “urgent reform of failing UK Nats. What we mean by urgent reform: sack Martin Rolfe.” The government has tasked the CAA to investigate Nats’ explanations for the major outage on 8 September, blaming a “millisecond’s software fault” for disruption to hundreds of thousands of passengers’ flights. The CAA is due to report next March. O’Leary said: We don’t need six months to learn lessons. The fundamental lesson to learn about Nats is it has an incompetent, overpaid CEO who needs to be dismissed. He said Ryanair’s costs had run to 4-5million euros, and the airline was still seeking compensation in court for the 2023 Nats outage. O’Leary meanwhile addressed his own recent €150m bonus deal, which was opposed by 40% of shareholders at Ryanair’s AGM this month. He said they would be consulting with shareholders to understand their concerns, but would not be changing the terms. Asked if it was a pointless consultation, he agreed and said “Welcome to the world of ESG,” [environmental, social, and governance rules]. The price of gold and other precious metals has fallen, under pressure from ⁠a stronger dollar and ⁠hawkish remarks from US Federal Reserve officials that reinforced expectations of near-term interest rate hikes. Spot gold fell 1.2% to $4,303 an ounce, while silver dropped 3% to $65.05 an ounce, platinum lost 2.8% to $1,779 and palladium declined 2.1% to $1,279. The dollar rose to its strongest level in two months, as traders priced in a 53% chance of an interest rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch Tool. Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin said on Tuesday that rate hikes could temper business inflation expectations and cool price increases without slowing down economic activity. The Fed last week lifted its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% – its first rate rise since 2023 – and ‌signalled another increase could come before year-end. Although gold is seen as a hedge against inflation, rising interest rates can reduce its attractiveness as investors pivot towards interest-bearing assets. On the geopolitical front, Donald Trump warned yesterday that he could “annihilate” Iran if there is no deal to end the war, ⁠but also suggested an agreement could come soon amid a diplomatic push at the United Nations general assembly in New York. BMI analysts said: In the long term beyond 2026, we expect gold prices to ease. The main driver of easing gold prices in the ‌long term will be greater risk-on sentiment as the global economy recovers in the later part of the decade. When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors. The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics. Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.” One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of ⁠OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a ⁠state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening. ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’ In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement. Young people are now now “waiting for promotions to come” rather than looking out for trainer brands’ latest footwear launches, the boss of JD Sports has said, as the retailer’s core customers remaiun under pressure from rising unemployment and an increase in the cost of living. Half-year sales at the group fell 0.8%, excluding exchange rate fluctuations, to £5.9bn, led by a 4% drop at established stores in North America where food prices have soared. Sales were down 3.3% in Europe and 1.4% in the UK as JD’s chief executive Régis Schultz said retailers around the world were having to discount sports footwear to clear stock having not recognised that the market was maturing as shoppers reined in spending and the global shift from wearing leather shoes to trainers had worked its way through. He said average selling prices were down in both the UK and Europe as shoppers were waiting for promotions to come. Three years ago customers were looking for a new launch, now they are looking for a new promotion and that’s having a negative impact on the industry. He said UK sales had been better than elsewhere as young people were buying more performance sportswear as “running clubs are the new nightclubs” and he said JD was rapidly adapting by adding more clothing in the US, including own-label, and bringing in new brands such as On and Salomon in footwear as the bigger brands such as Nike face new competition. Schultz called on the UK government to cut the cost of employing young people and to maintain flexibility on short-hours contracts as he said former chancellor Rachel Reeves’ increase on National Insurance contributions for employers and increase in the minimum wage for under 21s had been “really a wrong movement” and only pushed retailers to use more technology and hire fewer young people. While he said JD did not use self checkouts, he added: The more the cost of labour increases and the less flexibility [on working hours] the more retailers are inclined to invest in technology. Have a look at our visualisation of London buses, which have become slower and fewer in recent years. This is, unfortunately a global trend. As experts fear for future of UK capital’s bus network, some commuters are giving up entirely. London is not alone – with worrying implications for the poorest in society. A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange. Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures. The company is understood to be looking to raise about $800m (£601m) from the IPO and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to 9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years. Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year. Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately. Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao, said: From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future. We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here. Ferrao added: Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically. Legal & General has confirmed that it is cutting 1,000 jobs, with a voluntary-first approach in the UK, and excluding asset management. António Simões, the chief executive, said in an email to employees as he announced the voluntary redundancy programme: Over the past two and a half years, we have made significant progress executing our strategy, simplifying L&G, establishing three core businesses, and creating a more focused business. However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be. To deliver our strategy successfully, we now need to make sure the way we work reflects the business we are becoming. Across L&G, we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation. By the middle of next year, we expect to reduce the size of our organisation by around 1,000 roles. An L&G spokesperson said: Since 2024, L&G has become a simpler, more focused business. These changes represent the next stage of that transformation, ensuring that our organisation and ways of working reflect the business we are now building and the rapidly changing environment in which we operate. They will also help us focus our resources and investment on the areas where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term growth. We recognise and take seriously the impact on colleagues and are committed to supporting our people throughout the process and consulting with our unions. The British insurance and pensions firm Legal & General reportedly wants to cut 1,000 jobs by the middle of next year, amounting to a tenth of of its workforce. António Simões, the chief executive, is wielding the axe as he tries to simplify the company’s operations. The London-headquartered firm has kicked off a plan to eliminate about 1,000 roles by mid-2027, according to an email sent to employees on Wednesday seen by Bloomberg News. The programme will initially be voluntary redundancies in the UK but L&G will consider mandatory cuts depending on take-up, Bloomberg said, citing a source. The investment management division, which oversees £1.2 trillion in assets, is excluded as it already has its own restructuring plan underway. The Co-op has called on Andy Burnham’s government to “create an environment where we have confidence and certainty to invest” which it needs to support “lifeline stores” in urban and rural communities across the UK. Kate Allum, the interim chief executive of the mutual who stepped in after the unexpected departure of Shirine Khoury-Haq last year, said: We have no intention of closing any lifeline stores. We have a big estate and we want to continue to invest but what we need is confidence. We don’t want unintended consequences of decisions. The Co-op’s losses widened by £13m to £45m in the six months to 4 July, but the grocery retailer, funerals and insurance business said the step up was largely due to an accounting change. It said losses had not improved after last year’s cyber attack as it had been forced to invest in lowering prices and offering promotions to tempt back shoppers it lost when shelves lay empty for several weeks after the hack. Sales for the group rose 2.4% to £5.6bn led by growth in funeralcare and financial services while grocery sales increased 2.4%, behind the pace of inflation. Allum said the Co-op was optimistic about the second half of the year as the group had now regained sales momentum and won new members but she said consumer confidence is pretty uncertain. We talk to our members all the time and the cost of living has been their number one concern for a significant period of time. The pound has dipped below $1.33 this morning, as the dollar has strengthened against a number of currencies, on the back of expectations of interest rate hikes in the US. Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at the global financial services firm Ebury, said: The pound has sunk below 1.33 against the US dollar this morning, as investors prioritise hawkish Fed rhetoric and the upward repricing in US rates over any tailwinds to the UK economy from this week’s drop in global oil prices. The Bank of England has, of course, also placed outsized importance on the energy crisis for the path of its policy rate - suggesting that any hikes would be effectively contingent on a continuation of the conflict - so the recent pullback in oil prices should undercut the case for hikes just as much as it offers relief to UK growth. Today’s business activity PMI figures were a bit of a disappointment, as while the manufacturing index ticked upwards modestly (52.0 from 51.7), growth in the far more important services sector sector (51.7 from 52.5) slowed more than anticipated. Growth in Britain’s economy has been remarkably resilient so far this year, though we think that a slowdown is almost inevitable during the remainder of the year - energy costs have risen, borrowing costs are up, the jobs market continues to weaken and political uncertainty looks set to rear its ugly head again as we approach budget day next month. We expect this to keep sterling under pressure in the near-term, though we do contend that GBP/USD appears a bit oversold at current levels. Meanwhile, the latest PMI survey shows business activity in the UK eased this month, while inflationary pressures picked up. The flash UK composite output index fell to 51.7 in September from 52.5 in August, a three-month low. There was a loss of momentum in both the services and manufacturing sectors. The rate of input price inflation accelerated for the second month running to its highest since June. Companies pointed to increased energy, fuel and raw material costs. Service providers noted that subdued domestic economic conditions and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty were factors that held back business activity growth in September, although some firms again cited a boost in demand for technology services. AI investment and greater defence spending were highlighted as factors supporting manufacturing production, while weak consumer demand acted as a constraint. Total new work across the private sector fell slightly in September, which contrasted with marginal growth during July and August. This mostly reflected a renewed downturn in new business volumes at service sector companies. They talked of weak business and consumer confidence, in part due to pressures on discretionary spending amid the ongoing cost of living crisis. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said: September is seeing a worrying combination of disappointingly sluggish economic growth and intensifying inflationary pressures, with subdued business confidence and high costs meanwhile continuing to discourage hiring. Output growth across the manufacturing and services PMI surveys has slowed to a pace consistent with the economy growing at a mere 0.1% quarterly rate. Growth, business confidence and employment are all being hamstrung by high energy prices, elevated business costs, geopolitical worries, higher market borrowing costs and uncertainty over government policy at home in the run up to the autumn Budget. While the upturn in the survey’s price gauges suggest the Bank of England looks likely to keep a hawkish bias, the worryingly lacklustre pace of business growth underscores the risk to the economy from higher borrowing costs. The outlook for the UK economy has brightened, according to the Paris-based OECD, with inflation lower than expected while new government support measures are likely to boost growth. The think tank has significantly cut its inflation forecast for this year, from 3.7% to 3.1%, after prices rose less dramatically than expected. Economic growth for the UK is forecast at 1.1% for 2026, up from the 0.9% it had forecast in June and 0.7% in March, “with consumption expected to be supported by newly announced government support measures”. In response, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said: Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience. We will face these challenges together and we are already giving families space to breathe. We had the fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of the year and we are starting the big, long-term changes needed to create good jobs and growth in every postcode. Andy Burnham, who became the UK prime minister on 20 July, announced a cut in VAT on electricity bills as one of his first policy measures on coming to power in July, and has suggested there may be more measures to give consumers “breathing space” in next month’s budget. Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have seen UK borrowing costs rise sharply amid turmoil in global bond markets as ongoing conflicts have disrupted the oil supplies, driving up inflation. The world’s advanced economies have been warned they need to take action to reduce their borrowing and bring down debt levels, at a time of surging government borrowing costs, according to the head of the International Monetary Fund. Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC that global economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven” despite governments taking “no action to contain that service cost. [It’s] time to take that action,” Georgieva said, adding that courage was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps. The global economy has withstood the strains of the Iran war better than first feared but its outlook is “heavily dependent” on a lasting resolution to the conflict, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has warned. In its interim economic outlook, the Paris-based body suggested global growth had been more resilient than expected when the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February. The OECD on Wednesday pointed to the release of global oil stockpiles, a sharp decline in energy imports by China and the switch to other fuels including coal as factors helping to cushion the economic impact of limited Gulf oil supplies. However, it warned that the recent resurgence in oil and gas prices posed risks for the coming months. Global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved. In its quarterly forecast update, the OECD said it expects global economic growth to be 2.9% this year – a modest 0.1 percentage point upgrade from the 2.8% it forecast in June. At the same time it has trimmed the outlook for next year slightly, from 3.1%, to 3%. Oil prices fell back below $100 a barrel on Tuesday amid hopes of a potential agreement between the US and Iran, but the continued standoff between the two sides has sent energy costs soaring in recent weeks. The OECD warned that while more oil supplies were expected to resume as hostilities eased, “renewed or more persistent disruptions could result in both higher inflation and weaker growth”. The Paris-based organisation also identified the record-breaking El Niño weather system – expected to be the strongest in 1,000 years – as a “significant downside risk” to the global economy, warning that it could hit agricultural production and push up food prices. Other such risks include a further increase in the yields, or interest rates, on government bonds, which have risen in response to fears of higher inflation, and a loss of market confidence in the value of AI companies. The OECD said AI investment has helped to offset wider economic weakness, especially in the US economy. In the United States, countervailing forces are at work, with strong underlying momentum and further expansion of AI investment, but consumer spending that is increasingly constrained by declining purchasing power, softer labour force growth and depleted household savings. In the eurozone as a whole, private sector output growth hit a three-and-a-half year high in September, helped by the ramp-up in AI and defence spending, according to the latest PMI survey. The flash reading from S&P Global showed output rose at the fastest pace since April 2023 amid solid expansions in both the series and manufacturing sectors, reflecting high new orders. The composite output index rose to 53.1 in September from 52 in August, indicating faster growth. Any reading above 50 points to expansion. The services index jumped to 53 from 51.6, marking a 10-month high, while the manufacturing index edged up to 53.4 from 53.3, a four-and-a-half-year high. However, the rate of job creation remained muted as confidence in the year-ahead outlook eased to a three-month low. Rates of input cost and output price inflation were the strongest since May. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said: It’s no surprise to see inflationary pressures on the rise again in September, given the increase in energy prices emanating from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, but more encouraging is the resilience of economic growth being reported. Accelerating business growth means the flash PMI survey is indicative of GDP rising at a quarterly rate of 0.4%, with order book growth picking up further momentum across both manufacturing and services in September to hint at sustained momentum heading into the fourth quarter. Manufacturing, spearheaded by Germany, is enjoying its best growth spell for over four years, spurred by rising AI and defence spending, but service sector growth is also perking up to signal a broad-based improvement in the economic growth story. The rate of job creation remains subdued as business confidence continues to be dampened by caution over geopolitics, notably the ongoing impact on energy prices and the cost of living. However, employment has edged higher again in September, up for a second month, to suggest more companies are returning to the jobs market. The resilience of economic growth amid the headwinds of geopolitical issues and rising prices will likely embolden the European Central Bank to hike interest rates again before the end of the year, adding to the case for rates to rise sooner rather than later to put an October hike very much on the table. The picture also brightened in Germany, Europe’s largest economy. Businesses in Germany recorded a “solid and accelerated increase” in output of goods and services at the end of the third quarter, according to the latest PMI survey from S&P Global. This was despite firms reporting increased inflationary pressures, which they linked in large part to the rising price of fuel. The flash composite output index for September rose 53.8 from 51.8 in August, an 11-month high. The services business activity index increased to 52.9 from 49.7, a seven-month high and above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction. The manufacturing output index eased to 55.9 from 56.6, a two-month low, but stayed well above the 50 mark. Phil Smith, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said: German businesses reported further signs of resilience in September, with output growth picking up speed, expectations towards the outlook holding steady and employment rising for a second month running, all despite renewed pressure on the inflation front. The flash data pointed to the strongest rise in business activity for almost a year, with the service sector finally rejoining manufacturing in growth territory after a quieter period that followed the outbreak of the Middle East war. Rising inflows of new work were starting to put pressure on business capacity, however, as underlined by the accumulation of backlogged orders, which in turn helped strengthen labour market conditions. So far, recent job creation has been confined to the service sector, but factory employment continued to show signs of stabilising as goods producers reported rising levels of work-in-hand and greater optimism towards future output. In France, private sector activity bounced back in September, and rose at the fastest pace in more than two years. The first of the flash purchasing managers’ index (PMI) reports from S&P Global for September showed a strengthening of the eurozone’s second-biggest economy at the end of the third quarter as activity growth returned. The composite output index, measuring service and manufacturing activity, rose to 51.2 from 48.5 in August. Any reading above 50 points to expansion. This was driven by the services sector, where the business activity index jumped to 51.4 from 48, a 10-month high. The manufacturing PMI dipped to 50.3 from 51.1. Demand improved, reflecting rising sales activity in the service sector, although employment continued to decline and business optimism weakened further. Joe Hayes, senior principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said The French economy displayed surprising resilience in September, although the durability of this expansion is questionable given new orders barely rose and firms’ own expectations for activity deteriorated. There may also be some payback driving the uplift after the extreme heat seen in August disrupted some business activities, particularly in the service sector. Nevertheless, these data reinforce the narrative that European economies are weathering the war-induced inflation shock well. The pick-up in the PMI price measures seen in September should however be watched closely, particularly as we approach the winter months, as the risk of energy price inflation spreading to other areas of the economy undoubtedly rises. Input and output prices both rose at quicker rates for the first time since May as rising cost pressures were passed on to clients, the survey showed. The world’s advanced economies have been warned they need to “take action” to reduce their borrowing and bring down debt levels, at a time of surging government borrowing costs, according to the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC that global economic shocks have been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven”, and that governments have been taking “no action to contain that service cost”. “[It’s] time to take that action,” Georgieva said, adding that “courage” was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps. Her comments come at a time governments, including the UK and US, have seen their borrowing costs soar as ongoing global conflicts have disrupted the oil supply, driving up inflation. Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. Oil prices have fallen for a sixth session, dropping further below $100 a barrel on reports of increased supply from the Middle East, and amid hopes of progress in talks between the US and Iran. Several Asian stock markets have risen for a sixth session with the exception of Chinese indices, riding high on the artificial intelligence wave. Brent crude is down about $1 at $98.32 a barrel, after closing below $100 a barrel yesterday for the first time in more than two weeks. If the downward move is sustained over the day, the six-day declines would be the longest losing run for oil since August 2025, according to Bloomberg. Reuters reported, citing sources, that Saudi Arabia has restarted operations at its east-west pipeline and may have already resumed exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. Donald Trump talked of progress in talks with Iran in New York, but also threatened to “annihilate” the country if there was no deal. Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian addresses the UN general assembly later today and according to reports may meet with the US president. Chinese president Xi Jinping arrives in Washington later today for talks with Trump, with speculation a trade truce between the US and China will be extended, and hopes that they can agree a cooperation deal over AI. Trump commented on AI in his speech at the UN yesterday, calling it “super intelligence” and rejecting any attempts to control it. He said: I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution. The buzz around AI has lifted technology stocks and helped South Korea’s Kospi gain nearly 0.7% while the Taiwan stock market rose 0.75%. Japanese markets are closed for the silver holiday. China’s CSI 300 fell 0.5%. European and US stock futures are pointing to a higher open. There has been strong uptake of Meta’s new personal Muse agent, which has sat at the top of US app download charts since its launch a fortnight ago. The dollar has climbed to a two-month high on expectations of interest rate hikes soon. Sterling dipped 0.2% to $1.3316 while the euro eased to its weakest level since July, falling 0.2% to $1.1423. headline: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s approval rating: ‘somewhere between Ebola and Ed Sheeran’
trail_text: Late-night hosts discussed the decreasing popularity of the US president and how his latest attack on the press continues to backfire
body_text: Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump’s disastrous approval rating and his latest rambling speech at the UN. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host spoke about Trump’s new all-time low approval rating which is “somewhere between Ebola and Ed Sheeran” at just 29%. “If that number goes any lower, he’s gonna have to leave Melania for it,” he joked. This week has seen the president banning CNN and MS Now from press briefings leading to other stations suspending coverage in protest. The lack of coverage has made him “even crazier than he already is” as there is “nothing he loves more” than being on TV. His “dumb actions” have now meant that the only camera in the White House is a “ring camera that Melania has mounted on her bedroom door to keep him out of it”. The week also saw him meet with new UK prime minister Andy Burnham who was “visibly uncomfortable” as Trump bragged about his “very petty new attack on freedom of the press”. But Trump’s minions have been trying to defend his actions, from JD Vance to rightwing TV pundits. Kimmel said that it’s “increasingly difficult for these hand puppets of Trump to explain the unexplainable”. In response to the show of media solidarity that has led to Trump being removed from TV screens, he has started a “state-run media network” called Trump TV on YouTube. It started with just 8,000 viewers, which Kimmel joked that Trump will say means “bigger ratings than the final episode of Friends”. The quality is also “spotty and weak just like the president”. Kimmel also called Trumps’s UN speech “a rough, threatening, ugly ramble” that saw him brag about renaming artificial intelligence “super intelligence”. The host said that “his legacy will be renaming things that did not need to be renamed”. Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers spoke about Trump’s ribbon-cutting event at the White House this week, which had no audio as there was no press pool coverage thanks to his ban. “You really need to learn how to project,” Meyers said as advice to the president. Meyers said that even though we couldn’t hear what was being said, he was “either bragging or lying” and that we should “use the media as a baby monitor” when trying to check his emotional state. Meyers also spoke about Trump’s embrace of AI, showing a picture that the president posted of himself as the pope. “We shouldn’t be building datacenters, we should be building assisted living facilities,” he said. This week also saw Trump breaking with convention by endorsing Irish unification. “When isn’t he breaking with decades of US precedent?” the host asked.

headline: My (complicated) relationship with AI: often seductive, occasionally frustrating and always demanding vigilance
trail_text: As a multilingual academic, artificial intelligence has levelled the playing field. But I will continue to think, judge and develop ideas that are stubbornly mine
body_text: I am walking between carriages in search of a cup of tea on a train travelling over 100 miles an hour from Liverpool to London when I see half the people in my carriage in deep conversations with a machine: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to name a few. I am meant to be on sabbatical, the rare stretch of academic life reserved for slow thinking. Around me, almost nobody is thinking slowly. This is not limited to a train carriage. Half of the adults surveyed in one US study reported using an AI chatbot, one example of how fast people are entering a relationship with their AI tools, which now receive more of our questions, problems and drafts than our friends and colleagues do. I am one of them; I research advanced technologies for a living. I sceptically entered this relationship to satisfy my curiosity, and my very first request of ChatGPT was to proofread an email. The second was to plan a four-day holiday, and the third was to compare home loans. I sent that AI-proofread email, took that short holiday, and refinanced our mortgage with a better rate – all based on its advice. The relationship started growing and I started giving it more complicated tasks: summarise an article, collate recent findings on a specific topic and redesign my kitchen. What would have taken hours took only minutes. I trusted nothing and checked every line, as trust in any relationship accrues exchange by exchange. I did not like the kitchen design it produced. I was not alone; in an experiment published in Science, professionals using AI completed their writing tasks 40% faster and produced writing rated 18% higher in quality. The most interesting finding for me from the experiment sat silently in the middle: inequality between workers decreased. That hit close to home. English is my second language, and for years I paid copywriters thousands of dollars to proofread and smooth my drafts. These were outsiders with no knowledge of my field or the experience behind my arguments. Now it takes minutes, at any hour of the day, and at a fraction of the cost. For a multilingual academic, it is more than just convenience. It is the levelling of a field that was never level; it is workplace equity. The relationship is not rosy; at times it is unsettling and frustrating. The most seductive quality of AI is not its speed to produce lines of code, summarise meetings or synthesise complex patterns. It is its agreeableness and flattery, or what researchers call “sycophancy”, a phenomenon undermining self-correction and responsible decision-making. In a spectacular failure, investor Jason Lemkin watched an AI coding agent on Replit wipe his company’s live database during a code freeze. The agent did apologise for its “catastrophic failure”, using words a genuinely remorseful person would use. In this case, the apology did not restore anything. Replit deployed the fixes and the relationship continued, with caution. Findings from medicine are more concerning. Endoscopists who used AI to detect polyps in colonoscopies saw their detection rate fall six percentage points when they performed the procedure without AI support. Each endoscopist in the study had more than 2,000 colonoscopies behind them; the authors call it deskilling. In my line of work, editors at one reputable journal looked in their own back yard and found submissions rising and review reports carrying signs of AI writing. They concluded that human judgment is still holding the line, although at the cost of greater effort. They also found researchers writing in a second language, and new entrants to the field, were among the heaviest users. I am one of them, and I know the difference between asking AI to carry my argument into English and asking it to supply one. AI and its agents are not disappearing, and there is no returning to the world before them. Our relationship with AI only deepens from here. Mine now proofreads and smooths out my writing and acts as my research and personal assistant, but it still does not know what my dream kitchen looks like. So, where am I landing? Not in a divorce and not in a honeymoon. A real partnership that is sometimes useful and equalising, occasionally tiring, and always demanding vigilance. One thing AI cannot yet do is care; it has no stake in whether I am right. It will argue any side with equal confidence and apologise for any disaster with equal grace. I keep thinking, judging and developing ideas that are and will be stubbornly mine. Like it or not, we are in a relationship with AI. What we need to ask ourselves is not whether to be in it; it is whether to stay awake inside it or watch our thinking, knowledge and skills decay. • Dr Setareh Seyedghorban is director of teaching, resources and planning, and senior lecturer of operations and supply chain management at the Department of Management and Marketing, Faculty of Business and Economics at the University of Melbourne

headline: Trump’s UN speech was delusional and dangerous
trail_text: It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president like Trump
body_text: Donald Trump’s speech on Tuesday to the United Nations general assembly was an object lesson in his lawless rule and remarkable capacity for self-delusion. Disregarding the UN charter’s emphasis on the peaceful resolution of disputes, he doubled down on his violent unilateralism while denigrating the global issues that the UN is designed to address. For many, the headline remark was his musing about whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” of Iran. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” But it was probably less a genuine threat than a clumsy effort to influence negotiations where he has little leverage. Trump is in desperate quest of some face-saving gesture that will allow him to feign “victory” and extract himself from his disastrous war of choice. He spoke of destroying the “Islamic Republic”, which might imply the Iranian military, a legitimate military target. But his reference to precluding future generations suggests he meant to threaten the Iranian people. Attacking them would be a blatant war crime. In July, he already vowed to destroy Iran’s bridges or power plants – itself a threat to commit war crimes. The international criminal court (ICC) has charged four Russian military commanders for doing precisely that in Ukraine. Trump didn’t even bother to offer a coherent rationale for his threat. Once more, he proclaimed: “I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.” But Tehran has long disavowed that goal. He claimed that other American presidents “just wanted to ignore” the issue. But Barack Obama negotiated a deal to constrain Iran’s ability to build a nuclear weapon. Trump ripped it up, preferring his utterly counterproductive military solution, which has brought Iran far closer to a nuclear weapon than ever before. Preposterously, Trump claimed, “when it comes to Iran,” the midterm election “doesn’t even enter my mind.” No one believes that. If the Republicans face the disastrous showing that the polls now predict, he knows the election will be seen as a repudiation of his arbitrary tariffs and Iran war which have fueled inflation and aggravated the affordability crisis that he belittles. Trump also spotlighted his other acts of aggression. He celebrated the seizure of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro, emphasizing how some political prisoners have now been freed, although hundreds remain. But while Trump lauded his coerced deal with Venezuela’s remaining autocratic leaders to take a large chunk of the country’s oil, he said nothing about a democratic future. Instead, touting his might-makes-right beliefs, he proclaimed: “To the victor belong the spoils.” He noted the new agreement on Greenland without mentioning his earlier threat to seize the territory by force even though it has long been administered by Denmark, a fellow Nato member. He raved about slaughtering drug suspects at sea, claiming they are “at war with civilization” and “should be killed … as enemy combatants”. But there is no real war, only a rhetorical one. Drug traffickers form a criminal cartel, not an organized force in armed conflict with the United States. They should be arrested and prosecuted, not summarily executed by drone. The killings are murders and arguably crimes against humanity. Many of the victims were on boats registered in Columbia or Venezuela – both at the time members of the ICC. That would give the court jurisdiction over these crimes, which may be why Trump reprised his attack on this important institution of justice. Trump wants to be restrained only by his own warped “morality”. It has been reported that Trump may soon supplement his sanctions against 13 ICC personnel – judges and prosecutors – with sanctions against the court as a whole. But that would only compound the criminality of his conduct, because retaliation against court personnel for the performance of their official duties is obstructing justice under article 70 of the court’s statute. Trump emphasized his role as a peacemaker. “I have made peace,” he declared, as he claimed to have “settle[d] eight wars”. Yet the reality is more complicated. He said he had “ended the war in Gaza”. In fact, despite the “ceasefire”, Israel’s continuing attacks continue to raise the death toll. Trump mentioned his 20-point peace plan for Gaza without noting that virtually none of it has been implemented. Israel continues to kill Palestinians and block needed supplies, while Hamas has not disarmed. He didn’t even bother to mouth the word “Palestinian”. Indeed, the Trump administration has rejected a leading candidate for the next UN secretary general because she has publicly recognized that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, suggesting that Trump will accept only future UN leaders who are willing to deny this reality. He claimed to have “contribute[d] to peace” between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, without noting that Rwanda’s M23 militia continues to occupy large swathes of eastern DRC. Trump seems fine with that, so long as the murderous M23 brings the region’s mineral riches to the western market. He claimed to be making progress in securing peace in Ukraine, without acknowledging his prior suggestion to reward Vladimir Putin’s aggression by having Ukraine not only cede territory already illegally occupied by Russia but to hand over additional chunks of its territory as well. Meanwhile, Trump belittled the problems that the UN, able to convene the world’s nations, is ideally suited to address. He called the existential threat of climate change a “hoax”. Ignoring the enormous risks posed by artificial intelligence, he attempted to relabel AI as “superintelligence” and derided efforts to regulate it as “globalist.” This week Trump meets with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping. Yet rather than outline the important issues to be addressed, Trump chose to self-promote: “We’re leading now over China by a lot”. Most would say only that Trump is leading in national embarrassment. It is sad and dangerous that at such a perilous moment, the United States is saddled with a president who excels mainly in disseminating self-promoting fantasies while flouting the most basic rules of decency. His UN speech put that all on painful display. Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

headline: Italian pop legend takes the lead in Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi collection
trail_text: Milan show full of diaphanous dresses and visible bras celebrates ‘incredible feminist’ of the 1970s, Raffaella Carrà
body_text: Maria Grazia Chiuri has been having more fun with clothes since she decamped from Paris back to her native Rome to work at Fendi. “I have less of a uniform these days. I think it is because being back here makes me feel young again. I’m not sure my daughter appreciates [this attitude]! But I don’t care,” she said at a preview before her Milan fashion week show. Not that Chiuri doesn’t approach her work as a designer seriously. She described her second ready-to-wear season at Fendi not as a show, or a collection, but as “the second part of the project I am working on for them”. She is continuing the protocol she developed as the designer of Dior of using each event as a platform to celebrate women’s creativity. But instead of a ceramicist or a philosopher, her muse for this season is the Italian pop legend Raffaella Carrà. Carrà, once described as a “one-woman Abba”, had a Lady Gaga bob and a taste for sequined catsuits. She caused a sensation with her raunchy outfits – the first bare midriff ever seen on Italian TV, in 1970 – and her sex-positive lyrics (her song A Far L’Amore Comincia Tu translates as “Take the lead when making love”). “She was an incredible feminist, and her relationship with her clothes was so free,” said Chiuri of Carrà, who died aged 78 in 2021. On the catwalk, Carrà’s influence became diaphanous 1970s dresses with trailing hems, visible lace bras, embroidered waistcoats and vintage fur stoles, while men’s shirts were unbuttoned to the navel. The biggest and starriest show of this Milan fashion week belonged not to any designer, but to Vogue. Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, Milan’s glass-domed cathedral to retail, became a catwalk for a line-up that included Jennifer Lopez in Dolce & Gabbana and Cardi B in vintage Versace, with the singer Alicia Keys and the ballet dancer Roberto Bolle performing live. Vogue is leaning into live events to amplify its brand and strengthen its coffers as print income declines. Vogue World Milano follows last year’s Vogue World: Hollywood in LA, which generated $30m (£23m) in revenue. Billed as a celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the human touch in fashion, the event highlighted the stark reality of an increasing dependence on benefactors from Silicon Valley. Sponsors of the event included Meta Glasses and OpenAI, and the finale included two dancing robots, who were greeted with notably less enthusiasm by the stellar line-up of Italian designers in the front row than the rest of the show. “The landlords have entered the chat,” read one comment beneath a video of the robots circulating on social media.

headline: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
trail_text: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
body_text: Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting. “AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming. As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue. Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.” The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed. ‘Google is better now’ Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise! Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, Dublin I find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites. Peter Warb, 75, UK AI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches. Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, Texas AI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating. Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, Malta Far more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy. Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, Nigeria Much better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results. Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, Oregon It’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in. Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, London Greatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking. Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey ‘Search has gotten worse’ Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from. Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregon Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search. Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, Japan Worse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension. Chris Gibson, Dundee Absolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results. Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UK ‘It’s so bad I quit Google’ Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it. The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be. headline: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
trail_text: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety
body_text: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.
