headline: Judge seems inclined to side with media outlets who were banned from White House in lawsuit
trail_text: Due process was not followed, said judge, when CNN, MS Now and Politico were banned from White House
body_text: A US district judge on Wednesday heard arguments in the extraordinary showdown between Donald Trump and CNN, MS Now and Politico, suggesting in comments that he was more inclined to side with the media plaintiffs who sued the president on Monday. Lawyers representing the media organizations have asked Timothy J Kelly, a district judge, to force the White House to return the press badges that were taken over the weekend after Trump banned their journalists from the building. While the judge declined to rule on Wednesday, he acknowledged that due process had not been followed in revoking access. The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”. When he originally announced the ban in a Friday post on Truth Social, Trump cited “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”, rather than any violation of national security protocols. During a tele-hearing on Wednesday afternoon, Kelly cited past case law that clearly laid out the need for a distinct process that involved advance notice of an infraction and the opportunity to plead one’s case. “I think it is fair to say that the processes that the circuit laid out in those two cases wasn’t followed here,” the judge said, referring to two similar cases involving journalists who had either lost access or were denied access to the White House. The judge said that the cases made clear that “before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard”. Michael Kenneth Velchik, a justice department attorney representing the Trump White House, argued that such a process had been laid out in the letters, which informed each news organization that they had until 5pm on Friday to contest the ban. (The letters said that if the organizations did not submit such a challenge, it would become final.) Theodore Boutrous, a prominent first amendment attorney who has represented many media plaintiffs in press access lawsuits against the Trump administration, said the letters were post-hoc and woefully insufficient to serve as notice. He said the White House’s actions and process was “not even close to conforming to due process and the first amendment”. Judge Kelly also seemed to agree that the letters were insufficient. “I don’t know how a letter they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the standards that they’d have to conform their conduct to,” he said. “It’s a piece of paper they got saying, ‘You’ve already violated that.’” As he laid out in a blockbuster lawsuit filed on Monday, Boutrous argued that, once the White House has been opened up to reporters, access cannot be denied for viewpoint-based reasons. He called the press ban “an unprecedented and unreasonable and severe punishment on the plaintiffs because of their content and their viewpoint”. Because Trump explicitly tied the ban to the news outlets’ coverage, Boutrous called him the “lead witness” for the plaintiffs in arguing that the decision was content-based. Boutrous argued that the journalists at issue – dozens of hard-pass holders at the three news organizations – are suffering “irreparable harm” by losing access to the building. “These are urgent matters,” he said. “We’re at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington. We have [Artificial Intelligence] discussions … It’s urgent that we get a [temporary restraining order]. The harm is irreparable. The public interest favors striking down unconstitutional acts like that.” While Kelly did not rule from the bench, he said he would issue a determination expeditiously. Kelly ruled affirmatively for CNN in a similar press access case in November 2018, forcing the White House to return the hard pass of then-correspondent Jim Acosta after the Trump administration seized it. At the time, Kelly said the White House had not afforded Acosta due process and agreed that the journalist had suffered “irreparable harm” by being deprived of access to the building. Trump recently took aim at Kelly in a post on Truth Social, saying that CNN had drawn a “great judge” for them, someone he had “sadly” appointed in 2017. Seemingly predicting a loss in court, he wrote: “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.” The plaintiffs in the case have received overwhelming support from fellow news organizations and groups that advocate for press freedoms, and were backed by a friend-of-the-court brief filed this week by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the White House Correspondents’ Association and a coalition of 49 media organizations. In solidarity with CNN, a member of the primary television pool, the other four networks – NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News – have refused to provide video footage of the president for the time being. Some news organizations have also opted to not publish pool photos taken of the president, or to use audio from White House events, in the case of National Public Radio.

headline: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years
trail_text: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances
body_text: Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure on Andy Burnham to abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum. The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave. In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry. The intervention comes after Burnham declined to rule out promising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago. In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.” TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.” Blair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has called the Brexit vote a “catastrophic mistake” and said the party should aim to rejoin the bloc, while Burnham himself told the Guardian last year: “I hope in my lifetime I see this country rejoin the European Union.” But Burnham has said he does not wish to pursue membership of the union in the near term. When asked by reporters this week if it could be in the next election manifesto, he said it was a question “for another day”. Others are sceptical of the electoral wisdom of giving the appearance that the party wants to undo the result of the 2016 referendum, especially in areas of the country where Reform UK has made inroads in recent years. Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, dismissed the idea earlier this year as she warned against “reopening the circular arguments that we ended up in as a country”. However, pollsters suggest Labour could benefit electorally by promising to rejoin. A new megapoll conducted by YouGov on behalf of the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain suggests the party could more than double its seat total if it goes into the next election promising to rejoin. The survey of more than 13,000 people, undertaken in June before Burnham became prime minister, found that a pledge to seek membership would help unite progressive voters behind Labour while doing nothing to boost Reform’s vote. The results suggested the move could take Labour from a projected 136 seats to 321 – though those totals will have changed since Burnham came to office, which has given the party a poll lead for the first time in months. The TBI paper calls for Britain to try to accelerate European market reforms using possible re-entry as leverage. It argues that pro-reformers in Brussels would have a significant incentive to work with Britain on a project to make the EU more economically liberal and to reform its regulations on energy and technology. It adds that Burnham should scrap the government’s red lines of not rejoining, not allowing free movement and not entering the single market or a customs union. The paper argues that the prime minister should replace them with a single promise only to sign up to rules and initiatives that prove of economic or strategic benefit to the UK. TBI has advocated in recent years for the UK to slow down its push to achieve net zero carbon emissions and is a heavy backer of increased use of artificial intelligence in government. Its policy positions have brought scrutiny on some of the institute’s most high-profile funders, who include the technology billionaire Larry Ellison, and its clients, which include the government of Saudi Arabia.

headline: Trump greets Xi Jinping on arrival in rare move as US-China trade truce extended
trail_text: President lays out red carpet as treasury secretary announces extension of ‘Busan agreement’ pausing trade war hostilities
body_text: Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington. Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and the first lady, Melania, traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday evening. Xi’s visit comes as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations general assembly, although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012. “It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters. “I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’” Scott ⁠Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US ⁠and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan ⁠agreement – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies. Bessent, who met the Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire. The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events. The simmering trade war is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi must confront during the visit, including the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit. The White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday. There was one discordant note in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony, when Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed that while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men. The moment, which was widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later. The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development. Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week. The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China. Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year. Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi. “He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.” Robert Mackey contributed reporting

headline: Senator confirms ‘eight suicide attempts’ by US navy personnel assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln carrier group – as it happened
trail_text: Kirsten Gillibrand says acting US navy secretary told her of attempted suicides after carrier strike group’s lengthy deployment as part of US war in Iran. This blog is now closed.
body_text: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Democrats in Maine accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after ProPublica reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Trump derailed the inquiry. The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The judge said that the cases made clear that “before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard”. Congressman Ro Khanna, the progressive Democrat whose California district sits across a swath of Silicon Valley, has called for an agreement between the US and China to pace and monitor AI development as he led a “shadow hearing” on Thursday of Democrats on the House select committee on “the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party”. “The American people are deeply concerned about the future of AI and the potential risks,” Khanna said in a statement. “We urgently need an agreement with China on basic inspections and safety standards.” The virtual hearing included testimony from Geoffrey Hinton, British-Canadian computer scientist and Nobel laureate often called “the godfather” of artificial intelligence, on what kind of US-China agreement might be possible. Khanna said OpenAI and Anthropic had not agreed to testify. The progressive Democrat also said he’d sent letters to leading Chinese AI companies, including Moonshot AI, Alibaba, and DeepSeek requesting commitments to join American AI labs in a binding international agreement to responsibly pace the development of the technology. On Tuesday, members of the committee sent a letter to the White House saying that US calls to “pace the frontier” of AI “do not need to conflict with ensuring American AI leadership and maintaining our strategic edge against the PRC, which is also an imperative.” The signatories called on Donald Trump to use his summit with Xi in Washington tjis week to press for “a binding, enforceable, and verifiable international accord to prevent any country from losing control of AI or unleashing misaligned superintelligence on the world.” The letter acknowledged that when engaging with China on the issue, “the US cannot assume commitments will be upheld unless there are clear mechanisms for verifying compliance. We recognize that this is a complicated topic and there are no easy solutions.” The letter also requests that Trump meet with committee members after his sit-down with China’s leader. “Just as humans must be kept in the loop of this technology, Congress must be kept in the loop of your diplomacy,” it says. In remarks earlier this week at the Asia Society, Khanna addressed the issue of US-China AI competition, days after Trump proposed an “AI Force” and an AI czar as the issue of data centers have become a potent midterm issue. Kahnna was asked how managing competition between the two AI superpowers would be possible if the stated goal of the US is to win the AI race, leaving China with little incentive for China to co-operate. “Winning the AI war is like winning a nuclear war – it would just lead to devastation,” Khanna said. “I don’t think the US should be trying to win an AI war – I think we need to come to an agreement about basic safety and basic standards to prevent a loss of control and misuse.” The US, he added, could continue to have the best chips and researchers. “It’s like nuclear weapons,” he said. “Both sides want to have the most advanced weapons, but there are still arms control agreements.” The call for US-China co-operation comes after the congressman published a bill of rights proposal for managing data centers in the US. At the the meeting in New York, he told the Guardian that levies on data centers he proposes would not affect US competitiveness. “The data issue is about economic balancing at home. There are a lot of places in the US you can build data centers that are away from residential communities, but big tech has just been lazy in building them where its easy but they need to build them only where communities want them and where there is real community benefit.” “I believe we need to tax agentic AI and robots,” he added. “There should be a tax to have neutrality in our tax code so that we are not incentivizing the replacement of human beings.” Workers, he added should also benefit from increased productivity as a result of AI. “There has to be a value to social cohesion in this country,” he added. “We need to be on the side of workers more than tech billionaires in terms of how this AI revolution takes place.” Khanna said that in keeping with regulations and safeguards in place for the nuclear power industry, the AI industry should embrace oversight and monitoring. “If something negative should happen the call would be for total nationalization,” he warned. “It’s a reasonable proposal that the private sector should get behind.” A bill of rights around AI should include investment in communities around data centers because most of what was currently proposed in the US amounts to “data center extraction”. “There should be a fund of $10m per 100 megawatts of data processing power to invest in schools, parks, jobs programs and infrastructure” and that “could easily be paid by the companies setting these data centers up.” Commentators and news outlets on the left and the right of the US political spectrum mocked Donald Trump on Wednesday for visibly wincing during a loud flyover of US military jets he staged for his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. The leftwing streamer Hasan Piker, who featured the Sky News broadcast on his live Twitch stream, exclaimed “What the fuck was that face! Xi didn’t even flinch!” After replaying the moment, Piker added: “Oh my god! Fucking mogged! Trump, it’s your air show! How do you get scared at your air show?” The moment, from a different angle, was captured on a White House live stream, and then posted online with mocking captions by both the rightwing New York Post and the leftwing MeidasTouch. Lindell TV, the partisan rightwing news outlet published by Mike Lindell, a Trump supporter and 2020 election conspiracy theorist, which was chosen by the White House to provide pool video, zoomed out at exactly the moment Trump winced, so did not capture the president’s startled reaction in its video. At a joint press conference on Tuesday, vice-president JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced that the federal government was removing 760,000 enrollees from Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces.

headline: Australia launches investigation after OpenAI agent hacked healthcare database
trail_text: Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach
body_text: Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”. Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach. Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate were ongoing into how the agent had infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal healthcare system, as well as three others. They were the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. “This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said. “Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident and I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.” Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government was disappointing. “It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said. The email was sent to the public-facing email address publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au. That inbox is checked once a day: the email was not read until 11 September. Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September. A taskforce has been launched to explore the “legal situation” of the breach. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, and the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, on Thursday both said Albanese had informed them the OpenAI breach had affected state websites – NSW’s crime agency and Victoria’s health department. Minns and Carroll said it did not appear any personal information had been shared in the breach, though investigations were ongoing. “New South Wales will be working with commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said. How the hack happened Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia. The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending. Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do this, “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server”. The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week. Marles said the agent was non-human and he called the breach a “very serious incident”. “What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said. The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics and, in doing so, had approached, as well as the Medicare portal, the three other Australian websites. “In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way,” Marles told ABC radio on Thursday. “But in relation to the medical portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway. “It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.” ‘Legal situation’ under investigation Marles said the government had established a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet that was working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute. “We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way,” the acting prime minister said. “This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed.” The OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement. “In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.” He said the review had found aggregate health statistics and internal file names had been accessed but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”. Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”. Australians should be ‘worried’ Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the fact it took three months for OpenAI to tell the government showed that there needed to be “basic rules and standards for tech companies”. “Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said on Thursday. “The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.” The independent senator David Pocock said the OpenAI hack highlighted how slow the government had been to implement AI safeguards in high-risk settings. Pocock criticised the government’s decision to shelve plans for a National AI Safety Act, and its dilatory approach to legislating new standards. “We have these companies warning of existential threat and hacking critical government infrastructure and the Labor government’s response is ‘We’ll get to that next year’. “There is also a big question here around why we aren’t holding these big tech companies liable for this kind of data breach. If it was an Australian who hacked the system they’d likely be heading for jail, yet there’s no accountability for AI companies developing this technology.” Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC radio that Australians ought to “be worried”. “This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.” OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” Santo said. Describing the behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, he said. “If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI.”

headline: Venezuela being ‘reborn’, Rodríguez tells UN – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: We’re winding up this live coverage of day two of the UN general assembly and Xi Jinping’s arrival in the US for high-stakes talks with Donald Trump. You can read our full reports on the UN forum and the talks summit, and below is a recap of the day’s main news. Thanks for being with us. Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the US and took the rare step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at an air force base outside Washington DC as Xi began a three-day state visit. Xi said China and the US should be “partners rather than rivals” and that Chinese and US interests were “deeply intertwined”. “The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the goal of making America great again can fully go hand in hand,” he said in written comments. Trade, artificial intelligence and the Iran war are expected to be prominent in the talks. The US and China agreed to a two-month extension of their trade war truce to 10 January, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said as Xi arrived. The deal came after lengthy talks between Bessent and his Chinese counterpart, vice-premier He Lifeng. Venezuela’s interim leader told the UN her country was coming back strong after “setbacks” this year and thanked Trump for being willing to resume diplomatic relations after the US military spirited her predecessor Nicolás Maduro out of the country. “Today, Venezuela is being reborn,” Delcy Rodríguez told the general assembly in New York. Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian described the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US. But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk – see Patrick Wintour’s report here. Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Moscow that Ukraine would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia if the two sides ⁠could not agree a truce on energy ⁠attacks before the cold sets in. He urged leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts, while singling out Vladimir Putin’s role in driving the war. Polish president Karol Nawrocki warned that without accountability, international law was not more than “a declaration without any real power”. Asian markets were mixed on Thursday as traders eyed the Trump-Xi summit. Hopes of business deals have been dimmed by there being no Chinese CEOs in Xi’s delegation, Agence France-Presse quoted two sources as saying. Oil prices cooled after jumping sharply. President Javier Milei condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, while accusing the UN of being filled with “parasites”. See Daniel Boffey’s report here. Syria’s interim president Ahmad al-Sharaa harshly criticised Israel’s occupation of southern Syria and told the UN general assembly the Golan Heights was an inseparable part of his country. The US has invited Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit of world leaders being held in Miami in December, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said. Xi and Trump’s summit this week will be the second time the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. The last time – in Beijing in May – there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers but little by way of concrete outcomes. Few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week – but one area in which the two leaders may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Amy Hawkins and David Smith have more here: What’s high on the agenda as Donald Trump and Xi Jinping hold their high-stakes talks? The last time the Chinese leader was hosted in Washington – by Barack Obama in 2015 – the topics included cybercrime, technology, the climate crisis and human rights. This time Xi is meeting a US president who has overhauled the world order and recalibrated the US-China relationship. And Trump is contending with a China that is in a much stronger position than it was 10 years ago. Amy Hawkins goes through five things to watch for at the talks. Asian markets have been mixed on Thursday as traders eye the much-anticipated Trump-Xi summit. The Chinese leader’s arrival in Washington coincided with US treasury Scott Bessent saying the countries had agreed to extend their trade truce by two months to 10 January. But hopes of business deals have been dimmed by there being no Chinese CEOs in Xi’s delegation, Agence France-Presse reports two sources as saying. In contrast, top US tech bosses including the leaders of major AI companies are set to attend a state dinner for Xi Jinping on Thursday. Pre-summit talks between Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng included discussion of creating a communication channel for AI concerns. Hong Kong, Shanghai and Taipei were in the red on Thursday, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi was closed for a holiday. Japan’s Nikkei was up 1.6% as it reopened after a three-day break. Tokyo’s gains came as the benchmark 10-year JGB yield rose to 3.055%, hitting a 30-year high, after US bond yields jumped. Oil prices cooled after jumping sharply as world leaders at the UN general assembly offered little to suggest progress in ending the turmoil in the Middle East. Brent crude – the international benchmark – was down 1% in early Asian trade after soaring more than 3% the previous day. Hopes for a new China commitment to buy Boeing planes are sinking ahead of Thursday’s Trump-Xi summit, Reuters is quoting two sources as saying, with negotiations still in flux. The US aerospace giant is instead trying to finalise a May deal for China to buy 200 planes, rather than earlier hopes of securing new commitments for hundreds more jets, the people briefed ⁠on the matter said on condition of anonymity. The provisional ⁠deal struck in tandem with Donald Trump’s last summit with Xi Jinping in Beijing put Boeing back into competition for Chinese jetliner orders. Boeing had been effectively shut out since 2017, while European rival Airbus had continued to expand its market share ⁠in one of the world’s biggest aviation markets. More now on Xi Jinping saying China and the US should be “partners rather than rivals”. He also said: “The Chinese and US peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and our interests are deeply intertwined.” Xi’s written comments – published by state news agency Xinhua – came hours after he was greeting by Donald Trump on arrival in the US ahead their high-stakes talks. Trade, artificial intelligence and the Iran war – including Beijing’s support for Tehran – are expected to be prominent. The Chinese leader said he looked forward to “in-depth exchanges” with Trump on “major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation”, Xinhua reported. The countries should “work towards each other to foster a stable relationship characterised by cooperation as the mainstay, competition within bounds, manageable differences and peaceful prospects”, Xi said. The great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the goal of making America great again can fully go hand in hand. The two sides should “chart a correct path for two major powers” to get along, Xi was quoted as saying. I am confident we can achieve this. I believe that with the joint efforts of both sides, this visit will yield fruitful results, enhance the wellbeing of our two peoples and bring new hope for world peace. Uzbekistan’s representative Saidi Mirziyoyeva has just finished speaking to the UN general assembly and that concludes the day’s addresses – it’s almost 9.30pm in New York City. The speeches in the “general debate” continue on Thursday morning, with Zimbabwe’s president Emmerson Mnangagwa first up. In case you missed this, Delcy Rodríguez earlier celebrated what she called a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with him less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro. The former foes met at a five-star hotel a few blocks from Trump Tower in Manhattan late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Tom Phillips reports. The hotel is about 11km (7 miles) from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas in January. On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, a reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro – under whom she served as vice-president – during her stay in New York. She did not reply. But she did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of Venezuela’s diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. See the full report here: Returning to Venezuela for a moment, interim leader Delcy Rodríguez also told the UN her country would hold elections. “I want to state this very clearly before this general assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela,” she said, while giving no timeline. Many Venezuelans have been hopeful that the ongoing US-backed political transition talks between the interim government and parts of the opposition would lead to a democratic election, as AFP reports. But those hopes were dented early this month when Donald Trump – speaking shortly after striking a huge oil deal with Caracas – brushed off the notion of a vote in the near future. Rodríguez echoed those comments at the time. Rodríguez replaced president Nicolas Maduro after his ouster by US forces in January, and she has served as a pliant ally to Washington since then. As mentioned earlier, while addressing the UN general assembly she thanked the Trump administration for its “willingness to resume the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation with Venezuela”. Xi Jinping ‌said after arriving ‌that Beijing and Washington should be partners rather ⁠than rivals, Chinese state news agency Xinhua is reporting. With ‌joint efforts, the US visit was sure ⁠to be fruitful, Xi said in written remarks, according ‌to Xinhua. Separately Xi was also quoted as suggesting in his statement that the two sides “should move toward each other and work together to build a stable relationship – one where cooperation is the mainstay, competition is kept within proper limits, differences are managed and peace can be expected”. On returning to the White House, Donald Trump said of travelling to greet Xi’s plane on arrival: “I think they appreciate it, tremendous people.” On Xi Jinping’s arrival in the US, his plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 30-metre-long red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and first lady Melania Trump travelled to the military base just outside Washington DC to personally greet the Chinese leader and his wife Peng Liyuan’s on touching down. The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, a private tea with the US president and first lady and a tour of the National Archives, among other events. See the full report from Ariana Baio here: Venezuela’s acting president has told the UN her country is coming back strong after “setbacks” this year and thanked Donald Trump for being willing to resume diplomatic relations after the US military spirited her predecessor out of the country. “Today, Venezuela is being reborn,” Delcy Rodríguez said in addressing the general assembly for the first time since she came to power. Rodríguez took over in Venezuela after the US military’s raid in January that captured Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the US to face drug trafficking charges. This is the first trip to the US by a Venezuelan head of state since 2018, when Maduro travelled to New York to take part in the UN general assembly, the Associated Press reports. He is currently being held not far from the organisation’s headquarters as he awaits trial. “I do not promise you an easy way forward,” Rodríguez said, saying she was addressing her people. Rebuilding our national soul will be the priority. More on Scott Bessent saying the US and China had agreed to a two-month extension of their trade war truce, which had been due to expire on 10 November. The deal came after marathon talks between the US treasury secretary and his Chinese counterpart, vice-premier He Lifeng, in New York on Sunday and in Washington on Wednesday. The announcement came just as Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in the US on Thursday evening for a high-stakes summit with Donald Trump. “We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan agreement, the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on November 10th,” Bessent told Fox News. That is going to be extended until January 10th to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front. The truce, which took effect last year, came after Trump struck a deal with Xi. The agreement saw both sides agree to reduce tit-for-tat tariffs and for the US to extend certain tariff exclusions. Washington had also agreed at the time to suspend responsive actions after an investigation into China’s shipbuilding sector, as AFP reports. Bessent on Wednesday also flagged the possibility that both sides could reduce tariffs on $30bn of non-sensitive goods. A selection of pictures here from the cordial greeting given to Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan from Donald and Melania Trump at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, outside Washington DC. The US treasury secretary is saying the ⁠US ⁠and China have agreed to extend “the Busan ⁠agreement”. Scott ⁠Bessent’s comments to Fox News ⁠came after he met Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng before Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington this week. “We met today to see if ‌we could do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series of smaller things,” Bessent was quoted as saying on Wednesday. “We have agreed ⁠today that we will extend what we call the Busan agreement.” The extension would go until 10 January, he said. The Busan agreement refers to the trade war truce Trump and Xi agreed to in Busan, South Korea, in October last year. Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington and been greeted by Donald Trump at the airport instead of waiting for him to drive to the White House. The decision to greet the Chinese leader there has been reported as showing how far Trump is going to honour China’s leader as he makes his first state visit to the US capital in more than a decade. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump greeted Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan after the Chinese president descended from his plane at Joint Base Andrews, a military airfield outside Washington, for the start of a three-day state visit. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US. But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.” Here’s Patrick Wintour’s report. Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Moscow that Ukraine would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia, if the two sides ⁠cannot agree a truce on energy ⁠attacks before the cold sets in. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too,” Zelenskyy told member nations, as he urged leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts. Zelenskyy also used his address to single out Putin’s role in driving the war, repeatedly describing him derisively as “patient zero” and “the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further”. He said: “That is why ’patient zero’ must be stopped. He must be denied the space to act – and the space to spread this evil further.” Ukraine did not choose this war, he reiterated, stressing that partial victory (in Donetsk) would never be enough for Putin. Polish president Karol Nawrocki warned that without accountability, international law is not more than “a declaration without any real power”. “Russia is destablising the situation in Europe through open aggression, hybrid operations, acts of subversion and sabotage, and by ignoring successive resolutions of this assembly,” he said, adding: “If aggression is not met with an adequate response, it becomes an invitation to repeat it.” Javier Milei condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. In a caustic speech, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known in Argentina as the Malvinas. “An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Falkland Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory. Milei told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”. “Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.” Here’s Daniel Boffey’s report. Syria’s interim president harshly criticized Israel’s occupation of southern Syria and said the Golan Heights is an inseparable part of his country. In a speech to the UN General Assembly, Ahmad al-Sharaa said that Israel has carried out more than 500 air and artillery strikes on the country since he took power nearly two years ago. Israel has also carried out 1,200 land incursions and detained nearly 300 people, he said. The United States has invited Russian president Vladimir Putin to attend the G20 summit of world leaders being held in Miami in December, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with the people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with, so we’ve invited president Putin to the G20. Kenyan president William Ruto argued for the necessity of reforming the UN security council and for greater African representation. “On the greatest questions of war and peace, five nations possess a power that the other 188 do not,” Ruto said. Demanding a permanent seat on the council for Africa, he added: “We cannot manage transformation with institutions that refuse to transform themselves.” Namibian president Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah joined growing calls for a woman to be elected as the next United Nations secretary-general. Addressing member nations, Nandi-Ndaitwah noted that no woman has held the position since the organisation was established in 1945, and said the UN’s leadership should reflect the gender equality it promotes across the international system. “Namibia therefore, believes that it is time that a woman is elected as secretary-general of our Organisation,” she said. Earlier, Panama’s president, José Raúl Mulino, also called for for the Latin America and Caribbean region to have a permanent seat on the UN security council. I wish to reiterate before this general assembly the need for Latin America and the Caribbean to hold positions with greater decision-making power on the security council, specifically a permanent position, as a permanent member of this organization’s security council. We are a leading region in food, minerals, biodiversity, and [have] a deep commitment to peace and integration. He urged the UN to address urgent issues including migration and the climate crisis, adding: We must acknowledge that citizens do not believe these kinds of gatherings benefit them. Herein lies one of the reasons why trust must be restored. Our conclusion is unequivocal: the world does not need less United Nations; it needs a United Nations that works better. Polish president Karol Nawrocki spoke of the grave importance of accountability if there is to be lasting peace and “if international law is to be anything other than a declaration without any real power”. The absence of accountability in the international community has “sent a signal [to aggressive states] that violations of international law, aggression, and imperialist policies could go unpunished,” he told member nations. It is precisely this lack of justice - this sort of original sin of the postwar order - that creates space for the return of old aggressive ambitions and methods of operation. He went on: “Russia is destablising the situation in Europe through open aggression, hybrid operations, acts of subversion and sabotage, and by ignoring successive resolutions of this assembly.” Contempt for international law must not become the norm. As a country that neighbours Russia, he said he wanted to make it clear on behalf of Poland that “we are not the ones seeking confrontation”. We are strengthening our alliances, developing our military, and modernizing its equipment not to wage war, but to prevent it … Our goal is deterrence and defence. Nato remains the “guarantor of transatlantic security”, he said. “Russia is carrying out actions aimed at undermining the foundations of international stability,” Nawrocki went on. If aggression is not met with an adequate response, it becomes an invitation to repeat it. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev ⁠is heading to the United States on ⁠Wednesday, where ⁠he will meet with Trump administration representatives Steve Witkoff, ⁠Jared Kushner and others, two sources familiar with ⁠preparations for the talks have told Reuters. The ‌sources said ‌that Dmitriev’s visit to ‌the US, which was agreed upon with Vladimir Putin, will take place in New York on ‌the sidelines of the UN general assembly and will follow up on a meeting between Putin ⁠and US representatives at the Kremlin earlier this month. One source told Reuters that the ‌aim of the visit is to keep the Russia-US dialogue and the peace-making effort going. President of Panama José Raúl Mulino is now up. He kicks off by applauding multiculturalism and the role of the UN in a world of “such volatility”, but calls for greater leadership. “We must restore trust,” he says, warning that illegal people trafficking was taking a heavy toll on the country socially and economically, but also on some sensitive natural environments in Panama. “We must make headway together on the key issues,” he says. This includes world trade, with Panama’s canal playing a key global role, but he warns it is increasingly at risk from heavy rain and flooding which is worsening due to the climate crisis, despite Panama being a carbon negative country. President of the Central African Republic, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, is now on the podium, speaking about the country’s ongoing sectarian conflict and political instability. “A fragile country needs security for development,” he says, calling for international support. “Peace cannot be decreed, it must be built day after day through dialogue, justice and shared development.” “Holding out your hand to yesterday’s opponent is not a sign of weakness”, he says. He also warns about the worsening impacts due to the global climate crisis and calls for a greater role for women in public life to help end instability in the country. Some boast of ‌a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second. Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should ‌shame us all?” Macron also opted for tough language on settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, saying: “Look at what is happening in the West Bank, where every day violations are committed. In whose name? Hamas has never operated in the West Bank … What is happening there is building, day by day, the impossibility of a project that should be based on respect for the legitimate right of the Palestinian people to exist.” Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least one person died and seven were injured in this morning’s Russian attacks on Kyiv. In a series of updates, he said Russian drones struck a business centre, a transport facility, and a “non-residential building,” among others. Separately, Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta said Russia hit one of its petrol stations in the capital, ‌the sixth such facility attacked in recent weeks. Smoke ⁠was ⁠seen rising in the centre ⁠of Ukrainian ⁠capital Kyiv ‌after ‌a ‌Russian drone attack this morning, Reuters reported. More on that when we have it. Ukraine is set to feature prominently on Day 2 of the UN general assembly in New York, with leaders first joining the UN security council meeting on Ukraine, before president Volodymyr Zelenskyy takes to the podium to deliver his address to the assembly. It will be a key opportunity to rally international support behind Kyiv, bolstering Ukraine’s position ahead of any potential peace talks with Moscow. Zelenskyy did not get a chance to say much during his last night’s meeting with US president Donald Trump. “I hope we will end this war, and president Trump will help us end this war. We need to do it as quick as possible, before winter,” he said at the beginning of the meeting before Trump dominated the Q&A with reporters. He later said on social media that the pair discussed ending “the senseless war” before winter, with “potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy.” He also said Ukraine was “ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire” if Russia agrees to “not attack out energy system” Before we get to Zelenskyy late afternoon, we will hear from some other European leaders from Latvia, Romania, Czech Republic, Estonia, and Cyprus. I will monitor their speeches for any key lines. Lots to cover. It’s Wednesday, 23 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live. Good morning.

headline: An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so far
trail_text: Experts say ‘fairly minor’ breach is a portent of things to come and proprietary closed systems like OpenAI are ‘the least of the worries’
body_text: Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare and three other systems in June – and the company only notified Australia earlier this month. The prime minister has expressed his “extreme concern” over the incident, although he noted no personal information is believed to have been accessed in the breach. Here’s what we know. What happened? An artificial intelligence agent built by the American firm OpenAI hacked into Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system. The agent gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public files in the Medicare statistics reporting service portal. The actions of the agent have been described as “misaligned behaviour” after it was assigned a benign research task compiling health and medical statistics. The agent also accessed the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research. At this stage it is believed that no personal medical information has been compromised, but investigations are continuing. The prime minister has said: “this situation is obviously unacceptable”. What is an AI agent? An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools. OpenAI was co-founded by Elon Musk and Sam Altman (who remains CEO) in 2015. It is valued at more than US$1tn. Both have recently raised concerns about the pace of, and lack of controls around, the development of AI. “There are many things that AI cannot and should not automate,” Altman told the UN security council this week. “As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.” How did Australia find out? OpenAI, one of the best-resourced AI companies on Earth, sent an email to a public-facing Australian government address, three months after the hack. OpenAI said it found out about the agent’s access in August. On 10 September, it sent an email to a general Australian government email address which is monitored once a day, advising its AI agent had hacked the country’s universal healthcare system. The email was read on 11 September. On 15 September, Services Australia notified the Australian Signals Directorate. The minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, was notified on 17 September. Services Australia’s first interaction with OpenAI – asking for more specific details of the hack – was on Tuesday this week, 22 September. “It took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred,” Albanese said, “and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, met with Altman earlier in September, but Marles said Altman did not mention his company’s hack of Australia’s health system to Marles at that meeting. How did Australia respond? Albanese, currently in the US, said he spoke with Altman “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”. The prime minister announced he would establish a taskforce – involving the national cybersecurity coordinator, the office of AI, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia – to conduct an “urgent and immediate” review into the incident. Terms of reference for the investigation, released by the prime minister’s department on Thursday, cover reporting requirements for AI-driven cyber-incidents and vulnerabilities; governance and information sharing responsibilities for federal officials; obligations on AI firms for notification of future incidents; the adequacy of existing laws; and mechanisms to boost protections against hackings within the federal government. The incident has also been referred to parliament’s joint select committee on artificial intelligence. To date, OpenAI has not faced any sanction. How serious was this attack? At a press conference in Sydney, Marles said the incident itself was “relatively minor” and that it appeared no personal health information had been accessed. But he said the government regarded the hack as a “salutary warning … about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place”. Dr Joel Pearson, a professor of neuroscience and neurofuturism, and the deputy director of UNSW’s AI Institute, said the breach appeared to be a “fairly minor security incident”, but was a portent of more serious attacks to come. “What I would worry about is the latest open-weights and open-access models from China that are going to be used at scale by nefarious organisations and nations, perhaps particularly Russia: these things are going to be used at scale to do things much more damaging and much more costly to Australians than a small breach to some non-personal Medicare data.” Cory Alpert, a PhD student studying the impact of AI on democracy at the University of Melbourne, said OpenAI’s attack appeared to be the first instance of a frontier AI model hacking into another country’s government systems of its own volition. “This raises very important questions about the foreign attack vectors. Had this been a Chinese or a Russian model, the reaction would have been markedly different than a stern call to Sam Altman, and yet it is still a massive vulnerability.” Is Australia doing enough to address the risks posed by AI? Pearson said it was “pretty clear that we are way behind, the government is behind in all things cybersecurity, in most things AI”. “I would say that the least of the worries should be these proprietary closed systems like Anthropic and OpenAI. It will be the open-source Chinese models in the hands of spammers, scammers, and nefarious individuals and foreign nationals, and the spy agencies coming at us from all different angles. That will be the big threat and that’s where the government really has to step up.” Pearson said none of the frameworks established in Australia – government or private – were equipped to deal with the rising threat. “From the government all the way down to companies and boards and CEOs, everyone is scrambling, trying to understand and update frameworks, including the legal process. It’s just all moving too slow compared to the exponential speed of AI.” What does this incident say about big tech and transparency? A spokesperson for OpenAI said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity” during training and evaluation, and notified third parties whenever the review identified potential impacts to their systems. The spokesperson said “our models took actions we did not attend”, but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”. “Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues.” Prof Toby Walsh, the chief scientist at UNSW’s AI Institute, said he believed Australia should be prosecuting OpenAI, a company known to have “terrible agent governance”. “For a trillion-dollar company, their cybersecurity was woeful. The officers of this company need to be held accountable. These hacks could have easily been stopped, indeed never need to have taken place. We would prosecute humans who did such hacking.” Walsh said it displayed operational incompetence on the part of OpenAI. Dr Rob Nicholls, senior research associate at the University of Sydney, said the three-month delay in informing Australia of the breach exposed the ineffectiveness of Australia’s laws. “An AI agent broke into a government Medicare system and helped itself to non-public files, and OpenAI sat on that for three months before telling us. If a person had done this, we’d call it hacking. The fact it was an AI agent doesn’t make it less serious, it makes our disclosure laws more out of date. “This is the clearest case yet of an AI agent operating autonomously and breaching Australian government systems without a human directing it to. It is a live test of whether Australia’s AI and privacy settings can keep pace with agentic AI, not just chatbots.”

headline: OpenAI’s Medicare hack is a bleak opportunity for Australia to address its security shortcomings post-haste
trail_text: All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein and Daddy America
body_text: Whoopsie! Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein regrets to inform you he’s lost control of his OpenAI monster. It’s roving around doing things that provoke international legal investigation, and Australia has found out in the worst possible way. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, was obliged to announce from the United Nations summit on Thursday morning Australian time that an agentic AI from the OpenAI stable had gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public information from Australia’s Medicare website. The good news in this debacle is that so far it appears no personal information held in Medicare’s records was compromised. Pursuing “a benign task” of compiling some health statistics, the portal breach accessed non-sensitive data about spending. The good news, alas, ends here. OpenAI – a company worth US$852bn as per its last valuation – informed the government of the breach by … sending an email to its public email account three months after the hack occurred. Albanese revealed the date of Services Australia’s worst ever Inbox Zero was 10 September, and the Australian Cyber Security Centre was informed on 15 September. Albanese at the UN has proved a fairly nimble diplomat, much to the surprise of anyone who has been on the receiving end of his vengeance at home. One imagines that a desire to soften fierce Trumpian pushback to Labor’s attempts at “digital duty-of-care” regulations for – ha! – AI and social media inspired the PM’s epically cringeworthy grip-and-grin selfie with the unpopular president. It was “photo diplomacy” wisely followed by a well-publicised hug with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. After a direct meeting with Altman, the PM described the “obviously unacceptable” incident and his government’s “extreme concern”. Announcing immediate taskforces and urgent reviews into the breach and its national security implications, Albanese said Altman was aware “the company had not done good enough”. “Aware” may actually be underselling it, because Altman has been making speeches of his own at the UN – to no less than the UN security council, alongside his supposed corporate rival, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei – urging the governments of the world to collectively enforce regulations of the technology guided by democratic institutions. Begging the question: Dr Frankenstein, what the hell’s been going on in your lab? One longs for the tender innocence of last week when we could describe warnings from ex-Anthropic employees that AI could destroy the world within 10 years as merely utterly terrifying – because the attitude of the security council member representing the world’s richest democracy is that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. Here’s hoping one will turn up. In the unregulated, commercial AI environment where “crawler” AIs are autonomously finding their way around sovereign data protection systems to scrape information, the explanatory metaphor that leaps to mind is if nuclear weapons had been retailed and the world only found out about radioactive fallout once a 10-year-old playing with it in a back yard had permanently depopulated Baltimore. Is American laissez-faire fuckwittery to blame here? Yes – and Australians are right to be screaming that if OpenAI were a Chinese or Iranian company hacking into our systems ambassadors would be marching out of embassies with grand announcements and thundering speeches of condemnation. But they’d also be wise to remember that geographically isolated, distant middle power Australia has only been afforded grandiosity on the world stage because in the post-second world war, pre-Trump era, it had the umbrella protection of a meaningful alliance with Daddy America. And these days it’s Daddy America who’s a rules-free maniac whose sole political calculation is that money equals power and a literal “to the victor the spoils” foreign policy. To imagine Donald Trump’s US state department will be inspired into acts of responsibility due to Australian shaming it for data theft is some high genre alternate history. The man Trump pardoned who ran a stolen-data criminal marketplace spoke at the Republican convention in Dallas this year. Symbolic, no? Internationally, the realignment of powers in the wake of Trump’s thuggery advances, but what role Australia will be offered in that realignment is uncertain, and it is narcissistic to pretend otherwise. Locally, we’re not powerless. The Medicare breach is a bleak opportunity to address our revealed information security shortcomings post-haste, with full democratic transparency and accountability. All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from the new front in the information war. If Albanese’s new taskforce determines that ministerial oversight failed to protect Medicare or any other comprised dataset, heads must – publicly – roll. The ACTU has long been warning of US abrogation of AI security obligations, demanding the development of “sovereign AI” capacity to meet oncoming threats. Every one of us should back calls to regulate the living bejeezus out of all AI-capable foreign platforms seeking to operate here – or impose moratoriums on operations outright. I am not entrusted to represent Australia diplomatically, so let me say to Mr Altman what a prime minister on a diplomatic mission apparently can’t: if your creatures are thieving our data and you are too much of a coward to pick up the damn phone to tell us, your destruction may be individual, it may be collective – but it is ensured. • Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnist
