headline: Workers on 13 Bathla sites stood down as funding runs out – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: That’s where we’ll end our coverage for today. Here are the top stories today: A person has died and several other people have been injured after a multi-vehicle collision involving a bus. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June, and said the company only notified Australia earlier this month. The PM, who has been in the US, also announced Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion. The Australian Bureau of Statistics released data showing unemployment ticked up to its highest rate since the pandemic, with the key jobless figure lifting to 4.6% in August, from 4.5% the month before. A former senior National Gallery of Victoria employee was alleged to have funnelled $8m from the gallery over six years by buying and selling mobile phones. The government department that overseas Questacon was fined $140,000 for work, health and safety failures after a child’s hands caught fire at the science centre. More than 600 Qantas ground crew workers began a 24-hour strike across the country over an escalating industrial dispute. And children’s author Andy Griffiths remembered his friend and collaborator of 35 years, Terry Denton, after the latter’s death on Monday. Victoria’s Labor and Liberal leaders weigh in on twilight AFL grand final speculation Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has described herself as a “grand final traditionalist” while the premier, Ben Carroll, says he’d like to see the match played at twilight. With just two days until the AFL grand final, the perennial question about the match time was a topic of conversation at parliament. It follows a report in the Herald Sun suggesting that if the Liberal party were elected in November, it would look to use ministerial powers to block staging an AFL night grand final at the MCG. Wilson would not confirm the report but said: I’m the Grand Final traditionalist. I love the grand final. I love how big [an] event it is for Melbourne. It’s when Melbourne comes alive, and I think the Saturday afternoon grand final is a big part of that. But I’m also really focused on how the grand final can be an event for families, and I believe that the afternoon grand final is the best way to do that. Carroll, when asked, said he’d prefer a twilight start: I will leave it to the AFL and our experts at Visit Victoria, and all of our experts that make these decisions … not the politicians … I think that twilight is something that could be considered by the AFL. I certainly think it is the sweet spot in terms of family-friendly TV ratings and the weather. Victoria police have confirmed a woman died in the bus crash in Glenburn this afternoon. The force has just issued a statement saying the driver of one of the cars involved in the collision died at the scene. Detectives are investigating the crash, but police say they understand the bus collided with a white car and a blue Toyota on the Melba Highway near Two Hills Road about 2.40pm. The driver of the white car died at the scene, police say, while the driver and passenger of the Toyota sustained minor injuries. Policed say they believe there were 18 people inside the bus, including the driver. Two occupants of the bus were taken to hospital with serious injuries, two were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and the others were treated at the scene. This post has been amended. Owing to incorrect information in a police statement an earlier version misstated the gender of the person who died. The insolvency advisory Teneo has announced it is standing down workers and stopping construction on the embattled developer Bathla Group’s semi-finished properties. Bathla – one of Australia’s largest property developers – went into voluntary administration on 25 August, weighed down by almost $3.6bn in debt, leaving thousands of customers in limbo, some with semi-complete homes they’d bought off-the-plan. Its administrators at Teneo had been in crisis talks with private lenders to try to save Bathla and its many projects, saying their immediate priorities included finishing the estimated 2,000-2,500 homes on which construction had already begun. Teneo managed to secure short-term funding to temporarily continue construction on the 13 Bathla sites where construction was under way, but it announced this evening that the money had run out and it had not managed to secure further funding. Teneo said its discussions with lenders for further funding “have now concluded”. As a result, construction workers across 13 Bathla sites have been stood down and all construction operations have ceased, Teneo said. Teneo’s Stephen Longley said the administrators were now focused on working with lenders for an “orderly sale” of Bathla Group’s subdivision and land bank sites. He said: A core team of Bathla employees has been retained to assist with the management and realisation of the assets. The administrators will provide further updates to customers, employees, creditors, subcontractors and other stakeholders as the administration process progresses. At Bathla, 125 staff members were let go today, and 67 employees have been retained. We’ve asked Teneo to clarify if the 13 construction sites it is referring to encompasses all of Bathla’s current projects, as well as how many construction workers have been stood down. You can read more about Bathla’s downfall here: Ambulance Victoria has provided some more detail on this afternoon’s bus crash in Glenburn, a town north-east of Melbourne. The state’s ambulance service says its paramedics responded to reports of a collision involving a bus in Glenburn about 2.40pm today, and assessed 21 people at the scene. They say: A teenage male was treated at the scene and flown to the Alfred hospital in a serious condition with upper body injuries. A man in his 50s was treated and transported by road ambulance to Box Hill hospital in a serious condition. A teenage female was treated and transported by road ambulance to the Royal Children’s hospital in a stable condition. A teenage male was treated and transported by road ambulance to Maroondah hospital in a stable condition with upper body injuries. Sixteen other people assessed by paramedics at the scene did not require emergency treatment or transport. Ambulance Victoria asked journalists to speak to Victoria police regarding a fifth person who was injured, so we will bring you more information as soon as we can. Australian chefs have joined their global colleagues in refusing to serve ocean-farmed Atlantic salmon. The Gourmet Farmer Matthew Evans, Analiese Gregory and Josh Niland have signed an open letter, together with more than 120 leading chefs from 26 countries, and food-system campaigners such as Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall. The list includes chefs from some of the world’s best restaurants, holding more than 90 Michelin stars between them. The chefs have pledged to stop serving ocean-farmed salmon until it can be produced without harming wild fish, marine ecosystems and coastal communities. Tasmania produces virtually all of Australia’s farmed salmon. Evans, the host of Gourmet Farmer and What’s the Catch?, said he would never serve Tasmanian-farmed salmon at his Fat Pig Farm. Evans said: It’s clear that the way we produce salmon in open pens is done in a way that continues to harm Tasmania’s natural environment. It’s a dirty industry that refuses to clean up its act. Multiple people have been injured after a bus crash in Victoria. Ambulance Victoria paramedics are on the scene in Glenburn after reports of a crash involving a bus at about 2.40pm today. Paramedic crews are assessing multiple patients, with initial reports from on-scene crews suggesting 18 people may have been injured. “Our paramedics’ priority is with their patients. Further updates will be provided as information becomes available,” Ambulance Victoria said in a statement. Systemic racism to blame for Indigenous people’s wage disparity: landmark study Systemic racism is to blame for a glaring Indigenous pay gap that is costing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples billions of dollars a year, a landmark study has found, AAP reports. The Australian-first Towards Indigenous Pay Parity report released on Thursday revealed Indigenous employees earn 16 cents less for every dollar compared with the average Australian worker, culminating in an average $15,000 discrepancy each year. That figure climbs to 21 cents for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, who earn an average $41 per hour, compared with $52 for men overall. The UTS Centre for Indigenous People and Work report analysed Australian Tax Office and Australian Bureau of Statistics data from almost 230 occupations, identifying wage gaps in three quarters of sectors. The centre’s director, Prof Nareen Young, warned the pay gap cost Indigenous Australians a combined $3bn in 2022-23, with a total cumulative loss of $170bn possible by 2050. Exploring factors including education, age, job type and hours worked, the study found those elements accounted for less than one third of the average hourly pay gap. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast earlier today, Prof Young said: Having examined all of the usual things that explain a pay parity gap we can only put it down to systemic racism. When it’s up to the discretion of the employer or manager or a REM (remuneration) process or an HR process, the gap is wider, which is of real concern. New South Wales police say a 50-year-old man has died after he was spotted struggling in the water off a beach south of Sydney. Emergency services were called to Marley beach in the Royal national park about 12.50pm today, to reports two swimmers were struggling, police said. They said local police, officers from the Marine area command, surf lifesavers and three helicopter services assisted in the search and rescue operation. Police said a 20-year-old man was pulled from the water after being washed back to shore by waves. He was treated at the scene, winched out of the remote beach by helicopter and taken to St George hospital in a stable condition, police said. A short time later, police said officers attached to the Marine area command found the 50-year-old man’s body in the water. Police have said they will prepare a report for the coroner. Money markets are still predicting a 90% chance of the Reserve Bank raising interest rates next Tuesday. The surprise rise in unemployment to 4.6% in August data today would normally reduce the prospect of a rate hike but today’s data also showed hiring actually increased, just by less than new jobseekers. As a result, Commonwealth Bank, ANZ and NAB have all reaffirmed their predictions for a hike in the cash rate on Tuesday from 4.35% to 4.6%, as have analysts at AMP and UBS. That would take rates to their highest level in 14 years. (Westpac has not explicitly said whether it still agrees with that view.) For someone with an average-sized new mortgage of $731,000, paying a typical rate of 6.2%, a rate increase would add about $119 to their $4,477 monthly repayments. Rugby league tsar Peter V’landys has increased his grip on the game after being named executive chairman of the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC). The V’landys appointment adds the responsibilities of the NRL chief executive – a position held until July by new Tennis Australia boss, Andrew Abdo – to his existing duties as ARLC chair. The move is controversial, given the ARLC was established in 2012 with clear separation between management and operations within a sport plagued by political infighting. V’landys has the unanimous backing of NRL clubs and state associations, however, and resigned as Racing NSW chief executive earlier on Thursday to allow him to focus his energies on rugby league. A former senior National Gallery of Victoria employee is alleged to have funnelled $8m from the gallery over six years, AAP reports. He allegedly bought $8m worth of mobile phones using an NGV account, which he then sold for personal financial gain. The state’s corruption watchdog has charged the former employee with eight offences alleged to have taken place between September 2019 and September 2025. “IBAC will allege that mobile phones were purchased under an NGV account to the value of approximately $8 million and then sold for personal financial benefit,” the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission said in a statement on Thursday. The watchdog said it began investigating allegations of corrupt conduct in relation to theft and misuse of his position by the former senior employee earlier in September 2025. The man has been charged with seven counts of theft and one count of misconduct in public office. He is expected to appear before Melbourne magistrates’ court on 20 October. Founded in 1861, the NGV is Australia’s oldest and most visited art museum. NGV has been contacted for comment. Hello, thanks for reading so far. I’ll take you through the rest of the day’s news. That’s all from me. Catie McLeod will snag the blog from here. Take care. Violent, serious offences decrease as crime rate falls in Victoria The crime rate in Victoria has fallen by almost 4% in the past year, with police praising controversial “adult crime, adult time” laws as being responsible for a major drop in youth offending. AAP reports the state’s crime rate, which accounts for population growth, fell to 8,679.6 offences per 100,000 people, according to Victoria’s Crime Statistics Agency figures released on Thursday. Overall, the state recorded 624,624 criminal offences in the 12 months to June, a reduction of 13,360 offences compared with the previous financial year. Youth offending decreased by 8.1% in that time, but police maintain child offenders aged 10-17 continue to be over-represented in major violent crimes such as home invasions, aggravated burglaries and robberies. Police attributed some of the reductions to increased visible and proactive policing. But other areas of offending continued to rise. Drug offenders apprehended increased 11.6%, while the number of offenders processed for drug trafficking and dealing rose 18.5%. Police also recorded a 2.7% increase in retail theft, with 43,124 offences recorded. Last-minute decision to protect endangered birds from SA space project Conservation groups have welcomed an 11th-hour decision to protect “precious and important habitat” on South Australia’s Eyre peninsula from plans for a rocket launching facility. The Whalers Way “orbital launch complex”, which could see as many as 42 rockets a year take off from conservation land, had already been approved under federal and state planning and environment laws. But a recent decision by the state’s independent Native Vegetation Council could scuttle the space project, located about 32km from Port Lincoln. The 23-hectare site is protected under a longstanding heritage agreement, a type of covenant on private land designed to protect native wildlife and habitat in perpetuity. headline: Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year’s Oscars race stand?
trail_text: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey might be the one to beat but a crop of competitors is starting to materialise
body_text: Reporting from fall film festivals used to be a more streamlined process – what’s good, what’s bad, what’s being sold, what has Oscars chances – but with each year, the season arrives with larger, more existential questions. The 2025 run, from Venice to Telluride to Toronto, was notably underwhelming and took place months after Sinners went from box-office hit to legitimate contender and at the same time as One Battle After Another skipped festivals and went on to win best picture. The pipeline that had once birthed winners such as Birdman, Spotlight, 12 Years a Slave and The King’s Speech had no longer played as big of a part with Covid-affected Nomadland being the last fall festival film to win the top prize. Even without an awards hat on, there has been a more general lack of buzz, an excitement of something new that much harder to find as more films of considerably lower quality took up underserved space. If the trades are to be believed, a lot of it is down to studios choosing against the risk of bad buzz and potential embarrassment to A-listers because for every The Shape of Water or Poor Things, there’s a White Noise or Joker: Folie à Deux. So while this season might see new films starring Tom Cruise, Timothée Chalamet, Anne Hathaway, Christian Bale, Amy Adams, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Ben Affleck and Mikey Madison, none of them are braving a festival premiere. As Oscar nominations were being announced back in January of this year, the next crop of contenders started revealing themselves over in Park City where Utah hosted its final Sundance film festival. The biggest story was the return and reinvention of Olivia Wilde, who was the best part of Gregg Araki’s comedy I Want Your Sex and finally announced herself as a serious director with chamber comedy The Invite, a remake of the Spanish film The People Upstairs. It was the buzziest title of the festival and after a rapturous premiere, a heated auction led to A24 buying the rights and a summer release scored solid box office and sustained word of mouth. It didn’t automatically seem like an obvious Academy pick even if it might have been viewed as such years prior – a talky, human comedy about sex and relationships without much of a recent precedent – but it slowly seemed like a surer thing. Wilde could become the first woman ever to receive nominations for acting and directing while, as it stands, it seems like A24’s strongest contender. There was also support for John Turturro’s turn in simple, old-fashioned crime drama The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, a film that was purchased by Sony Pictures Classics, an Oscar campaign clearly in mind. Turturro has yet to receive an Oscar nomination and with a rare every-scene performance here, he could sneak into the best actor five. The festival’s big prize isn’t usually a predictor of Oscar success (recent winners have included Clemency, Atropia, Nanny and In the Summers), yet films such as Coda, Minari and Whiplash have managed to use this early win as the start of fruitful Oscar campaign. This year’s winner was Josephine, an acclaimed drama starring Channing Tatum that seemed like one of the bigger breakouts. But its uncomfortable subject matter – an eight-year-old girl spirals after witnessing a graphic sexual assault – made it a difficult watch for some (there were walkouts) and an even more difficult purchase for buyers, ultimately going to a small and untested new company called Sumerian Pictures. Tatum gives arguably his greatest performance yet (I would hand him the best supporting actor Oscar now if I could) and the film is thoughtfully made by writer-director Beth de Araújo, but it’s a steeper hill to climb due to its backers and content and it might have to unfairly settle for some critics circle prizes. The Berlin film festival hasn’t tended to produce many Academy-friendly movies over the years (Ethan Hawke in Blue Moon, Charlotte Rampling in 45 Years, four wins for The Grand Budapest Hotel) but with more doors open for international films at the Oscars, it’s become more present in the race. This year most eyes were on Sandra Hüller and her gender-switching turn in black-and-white drama Rose, which could find her on the outskirts of the best actress race. It helps that she’s also in three other acclaimed films of the year, one of which premiered soon after the festival finished … No one was quite sure what to expect of March’s sci-fi adventure Project Hail Mary, with star Ryan Gosling proving to be an unreliable box-office draw and directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller having not made a live-action film since 2014’s 22 Jump Street. But the film was a considerable win, both critically and commercially, and many believe it could follow in the footsteps of The Martian, also from author Andy Weir, a film that nabbed seven Oscar nominations. Amazon doesn’t have the best track record with the Academy but since the Academy seems to be once again favouring blockbuster fare (if F1 could get in …) this could easily become one of the final 10. Next came Cannes and a notable lack of many American movies, with most studios and stars choosing not to make the journey over. James Gray’s Paper Tiger, starring Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson, was well-received but like his other similarly well-received films, such as Armageddon Time and The Lost City of Z, it might not be to the Academy’s tastes (he has yet to score a single nomination). The biggest American breakout was Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid, a fairly conventional comedy about a gay man dealing with a son he didn’t know about, which scored strong reviews and interest from buyers, leading to an A24 pickup. It’s continued to play well at fall festivals but could be another beloved smaller indie from the company that appeals more to critic circles than the Academy (see also: Sorry Baby, Uncut Gems, The Souvenir and I Saw the TV Glow). The buzziest breakouts came from outside the US – from Spain to Japan to Romania. The Palme d’Or winner was Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord, a divisive culture wars drama starring Oscar nominees Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve. It was picked up by Neon, a company that knows a thing a two about turning this into Oscar success (they have previously secured noms and wins for previous Palme d’Or picks Anora, It Was Just an Accident, Parasite, Anatomy of a Fall and Triangle of Sadness). But Fjord has its fair share of hurdles (it went down poorly at Toronto, some have accused it of being too rightwing and Mungiu previously saw his last Palme d’Or honoree – 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days – snubbed by the Academy). A far safer bet would be the ambitious Spanish epic La Bola Negra, which tells the story of interconnected gay men across three different timelines. It had a 20-minute standing ovation and was snapped up for the US by Netflix, who are giving it an unusually generous theatrical window later this year. It also features a cameo from Penélope Cruz, having quite the year with this and an Oscar-tipped supporting turn in The Invite. Elsewhere, there were thumbs up (and some wavering) for Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s care home drama All of a Sudden that might not have the support that pushed his breakout Drive My Car to Oscar glory, but its star Virginie Efira could find her way into the best actress category. She’ll face competition from another performance by Hüller, who turned up again in her second black-and-white drama of the year, this time in Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, a 1940s-set father-daughter tale. Back in the US, an unlikely contender took shape at the start of the summer season. At last year’s Toronto film festival, micro-budget horror Obsession turned midnight madness screams into a $15m purchase by Focus Features, 20 times what it was made for. It became a smash hit in May, breaking multiple box-office records and energising gen Z audiences – and while none of this immediately screams Oscars, the ongoing acclaim for breakout star Inde Navarrette caused many to ask, well why not? The Academy’s slow appreciation for horror – with The Substance and Weapons recently breaking through – shows that the genre has finally scared voters into submission and with Focus behind it, who know a thing or two about FYC campaigns, it seems like at least Navarrette is in the race, with the film itself possibly joining her. A more traditional challenger came soon after, Christopher Nolan’s epic The Odyssey, which also became a box-office titan and, like previous best picture-winning Oppenheimer, it appealed to critics as much as it did with audiences. It’s by far the strongest across-the-board option we have at this stage with likely acting noms for Hathaway and Matt Damon as well as a range of craft nods. Even though Nolan did win director and picture so recently, it’s hard to see who can stop him from doing it again at this moment. It was then time for the fall festivals with Venice emerging, a little light on the bigger titles many had expected. It kicked off with Danny Boyle’s tabloid tale Ink, which received decent notices but not quite decent enough for the film to be deemed a major player, with Netflix unlikely to prioritise it over La Bola Negra and a more substantial Venice breakout, Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love. Lee’s last film, Burning, might not have made the cut (it was, however, the first Korean film to make it to the final nine-film shortlist) but rapturous reviews for his latest, along with timely themes of class and power as well as the might of Netflix behind it, could turn it into one of the year’s best international feature nominees. The major English language success story came from Martin McDonagh, who has previously used the festival as a springboard for Oscar nominations or wins for films such as Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin. His latest, Wild Horse Nine, might not have quite the same amount of universal acclaim but it’s hard not to see it picking up multiple nominations. Its most likely win would be for John Malkovich, who has two nods under his belt but is yet to take an Oscar home. There was also the world premiere of Primetime, the thriller that sees Robert Pattinson play To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen, but it felt more curio than contender, the only real thing anyone could agree on being the surprisingly effective supporting performance from Skyler Gisondo, who could factor into the race. The Golden Lion, again not always a predictor of Oscar success (winners have included Father Mother Sister Brother, Roma, The Room Next Door and Nomadland), was awarded to Woman Unknown, a well-regarded Danish thriller that will likely be an international feature competitor but might not break into other major categories. Next was Telluride with a more stacked lineup than Venice, led by two films that might well feature the season’s two lead acting winners. First was Elsinore, a drama starring Andrew Scott as the Chariots of Fire actor Ian Charleson as he plays Hamlet while dealing with the devastation of the Aids crisis. While some were sniffier about what was perceived as “Oscarbait” storytelling, virtually all agreed that Scott had acted his way to the front of the pack for best actor. Notably the film did go down well enough at Toronto to win the people’s choice award for international film, suggesting it may also receive some other high-profile nods. Meanwhile the best actress race found itself suddenly led by Julianne Moore for her all-in performance in Jesse Eisenberg’s offbeat theatre comedy The Debut. While it’s unusual for a turn quite so wildly comedic and devoid of much recognisable humanity to win (Emma Stone in Poor Things might be a recent example but that character did have some pathos), Moore is beloved by the Academy (one win and another four nominations) and while A Real Pain wasn’t embraced by the Academy as much as some expected (a win for Kieran Culkin and just one other nod), the film’s focus on acting will appeal to a lot of voters. The long weekend also saw the premiere of Tender Loving Care, what might well be Mike Leigh’s final film. It’s another humane, textured and universally adored comedy drama about the lives of recognisably real people and while critics circles will likely shower it, the Academy hasn’t gravitated towards his films for a while. Hard Truths was snubbed, Another Year had just one nod for screenplay (and criminally nothing for Lesley Manville), Peterloo received no noms, while his only winning film is Topsy-Turvy and that was for below-the-line craft. What might lift this one slightly for voters is both the fact that Leigh said it could likely be his swan song and the presence of Kate O’Flynn, still riding high after her Emmys triumph for Apple’s hit horror comedy Widow’s Bay. She may well see herself in the supporting actress category. Elsewhere, Carrie Coon impressed in cult drama The Liberation but the film had mixed notices. There was also a last-minute surprise screening of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder’s unconventional, almost three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary, which some are claiming could be an unlikely best picture nominee, though this would be a first in the category. A documentary nod seems more likely, although that branch has mostly favoured international films of late. Toronto came next with a lineup stacked with films but of a noticeably lower wattage than what once was. On the ground, it was mostly repeats of films that had premiered elsewhere that received the most attention, with The Debut, Elsinore and La Bola Negra in particular getting a substantial boost, the first foreign language winner of the people’s choice award since 2011. Of the festival’s world premieres, the biggest hit seemed to be Peter Farrelly’s making-of drama I Play Rocky, which had a standing ovation and was the runner-up for people’s choice. Farrelly previously saw his crowd-pleasing comedy Green Book go from Toronto hit to best picture winner, and while his Stallone biopic might not feel quite as primed with fewer social issues in its corner, its ability to energise audiences could see it land a nomination at the least. There were a number of failed best actress bids from Cynthia Erivo with a mostly loathed adaptation of award-winning play Prima Facie, Sarah Paulson with buzz-free dame v dame drama Closing Night and Naomi Watts with misfiring Nazi thriller The Housewife, none of which have found a US buyer as yet. Far more convincing was British Slow Horses star Rosalind Eleazar, who rose above Chris Rock’s otherwise patchy Hollywood saga Misty Green to impress with a turn that could see her sneak in, especially given how weak that category is this year. This week sees the kick-off of the New York film festival with more world premieres than usual. Andrew Garfield will be hoping his Sam Altman impression in OpenAI saga Artificial is good enough to reintroduce director Luca Guadagnino into the Academy’s good books, Tom McCarthy will be aiming to repeat his Spotlight glory with talky, 80s-set climate change drama A Statement, and Tony Gilroy’s music drama Behemoth! will try to launch Pedro Pascal as a late best actor challenger. Outside of festivals, two-time best director winner Alejandro González Iñárritu is dragging Tom Cruise out of his comfort zone in the darkly comedic satire Digger (which some are suggesting will be bigger for supporting actor John Goodman than its lead) the week before Aaron Sorkin tries to copy The Social Network’s success with follow-up The Social Reckoning led by best actress winner Mikey Madison. Soon we’ll also see one-time Oscar mainstay David O Russell return with the sports biopic Madden, starring Oscar winners Nicolas Cage and Christian Bale, his first film since 2022’s disastrous Amsterdam; Robert Eggers following Nosferatu, which surprised with four nominations, with another gothic horror called Werwulf; and the return of Dune, a franchise that has so far won eight Oscars, with the third and “final” chapter. Could we have a best picture-winning Return of the King on our hands? Seven safe-ish nominee bets Christopher Nolan – best director, The Odyssey Julianne Moore – best actress, The Debut Andrew Scott – best actor, Elsinore Inde Navarrette – best actress, Obsession John Malkovich – best actor, Wild Horse Nine Rashida Jones and Will McCormack – best adapted screenplay, The Invite John Goodman – best supporting actor, Digger

headline: Nick Clegg plays down fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity
trail_text: Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’
body_text: Nick Clegg has dismissed fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, calling it a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”. The former UK deputy prime minister said that tech bosses should focus on addressing known specific threats such as cybersecurity and bioweapons rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”. Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he said: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.” Clegg, who was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta and owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs, said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry. “They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said, noting that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”. “There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things,” he said. Asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face, Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency”. However, he said this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI. He also suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”. He added: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.” Asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, Clegg noted the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.” Clegg also disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence. Instead, he suggested: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”

headline: What’s on the agenda for the Trump-Xi summit, and what won’t they discuss?
trail_text: Two leaders could discuss tech safety issues and US-China trade ties but may skip over climate emergency
body_text: The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are meeting in the US on Thursday for Xi Jinping’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade. The last time the Chinese president was hosted in Washington (by Barack Obama in 2015), the issues on the agenda included cybercrime, technology, the climate crisis and human rights. The star of the day was Ne-Yo, who serenaded Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, with Peng reportedly singing along at the state dinner. This time, Xi is meeting Donald Trump, who has overhauled the world order and recalibrated the US-China relationship. Trump is contending with a China that is in a much stronger position than it was 10 years ago. Here are five things to look out for at the US-China summit. Artificial intelligence Although AI was surprisingly absent from talks the last time Xi and Trump met, in Beijing in May, it is expected to be high on the agenda. There are calls for the two leaders to agree some sort of AI safety framework to prevent the technology – about which there have been dire warnings in recent weeks – from spinning out of human control. But Trump has called warnings about safety a “hoax”, and although Xi has called for “safety and security in AI development”, China sees AI as the key to unlocking its own national potential and bristles at US efforts to contain its progress. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, recently suggested that the two countries establish a mechanism to communicate on major AI safety issues. Xi and Trump may discuss further details. But Amanda Hsiao, the China director at the Eurasia Group, says: “The question that’s going to raise is just how is it going to be operationalised, and will it be effective. Because the US and China have had a long history of having crisis hotlines, and they haven’t always been effective.” Trade The biggest thorn in the US-China relationship is trade. When Trump launched a global trade war last year, with the biggest target being China, it risked bringing the world economy to its knees. China reciprocated with tariffs on US goods approaching 150% and unveiled a host of other retaliatory measures, most notably restricting the export of rare earths that are vital for US manufacturing. Since then, a temporary truce in the trade war, and Trump’s war in Iran, have stabilised the US-China trading relationship, with the source of global economic pain coming from the Middle East rather than China. But the truce is set to expire in November. With Trump and Xi expected to meet two further times this year, there may not be a trade deal announced at this week’s summit. But although China has weathered the trade war better than expected, with exports to other countries booming, finding a longer-term agreement to restore the flow of goods to China’s biggest market will be a high priority for Xi. Taiwan China’s ambassador to the US, Xie Feng, published an article on Wednesday outlining “four red lines” for the summit. First on the list was Taiwan. Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, has become an increasingly sensitive topic for Beijing. China wants to isolate Taiwan on the world stage and put pressure on the US to reduce its support for Taiwan’s defences, both of which would make it easier for it to annex the island. After the May Xi-Trump summit, Trump agreed to delay a $14bn package of weapons sales to Taiwan, calling it “very good negotiating chip”. Beijing rejects the idea of bargaining over Taiwan, describing it as a domestic Chinese issue. Nevertheless, says William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, “the Chinese side definitely feels that Trump is a rare US president that might offer a rare window of opportunity for them to influence American policy on Taiwan, specifically on defence support”. The leaders may discuss conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, but China has been unwilling to get meaningfully involved in peace negotiations. Human rights Second on Xie’s list was democracy and human rights. In Trump, Beijing has found a US president who is less interested than any of his predecessors in lecturing China about its human rights record. In 2015, Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state, called Xi “shameless” for hosting a UN summit on women while “persecuting feminists” at home. Barack Obama, then the US president, skipped Xi’s session. Trump is unlikely to echo such sentiments, even though some in his inner circle, most notably his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, are sharply critical of China’s policies. But Trump may raise individual cases. In May he raised the case of Ezra Jin, a detained Christian pastor, which seemed to contribute to Jin’s release from prison weeks later. Yufang Rong, the wife of a US nuclear scientist who has been imprisoned in China since late 2024, said this week that the White House had assured her that Trump would ask Xi to free her husband. Trump may also raise the case of Min Zin, a US expert on Myanmar, who was arrested in China in June. The most difficult and high-profile case, however, is that of Jimmy Lai, a British pro-democracy activist who was jailed in Hong Kong on national security charges. Despite promising to secure Lai’s release during his presidential campaign in 2024, Trump conceded in May that Beijing was unwilling to budge on Lai’s case, calling it “a tough one”. Climate crisis Notably absent from the talks will be any meaningful discussion about the climate crisis. Tackling the climate emergency used to be described as one of the few areas where the US and China could meaningfully cooperate, with China’s huge strides in decarbonising its economy seen as an area where it could show leadership on US-endorsed goals. But Yang says: “The climate conversation is just not really a topic that Trump is interested in talking about.” Not only has Trump withdrawn the US from the Paris agreement but Beijing and Washington are too divided on a host of issues to talk about cooperation. “They are coming into this summit with very little agreement or consensus in common,” says Yang. headline: ‘Eat the rich, save the planet’: climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from reality
trail_text: Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City
body_text: On Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested while disrupting a closed-door AI health summit in the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters. The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job with a warning that intensified an already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Though it was far from the first time an AI expert had issued a doomsday message about the threat the tech poses, this time it dominated public attention, arriving as trust in big tech has hit an all-time low and communities across the country are trying to stop the building of datacenters. From 2024 to 2026, at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Today, bans have been passed in at least 18 states at the local or county level, and New York passed a statewide moratorium this summer. “They are claiming that they have the power to end humanity, but at the same time can’t get AI to do a lot of major things that they’re pushing for,” said Jonathan Westin of Climate Defenders and the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign, which organized the “unplug AI” week of action. Like Westin, many of the protesters at the anti-AI protests this week were part of climate organizations, in town for New York’s climate week, a global gathering of elected officials, policy experts and advocates timed to the meeting of the United Nations general assembly. Datacenters require significant amounts of water to function and an immense amount of energy to power, often using fossil fuels, bringing pollution into communities. Organizers are calling for more datacenter moratoriums and stronger commitments to protect water access and to block fossil fuels. They say tech companies’ greed is the real threat to the environment. Even Wall Street has warned the AI boom could cause another economic bubble to burst – one that, protesters say, will be carried on the backs of working Americans. “Regular people shouldn’t be left holding the bag for a bunch of billionaires and trillionaires to play Monopoly with our economy,” Westin said. Other groups at this week’s protests, like the anti-war organization Code Pink, called attention to how many big tech corporations work with the US military: the US has used tech made by Palantir, xAI and Anthropic to establish targets and rain down bombs in the war in Iran – all with far-from-perfect accuracy. Alex Hanna, director of research at the Dair Institute, an AI research organization centering communities facing environmental damage and extraction from AI, said the doomsday prophesying from tech companies and former employees are a distraction amid “the climate and ecological crisis, the rising fascism that is borne out of climate politics, the making of climate refugees, and the growing inability of people just to get by from day to day. It’s such a disconnect from what seems to be actually happening.” Some protesters outside the OpenAI offices Monday had traveled from New Mexico, where a planned datacenter threatens the already-sapped Rio Grande and a community facing a 20-year drought. Oracle’s Project Jupiter, which is contracted to OpenAI, was pitched as a job creator for the community, but organizers say the companies aren’t talking about how it would drain the area’s limited water resources. “There’s just so much misinformation that’s being sold, not only to the elected [officials], but to the community, and I think it’s really a disservice to the people of New Mexico for these companies to come in and just basically lie about what they’re going to do and how these projects are going to benefit communities,” said Daisy Maldonado, a resident of Doña Ana county, the planned site of the datacenter. At an AI sustainability conference elsewhere in the city on Tuesday, five protesters were arrested for disrupting a keynote on using AI to solve the energy grid crisis. Activists called out the conference framing as “greenwashing”, or using misleading descriptions to brand something as eco-friendly or less harmful. “We do not want to greenwash these datacenters that are being built,” said Adrosto de Silva, who also traveled from New Mexico to the OpenAI protest. “There is no way that you can do harm reduction in any sort of datacenter whatsoever.” At Monday’s protest, attendees – including the Tennessee state representative Justin Jones, who dropped in while in town for climate week – emphasized that many of these fights are happening in communities of color and poor communities, where the companies thought they wouldn’t face local backlash. “This building behind me is a danger to humankind,” said Jones, gesturing at the OpenAI offices. “The confluence of this techno oligarchy is a threat to us all. I’m here because if they come for one of us, they’re coming for all of us.”

headline: The eyes have it: Rory Stewart’s ‘magnificently strange’ Newsnight moment goes viral
trail_text: Clip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist is shared widely online
body_text: Rory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province. This week, he created a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: he fixed a beady gaze on a fellow Newsnight panellist for the longest four seconds in television history. Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics podcast with Alastair Campbell, appeared on the BBC programme on 18 September – but in the last few days, a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media. Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI). After Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus. Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour had not appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme,” he said. He only became aware of what had happened when several friends texted him. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.” He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.” Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019. “It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said. Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added. He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph, winked at the camera. “This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.” Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting. The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place. The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.” Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”

headline: AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’
trail_text: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents
body_text: Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s statistics website will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. OpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to the June hacking via an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”. But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident. “All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia. “Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them. “When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities. “All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Arabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here. Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable. Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute. “Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg,” she said. “Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.” The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches. “We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg but, either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk,” Shen said. “It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on. “This strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.” Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack. It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI and how government systems can be strengthened. The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US. “If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector and other things that are important to us,” he said. The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what the president, Donald Trump, knew about the attack. “This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” the Greens’ acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said. “The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”

headline: Parents and carers: how has your view on your children’s use of social media or AI changed?

body_text: AI and social media companies have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months for some of the ways the technology they’re building operates, especially when it comes to their younger users. AI developer OpenAI is facing dozens of lawsuits that allege its ChatGPT bot lacks safety guardrails. headline: Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?
trail_text: Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips
body_text: One is an authoritarian who represses the media and has a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party. Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries. “Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.” While Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt. And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”. That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China. The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X: “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…” Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet? “I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!” Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised. Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng. Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave. Trump touted his “truly ⁠great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries ⁠had made strides on trade since his trip to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist. The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.” He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”. Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill. But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”. Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead! Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will send two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta. Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower. But with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.” Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit). None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp? Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips. When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not. Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn, Trump reported: “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.” Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies. By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

headline: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
trail_text: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
body_text: Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase. “We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on. “We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, referring to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power. Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it. His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other. Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president. “President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said. Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.” He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday. Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.” The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac. Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on. Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches. Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures. “Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.” Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader. “President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said. Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together. “China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said. Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues. In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development. A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said. Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December. Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continued to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running. Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting • This article was amended on 24 and 25 September 2026. Misspellings of Xi Jinping in the headline and text were corrected. And China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus, not deficit.

headline: Trump touts ‘great meeting’ with Xi at White House – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: We’re going to close this live page now and continue our coverage of the Trump-Xi summit in our US politics blog here. As Robert Mackey has just reported, tonight’s state dinner in Xi Jinping’s honour will not be televised because the White House has continued to deny full access to the event to CNN journalists on Thursday, despite a court order. Read more here. Recapping some of the day’s key newslines: Xi called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course. He also said the Chinese and US economic and trade teams had reached a new joint agreement, which he called “good news for the global economy”. Xi said Beijing hoped the ⁠US ⁠adhered to ‌the “correct” position of opposing “Taiwan ‌independence” and handles the Taiwan ‌question with prudence. On the US-Israeli war with Iran, he said China supported ‌the US and Tehran returning to a June memorandum of understanding ‌that was meant to end the war and ⁠reopen the strait of Hormuz. Trump said he and ⁠Xi had a “great meeting” after ⁠the two leaders ‌met ‌at the White ‌House. Here’s a summary of the leaders’ remarks before the talks. There was no sign of breakthroughs on contentious issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan or the Iran war. In remarks after Xi’s arrival on Thursday, Trump emphasised his “truly great friendship” with the Chinese leader, rather than focusing on policy differences, and said the two ‌powers had made strides on trade since his trip to China in May. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship.” Xi said the two countries’ interests were deeply intertwined and that competition between them should be a “healthy one”. US companies were welcome in China, he said, ‌while expressing hope Chinese companies were “treated fairly” in the US. The head of ⁠the Airlines for America industry group said US carriers opposed adding more direct flights from China to America, while Xi said it might happen. As Donald and Melania Trump welcomed Xi Jinping and Peng Liyuan for the black-tie state dinner, outside the White House gate a group of loud demonstrators shouted slogans like “China out ⁠of Hong Kong”. The protests were clearly audible to the US and Chinese leaders ⁠as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps, Reuters is reporting. During a bilateral discussion in the afternoon, Xi urged the US to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua shortly after it concluded. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary of the talks. Xi had been expected to press Trump this week to halt arms sales to Taiwan. The 30-second ad, which uses audio of Donald Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” includes a rapid-fire montage of images from his second term displayed beneath the on-screen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN.
