Michael Oren, the former Israeli ambassador, said he expected Netanyahu’s UN address to resemble a “campaign speech,” leveraging his feud with the mayor of the largest Jewish city outside of Israel to boost his political position at home. “Maybe he’s thinking, ‘if I can attack Mamdani and attack the Iranians, somebody who was wavering between ‌voting for me and voting for (Gadi) Eisenkot may decide to vote for me’,” Oren told Reuters, referring to Netanyahu’s main political rival in next month’s Israeli general election. In a video statement earlier this week, Netanyahu falsely accused Mamdani, New York City’s first Muslim mayor, of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against the city’s Jewish population. Mamdani said earlier this year that he was looking into whether his office could arrest Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over alleged war crimes in Gaza, if he visited New York. But he later conceded that he did not have the legal authority to do so. The US is not a party to the ICC and does not recognize its authority. Despite his criticism of the Israeli government and staunch support for Palestinian rights, Mamdani is reportedly not taking part in the protests against Netanyahu scheduled to take place in New York. The New York Times reported that he will instead be visiting an LGBTQ+ centre with the prime minister of the Netherlands. The president of the Palestinian Authority, Mahmoud Abbas, will also be addressing the UN General Assembly via video. Like last year, Abbas was banned from entering the US by the Trump administration, with the State Department saying in a statement that the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments.” The news has been trickling in this morning from the White House reporters showing back up for work, but now it’s confirmed that all three outlets targeted in Trump’s White House press ban are saying they’re still being denied access to the building, after a judge’s order to let them back in. We’ll see as the morning wears on whether that changes. Yesterday evening, after briefly taking the case under consideration, a federal judge ordered the White House to temporarily restore access to CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, the three outlets the president banned from the building via a social media post last week. White House security may not have gotten the memo, according to Thursday morning reports from the three news outlets involved. All three reported that they had journalists turned away from the White House early in the morning. Politico wrote this morning that a reporter showing up for work was blocked from entering the White House on Thursday and had his press credentials seized. The alleged denial of entry came after a federal judge instructed the Trump administration last night to allow the news outlets their usual access while their lawsuit against the president over the ban moves forward. CNN reported that some its staff – including reporter Betsy Klein and a photojournalist – were barred from entering the White House early on Thursday around 6a.m., without receiving a reason for being denied entry. However, the channel said one of its producers gained entry to the building using their pass. Some CNN staff, however, were unable to gain access to the White House early Thursday morning. CNN reporter Betsy Klein and a photojournalist were denied access to the White House grounds in the 6:00 a.m. hour. The Associated Press also reported that a CNN journalist told the outlet she was denied access to the White House on Thursday morning. CNN said would it continue trying to gain access to the building as the day goes on. MS Now also reported on Thursday morning that one of its journalists had been barred entry. MS Now White House correspondent Laura Barrón-López said that a member of the secret service informed her that her press credentials were “still coming up as disabled” when scanned. “Then he confiscated my badge, and I had to leave the premises,” she said. Barrón-López said it was unclear whether the refusal of entry was in deliberate defiance of the court order or “incompetence or a lag in the system.” President Trump teased in a social media post this morning that artificial intelligence would be a major part of his talks today with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during his state visit to Washington. He also suggested that he would avoid entertaining any kind of agreement between the two nations limiting AI development. “A big day with President Xi of China,” Trump wrote in the post to his personal social media platform. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ! President DJT.” (Super intelligence is the term Trump has been pushing to refer to artificial intelligence. He pitched the language earlier this week in a tangent during his speech to the world leaders at the United Nations. It’s unclear at this point if anybody is going to take him up on it.) After an unusually warm red carpet welcome ceremony on the tarmac yesterday, Trump is scheduled to receive Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the White House South Portico. The pair will deliver remarks, exchange gifts, and watch a military review before a busy day of talks and diplomatic pageantry. Donald Trump has been raging about a story first reported by MS Now on Wednesday that he is seeking to rename the Ford Theatre in Washington DC, a site infamous for the assassination of president Abraham Lincoln, after himself. Last night he posted on Truth Social about the news item, blaming “Dumocrats” for the “ridiculous lie.” This morning, hours after the late night ruling from the judge that temporarily reinstated CNN, Politico, and MS Now, Trump (again) said: The Dumocrats make up lie after lie. The new one is that I want Ford’s Theater named after me. That’s where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. Who would want that? I don’t! It is FAKE NEWS started by MSDNC AND CNN. This is his first mention of the day of his lesser-favored media outlets. He has not acknowledged the judge’s ruling to restore them access to the White House – yet. We’ll bring you more lines as they come in. Some more background information on this ongoing situation between the Trump administration and the White House press correspondents: The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, saying the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They requested a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out. Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be ⁠able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” and justice department lawyers had ‌sought to justify the ban on national security grounds. A Justice Department lawyer told the judge the Trump administration provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the press passes in letters sent to the news outlets on Tuesday. But the judge signaled skepticism of that argument, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed. In a legal filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department argued that access to the ‌White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president has the authority to suspend access by news organizations. Good morning and welcome to the US politics live blog. We start now with breaking news from the late night hours: a federal judge has temporarily restored White House access to journalists from CNN, Politico and MS Now after president Donald Trump banned them due to their coverage of his administration. US district judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organizations filed ‌contesting the ban that the president announced on 18 September, saying it was ⁠likely unconstitutional. Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and issued a temporary restraining order that will be in effect for 14 days. headline: Friday briefing: How a ​grassroots ​film ​is ​turning ​climate anxiety ​into ​action
trail_text: In today’s newsletter: The People’s Emergency Briefing delivers a stark warning about ​o​ur future in a warming world. ​B​ut sharing difficult truths collectively​ shows us that there is still hope to be found
body_text: Good morning. Here we are, stumbling into an oddly warm autumn and with the aftermath of a ceaselessly dry summer all around us in our parched parks and fire-ravaged forests. With the change in season, the headlines are no less gruelling. At the start of the week, more than 450,000 people are predicted to die from an unprecedented El Niño over the next six months. At the end of the week, a report by UK intelligence chiefs reveals the extent to which the collapse of natural systems threatens security and defence around the world – a report which, as the Guardian revealed, was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer’s leadership. Meanwhile, as Hettie has written about in a previous newsletter, right-leaning climate sceptics continue to seed doubt about the glaring reality wherever they may. Overload, silencing and misinformation can generate fear, suspicion, grief, helplessness, a compulsion to look away or to focus on paying the next bill. But this summer, I’ve been hearing about another climate briefing – in film form – that aims to engage all of those emotions. It’s as much about giving people the information they deserve as it is about helping them deal with it once they have it. You won’t see it on Netflix, but your neighbour might be screening it at the local scout hall this weekend: for today’s newsletter, I spoke to Nick Oldridge, co-founder of the People’s Emergency Briefing, about how a film about the end of the world became a grassroots movement. First, the headlines. Five big stories UN general assembly | Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza. UK news | Far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy while a rescuer was onboard. Iran | Iran says it has told Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some frozen assets. Ukraine | Ukrainian refugees fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments. World news | Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over AI, trade and Taiwan. In depth: ‘It’s clear evidence that this model works for engaging politicians’ Have you seen that climate film yet? You know, the one you read about on the Guardian website and then a friend of a friend emailed you about it, but other things got in the way until your best pal watched it and said you absolutely had to see it and then you looked it up and realised there were screenings happening all around you. That was my experience, at least. The People’s Emergency Briefing began life, in real life. Last November, nine climate experts delivered a “first-of-its-kind national emergency briefing” to an audience of MPs, civic and business leaders in Westminster. It was, by all reports, a galvanising event. The organising team – including pioneer in carbon footprinting Prof Mike Berners-Lee and TV environmentalist Chris Packham – then crowdfunded to turn the in-person briefing into a film, which anyone can register to screen in their local village hall, faith centre, workplace or wherever else they can get bums on seats. I watched the briefing myself at an arts centre in Paisley on a sunny Friday evening last month. The 50-minute film felt like 15, as the roster of experts set out in plain language how global heating is affecting all aspects of life in the UK: the economy, food, healthcare, nature, national security. It’s a hard watch. The alarming – but never alarmist – message is that the climate is changing much faster than expected, and that we are woefully unprepared for it. The grinding frustration of these experts – who have been repeating these stark facts to a sclerotic government and a sceptical public for years – is evident, but there is also hope. The aim is to demand that the prime minister convenes a Covid-style primetime emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis, led by independent experts. As Packham says as he introduces the film: “I understand it’s human nature to prefer not to know, to try to bury our heads in the sand. But if we all take a breath and watch this together, well first of all that’s a huge relief and second we can figure out what to do about it.” *** Do it like Gogglebox What’s unique about the film is both how it’s framed and how it’s watched. “We knew you can’t just film people talking at podiums,” Oldridge explains, “so we decided: ‘We’ll do it like Gogglebox’.” Spliced between the expert commentary, members of the public sit on a sofa across from Packham and talk about what they’ve just watched. “This is the nub of it,” says Oldridge. “This film has got to be watched in groups, people who experience it together and then talk about it, instead of the isolated way we usually consume media.” Since the first community screening on 7 April, the film has become a word-of-mouth phenomenon – so far 2,789 screenings have taken place, with a further 1,395 planned. Readers across the country, from the south of England to north-east Scotland, have contacted the Guardian’s Environment desk to tell us about their involvement. Anna Taylor, trustee of Wendover Climate Action, who organised a packed screening in the Buckinghamshire village after reading about the original Westminster event in the Guardian, told me: “It’s spurred me on so that, if nothing else, my kids will know I tried to make things better for them”. Any group can register to host a screening, and will receive a carefully scripted guide for steering the discussion afterwards as viewers process some difficult material. Organisers have told me how essential it felt for people to sit together and share their immediate reflections on what was a shocking film for many, even those who considered themselves familiar with climate science. That was my experience: the lump in my throat got smaller as I listened to other people talking about their visceral shock, anxiety and plans to take action. Groups are also encouraged to invite local politicians – not to put them on stage to shout at but so they can sit among the audience as another community member. (Eleven were invited to the Paisley screening, none came – you know who you are!). *** Will it burst through the eco-bubble? One of the threads we unravelled in the discussion after my screening was how to normalise climate conversations: “How do we reach people who don’t even believe climate change is happening?” asked one woman. (It’s worth interjecting here that tracker polling suggests this summer’s extreme weather has prompted a big jump in voters’ ranking of the environment as an issue.) But it’s a question that the People’s Emergency Briefing team have wrangled with extensively. Inevitably there’s an element of self-selection with community screenings, but there’s ongoing work to bring the film to wider audiences at Quaker meeting houses, churches and cathedrals, the Women’s Institute, hospitals, school staff rooms, the national lottery, the V&A, Channel 4, and even here at the Guardian. All the organisers I heard from had plans to run more screenings and diversify audiences, while viewers reported feeling more hopeful, better informed and more motivated to act. “We first realised something was happening when we watched the booming community screenings,” says Oldridge. “But now all these big brands are doing it too. You’re always trying to break beyond the eco-bubble and I think we’ve got a very good chance of doing that now”. *** What difference can it make? In recent years, the orthodoxy around climate communications has tended towards telling only hopeful stories, with a recognition that the public were beyond capacity for bad news. “But we felt quite strongly that we need to reset the baseline of understanding,” says Oldridge. “Most surveys show people are worried, but they see it as a far away problem. And they don’t have all the facts that relate to the UK and their own lives.” This is especially salient when the right weaponise net zero as a threat to the economy. Mindful of this context, the film is trenchant in its optimism. It avoids finger-wagging; there’s no scolding of those of us who still fly or eat cheese. There’s a recognition that – however helpful individual effort can be – climate change isn’t a problem that isolated action can solve. Rather, it calls for an emergency response equal to that rolled out during the pandemic, or a war. “Our effort is focused purely on change driven by government, helping the public understand that they are one of the pieces of the jigsaw that enable the government to be bold enough to make those changes,” says Oldridge. A major academic study of the film’s impact will be published next month and early findings suggest that every screening in a constituency makes its MP more likely to back a televised emergency briefing. “It’s clear evidence that this model works for engaging politicians.” There is engagement too at the top of government, according to our environment editor Fiona Harvey. She reported this week how Ed Miliband brought the national security warnings to global attention at the UN general assembly in New York, with the backing of Andy Burnham. It marks a growing openness from the prime minister towards climate action, she believes, encouraged by Miliband and that goes beyond campaigning pragmatism ahead of the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Labour is taking on Green leader Zack Polanski. Perhaps there is room for guarded optimism, as there is in this devastating film about the systemic collapse of society that is paradoxically hopeful. As one member of the public says on screen: “It’s not as if we need to go off and invent all the solutions. They’re right there. We just need to use them”. What else we’ve been enjoying Our politics and graphics desks teamed up on this exclusive report into how, as it stands, tactical voting could push Reform into fourth and leave Labour clinging to a thin majority at the next election. (And here’s a bonus read on the five progressive groups they will need to satisfy to even have a chance). Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team This gallery of shots from French photographer Martine Barrat, of people in Harlem and the Bronx in the 70s and 80s, is beyond beautiful. Barrat had a deep love for these neighbourhoods, and their communities, and it radiates from every tender photograph. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team Fascinating piece for this week’s Moving the Goalposts newsletter by Elizabeth Payne on whether the time has come for separated home and away seating at women’s football. Charlie Before you write off this year’s Oscars battle as a one-(Trojan)-horse race, have a read of Benjamin Lee’s excellent run down of the contenders who might stop The Odyssey sweeping the boards. Lucinda For the Filter, Bay Garnett has an authoritative guide to secondhand shopping in 2026 – “Wear and tear isn’t necessarily a reason to put something back,” she rightly urges. Charlie Sport Football | Joao Felix scored the only goal as reigning Nations League champions Portugal opened their campaign with a 1-0 home win over Wales; and a stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 draw for the Netherlands against Germany. Cricket | Sri Lanka pulled off a dramatic 16-run win over England in the second one-day international at Headingley ⁠to level the three-match ⁠series despite a heroic effort from injured Jos Buttler. Rugby union | Harlequins, Northampton and Gloucester are attracting serious interest from overseas investors with Prem Rugby entering an expansionist phase before its first season as a closed league begins on Friday. Something for the weekend Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now TV The Great British Bake Off (Channel 4) | ★★★★★ The culinary competition’s newest judge, Nigella Lawson, is a soothing presence, bringing a streak of romance that perfectly complements Paul Hollywood’s ever-practical approach. Read Lucy Mangan’s full review. Music Gilla Band: Pugnello | ★★★★★ Your favourite band’s favourite band unleash a thrilling and relentless 42 minutes of monstrous noise whose precise instrumental source always remains discomfitingly unclear. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review. Film Remake (in cinemas now) | ★★★★★ Sherman’s March director Ross McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art. Read Leslie Felperin’s full review. Art Amar Kanwar (Serpentine North) | ★★★★☆ Having made lyrical films for over 40 years, about everything from the end of empire to sexual brutality, the unflinching Indian artist’s new exhibition continues his focus on the parts of gruesome stories that are often missed. Read Ben Eastham’s full review. The front pages The Guardian splashes on “Two-year delay in assessments of autism due to pressures on NHS”. The FT leads with “Xi urges rivals to ‘coexist in peace’ as Trump hosts White House visit” and the Independent has “Trump and Xi clash over AI at tense state visit”. Top story at the Times is “Met chief: Stop putting offenders before victims”, the Daily Mail has “Labour’s army of migrants” and The i Paper leads on “NHS corridor care killing 550 people every week”. The Telegraph reports “Fiennes kept in care home illegally”, the Sun goes with “Fergie’s squeaky bum time for royals” and the Mirror has “I was sexually assaulted by celeb at home” – in relation to the former England striker Andy Carroll. The Latest Rogue AI hacks government system for first time A government database has been hacked for the first time by a rogue OpenAI agent, which infiltrated part of the Australian healthcare scheme in June. OpenAI became aware of the hack in August, but only informed the government in September. Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has expressed his “extreme concern” about the hack, which raises serious AI security concerns for governments around the world. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s UK technology editor Robert Booth. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad It’s officially autumn, but you will have noticed that it’s also sometimes summer and sometimes winter. That can make it hard to figure out what to eat every day, but have no fear: for this week’s Feast newsletter, Honey and Co’s Itamar Srulovich and Sarit Packer scribbled down some ideas. From rice salads to red pepper orecchiette and roasted squash, dig in and find something comforting, no matter the weather. headline: PM rejects ‘nonsense’ suggestion he delayed revealing OpenAI Medicare hack as Labor considers changing laws
trail_text: Expert says Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime
body_text: The federal government could change Australian laws if the current legal framework could not respond to the unprecedented OpenAI hack of Medicare, ministers have confirmed. It comes as the prime minister denied accusations from the opposition he had held on to the information before announcing it at the UN general assembly in New York, and said it was released at the first possible opportunity. “It’s just nonsense … I was informed while I’ve been in New York,” Anthony Albanese told News24 on Friday. “Imagine if we had said there’s been a data breach, but we don’t know what has been sourced, we don’t know if your personal information is out there, that would have created a great deal of anxiety, which was unnecessary. “We had to ascertain the facts, and then we made the statements, as a matter of urgency, we also provided briefings to the opposition, as is appropriate.” The government services minister, Katy Gallagher, said she was informed about the breach on 17 September. Guardian Australia understands she informed the prime minister between Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September. Albanese left for the US on the Friday, where he first met Apple’s executive chair, Tim Cook, in California on Saturday morning, before flying to New York that afternoon. On Friday, the government said the review by spy agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, would consider whether legislative change was needed after Albanese revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare’s statistics website and three other systems in June. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email If current laws could not touch the tech company, they would need updating, environment minister, Murray, Watt said on Friday. “There’s now a review of this under way through that taskforce that we’ve appointed, and one of the things that they’ll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian federal police under current Australian law,” he told Channel Seven’s Sunrise program. “If that is possible to happen, then that will happen. If it’s not possible, then clearly that indicates that we need to change Australian laws, and that’s what we’ll be doing.” The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, acknowledged similar incidents would become “more and more prevalent into the future” and the government would need to be prepared. “That’s why we’re conducting a review of the incident as well as a review of the laws to determine exactly … whether there needs to be legislative change to recognise this type of incident conducted by an AI agent rather than directly by a person or a company,” Charlton told ABC radio. Albanese told the Asia Society on Thursday that the incident was a “wake-up call” about the risks of AI, and whether humans would remain in charge of the technology. “This technology is moving very, very fast, and we need to make sure that we have a responsibility to keep on top of it,” Albanese said. Labor has announced it would legislate an AI standard, which Charlton said would be informed by the rapid review. The government has said it wants the bill to be introduced by the end of the year. UNSW professor Lyria Bennett Moses, an academic expert in technology and law, said Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault, such as intention or knowledge, is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime. She said existing laws are clear if a human or corporation gains unauthorised access to restricted data, but it’s more complicated when an AI agent commits the physical element of the offence. “The person is not the AI agent, so it’s not about what the AI agent intended. It’s about how you attribute that intention and that knowledge back to a corporation,” Bennett Moses said. Bennett Moses said existing civil laws are more likely to deal with these sorts of incidents, that would allow a government or individual to seek compensation an AI company for harm “negligently caused by that corporation”. “If their systems have suffered harm and there is financial loss, and that harm was caused by the negligence of a corporation, you’ve got a potential for litigation to get compensation for that harm,” she said. “Here it seems to me much easier to hold a company liable, because if a company caused the harm, it’s not a defence to say that my bot did it.” Independent senator, David Pocock said the incident “raises serious questions” for the government after it initially, in 2024, considered mandatory guidelines for high-risk AI but then dropped them in late 2025. “It’s great to see the PM on the world stage saying that we need global cooperation on this. We absolutely do. This is a huge challenge facing us. But it’s a bit rich where at home you’ve shelved plans for an AI safety act.” The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told reporters the Coalition would be open to working with the government to hold companies accountable. “I’ve long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it … But we’ll wait and see what the government has in mind.” OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, said on Thursday the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement. Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

headline: Would you bet on the future of our planet?
trail_text: Prediction markets are focusing on extreme weather and the climate crisis. But as scientists warn of an increasingly unpredictable planet it’s led to questions about what exactly people are betting on
body_text: How hot will it get in your nearest city tomorrow? How quickly will the planet’s ice melt and its corals die off? How many huge, costly climate disasters will hit this year? If you’re inclined to do so, you can now place online bets on how the weather and the broader, longer-term climate crisis will play out. In the US, big online prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket are considering a new area of growth beyond mere sport and crypto: the climate itself. Kalshi recently reported 500% growth in weather and climate wagers over the past year, taking the market to a $1.1bn, and is now partnering with the Weather Company, which owns the Weather Channel, to boost its credibility in this new arena. What does this mean for our ability to predict the future of our climate? More, after this week’s most important reads. Essential reads Huge El Niño projected to cause more than 450,000 deaths by February ‘Planetary boundaries’ necessary for flourishing of life have been massively breached, scientists warn British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it | Andy Burnham In focus Betting on the weather isn’t new, but some climate scientists have been left feeling queasy about people placing bets on the well-documented breakdown of a stable climate, caused by the burning of fossil fuels. Such bets, they argue, trivialise and gamify raw human suffering, distancing people rather than rallying them to act on the climate crisis. Particular alarm has been raised about the consequences of betting on wildfires, after large wagers were placed on the Los Angeles fires last year (Kalshi and Polymarket stress they have banned such betting, due to unintended incentives for would-be arsonists). “I find it depressing because it’s distracting us from what we should be focusing on,” said Kaitlyn Trudeau, a scientist at the non-profit Climate Central. Trudeau’s own grandfather lost his home in the LA fires, and she was aghast to find that people had been betting on the disaster. “I’m not against prediction markets in general but we need to be clear about the downsides,” she said. “They aren’t going to reduce the risks of climate change or solve climate change.” When I covered the story this month, though, it was striking to me how these prediction markets, which are essentially a gauge of public opinion, see their role as forecasting events in the natural world. A Kalshi spokesperson told me the company sees itself as part of “well-calibrated forecasting data” – essentially using the wisdom of the market to help predict how hot it will get, how bad floods will become and other such environmental outcomes. A growing array of data, and the use of artificial intelligence in harnessing it, is indeed helping scientists work out thorny questions over how the climate crisis is set to unfold. Perhaps prediction markets will be able to add to this in some way. But recent evidence suggests that anyone predicting exactly what will happen to our planet – other than it generally getting hotter, more chaotic and more dangerous – over this century will have a tough task. The United Nations recently conceded that a foundational international target to restrain the global temperature rise to 1.5C beyond pre-industrial times – a promise made just a decade ago – is now already effectively trashed. Global heating is too rapid, and too unrestrained, to meet the 1.5C goal, which will cast billions of people into the throes of extreme weather, food insecurity and heightened risk of the sort of cataclysm we recently saw in Nepal. Conversely, the advance of clean energy means that the very worst previous scenario, a pathway known as RCP8.5 and lined with rampant coal burning, is now unlikely. The absolute worst, but also the most optimistic, scenarios have been swept from the table, all in just a handful of years. The world itself will have further surprises in store for us as we blunderingly fiddle with its chemistry. “Feedback loops” from natural systems such as thawing permafrost, supersized wildfires and overheating wetlands mean that planet-heating emissions coming from such sources could accelerate overall global heating by as much as 30%, a recent study found. This will add as much as 0.4C to the overall global temperature – a large chunk on top of what is already set to be a disastrous rise in heat. But even in this stark new study, researchers caution that there are uncertainties. While for now we still retain some control over our own destiny, the situation could still gallop away from humanity – the planet, once provoked, could unleash far hotter temperatures than this. Perhaps – hopefully – it will be less sensitive. But do you really want to bet on that? headline: Pocock calls for AI safety act after Medicare breach – as it happened
trail_text: Follow the day’s news live
body_text: That’s a wrap on our live coverage for today! Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines: Anthony Albanese has called the first reported artificial intelligence agent hack into an Australian government website a “wake-up call” of the dangers of the technology. James Paterson has questioned the timing of the prime minister’s announcement about the hack, saying he believed Albanese had chosen to make the announcement at the UN summit in New York, as part of his effort to stand up to “big tech” on AI. The PM has denied the suggestion and called it “nonsense”. Staying on the PM’s US trip, Albanese detailed Australia’s bid for a temporary seat on the UN security council for 2029 to 2030. Australia’s gen Z are the generation most willing to cut their spending way back to afford a home, according to new Cotality data. An investigation is under way after a police officer was killed in a crash in Sydney’s inner west. The commissioner has paid tribute to the young female cop. Renters in New South Wales will only need to provide their driver’s licences and passports if they are about to sign a lease, instead of including them in every rental application, under new laws. Thanks for joining us, and have a lovely weekend! The independent senator David Pocock says the recent AI agent breach raises serious questions about Australia’s approach to artificial intelligence regulation. Speaking on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Pocock said the incident demonstrated the need for the government to introduce an AI safety act. This is not a new problem. For many years now experts have been saying we need action on this. The crossbench has been pushing them. The government then said, ‘we’ll have some guardrails, we’ll put them on a website’ … that’s not enough. Clearly it’s not. This is a huge challenge facing us. Qld parliamentary review of liability bill chooses not to hear from sexual abuse victims A Queensland parliamentary committee reviewing a bill to overturn a ban on lawsuits by child sexual abuse victims against some employers has chosen not to hear from any victim-survivors. The state Labor MP Meaghan Scanlon tabled the bill last year. It reverses a 2024 high court judgment ruling that the Catholic church was not legally responsible for the actions of a priest, because they were not a direct employee. The judgment also applies to all other employers. Similar legislation has already passed parliaments in Victoria and the ACT. The Queensland parliament’s justice, integrity and community safety committee held a single two-hour hearing into the bill this morning. The committee, which has a government chair, chose only to hear from lawyers. Child abuse survivor Diane Carpenter said she was “devastated” not to be allowed to be heard by the inquiry and called for the bill to be passed. If the bill is not passed, many adults who, as children, were abused in institutional care, will have no pathway to justice. Currently, we have two classes of victims: those who can access justice and those who can’t. A new trial date has been set for a British musician and media personality accused of violently raping a fan in a hotel, after a jury was unable to reach a verdict, AAP reports. Rapper Yung Filly, who is legally known as Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, faced trial in July over his 2024 encounter with a 20-year-old woman after a Perth nightclub gig. The 31-year-old was found guilty of two assault offences and acquitted of three sexual penetration charges following an eight-day trial in Western Australia’s district court in July. The jury was hung on three other sexual penetration counts and Barrientos is set to be retried for the charges. He was not required to appear when the case returned to court on Friday and a fresh trial was listed for 2027. The trial, beginning on 15 June in the same court, is expected to run for eight days. Judge Linda Black previously permitted Barrientos to vary his bail so he could travel home to the UK while he awaits retrial. He is understood to have departed Perth in late August. Should dogs be allowed in pubs? We asked Melbourne pet owners With their poll numbers in the dog house, the Victorian Labor government is hoping something as universally loved as pooches will help them. Labor is promising to change the rules to allow people to bring their pups into pubs. Our Victorian state correspondent, Benita Kolovos, hit the streets to find out what people thought of the idea. Good afternoon! Thanks for sticking around, I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of the day’s news. That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take things from here. Take care! Who is James Ashby? Pauline Hanson’s ‘favourite son’ One Nation’s national director James Ashby wields as much – if not more – power over the party as Pauline Hanson herself. Rafqa Touma speaks to Guardian Australia senior correspondent Sarah Martin about Ashby’s rise from PR flack to Hanson’s “favourite son” as One Nation’s popularity soars. Australian shares on track for fourth straight losing week The Australian share market has fallen to a three-month low and is headed for its fourth straight week of losses, as oil prices and bond yields both moved higher, AAP reports. Near noon on Friday, the benchmark S&P/ASX200 index had fallen 0.43% to 8,664, its lowest level since mid-June, while the broader All Ordinaries had dropped 0.55%, to 8,848.2. With a few hours of trading left, the ASX200 was on pace to finish the week down 0.8%, and was also 0.6% lower since the start of the year. The Australian dollar was changing hands for 70.12 US cents, from 70.35 US cents at 5pm on Thursday. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says it’s “nonsense” to suggest the government may have released details about the OpenAI breach when it did because it suited him politically. He told Sky News earlier: It’s just nonsense. We were informed of this late. That’s one of the issues that I raised with Sam Altman when I spoke with him yesterday. I was informed while I’ve been in New York. When pressed if the details were released as soon as possible, the prime minister said: “Absolutely”. This was a unique situation. … We had to ascertain the facts, and then we made the statements, as a matter of urgency. Albanese said he briefed the opposition as appropriate, and said Angus Taylor’s criticism was uncalled for. He needs to act more like a responsible leader of an alternative government if he’s going to be taken seriously. This is a unique situation without precedence. Police have released a photo of Mia Lay, the officer who died in this morning’s crash Read more: More Queensland social housing dwellings vacant for longer More social housing dwellings in Queensland are sitting vacant for longer, according to new data released by the state government. The average downtime for a social housing dwelling has increased from 25.1 days last June to 42.7 days in July. Vacancy rates are slightly up from about 0.56% to 0.6%. The data was released yesterday in response to a parliamentary question. The number of people in the state’s emergency homelessness assistance scheme – which pays hotels and motels to accommodate them – has declined from 3,623 to 2,707. The state made many homeless people ineligible for the system last year. There has been a slight increase in the number of Queenslanders in the state’s public housing system, from 55,913 to 55,998, but a decline in the number on the social housing waiting list, from 53,874 last September to 46,037 in July. One Nation admits using party funds to build $56,000 shed on James Ashby’s private property One Nation has admitted using party funds to build a $56,000 shed on James Ashby’s private property. Guardian Australia revealed on Monday that a company linked to One Nation – Small Batch Brewing Pty Ltd – was the purchaser of the shed on Ashby’s property despite having no revenue stream and not being licensed to make or sell alcohol. Ashby is living in the shed on his Yeppoon property while he undertakes renovations. In an email sent to members on Thursday night, the party’s general manager, Kelvin Morton, said party funds had been used to build the shed. Read more here: Police say Lay died responding to reports of a stolen vehicle Continuing the police press conference, Commissioner Lanyon said Lay was responding to reports of a stolen vehicle when the crash occurred. The exact circumstances of the collision remain unknown and remain under investigation. Lanyon said: We have formed a critical investigation. The experts in examining road crashes, our crash investigation unit, are at the scene at the moment. We’re trying to examine every circumstance. Our officers were responding to an urgent duty, which is where they have lights and sirens on. Police said the investigation would examine factors including the vehicle’s speed and road conditions, with the aim of improving officer safety. When officers are actually travelling on urgent duty, when they have lights and sirens on they’re exempt under the Australian road rules. So they can exceed the speed limit. But we need to understand the circumstances. As the commissioner, what I’m keen to do to make sure our officers are as safe as possible and the best and the only to do that is to examine these scenes thoroughly so we understand what happened. Police commissioner pays tribute to officer killed in Redfern crash Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has paid tribute to constable Mia Lay, who died after a police car crashed into a tree in Sydney’s inner south. The police car was travelling along Gibbons Street in Redfern with its lights and sirens activated when it crashed at about 1.30am on Friday. Police said Lay died “instantly”. Lay had served with the force for 16 months, based in the South Sydney Police Area Command. She showed exceptional promise and was well loved. She would have been an outstanding police officer. And to lose her life both in its prime and just at the infancy of becoming a police officer is a terrible tragedy. Today is a terribly difficult day. We are here, we will support each other as police officers. We understand the risk of what we do. We put our lives in the way for the safety of the community, to prevent crime and to make sure the community is safe. Terribly on of those days, some police officers pay the ultimate sacrifice. To Mia, thank you for your courage. Angus Taylor had some harsh words for the prime minister this morning, saying Anthony Albanese is “swanning around New York” at the UN general assembly rather than tackling fuel prices at home. Taylor had this to say this morning: Australians are suffering. And that’s why our fuel price shield will bring down the price of fuel when the price is high … What we see is a prime minister swanning around New York, getting his global citizen of the year award, hanging out with the United Nations, instead of looking at and seeing the pain that Australians are feeling at the bowser and struggling to make ends meet. Get real, mate. Get back here and cut the price of fuel. Albanese issued robust calls for an end to the Iranian war during his address to the UN general assembly today. Taylor and the Coalition have proposed a cut to the fuel excise tax whenever oil prices are sustained at more than US$100 a barrel. Renters in New South Wales will only need to provide their driver’s licences and passports if they are about to sign a lease, instead of including them in every rental application, under new laws. Agents and landlords will also be required to use one standardised rental application form, which will not request details such as photos, social media accounts, details about children – or tattoos. The new rules also require landlords and agents to say if photographs of the property have been digitally altered or AI-generated to hide faults – including “fake furniture that hides structural damage or misrepresents room proportions”. In addition, it will become mandatory for agents to tell renters if a property is locked in to an embedded utility network – like a private electricity or gas system – which stops them from shopping around for the best price. Potential breaches will be up to $11,000 for individuals and $49,500 for corporations for privacy violations, and up to $22,000 for failure to disclose digitally altered photographs. Anoulack Chanthivong, the minster for better regulation and fair trading, said: This is a strong step forward to protect renters from false information in the rental market and is an important part of the Minns Labor government’s commitment to supporting the ethical use of AI across the state. These laws put an end to the practice of excessive and intrusive data collection in the rental process and make it fairer for renters and less stressful for landlords and agents. Whether you have a tattoo, or what school your kids go to, is not relevant to whether you’ll be a good tenant. Australia has a new chicken factory, but will it improve animal welfare? The sleek, rust-coloured saucer settles into the earth, mirroring the surrounding hills. It looks like an art gallery or a high-end conference centre – an architectural masterpiece designed to sit lightly on the land. Until you see the shed behind it. The sweeping lines are the gateway to a $600m poultry processing plant that will, at full capacity, process 3 million chickens a week. Jed Goodfellow, the director of policy and government relations at the Australian Alliance for Animals, said while the Baiada building may be state of the art, he believes “the welfare model behind it is anything but”. Read more here: Anthony Albanese posts a selfie with the Greek prime minister at the UN summit Albanese is back on the selfie game: he’s just posted a photo alongside the Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis. The post comes after another, much-talked about selfie with the US president, Donald Trump. You can read about that one here: ‘We can’t ignore AI or prevent it’, Albanese tells UN Albanese again addressed the AI hack of Medicare during his address, saying the episode reflected the need for greater regulation of artificial intelligence. He said: AI can improve lives, boost growth and productivity, provide revolutionary breakthroughs in healthcare and other fields – but leaders of AI companies themselves have warned of the potential risks to allow frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails. Recently, an artificial intelligence agent infiltrated an Australian government website. This is unacceptable. And it is why Australia has been leading the way in establishing Australian standards for AI. Standards to ensure that AI will work and deliver for people, not for other way around. We can’t ignore AI or prevent it. And it’s why we joined with other nations this week to call for action to shape artificial intelligence development, rather than be passively shaped by it. Albanese is detailing Australia’s bid for a temporary seat on the UN security council for 2029 to 2030. He said: We understand that the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers or the biggest countries or even the loudest voices alone. Nor can it be subcontracted to the world’s richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology. The world faces tough times and Australia wants to respond, to partner, and to make a difference. Should our security council bid prove successful, our purpose and approach will be consistent with how we have always conducted ourselves at the UN. We will listen with respect, we will partner as equals, and we will protect what matters most. Albanese addresses UN general assembly The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is addressing the UN general assembly in New York City. We’ll bring you some key moments from his address in a moment. Watt says government will do what it needs to after AI breach Murray Watt, the environment minister, also spoke about the AI hack this morning. He told Sunrise the timeline behind OpenAI’s notification was “completely unacceptable”, and that the sending of an “email to a generic inbox that isn’t monitored all the time” wouldn’t stand going forward. He added: We have commissioned a task force to do an investigation of this event, and if it is possible to press criminal charges, that will happen. But what it also highlights is that we do need to ensure that Australian laws are keeping pace with this new and emerging technology. But if we need to update our laws to improve the requirements for notification of these kind of events, then that’s what we’ll do. And of course, if there’s further safeguards that need to be put in place, that’s what we’ll do as well. AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s internal systems will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk. He said the government is still looking at any legal action and there were questions about liability as an AI agent was “not a legal person”. Australia’s gen Z are the generation most willing to cut their spending way back to afford a home, according to Cotality data reported by AAP. The figures show more than 75% of all Australians were curbing their outgoings in pursuit of property, meaning we are more likely to do so than our Canadian, US and UK peers (for whom the figures sat below 70%). Levels of discretionary spending, like eating out, owning a car, and even moving from the family home into a share house, have dropped among young adults in recent years. But it wasn’t just first-time buyers making significant financial sacrifices to climb the ladder. Millennials – the largest buyer cohort in the world – are readily forgoing small luxuries to afford homes large enough for their families. Prospective buyers were selling their second car or putting off holidays while their children were young, Capital Buyers Agency owner Claire Corby said. For many, it’s around delaying things like going away, or reducing things like dinners out. People are leaving where they want to live and buying in cheaper markets. Most Australians would not be persuaded to participate in the housing market until mortgage interest rates hit a 4.9% average, the data revealed. The average rate for an owner-occupier in August 2026 was 6.3%, meaning the market is likely to stay quiet for some time and allowing bold buyers to swoop in. People are being conservative and cautious. The opposition’s defence spokesperson, James Paterson, has questioned the timing of the prime minister’s announcement that an AI agent hacked Medicare. Paterson made the claim on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night after Anthony Albanese publicly disclosed that an AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and that the tech giant only notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”. Paterson told 7.30 he believed Albanese had chosen to make the announcement at the UN summit in New York, as part of his effort to stand up to “big tech” on AI. The senator said: The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did. But in terms of the nature of the potential of actual security breach this is the bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness. I don’t think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City. Paterson said he didn’t consider the breach to be overly serious because the data the AI agent accessed was made freely available to researchers and academics studying the health system, and was not personal or private in nature. He said the breach was cause for “being alert but not alarmed”. Nevertheless, he said Australians were “entitled to demand explanations and contrition” and to want high levels of confidence when entering into agreements with big tech companies such as OpenAI. headline: We all know a lack of exercise is bad for our bodies. So what is relying on AI doing to our brains?
trail_text: Most of my students use AI, and I worry about its corrosive effects. We must not entrust tech companies with our long-term health, says Prof Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
body_text: When I was a postgraduate student at the University of Oxford in the early 2000s, I interviewed for a major consulting firm. All my friends were being recruited, and I thought why not give it a shot? Aside from the usual maths-proficiency test (how quickly can you crunch numbers in front of a client and look smart), I was asked about what the future of streaming could look like. I gave a long-winded answer about the unintended consequences of changing how humans interact with each other when a new technology is introduced, and why this may not be in the best interests of health and society. I even remember saying something like: “Can you imagine just being stuck at home, alone, watching show after show and never having to move or see any other people? Why would anyone choose that over going out to rent a DVD at a local shop, or to a movie theatre?” You won’t be surprised to learn that I wasn’t invited for a follow-up interview. The partner at the consulting firm thought my answer was completely wrong. They saw the potential growth and profitability of streaming – and you could say, in hindsight, they had a point: Netflix’s global revenue continues to rise year on year, reaching $12.6bn (£9.5bn) in 2026. My answer, on the other hand, focused on its societal and health consequences. But if you look at the negative impact that excessive screen-time has had on health and wellbeing, especially on children, perhaps I wasn’t wrong after all. We know that social isolation is now widespread, anxiety and depression too, with sleep also negatively affected by how late we stay up watching content. And here I am, more than 20 years later, being asked to talk about AI and what it means for higher education, health and society at a conference at the University of Edinburgh, where I work as a professor. I know many people would say: “It’s wonderful! Our lives will all get easier.” But we’re also moving closer to a world where we don’t have to see anyone, move anywhere or use our brains, seemingly at all. And again I think, wonderful for who? Wonderful for the tech companies and those looking to cut costs by replacing humans with automation, but certainly not for the rest of us. There’s a comparison, for me, between the effects of streaming on our physical activity levels and health, and the probable effects of AI on our brains. The richer a country becomes, the more people move into non-manual labour, with sedentary activities in their free time. We can see evidence for this if we look at development in low- and middle-income countries: physical activity goes down as GDP per capita goes up. Over the past few decades, we have seen the health consequences of sedentary behaviour grow: higher rates of chronic disease such as cancers and type-2 diabetes, more chronic back and neck pain, and reduced quality of life. Physical movement has become a leisure activity to stay healthy, and is increasingly linked with higher socioeconomic status in places such as the UK. We know that not using our bodies is bad for our physical health – but what is regular reliance on AI doing to our minds? The true causal evidence might take decades to emerge, but we can link several trends together to guess at an answer. We know, for example, that AI use and daily screen-time averages are going up. At my university, I’d guess almost all students are using some kind of generative AI (gen AI) to produce their work, raising huge challenges when it comes to assessment. The 2026 Higher Education Policy Institute survey of students’ use of gen AI found this year that 95% of undergraduates reported using AI in at least one way, and 94% said they had used it in assessed work. We also know that overall educational attainment levels are decreasing: a recent OECD report noted that student performance across its member countries continued to decline, with the lowest average ever recorded for maths and reading. The report links these poor scores to longer screen-time, increased digitalisation in the classroom and the collapse in reading for enjoyment among children. All of this makes me wonder what will happen to our brains as we continue to outsource key cognitive functions to AI. We already have preliminary evidence from a study that used electroencephalography (EEG) sensors to measure electrical activity in the brain, titled Your Brain on ChatGPT: it showed those students using gen AI to write essays had weaker and less distributed brain connectivity than those writing fully on their own. We also know that a lack of mental engagement can lead to losing cognitive function over time. A study of more than 19,000 adults over the age of 50 found greater participation in cognitively stimulating leisure activities (such as crosswords or sudoku) was linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning in later life. Just as resistance training is important to maintain muscle mass as we age, our brains also need regular training. Use it or lose it. As we look to the future, will thinking, reading, writing and actively using our brains become activities from a bygone era? If we stop using our brains to think, socially interact, concentrate or problem-solve, what will be the impact on our quality of life and our chances of ageing healthily? Will we see a rise in chronic disease linked to the brain? And, maybe just as importantly, does anyone even care? It’s certainly not the concern of tech companies, which are in an arms race to go faster. And so we’re heading in that direction and being told it’s all wonderful. Yes, it is wonderful for certain tech companies. And probably terrible for the mental health and wellbeing of the rest of us. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

headline: Human skills, AI thrills: the initiative guiding young people into a radically changing job market
trail_text: With the world of work set to be transformed by AI, a new initiative from Barclays and supported by Atlassian Williams F1 Team is helping the next generation join the fast lane
body_text: The new academic year is now firmly in full swing. Teachers have finally nailed who’s who in their cohort, brand new jumpers are piling up in lost property and summer lie-ins feel like a distant memory. But the start of the 2026/27 year brings some fresh challenges, too. Today, many teachers will be familiar with the AI paradox: how quickly it’s embedding itself in the rhythm of students’ daily lives versus the need for human skills and critical thinking that will ensure they use it wisely, and to best effect. Educators now have a tricky balance to strike: how to help students harness AI without letting chatbots do all their thinking for them. In response to this, Barclays LifeSkills, supported by Atlassian Williams F1 Team has launched a new competition for schools, colleges, universities and youth groups, to inspire young people to build the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work. Accelerate Your Skills uses practical activities to help 11- to 25-year-olds apply AI responsibly to real-world challenges while simultaneously developing the human-centric skills they’ll need to thrive in the years ahead, such as communication, creativity and critical thinking. “AI is transforming the world of work at an incredible pace, creating exciting new opportunities but also changing the skills young people need to succeed. Which is why we’ve launched the Barclays LifeSkills Accelerate Your Skills challenge. We want to help young people build the human skills and experience that employers are saying are more important than ever to be able to confidently and practically work alongside AI,” says Kirstie Mackey, Barclays head of citizenship, UK and Europe. Accelerate Your Skills arrives at a time when many young people face a rapidly changing world of work. In May, the number of young people considered NEET (those aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training) surpassed 1 million for the first time in a decade, with a recent report by Alan Milburn, a former cabinet minister turned social mobility adviser, warning the UK is “at risk of a lost generation”. This uncertainty is reflected in young people’s confidence about entering the workplace. Recent research from Barclays found that fewer than a third of working age people are confident they understand the skills employers are looking for as AI and technology is more widely used in the workplace. “For many young people, taking their first steps into the world of work can feel daunting, with barriers ranging from a lack of experience to uncertainty about the opportunities available to them,” says Mackey. “By understanding the skills employers are looking for and taking opportunities to develop them, young people can break down these challenges, build their confidence, and unlock their potential. The more equipped they feel with the right skills, the more motivated and ambitious they can become about their future, helping them take positive steps towards rewarding careers and long-term success.” What teachers can expect Teachers needn’t worry about shoehorning Accelerate Your Skills into an already-crammed start-of-year timetable. Barclays LifeSkills has made it as easy for you as possible to enter, with a leaders’ toolkit packed with guidance and ready to use in class activities. The challenge? To raise awareness of Atlassian Williams F1 Team and turn young people into fans. Participants will need to research and brainstorm ideas, using generative AI as a wingman while they steer towards their best creative idea. Throughout the process, students will develop their communication, creativity, critical thinking, adaptability, ethical reasoning and problem-solving skills – combining their human skills with smart use of generative AI. James Vowles, team principal for Atlassian Williams F1 Team, says they have always been driven by innovation, teamwork and the relentless pursuit of performance. “As a team, we are constantly looking for ways to find our edge and extract even more performance on and off track. This competition challenges young people from across the UK to think in the same way, and imagine new opportunities for our organisation ahead of our 50th anniversary year. We look forward to seeing their entries.” What students can expect One of the most exciting things about Accelerate Your Skills is the practical, hands-on activities which mirror challenges people might face in the world of work. Along the way, students may find AI makes a great brainstorming partner, but the most original ideas still need human imagination and collaboration. Do well in the competition and your organisation might win up to £5,000 in national and regional cash prizes, with the winning team scooping a visit to Atlassian Williams F1 Team factory and further opportunities to collaborate with Barclays. More importantly, the activities will show students how to combine AI literacy with human judgment – a useful mix as they take their first steps into the world of work. These skills could prove invaluable for entry-level and early-career roles, such as project assistants or junior designers, while also giving them a headstart in apprenticeships, traineeships and higher education. With the possibility that AI will take on more technical or repetitive workplace tasks, Accelerate Your Skills aims to develop the human abilities that can’t easily be replicated by machines (if at all), which are for that reason now prized by employers. In fact, in a recent Barclays survey, employers identified critical thinking (51%), problem-solving (46%) and adaptability (37%) as among the hardest skills to source in job applicants, ahead of AI skills (19%), data analysis (16%) or coding or programming (12%). Yet, these same bosses also feel younger generations aren’t demonstrating these qualities. About a third of businesses (32%) feel school-leavers aren’t workplace-ready, with lack of employability skills cited by 60% of employers as a key factor. Accelerate Your Skills aims to remedy this. Support from Atlassian Williams F1 Team provides a natural fit too. As anybody who has watched its drivers, Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz, whiz around a track at 230mph will know, Formula 1 drivers require more than razor-sharp reflexes. They rely on communication, teamwork and split-second judgment, using vast amounts of data to make decisions under pressure – many of the same qualities Accelerate Your Skills aims to develop. From now until the competition’s finish line in December, teachers will get the chance to imbue these skills in their students, leaving them with a better grasp of AI, experiences worth shouting about on their LinkedIn profiles plus the confidence to take the wheel once they start their working lives. “We hope that the Accelerate Your Skills challenge can give young people a strong foundation for the future by helping them develop the skills that matter most in an AI-enabled workplace. We’re committed to backing the future of young people and help them to gain the skills that will support their success throughout their careers,” says Mackey. How to register Accelerate Your Skills has everything you need to run the competition including the full challenge brief, a step-by-step competition journey and activities ready-to-use with young people. To register and download the leaders’ toolkit, head to barclayslifeskills.com. The competition is open now, and all schools, colleges, universities and community groups have until 18 December to submit their entries. Good luck!

headline: First Thing: Netanyahu lambasts Israel’s critics at UN as New York protesters detained
trail_text: More than 100 people arrested while Israeli PM claims war on Gaza is ‘the opposite of genocide’
body_text: Good morning. Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, delivered an inflammatory address to the UN in New York, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and taking aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. He branded Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a “tyrant”, described Zohran Mamdani as the “antisemitic mayor of New York”, and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza was not a genocide, “it’s the opposite of genocide”. Netanyahu delivered his address just hours after the Palestinian leader, Mahmoud Abbas, said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting. Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage. What was the reaction on the streets of New York? More than 100 people were arrested outside the UN headquarters as hundreds of Jewish, Palestinian, Iranian and Lebanese New Yorkers, among others, protested during Netanyahu’s address. Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were among those detained. What has rapper Macklemore announced? The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after voicing his support of Palestine, has convened a Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations. The charity show will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced. Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days Iran has said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets. Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal due to the inclusion of demands over Lebanon. What happened in the Senate about the war? Senate Republicans have blocked a Democratic effort to end the US war against Iran, voting down a House-passed war powers resolution. The measure, which passed the House last week with bipartisan support, failed in the Senate by a 49-50 vote, attracting some Republican support, but not enough to pass. What other developments have there been in the Middle East? Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, with the latest attacks pushing oil prices ⁠to a one-week high over fears of spiralling supply disruptions. Texas woman triumphs as court upholds acquittal in voting error case The nearly decade-long case of a Black Texas woman who was sentenced to five years in prison in a controversial illegal voting case will end with an acquittal, the state’s highest criminal court has ruled in a 5-4 decision. Crystal Mason has been appealing ever since her 2018 conviction for casting a provisional ballot that ultimately was not counted. What is the latest voting controversy in Nevada? The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Why is there backlash against a sheriff in California over voting? The Republican sheriff Chad Bianco must return more than 650,000 ballots his department confiscated earlier this year in an unprecedented move that violated election law, a state supreme court has ruled. Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid a trap that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said. Mark Saunokonoko has this list of key takeaways from the summit. In other news … Mary Peltola’s campaign says reports of her using slurs and shoving a staffer are exaggerated, but acknowledges the Democratic nominee in Alaska’s pivotal Senate race struggled after the deaths of her husband and mother. Trump’s Food and Drug Administration commissioner nominee, Dr Heidi Overton, has said the MMR vaccine shot is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind Trump as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal”. US mortgage rates passed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s election there. Stat of the day: ICE has wasted tens of millions to carry out Trump’s mass detention agenda US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other federal agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing controversial plans to rapidly increase detention capacity – and the total will likely rise due to continuing mismanagement, congressional investigators have warned. Culture Pick: My dad was a monster! Sara Karloff on reviving Frankenstein, 95 years on Boris Karloff’s daughter and the composer Michael Shapiro, who has written a 21st-century musical score for the 1931 classic, talk to Pamela Hutchinson about how it became so loved – and the strange experience of watching your father be Dr Frankenstein’s creation as a teenager. Don’t miss this: Gavin Newsom condemns Democrats’ ‘climate hushing’, predicts Trump’s downfall and expects AOC to run in 2028 Mark Hertsgaard interviews the governor of California, a man who may still – if the circumstances are right for him – run for US president in 2028. … or this: Amid soaring living costs, America’s biggest convenience-store chains quietly overcharge consumers A Guardian investigation has revealed that 7-Eleven and Circle K stores often fail to honor advertised prices – charging more at the pump and register for gas, snacks and other items. Climate check: ‘We wanted to prove we didn’t need air conditioning’ – the airport cooled by natural ventilation Avoiding a planet-heating disaster will take innovative approaches, and at Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, a unique ceiling design funnels a light tropical breeze into the terminal, ending the need to run air conditioning. Last Thing: 55,000 fans and nowhere to hide – what it’s like to play in basketball’s biggest arena I still have nightmares about just a handful of people watching me flounder at sport in my younger years, so appearing at the sprawling Philippine Arena sounds terrifying. Jacob Uitti reports. Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. If you’re not already signed up, subscribe now.
