headline: Regrets? Even three decades on from Rats in the Ranks, legendary film-maker Bob Connolly has a few
trail_text: Documentary screened at more than 40 international film festivals and won multiple awards for its depiction of the Shakespearean skullduggery of local politics
body_text: It’s one of the most celebrated documentaries to come out of Australia, but film-maker Bob Connolly still harbours misgivings about Rats in the Ranks, a fly-on-the-wall tale of skullduggery at inner-Sydney’s Leichhardt council. “I have huge regrets about the film, huge regrets,” Connolly, 81, says on the 30th anniversary this month of the 1996 release of the film he made with his late partner, Robin Anderson. “The entire press coverage was basically: ‘we loved the film but we hated the councillors who are all low lives’. And it’s rankled with me for 30 years.” Some on the left were furious at what they saw as a film sending up a progressive council. Anderson, his professional and life partner, died in 2002 aged 51 after co-producing five award-winning feature-length documentaries. Her last film was Facing the Music, about a campaign to save the music department at the University of Sydney. “When we make five 90, 95-minute films, you live through a period of someone’s life which is very often stressful, which is lonely, which has high stakes,” Connolly says. “And you really do develop a duty of care for the subjects.” Connolly and Anderson’s subjects were the incumbent mayor of an inner-western Sydney council, independent Larry Hand, and 11 disparate councillors, including four Labor party representatives whose dysfunction is the heart of the drama. The duo spent 10 months following these characters around, using up 60,000 feet of 16mm film. The idea that an observational documentary about local government could sustain a feature-length film was not immediately clear to commissioning executives. If it hadn’t been for the couple’s solid record of producing consistently brilliant documentaries it may never have been approved. The couple’s first film, Franklin River Journey (1980), was followed by what became known as the Highland trilogy: First Contact (1983), which was nominated for an Oscar, Joe Leahy’s Neighbours (1988) and Black Harvest (1992). Shifting their focus to an urban landscape was serendipitous. In 1993 Connolly met his loyal mayor, Hand, when he asked for help to fight a development in Glebe. He was impressed by Hand’s ability to handle conflict. “Larry was smart, he was well educated, he obviously was a good politician, he was respectful,” Connolly says. “I think he quickly formed an opinion about the rights and wrongs of disputes, but never let that be shown.” Meanwhile, a project they had planned in Fiji fell through and they needed a new idea for a film. “I was putting out the garbage one day, and I remembered Larry had said to me ‘what you’ve got to remember about councils is that they’re a clearinghouse for conflict’,” Connolly says. “So we thought that’s a good idea for a film: the spreading suburbia and a lot of the decisions being made by the council.” Connolly approached Film Australia. “My gut feeling was that something interesting would very likely happen, but I couldn’t guarantee it,” he says. Chris Oliver, who was an executive producer at Film Australia when they pitched their project, remembers telling them: “Please tell me you’re joking.” Oliver said when he was shown footage of Hand in action he thought he had a “classic laconic larrikin feel about him” and approved the project. Funding was approved under Film Australia’s National Interest program. When filming started in December 1993 the mayoral election was 10 months away, and they had no plans to feature the political manoeuvrings in the run-up. It simply hadn’t occurred to them. “We went to a whole lot of site inspections and got some great stuff and then Robin looked at me and said ‘I’m getting worried’,” Connolly says. “We’d been at it six weeks and we were realising that everything was mosaic. There were a whole lot of small conflicts but no overarching narrative.” A conversation in a pub in Balmain after a site inspection changed everything. “We heard there’s going to be a shit fight this year because [ALP councillor] Evan Jones wants Larry out,” Connolly says. Suddenly they had a dramatic narrative: it wasn’t the councillors’ relationship with the ratepayers, it was the councillors’ relationships with each other. The opening scene of the film is a caucus meeting at which the ALP members do not hide their dislike for each other. Connolly still marvels at the access they had to a Labor caucus meeting, which he believes had never been filmed before. “We shot that scene three weeks before the mayoral election, and everything in the film was shot after that sequence. We shot 50,000 or 60,000 feet of film and we used virtually none of it.” Connolly says none of the extraordinarily candid scenes in the film would have been possible had they not spent months quietly observing the action until the councillors forgot they were there while they engaged in the universal practice of number crunching. “The classic example of that was in the early weeks we camped in Larry’s office and every now and again there’d be a very sensitive phone call coming in, some sort of politically ticklish thing, and he’d say, ‘look, I’m really sorry, but would you mind just going out for this?’. Well, about six or seven, eight weeks later, that had all gone.” Hand allowed the couple to film him as he made calls and tried to drum up support to serve as mayor for a fourth year. Adopting a conspiratorial tone Hand would look into the camera and say things no one would want to be heard saying publicly, such as: “She’s a dirty rotten traitor”; “She’ll vote for Kath [Hacking] on the basis that she’s hopeless” and “I find it so unethical”. Connolly: “Events are unfolding in this office, and we’re capturing them without having to do anything but point the camera. And the reason is that he has become comfortable with us being there. We became a sounding board for Larry. And it was all totally natural.” The film screened at more than 40 international film festivals and won multiple awards. At the now defunct Valhalla Cinema in Glebe, Rats in the Ranks played for five months and box office takings were more than $120,000, which according to Oliver, was a record for a feature documentary at the time. It has cemented its place as a critical masterpiece and is still available to rent on streaming services and the National Film and Sound Archive. Oliver says it “was the first real insiders’ fly-on-the-wall treatment of political trading” and it resonated across cultures. In the New York Times, Janet Maslin wrote that Rats in the Ranks appreciates ‘‘the dauntless energy and sheer Shakespearean conniving it takes to stay afloat’’ in the ‘‘shark-infested waters’’ of local politics. One of best known scenes in the film is one in which Anthony Albanese, then assistant general secretary of the ALP in NSW, refused to appear on camera at a meeting of the Labor caucus at Bar Italia. Unable to agree among them on who should be the mayoral candidate, Albo famously advised them to pull a name out of a hat. “I got presented with a trophy for the best non-appearance in a feature film,” Albanese told Guardian Australia in 2019. “I dunno where it is now, but I’ve still got it somewhere”. Coincidentally, in the days before we spoke to Connolly and Hand, the Sydney Morning Herald published a headline which rankled both men: Rats in the ranks: ICAC hears double-crosses, blackmail and broken promises. It was accompanied by a large photograph of the famous movie poster of Larry Hand grinning like a Cheshire cat in his red mayoral robes and chain. Connolly was furious the Herald had linked Hand with blackmail and corruption and drafted an angry letter to the editor. The article opened old wounds about some of the negative reaction to the film’s subjects from the media and sections of the left. Hand, who has been the secretary of the Balmain branch of the Labor party for a decade, was not impressed his photograph had been used alongside the word blackmail. “What sort of dimwit fucking editor would put the word blackmail next to a photograph of me,” he said. Connolly and Hand have remained friends, which drives Connolly’s regrets about the film. He says “the mayoral contest was a wonderful piece of drama. It was almost too wonderful.” Almost all the scenes of the councillors doing their duty in the electorate hit the cutting room floor. All that was left was the raw fight for power, and he feels bad because he got to know the characters. “They haven’t got a high status,” he says. “They’re part-time. They get paid peanuts. They’re often elderly. What I say is, one of the tyrannies of nonfiction film-making is you cannot invent anything.” One scene which did make the cut was the public applauding when Hand won the election in a dramatic turn of events. “It was a good moment because 99% of the people there wanted Larry to win because he was the smartest, the most able and the most honourable,” Connolly says. For his part, Hand, 71, believes “only a minority of people saw the councillors in a bad light”. “Most people would realise that you didn’t spend 24 hours a day plotting,” the former political adviser for state and federal ministers says. “You had other work to do. And that’s why in the film they deliberately put in a number of scenes to show the council doing their normal work. But of course, most of the film is about who’s going to be the mayor. That’s what the film was about. “If they had made a film, for instance, about the council sticking up for not being too pro-development or this or that it would have been like a Four Corners, which would have been interesting at the time. But you know what? No one would have watched it again.” • Rats in the Ranks is available to watch via streaming services and the NFSA website

headline: AFL grand final breaks TV audience records – as it happened
trail_text: This blog is now closed
body_text: Thanks for sticking with the blog today, here are some highlights: Richard Marles, the deputy prime minister, said the CEO of OpenAI didn’t tell him about the hack of Australian government websites when they met earlier this month. Jane Hume, the deputy Liberal leader, said she’s unsure “who they’re going to put in cuffs” after the AI breach. The partner of Mia Lay, the NSW police officer who died in a car crash while on duty, said she was the “happiest girl I’ve met”, calling her the love of his life. NSW said drone patrols picked up an average of 20 sharks a day at patrolled beaches over winter as aerial surveillance was being ramped up for the school holidays. The AFL grand final smashed viewership records, with millions tuning in to watch Kylie Minogue’s pre game performance. Have a lovely Sunday afternoon, see you tomorrow. Newcastle fans stymied by train delays, but services running again Transport NSW advised those travelling from Newcastle to Sydney’s Olympic Park for this afternoon’s NRL match to allow plenty of extra time due to a failed freight train at Warnervale. Trains have resumed their journeys between Newcastle and Wyong at slower speeds, with some buses helping supplement travel. Sydney Train’s head of rail operations, Jas Tumber, said earlier: Diversions are currently in place that will allow train services to move around the failed freight train, however, this is adding at least one hour to journeys. We apologise for this inconvenience and thank passengers for their patience. Pacific National have mobilised their repair crews to temporarily repair the failed freight train as soon as possible. The AFL grand final smashed viewership records for Seven yesterday, with the broadcaster saying it was the most watched one ever. Seven reported a total national TV audience of more than 4.5 million, with an audience reach of 6.5 million. Those figures make it the #1 program on Australian television this year, Seven said. The pre-game event featuring Kylie Minogue reached more than 4.3 million people, up 20% on the year prior. Chris Jones, Southern Cross Media’s director of sport, said: From the opening moments of our coverage outside the MCG, through Kylie Minogue’s show-stopping pre-game performance, an unforgettable match and the premiership celebrations, Australians were with us every step of the way. Earlier today the triple premiership-winning Brisbane team celebrated with fans at the Lions’ spiritual home at Brunswick St Oval in Fitzroy North. Rookie officer stabbed in Queensland, partner slashed A police officer has been stabbed in the neck and torso, while his partner reportedly was slashed across the forehead, after responding to a disturbance at a property in Brisbane’s south east. The police union general president, Shane Prior, told the Courier Mail the rookie officer was “a hero” who held on to his neck to stem the bleeding while trying to chase down and taser his assailant, before having to stop for loss of blood. The two officers were called to Bogong Street in Hemmant about 5:13am this morning. Police said “officers engaged with two men” before one stabbed the officer and fled on a bike, which he later dumped and continued on foot. He was arrested about 7am while one officer was transported to hospital and in a stable condition. OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue OpenAI said it has paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models as reports of AI agents going rogue mount. The Associated Press reports the decision to halt development came just hours after the company disclosed Friday that it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information. Separately, the AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a US Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed. Read more here: The defence minister has fired a warning shot at critics of a plan to sell a historic military barracks, painting the site as a glorified wine cellar that wouldn’t help prevent an attack on Australia. There are 67 military properties slated to be sold off by the Labor government to raise funds, including Sydney’s Victoria Barracks – a complex established in 1840. During the week, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, called the site the “spiritual home of the Australian Army” in comments to the Daily Telegraph. On Sunday, Marles was in no mood to appease his critics. “It is not my priority for defence to be a heritage organisation,” he told News24. It’s not my priority to see defence manage the oldest wine cellar in Australia. There are a few former generals who liked hanging out there, who are lamenting this. The mass sale of defence sites, announced in February, is expected to rake in $1.8bn. Victoria opposition wants to end prisoner sentence cuts for good behaviour in emergencies Prisoners shouldn’t have time shaved off their sentences for good behaviour during emergencies, the Victoria opposition argued in its latest election pledge. AAP reports convicted criminals in Victoria can receive compensatory sentence discounts for good behaviour in unforeseen circumstances, such as industrial disputes and lockdowns, known as emergency management days. The only laws of their kind in Australia would be abolished if the state’s opposition deposed the Labor government at the November election. “Labor’s freebie sentence reductions do not meet community expectations and are out of step with other states,” the opposition police and corrections spokesperson, Brad Battin, said on Sunday. Collectively, nearly 2,300 years were scrubbed from prisoners’ terms over a four years due to the scheme, according to freedom of information documents released to the coalition. Drones patrols have picked up an average of 20 sharks a day at patrolled beaches over winter as aerial surveillance is ramped up for the school holidays, AAP reports. Drone operators across NSW detected 1,225 sharks from 1 July to 31 August, fresh data has revealed. The shark sightings prompted 360 safety measures, including water evacuations, alarms to alert swimmers and surfers, and the deployment of inflatable boats and jetskis. Surf Life Saving NSW’s statewide drone operations recorded 49,000 flights, totalling 16,150 hours and covering 343,000 km. The NSW government released the figures on Sunday as it rolled out “the world’s largest and most advanced aerial shark surveillance program” in time for the state’s school holidays. ‘Competing priorities’ on copyright protections: Hume Jane Hume has left open the possibility of supporting changes to Australia’s copyright laws to attract more investment by AI companies, ahead of significant legislation expected in the next six months. On ABC TV, Hume was asked about the differing of views Coalition members on the need to maintain strong protections for Australian writers, musicians, film-makers, photographers and journalists – something the federal government is now considering. Labor’s AI bill is expected to be debated in parliament early in the new year. “The copyright laws are really important,” Hume said. “Making sure that we protect the work of authors, artists and journalists, that is fundamentally important.” Asked about the position of the Liberal frontbencher Michaelia Cash that any move to water down copyright protections would be wrong, Hume was less definitive and cited the role of a new parliamentary committee on AI. There are competing arguments here. If we want to make sure that any sovereign AI models are culturally relevant and appropriate, we want to make sure that that work is reflected. There’s a big difference between copying and using illegally other people’s work and learning from it. We want to work with the government on this to get it right, so that we protect our journalists, protect our authors, protect our artists, but at the same time don’t miss out on the really important access to those frontier AI models that we are going to need, not only to make sure that we are appropriately defended, but also to boost productivity and increase our economic growth into the future. Deaths in Queensland child protection system reach five-year high Queensland has recorded a five-year high of 92 deaths in the child protection system, according to new data. The Queensland Family and Child Commission reported the deaths of 452 children in its annual report, on Friday. The figure included 102 Indigenous children. The report found 94 children died from “external causes”, including 28 from suicide and 13 from an accident or neglect. Meanwhile, 92 children had engaged with the state’s child safety system in the year before they died, while seven died in care and a further 43 had open investigations or “intake events”. It is the highest number of deaths recorded in the state overall and the highest number in the child safety system in five years, up from 427 overall deaths and 57 in protection last year. The commission, which also administrates the state’s child death review board, was created to independently oversee the child safety system as a result of a inquiry called by the state’s former premier Campbell Newman. The state government recently tabled legislation to give the minister the power to sack its commissioner for any or no reason, but maintained the role would remain independent. ‘Not entirely sure who they’re going to put in cuffs’, Hume says Asked if possible legal action should be off the table, Hume said the liability was unclear: “I’m not entirely sure who they’re going to put in cuffs,” she said. The real alarm bell that was set off this week is the fact that the only reason we knew about this breach of the Medicare archive or data system is because OpenAI told us there was a breach. If they hadn’t told us that there was a breach, would we have known about it at all? That demonstrates that our cyber defences, particularly for Services Australia, were woefully inadequate. The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, has expressed scepticism revelations an OpenAI agent accessed Australian government data without authorisation should have legal consequences for the company. The hack was revealed last week, despite taking place in June. Government ministers have raised the prospect of possible referrals to the Australian federal police, but gaps in Australian law could make establishing criminal liability difficult. Hume told ABC TV on Sunday that AI was inevitably going to be a part of Australia’s future and it was important the country was part of the conversation. But certainly the way to go about that is not to threaten criminal action against US counterparts and those trusted partners that we’re relying on now to make sure that we can bring those frontier models, that we can do frontier model training here in Australia. I don’t necessarily think that finger-wagging at our trusted partners, or trying to gazump Donald Trump, is the way to go about that. Daniel Vasquez, the partner of NSW police officer Mia Lay, who died in a car crash while on duty, issued a statement on behalf of her family yesterday, saying he had lost the “love of my life”. Vasquez said: Mia loved what she did in the police. She was happy in the police, she was good at her job, and how loved she was by everyone in the community. She was the happiest girl I’ve met … I’d ask for everyone to remember how stunning and beautiful she was. She was a kind hearted person, gave so much love to everyone that she cared about … I’ve just lost the love of my life. She will be missed by everyone. And I ask that she is remembered. Marles defends Albanese’s global leadership award Richard Marles has defended the prime minister Anthony Albanese’s decision to accept an award for global leadership in UN last week, part of a black tie event in Manhattan hosted by the Atlantic Council. The opposition criticised Albanese for being in New York during difficult economic times for Australian households. The prime minister accepted an award about the way in which we are managing our place in the world, and specifically our place in the region. In terms of the alliances that we’ve struck with countries around Australia, such as Papua New Guinea and Fiji, the way in which we are pursuing the AUKUS arrangements, which are building Australian capability in what is a very challenging world. I think the recognition of the prime minister is deserved in respect of him. But it’s also a recognition of what his government has been doing to make sure that we are keeping Australians safe in a very challenging global environment, and that’s what we are seeking to do here. Trump White House wants Iran war to end: Marles The defence minister, Richard Marles, is on News 24 this morning and has been asked about the ongoing economic and geopolitical damage being caused by Donald Trump’s war in Iran. Marles says it clear that the White House wants the war to end. Clearly, the United States wants to see an end to the conflict. That’s to state the obvious, but they are seeking to to manage that through What is clear is that the global fuel supply chain is disrupted, and that is having an impact on the global economy ... and that’s what we are seeking to manage in terms of the way we manage the economy and the budget at home. Richard Marles says revelations last week that an OpenAI agent hacked into Australian government websites is very serious, despite the nature of the information accessed being less sensitive. Marles met with OpenAI boss Sam Altman earlier this month but the company did not disclose that it knew the agent had breached Australian government systems. He declined to speculate about whether Altman knew about the breach or not when they met. “The fact that we’ve got an artificial intelligence agent gaining unauthorised access to an Australian government website, that of itself is very serious,” Marles told News 24. “There’s no hiding that. This is the first time this has happened in the context of Australia, and so we’re not shying away from that. In fact, the information that it obtained, was minor in its nature, in as much as that information we’ve now made public anyway, it wasn’t anyone’s personal data. But in a sense, the seriousness doesn’t lie in the information that was obtained. It was the fact that we’ve got an unintended action of an AI agent gaining unauthorised access into an Australian government website. Interstate footy fans grappled with flight delays and cancellations on Saturday as they raced to reach Melbourne in time for the AFL Grand Final. Melbourne airport said some flights had been cancelled due to poor weather causing low visibility, with rain forecast for much of the morning and early afternoon. About 100,000 fans packed into the MCG on Saturday for an all-interstate final between the Fremantle Dockers and the Brisbane Lions starting at 2.30pm. A Qantas flight from Perth scheduled to land at 10.30am was cancelled and a further two were delayed, including another Qantas flight scheduled to arrive before the bounce at 1.40pm which was delayed by around an hour. Two Brisbane flights were cancelled and nine were delayed by up to two hours, meaning some fans landed after the 2.30pm starting time. Among those racing to make the game was journalist and TV host Brooke Boney, who was scheduled to land at 11.35am, which was pushed back by an hour. She made it to the ground just in time for Kylie Minogue’s pre-match entertainment. Anthony Albanese says he was not aware of other cases of AI agents wrongfully accessing classified information before he revealed OpenAI’s unauthorised infiltration of the Medicare Statistics Reporting portal in New York on Thursday, Australian Associated Press reports. “At the time we made our announcement … we weren’t aware of other occurrences,” the prime minister told reporters at Sydney airport on Saturday. “We were acting purely in our national interest.” The PM landed back in Australia on Saturday after a week in the US where he addressed the United Nations General Assembly on the international need to rein in AI. He said news that autonomous agents allegedly infiltrated American university and commerce department sites, as well as the US Securities and Exchange Commission, further proved that need. “We now know it wasn’t just the issue of the Australian sites that have been subject to AI agents accessing information without authorisation,” Albanese said. What this does is confirm that approach of making sure that it needs to be an appropriate national response, as well as an international response to make sure that humans are in charge of this new and emerging technology. Albanese said it was up to OpenAI to state why multiple breaches occurred. Good morning Welcome to our Sunday live blog. Flight delays and cancellations caused frustration and heartache for some footy fans racing to make it to Saturday’s AFL grand final before the first bounce. And the PM says the timing of his announcement of OpenAI’s Medicare hack was made “purely in the national interest”. More on both those stories shortly. Also, the Liberal deputy leader, Jane Hume, will be speaking on the ABC’s Insiders this morning. More on that coming up.

headline: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
trail_text: Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
body_text: Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence (AI), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”. “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.” Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.” Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”. “There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures. Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate. “It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.” Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale. His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods. The progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place. Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI. Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday. The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote. Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later. An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014. Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity. In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’” Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’ “So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”

headline: Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker. The rest say he is changing this year’s elections
trail_text: The popular Twitch streamer has been vilified by Republicans, but the socialist commentator has a large audience that some Democrats have courted
body_text: It’s only 9am and the latest media shitstorm is well under way. Hasan Piker scrolls through his social media feeds as he comes down the stairs of his home in West Hollywood. An interview with Axios, in which Piker said the US had committed more atrocities than al-Qaida, is blowing up his phone. Requests from reporters are streaming in. Comments on the interview flood his replies. Just another day, and just another news cycle, for a 35-year-old socialist streamer who has no elected or appointed power. Never mind that many voters don’t know who Piker is – and haven’t heard of Twitch, his streaming platform of choice – despite months of concerted efforts by political opponents to elevate his profile, and tie Democratic candidates to his most incendiary comments. Facing an uphill battle to retain control of Congress in November’s US midterm elections, and struggling to land on a coherent message to rally support, Republicans have fixated on Piker – and held him up as a representative of their political targets, from socialists and leftists to Muslims. Voters, so far, don’t seem to care about Piker – at least not more than the cost of gas, or the war in Iran, or healthcare, or artificial intelligence, or immigration, or corruption. Around the country, many told the Guardian they hadn’t heard of Piker, or they knew who he was and sometimes had opinions, but those opinions didn’t factor into their voting decisions. Still, Piker features in Republican campaign ads. A photo of him nearly nude, inexplicably, appeared on the jumbotron at the party’s midterm convention. And Republicans have tried hard to tie Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in the critical swing state of Michigan, to Piker after El-Sayed campaigned with him in the primary. (The candidate has since distanced himself from Piker.) Fielding questions in quick pockets of time around his hours of streaming, podcasts and media appearances, Piker says he is not overly troubled by such attacks. “Republicans believe this is an incredible narrative, for the record,” he says. “They truly believe that this is successful. I’m willing to bet it’s because they’re fucking brain-poisoned by the internet.” But the spotlight is glaringly bright. He was even called out from the stage of this week’s United Nations general assembly, as the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, singled out one of Piker’s most controversial remarks. Moderate Democrats have also used Piker as a proxy in their battle against their party’s ascendant left, which notched key upsets in primaries this year, challenging the centrist establishment. And Piker won’t shut up. He streams for seven hours nonstop each day, with hundreds of thousands of followers tuning in each hour. And even then, he’s not done. Depicted on the right as an extremist, Piker is trying to be tame, he says. “For the election season, I have tried to be as serious as possible,” he says in his signature suit and tie. Unlike the Democratic primaries, where he appeared alongside his chosen candidates from El-Sayed in Michigan to Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Piker isn’t campaigning for anyone in the general election. It has not escaped Piker’s notice that Republicans continue to target Democrats over their ties with him, and his more controversial statements. “It’s not necessarily my affiliation that’s so negative,” he suggests. But more questions about him mean fewer questions about policy and their opponents. It’s a missed opportunity when they constantly have to answer “What about Hasan Piker?” Piker says. News cycles focused on Piker are driven by a push to attack progressive candidates, according to him, while news outlets carry negative stories about him in an effort to chase clicks and protect their own relevance in the media ecosystem. But in the longer term, Piker also sees the focus on him as a wider test, for a potential 2028 presidential run from the left by candidate like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive congresswoman. “Most people on the left are in some way, shape or form connected back to my community, or myself, or organizations that I work with,” he says. “This is an active way to try and eliminate a political opponent before it becomes too big of a problem for them.” Who is this guy? Piker was born in New Jersey and grew up mostly in Turkey; his parents – his father a political scientist and his mother an architectural and art historian – are Turkish immigrants. While a student at Rutgers University in New Jersey, he got his start as an intern at the progressive outlet The Young Turks, which was co-founded by his uncle, Cenk Uygur. He went on to host a show on the network and started streaming on Twitch in 2018, eventually leaving The Young Turks to focus on his own platform. He now has more than 3 million followers on Twitch, nearly 2 million on YouTube and nearly 2 million on X. From the start, he made controversial comments – comments that now appear in political ads attacking candidates that Piker has supported. Perhaps the most notable, when in 2019 he said “America deserved 9/11,” features prominently in an ad by Mike Rogers, the Republican contender for US Senate in Michigan, to attack El-Sayed. (Piker has since said the comment was “inappropriate”.) A stream in August led to another round of condemnations. Piker, a frequent critic of Israel, said while talking about the Democratic Michigan congressional candidate Jeremy Moss: “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s going to come around and take action – not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” His anti-Israel views, in particular, took center stage in the Michigan Senate primary, where El-Sayed faced the pro-Israel congresswoman Haley Stevens. El-Sayed has worked since his primary win to bring in Jewish voters in the state. In the Axios interview that sparked the shitstorm earlier this month, Piker was asked whether he thought America was worse than al-Qaida, the terrorist group. “Pound for pound, as far as the number of deaths, yes,” he responded. “We have caused tremendous terror all around the world.” Earlier this year, the UK would not allow Piker or Uygur to enter the country to do speaking events, with the Home Office saying their visit “may not be conducive to the public good”. And in Australia in August, a program on the ABC that featured an interview with Piker led to a round of complaints to the national broadcaster. Trump this month called Piker a “terrible liability” who has “a power over some of these Democrats”. The Democratic National Committee chair, Ken Martin, said some of Piker’s comments were “absolutely disgusting and deplorable” and that he “does not represent the Democratic party” or its candidates. After 13 years on camera, Piker concedes that his sheer volume of talking means he is not always considered in his comments. After some 22,000 hours of extemporaneous commentary on hot-button issues, some of his remarks almost inevitably test what people find acceptable. His stream, he notes, is not prepackaged or scripted like the conventional programs of other political commentators. His audience is dedicated, albeit niche. Members of Congress have appeared on his streams, including Ocasio-Cortez in 2020. In 2025, he stepped more into campaigning for democratic socialist and progressive candidates, first with the then future New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani. In the 2026 cycle, he lent his name recognition to El-Sayed, Pennsylvania congressional candidate Rabb, Colorado’s Milat Kiros, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey and others. After Democrats lost the presidential race in 2024, their soul-searching included a quest for a “Joe Rogan of the left” who could counter the influence the right had on podcasts. Rogan, for what it’s worth, has more than 21 million followers on YouTube alone. This elevated Piker’s profile further, but misunderstood the realm of nonstop speaking to camera online. It is inherently not polished, and the potential for controversy exceeds the tolerance of most Democratic politicians. Piker has said that he isn’t the Joe Rogan of the left, that really there could be no such thing. Democrats were looking for someone with a platform like Rogan’s that would be a “lackey for the party”. “I’m not that person,” he says. He could elect to not answer a question posed like the al-Qaida one. He could soft-pedal or redirect or say something he doesn’t really believe. But instead, he takes the opportunity to be in front of larger audiences as a chance to find other people who will resonate with what he’s saying, even if it’s “intentionally provocative”. Candidates reached out to him, he says. It hasn’t brought him more money but has increased viewership on YouTube. If he were truly irrelevant, no candidate would risk associating with him, he says. They had made a calculation – and sometimes campaigns were open with him about that, saying they had tested him in their districts to see if he will help or hurt, he says. “This is bad content. It sucks to admit,” he says. “From my perspective, it’s much easier for me to stay the hell away from real campaigns, and I think part of the reason for why I’m getting attacked so much is so that that is what I do, I sit it out next time, or it’s a lesson for even progressive candidates that they shy away from entertaining my platform at all.” Voters don’t care For voters, Piker is mostly a distraction. “I kind of liken it to following Kim Kardashian,” Phil Verges, a farmer in Spring Valley, Wisconsin, said of Piker. “Now, I don’t – excuse my language – I don’t give a shit.” Verges, who votes mostly for Democrats, said he only started to hear Piker’s name while following El-Sayed’s campaign. The stream is “totally meaningless to me”, he added, “as Joe Rogan is to me”. Two things can be true at once. Piker has sway over a set of dedicated leftwing, often younger, people who can help increase a candidate’s profile in a Democratic primary. But many Americans do not care, or even know, about him. Despite the countless news cycles, a New York Times/Siena poll from mid-September found 62% of likely voters across three US Senate battleground states did not know who Piker was. Even in Michigan, where ads are running about Piker, 54% of voters didn’t know him. Guardian reporters who approached voters across the country encountered the same reality. Some said his name sounded familiar, or that they had only heard it in recent weeks in the media. Rabb, the Democratic congressional candidate in Pennsylvania’s solidly blue third congressional district, was the oldest candidate, at 56, in a crowded primary this year. He credits Piker with having brought awareness to his campaign among a demographic that would have otherwise been hard, and expensive, to reach. Whether Piker’s support won him the primary is “unknowable”, Rabb said, but it “significantly increased” his capacity to reach more people – and bring on more volunteers to talk about his candidacy. “What he could do in one stream could have taken me months to cultivate,” he said. Piker has all the while become a central focus of Republican attacks. A recent push poll in Georgia attempted to tie Piker to the Democratic US senator Jon Ossoff, a rising star in the party. The pair have not campaigned together once. At this month’s Republican convention, Piker proved an unlikely star, with speakers frequently citing him as the personification of a supposed communist and anti-Israel takeover of the Democratic party. Most of the 15 attenders interviewed by the Guardian had never heard of him. Even seasoned convention-goers were in the dark. Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, Texas, who has attended every Republican convention since 2004, assumed that Piker must be a British political candidate. But after months of pillorying on the right, the name did resonate with some. AJ Louderback, a Texas state legislator, dismissed him in stark ideological terms as “just another radical Muslim”, and remarked: “He doesn’t stand for American values.” Republicans, and rightwing media, were expert at creating a “boogeyman”, Piker notes, from transgender athletes to migrant caravans. But the attack isn’t as salient when it’s a “rabble rouser, Twitch streamer, random entertainer guy”, he says. “There’s just chaos everywhere, and people are just going about their daily lives, trying to make sense of it all and trying to find some kind of peace and stability and prosperity,” adds Piker. “No one is saying it’s because of a Twitch streamer. I’m not top of mind for anybody.” A day in Piker’s world At Piker’s house, the day begins with coffee delivery and checking his friend group’s standings in their fantasy football league. Piker grabs a new Zyn before getting on camera to record a pop culture podcast he does with his friends called Fear&. His dog, a fluffy Tibetan mastiff named Kaya, sits outside the podcast recording room. After almost two hours of podcasting, Piker moves over to the room where he streams on Twitch for seven hours. Art from fans, mostly of Piker, lines the walls around him. He scrolls through news stories, tweets and an endless chat window. Today he launches into the interview with Axios, which he calls a “hit job”, and as the circus around the interview spreads, suggests he maybe shouldn’t have done it, or didn’t expect it to become a clip show, or shouldn’t have used the term “pound for pound”, but that it wasn’t the “end of the world”. Piker spends the majority of each day on camera. He even eats on camera, taking breaks to use the bathroom. He works out and streams – that’s basically it – although he does have friends, who are around much of the time. At any given time, about 25,000 to 30,000 people are viewing the stream. Most of those do not watch for the duration, according to Piker, who says between 300,000 and 500,000 unique visitors will tune in each hour. In the chat, viewers lob questions, praise and criticism. “baby wake up, a new hasan bad press tour,” one person writes in the chat. “Rare hasan L shouldn’t have done this interview,” says another. Today’s stream focuses heavily on Piker himself. After a full streaming shift, he’s not done talking. Piker heads from his home studio to a live taping of Lovett or Leave It, a show from the Pod Save America co-host Jon Lovett that broadcasts on MS Now. (At arrival, a security guard asks me if I’m Piker’s publicist. A publicist, the streamer reflects later, would tell him not to do any interviews, even with friendlier outlets, at this point – when his whole job, really, is “dealing with the media”.) In his opening remarks, Lovett jokes, “If Democrats lose the midterms, we should not have to wonder if it’s because of missing mail-in ballots,” after talking about Trump’s efforts to derail mail voting. “We should know, without a shadow of a doubt, that it is because of Hasan Piker.” “I denounce you,” Lovett declares to Piker as he walks out on stage, a jocular nod to the string of condemnations of Piker’s statements that have featured during this year’s midterm campaigns. Lovett thinks Piker has said some “very stupid and bad” things, but also that a lot of his words have been taken out of context. But, he asks, how does Piker view his responsibility, given his influence and proximity to candidates who he wants to win? It’s a question Piker seems to wrestle with throughout the day. Still, he tells Lovett at one point, “The idea that a Twitch streamer is supposed to be held to a higher standard than the president is such an insane phenomenon.” “They’re elevating my status as this super-serious political commentator and then campaign consultant, campaign surrogate, when I’ve never wanted to be that,” he adds. Afterward, fans approach Piker for photos. One person, he says later, asks how he puts up with so much hatred coming his way for saying what he believes. He is both “very stubborn” and “very mission-oriented”, he explains. Has he considered talking less? “No,” he replies. “I mean, I talk less, I say the same stuff. Still going to be a problem.” David Smith contributed reporting

headline: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI
trail_text: ‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’
body_text: The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”. When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.” The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world with artificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their project in the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do. Everyday Americans are up in arms against the AI datacenters sprouting across their communities. Villages, counties, cities and states are imposing moratoria and bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development. Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits, according to a survey by the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society. Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastly more concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generally more mistrustful of the technology than people in other countries. This surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction has, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net. The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch of weird, sci-fi addled plutocrats to pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.” People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhury points out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whatever harm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law. The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters. Donald Trump remains steadfastly on the side of the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which could keep locals in the dark until construction starts. The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.” Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology. And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule. This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum. But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead, has flushed workers without a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI. One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them. Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach. The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest rates free from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest. But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.” The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.” Peter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued that democracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altman salivates about an “awesome” future in which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.” The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about a superintelligent Golem. Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to be answerable to no one and will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,” he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way. There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of the End of History in Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word. Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass: section 230 of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it. Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage. Reports of teen suicides and online bullying bred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed to hook users to their screens. When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny. By the time Covid hit in 2020, the former paragons of liberal democracy had found a new role as magnifiers of conspiracy theories, enemies of “woke”, partisans in a libertarian revolt against “government control”. Joe Biden’s attempts to use antitrust law and other regulations against the techno-plutocrats’ empires pushed them to the dark side, where Trump and his angry Maga movement awaited their embrace. How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising to punish European countries who dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which is proving so lucrative for him and his family. Still, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck. Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in a conversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.” Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.” Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

headline: I spent a full hour watching Trump TV. It’s a digital pathway to hell
trail_text: The streaming channel was full of the president’s vanity and myopia. It was also deeply, deeply dull
body_text: Are you currently at an airport? Strapped to a hospital bed, with various tubes protruding from your body? Maybe you’re on a treadmill or visiting an elder care facility? Chained to a radiator in the basement from the Saw movies? If you said yes to any of these questions, you might be watching cable news while reading this column. Or maybe you’re one of the hundreds of people currently watching Donald Trump’s answer to cable news, Trump TV – a YouTube streaming channel that airs nothing but White House-sanctioned content 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Kudos to you for multitasking, and thank you for the click. I know Jacob Soboroff is hard to look away from, but at least finish this. I don’t typically watch cable news. Or broadcast news. I feel like the best way to consume vital information is through the glorious written word, full of context and detail, rather than various “experts” yelling at each other about which one is the harbinger of the antichrist. Instead, I can yell all I want at a newspaper or an internet article and no one can tell me not to. Except the people in the dentist waiting room with me. Trump TV is kind of like cable news, if it served absolutely no purpose and had even fewer human beings watching. I gave myself the challenge of watching this neverending digital pathway to hell for one single hour, hoping I could capture whatever joy is being derived from this American horror story. When I first logged on to the stream, I was “treated” to an 11 March 2016 speech Donald Trump gave in Hebron, Kentucky – which Trump on more than one occasion pronounced “Keentucky”, presumably to mimic local speech patterns. That Donald Trump is just a good ol’ country boy, after all. I came in right smack-dab in the middle of the remarks, which very clearly were not prepared. As someone hyper-allergic to cable news, I don’t often witness the president’s speeches in full. I immediately felt as though I were succumbing to a form of intense psychosis, where reality had begun to melt before my eyes, like an ice-cream cone that’s sat out in the sun too long. Trump was describing the stairs at the event, stairs he had to walk up and down. Stairs that he traversed despite his own natural sense of self-preservation. “I might slip, it’s soaking wet,” he said of the stairs. “They’re steel stairs. Four sets of stairs.” I immediately begin to imagine him counting the stairs. Slowly. From there, he played his greatest hits and mocked Joe Biden for falling down. But the big swerve was a backhanded compliment to Barack Obama for not falling down. “The only thing is how he bobbed down. He bobbed. I couldn’t believe that he made it without a major, noticeable fall.” The shock on his face that a healthy adult man would not trip on his descent from an airplane certainly made me wonder. You can tell this man has thought a lot about the best ways to not fall down stairs. Eventually, Dr Oz showed up, and I needed to mute my computer. My Uber Eats order had just arrived, and I didn’t want my neighbors getting the wrong idea when I opened the front door. We got a brief respite from Trump up next, with a re-airing of Melania’s ad … excuse me, speech about how great artificial intelligence is, from 16 January. “The most powerful skill is knowing what to ask,” she declares. I realized the thing I should be asking right then was: “Why am I watching this?” I hung in a little longer for one more event: the National Prayer Breakfast from 6 February. Paula White-Cain, senior adviser to the White House Faith Office, opened the proceedings by saying: “No president in modern history or perhaps all of history has done more to elevate and protect religious liberty” than Donald Trump had. Except maybe George Washington, who presided over the ratification of the first amendment to the US constitution. The first amendment enshrined freedom of religion into the country’s laws. Also, awkwardly, freedom of speech and freedom of the press. You know, the press Donald Trump kicked out of the White House. Trump TV seems like the next escalation of the president’s obsession with and animosity toward cable news. I remain flabbergasted that someone could care about anything on television that much. At last census count, 342 million people live in the United States. Of that population, between 2 and 3 million watch cable news in a given day. The vast majority of those people watch Fox News. And the majority of that majority is over the age of 54. When I say “no one watches cable news,” I am only being mildly hyperbolic. To coin a term, I’m being “semibolic”. Just a “hint of bolic”. Yes, there are people who can’t seem to just turn their TV off out there, but MS Now, CNN and Fox News aren’t capturing the same level of enthusiasm as the latest episode of HBO’s Lanterns or your local bird-watching club. That cable news retains any significance in our daily discourse is a testament to how fiercely committed our nation’s leaders are to using it as a battlefield for their ideological warfare. And as a retirement community for ex-politicians. When Trump tried to ban CNN, MS Now and the website Politico for allegations of unfair, dishonest coverage of his administration, journalists had a reasonable fear for the state of freedom of the press in this country. Covering the goings-on at the White House is not, as Trump says, a “privilege”. It is a solemn duty. One that defines what’s left of our democracy. Maybe now, I’m being fully hyperbolic, but I’m a journalist. I should declare my own bias on this topic. Trump’s media blackout gambit backfired, as Fox News joined with their cable cousins to abandon coverage of the president’s activities, thereby ending the press pool that provided audio and video for news outlets. Without the press pool, no one can hear what Trump says during his speeches. Thankfully for those who use Trump speeches to calm their nerves before a midday nap, they can count on Trump TV to help them off to slumberland. Back to the Trump TV live stream. He was wearing the same purple tie at the prayer breakfast that he’d worn in Kentucky. If you were not an attentive viewer of Trump TV, you might think you were watching the same speech. I realized that just about everything on this stream is from this year, that we’ll probably never see anything from, say, 2020. But I couldn’t stick around long enough to find out, and Trump TV doesn’t seem to list its programming lineup anywhere. I left the house during the National Prayer Breakfast, just as Trump was getting going, declaring “something is wrong” with the Republican congressman Thomas Massie from … Kentucky. You know, the state Trump loves so much. I started to wonder if today’s Trump TV schedule was merely a troll directed at Massie, who lost his re-election bid in the Republican primary, to the former Navy Seal Ed Gallrein, whom Trump endorsed. The absurdity of using a 24/7 YouTube stream to subtly mock a political rival for an audience of 800 people seems far more possible when you remember the person behind this project is Donald Trump. I took a 30-minute walk with my dog, and when I got back to my desk, I was shocked to learn that Trump was still talking at the National Prayer Breakfast. Specifically about the size of our military budget, which I believe was a direct quote from 1 Corinthians 13:4–8. As Trump droned on (pun intended), the view counter kept going down. Even the diehards were getting bored. The launch of Trump TV has been a fairly obvious disaster. Unlike cable news, YouTube has real-time data to tell you how many people are watching something. Multiple media outlets took a swipe at Trump for this folly, though in his defense, most YouTube streams get pitiful concurrent viewership unless it’s MrBeast or live footage of a police chase on an LA freeway. Trump TV was obviously never meant to be anything significant. No one in charge of this stream is trying, unless you count trolling Thomas Massie as “trying”. There are no graphics or lower thirds other than a number to text for “updates” from the White House. There’s no slick editing or editorial perspective outside of the purple tie/Massie element. But is this any worse than the ideologically minded focus of cable news – with the three major channels pointing their rhetorical ICBMs at each other all day long? Maybe Trump TV is actually the best way to consume our sitting president. Nothing else presents him in all of his repugnant glory: vain, myopic and worst of all, deeply, deeply dull. This holiday season, turn on Trump TV for your conservative family members. There’s always a chance that the uncut, unfiltered lethal dose of nonsense will break the spell for good. Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

headline: British celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for Australia
trail_text: ‘People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,’ says the architect of the fightback in the UK
body_text: If you want to state the case against copyright reform in Australia, get Kylie Minogue’s phone number. If there is one lesson to be learned from a similar battle in the UK, high-profile members of the creative industries make a difference. They get your argument on the front of newspapers, in the news bulletins and on social media. In the face of this onslaught, the UK government backtracked on plans to let AI firms use copyright-protected work without permission. The many artists who put their name to various letters and protests against the reforms to create a virtual red carpet, included: Sir Elton John, Sir Paul McCartney, Abba’s Björn Ulvaeus, the actor Julianne Moore and the Radiohead singer Thom Yorke. John had one of the most memorable soundbites, calling the government “absolute losers” who were on course to “rob young people of their legacy and their income”. Overall, the campaign was more sophisticated than just rounding up irritated celebrities. Beeban Kidron, a member of the upper house of the UK parliament and an award-winning film director, marshalled an effective political campaign against the proposals by pushing legislative amendments that would have spiked the plans. She also helped organise celebrity opposition. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Kidron says the campaign struck a chord with the public. “People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,” she says. Polling backed this up, with seven out of 10 adults in the UK supporting the payment of royalties to copyright holders whose work had been used to train AI models. The Australian prime minister should take heed, Kidron says. “Albanese has been a leader in standing up to tech. He should not squander his reputation by selling Australian creatives down the river.” The campaign against copyright reform also benefited from the ingenuity of an industry that knows how to grab people’s attention. One of the most prominent figures in the movement against the proposals, Ed Newton-Rex, organised a “silent” album and an “empty” book, to warn of the consequences of watering down copyright law. “There is no one out there, who does not work for an AI company, who thinks AI companies should not pay for the content they use,” he says. “What we did in the UK was make the government understand that was the case.” Newton-Rex, a composer and former AI executive, put together an album featuring recordings of dormant music studios and performance spaces, called Is This What We Want? It was backed by more than 1,000 musicians, including Damon Albarn, Kate Bush and Annie Lennox. The author stunt, called Don’t Steal This Book, involved 10,000 writers listing their names in an otherwise empty paperback. Contributors included Kazuo Ishiguro, Philippa Gregory and Richard Osman. “The only way the government gets something like this copyright proposal through is if no one notices what they are doing. It will take just a moment for people to understand this is not fair,” says Newton-Rex. Albanese’s government needs to be wary of committing the same mistake as its centre-left UK counterpart, says Pierre Andrews, a former adviser on culture policy under Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government in 2023-2024. “The [UK] Labour government’s mistake was that it thought it could convince the creative industries to go along with it,” he says. Instead, the nation’s assembled artists and authors recoiled at a perceived betrayal by a party they thought would be on their side. “There was a strong sense of surprise within the creative community that Labour would even consider changing copyright to their detriment,” he says, adding that he foresees another government U-turn, but in Australia this time. The tech industry still believes in the win-win argument; that the UK could get behind a policy where domestic AI companies are able to train models on British shores using copyright-protected content, while the holders receive adequate compensation for their work. “The government recognised that it didn’t frame the initial consultation very well,” says Antony Walker, deputy chief executive of trade association techUK. “But I also think rights holders were extremely effective at shouting down the debate. It was a one-sided argument.” In March the then UK technology secretary, Liz Kendall, said the key proposal to let tech companies train on copyright protected material unless artists “opt out” of the process beforehand was no longer the government’s preferred option. The new prime minister, Smiths fan Andy Burnham, has yet to set out a new policy on copyright but would face a battle-hardened opposition if he took the unlikely step of taking on the creatives again. Over to you, Kylie, Baz and Hugh.
