headline: One Nation boss called David Farley an ‘asshole’ in lead-up to Farrer byelection, text messages reveal
trail_text: Exclusive:  Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteers
body_text: One Nation’s general manager, Kelvin Morton – brought in by the party to improve its vetting processes – referred to David Farley as an “asshole” just days before Farley’s historic Farrer byelection win for the party in May. In a series of text messages seen by Guardian Australia, Morton responds to a news article published in the Sydney Morning Herald about infighting among senior party figures over Farley’s previously undeclared support for the Labor party. “Shit stirring,” he writes. “We need to do way better with our candidate selection – we need to stop finding these assholes … or letting them find us. “I guess this might nail David’s colours to us a little more. He’s sworn allegiance in the face of all the concerns being raised – he’d look like a completely untrustworthy snake if he jumped ship after the election – he’d be ruined forever.” A One Nation party spokesperson said that Farley was “a dedicated One Nation MP”. “The comments made do not reflect the view of the party. “The only untrustworthy snake is the person who leaked the text messages.” Tensions between Farley and other One Nation MPs and staff have reportedly been high since he was elected to parliament, with the party having to publicly criticise him after he claimed One Nation’s migration policy was not dissimilar to the Labor government’s. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Morton, who claims on his LinkedIn to be a “strategic business transformation leader” with vast experience with some of the world’s biggest companies, was appointed as general manager in February. At the time, he said the party’s national executive had wanted him to build a “professional, scalable, and legally robust organisation capable of outright victory at the next general election”. He claimed to be introducing a new vetting process and was in his position when Farley was preselected. But while his appointment was heralded as a turning point for the professionalisation of the party, the Guardian can reveal that Morton has since clashed with staff at the party’s Brisbane headquarters and officials at one of the party’s most active branches. He was recently appointed to the One Nation national executive, replacing former treasurer Alex Jones. Documents seen by the Guardian show he wrote to the Lilley branch in Brisbane advising it of federal intervention, which included removing the entire committee of volunteers. This came after a dispute about access to promotional materials and a local fundraiser that raised $12,000 for the party. The dispute arose after Morton and the Lilley branch coordinator, Mark McGuire, clashed over access to promotional materials for a different event, which prompted Morton to suspend him. “Your membership will continue to remain suspended until a formal written apology is received by you,” Morton said, accusing him of removing promotional materials from head office and clashing with a staff member. McGuire told the Guardian he had accessed policy flyers to take to an event being run by the party’s Brisbane branch. Other volunteer branch members and the president, Deb Dalton, complained about McGuire’s treatment, advising head office that the branch committee would cease volunteering in protest. The letter from Morton sent in response stated that he accepted the board’s “resignation”, despite the branch members only advising they would cease volunteering. “The Federal Executive is now intervening in the management of the Lilley branch as its functioning and compliance are in question,” he writes. “All branch decisions and actions are now subject to direct review and management by the Federal Executive, which reserves the right to overturn any local decision which is not in the best interest of the Party.” Morton also accused the branch of not handing over $12,000 raised at a branch fundraising dinner last year and demanded it be transferred to party headquarters where it would be controlled by the party’s national executive. “You are reminded that … branches are strictly prohibited from maintaining independent bank accounts,” Morton said in a letter to the branch president. “All branch funds – including the $12,000 referred to by Mark McGuire in his phone call to me – must be managed centrally.” He said he would revoke the membership of all branch committee members, and that “ongoing membership is contingent upon the full and transparent return of all party property, financial records, and the $12,000 in raised funds”. McGuire told the Guardian that he believed the party’s volunteers had been treated unfairly and the $12,000 had already been paid automatically to central office when people bought tickets. “They were treated with no procedural fairness and total disrespect,” McGuire said. “They all put their own time in, they make a sacrifice for their own family. “The fact is that he’s got it wrong, the question is, where’s the 12 grand? Who’s had their sticky fingers in the pie? He needs to stand up and be accountable to show the whole of the branch where the 12 grand is.” A One Nation spokesperson said the party “does not provide comment on internal disciplinary actions”. “All branch donations are managed through a microsite that tags funds with the corresponding branch. Branch funds are quarantined for localised campaigns.”

headline: As more Australian universities use AI to mark students’ work, is it creating a ‘slop-cycle’?
trail_text: Educational institutions find themselves suddenly confronted with a fork in the road
body_text: Armin Alimardani has blue hair, is fresh faced, wears a smartwatch and describes himself as “a tech enthusiast”. He is an unlikely sentinel, perhaps, to warn that a drift towards academics using generative artificial intelligence to help mark students assignments could pose an existential threat to higher education. The Western Sydney University senior lecturer in law and technology has been studying and experimenting with AI for years – he is speaking from Palermo in Italy, where he is attending a series of university workshops on the technology. He says colleagues have been asking him lately if it could help lighten the burden of grading. Alimardani finds this talk “extremely concerning”. “We’ve got to be really careful where we are stepping here,” he says. “Because I think there’s always a risk, at the moment, for higher education to collapse”. AI being used to mark assignments is no theoretical prospect, but a fork in the road at which universities have suddenly found themselves confronted. Alimardani’s is among several universities in Australia that allow staff to use AI in marking assessments and giving students feedback. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Though limited, fellow critics say such use of AI risks universities replacing the work of human academics on campuses with algorithms in datacentres – and that it could create a so-called “slop-cycle”, in which students submit AI-generated assignments that academics mark with AI. “Students are already financially struggling,” Alimardani says. “If they are not receiving proper feedback, if they feel like their degree is not as meaningful for employers and if they think that having a university degree doesn’t help them that much with guaranteeing a job – why would they come to university, really?” The University of Newcastle, also in New South Wales, Deakin University and RMIT in Victoria and South Australia’s University of Adelaide all give similar allowances to WSU. In all those cases, it is a qualified green light for AI. Newcastle, for example, gives students the right to opt out and Deakin says staff can use AI to “improve efficiency and support assessment and administrative activities” but not “assign grades”. A spokesperson said WSU took “a human-centred approach to generative AI use in assessment” in which “the awarding of marks, grades and feedback must also always be the responsibility of academic staff”. “Academic staff may use AI tools to support certain aspects of assessment and feedback, however responsibility for academic judgment must always remain with university teaching staff,” the spokesperson said. Alimardani says AI does have the potential to improve the quality of marking by acting as a “second pair of eyes” – he is working to create models that can pick out inconsistencies in human assessment. And the promise of AI assistance comes at a time when many university staff are overworked to “breaking point”, he notes, with marking taking up a large portion of academics’ time. But claims of the potential benefit AI would bring to marking, he says, are largely untested, while the risk it poses is so great as to behoove a “really slow” and considered evaluation of those claims. Alimardani is not sure how AI could be used at scale to speed up assessments at all, without inviting disaster. Imagine 100 academics are given an AI marking tool but told to verify its assessments, Alimardani says. “Let’s say 80 do exactly as advised, there are going to be 20 who do not”. He calls this “verification drift”: after a few AI generated assessments appear fine, the human charged with its oversight – often overworked themselves – stops being as vigilant and AI hallucinations slip through as facts. Such scandals, as have been seen in courtrooms over recent years, would be almost inevitable, he says, tarnishing university reputations and fostering a sense of unfairness among students that would see them question the value of higher education. Which may explain several high-ranking universities – including University of NSW, the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney – draw the line at using generative AI in marking, despite enthusiastically allowing it in other aspects of the classroom. Jury still out For all those that have adopted a position on the matter, a number of universities say they are considering how they might use AI as a marking tool. A Monash spokesperson said “at this time, AI is not used in the marking process”, but that the university was “transforming assessment through a programmatic approach” in which “AI is integrated into teaching and assessment to support students’ learning”. Wollongong and James Cook universities responded similarly. Others appeared to dodge the question entirely. A University of Queensland spokesperson said its academics are “required to confirm that all specified learning outcomes are achieved and that grades awarded reflect the level of student attainment”. “UQ maintains an expectation that academics assess their students’ work and is actively developing policies to maintain this expectation in the age of AI,” the spokesperson said in response to a direct question. Similar jargon was deployed by the Queensland University of Technology in an email sent to staff in late August advising them of its “assessment uplift project”. “The project is a whole-of-university initiative to transform QUT’s assessment ecosystem so that assessment remains authentic, trusted, scalable and future-focused in an increasingly AI-enabled learning environment,” it read. “It is currently progressing through initiation, with broad consultation underway to understand current experiences, challenges, and opportunities across the assessment lifecycle.” Such “corporate speak” prompted one QUT academic to quip that it sounded like AI was writing to inform academics it was taking their job. While a senior colleague, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the reaction among staff was one of “widespread concern”. Though “worryingly vague”, the academic said the email “certainly seems to be flagging that we will use less human marking if we can”. They said sessional academics often rely on marking as a primary source of income in an already precarious line of work. “People are concerned their job might be made redundant,” they said. Why mark with AI if students can’t write with it? As well as some staff having concerns about the environmental and ethical considerations, many are a long way from being convinced that AI could reliably and accurately assess work, they said, given the poor quality of AI generated assignments they were seeing some students try to pass off as their own. “We are telling students all the time that there are integrity issues with their use of AI in assessment,” the academic said. “What message does it send if we then say: but we are going to use it to mark you?” For QUT creative and professional writing student Alex Cameron, the message would be clear. “At that point, we might as well just have AI everything,” he says. “Just get our degrees through AI and have AI write our assignments.” An editor at the university’s Glass Magazine, Cameron says his three years of higher education have been an “awesome” time in which he has been surrounded by like-minded and interesting people – “the whole point of universities”. But Cameron says he “wouldn’t pay $1000” for a degree in which he was marked with AI – and doesn’t think many of his cohort would be happy with the prospect. “I would be irate,” he says. “I would be absolutely bloody incensed. “We like to do human writing, we like to have humans look at it – and we like to get feedback from humans”.

headline: Australia is run on legacy systems that AI agents can easily exploit, former UN cyber negotiator warns
trail_text: Federal cabinet will discuss the OpenAI breach on Monday as the AI giant pauses testing of latest models amid fallout
body_text: Ageing computer systems used throughout Australia’s government and large sections of the economy are easily exploited by AI agents, increasing the risk that sensitive information could be compromised, Australia’s former chief UN cyber negotiator has warned. As the government urgently undertakes a forensic investigation into a rogue OpenAI agent accessing Medicare data, the AI expert and Tech Policy Design Institute executive director, Johanna Weaver, said huge vulnerabilities existed across older IT systems. “It is old legacy systems that present the huge vulnerabilities, because large amounts of information and data is stored on these systems that have been around since the beginning of the internet,” Weaver said. “They aren’t updated and maintained because either people have forgotten about them or it’s too costly, or there aren’t updates for systems any more. That creates an enormous vulnerability, and that is what these agents are going to be exploiting.” Monday’s meeting of federal cabinet will discuss the fall out, as OpenAI said on Sunday it had paused training of its latest artificial intelligence models amid growing reports of its agents going rogue. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here After the Australian hack was revealed on Thursday, the company disclosed moves to review several incidents in which OpenAI agents searching American government websites went far beyond what handlers asked of them. OpenAI said it would resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards” in place, adding that it expected it would have to “hit pause” again as AI developed and other issues emerged. Weaver, who completed her term at the UN in 2021, said thorough investigation and remediation efforts would be required to close vulnerability gaps, calling on AI companies not to release models they could not control on the internet. “We are not powerless. We can decommission old systems and move sensitive data off legacy systems. Think of it as a digital spring clean,” she said. “We must also draw a line in the sand and say that, if companies cannot control their AI systems, they shouldn’t release them. And if they do, and those systems cause harm, companies must be held accountable.” Government systems are commonly run on programs dating back decades, sometimes due to the cost and complexity of replacing them. The finance and government services minister, Katy Gallagher, said last week the agent had accessed Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, through legacy systems linked to Services Australia. On Sunday a spokesperson said the agency was working with the Australian Signals Directorate to track the AI agent’s movements in the June incident. A cross-government rapid review is under way, with the prime minister’s department, the national cybersecurity coordinator and the Australian AI Safety Institute all involved. Axios reported on Sunday that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers were investigating tens of thousands of incidents globally in which frontier models undertook problematic or unexpected actions. Incidents included bypassing safety guardrails, creating message boards, escaping testing systems, hijacking websites, so-called “self prompting” and the bypassing of monitors. OpenAI also halted development of its models in July, after the disclosure of a cyber-attack targeting AI startup Hugging Face. Growing scrutiny of AI models follows calls from the heads of OpenAI and rival Anthropic for an industry slowdown. The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, called on the companies to make executives available to answer questions in a parliamentary inquiry into AI. The chair, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, called on OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei to give evidence on Sunday. Hanson-Young’s inquiry is due to resume hearings in Canberra on Thursday. The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, was sceptical that the OpenAI hack should result in legal consequences for the company. “I’m not entirely sure who it is that they’re going to put in cuffs and drag through the city streets and put in the stocks,” the Liberal senator told ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday. “The real alarm bell that was set off this week is the fact that the only reason we knew about this breach … is because OpenAI told us.” The Albanese government has defended its response to the incident. “The fact that we’ve got an artificial intelligence agent gaining unauthorised access to an Australian government website, that of itself is very serious,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, told News 24. “There’s no hiding that. “This is the first time this has happened in the context of Australia, and so we’re not shying away from that. In fact, the information that it obtained, was minor in its nature, in as much as that information we’ve now made public anyway – it wasn’t anyone’s personal data.”

headline: ‘I can’t be the mum I want to be’: why does parenthood feel so impossible for millennial mothers?
trail_text: Women today are more educated, more employed and more engaged in childcare than generations before them. Is there any way out of the total overwhelm?
body_text: Early one morning, feeling desperate, Katherine went on to her phone and asked ChatGPT how to make her life work. She plugged in her work hours, her husband’s work schedule, the days she had childcare for her three-year-old, the school hours – plus before- and after-school care times – for her six-year-old; the flexibility her job offered her, the supports she had from grandparents, and asked AI if it could help her make things feel a bit better. She told the chatbot that she wakes up between 5am and 5.30am, so she can “get the jump on the kids”. She might use this time to shower in peace, or start preparing her daughter’s lunchbox, or, if she’s really doing well, get a quick workout in. The children wake between 5.30 and 6am and from that time it is a mad scramble to get them ready to leave for school and daycare by 7am. It is not the gentle start to the day that any of them would like. “They come down and they want to have a cuddle on the couch, and I’m constantly like, ‘I’m really sorry, I have to get lunch boxes packed,’” Katherine says. After the frantic domestic sprint, the girls head out the door with their dad, who drops them off on his way to work and picks them up at the end of the day. “Then I have a very short amount of time to get myself ready and then I run out the door and my bus trip is, like, me calming myself down.” At the end of the day, they do it all again but in reverse. Katherine is describing her dilemma beside an overheated indoor swimming pool in Sydney, where our kids have lessons on the same weekday afternoon. She and I don’t know each other outside the context of swimming lessons, but we both have six-year-old daughters who have started at local primary schools this year and three-year-olds who take turns trying to bolt from the pool when the lessons no longer spark joy, so we have fallen to talking. And the subject of the impossible juggle of millennial mothers – broadly, those born between 1980 and 1994 – comes up, as it almost inevitably does when women of our age and stage get together. Because while Katherine’s questions to ChatGPT may sound like desperate cries for help from a woman on the brink, the reality is she is not an outlier. Within minutes of meeting one another on the sidelines of football games, at daycare drop-offs and pickup from afterschool care, women pepper one another with questions. How are you doing it? What balls do you drop? Why does it feel like this? ‘You’re not getting to parent the way you always wanted’ Last week the spotlight was thrown on the economic toll of the juggle for today’s parents, with new research showing that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has only grown by 102% in the same period. Georgie Dent, the chief executive of The Parenthood, which published the research, says having children reduces the earnings of Australian women by an average of 55% over the first five years and that Australian families now need two incomes to stay afloat. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads This is not hyperbole. In a fairly seismic shift for the country’s labour arrangements, both parents working full-time became the most common setup for households with children under 15 in 2024 for the first time. Despite this, Dent says, there is less give in family budgets. Meanwhile, the latest federal government intergenerational report warns that fewer Australians are expected to be having fewer children over the coming decades. This economic reality is acutely felt, like a great oppressive scaffold, by Katherine. After plugging all the variables of her life into ChatGPT, the suggestions that came back from the chatbot were impossible. It suggested she work from home – not an option – or part-time. Katherine already works four days a week; doing any fewer days of paid work would mean the family would struggle financially. Her entire salary goes toward their mortgage. It used to cover the payments but, after the multiple interest rate rises, it no longer does. “If I could go to five days, it’s a 20% increase, which is not nothing. I’ve been really tempted to do that.” It would, however, mean even less time with her children. Going below four days a week would not only be a financial impossibility but mean she can no longer perform her job in a way she wants to, or in a way that would mean she is taken seriously. “I would be drowning and not worth employing,” she says. Eventually, the main thing that ChatGPT offered Katherine was sympathy and an unflinching mirror held up to her life. “ChatGPT was like, ‘Oh, that’s interesting, what you just said is you’re not getting to parent the way that you always wanted to parent and … you’re limited and I think that that’s a really common experience.’” The fact that a machine built to scour the furthest reaches of published human knowledge, synthesise all that information and return with diagnoses and a solutions could only offer her a blunt assessment of her life and no real answers broke her. “I just sat there with tears in my eyes. “It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.” A matter of time While the rising economic cost of having children sits underneath everything like a great rotten foundation, for many Australians it is just one part of the parenthood pinch. For many parents, whose lives feel like a rubber band pulled so tight it is translucent, the stretch comes also in time and wellbeing. According to a major study conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the most time-stressed group in the country were single mothers of children aged under 15, with 56% saying they were “always or often” rushed or pressed for time. Having a partner scarcely seems to makes a difference to how extremely time-pressured mothers feel – 54.6% of women with children under 15 who have a partner report being time-stressed. Men with young children have the highest rate of time stress (46.6%) of any group of men in the country. In couples with no children, the number of people feeling acutely pressed for time is about half that of their friends with children. Because, despite the huge increase in women’s paid work over the last 60 years, today’s mothers are not doing less childcare. One of the findings that is repeated again and again across sociological research globally is that parents today – of any gender – spend more time caring for children than parents did midway through last century. In one of the most comprehensive studies of the subject, researchers looked at data spanning 11 countries over nearly 50 years and found that in every single country the amount of time spent directly caring for children each day increased dramatically, on average doubling for mothers from 1965 to 2012 and tripling for fathers (though from a far lower base). In Australia, men (and this data refers to all men, not just fathers) have increased the amount of time they spend caring – for children and disabled or elderly relatives – by half an hour a week over the last 20 years – 5.5 hours a week in 2022, up from five hours in 2002. But women still do nearly double the number of care hours as men, and have seen their care work increase too – spending 10.7 hours a week caring in 2022, compared with 10.1 hours in 2002. Everyone’s workloads have gone up – women in the paid work sector, men’s at home, women’s at home – and there has been no counterbalancing drop in either men’s paid work or women’s care work. ‘The workplace is too greedy’ “It just feels to me like a lot of the Jenga pieces have been pulled out, one by one and the tower is tottering,” says Prof Lyn Craig, a leading researcher in gender dynamics and household labour at the University of Melbourne. “I think the pressures on young women particularly, but young people generally, are getting more and more.” There is less economic give, which gives people fewer options to scale back paid work when care needs increase. And while it’s more common for couples to assume that there will be a more equitable division of labour at home, the world has not changed to make that possible. “There hasn’t been enough attention paid, I think, in policy, as to how to lower the amount of time that is expected of households to be in the market now.” Craig says many people expected that as a result of women spending more hours in paid work, men would spend more time doing domestic labour. But while more than half of Australian women aged between 25 and 44 are now university educated, and volumes more are in paid work in ever more senior roles, that isn’t what has happened. The shifts at home have been far slower than the shifts in the workplace. “I just think the workplace is too greedy,” Craig says. Women are doing less housework than they used to but not less care work, even as they do more paid work. “People just do more at the same time,” Craig says. “They just double up.” This is because, as Craig writes in a paper from 2006: “Delegating the care of children is more potentially problematic than outsourcing other domestic tasks. Caregiving is a complicated mixture of work and love. “Balancing the needs of children for nurture and the needs of women for independence without overloading women is the outstanding challenge of feminism.” Twenty years after she wrote those words, I ask her, does she still see this as the outstanding, unmet challenge of feminism? “I think it is,” she says. ‘Who designed that?’ In 1963, Betty Friedan identified “the problem that has no name” – a pervasive despair among white, middle-class US housewives who were trapped by expectations that their domestic lives would offer them total fulfilment. But 60 years on, the feminine mystique has flipped. Millennial women, it seems, are not trapped by their homes but by an impossible expectation that they maintain everything – career, motherhood, partnership, self-care – simultaneously and without complaint. One of the hardest things about the problem for this generation of women is not that it has no name but that it feels like a problem with no solution. A friend, who has a big job in government, a husband who frequently has to travel for work and a one-year-old who has been sick and not sleeping, texts me at 7.30pm one night to tell me that her five-year-old has been “one big giant meltdown this evening”. I sympathise and ask if the five-year-old is now in bed and my friend can crash on the couch with ice-cream or wine and some trashy TV. She writes back: “Seriously though – when do people do this? Teach me your secrets. I look around after bedtime and the house is absolutely trashed, and by the time we’ve dealt with it – definitely not CLEANED it or anything, literally just put away actual food items and spilled hazards, it’s time for bed!” I respond with a picture of my living room, which looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them. “Current state of play,” I text back. “We have no secrets.” “That’s the problem,” Katherine says as we wrap our poolside chat because a three-year-old who may or may not have urine trickling down a leg has emerged from the water and is shivering on the concrete in front of us. “You’re just kind of making the same complaint to your friends over and over and no one has any idea how to navigate it aside from winning the lotto and then completely pissing off your career that you also care about.” I have spent months collecting stories from mothers around the country and one thing that rings through all their stories is a common feeling of total overwhelm, of zero margin, that the house is made of cards and has been built too high and that the slightest gust could knock it all down. “I’m now at a point professionally where I should be kind of at my maximum, like my peak professional moment,” says Annie (not her real name), a mother of two young children. “And I just feel jammed. I feel torn ... I can’t invest the time and the energy to deliver the professional product that I want to deliver and be the mum I want to be. “It’s too much.” As for how to solve the problem, for Annie, she says there is a need to correct what she calls “structural disasters”: the school hours that run from 9am until 3pm; the weeks of school holidays that dwarf any parent’s paid leave allowance. “For crying out loud! Who designed that?” she asks. “Working men with stay-at-home wives designed that.” Dent and her organisation The Parenthood propose policy solutions including parental leave that is longer and which men are incentivised to take alongside better access to affordable, quality childcare. Annie says: “I actually think the other thing – which is much harder – is reducing the hours that people work and the expectations of what it means to be a good professional.” In her industry, “success” is marked by a culture of long hours and visible busyness. Having a packed schedule and being busy beyond the telling of it. Maintaining a full but sustainable workload and doing your work well, but being home in the evenings for time with family, is not. “I don’t know how you change that sort of cultural pressure.” *** Despite the exhaustion, the financial pressure, the feeling that we are all furiously spinning our gears to keep our lives in motion, the women I have spoken to do not hate their lives. They do not regret being mothers. I am a millennial mother. I adore my children. If someone had been able to get me to feel the reality of what motherhood would be like before I ever became pregnant, I would choose to have these three delightful chaos agents again, without question. Many millennial parents are living a life we dreamed of – with jobs and families we love and fought hard for. We are grateful for that but it is all far harder than we imagined. Because equally if, before I became pregnant, someone had been able to get me to feel the reality of what motherhood would be like, I would have said: surely we can do better than this.

headline: Shannon felt a ‘sense of doom’ as she sought justice for sexual assault. A new NSW program hopes to alleviate that
trail_text: Exclusive:  Dedicated service to support sexual assault victim-survivors as they navigate legal system to open in NSW
body_text: It took Shannon Stokes two years and 11 days to successfully prosecute her former boyfriend for sexual assault and domestic violence offences. The lengthy trial left her feeling as though “there wasn’t going to be an end in sight”. Prosecutors secured convictions on nine of the 11 charges, and he was later sentenced to five years in prison. Stokes, 28, from New South Wales, said a “sense of doom” throughout the trial was compounded by a lack of appropriate legal assistance as she navigated the justice system, a world she said felt “so alien” to her. She recalled receiving pamphlets in the lead-up to the trial that she said were “more or less about how to look presentable” in court. “I also had a few pieces of paper handed to me on the day going into that courtroom, and that was what I had to kind of go off … it just makes you feel so isolated and like a number in the system rather than a person who has actually been victimised by violence.” Experts say Stokes’ experience is common among sexual assault victim-survivors pursuing justice. Sarah Rosenberg, the executive director of the victim-led network With You We Can and an advocate for justice reform, has long called for greater support for victim-survivors navigating the legal system. “They’re expected to navigate a very isolating, very complex system entirely alone,” she said. “They’d essentially have to become legal experts overnight just to figure out what is going on in a case that supposedly revolves around them.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Rosenberg said an adversarial justice system often further traumatises victim-survivors. “That process of having the victim-survivor be a witness opens them up to a lot of re-traumatising during the process … There is nothing that mimics the dynamics of abuse more than being relegated to just a witness in the accountability process.” This week, the NSW government announced it would establish the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Legal Service, operating through Legal Aid NSW. The $1.74m expansion will provide free legal support for a range of sexual assault matters, including advice about the criminal process, survivors’ rights during police investigations and prosecutions, and assistance with access to victims’ compensation. The pilot program is part of the state government’s $6.2m strengthening sexual violence justice responses package announced last month, which is backed by federal funding. Robyn Gilbert, a senior solicitor at Legal Aid NSW who will lead the service, said: “The point of the service is to bring some autonomy and choice back to survivors, to be better informed and have a clearer idea of their own rights and their role in the system.”She said the service would be “open to all callers” across the state. “Really, the only eligibility criteria is to have experienced a sexual assault,” Gilbert said. The NSW minister for the prevention of domestic violence and sexual assault, Jodie Harrison, said navigating the legal system could be overwhelming for many victim-survivors. “Accessing the right support at the right time is an important part of ensuring they are treated with dignity and respect throughout the justice process,” she said. Ged Kearney, the federal assistant minister for the prevention of family violence, said: “I have heard from many victim-survivors of sexual violence that their experience seeking legal advice after an assault can be traumatic during what’s already a very traumatic period.” Stokes said she experienced those challenges during her own trial, when questions were dismissed or repeated, and she was required to submit evidence for victims’ compensation more than once. The pilot program was a step towards addressing the trauma of navigating “a really hard legal system”, she said. “Having such a big time pass between my assault and going to court definitely affected me more mentally … I say it light-heartedly, but I think it actually traumatised me more than my actual assault did.”

headline: Extra 1,000 prison beds announced in NSW as union warns against arresting ‘our way out of domestic violence’
trail_text: Minns government to spend $47.1m to recommission part of Silverwater jail while PSA says prison alone will not end violent behaviour
body_text: The reopening of part of Sydney’s Silverwater jail will deliver hundreds of extra beds amid record numbers of prisoners on remand, the state government says, as the prison officers’ union warns against “arrest[ing] our way out of domestic violence”. The Minns government, responding to a surge in prisoners awaiting trial since domestic violence bail laws were tightened, announced on Monday it would spend $47.1m to recommission the 515-bed Dawn de Loas correctional centre at the Silverwater complex by early next year. It said alongside the “fast-tracked delivery” of more than 360 additional beds at Parklea correctional centre, returning to public hands next month, this would add nearly 1,000 beds to New South Wales’ prison capacity. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The premier, Chris Minns, told reporters at Dawn de Loas on Monday he believed the expansion was “a necessary decision for NSW, [which] we believe in the long run will keep the public safe. “Not arresting people for violent domestic violence offences will not solve them either.” But after the announcement, the Public Service Association (PSA) of NSW said the additional beds were “a response to a DV crisis that demands far more than extra prison capacity”. The PSA general secretary, Stewart Little, said, “We can’t just arrest our way out of domestic violence. “Prison can contain someone who poses a serious risk. It cannot, by itself, protect a person before violence occurs or stop an offender returning to violent behaviour after release.” The additional beds come amid desperate calls for action on domestic and family violence after the alleged murders of three women and two children this month. On 11 September this year, Daniel Billings was sentenced to 28 years in jail for the 2024 murder of Forbes woman, Molly Ticehurst. Ticehurst’s killing by her ex-boyfriend, who had been freed on bail a fortnight before, prompted strengthened domestic and family violence laws, with serious alleged offenders now needing to “show cause” as to why they should be released, and registrars no longer able to make bail decisions. The changes have driven record numbers of prisoners on remand, totalling 6,398 people – 46% of NSW’s adult prison population – as of September. The PSA has called for the government to run domestic violence services in-house through 15 centres across the state, as well as compulsory diversionary programs for alleged offenders on remand, and dedicated courts for domestic violence cases amid a backlog of cases. While it called for “properly resourced” domestic violence programs for people leaving custody on parole, the premier said the government had increased funding for domestic and family violence services. “People pitch these arguments as: ‘Look, it’s a waste of money to have the criminal justice system in place or to have long sentences for violent domestic violence offenders’. I don’t agree with that,” Minns said on Monday. Amid concerns that DV offenders were not being rehabilitated and about the effectiveness of rehabilitation programs in general, the premier said he could not make programs compulsory for prisoners on remand. Dawn de Loas temporarily closed in November 2022 amid a declining prison population and staff shortages during the pandemic. The government says about 150 staff will be recruited to support the reopening in early 2027. The government anticipates fast-tracking an additional 360 beds at Parklea correctional centre, one of two privately managed correctional centres in NSW, after Corrective Service resumes management in October. It says the 1,000 additional beds, which will be for minimum security remand and sentenced prisoners, will take the strain off Silverwater’s 24-hour Metropolitan Remand and Reception Centre (MRRC). On Monday, the corrections minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, ruled out closing Long Bay correctional centre’s Metropolitan Special Programs Centre (MSPC), where a 19-year-old man took his own life in May while on remand. The independent watchdog had previously recommended the unit be closed because it “simply cannot provide a safe environment”. The NSW opposition has proposed to close all of Long Bay to build 10,000 homes, calling for an upgrade to Goulburn correctional centre. Chanthivong confirmed the government had closed four Victorian-era wings at Goulburn which he said were “no longer fit for purpose”.

headline: Beau Lamarre-Condon told friend if he killed anyone he’d dump belongings in bin and take bodies to bushland, court hears
trail_text: Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024 – nine months after discussion with friend Georgia Cook
body_text: A Sydney police officer told a friend he would hide the bodies of anyone he killed in bushland and put their belongings in a dumpster, months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a court has heard. Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting the couple with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. At his double murder trial on Monday, Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court about a dinner in May 2023. The brief relationship between Baird and Lamarre-Condon had ended when the accused asked her what she would do if he told her he’d killed someone, Cook told the jury. He then asked what she would do if she killed someone and what she would do with their bodies, the court heard. Cook responded she had no idea. She said on Monday that Lamarre-Condon replied: “After I’d killed them I would take their stuff, I would put it in a dumpster, and I would take their bodies in bushland where nobody would ever find them.” Asked about her response, Cook said the situation in 2023 felt “very surreal”. “I didn’t know whether to believe anything I’d heard, or whether it was true,” she told the jury. “Hearing a person of power in the police force [say that] – it felt like I didn’t have anywhere to go and I was really scared by what I had heard.” After Lamarre-Condon allegedly shot Baird and Davies in February 2024, he dumped Baird’s bloodied belongings and furniture into a skip bin in Cronulla, the prosecution said during its opening statement last week. The two bodies were left on the fence line of a Greek Orthodox monastery in remote bushland in Bungonia – about 160km from Paddington, the court heard. Lamarre-Condon’s lawyers suggested he never told Cook he would dump a hypothetical body in the bush, and noted her statement to police about the conversation came months after news reports about Baird and Davies’ bodies being disposed of. She responded: “I could never forget these words being said to me.” The crown alleged in its opening that the police officer began planning to murder Baird in early 2024 after developing an “obsession and infatuation” with him. Lamarre-Condon’s work colleague Andrew Callus told the court the officer had become annoyed and unhappy when he discovered Baird had begun seeing Davies. Lamarre-Condon allegedly told Callus: “You know what I’m like … I can’t let things go, I hate losing.” He was “angry at the relationship, at being rejected by Jesse,” Callus told the court. The defence team has claimed Lamarre-Condon was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an UberEats rider and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings. Defence lawyer John Stratton SC said during his opening statement the two men were fatally shot in struggles with the policeman, who immediately began cleaning up the scene because he “panicked”. Lamarre-Condon sent messages from Baird’s phone after allegedly murdering him to give the impression he was alive, the prosecution has said. Messages were read to the court as a friend of Davies took the witness box on Monday. The morning of the shootings, the friend sent a message to Davies that went undelivered, before following up with an Instagram message that also went undelivered, the court heard. Knowing Davies was in a relationship with Baird, the friend then decided to send a message to Baird asking: “Hello is your wife alive?”, referring to Davies. Baird’s Instagram account replied that Davies had smashed his phone screen on the day of the alleged murders, the court heard. On 21 February 2024, the friend sent another message to Baird’s account that said: “Apparently police have found Luke’s wallet and called his mum. No one can get in touch with him and they’re freaking out. Have you spoken to him?” But he never received a response. That same day, a detective attended the Paddington terrace and spoke to Baird’s housemate, known to the court under the pseudonym Sarah King. King showed the detective a photo of the back courtyard, previously taken by their other housemate, showing surfboard bags and a blue tarpaulin next to a red pool of blood, the officer told the court on Monday. At the time of the officer’s visit, the items were no longer in the courtyard. Asked whether she had seen them before, King told the detective: “Nope. He’s never had surfboards here and he’s never spoken about surfing.” Baird and Davies’ bodies were eventually found in two surfboard bags, the prosecution alleged during its opening statement. The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

headline: Victoria police apologise over death of injured man taken to cells instead of hospital
trail_text: Inquest into 2023 death shown footage of John Makai struggling to stand after suffering serious head injury from being punched in head by son
body_text: Victorian police have apologised to the family of a man who died after being held for five hours in a police cell without medical treatment for a significant head injury. John Makai, a 58-year-old father of 10, died in 2023 from serious head trauma that went untreated despite him being unresponsive in a Broadmeadows cell, the Victorian coroner’s court heard on Monday. On the first day of an inquest into his death, footage was shown in court of Makai being dragged from a divisional van into police cells, and repeatedly failing to respond when officers checked on him through the cell door. The officers twice claimed that he had responded, despite the CCTV of the incident showing no such physical response, counsel assisting Rachel Ellyard told the court. After the footage was shown, a lawyer for Victoria police’s chief commissioner, Mike Bush, said he apologised for the death. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Andrew Imrie, for Bush, said that Makai’s care “was not at the standard that … any member of the Victorian community is entitled to expect”. He offered sincere condolences to Makai’s family and said it was “a situation Victoria police and all its employees work tirelessly to avoid”. Imrie said there was a failure to complete a medical checklist when Makai arrived at the Broadmeadows station. He also said there were failures to notice his deteriorating condition, to complete a risk assessment, and to conduct adequate checks. There had been disciplinary action taken against officers “where a basis was available”, he said. “At this stage it is unclear whether these shortcomings would have made any difference to the tragic outcome in this case,” Imrie told the inquest. The court heard that an ambulance was initially called – but was cancelled – after one of Makai’s sons punched him twice while the pair were drinking with another of his sons and a friend at a house in Sunbury. Police attended the house and in footage shown to the court could be seen watching on as Makai struggled to stand and then collapsed into a bookcase while trying to sit down. Police then had to support him to walk to the divisional van, and could be heard telling him to “get his legs up”. When they arrived at the Broadmeadows police station about 20 minutes later, Makai could no longer stand, and had to be dragged out of the van by his legs, with his head seen striking the floor and walls of the van. He was then placed seated on the ground, the footage showed. Officers lifted him under the arms to drag him into a cell, where he was placed in what is known as a “coma position”, the inquest heard. He made no verbal response during this transfer, nor at any other time at the station, the court heard. Police requested another ambulance at 1.25am, telling them that Makai had a minor facial injury and was in a very deep sleep because of his state of drunkenness, and they would like him to be checked by paramedics. Ambulance Victoria told police they were struggling with workload but would dispatch paramedics when they were available. “What was interpreted as deep sleep was in fact the increasing effects of traumatic brain injury and bleeding into the brain,” Ellyard said. The court heard that because of an issue with Triple Zero Victoria, the job was not actually logged as outstanding. An ambulance was not dispatched until the same police officer again requested another five hours later. The fresh call for an ambulance came after police entered Makai’s cell and could not get him to respond verbally. “I’ve got a guy been in custody a number of hours, he’s breathing, trying sternum rubs, all sorts of … we can’t get any verbals out of him, we’d like an urgent check on his welfare,” the police officer said in a recording of the call. “This request’s made since midnight, and for some reason it’s been cancelled at your end … I’m the custody sergeant, this guy’s breathing but we can’t raise any verbals from him.” When asked about his breathing, the sergeant responds he had been snoring heavily but not responding “since he came in, since midnight”. “Unconscious? And you haven’t had any response for six hours?” the Ambulance Victoria operator responds. The sergeant then goes on to say his officers had been checking on him every 15 minutes, which Ellyard said was proven incorrect in a review of the footage. When paramedics did respond, Makai was found to be showing signs of a brain injury, the court heard. He was transported via ambulance to hospital, where he was diagnosed with a non-survivable brain trauma. He died in hospital two days later. The first witness, Ryan Goon, the director of operations support for Triple Zero Victoria, said that the dispatcher wrongly cancelled the police request for an ambulance. This was because of an issue with “multiple associated events”, as the first person to call for an ambulance at the Sunbury house had later cancelled the request. Ellyard said the scope of the inquest – expected to run for two weeks – would consider the cause and the circumstances surrounding Makai’s death, including what treatment he could have received if he was taken to hospital rather than to a police station. It will also examine any changes to policies and reviews that had been completed after his death. The inquest before coroner Paresa Spanos continues.

headline: One Nation senator pays back more than $3,300 in taxi expenses; Cleary tells fans ‘I’ll be back’ – as it happened
trail_text: The days news, as it unfolded
body_text: Thanks for joining us today. Here are the key headlines: Australians along the east coast are reporting sightings of endangered bogong moths as the insects continue their long migration towards the country’s alpine regions. Australia’s key interest rate is expected to hit its highest level since 2011, drag down house prices and add more than $100 to typical monthly mortgage repayments. The former NSW premier Mike Baird will step down as the chair of Cricket Australia at the body’s next annual general meeting in October. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the final budget outcome showed the deficit came in “$6bn better than expected”. Perth’s popular City Beach is closed after a whale carcass washed up this morning amid concerns it could attract sharks. Petrol prices increased by more than 10 cents a litre last week to reach a national average of 237.5c/L, as global oil supply disruptions intensify. The Penrith Panthers star Nathan Cleary is out of surgery and told fans on social media he’ll “be back” after he suffered an ankle fracture in a hip-drop tackle during Sunday’s match. We’ll be back bright and early tomorrow with more news. The One Nation senator for Western Australia, Tyron Whitten, has paid taxpayers back $3,391.68 for taking dozens of taxi journeys across Perth, the area he represents, between July and November last year. Under the rules, the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority (IPEA) said Whitten should have used the private-plated vehicle or vehicle allowance MPs and senators receive. The IPEA review says Whitten said he did not yet have his private-plated vehicle and was not “adequately briefed about the payment of the allowance”. But the IPEA then noted Whitten had “attended education sessions for new parliamentarians arranged by the Department of Finance … and by IPEA where the allowance had been covered.” Whitten has now paid back the taxi expenses plus a 25% loading – coming to a grand total of $3,391.68. Australia accused of being ‘in denial’ after failure of criminal case against King Charles An Indigenous elder attempting to charge King Charles III with genocide says Australia is in denial over its crimes and their ongoing impacts, AAP reports. Uncle Robbie Thorpe has been pursuing legal action against the king since 2023 over the alleged genocide committed against Aboriginal people. On Monday, an application to appeal a decision preventing the case from proceeding was denied. Despite the loss, the Krauatungalung elder and uncle of Senator Lidia Thorpe said the effort has been worth it. He vowed to take the fight to an international jurisdiction. He told AAP: Australia is just totally in denial. If it wasn’t for the acts of terror and the policies of genocide, Australia wouldn’t exist. That’s my reality, and a lot of other people’s. Thorpe filed a charge sheet with the magistrates court of Victoria in 2023, naming himself as the informant and the king as the accused. The offences alleged were continuing acts of genocide committed since 28 September 2022 against First Peoples, contrary to common law, federal law concerning genocide and First Peoples’ sovereign laws. But the filing was knocked back by a senior registrar of the magistrates court on the grounds that it did not reference any “proper source of law”. A judicial review by the supreme court upheld the registrar’s decision. The court of appeal dismissed an application by Thorpe to appeal the decision on the basis it had no real prospect of success. The appeal court said: While acknowledging the significance of the questions raised by Uncle Robbie, the primary judge stated (correctly and self-evidently) that the only jurisdiction she could exercise was the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Victoria. The primary judge concluded that the senior registrar of the Magistrates’ Court acted lawfully ... as the charges alleged in the charge-sheet did not disclose an offence known to the law of Victoria. Panthers star Nathan Cleary is out of surgery and told fans on social media he’ll “be back” after he suffered an ankle fracture in a hip-drop tackle during Sunday’s match. Penrith lost to Newcastle 22-14 on Sunday, sending the Knights through to their first grand final in 25 years. Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a tackle that left Cleary with a compound fracture and dislocation of the ankle late in the first half. Cleary posted a picture to his social media earlier today from a hospital bed, with his thumbs up and his leg wrapped in a bandage. He wrote: Surgery done… Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable. Yesterday sucked but it’s all part of the journey [and] it’s made me even more grateful for the people I have around me. I’ll be back. ‘We need to fix the economy,’ Angus Taylor says ahead of expected rate rise Opposition leader Angus Taylor has accused the Albanese government of losing control of the economy ahead of an expected rate rise by the Reserve Bank tomorrow. He said: We need to restore hope, we need to fix the economy, and we need to protect our way of life. And that’s why we need a government that is going to take less, not more. Earlier today, treasurer Jim Chalmers announced an improvement of $6bn in the budget bottom line. Contact tracing under way in Adelaide after measles cluster spreads A woman has become the latest in a cluster of measles cases after she spent up to 24 hours in an emergency department while infectious, AAP reports. It brings South Australia’s total number of cases to nine, the highest it’s been in 10 years. SA Health was notified of the case on Sunday afternoon and confirmed it was linked to a cluster at Adelaide’s Brighton Secondary College, where three teenagers contracted the highly infectious disease. The health agency confirmed 24 exposure sites dating back a week, warning those who had come into contact with those areas and weren’t fully immunised to be ‘‘alert for symptoms’’ over the next few weeks. SA’s chief public health officer, Nicola Spurrier, said contact tracing was under way at the hospital to contain the spread: The area that concerns me the most is the Queen Elizabeth hospital because you’ve got other vulnerable patients there. Unfortunately she was there in an open space for a longer period of time. I think there could potentially be additional spread. Call for NSW to fund air-conditioning in major public housing estate The NSW government is being urged to provide funding for reverse cycle air-conditioning in a Sydney public housing estate undergoing a major redevelopment. Public housing advocacy group REDWatch said the developer of the Waterloo public housing estate, Stockland consortium, had not been required, in its contract with Homes NSW, to include air-conditioning in the redevelopment of Waterloo South. RedWatch said that Waterloo South Homes NSW, the team in charge of the redevelopment, had applied to Homes NSW requesting funding for air-conditioning. It comes after the City of Sydney voted unanimously in support of air-conditioning in Waterloo South. The motion, passed last week, said: Summer air temperatures are becoming increasingly hotter due to global warming. Energy efficient heating and cooling is especially important in social housing because of the medical needs of residents, many of whom are at higher risk of health impacts from extreme heat. RedWatch said tenants had also written to housing minister Rose Jackson urging the government to commit the funding. Hello, I’ll now be taking you through our rolling live news coverage for the next little while. That’s all from me! Jordyn Beazley will snag the blog from here. Take care! ‘Not all good news’ amid whale conservation anniversary Forty years on from an international moratorium on commercial whaling, the global community is meeting to consider new, unforeseen threats, AAP reports. The International Whaling Commission’s 70th meeting began on Monday at Hobart, with delegates from some 63 member nations in attendance. The commission was founded in 1946, at a time when whale populations had been decimated by decades of unregulated industrial whaling. While populations have in many cases rebounded – particularly since a 1986 moratorium on commercial whaling – whales remain under threat globally. “It’s not all good news,” environment minister Murray Watt told delegates. Among the main issues to be debated at the week-long meeting is a quarter-century old push for a whale sanctuary in the southern Atlantic ocean. The proposal, which was first raised by Brazil in 1998, would extend an existing protected area in the Southern Ocean, protecting whales from West Africa to South America. But pro-whaling nations have refused to back the plan, with some walking out of previous meetings to scupper votes. Albanese says government still focused on cost of living ahead of interest rate decision tomorrow The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said the government is continuing to take action on cost of living support amid tomorrow’s expected rate rise by the Reserve Bank. Albanese just held a press conference in Tasmania, where he was asked how mortgage holders should feel before tomorrow’s announcement. He said the government had supported a tax cut earlier this year, free Tafe and multiple health initiatives meant to lower costs. [That’s] all aimed at making a difference, because we know people are doing it tough. And will continue to, as well, take work, such as the $6bn reduction in the deficit compared with what was anticipated in our May budget. The prime minister also said the government continues to look into the OpenAI breach. Artificial intelligence can make an enormous difference. It can boost productivity, it can boost economic growth, it can give us health breakthroughs. But we need to make sure that human beings are in charge of this. Petrol prices increased by more than 10 cents a litre last week to reach a national average of 237.5c/L, as global oil supply disruptions intensify. The price of diesel, which is being squeezed by a shortage of refining capacity and high demand from commercial users, rose more than 13c to 286.7c/L, according to the Australian Institute of Petroleum. Economists have linked the recent price rises in crude oil, which affects petrol prices, to the enduring conflict between the US and Israel against Iran, and recent Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Elevated fuel prices are a major household expense and inflation trigger given they drive up costs across goods and services in the economy, pushing central banks, including in Australia, to consider rate hikes to keep a lid on inflation. The Reserve Bank is expected to lift the cash rate from 4.25% to 4.6% after its meeting tomorrow in what would be the fourth rate increase this year. AMP’s chief economist Shane Oliver has warned petrol prices could surpass $2.70/L. Rescue crews continue to search for Jordan Yap, 30, a Melbourne man who went missing during a hike on a remote trail in Peru. A widespread search is under way by private rescue teams, but they’ve so far failed to find any trace of Yap. He last made contact with friends and family on 14 September before setting out on the planned 10-day solo trek. He was last seen near the beginning of the hike across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, a challenging, high-altitude adventure. Yap is considered an experienced hiker and was meant to return from the trek last Wednesday. The Mountain Rescue Association in Peru said on Saturday a group of 12 rescuers had been deployed, the third group to look for signs of the Australian. A reconnaissance flight has also been carried out to look in difficult-to-reach areas and abysses. “The mission remains active and will resume when weather conditions permit the continuation of operations safely,” the group wrote overnight on Facebook. A GoFundMe to help fund the search has raised about $60,000. Perth’s popular City Beach is closed after a whale carcass washed up this morning amid concerns it could attract sharks. Surf Live Saving WA reported the carcass around 7.30am this morning Perth time. Officials said sharks may be present along the WA coast throughout the year, but people should exercise additional caution at this time. Officers from the WA Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development and other agencies are monitoring the situation. The Town of Cambridge is working to remove the carcass. SharkSmart, which monitors shark activity, has issued shark advice for the City Beach area due to the carcass. Tight New Zealand election campaign kicks off The starter’s gun has been fired on the closest New Zealand election campaign in decades, with both major parties staging campaign launches in a tightening race. AAP reports prime minister Chris Luxon’s ailing coalition faces a fight from Labour under Chris Hipkins to avoid being the first one-term government in half a century. The contest is close between both the major parties and the broader right and left blocs. On Sunday, both National and Labour held rallies in Auckland to fire up their bases for the poll push ahead. Based on those events, a month of mud-throwing awaits. Gallagher gives update on response to OpenAI incident Asked by Guardian Australia’s Tom McIlroy as to whether there was new information on the OpenAI incident last week, Katy Gallagher says she had a briefing from Services Australia this morning. They have all the technical information they need but there are some further information that is still being sought, and there will be follow-up meetings with OpenAI over the course of this week. I don’t think there is anything further I can update you on, other than that website will not be reactivated. It is the Medicare statistics reporting portal. The data that was on the Medicare portal had been moved to a public site, she says: The email that notification, that OpenAI came to, has been redirected to essentially be monitored 24-7, not once a day, so there has been some short-term responses that Services Australia put in. I expect the forensic investigation to be finished within a matter of weeks, no longer than that. I don’t have a specific date, and that will feed into the rapid review the PM&C are leading. In response to a question about the expected interest rate hike tomorrow from the Reserve Bank and whether the government is considering doing anything to take pressure off inflation, Chalmers says it is a “near universal expectation of economists and the market that rates will go up around the world, including in Australia”. Conflict in the Middle East in particular will put pressure on inflation, he says. On productivity, he adds: There is no quick and easy way to turn around two decades of underperforming on productivity but we are taking [the] challenge more seriously than our predecessors did. Gallagher details origins of lower spending The minister for finance, Katy Gallagher, says the $1.4bn lower spending had come from cutting back on spending on a few particular programs, including aged care, the PBS, across the childcare system and “a couple of national partnership payments”. Chalmers says improvement came from super and investor income, not commodities Chalmers says payments were down $1.4 bn, and receipts had increased $4.6 bn. He says the improvements in receipts did not come from commodities: It is also not from wage earners. It is overwhelmingly from higher super and investor income than what we anticipated in the Treasury’s forecasts in May. So to be really clear about that, this is not about wage and salary earners, it is not about commodity prices, it is about higher-than-expected super and investor income, higher than was anticipated in the May budget. Mining profits actually came in lower than was expected, so those are some important points of perspective. The federal treasurer, Jim Chalmers, and the minister for finance, Katy Gallagher, are speaking to the press about the final budget outcome for the 2025-2026 financial year. Chalmers says the final budget outcome showed the deficit came in “$6bn better than expected”. He says: We have made a lot of progress in the budget and we have made more progress since then, but we know that there is more work to do. The bottom line is better than we inherited, better than it was at the election and better than it was forecast to be in May. It is now around half the deficit for the year just finished, compared to when we came to office. Cafes and shoppers at a crossroads as surcharge ban looms A ban on card surcharges is supposed to deliver savings for Australian shoppers, but the reality could be quite different if retailers raise prices and the banks claw back losses by axing rewards. AAP reports that the reform, driven by the Reserve Bank of Australia, comes into effect from Thursday, when anyone paying with a debit or credit card will be spared the surprise of extra charges at the till. Under the new rules, retailers must either absorb the cost or build it into their prices. They could also offer a discount for cash or payment services such as PayID, which some experts think could lead to savings of up to 10% off the transaction price. However, dealing in cash means keeping a float and taking it to the bank at the end of the day, which can be difficult given the general decline in branches across the country, and does lay a burden on small business owners. For those sticking to tap and go, there’s a good chance some businesses will raise prices to offset the merchant fees they still pay to the banks and payment providers to process those payments, which they used to recoup under surcharges.
