headline: OpenAI announces ‘dots’ agent after scrapping launch of new AI model over safety concerns
trail_text: Company’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificial intelligence agent Muse
body_text: Less than 24 hours after OpenAI announced it would scrap the launch of an artificial intelligence model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of AI tools. During its annual showcase for developers in San Francisco on Tuesday, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, enthusiastically unveiled an AI agent called “dots” that he said was “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI”. “It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, to loud applause from the developers attending the event. “In the future, if you like, you can work with a whole team of dots.” OpenAI’s dots are colorful little blobs, donning berets or glasses, that appear on people’s phones or laptops, can be integrated into other apps and can follow commands. The agents can perform tasks without supervision such as schedule a meeting, book a flight or dole out assignments to colleagues. OpenAI says the “dots are an extension of you” and describes the tool as “frontier intelligence”. Dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s latest model. OpenAI said the previous evening it would halt the release of GPT-6.1 Astra because the updated model showed deceptive behavior during testing. OpenAI’s dots will compete with Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released two weeks ago. Meta’s product is aimed at everyday consumers more than business customers, as OpenAI’s is, though Meta announced a small business offering on Tuesday. The agent’s app, available in the US, has been downloaded more than 3m times. OpenAI also apologized on Monday for one of its AI agents going rogue and hacking an Australian government website. The apology came after the company has been plagued by reports and admissions that its AI systems have been acting independently and gaining access to various company and government websites. During OpenAI’s event on Tuesday, Altman touted the power of Astra and introduced similar potent AI tools. One model, called GPT-6.1 Sol, is cheaper and “smarter than Astra in many ways”, the CEO said. Altman also previewed a new “Ultrafast” mode for its AI coding models, which can generate outputs up to eight times faster than what’s available now. “People often talk about AI as a new industrial revolution, I find that quite off-putting,” Altman said at the end of his presentation. “There are some parts of life that we cannot and should not automate. I believe that the future, if we get this right, can be more like a new Renaissance than a new industrial revolution.”

headline: From One Nation to fossil fuels, Adam Bandt and Bob Brown reveal vision for Greens ahead of leadership showdown
trail_text: Senior Greens figures say Larissa Waters’ successor must stop Labor approving fossil fuel projects ‘by whatever means’
body_text: The former Greens leader Adam Bandt says the party’s new leadership team, which could be chosen as early as Wednesday, will face mounting pressure to block the Albanese government from approving any new coal and gas projects “by whatever means”. Bandt told Guardian Australia there would be no excuses for the new leader, likely to be elected at a two-day retreat in Sydney which begins on Wednesday, to allow Labor to approve any new fossil fuel development. Three separate tickets have declared an intention to stand for the leadership. On Tuesday, South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young announced she would run for the leadership, while deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi, has also announced her intention to run on a joint ticket with Nick McKim as her deputy. On Wednesday morning, senators David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May confirmed they will also stand for leadership positions. Larissa Waters announced she would step down from the Greens’ leadership on Monday night, revealing she has been managing a chronic kidney disease, but that her health had “declined significantly over the course of recent months”. She said while her prognosis for recovery was positive, the pressure of the party’s leadership, including additional travel demands, was detracting from a focus on her health. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Bandt, now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said there would be several key climate flashpoints for the next leader with Labor before the next election, including whether the government would approve Woodside’s Browse gas project near the Scott Reef in northern WA, whether it would allow gas fracking in the Beetaloo basin in the NT and whether datacentres would be permitted to use fracked gas. “In terms of what approach gets taken in parliament, the view from the movement is: look, there’s no excuse now, there’s no parliamentary blocker to stopping new coal and gas mines and to stopping deforestation,” Bandt told Guardian Australia. “Just get it done by whatever means, whatever it takes to make that happen, at whatever style people adopt while they’re in parliament.” Party grandee Bob Brown said Waters had been a “splendid” leader, but warned the next leader would have to show they could extract significant reforms from Labor. “The next leader has an opportunity to take on not just One Nation but the failures of Labor … It has to be a leader who can take it up with Anthony Albanese and Pauline Hanson,” Brown said. “You need a very, very strong and able negotiator, not just to make incremental changes, but very big changes.” While One Nation has seen its popularity surge in 2026, the Greens voter base has not significantly grown. The party received 12.22% of the primary vote in 2025 compared with 12.25% in 2022. In 2026, the Australian’s Newspoll showed the primary vote at 13% in August and September. Nine newspapers’ Resolve poll showed the party at a high of 15% in March before dropping to 13% in July and August, and recorded a dip to 11% in September, while Redbridge Group and Accent Research polls in the Financial Review showed the Greens at 14% in June, dropping to 12% in August. Former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather used an open letter to call for the Greens rank and file to elect the new leader, not just MPs. Bandt and Brown defended the party’s reach and said the Greens have been cutting through with the public, akin to the surge of support for progressives like the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Brown said the Greens “are the antidote to people who despair about politics”. “Under Larissa they have gone up in the polls and I expect that trend to continue, if not escalate. There’ll be surprises between now and 2028, and one of those will be the Greens because they often get taken for granted,” Brown said. Bandt added the progressive moment broadly has grown, pointing to a groundswell of public support for a gas export tax, despite the government abandoning any reforms. “Where they decide to go next will be a matter for the Greens party room … the progressive movement is quietly on the march and growing. We saw a big response to the gas tax campaign as it has mobilised over 70,000 people to call for a rethink of the decision to drill for gas off the Scott Reef,” Bandt said. NSW state Greens upper house member, Sue Higginson, said it was harder for her party to cut through the media and against other parties with significant financial backing. “It’s genuinely hard to cut through media narratives, and you’ve got to remember … when you have sort of dark money and dark interests influencing politics and political narratives, that is very hard to push back against.” Higginson said grassroots members expect the party leadership to take both conciliatory and activist approaches to policy.

headline: Trump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’
trail_text: The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
body_text: Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives. “It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week. “The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests. While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth. The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment. The document outlines four “layers of controls and audits” for AI companies. The first involves implementing internal safety monitoring during training – something that already exists at major labs and has failed to prevent testing failures thus far. The second calls for empowering an internal team to make sure the first layer of monitoring is operating correctly, while the third agrees to give an external auditor the ability to independently assess safety controls. Finally, the agreement calls for companies to designate an independent board to review reports about those safety controls. None of the controls listed in the agreement involve government regulators or include a commitment to publicly detail the findings of independent evaluations. The agreement also appears to allow companies to pick their own evaluators, appoint their own oversight boards and decide whether to publish their results. Trump made the remarks after holding a luncheon with tech leaders including Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO; Mark Zuckerberg, the Meta CEO; Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia; Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO; and other top industry executives. The tech industry, which has largely aligned itself with the Trump administration, has lobbied against strict regulatory oversight, arguing that it would stifle the economy. Zuckerberg, flanked by Trump and other tech moguls, told a press conference after the lunch that he was proud of the agreement and said that it was created to assure the American public that their technology was trustworthy. “This is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. “It was sort of a historic conversation.”

headline: A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?
trail_text: Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public
body_text: An image of Bianca Motley Broom, the mayor of College Park, Georgia, kissing a man who was not her husband in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it was fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people. “I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.” Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator. The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public. A poll taken in mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women. “The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and co-founder of Women Who Tech. The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota. A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”. Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories. Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said. “The public is deeply concerned,” she said. Fact from fiction Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic. “As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI-generated images, fake stories about the candidates – how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?” Warnock is among a group of Senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media. The outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.” Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation pre-empting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the Senate. State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry. Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them. While legislators in Georgia began debating deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation. Motley Broom said she believed she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.” While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said. “These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”

headline: Things are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots?
trail_text: Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat, warns a British civil servant
body_text: Another day, another apocalyptic warning about the likelihood that rampantly uncontrollable artificial intelligence will solve all of our problems, including the problem of being alive. Hot on the heels of disgruntled Anthropic researchers announcing the end of civilisation by 2030, we’ve now had the portentously named Hugging Face incident, as well as the Australian government’s grim discovery of a rogue AI’s attack on its Medicare website. Swarms of experts are now falling over each other to warn us that much, much worse is on the way. Thank God, then, that PM Uncle Andy has thrust Britain on to the bleeding edge of the fight against the rise of the self-improving machines. Except he hasn’t. Not really. Yes, Burnham went to the United Nations and risked enraging the Orange One with talk of Britain’s prospects of leading the drawing-up of international rules for AI. Slightly awkwardly, however, one of Burnham’s first acts after sweeping into office was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), the very department that had been leading work on AI safety. It’s a move that the Institute for Government warns will cause “real harm” and which former government AI adviser Matt Clifford has said “wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance”. Isn’t there something gloriously British about all this? Having failed thus far to regulate the technology effectively at home, we are going to world-beatingly coordinate its regulation everywhere else. Whatever it is, it doesn’t quite feel like the response of a state gripped by existential urgency. But perhaps that is because all of us – government ministers included – have already become desensitised to the risk of AImageddon. You can get used to anything. Sure, if one industry insider inadvertently leaks the news that scientists building a new technology believe it might kill everyone, a spot of existential panic is to be expected. But if you ram these tidings down our collective throat every couple of weeks, eventually the prospect of mass extinction acquires the urgency of that bowel cancer screening kit you’ve been meaning to send back to the doctor. Civil servants understand this aspect of human nature only too well. Like the prospect of the galloping climate crisis, we too are simultaneously terrified by AI and utterly bored by it. The extraordinary becomes familiar; the familiar becomes an item on a civil service risk register, after which the real fear is that someone will arrange a Teams call to talk about it. The median age of civil servants, remember, is 43 years, so many have already witnessed enough technological revolutions to choke a chatbot. Which means that, like me, there’s a large faction of the workforce that remembers the replacement of fax machines by email, and their first introduction to Clippy, that damnably moronic AI ancestor office assistant whose principal stab at sentience was appearing uninvited to chirp: “It looks like you’re writing a letter. Would you like help?” So it’s entirely possible that civil servants of my vintage might not yet have been compassionately euthanised by the time government departments such as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) or HMRC contain more AI agents than carbon-based officials. It may sound melodramatic, but that’s where we are headed. Ministers – convinced that harnessing AI will help keep Reform at bay by offering the tantalising possibility of slashing civil service jobs – have calmly and robotically emoted their concerns about the machines jumping their guardrails, while enthusiastically searching for things to give them. That’s amid civil service union concerns that the government is moving too quickly, citing the Fabian Society’s research finding that only 29% of those surveyed said they had been consulted about AI tools in their workplace. They’re right to be worried. Before DSIT was deleted, its permanent secretary, Emran Mian, reportedly had plans for AI to eventually replace almost every departing civil servant in his department rather than replacing them with humans. Elsewhere, the DWP has been busily experimenting with AI across the welfare state, directing its machine-learning systems to identify supposedly high-risk universal credit claims. And in response to “serious concerns” about transparency and the handling of personal data, the DWP has been careful to insist that humans retain the final decision and that AI does not determine entitlement. Is this just practical common sense, or the kind of world-beating complacency that some have pointed out is an echo of the government’s response to the climate emergency? Either way, the reassurances given by AI minister Kanishka Narayan to the parliamentary business and trade committee sound increasingly hollow after the spate of recent AI rampages. Civil servants – especially those in public-facing government departments – are acutely aware that saying “a human remains in the loop” is not the same thing as saying “a human remains in charge”. This really, truly, matters, because the commodity on which every government ultimately runs is not data, or productivity, or even money. It is trust, including the trust that – while below the OECD average – the British public still has in the civil service, and which, according to the public accounts committee, is being jeopardised by inadequate transparency and weak standards on AI. We already have a national catchphrase for what happens when human discretion – and the accountability that comes with it – disappears. Little Britain’s “computer says no” still resonates – thanks in part to the haunting legacy of the Post Office’s Horizon scandal. Everyone recognises the terror of the human being behind the desk surrendering responsibility to a system whose conclusion can’t be questioned because nobody in the room understands how the hell it got there. And that may be the real warning from Whitehall. Not that killer robots are about to lock the doors and announce the abolition of humanity. But that long before then, governments might quietly surrender thousands of small human judgments to a swarm of digital bureaucrats because doing so is cheaper, quicker and can be passed off in a ministerial speech as “transformation”. It will not feel like that to the public. The author works for the UK civil service

headline: First Thing: ‘Third country’ deportation can resume, US supreme court rules
trail_text: Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries other than their homeland
body_text: Good morning. The supreme court has ruled the Trump administration can resume deporting immigrants to “third countries”, or countries other than their homeland, without giving them any opportunity to contest their removals. The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a decision by a lower court that required the administration to provide immigrants sufficient notice and the opportunity to claim fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they were being sent. What has the administration asked the supreme court to rule on about trans prisoners? The administration asked the justices to allow it to deny gender-affirming care to transgender people in federal prisons. The solicitor general, D John Sauer, wrote that gender-reassignment surgeries, hormone therapy and social accommodations such as undergarments, makeup, padding and wigs “could no longer be justified.” Why is the EPA union suing the administration? The union, which represents more than 8,000 workers at the Environmental Protection Agency, has filed a lawsuit against the EPA and the agency’s administrator, Lee Zeldin, alleging it illegally terminated a collective bargaining agreement. Which legal battle has Trump appeared to have conceded? The president has agreed to stop fighting the disbursement of E Jean Carroll’s $5m verdict in her 2023 sexual abuse and defamation civil trial against him, a procedural development as the funds had already been distributed to her. Less than 24 hours after OpenAI said it would scrap the launch of a model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of artificial intelligence tools, including “dots”, agents it said were “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI.” Why is Greta Garbo making AI headlines? More than a century after her screen debut and decades after she was laid to rest, the actor has been reanimated by AI for a Swedish advert. Peter Bradshaw has given it a damning one-star review. US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank The US Senate rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. Why did an Israeli-bound plane make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia? A passenger jet travelling from Dubai made an emergency landing, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes. Reports said the incident stemmed from a feud between the plane’s two pilots, and everyone onboard was safe. What has Zohran Mamdani announced about antisemitism? The New York City mayor has debuted a sweeping plan to combat antisemitism. The strategy includes increased security funding for synagogues and an increased focus on incorporating Jewish history into public school education. The plan is seen as a move to assuage critics who see his steadfast denunciations of Israel as antisemitic. Why are two authors suing the city of Los Angeles? Jenan Matari, a Palestinian-American author, and Nora Lester Murad, a Jewish-American writer, are taking the action after public library officials scrapped their Read Palestine Week book talks. Texts about alleged Cornell gang-rape released after investigation reopened Excerpts of text messages reportedly exchanged by a defendant in the Cornell University gang-rape case and the woman who claimed she was assaulted were published by CBS News on Tuesday, a day after New York prosecutors said they were reopening a criminal investigation. Two of the alleged perpetrators were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell – while the other five were allowed to resume their studies at the Ivy League institution after writing an essay, attending a workshop, or serving a short suspension. headline: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia
trail_text: Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations
body_text: Years ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse. Now, all you need is AI. In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news, Anthropic recently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents. The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies. The experiment was ultimately ineffective once Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news. Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape. “AI can supercharge it in terms of you can make a lot more content that’s more personalised, quicker and cheaper,” says Harbath, who now heads the tech consultancy company Anchor Change. “But you still need a distribution mechanism, and at the moment, that’s still your more social media type platforms.” Anthropic detailed the Malaysia election operation in its latest threat assessment, released in September. The report revealed how actors used Claude to build networks of fake social media profiles and news websites that targeted audiences on six continents. Anthropic said the actors included “governments, state-aligned propaganda institutions and state media, as well as private firms selling influence”. ‘Flood the zone’ South-east Asia is no stranger to disinformation. In recent years Nobel laureate and Filipino journalist Maria Ressa has likened the Philippines to a “petri dish” for the weaponisation of disinformation and fake news, with techniques tried and tested in the south-east Asian nation later successfully replicated in the west. But AI makes it all much easier. “Basically AI is just mimicking what we would have, I guess, termed a few years ago, a troll factory,” says Rossine Fallorina of Sigla, a Philippine thinktank that researches AI. “Mostly because it speeds up the production process. So you don’t need 10 people to create a narrative or a story. You can just prompt it and then have it propagated.” Last year OpenAI banned accounts using AI to generate comments about Philippine politics and public officials across social platforms, with many fictitious comments generated in support of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Across south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper connected populations, some fear the divisive potential of AI on social media. “It feeds political polarisation and it feeds on divisions,” says Bridget Welsh, from the University of Nottingham Asia Research Institute Malaysia. “That’s really what’s concerning about the fragmented nature of what’s happening in Malaysia.” Malaysia’s general election could be called for late 2027, while the Philippines and Cambodia have polls in 2028, and Indonesia the following year. Already in the region, AI has been effective. In Indonesia, an AI-generated cartoon image of now-president Prabowo Subianto that helped soften his strongman image became wildly popular in the 2024 election. It has also been used to inflame tensions, such as inciting hatred toward ethnic Rohingya refugees who fled to Malaysia from Myanmar during the civil war, says Dr Ben Loh, a media lecturer at Monash University Malaysia. “It’s come to the point where people already have this deep-seated hate in their minds and when they see the content like this, even though it’s AI-generated to them, it’s merely reinforcing what they believe is already true,” says Loh. The Anthropic report notes that the fake news outlet scraped legitimate Malaysian reporting and had the model rewrite it several times before republishing it under fabricated bylines. It also republished articles from Russian and Chinese state-aligned foreign outlets, including TV BRICS, Xinhua, Sputnik/RIA, and CGTN, stripping them of attribution. Anthropic said in its threat assessment that in each case of identified political influence the company “disrupted the activity, used what we learned to strengthen our safeguards, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners, where appropriate”. In future, Harbath says AI could be used to “flood the zone” in an attempt to influence the large language models (LLMs) from which AI models draw their information. “If there’s any sort of news drought, or if you have a place where there’s mostly government-sponsored media,” she says, “It wouldn’t take very much money to kind of flood the zone.”

body_text: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: The latest in a series of pro-Trump ads the Trump administration is using taxpayer funds to air on television in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a 1-minute spot that celebrates his decision to go to war with Iran. Pete Hegseth announced that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, with Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House. An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released Wednesday. The latest in a series of pro-Trump ads the Trump administration is using taxpayer funds to air on television in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a 1-minute spot that celebrates his decision to go to war with Iran. The ad aired during a commercial break on Fox News Wednesday night, according video posted online by MeidasTouch, a leftwing outlet. A copy of the new ad posted on social media by Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, shows that it features audio taken from Donald Trump’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations in Iran. “This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States Armed Forces,” Trump can be heard saying over images of combat, some of which appear to be dramatizations or computer-generated. A cover version of John Lee Hooker’s Boom Boom provides the soundtrack. The audio then switches to comments made by Pete Hegseth the US defense secretary, in a briefing on the third day of the war. “He reminded the world, as he has time and time again, being an American means something unbreakable,” Hegseth says over slow-motion images of Trump walking down a corridor. “If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth says . “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it. Their war on Americans has become our retribution against their ayatollah”. As the words “Paid for by the U.S. Government” appear at the bottom of the screen, the ad’s audio switches back to Trump’s call for regime change in Iran in his announcement of the war in February. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump can be heard saying, over images of Iranian Americans in New York celebrating the US strikes on 1 March. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take.” The images of Iranian Americans demonstrating in support of Trump’s war in New York City, marching down 42nd Street and holding signs that read “Thank you president Trump”, were all previously included in a White House video posted on YouTube on 4 March. The focus of the ad on speeches and images of celebration that all came in the first three days of the war, when it looked like Iran’s government could collapse, makes its release now, as the war enters its seven month and continues to alienate Trump’s supporters, baffling. A federal judge on Wednesday dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit against Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, over his refusal to hand over unredacted, sensitive voter information to the Department of Justice. The justice department had demanded that the state’s senior election official email a copy of Georgia’s statewide voter registration list, including each voter’s driver’s license number, social security number and date of birth, arguing that the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law, entitled it to this information. The US district court judge, Victoria Marie Calvert, ruled that the federal law does not require states to disclose sensitive voter data to the federal government, and does not take precedence over Georgia’s state law protecting the privacy of information provided to the state by registered voters. Raffensperger was the Georgia state official Donald Trump called on 2 January 2021, in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election, asking him to “find 11,780 votes” for Joe Biden that could be tossed out as fraudulent, which would have allowed Trump to reverse his loss and win the state by one vote. In keeping with his near-constant use of his office for thinly disguised campaign events, Donald Trump had Alaska’s Republican senator Dan Sullivan by his side in the Oval Office on Wednesday when he announced that South Korea plans to spend $54bn to build a liquefied natural gas pipeline in Alaska. Sullivan is facing a strong challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola to retain his Senate seat in the November midterm elections. Unfortunately for Sullivan, the president wrongly suggested that an issue that is infuriating voters in his home state, the high price of gasoline and diesel, would be solved by the pipeline, which will transport an entirely different kind of petroleum, natural gas, when it is completed in three years. The Alaska LNG project includes an 807-mile (1,299km) pipeline to carry natural gas from the North Slope to a liquefaction facility on Alaska’s southern coast, allowing the fuel to be shipped to Asian markets. Asked by a reporter about whether there has been any discussion of building another oil pipeline in Alaska, given the high cost of gasoline for consumers, Trump appeared to confuse the liquefied natural gas, known as LNG, with gasoline, which is made from oil. “Well, this is going to bring those prices down. One of the reasons, Alaska prices are going to come way down,” Trump said of a project that has nothing to do with gasoline used to fuel cars. After Trump was informed that the the LNG pipeline is going to take three years to complete, which would lower the cost of LNG in Alaska, but have no impact at all on the cost of another petroleum product, gasoline, Trump turned back to reporters and said: “Gasoline prices in Alaska are going to tumble.” Trump also said that the Korean investment was part of a $200bn package of projects that would also include a 6-gigawatt ⁠power generation facility in Texas, another state where his party is in danger of losing a Senate seat. The announced investment follows pledges South Korea made in 2025 to invest up to $350bn in the US as part of a trade deal in exchange for lower US tariffs on South Korean cars, auto parts and other products. Without providing those details, Trump credited his tariffs for making the announcement possible, saying “our trade agreement with South Korea, they have to invest hundreds of billions of dollars.” “For doing that, I reduced their tariffs to 15%. But they paid to get them reduced,” Trump said. “And, part of that money is going into this project.” Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House. A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations. The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year. Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday that he had spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, about the security incident on a FlyDubai commercial flight from the United Arab Emirates to Israel on Wednesday. “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job,” Trump said, before giving a dramatic account of the intervention of a passenger who subdued the pilot who reportedly stabbed his co-pilot. Although witnesses on the flight said that an off-duty pilot then entered the cockpit, pulled the aircraft up and landed in Saudi Arabia, Trump told reporters that “an Israeli plumber” first subdued the attacker, “and this plumber, having never flown a plane, he took the stick, lifted it up, and leveled out the plane before it crashed. Now this is the story that I heard. I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story I got from Bibi.” Before we move on from Pete Hegseth’s lengthy address today, it is worth noting that the Pentagon’s in-house “rapid response” social media account, which is dedicated to battling with the media in the style of a political campaign’s opposition research unit, made a point of highlighting the defense secretary’s scathing criticism of the US press corps. The Pentagon account shared video and a partial transcript of Hegseth addressing reporters he called “the anti-American losers in our media” in prepared remarks that sounded more like a script written by one of Hegseth’s former Fox News producers than a speech by a US cabinet official. Hegseth went on to say: “The information space is a battle space. Yet our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable. Our media’s shameful lust for political retribution blinds them to the consequences of reckless, so-called ‘reporting’. So-called journalists – juiced up on Trump derangement syndrome – think they’re fighting against our president, but they’re really undermining you – our warfighters.” “Bottom line: too many of them hate the president more than they love the country. You see, it’s your movement and bases that they reveal to the enemy,” Hegseth told the troops before him. “And ultimately, it’s your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munitions stockpiles. “All for a banner that will scroll on TV for 30 seconds,” the former Fox weekend host said. “And I know a little bit about banners scrolling on TV for 30 seconds.” Pete Hegseth officially announced 20% cuts to generals and admirals “across the board” in the US military. The defense secretary added that the generals “who clung to the woke department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”. Hegseth appeared to downplay the ongoing mental health crisis in parts of the US military, particularly after eight navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment. Nonetheless, the defense secretary slammed the media, and insisted that there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”. It’s worth noting that Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, confirmed the suicide attempts in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand earlier this month. Throughout his address, Hegseth boasted touted his anti-diversity policies. He insisted that the Pentagon was “no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.” He also announced a new project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with department to study the “future of warfare”. “Their work will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes,” Hegseth said, noting the project’s findings would be completed and submitted within 120 days, culminating in a full public rollout. Meanwhile on Capitol Hill, Senate Democrats blocked legislation that would allow states and utilities to consider standards to ensure tech companies foot the bill for the additional energy costs associated with power-intensive datacenters throughout the US. In a 57-43 vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, four Democrats – Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – all broke with their party in support of the bill. However, the legislation failed to achieve the 60 votes needed to advance out of the Republican-controlled upper chamber. More here Earlier, Democrats in the Senate also blocked legislation that would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and their dependent children from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The Stop Insider Trading Act failed along party lines, in a 53-47 vote, failing to clear the 60-vote threshold. Despite widespread support for stopping members of Congress from trading stocks, many Democrats argued the bill didn’t go far enough to actually solve the issue. They also took issue with the fact that the House-passed bill also included a provision which would require photo identification when casting a ballot. More here Hegseth’s ‘State of the Force’ address also includes an announcement about partnering with a new group of higher education institutions. The defense secretary took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges – which the Trump administration has targeted routinely – as “DEI worshipping woke factories”. Hegseth said the department would now partner with other institutions– some of which are known for conservative values, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College. Other schools joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University. It’s worth remembering that Hegseth attended and graduated from Princeton and Harvard – both Ivy League universities. The defense secretary announced a new Pentagon project that will see Elon Musk, Palmer Lucky – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with department to study the “future of warfare”. “Their work will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes,” Pete Hegseth said, noting the project’s findings would be completed and submitted within 120 days, culminating in a full public rollout. If Palmer Lucky’s name sounds familiar to you, that might be because the Guardian has reported extensively about how his company, Anduril Industries, a major military contractor, has received billions in government contracts over the last year. The first of six announcements the defense secretary made today was the development of a top-level joint military organization, led by four-star generals, to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities. “The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,” Hegseth said. “The autonomous robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades.” Per my last post, Hegseth went on to boast about the retention rates in the US military, claiming they are at “record rates” – including “80% of the force on the USS Abraham Lincoln on their historic mission”. Hegseth appeared to downplay the ongoing mental health crisis in parts of the US military, particularly after eight navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment. Nonetheless, the defense secretary disparaged the media, again, and insisted that there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”. It’s worth noting that Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, confirmed the suicide attempts in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand earlier this month. The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war. As we noted earlier, Pete Hegseth officially announced 20% cuts to generals and admirals “across the board” in the US military. The defense secretary added that the generals “who clung to the woke department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”. As has become customary, Hegseth disparaged the press during his address. “As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment,” he said. “You can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it.” The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, is providing an update on the US military at his second “State of the Force” address, in Quantico, Virginia, one year after he berated “fat troops” and condemned the military’s “woke” policies. Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, Hegseth began his announcements by again boasting about his anti-diversity policies. “The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline, and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues, and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.” The defense secretary added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth said. An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released Wednesday. For over a year, Donald Trump has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair Jerome Powell around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal probe that was dropped in April. The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation. “At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said. Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018m by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027. The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be nonpartisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail. Trump latched onto the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features like a VIP dining room and a garden terrace. In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s. Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures. “It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.” The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said. During his White House event today, Trump spoke to his need for Republicans to secure the Hispanic and Latino vote in the upcoming midterms. “I loved you right from the beginning. I loved you for many years before I ever decided to do this political thing,” the president said. “You also know when I build a wall, I’m building a wall to keep bad people out. And you want, and you want those bad people kept out more than anybody.” This appeal comes after Trump won a record number of Hispanic votes for a Republican president in the 2024 election, but there is concern that the community is now fractured in its support for GOP candidates because of the administration’s immigration crackdown and the cost of living. More than 65% said they are unhappy with the president’s job performance, and 78% said they would prefer to see the Democratic party in control of Congress, according to a recent poll from the New York Times/Siena University. The president falsely claimed that “more oil has come out” of the strait of Hormuz in the past three days than at “any time in history”. While the transport of oil has rebounded in recent weeks, climbing close to prewar levels according to analysts, it has not exceeded that. The increase in flow through the vital waterway is encouraging, according to those tracking the movement, but it hasn’t yet been reflected in the price. The international benchmark for crude oil still sits just below $100 per barrel. Trump also welcomed the Pentagon’s news today that the US has finally completed its withdrawal from Iraq. “This day is a victory for the United States. It’s a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over Isis, which has been completely decimated,” the president said. “I decimated them and took them out in my first administration. So I don’t know what took them so long to be making the announcement that I’m making today.” Speaking at the White House today to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month, Donald Trump told those attending that they would be among the first to see and walk around the new ballroom when he opens the East Room doors after the event. Senate Democrats blocked legislation that would allow states and utilities to consider standards to ensure tech companies foot the bill for the additional energy costs associated with power-intensive datacenters throughout the US. In a 57-43 vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, four Democrats – Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – all broke with their party in support of the bill. However, the legislation failed to achieve the 60 votes needed to advance out of the Republican-controlled upper chamber. Earlier this month, the bill received overwhelming support in the House. However, many Senate Democrats say the bill is “toothless” and doesn’t do enough to actually curb costs for consumers. Datacenter construction and electricity consumption have grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has come increasing anxiety among voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills. Democrats in the Senate blocked legislation that would prohibit lawmakers, their spouses and their dependent children from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The House-passed bill would also require that lawmakers disclose that they intend to sell any stocks at least seven days (and up to two weeks) in advance, to curb the ability to profit from insider information. The Stop Insider Trading Act failed along party lines, in a 53-47 vote, failing to clear the 60-vote threshold. Despite widespread support for stopping members of Congress from trading stocks, many Democrats argued the bill doesn’t go far enough to actually solve the issue. “They can’t be serious. The Republican bill is a permission slip for corruption, not a stock-trading ban. This bill has no reform, no accountability, no substance,” said Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader. “Republicans want to explicitly allow members to continue trading stocks in privately held companies, including in companies the members oversee.” Democrats also took issue with the fact that the House-passed bill also included a provision which would require photo identification when casting a ballot. Pete Ricketts, a Republican senator from Nebraska who introduced the legislation in the upper chamber, and who is facing a tough re-election battle in the upcoming midterms, said it was “discouraging” to see his bill fail. The Pentagon announced on Wednesday that it has formally completed its withdrawal of US troops from Iraq, two years after the withdrawal was agreed to and 12 years since the US mission to fight the Islamic State started. After the announcement, Iran and its allies celebrated the departure as a victory, while Iraqi security experts worry that the withdrawal could give the Islamic State and others a chance to recover. “Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq,” the Pentagon said in a statement, adding that the departure of its forces “marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq”. The Pentagon noted it will continue to provide training and intelligence support to Iraq “to ensure ISIS can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory”. The US invaded Iraq in 2003 to oust its dictator, Saddam Hussein, who ruled the country for nearly 24 years. The invasion would lead to hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths, civil war and sectarian violence in Iraq, as well as the rise of the Islamic State militant group. In 2011, Barack Obama declared an end to the Iraq war and announced that all US troops would be withdrawn from the country by year’s end. At that moment, the US military presence in Iraq stood at under 40,000, and 4,400 US military members had been killed. But in 2014, Obama sent troops back to Iraq after Islamic State militants seized large swaths of territory, including Mosul. Then, a coalition of more than 80 countries led by the US was formed to fight Islamic State, which subjugated millions during a cruel war before losing its hold in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019. Finally, in 2024, during Joe Biden’s presidency, the US and Iraq agreed to wind down the US-led coalition operations. The justice department has also announced federal indictments against 10 foreign nationals accused of illegally registering and voting in Minnesota elections. Todd Blanche said a federal grand jury had returned indictments alleging nine counts of illegal voting by an alien and nine counts of falsely claiming US citizenship to register to vote. Charges include illegally voting in the general elections of 2022 and 2024, as well as the state’s primary election in August this year, the attorney general said. “Voter fraud erodes the public’s trust in our electoral system,” Blanche said, adding that a way to restore that trust “is by working to make sure that the only people voting in an election in the United States are American citizens who are eligible to vote”. Since Trump returned to office, according to Blanche, the DoJ has charged more than 90 people with voter-related fraud offenses, including 50 non-citizens in the last five weeks. There are hundreds of investigations going on across the country, he added. In the context of Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, his administration has made a big push to investigate and prosecute cases of alleged non-citizen voting. But the fact is, voter fraud in general, including voting by non-citizens, remains exceedingly rare. Case in point, as Blanche just announced these 10 indictments, there are over 3.9 million registered voters in the state of Minnesota. The justice department has filed a judicial misconduct ⁠complaint against judges in Minnesota who gave interviews to the New York Times ⁠about the immigration surge there, alleging that it was unethical and partisan. In September, ⁠judges in Minnesota told the Times (paywall) that the Trump administration had ‌a “disregard for ‌court orders” and warned that its actions posed “a grave threat to the rule of law”. Two did so on the record. The judicial misconduct complaint branded the judges’ conduct “particularly egregious”. The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, called the fact that the judges spoke ‌to the media a “clear violation of their ethical duties” and criticized them for commenting on pending cases. He also asked the judges to recuse themselves from any case involving the Department of Homeland Security, ⁠alleging they had bias against the administration. It is unusual for sitting judges to comment on the record about cases, particularly ‌those in the news, Reuters notes. The complaint was signed by the second- and third-ranking officials in the Department of Justice. Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes today, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month. A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters. Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure. headline: Steve Hilton, Xavier Becerra clash in testy California governor’s race debate
trail_text: The candidates running to replace Gavin Newsom sparred over taxes, immigration and regulating AI
body_text: Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton, the candidates running to be California’s next governor, clashed on Wednesday over taxes, immigration and regulating artificial intelligence in a testy debate held days before voters begin receiving their ballots in the heavily Democratic state. Hilton, the former Fox News host endorsed by Donald Trump, used the hourlong matchup, hosted by CNN in its studio in Burbank, California, to argue that Becerra, a former congressman who served as the US health and human services secretary during the Biden administration, was not actively campaigning and instead taking voters for granted. “He wasn’t even supposed to be the candidate,” Hilton, 57, said, referring to Becerra’s unexpected success after an unusually wild primary campaign. “I just want to ask every Californian: aren’t you tired of that?” Becerra, 68, pitched his experience as an asset, vowing to tackle the state’s punishing cost of living crisis while being a bulwark against the Trump administration’s policies. He accused Hilton of owing loyalty to Trump – and not the state that roundly rejected the president in each of the last three presidential elections. “If you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response,” Becerra said of Hilton’s reply to a question about regulating the development of AI. Hilton’s bid to succeed California’s term-limited governor, Gavin Newsom, is aimed at voter discontent with the political status quo in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican governor in two decades. But his pitch is complicated by his party identification and the president who has backed him. Though most Californians say the state is headed in the wrong direction, fewer than a quarter of likely voters approve of the president’s job performance, notably lower than the national average, and many cite “fight against Trump administration policies” as a priority. Recent polls show Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton, suggesting the onus was on the Republican hopeful to persuade voters partisan change was needed in Sacramento. The debate, the only scheduled face-to-face debate before the 3 November general election, comes just days before voters begin receiving their ballots by mail. Both candidates said they would oppose the so-called billionaire tax proposal, a November ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% tax on any California resident worth more than $1bn. Becerra’s opposition puts him at odds with progressives, including Senator Bernie Sanders, who will campaign for the measure in California this weekend. But they were at odds on Proposition 39, a ballot measure that would require voters to show a government-issued ID to vote in person. Like other Democratic leaders in the state, Becerra said he opposed the measure, calling it an initiative “backed by Donald Trump” that would make it harder for Californians to vote. Hilton said he supported the proposal, but insisted he had confidence in the state’s voting system despite Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of fraud. “I’ve got confidence in what we saw in the primary and in this process,” Hilton said. Without distancing himself significantly from Trump, whose Maga base he cannot afford to alienate, Hilton sought to draw subtle differences: “My whole aim here would be to lower the temperature.” An exchange over immigration policy became personal, when Becerra, the son of Mexican immigrants, accused Hilton, who grew up in England and was an adviser to the former UK prime minister David Cameron, of appearing to support measures that would “welcome immigrants who look like you” while wanting to “deport immigrants who look like me”. “What a disgraceful remark that was,” Hilton shot back. Becerra’s path to the general election was winding. After languishing in the low single digits for much of the race, he was catapulted to the front of the pack after the implosion of Eric Swalwell’s campaign amid a slew of sexual misconduct and assault allegations – claims the now former congressman denied. Becerra ultimately advanced first in the June primary, overcoming fierce opposition from his more progressive rival, the billionaire activist Tom Steyer. Hilton came in second, with Trump’s endorsement helping to consolidate conservative support and avert the risk of a Democratic lockout in the state’s non-partisan primary. But the president’s support risks being a liability in the general election as the unresolved war with Iran has spiked oil prices and kept US inflation stubbornly high. Since reaching the general election, Becerra has maintained a low profile, while Hilton has blitzed the state as he seeks to make inroads with voters who disapprove of Trump. “Thank you to CNN for bringing Xavier out of hiding,” Hilton said, slamming his opponent as a “career politician” who was the product of the “machine in Sacramento”. Becerra pushed back, arguing that the challenges facing the state and country were too great to risk rolling the dice on a political newcomer. “There aren’t training wheels in the governor’s office,” Becerra said, repeating a line he deployed in the primary. “You have to know how to do the job, and that’s why I’m asking California voters to vote for me for governor of state of California.”

headline: Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month
trail_text: The risks of AI aren’t what we think they are, as a recent security incident between China and the United States reveals
body_text: Amid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public. The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was the Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public’s, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions. The California governor, Gavin Newsom, issued a mandate to create an “AI kill-switch”; New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is similarly exploring the possibility of having “AI kill-switches”; and Senator Bernie Sanders and Congressman Greg Casar introduced legislation to “ban artificial superintelligence”. While so many of us were focused on fictional superintelligent machines that we were told could hypothetically cause human extinction, however, there was a more serious story being reported. A series of events almost got us to armageddon, not caused by “rogue, superintelligent AI”, but by government reliance on error-prone systems that are marketed by their manufacturers as being close to superintelligent. A CNN report published on 18 September, which hasn’t been verified by other major outlets, describes how the US “almost started a war” with China, based on an intelligence report that claimed a Chinese ship was transporting components of nuclear weapons. Military personnel made plans to intercept the Chinese vessel, complete with aircraft and soldiers ready to board the ship. A military skirmish of this kind between China and the US could quickly escalate and spiral into world war three. It was only moments before executing on the plan that American officials further investigated the intelligence report and found that it had been generated with the use of a chatbot and contained erroneous information about the vessel’s contents. Unlike the terminator, “rogue AI”, scenario, this incident didn’t galvanize lawmakers into announcing calls for regulation so as to avoid potential human extinction. Media outlet after media outlet didn’t warn the public that we almost triggered a war against a nuclear superpower because of our military’s reliance on error-prone chatbots. We describe the large language models (LLMs) powering these chatbots as stochastic parrots, that is, models that are designed to regurgitate the patterns of the data they are trained on. News coverage describing them as “powerful” “rogue” models that could render humanity extinct all on their own, bolsters perceptions of tools based on these models being infallible enough to merit usage in stakes as high as warfare. Even CNN’s more critical coverage describes the chatbot used by the US military as presenting “profound risks” because it is “powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology”. In fact, today’s LLMs and the chatbots they power are not poorly understood, nor are they powerful in the sense of being effective tools for this use case. They are systems for generating plausible-looking text, built out of enormous, haphazardly collected datasets and then “fine-tuned” (that is, further trained) to be especially appealing to their intended users. CNN wasn’t able to learn which chatbot product was used in this case, but the LLM powering the product was probably fine-tuned to output text with the stylistic hallmarks of intelligence reports. Both the basic functionality and the risks of such a model have been well-understood and well-documented for years, including in our 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big? Claims that system behavior is mysterious arise from deliberate mystification on the part of those selling those systems, and a misapprehension of what their output is by those procuring and using it. Unlike the unscientific and fantastical claims of OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs and those who uncritically repeat their talking points, the harmful, and well-documented, impacts of these companies’ products have arisen because people believe that the products are superintelligent, not because they actually are. From “AI” scribes used by hospitals erroneously classifying patients as illicit drug users, to governments killing children after relying on “intelligence analysis” systems which mistake schools for military facilities, we are seeing the predictable harms that come from misplaced faith in unreliable automated software. Meanwhile, the marketing campaigns from the companies selling this software warn of impending superintelligence, directing our attention away from the real risk to their fantasies of doom. It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high-stakes scenarios. Any automation used in military, medical or other life-and-death situations must be thoroughly evaluated within its use case and paired with usage norms that keep accountability with people who have actual power to make decisions. As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption from the law when it comes to AI: there are existing laws that federal agencies and other regulators can enforce to protect the public against the AI industry’s unsafe and unscientific practices of pushing unsound products while marketing them as “magic intelligence in the sky”. Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public. We call on journalists and lawmakers to hold companies accountable rather than parrot their marketing talking points. Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February. Emily M Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and co-author of The AI Con.
