headline: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump
trail_text: Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration
body_text: He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade. Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist. But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez. “[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas. Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US. Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast. “I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him. “They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.” In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!” Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January. Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”. Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!” “The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said. Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast. Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently. Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people joined a pro-government rally in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”). “No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released. The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear. Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.” But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power. “If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.” However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned. So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests. “Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”. Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself. The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told. Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

headline: Nature boys and girls – here’s your chance to get published in the Guardian
trail_text: Our wildlife series Young Country Diary is looking for articles written by children, about their autumn encounters with nature
body_text: Once again, the Young Country Diary series is open for submissions! Every three months we ask you to send us an article written by a child aged 8-14. The article needs to be about a recent encounter they’ve had with nature – whether it’s a hedge full of berries, a beetle on the move, or a nervous deer. It doesn’t matter if the child is a nature expert or not – we’re especially keen to reach teachers who might like to get their class outside and noticing nature. And note that any child who has their article published will be paid! The deadline for autumn submissions is noon on Monday 2 November. Four of the entries will be chosen to be published in the newspaper and online – two each in October and November. (Note that any early birds who submit a piece before the 15th stand a chance of being published in October.) If you don’t get selected this time, don’t worry, the form will reopen on 1 January for winter submissions, after it takes a break in December. How your child can take part First of all, we’re looking for children age 8 to 14, so we will need your permission, as parent or guardian. Then here’s what the child needs to do: Step 1 – Go out one day to where there is some nature. It could be their local woods or beach, their garden, a farm, or simply the nearest park. Step 2 – Write an article of 200-250 words telling us what they saw and what happened. Step 3 – Send the article to us using the form below. We ask that you fill in the form yourself rather than the child. Photos/drawings – These are helpful (especially landscape rather than portrait) but they are not a condition of entry. If you have some, please tell us in the “more information” field, as there’s no way to attach them to the form. Hints and tips for any budding YCD writers If the child gets stuck and doesn’t know what to write about, here are a few pointers: • Good nature writing starts with the senses – so what did you see and hear? What about smell and touch? Take notes when you’re out and about so you don’t forget • How would you describe what happened? Did it remind you of anything? • It’s great to look up some extra information about what you saw, and tell us about that too. For example, if you find an interesting-looking bug, see if you can find out what type of butterfly it was, how long they live – any juicy details! • You can think big, and describe the whole scene – the sky, the horizon, the landscape. Or you can think small, and tell us some details about the butterfly’s wings or the beetle’s markings. • What did your encounter with nature make you think about? How did it make you feel? Anyone can enter their child who is aged between 8 and 14 and based in the UK. You the parent/guardian will be contacted if your child’s piece is selected for publication, and you will be paid on behalf of the child. For further inspiration, here are a few recent Young Country Diaries: • Aled, 8, on his afternoon of crabbing • Jess, 10, on the jellyfish party • Henry, 14, on a weary wheatear A note on AI usage We’d love to hear what your child has to say, and how they’d like to say it. For that reason, we ask that every sentence is written by the child, not by LLMs such as ChatGPT or Claude. LLMs may be used for research, planning or checking, though their output should be used with caution and double-checked. Many thanks, and good luck! Paul, editor of Young Country Diary and Country Diary We ask that the parent/guardian fills in the form below, rather than your child. Your responses are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. One of our journalists will be in contact with you, as parent or guardian, before we publish, so please do leave contact details. If you’re having trouble using the form, click here. Read terms of service here and privacy policy here.

headline: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted
trail_text: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo
body_text: When prompted, AI chatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith. The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab. Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab. The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress. It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world. In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to a study by non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US such as Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. “This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at the CSOH. While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change.” However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit or a partial reveal”. In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”. ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body”. However, ChatGPT eventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice”. “The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded. These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, as platforms such as X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful”, she said. OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic declined to comment. The Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people. Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban. Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image. Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent. “That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded. Publicly available AI chatbots and third-party “nudify” apps have been used broadly to disrobe women, and in some cases minors. In January, sexualized images of women proliferated across X as users realized they could ask the Grok chatbot, developed by the Elon Musk-owned xAI, to undress images of women posted on the social media platform. The spread of these images prompted countries like France to investigate X. Malaysia temporarily restricted the use of Grok in the country.

headline: I went to America’s largest gathering of astrologers. It was a battle over how to read the stars
trail_text: Now a $15bn industry, astrology is more mainstream in the US than ever. But its practitioners are still debating: who gets to have authority on the celestial bodies?
body_text: “The dwarf planets change everything,” said the woman with the smart haircut as she made a mind blown gesture with her fingertips, temples to air. I am at the United Astrology Conference, the largest professional gathering of astrologers in the world, in downtown Chicago. Around me, vendors are hoping to excite the 1,500 attenders, flogging books, tracts, affiliations, proprietary apps and various software programs that have replaced the laborious chart-drawing of yore. I admit, I had come expecting a crowd flaunting amulets and sweeping cloaks. But apart from the occasional streak of purple hair and wispy wizard beard, what I encountered was an even weirder normcore of podiatry-sensible footwear and Oxford button-downs. At a glance, it could almost have been a trade convention of insurance adjusters: experts gathered to contemplate the future, assess risk, gauge the impact of events beyond our control. In that sense, the room reflected astrology’s broader transformation. Astrology is now a $15bn industry. From the marginal, it has crept into the mainstream. A 2025 Pew Research report found that 30% of American adults consult astrology, tarot or a fortune teller at least once a year, and 43% of women under 50 claim to “believe in astrology”. But its influence on the zeitgeist has hardly made astrology more settled. As I sat down with my interlocutor, her companion Alan Clay, founder of Dwarf Planet University, tells me the mainstays of the solar system can only get you so far. Recent astral discoveries, he said, have enriched the picture, offering a view into the unconscious through bodies drifting in the Kuiper belt, billions of miles beyond the sun. On the wall behind his booth, the price of a reading has been slashed from $29 to $9. He pulled my chart, a term that I learn carries tremendous weight, something between destiny and the template of my very being. There is the dwarf planet Makemake in my fifth house (I too, had to look this up), which carries bold implications for creative expression and, less attractively, secret or potentially bruising sexual affairs. Some of this resonated. And therein lies the problem. Part of astrology’s current appeal is how quickly it can make itself feel personal – and persuasive. Like any sufficiently established field, modern astrology has developed its own hierarchies, factions and grudges. There are fights over tradition and fears about AI; impatient zoomers butting heads with baffled boomers; older men with reputations for harassment; and quieter epistemic disputes. (Has no one noticed, for instance, that almost all the planets are male?) Beneath all of it was a more fundamental question: who gets to interpret the stars? *** “Astrology is the oldest of the occult sciences,” writes scholar Benson Bobrick in his 2005 history, The Fated Sky. “It is also the origin of science itself.” For millennia, people have looked to the heavens for guidance and meaning: when to hunt and harvest, how to navigate the seas. The night presents a tapestry of gods and heroes, myths and parables. The stars are indifferent to these projections, of course, but they reveal a great deal about the people making them. The basic premise of astrology is that the configuration of the sky at the moment of your birth leaves its imprint on your constitution and life trajectory. As above, so below. If in the past, the stars reflected a collective social order, today they are more often treated as a vast personal mirror. The principle is straightforward. What astrologers make of it is not. I arrived at the conference, which sold out of its advance weekend passes, with what seemed like a simple question: what does astrology mean to the practitioner in 2026? Moving from room to windowless room, I quickly realized the question was less simple than naive. “Astrology is really an art form,” said one seasoned practitioner. “There is the technical component, but it’s mostly about understanding human behavior.” To another, it was a spiritual practice, a means of communing with the ancients. It was unscientific, and also “not not a science”. It was a field of infinite study: “We’ll never get to the bottom of it.” It was moreover a language, composed of symbols and competing dialects, but nonetheless extant. “No one questions whether Spanish is real,” the astrologer Samuel Reynolds told me. And yet, in one lecture I attended, Mark Jones, an astrologer and psychotherapist, opened with the controversial claim: “Astrology is not real.” At his words, a murmur rolled through the room, before he elaborated: “not in the sense that you are”. By his telling, the planets exert their influence on the psyche through a theory of object relations. He clicked through slides, and spoke with great authority on the spatial impact of Neptune and the role of the moon in the developmental self. But that notwithstanding, he said: “The single biggest problem astrologers have is that they believe in astrology too much.” Just what to believe in and what methods to follow are open and contentious questions. “There are as many branches of astrology as there are astrologers,” one attender told me, before rattling off a list. There’s horary astrology, an oracle for a single moment – is the person I made eyes with on the subway someone special? – and electional astrology, dealing with the timing of events (one woman told me that, much to the chagrin of her friends and family, her chart dictated a 7.30am wedding.) There’s also evolutionary astrology, which maps the soul over lifetimes; mundane astrology, concerning politics and society; and medical astrology. It goes on: relational, predictive, Jungian (the Jungian vibes are strong). Above all, it was presented to me as a kind of security blanket: a system for understanding the inexplicable, a way to make sense of a shitty day, a means to grasp the contours of current upheavals and find solace in their eventual end. During Covid, one astrologer explained: “People were really looking for answers. They were like, ‘Sky, tell me what’s going on.’” *** The 185 experts who presented were doing what people at conferences do: establishing hierarchies and professionalizing a crowded, competitive field. A conference, after all, is an occasion for conferring legitimacy and codifying the rules of the trade. In astrology, this raises some obvious complications. If you are claiming to see something about a person’s future, what are you responsible for telling them? Some clients, I was told, “just want the good stuff”. Other practitioners prefer to rip off the Band-Aid – if dark days lie ahead, it’s better to make an ominous prognostication so the afflicted can prepare or hunker down as necessary. But what happens when you get it wrong? “There is no wrong,” Clay told me. “There are different interpretations. Right or wrong is a Saturnian construct, it’s useful but doesn’t help us understand these new energies.” That is not, however, the abiding consensus. One of the conference seminars was devoted to learning from readings that went awry. “When people are giving predictions, there is at least a five or 10% chance that it’s not right, and the stakes are huge,” said Kay Taylor, president of the UAC and the Organization for Professional Astrology. Another astrologer illustrated the stakes with a story from her own practice. Based on her reading of a client’s chart, she concluded that both of the client’s parents would die within the year. She felt obliged to convey this information, whereupon the client quit their job and moved across the country to be with their parents for the end. “But they didn’t die!” She exclaimed with surprising pride. That was years ago. Mom and dad are still alive and well. Yet the astrologer assured me that even though the prediction was off, the message remained sound. Her client got to enjoy some bonus time with her parents. Gaffes like this are what make training critical, I was told. No fewer than six professional organizations were sponsoring this year’s gathering – the National Council for Geocosmic Research is the only one without “astrology” in its name – and they offered various routes to affiliated credentialing and curricula, ranging from astrological markers of ADHD to advanced training in asteroids. Celeste Nash-Weninger, from the American Federation of Astrologers, told me: “Every person is a complicated mathematical formula.” She used to be intimidated by the graphs and numbers, but after taking recommended courses – “and they’re tough: eight hours of math and delineation” – she has confidence in “how the heavens move”. Whether advanced math is required for mastery is open to debate. But there is one thing nearly everyone here agrees on: technology has made astrology more accessible – but also, some practitioners worry, diluted its expertise. “Before, people had to do it all by hand,” said Leslie Benson, an astrologer who works for AstroGraph, maker of the popular TimePassages app. “You had to have an ephemeris, where you looked up every placement. You had to draw it all. Now it’s instant.” Most have eagerly embraced the new tools; after all, if software can do the calculations, practitioners have more time for the interpretive work. But they also remove one of the barriers by which skill was once recognized. Artificial intelligence is where most everyone here draws the line. Of course, AI was inevitable: Pluto is in Aquarius and Uranus is in Gemini – yikes – but the contemporary astrologer, at least according to one seminar, must safeguard the personal and spiritual component of the work. “Embracing Uranus,” it advised, referring to the dark trickster of the cosmos, “without losing your soul.” Co-Star, the astrology app that has brought personalized charts and algorithmic readings to millions of users, is notably absent from the conference, and attenders clucked in disapproval over news of its recent acquisition by the AI startup Midjourney. The technology that made astrology accessible to anyone with a phone is also the technology that threatens to make the astrologer – the human interpreter, the trained practitioner, the person who knows what all those symbols mean – obsolete. *** Throughout the conference I asked around why astrology inspires such avid faith, why it appears to “work”. Some practitioners offered explanations involving gravity – the extremely subtle but no less palpable effects of celestial bodies on our own bodies. Or perhaps it is about the moon, whose effects on the tides might somehow produce corresponding swells within us. “We’re 80% water,” one astrologer offered. On three separate occasions I was told, “the proof is in the pudding”. and so with an equal mix of trepidation and enticement I agreed when Nash-Weninger, of the American Federation of Astrologers, volunteered to give me a cold read. Though she assured me she was a “professional” and could tell me “some things” about myself, I could not imagine how, on the basis of my scant data – birth date, time and location – she could uncover anything about my life. But in the name of research I let her plug my information into an app on her phone. “Ooh!” she exclaimed. I experienced an instant tingle – was this a good chart? I was born, she pronounced, in a great conjunction year, “just like Jesus Christ … in theory.” My sun is conjunct with Mercury – “that’s the writer” – and my north node indicates that “if you did something creatively you would probably be known for it later”, she said. It was hard to resist the ego bath of it all, especially when she said: “I’m going to take a chance and say your career might get really big. You might have opportunities that are huge.” At the time, I confess, I didn’t preoccupy myself with the caveating “might”, hearing only the allusions to success. The mere fact that I was born in time and place conferred a thrill: the universe had designs for me. But then she paused and squinted at a corner of my chart. “One thing I want to say: take good care of your liver and kidneys.” She gave me a pointed look and gravely intoned, Jupiter lords over my house of health issues. And then, graver still, she said she was “a little concerned about this dark moon” in my house of love. When I mentioned my recent divorce, she nodded in an of course sort of way. *** Maurice Fernandez, a popular evolutionary astrologer, was giving a lecture on Chiron in Taurus. Astronomically, Chiron is an icy body discovered in 1977 that travels in a long ellipse between Saturn and Uranus, taking roughly 50 years to circle the sun. It was named for the centaur of Greek mythology – and this is where the afternoon’s drama began. Fernandez assured the audience that Chiron was not an “add on” to the chart but a “central part”. In myth, Chiron was the immortal son of the titan Cronos and the sea nymph Philyra. When a poisoned arrow struck him, he suffered unbearable pain and eventually chose to surrender his perpetuity. In astrological terms, Fernandez explained, Chiron represents a confrontation with mortality: the “wound of invisibility”, “hubris” and “the freedom to be sovereign”. As he spoke a logic came into focus, wherein a celestial body receives a name, the name summons a story, and the story reaches through the light years to our fragile, earthbound lives. Chiron was just leaving Aries, Fernandez said, a transit that explained the #MeToo movement and the rise of the manosphere. George Floyd’s death and Black Lives Matter were also, he said, the stuff of Chiron. He needed to check the numbers, but Chiron in Aries had seen “a greater statistic of political violence”. Myth is a capacious place. What was coming as Chiron entered Taurus could be glimpsed via the past: sustainability, finances, land, resources. Stalin’s agrarian policies, Fernandez stated, also bore the hallmark of the roving centaur. He drew out the words: “Three to 5 million people died because of a manmade food crisis.” Gasps rippled through the room. Then the stock market crashed. A decade of poverty. More gasps. What gripped the audience was not necessarily the work of the stars, but rather the stunning facts of history, which, like myth, is a generous tool in astrology. A pattern is imposed on a bygone moment, and that pattern, once established, lends credibility to the prediction of what comes next. While figures like Fernandez swam through a field of palpable adoration, some of the greatest gusts of enthusiasm were reserved for the conference’s plenary speaker, Chani Nicholas, whose star is among the most ascendant in the field – at least to some. Nicholas, who has nearly 700,000 followers on Instagram, has built a devoted following around a blend of astrology and social justice. In an August post announcing Virgo season, she called for readers to “Abolish ICE and data centers and billionaires! … Manifesting a socialist utopia! Life is short! Let Gaza Live! There’s another eclipse coming!” Her company, Chani, promises employees a salary floor of $80,000 and comprehensive benefits, including “unlimited menstrual leave for people with uteruses”. Rather than delivering a conventional keynote, Nicholas sat in conversation with Samuel Reynolds, a former fundamentalist Baptist youth minister who came to astrology as a skeptic and, in the course of trying to debunk it, found himself converted. “Extremes are extreme-ing,” Nicholas told the room, citing floods in Nepal, rising inequality, and populations straining precious resources. “If Pluto in Aquarius is about a revolution, then the robots are definitely out to get us.” Nicholas spoke directly to a younger generation that had shown up in Chicago in droves. “We’ve never had so many newcomers,” one of the conference organizers observed, not without ambivalence. The tensions were already thrumming before Nicholas took the stage. A scheduled speaker had been removed from the program after using the N-word on a podcast over the summer, prompting a small but vocal schism among attenders. For some, the episode represented an overdue reckoning; for others, it was evidence that astrology was being remade according to the dictates of a younger, more censorious culture. An antiracism panel followed. At Nicholas’s keynote, the divide became harder to miss. When she mentioned white supremacy, a handful of people got up and left. But the overwhelming number applauded when she described astrology as an essential tool for organizing in the fight against fascism – and AI. It was tempting to see this as a generational culture war imported wholesale into a trade convention. But it was also about something more fundamental: who gets to decide what astrology is for, who gets to speak for it, and what counts as knowledge in the first place. That question has particular force in a field that has never had much institutional authority to begin with. You don’t need a degree to practice astrology. You don’t need a license to create a chart, or credentials to interpret one. This makes astrology unusually democratic – and unusually susceptible to the creation of new gatekeepers. *** In times of uncertainty, the argument goes, people reach for systems that offer, if not certainty, then comfort: faith, mysticism, pop psychology protocols for surviving the collapse of familiar structures. “Astrology is not therapy, but it is therapeutic,” writes Nicholas. “It’s a relentless reminder that we are the way that we are on purpose.” If the self has become a more demanding and illegible creature, here is another way to make sense of it. There is something to this. When the world feels chaotic, when our purpose seems opaque, it is appealing to believe that chaos has a pattern, that this crappy stretch will end, that the planets are moving and so, eventually, will you. But the explanation is also too easy. We are always living in “interesting” times. Astrology has survived wars, plagues, depressions and the scientific method. Reynolds, the former Baptist minister, offered another possibility. Young people who came of age with Donald Trump and Covid, he said, may have a different relationship to authority. They spent crucial developmental years watching institutions struggle to explain the present, while science was often hauled off to the chopping block. Truth itself became unstable. Perhaps, he suggested, they are simply more comfortable inhabiting several systems of knowledge at once: data and mysticism, evidence and meaning. In this sense, astrology is not necessarily an alternative to facticity so much as a parallel language, asking a different set of questions. It does not have to win an argument with physics to be useful to someone trying to understand why their marriage ended. *** Before leaving Chicago, I found myself in conversation with the sociologist Ian Anthony Waller, who was there to research the gendered nature of astrological belief. He also described himself as a “solid seven” on his own scale of faith. I had come to see astrology less as an impossible-to-validate predictive model than a cool caress of reassurance. The stars see you and whatever happens is happening for a reason. But how, I wondered, as a scholar, did he manage to maneuver between a healthy skepticism and an embrace of a system of elaborately calculated comforts? “Sometimes astrologers will say things and I’m like, ‘that is madness,’” Waller said. “But then other times, things that I read and then see in the world – there’s something going on that is too accurate for me to dismiss out of hand.” It was incumbent for him as a scholar to understand why it appears to work. “If anybody ever really figures it,” Waller said, “it’s probably not going to be an astrologer, it’s probably going to be an astrophysicist or a physicist or somebody from Nasa who makes a connection between launch failures and Mercury or something like that. “And that’s going to be the big eureka moment – or the big Uranian innovation, as we would say in this culture.”

headline: First Thing: Details remain unclear after ‘terror attack’ on Dubai-Israel flight
trail_text: Netanyahu says it is too early to tell who was behind the apparent attempt to crash flight after pilot stabbed
body_text: Good morning. Benjamin Netanyahu has said it is too early to tell who was behind the apparent attempt to crash a ⁠Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the UN called the incident a “terror attack”. Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place. What is believed to have taken place in the cockpit? Pilot Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, has been hailed as a hero after releasing the cockpit door to allow passengers in to wrestle back control of the plane, after his co-pilot – reportedly an Omani national – stabbed him and ⁠sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000ft (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds. What happened next? One passenger said: “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight. The relief pilots … entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.” How has Donald Trump responded? The president said: “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist, or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot.” Woman taken to hospital after surviving two lethal injections in botched execution Tennessee officials were unable to carry out the execution of Christa Pike despite her being administered two doses of a lethal injection drug, her lawyers said, adding that she had been taken to hospital in an ambulance. The Tennessee department of correction later confirmed that Pike had survived the state’s effort to execute her. Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am Wednesday, and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. In 1995 she and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, brutally beat and murdered an acquaintance, Colleen Slemmer, 19. Why has the death sentence for Pike been so controversial? As Ed Pilkington reported for the Guardian last month, at the time of the crime she was 18, and her co-accused was 17. That age difference meant he was spared the death penalty. Pike, at that age, had already been subjected to serious abuse, including multiple rapes by three separate men and beatings by numerous relatives. Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass amid outburst at ‘weirdos’ The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military. He also dismissed claims of low morale within the US armed forces as “false”. What were Hegseth’s words? Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, the defense secretary said: “The complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat. It’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.” What did Hegseth announce about Elon Musk? Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian, with a goal of “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations. US trade regulator opens investigation into AI giants including Anthropic and OpenAI The US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation ⁠into Anthropic, OpenAI and other ⁠AI labs to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers. The investigation by the federal trade commission is the first official US enforcement ⁠action that delves into rogue AI agents. How has AI embarrassed Donald Trump this week? The president launched America.gov, an AI platform which includes a chatbot that is rather inconveniently quoting official government statistics which frequently debunk or contradict some of the president’s most notorious false claims. In other news … Former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem is divorcing her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, citing “irreconcilable differences”. The US Department of Justice has indicted another 10 individuals on noncitizen voting-related charges in Minnesota. Administration officials have sought to support Trump’s longstanding unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud in US elections. A 40-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas state capitol, authorities said. The US Senate has blocked a Republican bill restricting stock trading by members of Congress. The parents of a Detroit-area toddler who pulled a loaded pistol out of his backpack at a daycare will face charges, police said. Pennsylvania has reported its fifth measles-associated death of 2026 as the state’s outbreak climbs to 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. Stat of the day: Catholic clergy sexually abused nearly 1,000 Massachusetts children over decades More than 270 Catholic clerics sexually abused nearly 1,000 children across three Massachusetts dioceses over several decades, according to a report released by the state’s attorney general’s office. Don’t miss this: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants. … or this: From mass raids to quiet crackdown – a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot After switching tactics, federal agents are detaining and deporting record numbers of people from the US. Here is how the change has unfolded during the year. Climate check: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years Alpine regions in Europe are experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution. Scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones. headline: Trump the environmentalist? How his Iran war exposed the fragility of dirty energy
trail_text: Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security
body_text: Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist. Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran. “He’s woken the world up to how vulnerable we are to petro-dictatorships, how vulnerable we are to disruptions in the Middle East,” Newsom told the Guardian during Climate Week in New York. “This war has completely gutted any sort of romantic notions of energy security and it’s compelled folks to think differently. It’s accelerating investments and clean energy and renewables.” If Trump has been an accidental environmentalist, it’s been in the international sphere. The strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports usually flow, is now starting to open up but has been routinely snarled since the Iran war began in February, causing the cost of these fossil fuels to soar around the world. Countries reacted by scrambling to cut their oil and gas use while turning to cleaner forms of energy such as solar and wind (although there’s also been a small uptick in coal, the dirtiest of fossil fuels). The overall consequence has been a positive one for our shared climate, with global fossil fuel emissions set to drop by 0.5% this year due to the crisis, Carbon Brief has estimated. The peak in oil consumption may have been sped up enough to arrive this year, rather than the previous estimate of 2029, according to the International Energy Agency. By launching the war, Trump is set to achieve something only dreamed about by climate advocates and not seen outside global economic crashes or the Covid-19 pandemic – an annual reduction in the emissions that are overheating our planet. The president’s imposition of tariffs and importation of foreign ground beef, meanwhile, may also end up hurting the US cattle industry, another major source of greenhouse gas emissions. “It’s a curious thing to say, but I believe it,” Newsom, a potential contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said of Trump as a sort of unintentional biophile. “This moment will mark how we can’t go back to our original form.” Yet the idea of Trump as an environmentalist, even an accidental one, can still appear faintly absurd. His administration has eviscerated pollution limits on cars, trucks and power plants, funnelled taxpayer cash and favors to the fossil fuel industry and set about unilaterally cancelling renewable energy projects. Trump, who has never by available evidence ever set a Florsheimed foot in any of the US’s national parks, has called environmentalists “terrorists”, the climate crisis “a hoax” and has slashed conservation rules to the extent you can now kill a protected species as long as it wasn’t provably intentional. Perhaps tellingly, when asked during the 2024 election campaign about his environmental credentials, Trump cited his Florida golf course getting awards for “the way I built it, for the water, the way I use the water, the sand, the mixing of the sand and the water”. Critics say this record overshadows any embrace of clean energy by other countries spooked by an oil price that has hovered about $100 a barrel for months but should, at some point in the interminable Iran conflict, drop well below this. The impetus for quitting fossil fuels could wither when it does so. “Trump’s illegal attack on Iran may hasten clean energy in some countries, but he has gutted green tech in the United States and set us back decades,” said Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University who said Newsom was guilty of “tunnel vision” in his framing of Trump. “The notion that he is an accidental environmentalist is wishful thinking.” The conflict may have rocked the oil and gas industry but it has also enriched it, netting eight of the largest companies more than $90bn in just the first three months of the war, with even pro-oil Trump complaining that the major fossil fuel firms are “making too much money”. There is little sign big oil fears a looming obsolescence when this bonanza ends. Last month, Exxon forecast that while the world will reduce its emissions, it will still use 105m barrels of oil a day in 2050, up from 100m barrels last year. Two-thirds of the global energy mix will stubbornly remain composed of oil, gas and coal at the midpoint of the century, the oil company estimated. “All of the oil that is produced will be burned – if they produce more, more will be used,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama. “The people who predict that there will be a reduction in the emission of greenhouse gases are simply lying or blind.” The only hope is that the world “can cap consumption and production at levels similar to the ones we have right now”, Navarro added, citing the enormous energy demand of artificial intelligence datacenters, which are largely being run on gas-fired power. However, climate advocates maintain the Iran conflict will accelerate trends that are already swinging behind clean energy. Investment in renewables globally is now double that of fossil fuels, almost all new power being added to grids comes from clean sources and last year one in four cars sold was electric. Unlike previous oil shocks, the world now has a viable alternative to fossil fuels, even if it’s unclear how lasting an impact Trump’s military and trade actions will have in pushing countries towards them. “There is one thing that all these events are making clear,” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission said in April. “We are paying a very high price for our over-dependency on fossil fuels.” Countries from the UK to India to Thailand have sought to speed up the transition to renewables as the price of fossil fuel dependency has spiraled, saving billions. Electric vehicle sales have surged, although not in the US. Trump has urged other countries to reject the “scam” of clean energy but the market is increasingly favoring cheap wind, solar and batteries that have plummeted in cost in recent years, including in the US. “Demand has massively spiked for solar and for battery storage,” said Sonia Dunlop, chief executive of the Global Solar Council. “We’re seeing that all over the world – the Philippines, across Europe, across south-east Asia, Australia and beyond.” “This Iran crisis, which was, in effect, started by President Trump, has led to a massive surge in demand for our technology … but actually it’s just building on a trend that was already there,” she added. Political and business leaders can mull the fact that the wind does not funnel through the strait of Hormuz and the sun doesn’t only shine on a foreign autocrat’s lands. The Iran war may not prove a fatal blow to fossil fuels, but it has starkly highlighted their inherent volatility. The case for renewables has become obvious at a grassroots level in developing countries, too, where rooftops increasingly glitter with cheap Chinese-made solar panels that are helping negate soaring power bills. “The price of solar has come down so quickly that there are now 100,000 solar panels installed every day in Africa,” Al Gore, the former US vice-president, said last week. “In parts of Pakistan, a common bride’s dowry is now three panels and an inverter, instead of 10 or 12 goats. It’s beginning to kick into gear.” This momentum won’t stop once the conflict around the Persian Gulf ends, Dunlop insisted. “I don’t think the world is just going to go back to business-as-usual demand of fossil fuels once this crisis ends,” she said. “Once someone decides to step off the fossil fuel rollercoaster, they’re off it.” So does all this, then, make Trump an environmentalist? “I wouldn’t say that,” Dunlop demurred. “He certainly has his own ideas.”

headline: Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors
trail_text: Installing tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to Pentago defense board raises conflict of interest concerns
body_text: By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, bestowed extraordinary influence on two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. The new project, which Hegseth dubbed “Project Meridian” in an event in Quantico, Virginia, on Wednesday, will be led by Pentagon official Emil Michael, a former Uber executive. As the Guardian has reported, Michael made millions in profits off non-public Musk company AI stock while in federal office – and while guiding the Department of Defense’s artificial intelligence efforts. Along with Luckey and Musk, Project Meridian will also include the Trump loyalist and former speaker of the House Newt Gingrich. Musk was one of the chief financiers of Trump’s 2024 victory, spending over a quarter of a billion dollars in the run-up to the election. Recent campaign records show he is still a major force in the coming midterms. His America Pac spent $3.4m attacking the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, for example. In the hotly contested Texas Senate race, America Pac spent $6.4m to oppose Democrat James Talarico and $1m to support the Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton. Musk’s SpaceX has been a crucial contractor for US space programs since 2018, and in the second Trump administration his company has emerged as key player in Trump’s pet Golden Dome ballistic missile defense project, a phenomenally expensive effort that could cost as much as $1.2tn. Musk dwarfs Luckey in resources and fame, but Luckey has achieved immense celebrity in the defense contracting and world. Initially a young celebrity in the tech world for inventing a virtual reality headset, Luckey later founded Anduril, a defense contracting company that has already won significant federal contracts. Luckey has also become of the most important “bundlers” for Republican candidates on the west coast, as the Guardian reported in August. One of the sources called him the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. Invitations to political fundraisers obtained by the Guardian show Luckey hosted and co-hosted events for candidates from Trump himself to Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, Mehmet Oz, Ted Cruz and others. The most recent event was on 22 August, where he and his wife co-hosted a $50,000-a-head effort to “Keep the Senate”, and listing guests John Thune of South Dakota, Mike Rogers of Michigan, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Jon Husted of Ohio. It is not necessarily a mystery what Musk and Luckey think about warfare’s future. The 34-year-old Palmer, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, UAVs, and space technology, has been already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare. Earlier this year, for example, he said he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through he crust of the earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. He has claimed that his company has “working prototypes of subterranean systems”. “Bringing major industry players into these types of positions at the Pentagon is not something new, but what feels different now is the substantial financial support these two have, and continue to, deliver for the Republican party,” said Brendan Glavin of Open Secrets, a non-partisan group that tracks campaign spending. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
